items.note: In 735 the land should be free from உட்பகை, which Parimelazhagar glosses as robbers, slanderers and even wild animals. In 881 the same commentator takes the word as kin. The term shrinks from a realm's internal troubles to a family's, and it hurts more in the smaller frame.

333 says wealth has the nature of not staying (அற்கா இயல்பிற்று) and concludes that on getting it one should at once do what stays; 592 also says goods do not stay (நில்லாது நீங்கிவிடும்) and concludes that the lasting possession is the inner drive (உள்ளம் உடைமை). Starting from the same fact, the Book of Virtue points to enduring deeds and the Book of Wealth to an inner resource that can make wealth again.

669 says to carry through the worthwhile deed despite the pain it brings at first. 611 says one must not slacken on the thought that a thing is hard (அருமை உடைத்தென்று அசாவாமை), since effort gives the greatness needed. Both refuse the difficulty of a task as a reason to hold back; 611 speaks of effort and 669 of resolve (துணிவு).

886 says that if disunity arises among those who are one with a ruler (ஒன்றாமை ஒன்றியார் கட்படின்), it is always hard for him to escape perishing. 764 defines an army as one that is not destroyed, cannot be undermined from within (அறைபோகாதாகி) and has inherited hardness. Both treat the loyalty of one's own side as a condition of survival, stated once as a warning and once as a requirement.

306 says anger burns even the safe raft called one's own people (இனமென்னும் ஏமப் புணை). 1068 calls asking a boat without safety (ஏமாப்பில் தோணி) that breaks on concealment. The same word for safety (ஏமம், ஏமாப்பு) marks the vessel in both: one's people are the safe one in 306, and asking is named the unsafe one in 1068.

Both verses play on இறந்தார் and துறந்தார். 310: those who go beyond bounds in anger (இறந்தார்) are like the dead, and those who have renounced anger are equal to renouncers (துறந்தார் துணை). 159: those who endure harsh words from the mouths of those who go beyond bounds (இறந்தார்வாய் இன்னாச்சொல்) have the purity of renouncers (துறந்தாரின் தூய்மை). In both, a householder's control over anger, his own or his response to another's, earns the standing of renunciation.

1063 calls hard the thought that poverty can be ended by begging (இரந்து தீர்வாம்). 1068 gives a picture of why: begging is a boat without safety (ஏமாப்பில் தோணி) that splits when it strikes the rock of concealment (கரவென்னும் பார்). Manakkudavar says 1068 states the cause of poverty not ending, which makes it the reason behind 1063's claim.

734 lists what must not reach a land from outside or by nature: hunger, disease and the enemy who destroys (செறுபகை). 735 lists what must not exist inside it: many factions (பல்குழு), the inner enemy that lays waste (உட்பகை) and murderous bands that harass the king. The two verses divide the threats into external and internal.

1091 finds two looks in her eyes, one that gives the sickness and one that is its medicine (அந்நோய் மருந்து); 1275 finds in her covert behaviour a medicine that ends great sorrow (உறுதுயர் தீர்க்கும் மருந்து). In both the remedy is not anything she says but something to be read in a sign she gives.

Both verses turn on the word உள்ளினும். In 1201 the man says remembering gives unending joy (தீராப் பெருமகிழ்); in 1207 the woman says that even while she remembers, her heart burns (உள்ளினும் உள்ளம் சுடும்), which Parimelazhagar explains as the separation burning her despite the memory. These are two speakers in two moods, so it is a limit on the first claim and not a contradiction in the book's teaching.

605 lists delay, forgetting, sloth and sleep as the craft that those of a ruin-bound nature desire (கெடுநீரார் காமக் கலன்). 920 lists double-minded women, liquor and dice as the company of those Fortune has cast off (திருநீக்கப் பட்டார் தொடர்பு). Both verses give a short catalogue and tie it to people already marked for ruin, leaving open whether the listed things cause the ruin or are its sign.

113 tells one to let go, that very day, of gain that comes from leaving fairness even if it brings only good (நன்றே தரினும் நடுவிகந்தாம் ஆக்கத்தை). 311 refuses wealth that would require hurting others (பிறர்க்கு இன்னா செய்யாமை). Both grant that the gain is real and still rule out the means, one in the householder's ethics and one in the renouncer's.

266 says those who do austerity do their own work, and the others, caught in desire, do what is futile (அவஞ்செய்வார் ஆசையுட் பட்டு). 367 says that if craving is cut off thoroughly, the deed that does not fail (தவாவினை) comes in the way one wishes. They state the same link from opposite sides: desire makes action futile, and its removal makes action unfailing.

1330 calls sulking the pleasure of love, provided the embrace follows (கூடி முயங்கப் பெறின்). 1307 fastens on that proviso: because one cannot be sure the union will not be long delayed (புணர்வது நீடுவது அன்றுகொல்), the sulk has its own pain. 1307 is the reservation built into 1330's praise.

803 asks what use long friendship is if one does not accept a friend's liberty as though one had done it oneself (செய்தாங்கு அமையாக் கடை). 790 says friendship looks shabby even when friends describe each other as 'they are this to us, we are that to them'. Both deny a separation of 'mine' and 'theirs' between friends: 790 in how they speak of each other, 803 in whose act an act is counted to be.

967, on honour, says that being called ruined is better than living by going behind those who do not accept one (ஒட்டார் பின் சென்று ஒருவன் வாழ்தலின்); Parimelazhagar takes this of following scorners for gain. 1248 calls her heart a fool for going behind the one who left without grace (பிரிந்தவர் பின்செல்வாய் பேதை). The standard of honour from the Book of Wealth is the one she applies to her own heart, though in love she cannot enforce it.

726 says books are nothing to one who fears a subtle assembly. 647 says the one who can speak, does not slip and does not fear (அஞ்சான்) is hard for anyone to defeat, and Parimelazhagar takes that fearlessness as fearlessness of the assembly. 647 states positively the condition whose absence 726 says makes learning useless.

722 says those who make what they have learned go home before the learned (கற்ற செலச் சொல்லுவார்) are called learned among the learned. 424 defines understanding with the same verb: saying things so that they go in easily (எண்பொருளவாகச் செலச்சொல்லி) and seeing the subtle meaning in what others say. Both measure learning or understanding by whether it reaches the hearer, not by what the speaker holds.

864 says the man who does not let go of anger and has no நிறை (நிறையிலன்) is easy prey for anyone, at any time and place. 917 says those without நிறைநெஞ்சம் are the ones who go to women whose hearts are set on something else. In both the lack of self-command is what exposes a man, to enemies in 864 and to women who want what he has in 917.

419 says humble speech is hardly to be had without fine listening. 844 defines வெண்மை, shallowness of understanding, as the conceit that says 'we have brightness' (ஒண்மை உடையம் யாம் என்னும் செருக்கு). The pair links lack of instruction and self-praise from both ends: 419 says the uninstructed will not speak humbly, and 844 says boasting of one's understanding is itself the mark of lacking it.

771 is a warrior's boast about a might that turns opponents into memorial stones. In 1088 a lover says his பீடு, which even enemies who had not met him feared in battle (ஞாட்பினுள் நண்ணாரும் உட்கும்), has broken before her bright forehead. The Book of Love borrows the same figure of the warrior whose name alone frightens foes, here as a speaker's way of measuring her effect on him.

997 says those without human courtesy are like trees even if sharp as a file (மரம்போல்வர்); 600 says those without abundance of drive are trees, differing only in having human form (மரம் மக்களாதலே வேறு). The tree marks the person who lacks what makes one human, but the two verses name different lacks: fellow-feeling in 997, inner drive in 600.

869 says joy does not go far from those who fight if they get enemies who are ignorant and afraid. 772 says holding the spear that missed an elephant is sweeter (இனிது) than holding the arrow that hit a forest hare. One locates the pleasure of fighting in the easy opponent and the other in the hard one; the conflict holds if both are read as claims about what a fighter should want, and eases if 869 is a king's reckoning of advantage and 772 an individual warrior's sense of honour.

953 puts giving and not scorning (ஈகை ... இகழாமை) side by side among the marks of a good family; Parimelazhagar takes all four as the way one meets the poor who come. 1057 gives the receiver's side: on seeing those who give without scorn or contempt (இகழ்ந்தெள்ளாது ஈவார்), the asker's heart rejoices within. The pairing shows why 'not scorning' sits next to 'giving' in the list.

399 assumes the learned person's learning gives the world joy. 650 says those who cannot unfold what they have learned so that others grasp it (கற்றது உணர விரித்துரையாதார்) are like a cluster of flowers in bloom without scent. It adds the condition 399 leaves unstated: the world's delight depends on being able to convey the learning.

843 says the suffering those without understanding inflict on themselves is hard even for their enemies to inflict (செறுவார்க்கும் செய்தல் அரிது). 165 says that for the envious, envy is enough: it brings ruin even when enemies fail to (ஒன்னார் வழுக்கியும் கேடீன்பது). Both measure an inner defect against an outside enemy and find the defect the more effective.

341 says that whatever one has left (யாதனின் நீங்கியான்), from that one has no pain (நோதல் இலன்). 626, in the chapter on not being undone by trouble, asks whether those who never guarded wealth saying 'we have got it' (பெற்றேமென்று ஓம்புதல் தேற்றாதவர்) would grieve saying 'we have lost it' (அற்றேமென்று). The renouncer's rule reappears in the book of wealth as a habit of mind for someone who still owns things.

In 1277 her bangles understood before she did that the lord of the shore had parted from her (நம்மினும் முன்னம் உணர்ந்த வளை). In 1185 the pallor spreads while he is still in sight. Both make the body register the parting faster than the mind or the facts do; 1277 pushes it to before the event.

1330 says sulking is the pleasure of love, and the pleasure of sulking is to come together and embrace (ஊடுதல் காமத்திற்கு இன்பம்). 1294 has the woman want exactly that order, first make a quarrel and then enjoy (துனிசெய்து துவ்வாய்), and complain that her heart will not do it. The book's closing statement of how a sulk should work is, in 1294, a plan she cannot carry out.

905 says the man who fears his wife fears to do good to the good; 908 says those who act as she wishes (பெட்டாங்கு ஒழுகுபவர்) neither meet their friends' needs nor do good (நன்றாற்றார்). Both state the cost to others: the wife-ruled man fails the good in 905 and his friends in 908.

35 defines virtue as what proceeds without slipping into four things, the last being painful speech (இன்னாச்சொல்). 96 says virtue grows and its opposite wears away when one speaks good things sweetly (அல்லவை தேய அறம்பெருகும்). 35 only requires avoiding harsh words; 96 adds that the positive practice of sweet, well-chosen speech actively increases virtue.

691 compares the king to a fire one warms at from a measured distance. 896 says one burned by fire may still survive, but those who go on offending the great will not (எரியால் சுடப்படினும் உய்வுண்டாம் உய்யார் பெரியார்ப் பிழைத்தொழுகுவார்). Read together, the fire in 691 understates the danger: 896 ranks the offended great above fire, though Parimelazhagar takes its பெரியார் as those great in austerity, not kings.

998 calls it lowness (கடை) to fail in courtesy even toward those who act without friendship or kindness. 579 calls it the highest thing (தலை) to extend kindly regard and bear with even those whose nature is to hurt (ஒறுத்தாற்றும் பண்பினார் கண்ணும்). The verses mark the two ends of the same scale: good conduct toward the hostile is தலை, and its failure is கடை.

1246 tells the heart that when it sees the lover it cannot stay in a sulk, so its present anger is false (பொய்க்காய்வு). 1284 is that prediction coming true: she set out to sulk and the heart forgot it and went to unite (அதுமறந்து கூடற்கண் சென்றது).

484 says that even if one has the world in mind, it comes to hand when one considers the time and acts by the place (ஞாலம் கருதினும் கைகூடும் காலம் கருதி இடத்தாற் செயின்). 485 reverses the same words: those who have the world in mind wait, unshaken, considering the time (காலம் கருதி இருப்பர் கலங்காது ஞாலம் கருதுபவர்). 484 states the condition for acting and 485 its other side, that until the time comes the ambitious do not move.

1277 says her bangles knew of his parting before she did; 1278 says her body has been pale for seven days though he left only yesterday. The two adjacent speeches make the same point with different signs: her body responds to his intention to leave before the leaving is an acknowledged fact.

372 says a fate of loss makes a person foolish and a fate of gain, when it arrives, widens understanding (அறிவகற்றும் ஆகலூழ் உற்றக் கடை). 859 says that when gain is coming a person does not look at hostility (இகல்காணான் ஆக்கம் வருங்கால்), and to bring ruin on himself he looks to excel at it. In both, approaching gain or ruin shows first as a change in the person's own judgement.

120 says true trade for traders is to look after others' things as their own (பிறவும் தமபோல்). 315 asks what use understanding is if one does not guard against another's pain as one's own (பிறிதின்நோய் தந்நோய்போல்). The same 'as one's own' (தம்போல்) test is applied to goods in the market and to suffering in the chapter on not hurting.

135 argues by comparison: as there is no gain in the envious, there is no elevation in one without conduct (அழுக்காறுடையான்கண் ஆக்கம் போன்று இல்லை). 170 states the premise on its own: none have grown great through envy (அழுக்கற்று அகன்றாரும் இல்லை). 135 takes chapter 17's claim as already known and builds its point about conduct on it.

1150 says the town is raising the gossip 'we want' (யாம்வேண்டும் கெளவை), and the lover will grant what is asked if he wishes. In 1143 the man asks whether the gossip the town knows is not his to have, since it is like gaining what he has not gained. Both sides welcome the talk: for him it stands in for union, and in 1150, on Parimelazhagar's reading, it is the ground for asking him to take her away.
549 clears the king: punishing crime is no blemish but his work. 567 marks where that clearance ends, since punishment past the limit becomes a file on his own strength.

532 says heedlessness kills fame (பொச்சாப்புக் கொல்லும் புகழை). 601 says the undimmed lamp called family goes out when the grime called sloth creeps over it (மடியென்னும் மாசூர மாய்ந்து கெடும்). In both, an inner lapse, not an outside enemy, destroys a standing built up over time.

In 1213 her life continues because in dreams she sees the man who gives no grace in waking life (நனவினால் நல்காதவரை). In 1199 the man who gives no grace (நல்கார் எனினும்) still sweetens her ears by any word of him. In both she is sustained by a substitute for his presence, a dream or a report, while saying outright that he withholds himself.

890 says that life with those who are not in accord (உடம்பாடு இலாதவர்) is like living with a snake in a hut. 825 says those whose minds are not settled with yours (மனத்தின் அமையாதவர்) are not to be trusted on their words. Both make inner agreement, not outward closeness or speech, the thing that decides whether a person near you is safe.

208: the ruin of those who did evil is like a shadow that never leaves a person. 36: virtue done now is, at the time one perishes, a companion that does not perish ('பொன்றுங்கால் பொன்றாத் துணை'). Both say a person's deeds stay with him; the good deed stays as a companion and the evil deed's ruin as a shadow at his heel.

403 says even the unlearned are very good if they can keep from speaking before the learned (கற்றார்முன் சொல்லாதிருக்கப் பெறின்). 715 says the best of all good things is the restraint of not speaking first among elders (முதுவருள் முந்து கிளவாச் செறிவு). 715 turns the rule 403 gives the unlearned into a general virtue of the assembly that binds capable speakers too.

591 says ஊக்கம், inner resolve, is the only true possession. In 1263, the woman names a very similar quality in உள்ளம் as his companion in leaving her. The virtue the Book of Wealth values most is what she has been left for.

1286: seeing him, she sees no faults; not seeing him, she sees nothing else. In 1297 she calls her heart மடநெஞ்சு, and Parimelazhagar defines that மடமை as exactly this reversal: remembering when he is absent, and forgetting when he is present, faults that ought to be remembered at sight and forgotten in absence. On his reading 1297 names and blames what 1286 only describes.

722 says those who can make what they have learned go home before the learned are called learned among the learned (கற்றாருள் கற்றார்). 683 uses the same construction for the envoy: he must be strong in the treatises among those who know treatises (நூலாருள் நூல்வல்லன்). Both measure learning by standing among the learned, not against the unlearned.
The same formula for two wealths: an army is தலை among a king's riches and listening is தலை among a person's. The phrase shows that 'chief of wealth' is relative to whose life is being described.

145 says one who crosses into another's home thinking it easy (எளிதென இல்லிறப்பான்) gets blame that stands forever without dying (விளியாது நிற்கும் பழி). 284 says a love grown strong in theft (களவின்கண் கன்றிய காதல்) yields at harvest a distress that does not die (வீயா விழுமம்). The same logic, a desire for what is another's that looks light at the start and has a permanent result, is applied to another's wife and to another's goods.

926 says that drinkers are eating poison. 1201 says love is sweeter than liquor because it delights even in memory, taking liquor's delight as the benchmark. The book of love borrows, without judging, the pleasure that this chapter condemns.

792: the friendship of one who does not take it after examining again and again ends in grief that kills him (ஆய்ந்தாய்ந்து கொள்ளாதான் கேண்மை). 1172, on Parimelazhagar's reading: the eyes looked that day without examining and understanding what would follow (தெரிந்துணரா நோக்கிய) and now suffer. The rule about forming ties without scrutiny is applied to a look. Manakkudavar reads the first phrase differently, as having looked with knowledge.

427 makes knowing what is to come the mark of having understanding, as if it were a trait of the person. 372 says a fate of loss makes a person foolish (பேதைப்படுக்கும் இழவூழ்) and a fate of gain, when it arrives, widens understanding (அறிவகற்றும் ஆகலூழ்). Read with 372, the division in 427 is not fixed: the same person may see ahead or fail to, depending on what fate is at work.

152 says to bear transgression always (என்றும்) and better still to forget it. 488, advising a king on timing, says: on seeing enemies, bear them (சுமக்க); when their end is seen to have come, the head goes down (கிழக்காம் தலை). In 488 the bearing is temporary and is kept in mind until the moment to act, where 152 asks for a bearing with no end that passes into forgetting. The Book of Wealth thus limits to a tactic what the Book of Virtue states without condition.

216 says wealth with a person of நயன் is like a fruit-bearing tree ripening in the middle of the town (பயன்மரம் உள்ளூர்ப் பழுத்தற்று). 1078 says the base are like sugar-cane (கரும்புபோல்), of use only when crushed. Both use a plant's yield (பயன்) as the figure for how a person's wealth reaches others: the tree offers its fruit in the open, and the cane gives nothing until it is pressed.

701 praises the one who knows what is meant by looking, without its being said (கூறாமை நோக்கிக் குறிப்பறிவான்). 1100, in the love chapter that has the same title குறிப்பறிதல், says that when eyes agree with eyes in their look, spoken words have no use (வாய்ச்சொற்கள் என்ன பயனும் இல). Reading without speech is a minister's rare skill in 701 and the ordinary condition of two lovers in 1100.

582 makes it the king's work to know quickly, at all times (எஞ்ஞான்றும் வல்லறிதல்), all that happens to everyone; 553 says a ruler who does not inquire daily and do justice (நாடொறும் நாடி முறைசெய்யா) loses his land day by day. 553 gives the purpose and the cost: the daily knowing of 582 exists to feed daily justice, and its absence is paid for in the kingdom itself.

163 says the one who does not cherish another's prosperity (பிறனாக்கம் பேணாது) and envies it is called one who wants neither அறன் nor ஆக்கம். 1079 shows the same reaction in the கீழ்: on seeing others clothed and fed (உடுப்பதூஉம் உண்பதூஉம் காணின்) he is quick to find a fault in them. The later verse gives the behaviour that the earlier one judges.

57 says confinement does little to guard women, and that the guard kept by their own நிறை, firmness, is the chief one. 917 says it is men without a heart of நிறை (நிறைநெஞ்சம் இல்லவர்) who touch the shoulders of women who embrace while their hearts tend other things. The same inner firmness that 57 names as a wife's real protection is here named as what a man lacks when he goes to such women.
824 fears hostility that does not show. 826 says an enemy's fine words are soon seen through. The chapter holds two views on whether concealment can succeed.

485 says those who have the world in mind wait, unshaken, with their mind on the time (காலம் கருதி இருப்பர்). Manakkudavar reads the second half of 673 in that sense: when the deed is not possible, keep it in mind and act on seeing the place where it becomes possible. Parimelazhagar reads 673 differently, as open force where one is stronger and one of the other three expedients where one is not, so the link holds on Manakkudavar's reading.

410 says the unlearned differ from the learned as beasts from people, though all are human in form. 1071 says the base look exactly like people (மக்களே போல்வர் கயவர்), a likeness the speaker has seen nowhere else. Both deny full human standing to some who have the human shape, for lack of learning in one and for baseness in the other.

230 holds death sweet for one who can no longer give. 968 asks whether a life of tending the flesh is any medicine once greatness has lost its dignity (பீடழிய வந்த இடத்து). In both a life is not worth keeping once the thing that gave it worth is gone: giving in 230, honour in 968.

1308 asks what use it is to suffer where there is no lover who knows 'this one is hurt' (நொந்தார் என்று அஃது அறியும் காதலர் இல்லா வழி). 877, in the chapter on enemies, advises: do not voice your hurt to those who do not know you are hurt (நோவற்க நொந்தது அறியார்க்கு). The same roots நோ and அறி carry one rule in love and in statecraft: displayed pain is wasted on someone who does not perceive it.

219 redefines poverty for the benevolent man: it is not lacking goods but being unable to do good with them. 89 redefines it from the other side: poverty in the midst of having ('உடைமையுள் இன்மை') is the folly of not tending guests. In both verses poverty is measured by what one does for others and not by what one holds.

391 tells one to learn what is to be learned without flaw (கற்க கசடற) and then stand by it. 845 uses the same phrase for what a person has truly mastered (கசடற வல்லதூஉம்) and says that carrying on as if one knew what one has not learned (கல்லாத மேற்கொண்டொழுகல்) brings doubt even on that. Pretence undoes the standing of the very learning 391 asks for.

662 gives two rules as the way of those who have studied the matter: avoid harm (ஊறொரால்) and do not give way once it has come (உற்றபின் ஒல்காமை). 442 tells a king to cherish those who remove the trouble that has come (உற்றநோய் நீக்கி) and guard beforehand against what has not (உறாஅமை முற்காக்கும்). The same before-and-after pair appears as the doer's own discipline in 662 and as the quality to look for in advisers in 442.

860 credits நகல், glad friendliness, with producing good conduct and its dignity. 999 describes those without the capacity: for people not able to laugh with others (நகல் வல்லர் அல்லார்) the wide world lies in darkness even by day. 860 gives what நகல் yields and 999 what its absence costs; Parimelazhagar reads நகல் in both as rejoicing in company with others.

86 says one who tends the departing guest and watches for the next (வருவிருந்து பார்த்திருப்பான்) will be a good guest to those in the sky (வானத்தவர்க்கு). 50 says one who lives on earth as one should (வாழ்வாங்கு வாழ்பவன்) will be placed among the gods who dwell in the sky (வான்உறையும் தெய்வத்துள்). 86 names one specific practice that earns what 50 promises the householder in general, and turns it into a reciprocity: the host becomes the guest. (This edition prints நல்வருந்து in 86 and உநற்யும் in 50; both are typos.)

The same earth responds in two ways. In 151 it supports even those who dig into it, the model of patience. In 1040 it laughs at those who won't dig. Being dug is what it tolerates and even wants, so the virtue chapter's image becomes a joke on the idle.

29 speaks of those who have climbed and stand on the hill called good qualities (குணமென்னும் குன்றேறி நின்றார்), whom Parimelazhagar takes to be ascetics; 124 says the restrained person's stature is greater than a mountain (மலையினும் மாணப் பெரிது), and Parimelazhagar reads நிலை there as the householder's state. On his readings the renouncer stands on a hill while the householder who stays restrained in his own station is said to overtop one.

752's 'everyone' (எல்லாரும்) scorns the have-nots. 1047 carries that to the limit case: one in poverty not joined to virtue is looked on as a stranger even by the mother who bore him (ஈன்ற தாயானும் பிறன்போல). The pairing shows how far 'everyone' reaches, with 1047 adding the condition அறஞ்சாரா.

449 says there is no standing (நிலை) for those without the support of a prop (மதலையாம் சார்பு). 1030 says a family with no good person to stand by and prop it (அடுத்தூன்றும் நல்லாள் இலாத குடி) falls when trouble cuts at its base. The image of a structure that needs a prop is applied to a king in one verse and to a household in the other.

1245 asks whether she can abandon as hostile (செற்றார் எனக் கைவிடல் உண்டோ) the man who does not answer her love. 1255 turns that private question into a general statement: not following the hostile (செற்றார் பின் செல்லா) is a dignity unknown to those with love's sickness (காமநோய் உற்றார் அறிவதொன்று அன்று). The word செற்றார் links them, and the second explains why the first could only be a rhetorical question.

882 says not to fear enemies who are like swords but to fear the bond with enemies who are like kin (கேள்போல் பகைவர் தொடர்பு). 822 says the friendship of those who seem one's own and are not (இனம்போன்று இனமல்லார்) will turn. Both identify the enemy in the guise of kin as the dangerous one; 882 gives the instruction and 822 the reason, that such a bond does not stay what it looks like.

807, on old friendship, says that those whose bond came by the way of love do not cut off love even when ruinous things are done to them (அழிவந்த செய்யினும் அன்பறார்). 1245 asks whether she can let him go as an enemy merely because he does not return her closeness. The logic of long friendship in the Book of Wealth, that injury does not license abandonment, reappears as a lover's rhetorical question.

995 says courtesy is present even in enmity (பகையுள்ளும் பண்புள) in those who understand others. 874 says the world rests in the greatness of the person of courtesy who treats enmity as friendship (பகை நட்பாக் கொண்டொழுகும் பண்புடையாளன்). 874 takes the step beyond 995, from staying courteous toward an enemy to turning him into a friend; Parimelazhagar reads 874 as a matter of policy.

693 says those who would guard themselves should guard against the gravest things (போற்றின் அரியவை போற்றல்), which Parimelazhagar reads as faults a king cannot forgive. 891 says not slighting the power of those able to act is the chief of all the guarding done by those who guard themselves (போற்றுவார் போற்றலுள் எல்லாம் தலை). Both use போற்றல் for self-protection and locate its first object in one's dealings with the powerful.

637 says that even when one knows the method of doing a thing, one should act knowing how the world goes (செயற்கை அறிந்தக் கடைத்தும் உலகத்து இயற்கை அறிந்து செயல்); Parimelazhagar glosses the method as what the treatises teach. 949 addresses the one who has learned (கற்றான்) and still requires him to consider this patient, this illness and this moment. Both hold that book learning has to be fitted to the particular case.

358 speaks of 'the folly called birth' departing when the real is seen. 835, in the chapter on folly in the book of wealth, says a fool can in one birth's doing make the mire he will sink into for seven (எழுமையும் தான்புக் கழுந்தும் அளறு). Both tie பேதைமை to the chain of births, 358 as its root and 835 through the fool's deeds.

252 takes it as given that holding wealth is not for those who do not look after it (பொருளாட்சி போற்றாதார்க்கு இல்லை). 376 says what is not one's portion will not stay however anxiously it is guarded, and what is one's own will not leave even if carried out and poured away (பரியினும் ஆகாவாம் ... சொரியினும் போகா தம). The conflict holds if ஆட்சி is read as possession, as Manakkudavar and Pope read it; Parimelazhagar reads it as getting the benefit of wealth, which softens it.

201 says those given to evil deeds do not fear, and the excellent do fear, the intoxication called evil deed (தீவினையார் அஞ்சார் விழுமியார் அஞ்சுவர்). 1072 says the base are more fortunate than those who know what is good, because they have no distress in the heart (நெஞ்சத்து அவலம் இலர்). 1072 puts 201's fact in mock praise: Parimelazhagar says the verse scorns by implication, and that the point is their not fearing blame.

794 picks out as a friend the well-born person who is ashamed of blame (பழிநாணுவான்). 951 says that integrity and shame together are found by nature only in those born in a good house (இற்பிறந்தார் கண்அல்லது இல்லை ... செப்பமும் நாணும்). 951 gives the book's reason for 794 pairing birth with shame as the test.

306 says anger burns the safe raft that is one's own people (இனமென்னும் ஏமப் புணையைச் சுடும்). 1134 says the flood of love sweeps off the raft that is shame and good manliness (என்னும் புணை). In both a passion destroys the thing figured as the raft that keeps a person afloat: anger in the chapter on not being angry, desire here.

Verse 26 divides people by whether they can do what is hard to do. Verse 664 says saying is easy for anyone and doing as one has said is hard (அரியவாம் சொல்லிய வண்ணம் செயல்). The chapter on firmness in action applies the renouncer's standard to statecraft and names what is hard in a deed: carrying it out as announced.

201 says those practised in evil do not fear 'தீவினை என்னும் செருக்கு' while the excellent (விழுமியார்) do. 428 gives the general rule in the chapter on understanding: not fearing what is to be feared (அஞ்சுவது அஞ்சாமை) is folly, and fearing it is 'அறிவார் தொழில்'. Read together, the fear in 201 is a working of knowledge and not timidity; Parimelazhagar on 428 lists sin, blame and ruin among the things to be feared.

867 advises paying to have a certain man as an enemy rather than keep him near. 800 advises paying to be rid of a certain friend: give something (ஒன்று ஈத்தும்) and leave the friendship of those who are not a match. Both accept a cost to end a harmful closeness; the commentators differ on who the man in 867 is, Parimelazhagar taking him as one who begins a task and acts unsuitably, Kalaignar as one who stays beside you.

1202 claims that thinking of the beloved brings no pain. In 1296 the woman says that when she sat alone and thought (தனியே இருந்து நினைத்தக்கால்), her heart stayed only to eat her (என்னைத் தினிய); Parimelazhagar specifies that what she thought of was his cruelties. The two speeches mark out the cases in which remembering comforts and in which it wounds.

50 says one who lives on earth as life should be lived will be placed among the gods who dwell in the sky (வானுறையும் தெய்வத்துள் வைக்கப்படும்). 346 promises the one who ends 'I' and 'mine' a world higher than the gods' (வானோர்க்கு உயர்ந்த உலகம்). Set side by side the two verses give a scale: the good householder reaches the gods, the renouncer goes beyond them.

277 uses the kunri seed for its two colours, red body and black tip; 965 uses it for its size, saying even those like a hill sink if they do a lowering thing as small as a kunri (குன்றி அனைய). The same seed serves both verses as a figure for a small dark flaw in something that otherwise looks fine, by colour in one and by measure in the other.

608: if sloth lodges in one of family standing it puts him into slavery to his enemies (அடிமை புகுத்தி விடும்). 616: absence of effort puts one into want (இன்மை புகுத்தி விடும்). The identical closing phrase makes sloth an agent that ushers a person into a condition; the neighbouring chapters thus name two destinations, poverty and subjection, and Parimelazhagar links them in his note on 616, where want leads to destruction by enemies.

467 fixes the order for action: think first, then resolve, and no thinking postponed until after. 509 fixes the same order for trusting people: trust no one without examining, and after examining, trust what is to be trusted (தேறற்க யாரையும் தேராது தேர்ந்தபின் தேறுக). In both the examination belongs wholly before the commitment, and the commitment is then not to be reopened.

41 names the householder the support of 'the three of proper nature' (இயல்புடைய மூவர்); 42 repeats the frame இல்வாழ்வான் என்பான் துணை and adds three more: துறந்தார், துவ்வாதவர், இறந்தார். Parimelazhagar takes these as the abandoned, the poor and those who died with no one of their own, so the pair moves from the recognised orders to people with no claim on anyone. Pope and Kalaignar read துறந்தார் as ascetics, which would make 42 overlap 41 rather than extend it.

1067 asks beggars not to beg of those who conceal (கரப்பார்). 1077 describes such people from the other side: the base will not even shake a wet hand (ஈர்ங்கை விதிரார்) for anyone but those whose fist would break their jaw. 1077 shows what asking a concealer comes to, and why 1067 pleads against it.

71 asks if there is any bolt to shut love in, since the small tears of the loving announce it (புன்கணீர் பூசல் தரும்); 1271 says her eyes tell something despite her concealment. The claim that affection cannot be locked away and that the eyes give it out appears in the book on virtue as a general truth about அன்பு and in the Book of Love as a scene.

1085 asks whether her look is Death, an eye or a doe, and says it has all three (இம்மூன்றும் உடைத்து); Parimelazhagar comments that it gives pleasure and pain together. 1091 states that plainly as two looks, one the sickness and one its cure. The puzzled question of 1085 is resolved into a doubleness he can name.

410 makes the unlearned like beasts beside the learned. 729 places a kind of learned person below the unlearned. Learning that seemed to separate humans from animals is here worth less than nothing if the learned can't speak.

1207 says she does not know forgetting, and even remembering burns her heart (உள்ளினும் உள்ளம் சுடும்). 1296 says that when she sits alone and thinks (நினைத்தக்கால்), her heart consumes her. Both make thinking of him in his absence the source of the pain; in 1207 the heart is what is burned, in 1296 it is what does the harm.

1248 calls the heart a fool for going after the man who left (பிரிந்தவர் பின்செல்வாய்) while grieving that he gives no grace. 1293 asks the heart whether it follows him as it likes (பெட்டாங்கு அவர் பின் செலல்) because the ruined have no friends. Both speak of the heart 'going behind him' as a desertion of her that she can see but not stop.

Both end on the phrase 'என்னும் செருக்கு'. In 201 it is 'தீவினை என்னும் செருக்கு', which Parimelazhagar glosses as a delusion (மயக்கம்) and Manakkudavar as an exhilaration (களிப்பு) that the good fear; in 180 it is 'வேண்டாமை என்னும் செருக்கு', the pride of not wanting, which yields victory (விறல்). The same word names a heady state to be dreaded in one verse and a state worth having in the other, depending on what it rests on.

7 says that only those who join the feet of the incomparable one can be rid of grief. 350 repeats the structure with attachment. Parimelazhagar himself notes that the generic word is kept to match the invocation chapter.

911 says the women who desire wealth rather than the man bring ruin through sweet words. 813 applies the same logic to friends who calculate, and the comparison runs the other way: chapter 92's accusation is made first of men's friendships.

504 tells the king to examine a person's qualities and faults (குணம்நாடிக் குற்றமும் நாடி) and take whichever predominates. 793 tells one to know a person's qualities, family, faults and kin (குணமும் குடிமையும் குற்றமும் ... இனனும்) before forming a friendship. The same inventory is used in both domains, but only 504 says how to decide when the inventory is mixed.

Both lovers are awake at midnight, with the same word யாமத்தும். The man in 1136 says his eyes will not close and even at midnight he thinks of mounting the palmyra horse; the woman in 1167 says that even at midnight she alone is there (யானே உளேன்), swimming without sight of shore. Sleeplessness in the dead of night is given to both sides.

761 counts the army as a form of the king's wealth (வெறுக்கை). 759 counts wealth as a weapon, the sharpest steel against foes (எஃகு). The two neighbouring chapters describe each thing in terms of the other: wealth is a weapon and the army is wealth.

1202 says love is sweet in every way since no pain comes from thinking of the one you love (நினைப்ப வருவதொன்று இல், as the commentators read this edition's garbled line). In 1209 the woman's dear life is wasting because she thinks hard on his lack of tenderness (அளியின்மை ஆற்ற நினைந்து). The pairing shows that the sweetness of 1202 depends on what is remembered: the shared days, not the present neglect. Manakkudavar in fact reads 1202 as conditional, 'if no pain comes'.

849 says one who tries to show something to a person who does not see ends up the unseeing one, while that person goes on having seen it his own way (கண்டானாம் தான்கண்டவாறு). 929 says giving reasons to a drunk man is like searching with a flame for someone sunk under water (கீழ்நீர்க் குளித்தானைத் தீத்துரீஇ அற்று). Both describe instruction that cannot reach its target, and in both the effort reflects on the one making it.

848 calls the life of one who neither heeds nor understands a disease until it leaves (போஒம் அளவுமோர் நோய்); Parimelazhagar takes this as a burden hard for the earth to bear, while Kalaignar takes the disease as the person's own. 572 says the existence of those without kindly regard is a weight on the earth (உண்மை நிலக்குப் பொறை). On Parimelazhagar's reading the two share the figure of a person whose mere being alive is an affliction to the world.

527 ties gain (ஆக்கம்) to those who, like the crow, call others before eating. 227 says the disease of hunger does not touch one who is habituated to sharing his food (பாத்தூண் மரீஇயவனை). Both hold that sharing food protects the sharer's own fortune, stated in the Book of Virtue as freedom from hunger and here as prosperity.

762 says steadfastness in defeat is rare except in an old army (தொல்படை). 764 defines an army by courage that has come down to it (வழிவந்த வன்கண்), along with not collapsing and not being turned by subversion. 764 makes a requirement of what 762 observes, and both use வன்கண் for the quality.

1073 says the base are like the gods because they too act as they please (மேவன செய்தொழுகலான்). 1075 says that where the base show proper conduct (ஆசாரம்) it is fear, and beyond that a little if there is something they desire. 1075 marks the limit on 1073's freedom: their doing as they please stops only at fear or gain; Parimelazhagar says doing what they like is their nature and conduct is not.

846 treats clothing the body as trivial beside dealing with one's faults. 1012 says food, clothing and the rest are no different for any living being, and the distinction of humans is having shame (ஊணுடை எச்சம் உயிர்க்கெல்லாம் வேறல்ல நாணுடைமை மாந்தர் சிறப்பு). 1012 gives the reason behind 846: dress is common to all, and what marks a person is shame at fault.

282 says even thinking in the mind (உள்ளத்தால் உள்ளலும்) of taking another's goods by stealth is wrong; 317 says the highest thing is not to do, with the mind (மனத்தானாம்), anything ill to anyone at any time in any degree. Both place the fault at the level of intention before any act, for theft in one and for harm in general in the other.

940: as the gambler loves the game more with each loss (இழத்தொறூஉம் காதலிக்கும் சூதேபோல்), the living being loves life more with each suffering. 1288: liquor is wanted by the drunk even as it does them shameful harm, and so is his chest. Both explain an attachment that grows through injury by a vice from the same group of chapters (dice in 940, liquor in 1288).

735 says a land has no murderous bands that harass the king (வேந்தலைக்கும் கொல்குறும்பு). 550 says a king's punishing the cruel with death (கொலையிற் கொடியாரை வேந்தொறுத்தல்) is like weeding the young crop. 550 gives the ruler's means of producing the condition 735 describes; Parimelazhagar on 735 likewise says these three are to be removed by the king and the inhabitants.

565 says the great wealth (பெருஞ்செல்வம்) of an inaccessible, grim-faced man is as if seen by a demon; Parimelazhagar explains that no one approaches him, so the wealth is of use neither to him nor to others. 1000 says the great wealth (பெருஞ்செல்வம்) gained by one without courtesy (பண்பிலான்) is like good milk spoiled by its vessel. Outside the court the same judgment holds: the holder's manner ruins wealth that is sound in itself.

126 says that drawing in the five like a tortoise in one birth is a protection through seven (ஒருமையுள் ... எழுமையும் ஏமாப்புடைத்து); 398 says the learning one gains in one birth is a protection through seven (ஒருமைக்கண் ... எழுமையும் ஏமாப்புடைத்து). The closing formula is identical, so sense-restraint and learning are set side by side as the two acquisitions that carry across births.

In 91 sweet speech comes from a love-soaked and guileless mind. 959 uses speech as a sign of what lies underneath, as the sprout shows the soil. Together they make speech a surface that discloses the source.

879 speaks of those who remove the thorn tree with the word களையுநர், weeders. 550 compares a king's putting the cruel to death to weeding the green crop (பைங்கூழ் களைகட்டதனொடு நேர்). Both picture the removal of dangerous people as a cultivator's weeding; 879 adds that timing matters, since the weed grown hard injures the weeder's hand.

431 lists செருக்கு first among the faults whose absence gives prosperity its dignity. 180 names a செருக்கு it approves of, 'வேண்டாமை என்னும் செருக்கு', the pride of not wanting, which yields victory (விறல் ஈனும்); Parimelazhagar there glosses the word as wealth. Read together they separate arrogance from a pride that consists in refusing to covet.

303 says to forget anger toward anyone, because evil is born of it. 487 keeps anger alive in secret until it can be used. The Aram book treats anger as something to give up, while the Porul book treats it as something to store.

203 asks only for restraint: do no evil even to enemies. 987 asks what worth (சால்பு) is good for if it does not do pleasant things even to those who did one harm ('இன்னா செய்தார்க்கும் இனியவே செய்யாக்கால்'). The Book of Wealth's ideal of the சான்றோர் goes one step beyond the householder's rule, from not returning harm to returning good.

121 says restraint brings one among the immortals (அமரருள் உய்க்கும்); 50 says one who lives on earth as one should will be placed among the gods who dwell in the sky (தெய்வத்துள் வைக்கப்படும்). Both promise a place among the gods to a person living an ordinary household life well, without renunciation, and 121 names restraint as the quality that does it.

In 1113, he went over her body part by part, comparing it to shoots, pearls and spears, and she was pleased to be praised. In 1320 she treats that very habit of comparing part by part as evidence that he has others in mind. The praise of chapter 112 is the root of the suspicion.

393 says those who are called 'people with eyes' are the learned (கண்ணுடையர் என்பவர் கற்றோர்). 577 says those without kindly regard are eyeless and those who have eyes do not lack it (கண்ணுடையார் கண்ணோட்டம் இன்மையும் இல்). The same title, கண்ணுடையார், is awarded on two different tests, learning and kindly regard; the verses do not conflict, but a reader should see that the book defines 'having eyes' twice.

218 says those whose sight knows what is due (கடனறி காட்சியவர்) do not falter in ஒப்புரவு even when they lack means. 1053 uses the same description, கடனறிவார், for the people before whom asking has a beauty; Manakkudavar glosses them as those who know ஒப்புரவு. The pairing identifies the fit giver of the begging chapter with the person 218 describes.

707 says the face is ahead of the person in showing pleasure or anger (தான் முந்துறும்). In 1277 a woman says her bangles knew before she did that her lover had left (நம்மினும் முன்னம் உணர்ந்த வளை). Both give the body a knowledge that arrives before the mind's own, a general observation in 707 and a lover's remark on her thinning arms in 1277.

709 says the eye itself declares enmity and friendship to those who can read it. 828 says a weapon is hidden even in an enemy's hands folded in worship, and the tears his eyes shed are the same (ஒன்னார் அழுதகண்ணீரும் அனைத்து). On the reading that the eye cannot conceal, which Parimelazhagar states under 710, the weeping eye of 828 should not be able to deceive; 828 holds that it does.

On Parimelazhagar's reading of தோன்றுதல் as birth, 236 treats being born with renown as good and not being born as only the better alternative for those without it. 362 says that if one wants anything it should be not to be born (வேண்டுங்கால் வேண்டும் பிறவாமை), with no exception. The conflict depends on the birth reading; on Kalaignar's reading, where 236 is about entering a field of activity, the two do not meet.

508: one who trusts an outsider without examining (தேரான் பிறனைத் தெளிந்தான்) gets trouble that does not end, extending to his descendants (வழிமுறை தீரா இடும்பை). 792: the friendship of one who does not inquire again and again ends in a grief that kills him (கடைமுறை தான்சாம் துயரம்). The same structure, unexamined acceptance followed by lasting harm, is stated for a king's officer and for a friend.

In Parimelazhagar's reading, 1120 is the man refusing to elope because her feet can't bear even swan's down. In 1279 she looks at those same feet, her way of saying she will walk. The compliment had been an excuse, and her glance answers it.

1245 asks the heart whether one can abandon as an enemy (செற்றார் எனக் கைவிடல் உண்டோ) the man who does not respond when she draws close (யாம் உற்றால் உறாஅதவர்). 1292 complains that the heart, even having seen that he is not close (உறாஅதவர்க் கண்ட கண்ணும்), goes to him on the thought that he will not be hostile (செறாஅர் என). The two share the pair உறாதவர் / செறு, and show the same refusal to treat coldness as enmity, once owned by her and once blamed on the heart.

437 says the miser's wealth perishes because he does not do what should be done with it; Parimelazhagar lists these as virtue, increase of wealth and enjoyment. 1006 says one who neither uses his wealth himself nor gives to the deserving (தான்துவ்வான் ... ஈதல் இயல்பிலாதான்) is an ஏதம், a harm, to great wealth. 1006 spells out the two uses left undone and turns the miser himself into the wealth's affliction.

476 warns that one who has climbed to the tip of a branch (நுனிக்கொம்பர் ஏறினார்) and pushes further loses his life; in 1264 her heart, thinking of his return, கோடுகொடு ஏறும், which Manakkudavar and Kalaignar read as climbing a tree's branches to look for him (Parimelazhagar reads it as swelling up like a tree putting out branches). On the climbing reading the same image marks reckless overreach in the book on statecraft and eager hope here.

52 says that if excellence of the home (மனைமாட்சி) is not in the wife, the life is nothing, whatever excellence it has (எனைமாட்சித் தாயினும் இல்). 750 says that whatever excellence a fort has (எனைமாட்சித் தாகியக் கண்ணும்), it is as nothing in those who lack excellence in action (வினைமாட்சி இல்லார்கண் இல்லது). The two share the phrase and the argument: the outward assets of a home or a fortress count for nothing without the quality of the person inside who runs it.

444: to conduct oneself so that those greater than oneself are one's own is the chief of all strengths (வன்மையுள் எல்லாம் தலை). 891: not slighting the power of the able is the chief of all the safeguards of those who guard themselves (போற்றலுள் எல்லாம் தலை). The two verses use the same ranking formula for the two sides of dealing with the great, winning them as the highest strength and not offending them as the highest protection.

864 says one who doesn't let go of anger is easy prey for anyone. 899 makes the anger of the exalted able to bring down a king. Anger is weakness or supreme power depending on who has it, and 306 warns that it burns the one who has it.

1310 calls the heart's wish to join with one who neglects it mere craving. In 1255 the woman says the dignity of not going after those who have turned away (செற்றார் பின் செல்லாப் பெருந்தகைமை) is something the love-sick do not know. Both admit that desire overrides self-respect toward an indifferent partner.

183 ranks death above a life kept up by backbiting and pretence. 230 says nothing is more bitter than death (சாதலின் இன்னாத தில்லை), yet even it is sweet when one cannot give. Each verse measures a fault or lack by setting death beside it and finding death the better; the pairing shows how the book uses that comparison for both a wrong done and a good left undone.

395 praises learning in the stance of one who lacks before one who has. 724 tells even the learned to state what they have learned before the learned and take more from those who know more (மிக்காருள் மிக்க கொளல்). The asking stance of 395 is thus not only for beginners; it continues among the learned.

In 1168 she calls the night அளித்து, pitiable or kindly, because having put every living thing to sleep it has no companion but her. In 1256 she uses the same word of her grief (அளித்தரோ ... துயர்), which Parimelazhagar takes as scorn. In both she speaks to her tormentor in the language of grace and pity, which is how these monologues voice bitterness.

129 says the scar left by the tongue never heals; 159 says those who bear the harsh words from the mouths of people who exceed all bounds (இறந்தார்வாய் இன்னாச்சொல் நோற்கிற்பவர்) are as pure as renouncers. 129 gives the reason 159's praise is so high: what the forbearing person takes without retaliation is the one kind of wound the book says does not close.

In 1235 the friend, in Parimelazhagar's reading, says the shoulders with bangles lost and old beauty faded declare the cruelty of the cruel one (கொடியார் கொடுமை உரைக்கும்). In 1236 the woman answers that with bangles and shoulders slackening, what pains her is the saying that he is cruel (அவரைக் கொடியர் எனக்கூறல் நொந்து). The second verse limits the first: the body's evidence stands, but she refuses the charge drawn from it.

435: the life of one who doesn't guard before it comes (வருமுன்னர்க் காவாதான்) perishes like straw before fire. 535: one who slipped by not guarding beforehand (முன்னுறக் காவாது இழுக்கியான்) will later grieve over his own error. The same failure is given two outcomes, sudden destruction in 435 and late regret in 535.

668: in a task one has seen clearly and decided on (கலங்காது கண்ட வினை), act without wavering and without delay (தூக்கங் கடிந்து). 671, opening the next chapter, says deliberation ends in reaching resolve (துணிவு) and it is bad for that resolve to rest in delay (தாழ்ச்சியுள் தங்குதல் தீது). The same rule closes the chapter on firmness and opens the chapter on method: once the thinking is done, delay is the fault.

1145 takes drinking as the model for love: each exposure makes love sweeter as each bout makes drink wanted. 1281 says being intoxicated at a thought and glad at a sight belong to love and not to liquor (கள்ளுக்கில் காமத்திற்கு உண்டு). So the likeness in 1145 has a limit the book itself states: liquor works only when drunk, love without contact.

511 says the man to employ is one whose nature, having looked into good and bad (நன்மையும் தீமையும் நாடி), has taken to the good (நலம்புரிந்த தன்மையான்). 422 defines understanding as not letting the mind go wherever it goes but turning it from bad to good (தீதொரீஇ நன்றின்பால் உய்ப்பது). The test for a king's officer is the book's general definition of அறிவு applied to a person at work.

113 says to let go, that very day, of gain that comes from leaving fairness even if it yields only good (நன்றே தரினும்). 931 uses the same concession, 'even if you win' (வென்றிடினும்), and still refuses the gain, calling it a swallowed hook. In both the apparent success of a wrong source is conceded and set aside.

360 lists desire, anger and confusion as what must perish for pain to end. 431 lists three faults whose absence gives a ruler's prosperity its dignity: arrogance, anger and smallness (செருக்கும் சினமும் சிறுமையும்), which Parimelazhagar glosses as pride, anger and lust. A similar triad, sharing anger and, on that gloss, desire, is the obstacle to release in one book and to good rule in the other.

93 says virtue lies in sweet words that come from within (அகத்தானாம் இன்சொலினதே அறம்), after a glad face and a kind look. 34 says being spotless in mind is the whole of virtue and the rest is noisy show (ஆகுல நீர பிற); Parimelazhagar counts speech and outward guise among that rest. 93's word அகத்தானாம் is what keeps sweet speech on the right side of 34's line: it counts as virtue because it issues from the mind.

Verse 21 rests its claim on பனுவல் துணிவு, the settled conclusion of the texts. Verse 533 uses the same appeal: that the heedless have no fame is the conclusion of authors of every school (எப்பால் நூலோர்க்கும் துணிவு). These are two places where the Kural, which usually argues from observation, cites the agreement of the books as its ground.

642 gives the general rule: since gain and ruin come from speech, guard against a lapse in it (சொல்லின்கட் சோர்வு). 716 applies it to one setting, a slip before the widely learned, and measures the damage by comparing it to falling from the path (ஆற்றின் நிலைதளர்ந்தற்று), which Parimelazhagar reads as a renouncer's lapse from the good path.

708 says that if one has people who look within and understand what has happened, it is enough to stand looking them in the face (முகம்நோக்கி நிற்க அமையும்). 1100 says that once eyes agree with eyes, spoken words are of no use. Both make speech unnecessary between the right pair; Parimelazhagar adds for 708 that going on to speak would lessen both parties, a concern for dignity the love verse does not have.

174 says those of faultless sight who have conquered the senses will not covet on the thought 'we have nothing' (இலமென்று வெஃகுதல் செய்யார்). 205 forbids doing evil on the same plea (இலன் என்று தீயவை செய்யற்க) and adds that doing so makes one poor again. Both name poverty as the excuse and reject it; 205 gives the consequence that 174 leaves unstated.

1182 has the pallor ride over her body with the pride of saying 'he gave me' (அவர்தந்தார் என்னும் தகையால்). 1183 uses the same verb of giving for an exchange: he took her grace and modesty and gave sickness and pallor (நோயும் பசலையும் தந்து). The pallor that boasts of being his gift in one verse is entered as his payment in the next.

34 says being spotless in mind is the whole of virtue and the rest is noisy show (ஆகுல நீர பிற); 272 says a sky-high appearance (வானுயர் தோற்றம்) does nothing when the heart is in known fault. 272 applies the general rule of 34 to the specific case of the ascetic's appearance.

609: when a man ends the rule of sloth over him (மடியாண்மை மாற்ற), the fault that came into his குடியாண்மை is gone; Parimelazhagar splits the word into family and manhood, Manakkudavar reads it as the management of the family. 1026 says good manhood is making the management of the house one was born in one's own (நல்லாண்மை ... இல்லாண்மை ஆக்கிக் கொளல்). 1026 supports reading the two terms of 609 together: manhood is measured in the household, and sloth is what unseats it.

162 says that among excellent gains (விழுப்பேற்றின்) nothing equals being free of envy toward anyone (அஃதொப்பது இல்லை). 363 says there is no excellent wealth (விழுச்செல்வம்) like வேண்டாமை, here or there (அஃதொப்பது இல்). The same formula ranks an absence, of envy in the householder book and of wanting in the ascetic book, above every positive possession.

802 calls it the duty of the worthy (சான்றோர் கடன்) to take a friend's liberties well. 981 says that for those who take on worthiness knowing what is due, all good things are கடன். 802 is one instance of 981's general statement, with the same word கடன்.

1174 reports that the eyes have dried up and cannot weep (நீருலந்த). 1177 wishes exactly that on them: may the eyes that longed and melted to see him suffer on until their inner water is gone (உள்நீர் அறுக). What one verse states as their condition the other pronounces as a curse.

620 ends 'தாழாது உஞற்றுபவர்', those who labour without delay, and says they see fate's back. 1024 ends with the same phrase, 'தம்குடியைத் தாழாது உஞற்றுபவர்க்கு', and says that for them the outcome arrives by itself without deliberation (சூழாமல் தானே முடிவெய்தும்). The same people are described twice, once as defeating an opposing power and once as finding the result come unsought.

395 uses the poor standing before the rich (உடையார்முன் இல்லார்போல்) as its figure for the learner, and on Parimelazhagar's reading those who learned standing so are foremost while those who would not are lowest. 1066 says nothing is more degrading to the tongue than asking (இரவின் இளிவந்தது இல்), even asking water for a cow. Read together, the posture the book calls degrading when the object is goods is the one it honours when the object is learning.

In 1085 the doe (பிணை) is one of three things her look might be, beside Death. In 1089 her doe-like artless look (பிணையேர் மடநோக்கு) and her modesty are ornament enough, so added jewels are pointless. The same doe glance is first one part of a threat and then her natural adornment.

1052 says even begging is a pleasure to a person if what is begged for comes without pain (இன்பம் ஒருவற்கு இரத்தல்). In 1329 the man wants the sulk and the night prolonged so that he may beg (யாம் இரப்ப), treating the pleading itself as something to enjoy. Begging, which chapter 107 calls degrading, is here a pleasure because the giver is not in doubt, which is the condition 1052 sets.

In 129 a burn from fire heals inside but the scar burned by the tongue (நாவினாற் சுட்ட வடு) does not; in 293 the liar's own heart burns him (தன்நெஞ்சே தன்னைச் சுடும்). Both use burning for the lasting damage of speech: the harsh word burns the hearer, the false word burns the speaker.

Both say that no gain surpasses this, in the same formula (ஊங்கு), but 32 says it of virtue and 122 of restraint. The superlatives compete, as also in 61 on children, which suggests that the formula praises and doesn't actually rank.

571 says this world exists because the great beauty called kindly regard exists (கண்ணோட்டம் ... உண்மையான் உண்டிவ் வுலகு). 996 says the world exists by resting on people of courtesy, and would otherwise sink into the earth and perish (பண்புடையார்ப் பட்டுண்டு உலகம்). Both use the same construction, உண்டு உலகு, to say that a human quality and not power keeps the world going; 571 says it in a chapter on kings and 996 of people in general.

46 asks what one who conducts household life in the way of virtue would gain by going to the outside way (புறத்தாற்றில் போஒய்ப் பெறுவது எவன்); Parimelazhagar and Pope take the outside way as renunciation. 348 says those who have renounced completely (தீரத் துறந்தார்) have reached the head, and the rest (மற்றையவர்) are confused and caught in the net. If புறத்தாறு is renunciation and the question in 46 is rhetorical, 46 denies the gain that 348 reserves for renouncers alone; if புறத்தாறு means only ways outside virtue, the conflict disappears.

425 says embracing the world is brightness (உலகம் தழீஇயது ஒட்பம்). 544 uses the same verb twice: the world stands embracing the feet (அடிதழீஇ நிற்கும் உலகு) of the king who rules embracing his people (குடிதழீஇ). In 544 the embrace is returned, which gives a concrete reason why 425 counts drawing the world close as intelligence. Parimelazhagar narrows 'the world' in 425 to the high-minded.

119 makes unbent speech count as rectitude only if the mind too is unbent (உட்கோட்டம் இன்மை பெறின்). 295 praises one who speaks truth together with the mind (மனத்தொடு வாய்மை மொழியின்) above those who do austerity and give. Both attach the same condition to good speech, agreement between word and mind, in the fields of fairness and of truthfulness.

1101 says all five senses find their objects in her; in 1266 she will 'drink' him (பருகுவன்), which Parimelazhagar explains as drinking that nectar through all five gateways of sense. On his reading 1266 is the woman's version of 1101, with the five-sense enjoyment compressed into a single verb.
507 condemns trusting on fondness alone. 513 puts love first among four qualities, so the fault in 507 lies in the 'alone', not in the love.

90 gives the negative case: a face that turns (முகந்திரிந்து) and looks makes the guest wilt. 93 gives the positive rule in nearly the same terms: with a glad face, looking sweetly (முகத்தான் அமர்ந்து இனிது நோக்கி), then sweet words from the heart. The last verse of the hospitality chapter and the third of the next share the face-and-look sequence; Parimelazhagar on 90 also lists the glad face, the sweet word and the good deed as successive stages of welcome.

1204 asks whether she too is in his heart, since he is always in hers (யாமும் உளேங்கொல் அவர் நெஞ்சத்து). 1243 gives her own bleak answer: a compassionate thought of her does not exist in the one who caused the sickness (பரிந்துள்ளல் பைதல்நோய் செய்தார்கண் இல்). The question of 1204 has by chapter 125 become a settled premise for scolding her heart.

445 tells the ruler to choose his counsellors after deliberation (சூழ்வாரைச் சூழ்ந்து கொளல்), since they serve as his eyes. 462 says nothing is out of reach for those who act after considering a matter with chosen company (தெரிந்த இனத்தொடு தேர்ந்தெண்ணி). Both put the selection of the people one deliberates with before the deliberation itself.

629 makes freedom from pain depend on not desiring pleasure when it is present (இன்பத்துள் இன்பம் விழையாதான்). 4 describes the Lord as one without wanting or not-wanting (வேண்டுதல் வேண்டாமை இலான்) and says those who reach his feet never have இடும்பை. The same link between having no pull toward or away from things and having no suffering appears as a divine attribute in Book 1 and as a human discipline here.

771 dismisses the enemy by pointing to the many (பலர்) who faced his lord and became stones. 763 asks what it matters if a host of rats roars like the sea, since they perish when the cobra merely breathes (நாகம் உயிர்ப்பக் கெடும்). Both say numbers on the other side count for nothing against one real fighter; Parimelazhagar reads 763 as the hero not fearing a crowd of non-heroes.

55 says that when a wife who worships her husband says 'rain', it rains (பெய்யெனப் பெய்யும் மழை). 559 says that when a king bends justice, the sky will not rain (ஒல்லாது வானம் பெயல்). In both, rain responds to a person's keeping or failing the duty of their station, the wife's in the household and the king's in the realm.

1122 says their bond is like that of body and life. 1124 draws the consequence: together she is to his life what living is (வாழ்தல்), and when she leaves she is what dying is (சாதல்). The comparison in 1122 becomes a statement of what separation will mean.

1041 says that the only thing as painful as poverty is poverty itself (இன்மையின் இன்மையே இன்னாதது). 230 opens by saying nothing is more painful than death (சாதலின் இன்னாதது இல்லை), then reverses it for the person who cannot give. Taken together, 230's second half brings it into line with 1041: the want that stops giving is placed above death in bitterness.

498 says the drive of a commander with a large army is destroyed (உறுபடையான் ஊக்கம் அழிந்து விடும்) if he enters ground suited to a small army. 744 defines a fort as having little to guard and much room, and as destroying the drive of the foe who comes against it (உறுபகை ஊக்கம் அழிப்பது அரண்). The shared phrase shows that a fort is the built form of 498's principle: ground chosen so that numbers stop counting.

458 says that even for the worthy who have goodness of mind in full, goodness of company is a safeguard (ஏமாப்பு உடைத்து). 448 says a king without the guard of people who rebuke him (இடிப்பாரை இல்லாத ஏமரா மன்னன்) perishes even with no one to ruin him. Both use the same word for protection (ஏமம்), and 448 shows what the company protects against: one's own unchecked faults.

Verse 39 says only what comes through virtue is joy (அறத்தான் வருவதே இன்பம்) and everything else lies outside it. Verse 75 traces the joy and distinction people reach in the world to a life settled in love (அன்புற்று அமர்ந்த வழக்கு). Set side by side, 75 adds love to the source that 39 confines to அறம், which agrees with verse 45's coupling of the two.

385 defines a king as one able to create sources of wealth, gather it, guard it and apportion it (இயற்றலும் ஈட்டலும் காத்தலும்). 933, which Parimelazhagar reads of a king, says both the gathered wealth and its sources (பொருள் ஆயம்) leave him if he keeps at the dice. One habit undoes the gathering and the guarding that 385 makes the mark of rule.

344 makes possessionlessness the nature of austerity. 263 asks whether the others have forgotten austerity out of a wish to provide for those who have renounced (துறந்தார்க்குத் துப்புரவு வேண்டி). The pairing shows that the ascetic's having nothing is sustained by householders who keep possessions in order to give.

Both verses explain அருள் by putting it beside பொருள்: 247 says that world is not for those without அருள் just as this world is not for those without wealth, and 252 says holding அருள் (அருளாட்சி) is not for flesh-eaters just as holding wealth (பொருளாட்சி) is not for those who do not guard it. 252 takes the comparison one step on: அருள், like wealth, is something that can be lost through carelessness.

1068 calls asking a boat without safety (ஏமாப்பில் தோணி) that splits on the rock of concealment; the commentators supply poverty as the sea it was meant to cross. In 1164 the woman says the sea of love exists but the safe raft to swim it (ஏமப் புணை) does not. Both use the figure of a sea that must be crossed and a vessel that fails, 1068 as a teaching about begging and 1164 as a lover's complaint.

615 praises the one who wants the work (வினைவிழைவான்) and not pleasure. 901 says those who desire the wife do not reach the excellent fruit, and that this is the very thing those who desire action do not want (வினைவிழையார் வேண்டாப் பொருளும் அது). Both set the desire for action against a desire for enjoyment and use nearly the same word for the man of action.

1039 describes neglected land with the Book of Love's words for a lovers' sulk: it resents and sulks like a wife (புலந்து ... ஊடி விடும்). 1304, in the chapter on sulking, says that not appeasing one who has sulked (ஊடியவரை உணராமை) is like cutting a withered creeper at the root. The figures run in opposite directions: the land is compared to a sulking woman in 1039, and the neglected sulking woman to a plant in 1304.

954 says the well-born will not do diminishing things (குன்றுவ) even if they get crores piled up (அடுக்கிய கோடி பெறினும்). 311 says the stainless hold to not hurting others even if it would bring wealth that gives distinction (சிறப்பீனும் செல்வம் பெறினும்). Both use the same 'even if they gained' (பெறினும்) form to set a fixed refusal against a large reward, once for family standing and once for non-harm.

658: forbidden deeds done without shunning them bring anguish even if they succeed (முடிந்தாலும் பீழை தரும்). 113: give up at once gain that comes from leaving fairness, even if it brings nothing but good (நன்றே தரினும்). Both concede success in advance and still reject the act, so the objection is not that such means fail.

281 tells one who wants not to be scorned to guard his heart from stealing anything at all (கள்ளாமை காக்க தன் நெஞ்சு); 178 says that what keeps one's wealth from shrinking is not coveting the goods in another's hand (வெஃகாமை ... பிறன்கைப் பொருள்). Each gives restraint toward others' property as the means to something one wants for oneself, standing in 281 and one's own wealth in 178; Parimelazhagar reads 281 differently, as about one esteemed for not despising release.

204 says that if one plots another's ruin, அறம் plots the plotter's ruin; 1018 says that if one is not ashamed, அறம் is ashamed. In both, virtue is an agent that answers the person's act in the terms of that act, with a penalty in 204 and with withdrawal in 1018.

421 calls understanding an inner fortress enemies cannot destroy (உள்ளழிக்கலாகா அரண்); 1016 calls shame a fence (வேலி), which Parimelazhagar explains as keeping blame and sin from entering. Both give an inner quality the work of a defensive structure, one against ruin and one against disgrace.

615 praises the man who wants the work and not pleasure (இன்பம் விழையான் வினைவிழைவான்) as a pillar to his kin; in 1263 the wife describes her husband as gone desiring victory with his own resolve for company (உரன்நசைஇ உள்ளம் துணையாக), which Parimelazhagar glosses as not desiring enjoyment. 1263 shows the same man from inside the house: she stays alive only by desiring his return (வரல்நசைஇ இன்னும் உளேன்), the same verb நசைஇ set against his.

808 speaks of those with the strength of intimacy not to listen to talk of a friend's lapse (கேளிழுக்கம் கேளா); Parimelazhagar takes this as not accepting it even when others report it. 510 says that doubting one who has been trusted after examination (தெளிந்தான்கண் ஐயுறவு) brings endless trouble. Both rule out reopening a settled trust, in friendship and in a king's appointments. The second half of 808 is read in opposite ways by Parimelazhagar (the day of the lapse is a day well spent) and Kalaignar (the days are wasted), so the link rests only on the first half.

90 says a guest wilts when looked at with an altered face (முகந்திரிந்து நோக்க). 707 says nothing is as knowing as the face, since whether one is pleased or angry it gets there first (உவப்பினும் காயினும் தான்முந்துறும்). 707 explains why 90's guest is hurt before a word is spoken: the face has already reported the host's mind.

705 says eyes that cannot read another's meaning are of no use. 393 says only the learned have eyes, and the unlearned have two sores in the face (முகத்திரண்டு புண்ணுடையர் கல்லாதவர்). In both the physical eye is treated as worthless without a trained capacity behind it, learning in one and the reading of signs in the other.

In 1129 she does not blink for fear of losing sight of him, and for this the town calls him a stranger without love (ஏதிலர் என்னும் இவ் வூர்). In 1220 the people of the town say he has left her in waking life, and she asks whether they do not see him in dreams (கனவினால் காணார்கொல்). In both she sets the town's outward evidence against her inner experience of his presence, first in the eye and then in the dream.

Verse 61 says that among all things gained (பெறுமவற்றுள்) 'we' know of nothing to set beside knowing children. Verse 162 says that among excellent gains (விழுப்பேற்றின்) nothing equals (அஃதொப்பது இல்லை) being free of envy. The two top rankings conflict only if each superlative is read literally as a ranking across all gains; read as each chapter's idiom of praise they do not.

1061 says that not begging (இரவாமை), even from those who give gladly without concealing (கரவாது), is worth ten million times more. 1035 says those whose way is to eat what their own hands produce do not beg (இரவார்) and give to askers without concealing (கரவாது ஈவர்). 1035 names the livelihood that makes the ideal of 1061 possible, and puts the farmer on the giving side of the same exchange.

The adjacent chapter says fearless speech in assembly is rarer than courage in battle. 715 says that the best of all good things is holding back among elders. The chapters are a pair and Parimelazhagar reconciles them with precision: only speaking first is restrained.

969 praises those who give up life at the loss of honour, like the yak with its hair. 680 describes the weak who bow and take the terms to keep their people steady. Parimelazhagar sees this: the honourable would not choose it, so the verse only reports it.

361 says craving is the seed that yields unceasing birth for all beings (தவாஅப் பிறப்பீனும் வித்து). 349 says the moment attachment is cut off, that cuts off birth (பற்றற்ற கண்ணே பிறப்பறுக்கும்). One verse names the cause and the other states what follows when the cause is removed; Parimelazhagar makes the same cause-and-effect point under 349.

304 asks whether there is any other enemy than anger (சினத்தின் பகையும் உளவோ பிற), which kills smile and joy. 165 says the envious need no enemy since envy itself brings ruin. Two of the four things 35 excludes from virtue, anger and envy, are each described as the person's own enemy.

In 1311 her objection is to other women's eyes on him (கண்ணின் பொது உண்பர்). In 1320 it is to his eyes on her, which she thinks are really on another woman; Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar both explain that she supposes he is matching her limbs against someone else's. The chapter opens and closes on the look as the place where she locates unfaithfulness.

623 says those who do not suffer at suffering (இடும்பைக்கு இடும்பை படாஅதவர்) make suffering itself suffer; Parimelazhagar places this in the middle of an undertaking. 261 makes bearing the pain that comes (உற்றநோய் நோன்றல்) half of the form of தவம். The same endurance is a means to finishing work in one book and the definition of austerity in the other.

Parimelazhagar reads 491's முற்றும் இடம் as a place from which the enemy can be encircled, and tells the king neither to act nor to scorn the foe before finding one. 747 defines a fort from the other side as what cannot be taken even by encircling (முற்றியும் ... பற்றற்கு அரியது). The shared siege verb shows attacker and defender reasoning about the same ground; Manakkudavar instead reads 491 as 'the place where the task can be completed', which would loosen this link.

400 says learning is the imperishable, excellent wealth and other things are not wealth (மாடல்ல மற்றையவை). 411 says the wealth of the ear is the wealth among wealths and the head of them all (செல்வத்துளெல்லாம் தலை). Adjacent chapters use the same 'true wealth' figure for study and then for listening, without ranking the two against each other.

326 calls Death 'the life-eating' (உயிருண்ணுங் கூற்று) and says it does not advance on the days of one who does not kill. 1221 gives the same epithet, உயிருண்ணும், to the evening that comes on women parted from their husbands. The pairing shows the woman addressing evening in the book's own language for Death; Parimelazhagar's note on 1229 says she thinks of evening as கூற்றம்.

83 says daily hospitality never brings a household to ruin (பாழ்படுதல் இன்று), which Parimelazhagar takes to mean the host's goods are not used up. 480 says helpfulness that does not weigh the extent of what one has (உளவரை தூக்காத ஒப்புரவாண்மை) quickly ends one's wealth (வல்லைக் கெடும்). The Book of Wealth thus attaches a condition of measure to the kind of promise 83 makes without one.

In 1081 the man, at first sight, cannot tell whether she is a goddess, a peahen or a woman, and his heart reels (மாலும் என் நெஞ்சு). In 1116 the confusion is moved to the sky: the stars cannot tell the moon from her face (அறியா) and wander from their places (பதியின் கலங்கிய). The lover's own bewilderment about what she is becomes, in the praise chapter, a bewilderment he attributes to the stars.

Manakkudavar reads 785 as saying many days of acquaintance are not needed to judge a friendship, because for those of the same understanding (உணர்ச்சி) one meeting gives the claim. 792 says the friendship of one who does not examine again and again (ஆய்ந்தாய்ந்து கொள்ளாதான்) ends in grief that kills him. On Manakkudavar's reading the two differ on whether friendship can safely be formed quickly; on Parimelazhagar's, 785 only says that feeling, more than contact, is what makes the bond, and there is no conflict.

1088 reports the first loss: his battlefield strength breaks at the sight of her forehead. 1134 says the fierce flood of love carries off the raft of shame and good manliness (நாணொடு நல்லாண்மை என்னும் புணை). The later verse generalises what 1088 exclaims, with manliness now lost along with shame.

465 says setting out without thinking through every aspect is a way of setting one's enemies in a planting bed (பகைவரைப் பாத்திப் படுப்பது); Parimelazhagar reads this as establishing them in ground where they grow. 718 says speaking before those who understand is like pouring water into the bed of a growing plant (வளர்வதன் பாத்தியுள் நீர் சொரிந்தற்று). The same garden bed stands for fostering growth in both, wanted in 718 and brought on oneself in 465.

443 calls winning the great as one's own the rarest of rare things (அரியவற்றுள் எல்லாம் அரிது). 781 asks what is as hard to make as friendship (செயற்கரிய யாவுள நட்பின்), and what guard is as hard for an enemy's work to get past. Both rank a bond with others as the hardest thing to obtain, and 781 adds that it is also the strongest protection, which is what chapter 45 goes on to claim for the great.

465 says rising without full deliberation (வகையறச் சூழாது எழுதல்) benefits the enemy. 473 says many who did not know their own strength pressed on in enthusiasm and broke midway (ஊக்கத்தின் ஊக்கி இடைக்கண் முரிந்தார் பலர்). 473 names one of the things left unconsidered, one's own strength, and shows the cost to oneself where 465 shows the gain to the enemy.

410 says others stand to those who have studied the shining books as beasts stand to people (விலங்கொடு மக்கள் அனையர்). 420 calls those who know taste by the mouth and not by the ear மாக்கள், and asks what it matters whether they die or live. The next chapter carries the comparison on, from those who have not studied to those who do not even listen.

582 makes it a king's work to know everything happening to everyone, swiftly and always. 695 tells those near him not even to listen in on his secrets. Knowledge flows one way, and the Kural presents this imbalance as prudence, not as a problem.

861 advises avoiding opposition to the stronger (வலியார்க்கு மாறேற்றல் ஓம்புக) and pursuing enmity against the weaker. 493 says the weaker side can still become strong and win when it knows the ground and protects itself. 493 therefore sets a condition under which 861's rule about relative strength does not settle the outcome.
