717 says the learning of those who have studied and understood shines among those able to examine words without fault (சொல்தெரிதல் வல்லார் அகத்து). 404 says the wise do not accept an unlearned person's brightness (ஒட்பம்), however good it is. The same expert hearers decide both cases: before them real learning becomes visible and untaught cleverness is not accepted.

188 asks what those who spread even the faults of their closest (துன்னியார்) will do to strangers (ஏதிலார் மாட்டு). 1300 argues that when one's own heart is not one's own, strangers (ஏதிலார்) not being one's own is a slight thing. Both reason from the nearest relation to ஏதிலார்: if the bond fails at the closest point, nothing can be expected further out.

407 compares the good looks of one without fine, penetrating understanding to a well-decorated clay doll (மண்மாண் புனைபாவை). 1020 compares the movements of those with no shame within to a wooden puppet (மரப்பாவை) made to seem alive by its string. Both use a doll for a human form missing its inner part, understanding in one and shame in the other.

828 warns that a weapon lies hidden inside an enemy's hands folded in worship (தொழுதகையுள்ளும் படையொடுங்கும்), and his tears are the same. 1324 finds a weapon (படை) inside the lovers' sulk, which Parimelazhagar explains as the other's bowing and humble words. Submission as a concealed weapon is a danger to be detected in false friendship and, in love, the means by which the sulk is ended.

453 says perception comes from the mind, but the word that one is 'such a person' comes from one's company (இன்னான் எனப்படும் சொல் இனத்தான் ஆம்). 505 says the touchstone of greatness and smallness is each person's own deeds (தத்தம் கருமமே கட்டளைக் கல்), which Parimelazhagar glosses as that and nothing else. If 453 is read as saying what a person really is, and not only what people call them, the two name different tests of character: company or deeds.

In 1169 the woman herself speaks of the cruelty of the cruel one (கொடியார் கொடுமை) when she says the long nights are crueller still. In 1236 she is pained when he is called cruel (கொடியர்). The pair shows that she uses the word in her own lament and does not accept it from another's mouth; these are different moments of a dramatised speaker, not a contradiction in teaching.

159 says those who endure (நோற்கிற்பவர்) the harsh words of transgressors are as pure as renouncers. 48 says a household life that keeps others on their path and does not slip from aram has more endurance than those who do penance (நோற்பாரின் நோன்மை உடைத்து). Both apply the ascetic's verb நோல் to the householder and set him level with or above the ascetic; Parimelazhagar on 159 adds that these are people who remain in household life.

106 commands: do not abandon (துறவற்க) the friendship of those who were a support in distress. 806 states it as a description: those who keep within the bounds will not abandon (துறவார்) the tie of long-standing friends even in ruin (தொலைவிடத்தும்). The same verb is used in both, with the direction reversed: 106 is loyalty owed for help received in one's own trouble, 806 loyalty kept when trouble comes.

752 says everyone scorns those who have nothing and everyone honours the rich (இல்லாரை எல்லாரும் எள்ளுவர்). 1293 has the woman quote the same worldly observation as a saying, கெட்டார்க்கு நட்டார் இல், and ask her heart whether that is why it leaves her and follows him. The pairing shows a hard fact from the chapter on wealth being used in the Book of Love as a taunt, with the woman as the ruined one and her heart as the fair-weather friend.

247 mentions as an aside that this world is not for the penniless. 751 makes that its full subject: nothing but wealth makes nobodies into somebodies. The section on virtue quietly grants the premise of the section on wealth.

1051 says ask when you find those fit to be asked (இரத்தக்கார்க் காணின்), and if they withhold, the blame is theirs. 1067, in the chapter on the dread of begging, says: if you must beg, do not beg from those who conceal (கரப்பார் இரவன்மின்). The two chapters take opposite attitudes to begging but give the same rule about whom to ask.

1077 says the base give only to those who would break their jaw. 1078 states the same with a contrast and a figure: the worthy are of use at a word (சொல்லப் பயன்படுவர்), and the base, like sugar-cane, when crushed (கொல்லப் பயன்படும்). Parimelazhagar treats the two verses as a pair on how the base give.

520 requires the king to examine the worker daily. 584 defines the spy as one who examines everyone, beginning with those who do the king's work (வினைசெய்வார்), then his kin and his enemies. 584 supplies the means by which the daily examination of 520 is carried out.
Virtue as a kind of fear: in 201 the excellent fear evil deeds, and in 366 what is to be feared is craving, which is behind those deeds. It is the same moral fear moved one step closer to its source.

வன்கண் is the same word in both. In 1156 he is hard because he could speak of leaving. In 1198 she calls herself hard for going on living without a word from him. The accusation has moved from him to her.

460 is built on the form 'nothing beyond X as support, nothing beyond Y as affliction' (நல்லினத்தின் ஊங்கும் துணையில்லை). 32 uses the same form and the same word ஊங்கு for virtue: no gain beyond virtue, no ruin beyond forgetting it (அறத்தினூஉங்கு ஆக்கமும் இல்லை). The pairing shows good company being given, in the book on statecraft, the kind of unqualified ranking the opening chapters give to virtue.

1021 says no greatness has more dignity (பீடு) than that of the one who says 'I will not stay my hand' (கைதூவேன்) from the work. 611 says not to slacken at a task's difficulty because effort itself gives greatness (பெருமை முயற்சி தரும்). Both locate பெருமை in persistence rather than in rank or result; 1021 applies it to the work of raising one's family.

In 1149 the woman asks whether she can be ashamed at gossip (அலர்நாண ஒல்வதோ) now that he has left her. In 1297 she says she has forgotten even shame (நாணும் மறந்தேன்), caught in a heart that cannot forget him. In both her shame gives way, in 1149 because his leaving has made it pointless and in 1297 because her own heart overrides it.

406 says the unlearned are no more than 'they exist' (உளரென்னும் மாத்திரையர்) and are like barren saline ground that yields nothing. 730 says those who, fearing the arena, cannot convey what they have learned are, though they exist, equal to those who do not (உளரெனினும் இல்லாரொடு ஒப்பர்). The same bare-existence wording puts the learned who cannot speak in nearly the place of the unlearned.

In 1130 she is sure that he lives in her heart, and gladly (உவந்துறைவர்), against the town's talk. In 1204 she affirms the same thing, that he is always in her heart (எந்நெஞ்சத்து ஓஒ உளரே அவர்), and then asks whether she too has a place in his (யாமும் உளேங்கொல் அவர்நெஞ்சத்து). The confidence she shows the town in 1130 does not answer the doubt she admits in 1204: his presence in her heart says nothing about her place in his.

220: if ruin comes through ஒப்புரவு, that ruin is worth getting even by selling oneself ('விற்றுக்கோள் தக்கது உடைத்து'). 780: a death at which the eyes of one's lord fill with tears is worth getting even by begging ('இரந்துகோள் தக்கது உடைத்து'). The same closing formula takes something normally shunned, ruin or death, and declares it worth a degrading price, once for the benefactor and once for the soldier.

177 says not to want gain that comes by coveting, since at its ripening (விளைவயின்) the fruit is hard to make good. 284 says the love grown strong in stealth yields, at its ripening (விளைவின்கண்), a sorrow that does not die. Coveting in the householder book and theft in the ascetic book are both judged by the harvest image, where the gain looks sound until it ripens.

840 likens a fool entering an assembly of the worthy to setting an unwashed foot on a bed (கழாஅக்கால் பள்ளியுள் வைத்தற்று). 720 likens speaking before those not of one's own kind to nectar spilled in an unclean yard (அங்கணத்துள் உக்க அமிழ்து). The two are mirror images of the same mismatch: the unclean thing brought into the clean place, and the precious thing let fall in the unclean place.

1289 says few attain love's செவ்வி, its right moment or condition. 1306 gives a figure for missing it on either side: without துனி and புலவி love is like fruit over-ripe or unripe (கனியும் கருக்காயும் அற்று). Parimelazhagar places 1289 in a sulk that will not yield to appeasement, so the fineness it speaks of is the same fineness of timing that 1306 puts in terms of ripeness.

645 says to speak a word only after knowing that no other word can defeat it (வெல்லுஞ்சொல் இன்மை அறிந்து). 467 says to think and then commit to a task, and that saying 'we will think after committing' is a fault (எண்ணித் துணிக). Both put the testing before the irreversible step; 645 applies to an utterance the rule 467 gives for action.

1126 says he never leaves her eyes though the town thinks him gone. 1218 says that when she sleeps he is on her shoulder and when she wakes he hurries into her heart (நெஞ்சத்தர் ஆவர் விரைந்து). Parimelazhagar frames both as her defence of him against the charge of absence: she answers by locating him somewhere inside herself at every moment.

604 says that for the slothful the family dies and faults multiply (குற்றம் பெருகும்). 609 says the fault is destroyed (குற்றம் ... கெடும்) once a man changes his sloth. 609 makes 604's decline reversible; Parimelazhagar goes further and takes 609's faults to include ones that arose from other causes.

561 makes the king the one who punishes in proportion (ஒத்தாங்கு ஒறுப்பது வேந்து), while 579 calls it the highest quality to show kindly regard and bear with even those whose way is to hurt (ஒறுத்தாற்றும் பண்பினார் கண்ணும் ... பொறுத்தாற்றும் பண்பே தலை). The same root ஒறு sits on opposite sides. Parimelazhagar separates the cases: 561 concerns wrongs done to weaker subjects, 579 wrongs done to the ruler himself, so forbearance is limited to injuries that are the ruler's own to forgive.

In 1312 the woman says he sneezed while she was sulking, knowing (அறிந்து) she would have to say 'live long' and so speak to him. In 1253 the sneeze is the example of what happens without intention: desire comes out குறிப்பின்றித் தும்மல்போல். Parimelazhagar notes that 1312 treats a natural sneeze as a deliberate one, which is the subtlety the chapter title names.

437 says the wealth of the miser who does not do with it what should be done (செயற்பால செய்யாது) perishes without anything surviving. 333 says wealth does not stay and should be turned at once into what does. The Book of Wealth gives the same instruction negatively: unused wealth is simply lost.

875 advises a ruler caught alone between two enemies to make one of them an ally. 633 lists among a minister's abilities dividing (பிரித்தல்), which Parimelazhagar explains as separating the enemy's supporters from him, and rejoining those who broke away (பிரிந்தார்ப் பொருத்தல்). The advice to the king in 875 is the skill required of the minister in 633.

189 speaks of the backbiter as a weight the earth bears (வையம் ... பொறை). 572 says the existence of those without kindly regard is a burden to the earth (நிலக்குப் பொறை). The figure of a person as dead weight on the ground is used in both for someone who fails others in ordinary dealings, by malicious speech in one and by lack of regard in the other.

319 states a rule: hurt done to others in the forenoon (முற்பகல்) comes back to oneself in the afternoon (பிற்பகல்), of itself. In 1225 the woman asks what good she did to morning (காலைக்குச் செய்த நன்று) and what enmity she did to evening (மாலைக்குச் செய்த பகை). Her question assumes the same logic of return, that suffering answers something one did, and finds no deed of hers to explain evening's hostility.

Verse 63 says people call their children their wealth (தம்பொருள் என்ப தம் மக்கள்), and ties that wealth to deeds (வினையான் வரும்). Verse 114 says whether people are worthy or not is seen from their எச்சம், what they leave behind, which Parimelazhagar takes as their offspring and Kalaignar as the name they leave. On Parimelazhagar's reading the pair makes children both a person's property and the evidence by which that person is judged.

798 says not to take the friendship of those who cut away in distress (அல்லற்கண் ஆற்றறுப்பார்). 106 says not to give up the friendship of those who were one's strength in sorrow (துன்பத்துள் துப்பாயார் நட்பு துறவற்க). The two prohibitions, கொள்ளற்க and துறவற்க, are complementary: how a friend behaves in trouble decides both whom not to take and whom not to drop.

1039 says that if the owner (கிழவன்) stays away and does not go to it, the land turns against him and sulks like a wife. 553 says the king who does not look into things and do justice every day loses his land day by day (நாடொறும் நாடு கெடும்). In both, land is lost through the owner's or ruler's lack of personal attention; Parimelazhagar reads 1039 too as requiring a daily visit.

265 says austerity is practised because through it whatever is wanted is obtained as wanted. 362 says that if one must want, one should want not to be born, and that this comes by wanting not to want (வேண்டாமை வேண்ட வரும்). 362 narrows what the வேண்டிய of 265 should be; Parimelazhagar reads 265 itself as referring to results in the next life and release, while Manakkudavar takes it to include enjoyments.

504 tells the king to examine a man's qualities and faults and judge by what predominates (குணம்நாடிக் குற்றமும் நாடி ... மிகைநாடி). 511 uses the same verb நாடி, but now it is the candidate who examines good and bad and settles on the good. The king's weighing of the man in chapter 51 becomes, in chapter 52, a check on how the man himself weighs.

469 says there is error even in doing good when it is done without knowing each person's character (அவரவர் பண்பறிந்து ஆற்றாக்கடை). 1078 says the worthy are of use at a word, while the base, like sugar-cane, are of use only when crushed (சொல்லப் பயன்படுவர் சான்றோர் கரும்புபோல் கொல்லப் பயன்படும் கீழ்). 1078 is an instance of the difference in character 469 says must be known first: the approach that works on one kind of person does nothing with another.

Verse 211 asks what the world does for the rain-cloud in return (மாரிமாட்டு என் ஆற்றுங் கொல்லோ உலகு) and makes it the model of duty that wants no repayment. Verse 17 says even the long sea loses its nature if the cloud, having taken from it (தடிந்து, as Parimelazhagar reads it), does not give back. On that reading the cloud is not a pure giver: it returns what it drew from the sea, and the sea suffers if it withholds. Manakkudavar takes தடிந்து as lightning flashing, and on his reading the qualification falls away.

798 warns against taking the friendship of those who cut away in distress (அல்லற்கண் ஆற்றறுப்பார் நட்பு). In 1293 the one who deserts in distress is her own heart, which cannot be declined as a friend. The verse turns the advice of the friendship chapters into a predicament with no remedy.

671 calls it a fault when a resolved deed lingers in delay (தாழ்ச்சியுள் தங்குதல் தீது). 672 immediately limits this: there are deeds to be done slowly, and over those one should take time (தூங்குக தூங்கிச் செயற்பால); only the deed that must be done without delay must not be slept on. Delay is therefore wrong by the nature of the task, not in itself.

605 makes four habits a boat (கலன்) that the ruin-bound love to board; Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar both read it as a vessel that drops its passengers mid-sea, though Parimelazhagar notes others read கலன் as an ornament. 1068 makes begging an unsafe boat (ஏமாப்பில் தோணி) that splits on the rock of refusal. In both a way of living is a vessel trusted by the person in it and bound to fail him.

368 says there is no suffering for those without desire. 1043 makes poverty itself into desire, which Parimelazhagar glosses as: without craving there's no poverty. An ascetic insight enters the chapter on economic misery, while the rest of the chapter denies it.

629 says one who does not crave pleasure in the midst of pleasure does not suffer in the midst of pain. 115 says loss and increase are both part of life and that not letting the heart bend (நெஞ்சத்துக் கோடாமை) is the ornament of the worthy. Both ask for the same evenness across good and bad turns; 115 treats it as fairness of mind, 629 as protection against pain.

408 says wealth lodged with the unlearned (கல்லார்கண் பட்ட திரு) is more painful than poverty lodged with the good. 837 shows what happens when a fool gets great wealth: strangers feast and his own people go hungry. 837 gives one concrete form of the harm; Manakkudavar likewise reads 408 as harm done to others.

433 says the blame-fearing treat a millet-sized fault as palmyra-sized. 965 says even people like a hill are diminished if they do a lowering thing the size of a குன்றி seed. 965 gives the outward fact, that a tiny act does lower the great, which makes the inward magnifying in 433 an accurate estimate and not an exaggeration.

115 says loss and increase are not absent from life, and that not bending in the heart (நெஞ்சத்துக் கோடாமை) is the ornament of the worthy. Parimelazhagar records a second reading of 425, in which the opening and closing are expanding in wealth and shrinking in want. On that reading the two verses say the same thing, that a person should stay the same through gain and loss, one under the heading of fairness and the other of understanding.

930 asks whether a drinker, when sober and seeing another man drunk (களித்தானைக் காணுங்கால்), does not reflect on the slackness of his own drinking (உள்ளான்கொல் உண்டதன் சோர்வு). 539 tells one elated with joy to reflect (உள்ளுக) on those whom negligence ruined. Both correct an intoxicated state by looking at its effect in other people, and 930's word சோர்வு is the one 531 uses for the slackness of joy.

831 says folly is to let gain go (ஊதியம் போக விடல்). 797 uses the same two words to say what gain is: giving up and leaving the friendship of fools (ஊதியம் என்பது ... பேதையார் கேண்மை ஒரீஇ விடல்). The fool lets gain go, and for everyone else letting the fool go is the gain.

431 praises those without desire, and 440 tells one how to enjoy desire safely. Parimelazhagar resolves this by making the fault excess in 431, but the verses themselves pull apart. Removing and hiding are different programmes.

202 ranks evil deeds above fire as a thing to fear. 896, in the Book of Wealth, says one burned by fire may still survive ('எரியால் சுடப்படினும் உய்வுண்டாம்') but those who keep wronging the great will not. The same comparison, fire as the survivable danger, is applied once to one's own deeds and once to the anger of the powerful.

141 says the folly of desiring a woman who is another's (பிறன்பொருளாள்) is not found in those who have seen அறம் and பொருள். 163 says the envier of பிறனாக்கம் is one who wants neither அறன் nor ஆக்கம். In adjacent chapters a wrong attitude to what is another's is measured against the same pair, virtue and wealth.

292 makes good results decisive: a falsehood that yields faultless good (நன்மை பயக்கும் எனின்) counts as truth. 113 says gain got by leaving fairness is to be dropped that very day even if it yields nothing but good (நன்றே தரினும்). The conflict holds only if both are read as answers to whether a good outcome can license a breach of a norm; 113 is about gain and 292 about speech, and 292's புரைதீர்ந்த (free of fault) may already exclude what 113 forbids.

184 concedes speaking without kindly regard to a person's face (கண்ணின்று கண்ணறச் சொல்லினும்) and forbids only the word said in his absence that does not look to what follows (முன்னின்று பின்நோக்காச் சொல்). 795 goes further and tells one to seek out friends able to speak so that one weeps and to rebuke (அழச்சொல்லி ... இடித்து). What 184 merely tolerates, hard speech face to face, 795 treats as a mark of the friend worth choosing.

740 says that a land with every excellence is of no use without accord with its king. 770 says that though an army has plenty of steadfast men (நிலைமக்கள் சால உடைத்தெனினும்), there is no army where there are no leaders (தலைமக்கள் இல்வழி இல்). In both, a body that is complete in its own parts is counted as nothing without its head.

49 says that what is called aram is household life, and that it is good if there is nothing in it that another blames (பிறன்பழிப்பது இல்லாயின்). 147 says the householder living by aram is the one who does not desire another's woman. 147 can be read as naming a specific condition under which the household life of 49 stays free of others' blame; chapter 15 itself (145, 146) names பழி as the result of the offence.

1308 says the man's hurt is useless without a lover who recognises it. 1309 gives the general form: as water is sweet in shade, sulking is sweet only with those who love (வீழுநர் கண்ணே இனிது). Parimelazhagar assigns both to the man, in a sulk that she is not answering.

583 denies victory to a ruler who has things spied out but does not discern their meaning (ஒற்றிப் பொருள்தெரியா); 423 defines understanding as seeing the true substance of whatever is heard from anyone (அப்பொருள் மெய்ப்பொருள் காண்பது). The pairing shows the spy chapter applying the general rule about hearsay to intelligence: collecting reports is not yet knowing.

423 defines understanding as seeing the true thing (மெய்ப்பொருள் காண்பது அறிவு) in whatever one hears from anyone. 857 says those of harmful understanding who are attached to hostility (இகல்மேவல் இன்னா அறிவினவர்) do not see the மெய்ப்பொருள் that carries victory. So 857 names hostility as one thing that turns அறிவு against its defining task; Parimelazhagar narrows மெய்ப்பொருள் here to the content of the treatises on statecraft and says hostility clouds the understanding.

1205 complains that he keeps her out of his heart while entering hers without pause (எம்நெஞ்சத்து ஓவா வரல்). 1291 states the same imbalance to her own heart: his heart stays his (அவர்நெஞ்சு அவர்க்காதல்), so why is hers not hers? In 1205 she blames him for the unequal exchange, and in 1291 she blames her own heart.

797 counts leaving the friendship of fools as gain (ஊதியம்). 450 says that letting go the tie with the good (நல்லார் தொடர் கைவிடல்) is ten times worse than taking on the enmity of many. Whether breaking a tie is profit or harm depends on who is at the other end of it.

741 says a fort matters to those who fear attack and look to their own safety. 569 says a king who has not made his defences (சிறைசெய்யா வேந்தன்) will, when war comes, be struck with fear and quickly perish (வெருவந்து வெய்து கெடும்). 569 states the cost of ignoring 741: without a fort prepared beforehand, fear has nowhere to turn.

Both redefine manliness away from dominance over others. 148 gives பேராண்மை to the man who doesn't look at another's wife, and 907 finds the opposite failure in a man who takes a woman's orders: in each case ஆண்மை is measured by self-command.

696 tells one who serves a king to say what is needed and not disliked, in a way that is wanted (வெறுப்பில வேண்டுப வேட்பச் சொலல்). 685 has the envoy remove what offends and speak so as to please (தூவாத நீக்கி நகச்சொல்லி) while securing good for his own side. The same manner of speech is prescribed toward one's own king in 696 and toward a foreign king in 685; in both the pleasing manner serves what has to be said.

34 says being spotless in mind is the whole of virtue (மனத்துக்கண் மாசிலன் ஆதல் அனைத்து அறன்). 364 defines purity as the absence of craving (அவாவின்மை). Taken together, 364 names the stain that 34 leaves unnamed.

1090 uses liquor as the lesser pleasure that love outdoes. 1288 uses it as an exact likeness: 'your chest is to us as liquor is to those who are drunk on it (களித்தார்க்குக் கள்ளற்றே), though it does shaming harm (இளித்தக்க இன்னா)'. The later verse grants what 1090 leaves unsaid, that the pull likened to drink goes on despite disgrace.

155 says the wise do not count as anything those who punish in return (ஒறுத்தாரை ஒன்றாக வையார்) and keep those who forbear like stored gold. 314 keeps the word ஒறுத்தல் and gives it a new content: the way to punish those who have done harm is to shame them by doing them good (அவர்நாண நன்னயஞ் செய்து விடல்). 314 thus shows the only form of 'punishing' that 155's judgment leaves open. (The Parimelazhagar text displayed for 314 in this edition belongs to 315.)

In 1119 the man tells the moon that to resemble her face it must not appear for many to see (பலர்காணத் தோன்றல்). In 1311 the woman refuses the man's chest because all women feast on him in common with their eyes (கண்ணின் பொதுஉண்பர்). Each lover applies the same standard from the other side: what is shared with every onlooker is no longer one's own.

967 prefers being called ruined to a life got by following those who reject you. 230 says nothing is more bitter than dying, yet even that is sweet when giving is out of reach (ஈதல் இயையாக் கடை). In both, a life that cannot be lived on one's own terms, without honour or without the power to give, is ranked below death.

In 1123 the man orders the image in the pupil of his eye (கருமணியிற் பாவாய்) to leave, since otherwise there is no room for the woman he loves. In 1126 the woman says her lover never leaves her eyes (கண்ணுள்ளின் போகார்) and is too subtle to be hurt when she blinks. Both lovers place the other inside the eye; he has to make room for her, and she has him there already.

501's fourth test is fear for one's life (உயிரச்சம்). 690 defines the envoy as one who, even if it brings his end (இறுதி பயப்பினும்), does not fall short in securing his lord's good. The envoy chapter shows what passing that fourth test looks like in service.

657: the extreme poverty of the worthy (சான்றோர் கழிநல்குரவு) is better than wealth got by taking on blame (பழிமலைந்து எய்திய ஆக்கம்). 408: wealth lodged with the unlearned (கல்லார்கண் பட்ட திரு) is more painful than poverty lodged with the good (நல்லார்கண் பட்ட வறுமை). The same comparison of good people's poverty with bad people's wealth is made from each side, once about how wealth was got and once about who holds it.

The two verses open with nearly the same words, நனவினால் நல்காதவரை and நனவினால் நல்காக் கொடியார், and reach opposite verdicts on the dream. In 1213 seeing him in dreams keeps her alive; in 1217 she asks why the cruel one torments her in dreams (எம்மைப் பீழிப்பது). Parimelazhagar places 1217 after she has woken and found him gone, so the dream comforts while it lasts and wounds once it has ended.

112 says the wealth of a person of rectitude (செப்பம் உடையவன் ஆக்கம்) does not decay and is a security to his descendants. 169 admits the opposite case occurs: the prosperity of the crooked-hearted and the ruin of the upright (செவ்வியான் கேடு) are things to be pondered (நினைக்கப்படும்). 169 thus limits 112 to the usual course of things; Parimelazhagar explains the exceptions by deeds of earlier births.

704 says readers of the unspoken and others share the same limbs but are different (வேறு). 1071 says the base look just like people (மக்களே போல்வர் கயவர்), a resemblance the speaker has seen nowhere else. The same figure of outward human likeness hiding an inner difference serves a point about intelligence in 704 and about moral baseness in 1071.

616 says effort creates prosperity and the absence of effort brings in want (முயற்றின்மை இன்மை புகுத்தி விடும்). 270 says the have-nots (இலர்) are many because few practise austerity (நோற்பார் சிலர்). Both trace poverty to something people fail to do, but they name different things: present exertion in the chapter on labour, and austerity here, which the commentators take to bear fruit across births.

In 1086 the man says her eyes cause him trembling pain (நடுங்கஞர்) and wishes them screened. In 1171 the woman asks why her own eyes weep, since they showed him to her and so gave her this unending sickness (தண்டாநோய் தாம்காட்ட). Each lover names eyes as the cause of the pain; for him it is hers, for her it is her own.

Verse 11 gives rain the name அமிழ்தம் because the world's life continues through it. In 1106 the lover says her shoulders must be made of amrita (அமிழ்தின் இயன்றன தோள்) because his life puts out new shoots at each touch (உயிர் தளிர்ப்ப). Both verses award the word for the same reason, that the thing keeps life going, once for the whole world and once in a lover's speech about himself.

1134 has the flood of love carry away the raft called shame and good manliness (நாணொடு நல்லாண்மை என்னும் புணை). 1251 has the axe of desire break the door called restraint, bolted with the bar of shame (நிறையென்னும் நாணுத்தாழ் வீழ்த்த கதவு). Both make shame a built defence that love's force destroys, one in the man's voice and one in the woman's.

596 says that whatever one thinks of, one should think of rising (உள்ளுவதெல்லாம் உயர்வுள்ளல்), and that even if this is thwarted it is as if it were not. 476 says that those who have climbed to the tip of a branch and push beyond it (அஃதிறந்து ஊக்கின்) end their lives. 596 sets no ceiling on aspiration, while 476 sets one on action: there is a point past which striving higher is fatal.

1018 sees shame as the condition of virtue, with virtue itself ashamed to approach the shameless. 1075 is a kind of counter-case: the base still have conduct, with fear and desire in place of shame. Their conduct looks alike and differs in its source.

424 makes it part of understanding to put things so that hearers take them in easily. 650 says those who cannot lay out what they have learned so that others understand (கற்றது உணர விரித்துரையாதார்) are like a cluster of flowers in bloom with no scent. 650 gives the failure case of 424's first half: learning that cannot be conveyed is counted as lacking something essential. The first word of 650 is misprinted in this edition, though the image is clear from the commentary.

442 describes the people a ruler should keep: they remove the trouble that has come and guard in advance against more. 787 describes friendship in similar terms: it removes what leads to ruin (அழிவினவை நீக்கி), sets one on the path, and shares the suffering when ruin comes. The great adviser and the friend are given the same protective work, though 787 adds a sharing of suffering that 442 does not ask of the adviser.

787 ends with the friend who suffers along in ruin (அழிவின்கண் அல்லல் உழப்பது). 799 says the friendship of those who abandon one in ruin (கெடுங்காலைக் கைவிடுவார்) burns the heart even when remembered at the hour of death. 799 shows the cost of the failure of the third duty that 787 lists.

1049 says that in poverty the eyes cannot close by any means (யாதொன்றும் கண்பாடு அரிது). In 1136 the man says his eyes will not close because of the girl, even at midnight (படல் ஒல்லா ... என் கண்). The same sign, eyes that cannot close, marks want in the Book of Wealth and longing in the Book of Love; 1136 is a lover's speech, so this is a shared figure and not a shared teaching.

Both use a tiny seed against a huge effect. In 104 a millet-seed favour counts as large as a palmyra to those who understand it, and in 889 a sesame-seed enmity holds complete ruin. Small things turn out to be large in the Kural in both moral directions.
Both treat wealth as worse for being held by the wrong person, but 1000 faults character and 408 faults learning. 1000's spoilt milk also shows the damage to the good thing, not only to others.

129 sets a fire-burn, which heals, against the tongue's scar, which does not; 1049 says one can even sleep in the middle of fire but cannot close an eye in the middle of poverty (நெருப்பினுள் துஞ்சலும் ஆகும்). The book repeatedly takes fire as the measure of bearable pain and places a non-physical hurt beyond it.

521: kin keep honouring old ties (பழைமை) even when all is lost. 806: those who keep within the bounds do not give up, even in ruin (தொலைவிடத்தும்), the bond of those who have stood with them from of old (தொல்லைக்கண் நின்றார் தொடர்பு). Loyalty to a long tie when fortune is gone is claimed as the mark of kin in one chapter and of true old friends in the other.

1039 says land whose owner stays away sulks like a wife (இல்லாளின் ஊடிவிடும்); 1007 likens ungiven wealth to a beautiful woman who ages alone (தமியள் மூத்தற்று). Both picture a good left unattended as a woman without her partner, for farmland in one verse and for money in the other; Parimelazhagar notes for 1007 that the wealth itself loses its fruit.

430 says those without understanding have nothing, whatever they have (என்னுடையரேனும் இலர்); 1005 says the same of those who neither give nor enjoy, even with crores. The same form of argument, that owning is not having unless some further quality is present, is used for understanding in one place and for use and giving in the other.

833 puts shamelessness (நாணாமை) first among the fool's traits. 1018 says what that trait costs: if one is not ashamed of what makes others ashamed, the fault is one that virtue itself would be ashamed of (அறம் நாணத் தக்கது உடைத்து); Parimelazhagar reads it as virtue leaving him. 1018 supplies the consequence that 833 leaves unstated.

771 has a warrior warn enemies not to stand before his lord (என்ஐமுன் நில்லன்மின்), since many who did now stand as memorial stones (கல்நின்றவர்). 894 states the rule behind the warning: for the unable to do harm to the able is like beckoning Death with the hand (கூற்றத்தைக் கையால் விளித்தற்று). The battlefield taunt and the political maxim give the same counsel, one from the strong side and one addressed to the weak.

1078 says the worthy are of use as soon as they are told (சொல்லப் பயன்படுவர் சான்றோர்). 223 says not uttering the misery of 'I have nothing', and giving, belong to one of good family; Parimelazhagar records a second reading on which the giver gives before the asker has to say it. On that reading 223 goes one step beyond 1078: the worthy of 1078 give at a word, and the well-born of 223 give before the word.

164 says people do no wrong out of envy because they know the harm that comes of the wrong path (ஏதம் படுபாக்கு அறிந்து). 172 says people do nothing blameworthy out of coveting because they are ashamed of unfairness (நாணுபவர்). The neighbouring chapters use the same sentence shape, ending in செய்யார், with knowledge of consequences as the check in one and shame in the other.

843 states generally that those without understanding torment themselves (தாந்தம்மைப் பீழிக்கும் பீழை). 847, in the same chapter, names one way it happens: the person without understanding lets the precious மறை slip and so does great harm to himself by himself (பெருமிறை தானே தனக்கு). 847 is a specific instance of 843's claim, with the same stress on தானே.

Verse 20 ends the chapter by saying nothing in the world, for anyone, holds without the sky. Verse 55 says that for the wife who rises worshipping her husband, it rains when she says 'rain' (பெய்யெனப் பெய்யும் மழை). Three chapters after rain is made the condition of everything, the rain is said to answer to one person's steadfastness.

In 1281 love is set above liquor: it delights at a thought and a look, which liquor cannot do. In 1288, in the same chapter, his chest is itself like liquor to those who have got drunk on it (களித்தார்க்குக் கள்ளற்றே), wanted though it does shameful harm (இளித்தக்க இன்னா செயினும்). The chapter uses the one image both ways, first to say love exceeds drink and then to say it compels like drink.
Parimelazhagar himself cites 963 here: the poor must stand tall, and asking without speaking lets them do so. The honour chapter's demand shapes how begging can be done at all.

187 says that those who cannot make friends by pleasant speech will divide even their own people by divisive talk (பகச்சொல்லிக் கேளிர்ப் பிரிப்பர்). 808 describes the friend on whom that does not work, who does not listen to reports of a friend's lapse. 187 gives the talebearer's side and 808 the hearer's refusal.

127 says whatever else they fail to guard, let them guard the tongue, or they will grieve through a fault of speech (நாகாக்க காவாக்கால் சோகாப்பர்); 305 says if you would guard yourself, guard against anger, or anger will kill you (சினங்காக்க காவாக்கால் தன்னையே கொல்லும்). The sentence frame காக்க / காவாக்கால் is the same, and in both the harm of the unguarded thing falls on the person who failed to guard it.

881 says even shade and water are bad when they do harm (நிழல்நீரும் இன்னாத இன்னா), and so is the nature of one's own people when it does harm. In 1309 the man says water is sweet in the shade (நீரும் நிழலது இனிதே), and sulking is sweet only with those who love. Both take shade and water as the standard of what is pleasant and then make the pleasantness depend on a condition, which in both cases is the real disposition of those closest to one.

154 says that one who wants நிறையுடைமை never to leave should guard forbearance; Parimelazhagar glosses நிறை here as சால்பு. 987 asks what use சால்பு is if one does not do pleasing things even to those who have done one harm (இன்னாசெய்தார்க்கும் இனியவே செய்யாக்கால்). On Parimelazhagar's reading the two say the same thing from both ends: forbearance keeps சால்பு in place, and சால்பு that does not show in the treatment of offenders is worth nothing.

666: what one has thought of is obtained as thought, if one is firm. 309: all one has thought of is obtained at once (உள்ளிய தெல்லாம் உடனெய்தும்), if one does not think of anger in the heart. The same promise is attached to two different inner conditions, one positive (firmness) and one negative (absence of anger).

1322 says tenderness may wilt (வாடினும்) under the small pain of a sulk and still come to greatness. 1304 uses the same verb for the limit: not reconciling one who has sulked is like cutting an already wilted creeper at the root (வாடிய வள்ளி முதலரிந்தற்று). The wilting is harmless only if the sulk is ended; Parimelazhagar reads 1304 as the woman speaking of his other women.

148 praises not even looking at (நோக்காத) another's wife; Parimelazhagar glosses this as not taking her into the mind. 282 says that even thinking in the heart (உள்ளத்தால் உள்ளலும்) of taking another's goods (பிறன்பொருளை) by stealth is wrong. In both chapters the prohibition is moved back from the act to the look or the thought, for another's wife and for another's property.

131 says conduct is to be guarded more than life because it gives excellence (ஒழுக்கம் உயிரினும் ஓம்பப்படும்); 1017 says those ruled by shame will give up life for shame and will not give up shame for life (நாணால் உயிரைத் துறப்பர்). Both place a quality of character above life itself; 1017 states as what such people actually do what 131 states as a rule.

497 says that one who thinks everything through and acts by the place needs no support but fearlessness (அஞ்சாமை அல்லால் துணைவேண்டா). 534 says the fearful have no fortress (அச்சமுடையார்க்கு அரணில்லை): Parimelazhagar explains that forest or hill forts are of no use to a frightened mind. The pair shows the two sides of one claim: place is enough given courage, and place is worthless without it.

In 1088 the man, on first seeing her, says his might (பீடு), which enemies dreaded in battle, has broken before her bright forehead. In 1133 he says the shame and good manliness he once had are replaced by the palmyra horse. The later verse carries the first collapse through to its end: what broke at first sight is now given up publicly.

405 says an unlearned person's standing collapses once he converses. 717 says the learning of those who have studied and understood shines out (விளங்கும்) among those able to examine words without fault. Conversation with the competent is the test in both, with opposite results for the unlearned and the learned.

934 says nothing gives poverty like gambling, which does many small harms and ruins standing (சிறுமை பலசெய்து சீரழிக்கும்). 1045 says that within the one affliction called poverty many sufferings arrive (பல்குரைத் துன்பங்கள் சென்று படும்). Read together they form a chain: gambling brings harms on the way to poverty, and poverty then brings its own.

588 says that even what one spy found and brought should be confirmed through another spy (மற்றுமோர் ஒற்றினால்); 589 adds that spies should be run so that one does not know of another, and that what three say in agreement is to be accepted (மூவர் சொற்றொக்க தேறப்படும்). 589 turns the second opinion of 588 into a procedure: sources kept independent, and a threshold of agreement.

389 says the world rests under the umbrella (கவிகை) of a king who can bear bitter words. 1034 says those who have the shade of grain will see the shade of many umbrellas come under their own umbrella (தங்குடைக்கீழ்), which Parimelazhagar takes as their own king's. Both use the royal umbrella's shade for dominion, but 389 credits the king's character and 1034 credits the farmers' harvest.

In 1162 she cannot hide the sickness, and telling the one who caused it brings shame (உரைத்தலும் நாணுத் தரும்). In 1181 the question widens to யார்க்கு உரைக்கோ, to whom can I tell it at all, because she herself agreed to his going; Parimelazhagar adds that telling a self-made sorrow would itself be blame. The pair traces how the possible hearers for her complaint run out.

44 opens with பழியஞ்சி: the household life that fears blame and shares its food keeps its line. 49 calls household life virtue itself, then adds that it is good if there is nothing others blame (பிறன் பழிப்பது இல்லாயின்). On Manakkudavar's reading, where அஃதும் still refers to household life, 49 makes absence of blame the condition on the chapter's whole praise of the householder, which 44 had already built into its description.

490 says to be like the heron in the season for folding up (கூம்பும் பருவத்து) and like its strike when the moment is right (சீர்த்த இடத்து). 672 gives the same double instruction without the image: take time over what is to be done slowly, and do not delay what must not be delayed. Both hold that waiting and speed are each correct in their place.

202 says evil deeds are to be feared more than fire ('தீயினும் அஞ்சப்படும்') because they yield evil. 129 sets fire against the tongue: a wound burned by fire heals, the scar burned by the tongue does not ('ஆறாதே நாவினாற் சுட்ட வடு'). In both, fire is the harm that ends, used to measure a harm that lasts; Parimelazhagar on 202 makes this explicit, saying fire cannot follow one into another time, place or body.
131 says that conduct must be guarded above life. 969 and 970 turn that ranking into an actual death, and show what the abstract comparison costs.

946 says disease stays with the one of very great feed (கழிபேர் இரையான்), as pleasure stays with the one who eats knowing to stop short (இழிவறிந்து உண்பான்). 420 asks what it matters whether those live or die who know taste only by the mouth and not by the ear, and calls them மாக்கள். Both verses use a word with an animal sense for the person ruled by the mouth: இரை, feed, and மாக்கள்.

889 holds that inner enmity is ruinous even at the size of a split sesame seed. 433 says those who are ashamed of blame take a fault the size of a millet seed (தினைத்துணை) to be as large as a palmyra. 433 describes the attitude that 889 calls for: treating the small thing at its eventual size.
203 only asks one to refrain from harming an enemy. 314 goes further and makes kindness to the wrongdoer the punishment itself. Prudent restraint becomes active shaming.

787 defines friendship as turning a friend from ruin and, when ruin comes, sharing the suffering (அழிவின்கண் அல்லல் உழப்பதாம் நட்பு). The saying in 1293, that the ruined have no friends, describes how the world behaves and not what friendship is; by the standard of 787 her heart, which goes after him as it pleases (பெட்டாங்கு அவர்பின் செலல்), has failed as a friend. The woman's question, என்பதோ, shows she is quoting the saying to reproach, not endorsing it.

1204 asks whether she too is in his heart, since he is always in hers (யாமும் உளேங்கொல் அவர்நெஞ்சத்து). 1205 gives the answer as an accusation: he has put a guard on his heart against her (தம்நெஞ்சத்து எம்மைக் கடிகொண்டார்) and yet comes unceasingly into hers. Manakkudavar reads 1205 as the woman, having doubted, now deciding that he does not think of her.

229 says eating alone in order to fill up one's store (நிரப்பிய தாமே தமியர் உணல்) is more bitter than begging; 1001 takes the case one step further, the man who does not even eat it (அஃதுண்ணான்), and calls him dead. Read together they grade the misuse of wealth: unshared use is wretched, no use at all is not living.

93 places virtue in a glad face followed by sweet words from within (அகத்தானாம்). 824 warns that deceivers who smile sweetly with the face and are bitter within (முகத்தின் இனிய நகாஅ அகத்தின்னா வஞ்சரை) are to be feared. 824 describes the counterfeit of 93's first half, so the outward signs 93 begins with cannot by themselves be taken as proof of the inner part.

97 asks for speech that has both benefit (பயன்) and pleasantness (பண்பு), and credits it with producing நயன். 197 says the worthy may say what lacks நயன் if they must, but should not say what lacks பயன் (நயனில சொல்லினும் சொல்லுக ... பயனில சொல்லாமை நன்று). 197 thus ranks the qualities 97 holds together: use is the one that cannot be given up. Parimelazhagar takes நயன் in 197 as justice; Subramuniyaswami takes it as pleasantness, which makes the limit on chapter 10 more direct.

1206: she exists only by remembering the days she had with him (உற்றநாள் உள்ள உளேன்), and asks what else she could live by. 1213: her life exists because she sees in dreams the man who gives nothing in waking (கனவினால் காண்டலின் உண்டென் உயிர்). Both make survival in separation depend on a mental substitute for his presence, memory by day and dream by night.

464 says those who fear disgrace do not begin what is not clear to them (தெளிவு இலதனைத் தொடங்கார்). 491 gives the same ban on beginning (தொடங்கற்க எவ்வினையும்) a concrete test: until the place has been seen (இடங்கண்ட பின் அல்லது). Read together, knowing the ground is one specific form of the clarity 464 demands before any start.

59 says that without a home that seeks renown there is no walking with a bull's (Parimelazhagar: lion's) proud gait, ஏறுபோல் பீடு நடை. 1014 says shame is an ornament to the worthy, and without it their பீடு நடை is a disease. The proud walk appears twice as something that must be earned by an inner or domestic quality, the household's good name in one verse and a sense of shame in the other.

910 says those with deliberation and firmness of heart never fall into the folly of attachment to a woman. 917, in the next chapter, says it is those without a firm heart (நிறைநெஞ்சம் இல்லவர்) who touch the shoulders of women who embrace with their minds on other things. Both locate the safeguard in the man's own நெஞ்சம், stated positively in 910 for the wife-ruled man and negatively in 917 for the client of courtesans.

233 says only renown stands undying. 156 says those who punish have a day's pleasure, while those who forbear have renown பொன்றுந் துணையும், which Pope and Parimelazhagar take as until the world ends. 156 measures a virtue's reward by the lasting quality that 233 attributes to renown, and gives it a source other than giving.
42 makes the householder the support of renouncers, and 1036 sets the farmer a level below, as the support of renouncing itself. The chain of dependence runs lower than the book of virtue showed.

393 denies real eyes to the unlearned. 418 says ears not pierced by listening (கேள்வியால் தோட்கப்படாத செவி) are of a deaf kind even though they hear. The next chapter repeats the pattern for the other sense: an organ counts only when it has been trained by learning or listening.

117 says the world will not set down as ruin (கெடுவாக வையாது) the low state of one who stays in what is right through fairness. 169 lists the ruin of the upright (செவ்வியான் கேடு) as something to be pondered. 117 limits how that கேடு should be counted: the upright person's decline is not regarded as real ruin.

99 asks why one who sees how sweetly sweet words yield (இன்சொல் இனிதீன்றல் காண்பான்) would use harsh words (எவன்கொலோ வன்சொல் வழங்குவது); Parimelazhagar takes it as one who has felt the pleasure of others' kind words to himself. 318 asks why one who knows what is painful to his own life does painful things to other lives (என்கொலோ மன்னுயிர்க்கு இன்னா செயல்). The two rhetorical questions have the same form and the same argument from one's own experience to the treatment of others, applied to words in 99 and to harm in general in 318. (The first line of 318 is misprinted in this edition, but the verse is recoverable.)

1000 says great wealth obtained by one without courtesy is like good milk spoiled by the fault of its vessel (கலந்தீமையால் திரிந்தற்று). 1008 says the wealth of a man nobody seeks out is a poison tree bearing fruit in the middle of the village (நச்சு மரம் பழுத்தற்று). Both say a good thing is made useless or harmful by the character of its holder; Parimelazhagar reads 1000 as wealth that benefits no one.

150 says not desiring another's woman is good even in one who practises no aram and does wrong; 297 says that if one can keep to not lying, then not doing the other virtues (அறம்பிற செய்யாமை) is still good. Both isolate a single restraint and say it holds its value without the rest of virtue. Set side by side, the book makes this kind of claim for more than one virtue, so each is better read as emphasis than as a ranking.

1313, 1319 and 1320 share the frame '…even if I do X, she is angry (…இனும் காயும்), saying …'. In 1313 the act is wearing a wreath; in 1320 it is only sitting and looking at her (நினைத்திருந்து நோக்கினும்), which she takes as comparing her with someone (யார் உள்ளி நோக்கினீர்). The series runs from adornment down to a silent look, so that no act of his is left free of suspicion.

509 says to trust no one without examining and, after examining, to trust what is to be trusted (தேர்ந்தபின் தேறுக); 589 says to run spies unknown to one another and to accept what three say in agreement (தேறப்படும்). Both give the same two-step rule, test first and then commit, 509 for persons and 589 for reports.

938 lists what gambling does: it destroys wealth (பொருள் கெடுத்து), makes one take up lying, destroys compassion (அருள் கெடுத்து) and drives one through misery. 248 ranks two of these losses: those without wealth may flower again one day (பூப்பர் ஒருகால்), but those without அருள் are finished. By 248's measure the third item in 938's list is graver than the first.

In 1102 the man says that medicine for a disease is normally something else, but she is herself the medicine for the sickness she causes (தன்நோய்க்குத் தானே மருந்து); in 1266 the woman says that if he comes for one day she will drink him in so that all her sickness is destroyed (பைதல்நோய் எல்லாம் கெட). Each lover names the other as both the cause and the only cure.

1306 puts it negatively: without quarrels, serious and light, love is fruit at the wrong stage. 1330 puts it positively: sulking is the pleasure of love (ஊடுதல் காமத்திற்கு இன்பம்), and the pleasure of sulking is the embrace that follows. The chapter 133 verse states as a conclusion what 1306 argues by image.

209 assumes that doing evil is acting against oneself: one who loves himself stays away from it. 843 says the suffering that those without understanding inflict on themselves is hard even for their enemies ('செறுவார்க்கும்') to inflict. 843 describes the person who fails 209's test, and Parimelazhagar's comment there names poverty, blame and sin as what such people bring on themselves.

704 stops at saying that those who cannot grasp the unspoken are 'different' (வேறு) from those who can. 410 says others stand to those who have studied the shining books as beasts stand to people (விலங்கொடு மக்கள் அனையர்). Parimelazhagar glosses the வேறு of 704 with this very comparison, the idea being that they are animals, so 410 states outright what 704 leaves implied.

877 advises not telling one's pain to those who do not know it (நோவற்க நொந்தது அறியார்க்கு). 1140 shows the reason from inside: those who have not suffered what the speaker suffered (யாம்பட்ட தாம்படா) laugh at her in plain sight. The statecraft maxim and the lover's complaint agree that pain gets no hearing from those who have not felt it.

94 says want that brings suffering (துன்புறூஉம் துவ்வாமை) does not come to those whose sweet speech gives joy to everyone. 566 says that if a ruler is harsh of speech and without kindly regard (கடுஞ்சொல்லன் கண்ணிலன்), his long-standing wealth perishes on the spot. The two verses state the same link between speech and prosperity from opposite sides, for anyone in the Book of Virtue and for a king in the Book of Wealth.

897 asks what a life excellent in every part and lofty wealth (வகைமாண்ட வாழ்க்கையும் வான்பொருளும்) come to if the worthy of great stature are angered (தக்கார் செறின்). 900 says even those with support beyond measure (இறந்தமைந்த சார்பு) do not survive if those of the highest distinction are angered (சீரார் செறின்). The two close on the same word செறின் and between them cancel a person's own assets and then his outside supports.

320 says all pains fall on those who caused pain (நோயெல்லாம் நோய்செய்தார் மேலவாம்). 169 admits that the crooked-hearted prosper and the upright meet ruin, and says only that this is to be pondered (நினைக்கப் படும்). 169 concedes cases that 320's rule does not show on its face; Manakkudavar's reading of 320, that present pain comes from hurt done earlier, and Parimelazhagar's of 169, that such cases are to be examined for causes, are the way the commentators reconcile them.

450 weighs losing the good against the enmity of many and finds it ten times worse. 816 weighs close friendship with a fool against being a stranger to the wise and finds the second ten million times better (கோடி உறும்). Both rank relationships by a multiplied comparison, and in both the quality of the person outweighs whether the relation is friendly or hostile.

1072 calls the base fortunate (திருவுடையர்) for having no distress of heart, and 1073 calls them like the gods (தேவர் அனையர்) for doing as they please. Both give praise that is meant as blame; Parimelazhagar says so of each. The two together describe one condition, no inner check in 1072 and no outer one in 1073.

368 says those without craving have no sorrow, and where craving exists sorrow comes on and on without fail (தவாஅது மேன்மேல் வரும்); 284 says desire hardened in stealing (கன்றிய காதல்) yields sorrow that does not die (வீயா விழுமம்). 284 is the general law of 368 applied to one desire, with the same stress on sorrow that does not end.

461 lists the outcomes to be weighed before acting: loss, gain and later yield. 471, opening the next chapter with the same imperative, lists the strengths to be weighed: of the deed, oneself, the opponent and the allies (வினைவலியும் தன்வலியும் மாற்றான் வலியும் துணைவலியும் தூக்கிச் செயல்). The second supplies what the first's calculation of gain and loss depends on.

681 asks of the envoy 'qualities that kings desire' (வேந்தவாம் பண்புடைமை) without saying what they are. Manakkudavar glosses the phrase as not desiring what the king desires, which is the content of 692 (மன்னர் விழைப விழையாமை), and Parimelazhagar says this quality is obtained from the following chapter on conduct around kings. 692 therefore supplies, on the commentators' reading, what 681 leaves unstated.

1251 says the axe of desire breaks the door of restraint bolted with shame (காமக் கணிச்சி உடைக்கும் நிறையென்னும் ... கதவு). 1324 uses the same verb for the resolve to keep sulking: a weapon arises that breaks the heart (உள்ளம் உடைக்கும் படை). What was a breach forced during separation in 1251 becomes, inside the sulk, a breaking that leads to the embrace that does not let go (புல்லி விடா).

786 distinguishes the laugh of the face from the laugh of the heart in friendship. Parimelazhagar takes 999's laughter as inner joy in others' company, so a failure of that capacity darkens the world and not merely a friendship.

In the same chapter, 423 demands testing every claim for yourself and 426 says live as the world lives. The tension is softened if உலகம் means the worthy, as Manakkudavar has it, but the verse doesn't say so.

406 says the unlearned can only be said to exist (உளரென்னும் மாத்திரையர்) and are otherwise like saline ground that yields nothing (பயவாக் களர்). 420 says of those who have no taste for what the ear takes in that their dying or living makes no difference (அவியினும் வாழினும் என்). The chapters on not learning and on listening reach the same verdict, a life that merely exists; Manakkudavar reads 420, as Parimelazhagar reads 406, as about being of no use to others.

755, in the chapter on making wealth, says wealth that does not come with grace and love (அருளொடும் அன்பொடும் வாராப் பொருளாக்கம்) should be let go and not embraced. 311 makes not hurting others the settled stand of the stainless even at the cost of wealth. The condition that 311 states for the pure is repeated in the Book of Wealth as a rule for acquisition itself.

43 lists five quarters to be tended (ஐம்புலத்தாறு ஓம்பல்): ancestors, gods, guests (விருந்து), kin and oneself, and calls this the chief thing (தலை). 81 says that all of staying, guarding one's goods and living at home (இருந்தோம்பி இல்வாழ்வதெல்லாம்) is for the sake of tending guests and doing them good (விருந்தோம்பி வேளாண்மை செய்தற் பொருட்டு). One of the five items of 43 is taken up, with the same verb ஓம்பு, and made the purpose of the whole household.

475 says that feathers, light as they are, break an axle when piled too high. 889 says that enmity within, though as small as a split sesame seed (எட்பகவன்ன சிறுமைத்தே ஆயினும்), has ruin in it. Both warn against judging a danger by the smallness of its unit, 475 because small things add up and 889 because of where the small thing sits.

1198 calls hard those who live without receiving a sweet word from the beloved (இன்சொல் பெறாஅது). 1199 defines how little would count: though he gives no grace, any report of him is sweet to her ears (அவர்மாட்டு இசையும் இனிய செவிக்கு). Parimelazhagar reads இசை as any word at all, even that he is not coming, and links the two verses on that basis; Kalaignar takes இசை as his praise.

464 says those who fear the harm called disgrace do not begin what is not clear to them (தெளிவிலதனைத் தொடங்கார் ... அஞ்சுபவர்). 172 has the same form: those ashamed of unfairness do not do blameworthy things out of desire for the gain (பழிப்படுவ செய்யார் நடுவன்மை நாணுபவர்). In both a fear or shame is what holds a person back, in 172 from a wrong act and in 464 from an unexamined one.

Verse 72 says those who have love belong to others even in their bones (என்பும் உரியர் பிறர்க்கு). Verse 220 says that if ruin comes through ஒப்புரவு, that ruin is worth buying even by selling oneself (விற்றுக்கோள் தக்கது). Both carry giving past one's goods to one's own person, 72 as a description of love and 220 as the price of duty to the community.

1236: with bangles and arms slackening, what pains her is hearing him called cruel (அவரைக் கொடியர் எனக்கூறல் நொந்து). 1219 goes from that pain to a rebuttal: those who blame him (நோவர்) are people who have not seen a lover in their dreams. Parimelazhagar gives both verses the same occasion, the friend speaking ill of the man, and says she puts her reply in 1219 on strangers out of displeasure with the friend.

922 forbids drinking and adds that if anyone drinks, it should be those who do not want to be counted by the worthy (சான்றோரான் எண்ணப்பட வேண்டாதார்). 656 forbids any act the worthy condemn (சான்றோர் பழிக்கும் வினை), even to relieve one's own mother's hunger. In both the judgement of the சான்றோர் is the measure of conduct; 922 states it as the price a drinker must be willing to pay.

960 says one who wants lineage must want humility toward everyone (யார்க்கும் பணிவு). 125 says bowing is good for all (எல்லார்க்கும் நன்றாம் பணிதல்) and is a further wealth for the rich. Both make humility general, and each singles out the highly placed, by family or by wealth, as those it most becomes.

A flimsy vessel breaks up in both. 1134's raft of shame and good manliness is swept away by the flood of love. 1068's boat of asking is split by the rock of concealment. Each shows a failed crossing, but the vessel in 1134 is what one is proud of.

169 says the prosperity of the crooked-hearted and the ruin of the upright are things to be pondered (நினைக்கப்படும்), and gives no answer; Parimelazhagar says the wise look for the earlier deed behind it. 374 notes a like mismatch between wealth and understanding and gives it as the two-fold nature of the world. One verse separates wealth from goodness and the other separates it from wisdom.

507 warns that trusting those without understanding out of fondness brings all folly on the one who trusts. 836 describes the result from the other side: when a fool who does not know how takes up a task (கையறியாப் பேதை வினைமேற் கொளின்), it fails and he ends in fetters. 836 shows the outcome that 507's warning anticipates.

57 says confinement does little to guard women and the guard kept by their own firmness (நிறைகாக்கும் காப்பு) is best; 1016 says the high have shame for their fence (நாண்வேலி). In both the effective guard is a quality inside the person and not an outer barrier, for a wife's fidelity in one and for the conduct of the high in the other.

1259 narrates one occasion: she went away to sulk and embraced him when she saw her heart joining him. 1260 turns it into a general question about people whose hearts melt like fat in fire, and whether 'we will stand in a sulk' (ஊடி நிற்பேம் எனல்) is even open to them. The second verse gives the reason for the first.
471 says act after weighing strengths. Parimelazhagar's 485 says that even with greater strength, wait for the time. So a favourable reckoning from 471 still isn't enough.

496 says chariots with strong wheels do not run on the sea and sea-going ships do not run on land (கடலோடா ... நாவாயும் ஓடா நிலத்து); Manakkudavar takes it to mean that instruments must be made to suit the place. 675 lists means and place together (கருவி ... இடனொடு ஐந்தும்) among the five things to think through before acting. 496 shows why the two items in 675's list cannot be weighed separately: a tool is only a tool in its own medium.

104 says a millet of good is taken as a palmyra by those who know its worth. 109 says even harm like killing (கொன்றன்ன இன்னா) vanishes when one thinks of a single good the person did (ஒன்று நன்று உள்ளக் கெடும்). Parimelazhagar connects them in his note on 109: because the small good is held as large, that one good can cancel the later harm.

Both verses end on the word விருந்து, a feast. In 1211 the woman (for Parimelazhagar) asks what feast she can make for the dream that came bringing her lover's messenger (யாதுசெய் வேன்கொல் விருந்து). In 1268 the man, away on the king's work, looks forward to the evening feast at home once the king has won (மாலை அயர்கம் விருந்து). The real feast waits on his return, and meanwhile she can offer hospitality only to a dream.

351 says a joyless birth comes from the delusion (மருள்) that takes the unreal for real. 358 goes a step further and calls birth itself a folly (பிறப்பென்னும் பேதைமை); Parimelazhagar explains this as naming the effect in place of its cause. The chapter moves from delusion as the cause of birth to birth and delusion spoken of as one thing, removed together by seeing the real.

1129 and 1130 end with the same line, ஏதிலர் என்னும் இவ் வூர். 1129 gives the town's ground for blame, her sleeplessness, which she explains as refusing to blink. 1130 states her answer directly: he lives gladly in her heart always (உவந்துறைவர் உள்ளத்துள் என்றும்), while the town says he lives apart.

761 calls a fearless army the chief of a king's assets. 546 says it isn't the spear but the sceptre that gives victory. Porul itself has two answers to what wins wars, one in its justice chapter and one in its army chapter.

326 says Death that eats life (உயிருண்ணுங் கூற்று) does not advance on the days of one who lives by not killing. 1084 says the eyes of this womanly, artless girl have a look that eats the life of those who see them (கண்டார் உயிருண்ணும் தோற்றம்). The lover gives her eyes the standing epithet of Death, which the previous verse (1083) has just named.

636 asks what subtle scheme can stand before those who have native acuteness together with book-learning (மதிநுட்பம் நூலோடு உடையார்). 915 says those whose knowledge is made excellent by goodness of intellect (மதிநலத்தின் மாண்ட அறிவினவர்) do not touch the favours of women common to all; Parimelazhagar reads this too as natural intellect perfecting acquired knowledge. The pairing shows the same compound of mind being credited in statecraft with seeing through stratagems and here with keeping a man from a private vice.

42 says the householder is the support (துணை) of renouncers, the destitute and the dead. 1032 says the ploughmen bear (பொறுத்து) everyone who does not plough. Both verses identify one group whose ordinary work holds up all the others: the householder in the Book of Virtue, the farmer in the Book of Wealth.

920 names women of two minds (இருமனப் பெண்டிர்), which Parimelazhagar explains as a mind that joins and does not join a man at once. 974 says greatness, like women of one mind (ஒருமை மகளிர்), exists only by guarding oneself. The two phrases are opposites, and where single-mindedness is 974's model for keeping greatness, doubleness in 920 goes with dice and drink as the company of the unfortunate.

764 says an army has courage that has come down to it (வழிவந்த வன்கண்). 766 lists the four things that protect an army: valour, honour, walking the excellent path of those before (மாண்ட வழிச்செலவு) and தேற்றம். 766 spells out the inherited quality of 764 as following the path of earlier warriors, which is how Parimelazhagar reads வழிச்செலவு.

444 places the chief strength in attaching oneself to those greater than oneself; Parimelazhagar adds that this means following their lead. 985 says the strength of those who accomplish things is to bow (ஆற்றுவார் ஆற்றல் பணிதல்). Both locate strength in deference and not in standing alone.

566 says that if the ruler is harsh of speech and 'eyeless' (கண்ணிலன்), his long-standing wealth perishes at once; Parimelazhagar takes கண் here to stand for கண்ணோட்டம். 577, in the next chapter, states the equation directly: those without kindly regard have no eyes (கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லவர் கண்ணிலர்). The single word in 566 is the idea the following chapter spells out.

798 begins: do not think of what makes the spirit shrink (உள்ளற்க உள்ளம் சிறுகுவ). 596 gives the positive form: in all one thinks, think of rising (உள்ளுவதெல்லாம் உயர்வுள்ளல்). Both treat the direction of one's thoughts as something to be chosen for the sake of the spirit; 798 then sets fair-weather friends beside the shrinking thoughts as things to refuse.

462 says nothing is hard to attain for those who act after examining a matter with chosen company (தெரிந்த இனத்தொடு) and thinking it over themselves. 677 narrows whose counsel counts for a particular task: the one who knows that deed from inside (அவ்வினை உள்ளறிவான்), whom Parimelazhagar takes to be someone who has done it before. General consultation in 462 becomes, in 677, learning the mind of the person with experience of the task.

110 says those who kill any good may have an escape (உய்வுண்டாம்), but there is none for one who kills a good done to him (செய்ந்நன்றி கொன்ற மகற்கு). 207 has the same shape: those who incur any enmity (எனைப்பகை உற்றாரும்) escape (உய்வர்), but the enmity of one's deeds follows and kills. Both use 'everything else can be survived' to single out one thing, ingratitude in 110 and evil deeds in general in 207.

1059 asks what distinction givers could have if there were none who wished to ask and receive (இரந்துகோள் மேவார் இலாஅக் கடை). 256 says none would bring flesh to sell if the world did not kill for eating. Both reason from a counterfactual about one party to the existence of the other: askers make givers possible, and eaters make sellers of flesh possible.

607: the slothful end up hearing words of scorn (எள்ளுஞ் சொல்). 1040: seeing those who sit idle saying 'we have nothing', the good woman called Land laughs (நிலமென்னும் நல்லாள் நகும்). Both give idleness the same penalty, being laughed at, once from people and once from the personified earth.

488 advises that on meeting an enemy one should bear him, which Parimelazhagar glosses as bowing, until his end is in sight (செறுநரைக் காணின் சுமக்க இறுவரை). 827 says not to accept an enemy's bowing speech (சொல்வணக்கம்), because the bending of a bow signals harm. The humility 488 teaches as a tactic is the humility 827 teaches one to distrust in the other side.

1273 compares her unspoken meaning to a thread that shows through the gems (திகழ்தரு); 1274 compares it to the scent inside a closed bud (முகைமொக்குள் உள்ளது நாற்றம்). Parimelazhagar distinguishes them: the first lies within yet is visible outside, the second is not visible outside at all, so the pair moves from a sign that can be seen to one that can only be inferred.

1170: if her eyes could go where he is as her heart does (உள்ளம்போன்று உள்வழிச் செல்கிற்பின்), they would not be swimming in a flood of tears. 1244 turns the wish into a request: heart, take the eyes along when you go (கண்ணும் கொளச்சேறி), for they consume her in wanting to see him. Both rest on the idea that the heart can travel to him and the eyes cannot.

834 presents a puzzle: a person who has studied, understood and taught, and still does not restrain himself. 373 offers the chapter on fate's account of such a person: however many subtle books one studies, one's own underlying understanding prevails (தன் உண்மையறிவே மிகும்), which Parimelazhagar takes as the folly given by fate. 373 explains how the fool of 834 is possible.

487 says the bright do not flare up outwardly at once but watch for the time and burn within (காலம்பார்த்து உள்வேர்ப்பர்). 821 warns that those who keep close without inner consent will strike when they see the right place. The patience the book recommends to a ruler in 487 is the same conduct it tells him to expect from a false friend in 821.
A spy in 587 hears the hidden and knows it without doubt, and in 1076 the base also hear it, but proclaim it. Trading in secrets is a skill or a vice according to whether one can hold them.

1086 wishes her brows would screen her eyes (மறைப்பின்), for then the eyes would not cause him trembling pain. 1087 says the cloth over her breasts is like the face-cloth over a rutting elephant's eyes (கட்படாம்). Both are about a covering over something that harms him: one he wishes for and one he sees, and Parimelazhagar says of the second that the cloth keeps them from killing.

In 1321 the woman says he has no fault (இல்லை தவறவர்க்கு), yet the way he shows tenderness (அவர் அளிக்குமாறு) is able to produce a sulk. In 1325 the man says that even when men are faultless (தவறிலர் ஆயினும்), being kept from the soft arms of the one they love 'has a certain something' (ஆங்கொன்று உடைத்து). The chapter opens each speaker's side with the same concession: the sulk it praises needs no offence.

429 credits freedom from shock to an understanding that guards against what is coming. 442 tells a ruler to cherish and keep those who can remove the trouble that has come and guard beforehand against what has not (உறாஅமை முற்காக்கும் பெற்றியார்). 442 shows that the foresight of 429 need not be the ruler's own: it can be secured by choosing the right people.

430 says those with understanding have everything, and those without it have nothing whatever they have (என்னுடையரேனும் இலர்). 841 says lack of understanding is the lack among lacks (அறிவின்மை இன்மையுள் இன்மை), and the world does not count other lack as lack. 841, opening the chapter on shallow understanding, restates 430 from the side of poverty.

517 says that once the king has reasoned 'this man will finish this by this means', he should leave it with him (அதனை அவன்கண் விடல்). 510 says that doubting one who has been examined and trusted brings endless trouble. Leaving the task with the man is the practical form of 510's rule: examination comes first and is then followed by a real handing over.

Verse 72 says the loveless belong to themselves in everything (எல்லாம் தமக்குரியர்) while the loving belong to others (பிறர்க்கு) even in their bones. Verse 1009 says wealth piled up by putting love aside (அன்பொரீஇ), denying oneself and ignoring virtue will be taken by others (கொள்வார் பிறர்). 1009 gives the outcome of the stance in 72: what the loveless keep for themselves ends with பிறர் anyway.

155 says those who punish (ஒறுத்தார்) are not counted as anything. 549 says that guarding the people and removing wrongdoing (குற்றம் கடிதல்) is no stain on a king but his work (வடுவன்று வேந்தன் தொழில்). Parimelazhagar restricts 155 to a harm done to oneself, and 549 concerns a ruler acting for his subjects, so 549 marks the limit of 155: the low regard for punishing applies to personal retaliation and not to the office of justice.

182 calls it worse than denying virtue to slander someone when absent and smile at him when present. 820 tells one not to come near those who are friendly in the house and blame you in the assembly (மனைக்கெழீஇ மன்றில் பழிப்பார்). 820 turns the moral verdict of 182 into practical advice about which friendships to refuse.

719 forbids speaking good things in a mean assembly. 849 gives a reason in another chapter: one who shows something to a person who does not see becomes himself unseeing (காணாதான் காட்டுவான் தான்காணான்), while that person goes on seeing as he saw. Parimelazhagar makes the same point on 719, that both assemblies would then look down on the speaker.

262 says that for those without தவம், undertaking it is futile. 620 says those who toil on without flagging or delay will see the back even of fate (ஊழையும் உப்பக்கம் காண்பர்). If the தவம் one must already have is merit from former births, as Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar read it, then 262 makes present effort useless without a prior endowment, which is what 620 denies. On Kalaignar's reading, where it means present firmness and self-control, the conflict disappears.

904 denies வீறு (distinction) to the action of the wife-fearing man: வினையாண்மை வீறெய்தல் இன்று. 665 says the firmness in action (வினைத்திட்பம்) of those who have attained distinction (வீறெய்தி மாண்டார்) reaches the king and is held in regard. The same phrase வீறு எய்து names what capable action normally earns and what, in 904, fear of the wife withholds.

1325 says that being kept from her arms by a sulk has a pleasure of its own (ஆங்கொன்று உடைத்து). 1307 says sulking also holds one pain: the thought of whether union will be delayed or not (புணர்வது நீடுவது அன்றுகொல் என்று). Parimelazhagar gives both to the man, 1325 after the making up and 1307 during the sulk, so the pleasure of 1325 is one judged in hindsight.

428 says fearing what should be feared is the work of the knowing (அஞ்சுவது அஞ்சல் அறிவார் தொழில்) and leaves the object open. 366 names an object, craving, and calls the fear of it virtue (அஞ்சுவதோரும் அறனே). The general rule about right fear in the book of statecraft gets a specific content in the renouncer's chapter.

490 holds up the heron, which stays still until the moment and then strikes, as a model for acting on enemies. 274 says that doing wrong under cover of austerity is like a hunter hiding in a bush to snare birds (புதல்மறைந்து வேட்டுவன் புள்சிமிழ்த்தற்று). The pattern of stillness that hides a coming strike is the same in both. It is recommended to the king waiting for his time, and it is the figure of fraud in one who wears the ascetic's appearance.

447 speaks of the ruler who keeps rebukers. 638 gives the matching duty of the one beside him: even if the king rejects knowledge and knows nothing himself, the one at his side is bound to tell him what is sound (உறுதி உழையிருந்தான் கூறல் கடன்). 638 extends the idea to the case where the king is not the willing listener 447 assumes.

43 puts kin (ஒக்கல்) among the five the householder must tend. 524, in the chapters on kingship, says that living so as to be surrounded by one's kin (சுற்றத்தால் சுற்றப்பட ஒழுகல்) is the fruit of having gained wealth. The household duty of Book 1 reappears in Book 2 as the point of a ruler's prosperity.

428 says the knowing fear what should be feared. 451 names one such object, a surprising one: not a danger, but a social circle. It only makes sense given 452's claim that company changes understanding.

126 says that drawing in the five like a tortoise in one birth is a protection for seven. 354 says the attained fivefold awareness yields no fruit without true perception; Parimelazhagar reads ஐயுணர்வு as the mind withdrawn from the senses and held under control, and the missing fruit as release, while Manakkudavar reads it as knowing all that the five senses can know. On Parimelazhagar's reading sense-restraint earns protection across births, as 126 says, but not the end of birth.

572 says the existence of those without kindly regard is a burden to the earth (அஃதிலார் உண்மை நிலக்குப் பொறை). 1003 says the very appearance of men who cling to accumulation and do not want renown is a burden to the earth (தோற்றம் நிலக்குப் பொறை). The phrase is identical, and in both the people called a burden are those who are of no use to others.

731 makes unfailing yield (தள்ளா விளையுள்) one of three things that must come together (சேர்வது) for a land. 545 says rain and yield (பெயலும் விளையுளும்) gather (தொக்கு) in the land of the king who wields the sceptre as it should be wielded. Read together, the yield that defines a land in 731 is traced in 545 to just rule.

111 says the virtue called தகுதி is good if one keeps to what is due in each case (பகுதியால் பாற்பட்டு ஒழுக); Parimelazhagar takes பகுதி as enemy, stranger and friend. 541 defines a king's justice (முறை) as inquiring, showing favour to no one (யார்மாட்டும் கண்ணோடாது) and acting after consideration. The householder's impartiality of 111 reappears as the procedure of the ruler's court.

Verse 16 says that unless drops fall from the sky (விசும்பின் துளிவீழின் அல்லால்) not even the tip of green grass can be seen. Verse 557 says that what lack of drops (துளியின்மை) is to the earth, the king's lack of tender regard (அளியின்மை) is to those who live under him. Verse 16 supplies the picture that 557's comparison assumes: without the king's அளி, the people are the bare ground.

502 lists good family first and shame last among the grounds for trust. 951 says integrity and shame are found together by nature (இயல்பாகச் செப்பமும் நாணும் ஒருங்கு) only in those born to a good house. 951 supplies the reasoning 502 leaves unstated: family is asked for because it is taken to be where shame comes naturally.

92 treats giving with a glad heart (அகனமர்ந்து ஈதல்) as a real good, surpassed only by a glad face and sweet speech. 842 takes the same act, giving with a glad heart (நெஞ்சுவந்து ஈதல்), and says that in a person without understanding it reflects only the receiver's merit. 842 limits 92's valuation: the glad gift counts for the giver only when understanding is behind it, which is how Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar both read it.

616 says effort produces fortune and lack of effort brings want (முயற்சி திருவினை ஆக்கும்). 468 says exertion that is not made by the right way (ஆற்றின் வருந்தா வருத்தம்) will give way even if many stand guarding it. 468 puts a condition on 616's praise of effort: it has to follow the proper method, and neither strain nor helpers make up for that.
