253 uses the weapon-holder as the model of a mind closed to good. 774 celebrates a warrior who plucks a spear from his own body and laughs. The Kural honours in the section on polity the same figure that it distrusts in the section on virtue.

598 says the person without drive does not attain the pride of generosity; 614 says the beneficence of one without effort comes to nothing, like a sword in the hand of a பேடி. 614 adds what happens when such a person tries anyway: the means are present but the capacity to use them is not.

301 says that the one who truly guards against anger guards it where it can take effect (செல்லிடத்துக் காப்பான் சினங்காப்பான்); where it cannot, guarding or not makes no difference. 487 has the bright hold back anger now, when showing it would not serve, and keep it inside for the right time. On the reading that 487's anger is to be released when it can succeed, it describes the restraint that 301 says does not count, and withholds the one that does.

805 says a hurtful act by a friend is to be understood as folly or as great intimacy (பெருங்கிழமை). 109 says that even an injury like killing is cancelled when one thinks of a single good the person did. Both teach a way of reading an injury so that the bond survives it; 109 does it by remembering a past benefit, 805 by a charitable account of the cause.

846 asks whether covering one's nakedness is not itself small-minded when one's faults are left uncovered (தம்வயின் குற்றம் மறையா வழி); Parimelazhagar takes covering faults to mean removing them. 278 speaks of many who, with stain in the mind, bathe and go about concealed (மனத்தது மாசாக ... நீராடி மறைந்தொழுகு). Both set a bodily propriety, clothing or bathing, against an inner fault it does nothing about.

56 gives the wife's self-guarding, தற்காத்து, as what makes a woman. 974 makes the same self-holding the condition of greatness in anyone. A gendered virtue is universalized, and the phrasing reaches back across the book of virtue.

470 tells the one who acts to avoid what the world will scorn and not accept. 280 tells the ascetic that neither shaving nor matted hair is needed if he gives up what the world has condemned (உலகம் பழித்தது ஒழித்து விடின்); Parimelazhagar takes 'the world' there as the high-minded. The same measure, what the world rejects, governs a king's policy in one verse and a renouncer's conduct in the other.

463 says the wise do not undertake what loses the principal in hope of gain. 932 asks whether gamblers, who get one and lose a hundred (ஒன்றெய்தி நூறிழக்கும் சூதர்), have any way of living well. The gambler is the plain case of the venture 463 rules out, a small gain pursued at the cost of what one already had.

146 lists four things that never leave the man who crosses into another's home: enmity, sin, fear and blame (பகை பாவம் அச்சம் பழி). 171 says that one who covets another's good property without fairness finds his family ruined and fault brought on at once (குடிபொன்றிக் குற்றமும் ஆங்கே தரும்). Coveting another's wife and coveting another's goods are both given immediate, compound consequences; Parimelazhagar reads the பழி of 146 as blame on the family (குடிப்பழி), which brings it closer to the குடி of 171.

1307 finds a pain inside sulking (ஊடலின் உண்டு ஆங்கு ஓர் துன்பம்): the thought of whether union will be delayed or not. In 1152 the woman says union itself holds the misery of fearing separation (பிரிவு அஞ்சும் புன்கண் உடைத்தால் புணர்வு). In both, a state counted as pleasant carries worry about what comes next.

624 says trouble is troubled by one who hauls on like an ox through every blocked place. 620 carries the claim to its limit: those who labour on without flagging (தாழாது உஞற்றுபவர்) see the back even of fate (ஊழையும் உப்பக்கம் காண்பர்). What 624 says of obstacles in the road, 620 says of the power behind them.

123 calls restraint செறிவு and says that, recognised, it yields distinction; 715 calls not speaking first among elders a செறிவு and ranks it the best of good things (முந்து கிளவாச் செறிவு). The shared word shows the general restraint of chapter 13 turning up in the assembly as a concrete act, holding back one's speech before those who know more.

209 says that if a person loves himself (தன்னைத்தான் காதலனாயின்) he should not come near evil deeds, however small. 318 asks why one who knows what hurts his own life does hurt to other lives. Both reason from self-regard, by different routes: 209 from the doer's own interest, 318 from the doer's own knowledge of pain.

1234 and 1235 share the line தொல்கவின் வாடிய தோள், shoulders whose old beauty has faded. 1234 describes the loss: with her partner gone (துணை நீங்கி) they have lost their fullness and the bangles slip. 1235 turns the same shoulders into testimony that declares the cruelty of the cruel one (கொடியார் கொடுமை உரைக்கும்), so the repeated line moves from description to accusation.

229 condemns those who eat alone to build up their own wealth. 527 says crows do not hide their food but call and eat (காக்கை கரவா கரைந்துண்ணும்), and that gain belongs only to those of that nature. The rule against eating alone appears in the ethics of giving in 229 and as advice on keeping kin and prosperity in 527.

505 makes each person's own deeds the touchstone of greatness and smallness (தத்தம் கருமமே கட்டளைக் கல்). 514 says tests of every kind before the appointment still leave many who change once in the work. Both put the decisive evidence in action, and 514 adds that the action that counts is the work itself, after trust has been given.

1198 says no one in the world is harder than those who go on living without getting even a kind word from the one they love (வாழ்வாரின் வன்கணார் இல்). 1213 has the woman living on though he gives her nothing in waking life (நனவினால் நல்காதவரை), and explains it: her life exists because she sees him in dreams (கனவினால் காண்டலின்). The second verse answers the first's charge of hardness by naming what keeps her alive.

836 describes the fool as கையறியா, not knowing how to act. 925 uses the same compound, கையறியாமை, as the cause of paying money to lose awareness of oneself in drink. In both verses the word names a practical ignorance that ends in the person binding or losing himself.

751 says nothing but wealth makes people of no account into people of account (பொருளல்லது இல்லை பொருள்). 1002 names nearly the same thought, பொருளானாம் எல்லாம், as what the miser thinks, and says that when it leads to not giving (ஈயாது இவறும்) it is delusion. The chapter on making wealth is thus limited here: the claim holds only for wealth that is given and used.

309 says all one has thought of is gained at once (உள்ளியதெல்லாம் உடனெய்தும்) if one never thinks of anger in the heart. 540 says gaining what one has thought of is easy (உள்ளியது எய்தல் எளிது) if one can keep thinking of it. Both promise the same result in nearly the same words and set a condition on the mind: one removes a thought, the other holds one.

1101 says the objects of all five senses are found in her alone. 1105 says her shoulders are like whatever one craves, at the time one craves it. The first claim is about range, that she holds every kind of pleasure; the second adds timing, that she answers each wish as it comes.

Chapters 71 and 110 share the title குறிப்பறிதல். 709 has the eye say what kings won't, and 1100 says that when lovers' eyes agree, words are useless. A single theory of the speaking eye serves both state intelligence and love, and neither treats speech as the deeper channel.

497 says no ally is needed (துணைவேண்டா) beyond fearlessness when the plan is complete and the ground right. 875 advises one who has no ally and two enemies (தன்துணை இன்றால் பகையிரண்டால்) to make one of the enemies a pleasing ally. 875 shows that the book does not treat being without allies as generally safe; 497's claim holds only under its stated condition of complete planning and the right place.

728 and 140 have the same form: 'though they have learned much'. In 140, those who have not learned to live in accord with the world are without understanding though they have learned much (பலகற்றும்). In 728, those who cannot speak well in a good assembly are without use though they have learned many things (பல்லவை கற்றும்). Each names a practical ability without which the amount learned does not count.

298 says outer purity comes by water and inner purity is seen through truth (அகந்தூய்மை வாய்மையால் காணப்படும்). 688 names தூய்மை first among the envoy's marks and then requires வாய்மை along with all three. 298 gives the reason the two words belong together: truthfulness is how inner purity shows.

331 calls lowest the paltry understanding that takes what does not last for lasting (நில்லாதவற்றை நிலையின என்றுணரும்). 351 says a joyless birth comes from the confusion that takes what is not real for real (பொருளல்லவற்றைப் பொருளென்று உணரும் மருள்). The two verses are built on the same sentence frame; 331 applies the misperception to duration and 351 to reality, and 351 adds the consequence, rebirth.

Verse 18 says that if the sky dries up (வானம் வறக்குமேல்), festival and worship for the gods will not go on here (சிறப்பொடு பூசனை செல்லாது). Verse 560 says that if the guardian does not guard (காவலன் காவான் எனின்), the cows' yield shrinks and those of the six duties forget their book (நூல் மறப்பர்). Both say religious practice has a material precondition that can fail; chapter 2 names the rain and chapter 56 names the king.

510 says doubting one who has been trusted (தெளிந்தான்கண் ஐயுறவு) brings endless trouble. 519 says fortune leaves the one who thinks otherwise of the closeness of a man devoted to his work (கேண்மை வேறாக நினைப்பானை நீங்கும் திரு). Both make the ruler's unfounded suspicion of a proven servant a cause of his own loss.

481 says the crow beats the owl by day (பகல்வெல்லும் கூகையைக் காக்கை), and Parimelazhagar notes that the owl is the stronger bird. 500 says a jackal kills a fearless war elephant in mud where its feet sink (காலாழ் களரில் நரியடும்). In both a weaker animal defeats a stronger one through a circumstance, time in 481 and ground in 500, which is how the two adjacent chapters make their cases.

Verse 79 says the outer limbs are of no use without the inner limb, love. Verse 407 says the fine looks (எழில்நலம்) of one without subtle, penetrating understanding are like those of a well-made clay doll (மண்மாண் புனைபாவை). Both set a complete exterior against a missing interior, love in Book 1 and understanding in Book 2.

96 says that if one seeks out good things and says them sweetly (நல்லவை நாடி இனிய சொலின்), what is not virtue wears away and virtue grows. 128 says that if even one harmful word has its effect (ஒன்றானும் தீச்சொல் பொருட்பயன் உண்டாயின்), what was good turns out not good. Together they give speech power over one's stock of virtue in both directions: good words build it and a single bad word undoes it.

1084: her eyes have a look that eats the life of those who see them (உயிருண்ணும்). 1221: the woman tells evening it is not evening but a time that eats the life of those once wed (மணந்தார் உயிருண்ணும் வேலை). The same phrase marks what kills each lover: for the man her eyes at first sight, for the woman the evening hour in his absence.

2 asks what learning has achieved (கற்றதனால் ஆய பயனென்கொல்) if the learned do not bow at the feet of the one of pure knowledge. 354 says command of the five senses has no benefit (பயமின்றே) for those without perception of the real. Both verses grant an attainment and then deny its fruit when the final step is missing, learning without worship in one and discipline without insight in the other.

741 allows that a ruler may fear and protect himself behind walls. 775 counts even a blink before a spear as flight. The chapter on the state and the chapter on the warrior hold different standards for fear, and both are the Kural's.

757 says grace is raised by wealth. 755, in the same chapter, says wealth that does not come with grace and love (அருளொடும் அன்பொடும் வாரா) is to be let go. The dependence runs both ways: grace needs wealth, but only wealth that itself came with grace and love.

In 1139 the woman's love, thinking 'not everyone knows' (அறிகிலார் எல்லாரும் என்றே), goes reeling through the street (மறுகின் மறுகும்). In 1180 she says the town easily learns the secret of those whose eyes are beaten drums (அறைபறை கண்ணார்). In both the secret is given away by the lover herself and not by the town: by her love going about in 1139, by her eyes in 1180.

In 1314 he says 'we love more than anyone' (யாரினும் காதலம்) and she turns it on him: 'than whom, than whom?' (யாரினும் யாரினும்). 645 advises speaking a word only after knowing there is no other word that can defeat it (வெல்லுஞ்சொல் இன்மை அறிந்து). The love scene shows that rule failing in a comic way: his own word, repeated back, is the one that beats him.

509 says that once a person has been examined, what is to be trusted should be trusted. 588 says even what a spy has found and brought back should be checked through another spy (மற்றுமோர் ஒற்றினால் ஒற்றிக் கொளல்). For intelligence reports the book keeps verifying after the agent is chosen, which bears on 509's phrase தேறும் பொருள்: Manakkudavar reads it as the matters in which the person is reliable, not everything.

1137 says nothing has greater worth than womanhood that suffers a sea of desire and still does not mount the palmyra horse (மடலேறாப் பெண்ணின் பெருந்தக்கது இல்); 1280 says that telling love's sickness with the eyes and pleading (கண்ணினால் காமநோய் சொல்லி இரவு) is womanhood upon womanhood. Both praise as specifically womanly the refusal to declare desire openly, 1137 by what she will not do and 1280 by the silent means she uses instead.

1190 hopes that her pallor can be talked of without his நல்காமை being talked of. In 1232 the friend says her pale, weeping eyes themselves seem to tell of the unkindness of the one she desired (நயந்தவர் நல்காமை சொல்லுவ போலும்). The same word நல்காமை shows the limit of her wish: the pallor is itself the report against him.

285 opposes having அருள் in view to having பொருள் in view; 757 says the child அருள், born of அன்பு, is reared by the wealthy foster-mother பொருள். 757 limits how far 285 can be taken: the opposition holds for goods taken from others by watching for their lapses, not for wealth as such, which 757 makes the support of the same அருள் and அன்பு that 285 names.

91 says sweet words are the speech of those who have seen the செம்பொருள் (செம்பொருள் கண்டார் வாய்ச்சொல்), which Parimelazhagar glosses here as those who know virtue. 358 defines understanding as seeing the செம்பொருள் so that the folly of birth departs (செம்பொருள் காண்பது அறிவு). The same phrase links ordinary kind speech to the insight the renunciation chapters describe, though the commentator gives the word a more modest sense in 91.

954 says no amount of wealth makes the well-born do what lowers them. 657 says the extreme poverty of the worthy (சான்றோர் கழிநல்குரவு) ranks above gain reached by taking on blame (பழிமலைந்து எய்திய ஆக்கம்). Both rank standing above wealth; 657 states the comparison outright, in the context of a minister's clean action.

Parimelazhagar reads 152 as telling one to bear a wrong even when one is able to punish it (தாம் ஒறுத்தற்கு இயன்ற காலத்தும்). 301 states that condition outright: only the one who holds back anger where it can take effect (செல்லிடத்துக் காப்பான்) truly holds it back, and where it cannot, it makes no difference. 301 supplies the reason the commentator's condition matters: forbearance toward those one cannot hurt is not yet forbearance.

In 1266 the waiting wife says that when her husband returns she will drink him in (பருகுவன்) so that her pain ends. 811 uses the same verb for friends who look as though they would drink one up (பருகுவார் போலினும்), which Parimelazhagar glosses as from excess of love. The pair shows 'drinking' as the book's figure for consuming affection, sincere in the wife's mouth and only an appearance in the bad friend.

472 promises that nothing fails for one who knows his capacity (ஒல்வது அறிந்து ... செல்லாதது இல்). 483 asks whether anything is hard for one who acts with the means and knows the time (அருவினை என்ப உளவோ கருவியான் காலம் அறிந்து செயின்). The chapters on knowing strength and knowing time each make the same claim for their own subject, which suggests each is meant as one necessary condition, not a sufficient one.

111 asks that fairness be kept alike across the divisions of people, on Parimelazhagar's reading toward enemy, stranger and friend. 528 says a king should not look on all in common (பொதுநோக்கான்) but according to rank or merit (வரிசையா நோக்கின்), and many will then stay by him. Together they show that impartiality in 111 does not mean identical treatment: one may not favour by relationship, but one should distinguish by desert.

210: know ('அறிக') that one who does not turn aside to do evil has no ruin. 116: if one's heart leaves what is fair and does wrong, let one know ('அறிக') 'I shall perish' ('கெடுவல் யான்'). They state the same law from its two sides with the same imperative, 210 for the one who keeps straight and 116 for the one who leaves the middle.
157 asks for not retaliating, and 314 goes further: punish the wrongdoer by doing him good so that he's ashamed. What starts as restraint becomes a strategy.

226 says ending the ruinous hunger of the destitute (அற்றார் அழிபசி தீர்த்தல்) is the place where one who has got wealth stores it. 1007 says the wealth of one who does nothing for the destitute (அற்றார்க்கொன்று ஆற்றாதான்) is like a very beautiful woman growing old alone. 226 says where wealth is kept safe; 1007 shows what happens to wealth kept anywhere else: it passes its time unused.

683 sets two groups side by side: among spear-bearers (வேலாருள்) the envoy speaks of victory, and among treatise-knowers (நூலாருள்) he is master of the treatise. 727 pairs the same two things as a simile: the treatise learned by one who fears the assembly is a bright sword in the hand of a பேடி among enemies. In both the treatise is treated as the speaker's weapon, and 727 adds that it is useless without the nerve to use it.

In 1187 pallor seizes her the moment she shifts a little in his embrace (புடைபெயர்ந்தேன் அவ்வளவில்); in 1265 she says the pallor on her shoulders will leave once she has seen him to her eyes' fill (கண்ணாரக் கண்டபின் நீங்கும்). Together they give pallor's rule in the Book of Love: it comes with the slightest distance and goes only with his presence, which Parimelazhagar underlines by noting that merely hearing of his return will not do.

754 says wealth that comes by right means and without wrong yields virtue and also pleasure (அறன் ஈனும் இன்பமும் ஈனும்). 909 lists the same three goods as missing in men who do a woman's bidding (பெண்ஏவல் செய்வார்கண் இல்). Where 754 treats the three as flowing from one sound source, 909 treats them as shut off by one fault.

852 and its chapter say it is best not to return harm and to lean away from hostility. 879 says to kill the threat while it is young. One counsels letting enmity die by itself and the other warns that it won't, and both claim the outcome is self-preservation.

972 denies that birth settles distinction, and 992, two chapters later, places birth among courtesy's two sources. Parimelazhagar's gloss, which turns birth into conduct, can be seen as a way of closing the gap.

836 says that when a fool who does not know the way of doing (கையறியாப் பேதை) takes up a task, the task fails (பொய்படும்) and he himself ends in fetters. 468 says effort not made by the right means will collapse (பொத்துப் படும்) even with many standing by to protect it. Parimelazhagar glosses both verbs as புரைபடும்; 468 states the rule about method and 836 adds the cost to the doer.

991 and 548 share the word எண்பதம், easy access. In 548 a king who is not accessible (எண்பதத்தான் ஓரா) and does not examine and do justice falls and perishes by himself; in 991 being accessible to all makes courtesy easy to attain. The quality whose absence ruins a ruler is the one whose presence makes a person courteous.

698 forbids belittling a king on the grounds of youth or kinship (இளையர் இனமுறையர் என்றிகழார்). 667 says one must not scorn by outward form, since the great rolling chariot depends on its linchpin (உருவுகண்டு எள்ளாமை வேண்டும்). Both reject judging a person by a surface measure, whether age, family relation or size, and point instead to the function he carries.

381 lists the six things a king must have, among them people and resources (படைகுடி கூழ்...). 554 says a king who bends the sceptre and acts without reflection loses resources and people together (கூழுங் குடியும் ஒருங்கிழக்கும்). The two things injustice costs him in 554 are two of the six that make a king in 381.

751 treats wealth's power to give standing to persons of no account as its distinction. 241 notes the same fact, that material wealth is found even among the base (பொருட்செல்வம் பூரியார் கண்ணும் உள), and uses it to rank wealth below grace, the 'wealth among wealths'. What 751 counts in wealth's favour, 241 counts against it.

290 gives the two outcomes of stealing and not stealing: loss of உயிர்நிலை, and the world of the gods (புத்தேள் உலகு) not failing; 121 gives the two outcomes of restraint and its lack: a place among the immortals (அமரருள்) and thick darkness. Each closes or opens its chapter with the same two-sided reward and penalty attached to a single virtue.

95 says humility and sweet speech are a person's ornament and other things are not (அணியல்ல மற்றுப் பிற). 1014 asks whether shame is not the ornament of the worthy (அணிஅன்றோ நாணுடைமை சான்றோர்க்கு), and 575 names kindly regard as the eye's ornament. The exclusive wording of 95 is therefore the chapter's emphasis: other chapters award the same title to other inner qualities, while agreeing with 95 (as Parimelazhagar reads it) that bodily ornaments are not meant.

726 asks what a sword is to those who are not hard-eyed, and what books are to those who fear a subtle assembly (நுண்ணவை அஞ்சுபவர்க்கு). 534 says the fearful have no fortress (அச்சமுடையார்க்கு அரணில்லை), which Parimelazhagar explains as a fortress being of no use to them. In each, fear cancels an instrument that is sound in itself: sword, books, fort.

301 counts restraint of anger only where the anger could have its way. 153 says the strength of strengths is bearing with fools (வன்மையுள் வன்மை மடவார்ப் பொறை). Both locate the real test of forbearance where one has the upper hand and nothing outside compels it.

64 says the gruel one's children have stirred with their small hands is far sweeter than amrita (அமிழ்தினும் ஆற்ற இனிது). 1121 says the moisture at her white teeth is like milk mixed with honey (பாலொடு தேன்கலந் தற்று). In both, affection makes something bodily and ordinary taste better than the finest food, for a parent in one verse and a lover in the other.

720 says holding forth before those not of one's kind is like nectar spilled in a dirty yard (அங்கணத்துள் உக்க அமிழ்து). 1000 says great wealth in the hands of one without courtesy is like good milk spoiled by the fault of its vessel (கலந்தீமையால் திரிந்தற்று). Both describe a fine liquid ruined by where it lands, and so place the loss in the receiver and not in the thing given.

347 says sorrows hold and do not let go of those who hold attachment and do not let go (பற்றி விடாஅ இடும்பைகள்). 368 says that where craving exists sorrow keeps coming without fail, one after another (தவாஅது மேன்மேல் வரும்). Both describe suffering as continuing for as long as its cause is kept.

473 says many who did not know their own strength pressed on out of zeal and broke midway (ஊக்கத்தின் ஊக்கி இடைக்கண் முரிந்தார்). 498 says the large army's zeal (ஊக்கம்) is destroyed when it enters the small army's ground. In both, drive that outruns a sober measure, of one's strength in one chapter and of the ground in the other, is what gets broken.

585 requires of a spy an unsuspected appearance, not flinching before eyes (கண்ணஞ்சாது) and never letting anything out; 686 requires of an envoy that he not fear the eye (கண் அஞ்சான்), which Parimelazhagar glosses in both verses as the angry look of the other side. The open agent and the covert one are given the same nerve; what differs is that the envoy must speak so it goes home, and the spy must give nothing away.

1131 has the man say that for those worn down by love there is no strength that is a safeguard (ஏமம்) except the palmyra horse (மடலல்லது இல்லை வலி). In 1164 the woman says the sea of love exists but the safe raft to swim it does not (ஏமப் புணைமன்னும் இல்). The one ஏமம் he names is a man's recourse; her verse shows a sufferer for whom even that is missing.

1053 says that even asking has a beauty of its own (இரப்புமோர் ஏஎர் உடைத்து) when done before those who know their duty and do not withhold; 1280 says her asking (இரவு), done with the eyes, has a womanliness of its own (பெண்மை உடைத்து). The word for begging is the same, and both grant it a grace under conditions, though the chapter on begging means alms and 1280 means a lover's plea.

87 calls hospitality a வேள்வி (sacrifice) whose fruit has no fixed measure; Parimelazhagar notes it is one of the five great sacrifices. 259 says not taking a life and eating it is better than pouring oblations in a thousand sacrifices (அவிசொரிந்து ஆயிரம் வேட்டலின்). In both verses the ritual word is used to rank an ethical practice: one is named a sacrifice, the other is set above a thousand of them.

475 says even a cart loaded with peacock feathers breaks its axle if too many are piled on (பீலிபெய் சாகாடும் அச்சிறும்). 667 says not to scorn people for their appearance, since there are those who are like the linchpin of a great rolling chariot (உருள்பெருந்தேர்க்கு அச்சாணி அன்னார்). Both use the axle of a vehicle to say that size misleads: the light thing can break it and the small thing holds it.

134 treats forgetting the Veda (மறப்பினும் ஓத்துக் கொளலாகும்) as a loss that can be made good; 560 lists among the effects of a king who does not protect that those of the six occupations forget their books (அறுதொழிலோர் நூல்மறப்பர்). The same forgetting appears as a private, repairable lapse in 134 and as a sign of public ruin in 560, while 134 keeps conduct as the loss that cannot be repaired.

519 says fortune leaves the one who thinks otherwise of the closeness of a man devoted to the work (கேண்மை வேறாக நினைப்பானை நீங்கும் திரு). 808 praises those with the strength of intimacy not to listen to talk of a friend's lapse (கேளிழுக்கம் கேளாக் கெழுதகைமை). The duty not to reinterpret a close person's conduct appears in kingship and in friendship; Parimelazhagar reads 519 as the king being turned by the words of those who resent the officer, which is the situation 808 names.

706 says the face shows what fills the heart, as crystal shows what is beside it. 959 says the sprout shows what lay in the ground, and the spoken word shows the lineage of the one born in it (நிலத்தில் கிடந்தமை கால்காட்டும்). Both rest on காட்டும்: something visible discloses a hidden source, mood in the face and family in speech.

470 says to think and do what will not be scorned, because the world does not accept what does not accord with oneself (கொள்ளாத கொள்ளாது உலகு). 140 says those who have not learned to conduct themselves in accord with the world lack understanding, however much they have studied (உலகத்தோடு ஒட்ட ஒழுகல்). Both make the world's acceptance a test that sound judgement has to meet, 470 for a ruler's choice of action and 140 for conduct in general.

1056 says that on seeing those free of the affliction of concealing, all the affliction of poverty perishes at once (நிரப்பிடும்பை எல்லாம் ஒருங்கு கெடும்). 1063 says nothing is harder than the hardness of thinking 'we will end the affliction of want by begging' (இன்மை இடும்பை இரந்து தீர்வாம்). They conflict on whether asking can end poverty's distress, if 1056 is read as a general claim; Parimelazhagar removes the conflict by reading 1063 as blaming the choice of begging over effort.

Verse 73 says the tie of the life with the body (ஆருயிர்க்கு என்போடு இயைந்த தொடர்பு) is, they say, a matter of being joined with love (அன்போடு இயைந்த வழக்கு); Parimelazhagar takes embodiment as the result of a course meant for joining with love. In 1122 the lover says the bond between him and the woman is what the bond between body and life is (உடம்பொடு உயிரிடை என்ன). 73 explains the union of body and life by love, and the lover in 1122 measures his love by that union.

1169 calls the long nights of separation crueller than the cruel man himself (கொடியார் கொடுமையின் தாம்கொடிய). 1216 wants the night's state never to end, with waking itself abolished (நனவென ஒன்றில்லை ஆயின்). The difference is sleep: the night is an enemy when she lies awake and a refuge when it brings the dream, and Parimelazhagar accordingly has her call waking a villain (பாவி).

394 says the work of the learned is to meet so that others are glad and to part so that others think of them (உள்ளப் பிரிதல்). 839 says, ironically, that friendship with fools is very sweet because parting from them (பிரிவின்கண்) brings no pain at all. Both judge a person by what the parting leaves behind; the fool is the case where it leaves nothing.

213: neither in the world of the gods nor here ('புத்தேள் உலகத்தும் ஈண்டும்') is it easy to find another good like ஒப்புரவு. 363: there is no excellent wealth here like not wanting, and nothing there equals it either ('ஈண்டில்லை ஆண்டும் அஃதொப்பது இல்'). The same two-world formula crowns benevolence in the householder's section and desirelessness in the renouncer's; taken literally the two superlatives compete, and the pairing shows each section naming its own highest good.

646 pairs speaking well with drawing the benefit from others' words. 724 sets that pair in the assembly of the learned: make what you have learned go home to them (கற்ற செலச்சொல்லி) and take what is more from those who know more (மிக்காருள் மிக்க கொளல்). 724 adds what 646 leaves open, that listening is how the speaker's own knowledge grows.

232 says the world's speech settles as praise on the giver. 387 says that for one able to give and protect with sweet words (இன்சொலால் ஈத்தளிக்க வல்லார்க்கு), this world is as his own word would have it. In the chapter on kingship the same giving that earns the world's words in 232 earns its compliance.

In 1247 she cannot bear desire and shame together and asks her heart to give up one (காமம் விடு ஒன்றோ நாண் விடு). In 1257 the matter is settled in his presence: when he does what she longs for, shame is simply not known to her. The conflict that is unbearable in his absence does not arise once he is there.

133 says a lapse from conduct turns into low birth; 1019 says a lapse in கொள்கை burns one's lineage (குலஞ்சுடும் கொள்கை பிழைப்பின்), and Parimelazhagar glosses கொள்கை there as ஒழுக்கம். Both say family standing is lost through the individual's failure in conduct, one calling the result a low birth and the other a burning.

275 warns that the hidden conduct of those who say 'we are free of attachment' (பற்றற்றேம் என்பார்) brings many harms. 365 says who may rightly be called freed (அற்றவர் என்பார்): only those freed of craving. 275 shows the claim made falsely; 365 gives the inner criterion that the claim has to meet.

445 says a ruler proceeds with his counsellors as his eyes (சூழ்வார் கண்ணாக) and so must choose them with thought. 581 says a ruler should hold spies and the respected treatise as his eyes (மன்னவன் கண்). The king's 'eyes' are advisers in one verse and intelligence plus learning in the other, and in both he sees through something other than himself. This follows Parimelazhagar's reading of 445; Manakkudavar takes its second line differently.
222 calls giving good even with no reward in any world. 231 calls giving, with renown, the sole profit of a life. The same act is valued for itself in one and as a gain in the other.

In 1177 she curses her eyes to weep themselves dry. In 1244 they are eating her, and she wants them gone. The eyes haven't stopped, and her conflict with them has moved from revenge to getting rid of them.

320: all pain falls on those who caused pain (நோயெல்லாம் நோய்செய்தார் மேலவாம்). 1174: the eyes that fixed an inescapable sickness in her (உய்வில்நோய் என்கண் நிறுத்து) have themselves dried up and cannot weep. Parimelazhagar reads 1174 in these terms: having done her harm first, harm came to them of itself.

993 says likeness of limbs is not likeness among people; the likeness that counts is of character (பண்பொத்தல்). 1012 says the bodily needs are shared by all and shame is what sets people apart. Both refuse to take what is physically common as the measure of a human being.

Verse 15 says it is rain that ruins (கெடுப்பதூஉம்) and rain again that stands by the ruined and lifts them (எடுப்பதூஉம்); Parimelazhagar explains that it ruins by not falling. In 1102 the lover says that for other diseases the medicine is something else, but she is herself the medicine for the sickness she causes (தன்நோய்க்குத் தானே மருந்து). The pattern of one thing being both the harm and the only remedy appears for rain and the world and, in a lover's speech, for the beloved.

102 says help done at the time of need (காலத்தினால் செய்த நன்றி), though small, is greater than the earth. 788 makes that timeliness the definition of friendship: it removes distress there and then (ஆங்கே இடுக்கண் களைவது), like the hand going to a slipping garment. 102 values the help by its moment; 788 says what kind of helper acts in that moment.

743 defines the fort as a wall complete in four measures: height, breadth, strength and difficulty of approach (உயர்வு அகலம் திண்மை அருமை). 421 calls understanding the tool that guards against ruin and an inner fort that enemies cannot destroy (செறுவார்க்கும் உள்ளழிக்கலாகா அரண்). 421 moves the fort inside the person: the quality 743 seeks in masonry, that it cannot be broken into, 421 claims for understanding.
320 says that all pain rests on those who caused pain, looking forward. 330 turns this around and reads a past killing from present suffering.

636 asks what subtle scheme can stand before those who have keen intelligence together with the treatises (மதிநுட்பம் நூலோடு உடையார்க்கு). 684 requires of the envoy understanding and well-examined learning (அறிவு ... ஆராய்ந்த கல்வி) held together. Parimelazhagar glosses the first term in each verse as natural intelligence and the second as acquired learning, so both verses ask for the two in combination, for the minister and for the envoy.

Parimelazhagar reads 'ஒத்தது' in 214 as the way of the world (உலகநடை): one who knows and follows it lives. 140 says those who have not learned to conduct themselves in accord with the world ('உலகத்தோடு ஒட்ட ஒழுகல்') lack understanding however much they have studied. On that reading both make accord with the world the test of a person, of being alive in 214 and of having understanding in 140; Manakkudavar instead takes ஒத்தது as ஒப்புரவு itself.

376 says what is not one's portion will not stay however it is guarded, and what is one's own will not go even if thrown out (பரியினும் ஆகாவாம் பாலல்ல ... சொரியினும் போகா தம). 332 says wealth comes and goes like a crowd at a show. 376 puts a cause behind 332's picture: coming and going follow one's allotted portion; Parimelazhagar reads 332 the same way, the crowd coming for the dance and leaving when it ends.

34 locates virtue in the mind being without stain; 288 says virtue stands in the heart of those who know அளவு just as concealment stands in the heart of those who know stealing (நெஞ்சத்து அறம் ... நெஞ்சில் கரவு). 288 adds to 34 that the heart is occupied either way: what one practises, measure or theft, decides whether virtue or deceit takes up residence there.

725 says to learn by the proper path and with measure (ஆற்றின் அளவறிந்து கற்க) in order to reply in the assembly without fear; Parimelazhagar takes அளவு as the science of logic. 645 says to speak a word only after knowing no other word can defeat it (வெல்லுஞ்சொல் இன்மை அறிந்து). 725 names the training that makes 645's test possible.

656 forbids the blameworthy deed even when the need is a mother's hunger. 961 says to give up things that would diminish one (குன்ற வருப விடல்) even if they are indispensable (இன்றி அமையாச் சிறப்பின ஆயினும்). Both deny that necessity licenses a degrading act; 961 states the principle abstractly under honour, 656 gives it a concrete and painful instance.

156 grants the retaliator one day's pleasure and gives the forbearing renown to the end. 856 says that the life of one who says it is sweet (இனிது) to prevail in hostility is close to failure and ruin (தவலும் கெடலும் நணித்து). Both admit that getting the better of an opponent tastes sweet and both say the sweetness is brief; the verse in the Book of Wealth names ruin where the verse in the Book of Virtue names only the loss of lasting fame.

483 asks whether anything is hard for one who acts with the right means and knowing the time (கருவியான் காலம் அறிந்து செயின்). 375 says that in making wealth all that is good turns bad and bad turns good (நல்லவை எல்லாஅந் தீயவாம்); Parimelazhagar takes the good and bad things to be time, place, means and action, reversed by fate. On that reading the favourable conditions 483 relies on do not secure the result, and the two conflict. Kalaignar reads 375 differently, as good and bad deeds turning out contrary to intent.

779 asks who could fault for failure (பிழைத்தது ஒறுக்கிற்பவர்) those who die so as not to break what they vowed (இழைத்தது இகவாமை); Parimelazhagar explains that dying before the vow is accomplished still counts as keeping it. 772 says the spear that missed (பிழைத்த வேல்) the elephant is better to hold than the arrow that hit a hare. Both verses turn on பிழை, a miss, and deny that it is a disgrace when the attempt was great.

1052 says even asking is pleasure to a person (இன்பம் ஒருவற்கு இரத்தல்) when the thing comes without pain. 1066 says nothing is more degrading to the tongue than asking, even asking water for a cow (நாவிற்கு இரவின் இளிவந்தது இல்). They conflict if 1052 is read as commending asking under good conditions; 1052 speaks of pleasure and 1066 of disgrace, so the conflict depends on taking a disgraceful act as unable to be a pleasant one.

998 requires courtesy even toward those who do unfriendly, unkind things. 852 says that even if someone does what one cannot bear, intending division (பகல் கருதிப் பற்றா செயினும்), it is best not to do harm in return out of hostility. 852 gives the minimum, no retaliation, and 998 asks for more, that courtesy itself not lapse.

883 says to fear the enemy within and guard oneself (உட்பகை அஞ்சித் தற்காக்க), or it will destroy one. 305 says that if you would guard yourself, guard against anger (தன்னைத்தான் காக்கின் சினங்காக்க); unguarded, anger kills oneself. The same formula of self-guarding against something lodged inside is applied in one verse to people within the household or court and in the other to a passion within the mind.

775 treats a single blink (இமைப்பின்) before a flung spear as equal to flight. In 1129 the woman says she will not blink because her lover, who lives in her eyes, would be hidden (இமைப்பின் கரப்பாக்கு அறிவல்). Both make the refusal to blink a measure of devotion, to valour in one and, in the speaker's conceit, to the beloved in the other.

151 says that bearing with those who scorn one, as the earth holds up those who dig into it (அகழ்வாரைத் தாங்கும் நிலம்போல), is the highest thing. 488 uses a verb of carrying for the same act, bearing with those who would harm one (சுமக்க), and makes it a means: one bears them until their end comes and their head goes down. The two conflict if both are read as answers to how one should treat those who wrong one, since forbearance is the goal in 151 and a way to the enemy's fall in 488. 151 is addressed to the householder and 488 to a king, which is the other way to read them.

599 says an elephant, though huge and sharp-tusked, fears when a tiger attacks; 763 says a sea of roaring rats perishes when the cobra merely breathes. Both animal pairs teach that bulk or numbers do not decide a contest against an opponent with spirit, 599 of a person's drive and 763 of an army.

703 urges the king to pay any price for those who read signs. 445 says that since counsellors serve as the ruler's eyes (சூழ்வார் கண்ணாக ஒழுகலான்), he must choose them with care. 445 gives the reason behind 703: the king sees through his advisers, so an adviser who can read what is unsaid is worth what Parimelazhagar lists as wealth, land, elephants and horses.

In 1315 a promise limited to this birth (இம்மை) makes her weep. 107 says the good remember through all seven births (எழுமை எழுபிறப்பும் உள்ளுவர்) the friendship of those who removed their distress. Her complaint measures his promise against the span the book itself uses for lasting bonds.

1185 points there to the lover going and here to the pallor spreading (உவக்காண் ... இவக்காண்); Parimelazhagar takes it as an earlier occasion when he had gone only a short way. 1278 says he left only yesterday and her body has been pale seven days (நெருநற்றுச் சென்றார் ... எழுநாளேம் மேனி பசந்து). One verse measures the pallor's speed in space and the other in time.

908 describes men who live as the woman wishes, பெட்டாங்கு ஒழுகுபவர்; 141 speaks of the folly of living in desire for another man's woman, பெட்டொழுகும் பேதைமை. The same pairing of பெட்டு (desire, wish) with ஒழுகு (to conduct oneself) describes a life steered by desire in both, in 141 the man's own desire for a forbidden woman and in 908 the wishes of his own wife.

248 says those without அருள் are finished and can't become anything. 250, which Parimelazhagar calls the means of arousing அருள், assumes that the person going against the weak can still acquire it. The verdict is absolute, and the very next step offers a way out.

700 says intimacy that does what is improper brings ruin (பண்பல்ல செய்யும் கெழுதகைமை கேடு தரும்). 805 says that when friends do something hurtful one should understand it as folly or as great intimacy (பேதைமை ஒன்றோ பெருங்கிழமை என்றுணர்க நோதக்க நட்டார் செயின்). The conflict holds on Manakkudavar's gloss of 700, which speaks of the nature of friendship in general; on Parimelazhagar's, 700 concerns a king and the two verses address different relationships.

1186 is the woman's account: pallor watches for a gap in her husband's embrace (முயக்கற்றம் பார்க்கும்) as darkness watches for a lamp to fail. 1238 is the man's memory of the same thing: he loosened the arms that held her and her forehead turned pale (முயங்கிய கைகளை ஊக்கப் பசந்தது). The two speakers confirm each other from either side of the embrace.

Verse 66 says only those who have not heard their own children's prattle call the flute (குழல்) and the lute sweet. In 1228 the woman left alone says the herdsman's flute (ஆயன் குழல்) is now a messenger of the burning evening and a weapon that kills; Parimelazhagar notes that it had been sweet to her before. In both the flute stands for accepted sweetness, and in both that sweetness is made to depend on the hearer's situation.

Verse 69 has the mother's joy grow when she hears others call her son worthy (சான்றோன் எனக் கேட்ட தாய்). Verse 1047 says one in poverty unconnected with virtue (அறஞ்சாரா நல்குரவு) is looked on as a stranger even by the mother who bore him (ஈன்ற தாயானும் பிறன்போல நோக்கப்படும்). In both the mother's regard follows the son's standing, rising with his name in 69 and withdrawn in 1047.

In 1310 the man, on Parimelazhagar's reading, says that his heart's intent to join with one who leaves him to wither in the sulk (ஊடல் உணங்க விடுவாரோடு) is just craving (அவா). In 1292 the woman scolds her heart for going to him even after seeing that he is not close to her (உறாஅதவர்க் கண்ட கண்ணும்). Each blames the heart for running to someone who has shown no care.
After a chapter that places the unlearned among beasts, 414 opens a door: though you haven't studied, listen. The next chapter quietly withdraws the finality of this one.

224 gives the giver's side: being asked is painful (இன்னாது இரக்கப்படுதல்) until one sees the asker's glad face (இன்முகம்). 1057 gives the asker's side: on seeing those who give without scorn or contempt, the heart rejoices deep within (உள்ளுள் உவப்பது உடைத்து). The two describe one moment from both ends, and the asker's gladness in 1057 is what ends the giver's discomfort in 224.

1015 praises one who feels shame even for others' disgrace; 1018 describes one who does not feel shame at what makes others ashamed (பிறர் நாணத்தக்கது தான் நாணான்). The two set out the ends of a scale inside the chapter: shame that extends beyond oneself, and shame that fails even for one's own act.

933 says that if one keeps calling the rolling dice-throw (உருளாயம்), wealth and its income (பொருளாயம்) go and fall outside (புறமே படும்); Parimelazhagar takes 'outside' as into enemies' hands. 1009 says the wealth a miser gathered without love, self-regard or virtue is taken by others (கொள்வார் பிறர்). The gambler and the hoarder, by opposite habits, both end with their wealth in strangers' hands.

415 presents the words of people of conduct as the staff that keeps a person upright on slippery ground. 447 asks who can ruin a ruler who keeps as his own those who will rebuke him (இடிக்குந் துணையார்). Both verses locate safety in another person's speech; 447 applies it to a king and makes the helpful words explicitly unwelcome ones.

1255 states in general terms that the lovesick do not know the dignity of not going after one who is hostile. 1256 applies it to herself with irony: how gracious (அளித்தரோ) is this grief, which wants her to go after the one who is hostile (செற்றவர் பின் சேறல் வேண்டி). The pair moves from a maxim about lovers to her own case, and Parimelazhagar reads அளித்து as mockery.

899 says that if those of exalted resolve flare up (ஏந்திய கொள்கையார் சீறின்), even the king breaks midway and loses his rule. Parimelazhagar reads them as people of high vows, and Pope likewise. This is the power of 264, ஒன்னார்த் தெறல் through austerity, seen from the side of the king who must not provoke it.

612: guard against the work failing in the doing, because the world has left those who left the work's need undone (வினைக்குறை தீர்ந்தாரின் தீர்ந்தன்று உலகு), on Parimelazhagar's reading; Manakkudavar takes the second line the other way, that the world does not leave those who finish. 670: whatever other firmness they have, the world does not want those who do not want firmness in action (வேண்டாரை வேண்டாது உலகு). Both make the world's regard answer in kind to how a person treats the task.

Two kinds of invincibility, each put as 'don't attempt it'. 771's warrior warns that those who stood before his lord now stand as stones. 855's person is unbeatable because he leans away. One's strength is in striking and the other's in declining.

874 praises the one who takes enmity as friendship (பகைநட்பாக் கொண்டொழுகும்) without saying how it is done. 985 names a means: bowing (பணிதல்) is the weapon by which the worthy change their opponents (மாற்றாரை மாற்றும் படை). Parimelazhagar glosses this as ending the opponents' enmity, so 985 reads as the method behind 874.

1131 calls the palmyra horse the only safeguard for those who suffer in love. 1137 praises womanhood that suffers a sea of desire (கடலன்ன காமம் உழந்தும்) and still does not mount it (மடலேறா). The same verb உழந்து marks the same suffering, so 1137 limits 1131: the remedy is one a woman forgoes, and forgoing it is counted as worth.

56 defines the woman as one who guards herself (தற்காத்து), cares for her husband and guards the good name (சொற்காத்து) without flagging. 57 asks what guarding by confinement (சிறைகாக்கும் காப்பு) can do, and says the guard women keep by their own நிறை is the chief one. 57 explains why 56 makes her the subject of the verb 'guard': the guarding that counts cannot be done by anyone else.

793 includes a person's இனன், his circle, among the things to learn before befriending him (Parimelazhagar takes it as kin). 453 says that the word 'he is such a one' comes from a person's company (இனத்தானாம் இன்னான் எனப்படுஞ் சொல்). 453 gives the reason the circle belongs on 793's list: it is where a person's character is read from.
Fortune as a goddess who leaves or stays: 617 places her at the feet of the unidle man, and 920 says the ones she has dropped can be known by their company.

118 praises being level like the scale-beam and not leaning to one side (ஒருபால் கோடாமை) as the ornament of the worthy. 1196 applies the same test to love: borne on one end (ஒருதலையான்) it hurts, and on both it is sweet. Evenness between two sides is a mark of justice in the Book of Virtue and a condition of happiness here.

45 says that when household life has love and virtue (அன்பும் அறனும்), these are its character and its fruit (பண்பும் பயனும்); Parimelazhagar takes the love as that owed to one's wife. 901 says those who fix their desire on the wife (மனைவிழைவார்) miss the excellent fruit (மாண்பயன்). The pair marks a line between love within the household, which is its fruit, and விழைவு that lets the wife rule the man, which loses it; Parimelazhagar reads 901 as men who follow the wife's lead for pleasure's sake.

79 asks what all the outer limbs can do for those who lack love, the inner limb (புறத்துறுப் பெல்லாம் எவன்செய்யும் ... அன்பிலவர்க்கு). 573 asks the same kind of question of the eye that lacks kindly regard. In both a visible organ is counted useless without the inner quality it should serve.

In 1167 she herself swims the fierce flood of love and sees no shore; in 1170 it is her eyes that swim in flood water (வெள்ளநீர் நீந்தல), which is her tears. The chapter's water figure for love ends as literal water in the eyes.

In 1211 the dream arrives as the carrier of his message (காதலர் தூதொடு வந்த கனவு). In 1212 she wants to use the dream in the other direction: if her eyes would sleep, she would herself declare to him that she survives (உயலுண்மை சாற்றுவேன்). Parimelazhagar says this is spoken when she was thinking of sending a messenger, and that she would tell him in full what she would hold back from one.

516: examine the doer, the deed and the fit with the time, then act (காலத்தோடு எய்த உணர்ந்து செயல்). 949: the trained physician acts after considering the measure of the patient, the measure of the illness and the time (உற்றான் அளவும் பிணியளவும் காலமும் ... கருதிச் செயல்). Both end in செயல் after a three-part assessment of person, matter and time, the same procedure in statecraft and in medicine.

185 reads a man's inner lack of virtue from his backbiting. 959 says that as the sprout shows what lies in the soil, the words of the mouth show the family one is born in (காட்டும் குலத்தில் பிறந்தார் வாய்ச்சொல்). Both treat speech as the visible sign of something hidden, the heart in one case and lineage in the other.

983 calls its five qualities the pillar planted to bear worth (சால்பு ஊன்றிய தூண்). 615 calls the man who wants the work and not pleasure a pillar that wipes away his kin's troubles and props them (துடைத்து ஊன்றும் தூண்). The same figure, with the same verb ஊன்று, is used once for qualities holding up a character and once for a person holding up a family.

222 says taking is bad even if it is called a good path (நல்லாறு எனினும் கொளல் தீது). 1066 says that even if one asks for water for a cow (ஆவிற்கு நீரென்று இரப்பினும்), nothing is more degrading to the tongue than asking; Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar both take the cow as a case of asking for the sake of virtue. Both verses deny that a good purpose removes what is wrong with asking or receiving.

The second half of 659 says what comes from good ways (நற்பாலவை) yields later even if it is lost (இழப்பினும் பிற்பயக்கும்). 112 says the wealth of a person of rectitude (செப்பம் உடையவன் ஆக்கம்) does not decay and is a security for those who come after (எச்சத்திற்கு ஏமாப்பு). Both give rightly got wealth a benefit that outlasts the moment, 659 for the person later and 112 for descendants.

967 says it is better to be called ruined where one stands than to live by following those who do not accept one (ஒட்டார்பின் சென்றொருவன் வாழ்தலின்). In 1298 the heart, described as loving life (உயிர்க்காதல் நெஞ்சு), counts scorning him as the disgrace and goes on dwelling on him. The chapter on honour ranks honour above life; the heart in 1298 keeps the vocabulary of disgrace (இளிவு) but, out of attachment to life, applies it so as to stay with the one who slighted her. This is the heart's reasoning as she reports it, not a rival doctrine.

952 says the well-born do not slip in three things: conduct, truthfulness and shame (ஒழுக்கமும் வாய்மையும் நாணும்). 1019 says what happens when two of those three fail: a lapse in conduct burns the family, and shamelessness that stays burns every good. The chapter on good family gives the mark and 1019 gives the cost of losing it.

955 says an ancient family (பழங்குடி) does not part from its character when its means shrink. 1043 says poverty destroys together one's ancient descent and one's speech (தொல்வரவும் தோலும் கெடுக்கும்). They conflict if 1043 is read as plain poverty undoing lineage; the conflict eases on Parimelazhagar's reading, which stresses that 1043 calls poverty a craving (நசை), so it is the wanting, not the lack, that ruins.

290 says that for those who steal the உயிர்நிலை fails, while for those who do not steal the world of the gods does not fail; 255 says உயிர்நிலை rests in not eating flesh, and that hell will not open its mouth for one who eats it. Both verses hang உயிர்நிலை, the standing of life in the body on Parimelazhagar's gloss, on one abstention and pair it with a fate after death; Manakkudavar reads the word in 290 as release itself.

Both end with தான்முந்துறும், 'it gets there first'. In 380, fate gets ahead of any plan. In 707, the face gets ahead of any words. 1023 uses it again of a deity. The repeated phrase pictures a force that outruns human intention.

166 says the kin of one who envies a gift perish without anything to wear or eat (உடுப்பதூஉம் உண்பதூஉம் இன்றி). 939 begins its list of what gaming keeps away with the same pair, clothing and food (உடை ... ஊண்). Envy and gambling are both measured by the loss of the plainest necessities.

758 says doing a task with something in one's own hand (தன்கைத்தொன்று உண்டாக) is like watching an elephant fight from a hilltop, which Parimelazhagar explains as acting without fear or strain. 449 says those without capital have no profit (முதலிலார்க்கு ஊதியம் இல்லை). Both make resources in hand the precondition of an undertaking; 758 adds the safety they give.

735 requires a land to be without the inner enemy that lays waste (பாழ்செய்யும் உட்பகை). 889 says inner enmity, though as small as a split sesame seed (எட்பகவு), holds ruin within it (உள்ளதாங் கேடு). 889 explains why 735 demands its complete absence and not just its reduction.

In 788 the hand goes at once to the slipping garment (உடுக்கை). In 1023, for one who says he will raise his family, தெய்வம் tucks up its garment (மடிதற்று) and goes ahead of him. Both use a gesture with one's clothing for help that comes unasked and promptly, from a friend in one and from the divine in the other.

750 says a fort, whatever its excellences, is as nothing with those who lack excellence in action (வினைமாட்சி இல்லார்கண் இல்லது அரண்). 534 says the fearful have no fort and the heedless have no good (நன்கு). Both hold that an outward advantage counts for nothing without the inner quality needed to use it, and both use the fort to say so.

24 says one who guards the five with the goad called firmness (உரனென்னும் தோட்டியான் ஓரைந்தும் காப்பான்) is a seed for the highest ground; the goad makes the senses elephants, as Parimelazhagar spells out. 422 gives understanding a similar job, not letting one go where one has gone (சென்ற இடத்தால் செலவிடா), which Parimelazhagar explains with a rider directing a horse. 422 goes a step past 24's holding back: it also sorts good from evil and steers toward the good.

126, in the householder's chapter on restraint, speaks of drawing in the five like a tortoise (ஆமைபோல் ஐந்தடக்கல்), which protects through seven births. 343 uses a harder verb for the renouncer: the field of the five must be killed or crushed (அடல்வேண்டும் ஐந்தன் புலத்தை), and every wanted thing dropped at once. Read together they show two degrees of the same discipline, withdrawal that can be reversed and destruction that cannot.

440: if a ruler can enjoy what he loves without the love being known (காதல் அறியாமை உய்க்கிற்பின்), his enemies' designs come to nothing. 866, from the enemy's side, says one of blinding anger and excessive desire (கழிபெருங் காமத்தான்) is an opponent whose enmity is worth having. Together they show the reasoning: a visible passion is an opening for an enemy, which Parimelazhagar states in his note on 440.

987 says worth is useless unless it does good even to those who did harm. 998, in the next chapter, says failing in courtesy even toward those who act without friendship or kindness (நயமில செய்வார்க்கும்) is lowness (கடை). Both verses use the particle 'even to' (-க்கும்) to extend the virtue to hostile people, one for சால்பு and one for பண்பு.

510 says that doubting a person one has examined and trusted (தெளிந்தான்கண் ஐயுறவும்) brings unending trouble; 584 has spies examine everyone (அனைவரையும் ஆராய்வது), including the king's own officers. The conflict holds if standing surveillance of appointed officers counts as the ஐயுறவு that 510 forbids; if spying is read as routine inquiry and not suspicion of a particular person, the two can stand together.

Parimelazhagar reads 236 as: if born human, be born with the qualities that lead to renown. 972 says birth is alike for all living beings (பிறப்பொக்கும் எல்லா உயிர்க்கும்) and distinction differs through the difference in what they do. On the birth reading, 972 limits 236: no one is born with renown, so the 'appearing with renown' has to be made by deeds.

47 says the one who lives household life according to its nature is first among all who strive (முயல்வாருள் எல்லாம் தலை). 266 says those who do தவம் are doing their own work and the rest (மற்றல்லார்), caught in desire, do what is futile (அவஞ்செய்வார்). On Parimelazhagar's reading of 47, where the strivers are those working to leave the senses, the householder is ranked above ascetics, while 266 counts everyone but the ascetic as wasting effort. Manakkudavar reads முயல்வார் as those who strive for wealth, and on that reading the two do not collide.
97 requires speech to be useful and gentle, and 200 says to speak only what is useful. The later chapter keeps the usefulness test and drops the sweetness, which shows the two tests are independent.

466 says both doing the unfit and leaving the fit undone bring ruin. 672 gives the same two-sided rule for timing: delay what should be done slowly, and do not delay what must be done without delay (தூங்குக தூங்கிச் செயற்பால தூங்கற்க தூங்காது செய்யும் வினை). 672 carries 466's point, that holding back is no safer than acting, into the question of when to act.

348 sets those who have fully renounced above everyone else. 276 says none are harder-hearted than those who have not renounced in the heart (நெஞ்சின் துறவார்) and live by deceiving as though they had (துறந்தார்போல் வஞ்சித்து). The praise in 348 therefore applies to renunciation of the heart; the outward form without it is placed among the worst.

315 asks what understanding has achieved if one does not guard another's pain as one's own (பிறிதின்நோய் தந்நோய்போல்). 251 sets the same pair, self and other (தன் ஊன் / பிறிது ஊன்), the wrong way round: the other's flesh serves one's own. 315 gives the general test that 251's rhetorical question about அருள் applies to eating.

Verse 14 says ploughing stops when the rain's bounty declines. Verse 1036 says that if the ploughmen's hands fold (உழவினார் கைம்மடங்கின்), even those who say they have given up desire cannot hold their state. Verse 14 names one cause that would fold those hands, so the failure of rain reaches as far as the renouncer.

775 asks whether it is not a rout (ஒட்டு in this edition, which Parimelazhagar glosses as turning the back) for the fierce if the eye glaring at the enemy closes in a blink when a spear is thrown. 686 requires the envoy to be one who does not fear the eye (கண் அஞ்சான்), which Parimelazhagar explains as the hostile king's angry stare; 585 says the same of the spy. Holding one's gaze under threat is a test in the court as on the field.

1167 says she swims the flood of desire and sees no shore, and even at midnight only she is awake (யாமத்தும் யானே உளேன்). 1252 says desire has no pity (கண் இன்று), for it sets her heart to work even at midnight (யாமத்தும் ஆளும் தொழில்). Both mark midnight, when Parimelazhagar notes all others rest, as the hour that shows desire does not release her.

347 uses பற்று for attachment in general and says its holders are held by griefs. 438, on a ruler's faults, names miserliness as 'the clinging heart' (பற்றுள்ளம் என்னும் இவறன்மை) and says it is not to be counted with any other fault. The same word and the same refusal to let go appear in the domain of wealth, where Parimelazhagar glosses it as not releasing goods when they ought to be released.

966 says standing in the train of those who scorn you brings neither renown nor the gods' land. 1053 says that even asking has a certain beauty (ஏஎர் உடைத்து) when one stands before those of unconcealing heart who know what is due (கரப்பிலா நெஞ்சின் கடனறிவார் முன்நின்று). What 966 rejects is therefore not dependence as such but dependence on people who despise the one who comes to them.

574 says eyes without kindly regard in due measure (அளவினால் கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லாத கண்) do nothing but seem to be in the face; Parimelazhagar takes அளவினால் as excluding excessive indulgence. 578 says what the measure is: kindly regard shown without ruining the task (கருமம் சிதையாமல் கண்ணோட வல்லார்). The one word of limit in 574 becomes the whole subject of 578.

620 says those who toil on without flagging will see the back even of fate (ஊழையும் உப்பக்கம் காண்பர்); 269 says even getting past Death (கூற்றம் குதித்தலும்) is within reach of those with the power of austerity. Each uses the particle உம், 'even', to name the one thing thought unbeatable and then says sustained effort beats it: labour in the book of statecraft, austerity in the book of virtue. (The edition's text of 269 ends with a stray letter, தலைப்பட்டவர்க்குல்.)

928 tells the drinker to stop saying he has never been drunk, because what he hid in his heart shows all the more at that moment (ஒளித்ததூஉம் ஆங்கே மிகும்). In 1161 a woman says she would hide her pain, but like spring water for those who draw it, it increases (ஊற்றுநீர் போல மிகும்). Both end on மிகும்: the attempt to conceal an inner state is answered by its overflowing, in drink and in love.

306 says anger, the fire that kills what it adjoins (சேர்ந்தாரைக் கொல்லி), burns even the safe raft of one's own people (இனமென்னும் ஏமப் புணை). 526 says no one on earth has more people around him than one who gives greatly and does not cherish anger (பேணான் வெகுளி). The two give the loss and the gain of the same fact: kin stay with the one who is free of anger.

185 says that a man's heart does not really speak virtue is seen from the meanness of his backbiting (புறஞ்சொல்லும் புன்மையாற் காணப்படும்). 193 says that expansive talk of useless things itself declares the speaker to be without நயன் (நயனிலன் என்பது சொல்லும்). In both a kind of speech is treated as evidence about the speaker, whatever he professes.

638 says that even if the king destroys good counsel and knows nothing himself, the one at his side owes it to him to say what is good for him (உறுதி ... கூறல் கடன்). 690 says the envoy secures the lord's good (உறுதி) even at the cost of his own life. Both use உறுதி for the king's real interest and hold the servant to it under threat, from his own king in 638 and from a foreign one in 690.

228 says only that the hoarder keeps his goods and loses them. 1009 says how: bright wealth gathered by giving up love, denying oneself and ignoring virtue is taken by others (கொள்வார் பிறர்). The later verse fills in the 'losing' of 228.

1263 describes the man as having left with his own heart or resolve for companion (உள்ளம் துணையாகச் சென்றார்). 1299 asks who can be a companion in grief when one's own heart is no companion (நெஞ்சந் துணையல் வழி). The heart as துணை is what he had on setting out and, on Parimelazhagar's assignment of 1299 to the man, what he lacks when she will not be reconciled; Manakkudavar gives 1299 to the woman.
228 asks whether hoarders know the joy they forfeit. 1001 gives the outcome: he dies without eating what he amassed, and nothing remains to be done with it.

19 says that if the sky does not give, giving and austerity will not remain in the wide world (தானம் தவம்இரண்டும் தங்கா). 560 says that if the guardian does not guard, cows' yield declines and the six-occupation men forget their book. In both, religious and learned life depends on a provider, the rain in 19 and the king in 560, and fails when the provider fails.

765 defines an army as the force that can stand together even if Death comes raging at it (கூற்றுடன்று மேல்வரினும்). In 1083 the man says he now knows what is called Death (கூற்று): it has womanly grace and large warring eyes (பேரமர்க் கட்டு). Both set கூற்று in a battle; the Book of Wealth imagines standing against it, and the lover says he has met it in her eyes.

229 names something worse than begging; 1066 says that nothing disgraces the tongue more than begging, even for a cow's water. Their standards differ: the misery of a life against the shame of an act.

Both verses rank their subject first by the author's own witness in the first person plural: 61 has யாமறிவது இல்லை ('we know of none') for knowing children, 300 has யாமெய்யாக் கண்டவற்றுள் இல்லை ('among what we have seen as true there is none') for truthfulness. The pairing shows the same rare device, the poet's 'we', used to vouch for a household good and for a virtue of speech.

103 praises help from those who do not weigh the return (பயன்தூக்கார்), calling its good greater than the sea. 813 uses the same weighing verb for the opposite case: friends who weigh what they will get (உறுவது சீர்தூக்கும் நட்பு) are put level with thieves. The pair shows the book judging help and friendship by one test, whether the giver was calculating.

1234 describes separation's effect: the shoulders lose their fullness and old beauty and the bangles slip (பைந்தொடி சோரும்… தோள்); in 1279 she looks at bangles and soft shoulders (தொடிநோக்கி மென்தோளும் நோக்கி) and then at her feet. Read with 1234, her first two glances name what will happen if she is left, and the third, as Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar take it, names her alternative of walking with him.

430 defines having by understanding: the wise have all, and the unwise have nothing whatever they own. 591 uses the same turn for energy of mind: it is what makes someone 'one who has' (உடையர் எனப்படுவது ஊக்கம்), and those without it do not really have what they have (உடையது உடையரோ). The book redefines possession in the same words for two different inner qualities.

Parimelazhagar takes விளையுள் in 731 to stand for the cultivators, since the verse lists it beside two kinds of people (தக்கார், செல்வர்). 1032 calls those who plough the linchpin (ஆணி) of the world because they carry all who go off to other work. 1032 gives the reason the cultivators come first in 731's list.

1286 says that when she sees him she sees no faults, and when she does not see him she sees nothing but faults (காணுங்கால் காணேன் தவறாய காணாக்கால் காணேன் தவறல்லவை). 1246 calls the heart's anger in his absence false because it never survives the sight of him (காதலர்க் கண்டால் புலந்துணராய்). 1286 states the pattern plainly; 1246 uses it to discredit the anger felt while apart.

In 1142 the man says the town, not knowing how hard the flower-eyed woman is to reach (அருமை அறியாது), has given him gossip (அலரெமக்கு ஈந்தது). In 1150 the speaker says the town is raising the very talk 'we want' (யாம்வேண்டும் கெளவை எடுக்கும் இவ்வூர்). Both treat the town's gossip as an unintended service; Parimelazhagar reads ஈந்தது as help given, and reads 1150 as the friend counting on it.

172 says those ashamed of unfairness (நடுவன்மை நாணுபவர்) will not do blameworthy things out of desire for the gain to be had (படுபயன் வெஃகி). 113 gives the instruction that goes with it: gain that comes from leaving fairness (நடுவிகந்தாம் ஆக்கம்) is to be dropped that very day, even if it brings only good. 172 describes the character and 113 the rule it follows.

In 1237 she asks her heart whether it will win any glory by telling the cruel one, as Pope renders it, of the uproar over her wasting shoulders (பாடு பெறுதியோ நெஞ்சே ... உரைத்து). In 1200 she tells the heart that reporting its pain to one who is not close is harder than filling the sea. Both are addresses to the heart that reject sending him word of her suffering.

1302 says sulking is like salt in the right amount and is spoiled only by being prolonged a little (உப்பமைந் தற்றால் புலவி). 1282 says that when love is full to a palmyra's measure, not even a millet of sulking is wanted (தினைத்துணையும் ஊடாமை வேண்டும்). Read together, 1282 states a condition, காமம் நிறைய வரின், under which the measured sulk that 1302 recommends falls to nothing; Parimelazhagar takes 1282 as the woman voicing her own haste in the form of general advice.

947 says that if one eats greatly without discerning the measure of the fire within (தீயளவு), disease arises without measure (நோயளவின்றிப் படும்). 475 says even a cart loaded with peacock feathers breaks its axle if they are piled too high (சால மிகுத்துப் பெயின்). In both a fixed capacity, the digestive fire or the axle, is what excess breaks, whatever the quality of the load.

753 says wealth cuts away darkness (இருளறுக்கும்), which Parimelazhagar takes to be enmity. 759 says no steel is sharper than wealth for cutting the pride of foes (செறுநர் செருக்கறுக்கும்). Both use the verb அறு for what wealth does, once as a lamp and once as a blade; on Parimelazhagar's reading of 753 they make the same claim.

For Parimelazhagar, the schools conflict on everything in 242 and yet converge on அருள். On 353, he says that their conflict leaves doubt only experience can settle. Together they give his view of religious pluralism: agreement in ethics, and no resolution by argument in metaphysics.

1257 says she knows nothing of shame when the one she cherishes does, in desire, what she wants (பேணியார் பெட்ப செயின்). 1283 reuses the two words with the sense turned round: even if he does only what he himself wants, without cherishing her (பேணாது பெட்பவே செய்யினும்), her eyes will not rest without seeing him. The second verse removes the condition of the first: her yielding does not depend on his doing what pleases her.

759 says to make wealth, since no steel is sharper for cutting the pride of foes (செறுநர் செருக்கறுக்கும்). 878 says the pride found in enemies dies (மாயும் பகைவர்கண் பட்ட செருக்கு) when one knows the way, builds oneself up and guards oneself (தற்செய்து தற்காப்ப). Both aim at the enemy's செருக்கு; Parimelazhagar glosses 878's தற்செய்து as enlarging oneself, and 759 names wealth as the means.

460 says there is no support greater than good company and nothing that afflicts more than bad company (தீயினத்தின் அல்லற் படுப்பதூஉம் இல்). 450 says letting go the tie with the good is ten times worse than taking on the enmity of many (பல்லார் பகை கொளலிற் பத்தடுத்த தீமைத்து). 460 names keeping bad company as the worst harm and 450 names losing good company; both rank these above open enemies, and Parimelazhagar glosses 460's second half as enmity.

1047 says the person in poverty unconnected with virtue (அறஞ்சாரா நல்குரவு) is looked on as a stranger even by his own mother. 117 says the world does not count as ruin the low state of one who stays in virtue (நன்றிக்கண் தங்கியான் தாழ்வு). The qualifier அறஞ்சாரா in 1047 marks the boundary 117 draws: estrangement follows poverty without virtue, while poverty with virtue is not held against a person.

Verse 62 says evils will not touch a person in all seven births (எழுபிறப்பும் தீயவை தீண்டா) if they get children of character who bring no blame. Verse 398 says the learning gained in one birth is a protection in seven (எழுமையும் ஏமாப்புடைத்து). Both name a good of this life whose protection outlasts it by seven births: in one case one's children, in the other one's own learning.

618 separates what is no disgrace (having no luck) from what is (not working). 988 says want is no disgrace to a person who has the firmness called worth (இன்மை ஒருவற்கு இளிவன்று). Both refuse to count an outward lack as shame and move the test to something in the person, effort in one and character in the other.

1081 only asks whether she is an அணங்கு. In 1082, once she returns his look (நோக்கெதிர் நோக்குதல்), he says it is like an attacking அணங்கு (தாக்கணங்கு) who has also brought an army. The doubt of the first verse becomes a felt assault in the second, and Parimelazhagar reads 1082 as spoken after he has settled that she is human.

940: as a gambler loves the game more with each loss (இழத்தொறூஉம்), life loves itself more with each suffering (உழத்தொறூஉம்). 1110: each closeness shows love to be more than he knew, as each learning shows ignorance. Both describe an attachment that grows through its own repetition; the gambling chapter gives it as a warning and the lover as a delight.

427 separates the wise from the unwise by whether they know what will be (ஆவது). 461 tells one to act after weighing what will be lost, what will come of it (ஆவதூஉம்), and the gain that follows later. 461 turns the foresight of 427 into a procedure, a reckoning of outcomes made before acting.

Both verses turn on the quoted plea 'I have nothing': 223 has இலன் என்னும் எவ்வம், 205 has இலன் என்று தீயவை செய்யற்க. In 205 the plea is an excuse for doing evil and is answered with the warning that one will have nothing all over again; in 223 it is a plea the well-born do not voice. In both the book refuses to let want serve as a reason.

Both open with செய்யாமல், 'without (the other) having done anything first'. 101 applies it to help: unprompted help is beyond repayment. 313 applies it to hatred: even toward those who hate you though you did nothing (செய்யாமல் செற்றார்க்கும்), doing hurt brings sorrow with no escape. Read together, the unprovoked good creates a boundless debt while the unprovoked wrong still gives no licence to retaliate.

156 says those who forbear have renown until the end (பொன்றுந் துணையும் புகழ்), against one day's pleasure for those who retaliate; 145 says the man who violates another's home thinking it easy gets blame that never dies (விளியாது நிற்கும் பழி). The adjacent chapters use the same accounting, a brief gratification weighed against a permanent reputation, with புகழ் on one side and பழி on the other. Manakkudavar takes பொன்றுந் துணையும் as until the person's own death, Parimelazhagar as until the world ends.

The two verses share a formula: வேண்டிய வேண்டியாங்கு எய்தலால் (265), what is wanted is obtained as it is wanted, and எண்ணிய எண்ணியாங்கு எய்துப (666), what is thought of is obtained as it was thought. 265 gives this as the reason austerity is striven for; 666 makes it depend on the planner's firmness (திண்ணியர் ஆகப் பெறின்). The promise made for austerity in the book of virtue is made for resolute action in the book of statecraft.

516 asks the king to examine the doer, examine the deed, and act seeing how they fit the time (செய்வானை நாடி வினைநாடிக் காலத்தோடு எய்த உணர்ந்து செயல்). 675 lists five things to think through before acting: resources, means, time, the deed and the place (பொருள்கருவி காலம் வினையிடனொடு ஐந்தும்). Deed and time are in both lists; 516 adds the one item 675 lacks, the person who will do it, which is the concern of a chapter on employing people.

In 1126 she says her lover does not leave her eyes and is not hurt even if she blinks (இமைப்பின் பருவரார்), because he is so subtle. In 1129 she will not blink, knowing he would be hidden (இமைப்பின் கரப்பாக்கு அறிவல்). The same conceit is used both ways within one chapter: blinking is harmless in the first verse and a risk in the second, which shows these are playful defences of him and not one consistent picture.

484 says a king who considers time and place can gain even the world (ஞாலம் கருதினும் கைகூடும்). 610 says a king without sloth gains at once all the expanse crossed by the one who measured with his foot (மடியிலா மன்னவன் எய்தும் அடியளந்தான் தாஅயதெல்லாம்). Both promise the whole earth, one to timing and the other to unremitting effort, so the two chapters make the same claim for different qualities.

The same logic is used in two domains: the passion is its own executioner. Envy needs no enemies, and in 305 anger left unguarded kills its owner. The book treats inner states as weapons pointed inward.

379 asks why those who see things as good when good comes should grieve (அல்லற்படுவது எவன்) when it does not. 626 asks whether those who never clutched at wealth saying 'we have got it' would grieve (அல்லற்படுபவோ) saying 'we have lost it'. Both are rhetorical questions with the same verb and the same symmetry between gain and loss. 626 adds the practical point that grief at loss depends on how one held the gain.

1290 remembers her sulk ending because her eagerness to embrace was greater than his. 1327 states the rule the man later draws: in a lovers' quarrel the one who loses has won, as is seen in the union (ஊடலில் தோற்றவர் வென்றார்). Her giving way in 1290 is a case of the defeat that 1327 counts as victory.

835 says a fool can make, in one birth, the mire he will sink into for seven (எழுமையும் தான்புக் கழுந்தும் அளறு). 538 says those who neglect what is praised have no good through seven births (எழுமையும் இல்). Both attach a seven-birth consequence to conduct in this life, folly in one and neglect of duty in the other.

790 distrusts the declaration of how close two friends are; Parimelazhagar says that speaking of 'they' and 'we' already introduces a separation. In 1209 a woman says her life is ending as she thinks of the unkindness of the man who used to say 'we are not separate' (வேறல்லம் என்பார்). Her complaint is a speaker's case of what 790 states in general: saying the closeness did not make it so.

Here the sage's unstoppable anger shows his stature. In 301, real restraint means holding anger back exactly where it can hurt. By the standard of 301, the anger praised in 29 is what should be held back.

374 states as a general fact that wealth and clear understanding are separate lots. 408 judges one result of that: wealth lodged with the unlearned is more painful than poverty lodged with the good (கல்லார்கண் பட்ட திரு). 408 takes for granted the mismatch that 374 explains.

On Parimelazhagar's first reading, 223 says the well-born do not speak to others the beggar's degrading word 'I am poor'. 1044 says that even in the well-born (இற்பிறந்தார் கண்ணேயும்) poverty produces the lapse from which degrading words are born (இளிவந்த சொற்பிறக்கும் சோர்வு). The conflict depends on that reading of 223; if 'இலன்' is the giver's refusal to an asker, as Pope takes it, the two speak of different utterances.

644 asks for speech fitted to its hearers and says no virtue or gain exceeds it. 696 applies this to a single hearer, the king: know his mood, consider the time, and say what is needed in a way he will want (குறிப்பறிந்து காலம் கருதி ... வேட்பச் சொலல்).
