The general rule for a minister's speech becomes a specific rule for speech to power.

In 1192 a woman says that the tender care a lover gives the one who loves him (வீழ்வார் அளிக்கும் அளி) is like the sky giving rain to those who live by it (வாழ்வார்க்கு வானம் பயந்தற்று). 557 says a king's lack of அளி is to living beings what lack of rain is to the earth. The same word அளி and the same rain comparison describe dependence on a ruler in one book and on a beloved in the other.

1305 says that for men good in their qualities (நலத்தகை நல்லவர்க்கு) the beauty (ஏர்) is the sulking in flower-eyed women; Parimelazhagar reads this as 'even for the faultless, sulking is sweet'. 1325 says the same in plainer terms: though without fault (தவறிலர் ஆயினும்), being kept from the soft shoulders of the one they love has something in it (ஆங்கொன்று உடைத்து). Manakkudavar reads 1305 differently, taking நல்லவர் as the other women.

100 pictures someone who has ripe fruit at hand and takes the unripe: unpleasant words chosen while pleasant ones exist (இனிய உளவாக இன்னாத கூறல்). 831 defines folly as taking hold of harm and letting gain go (ஏதங்கொண்டு ஊதியம் போக விடல்). Harsh speech in 100 is an instance of exactly the choice 831 names as folly, which fits the chapter's closing argument that harsh words are a bad bargain for the speaker as well as wrong.

1055 says askers take up standing before others because people who do not conceal exist in the world (கரப்பிலார் வையகத்து உண்மையால்). 1059 says givers would have no renown if there were none who wished to ask and receive (இரந்துகோள் மேவார் இலாஅக் கடை). The two verses state the dependence in both directions: asking exists because of givers, and givers' standing exists because of askers.

1195 asks what the one she loves can do for her when he has no love for her (தாம்காதல் கொள்ளாக் கடை). 1245 asks her heart whether a man who does not respond when she draws near (உற்றால் உறாஅதவர்) can be dropped as one who hates her (செற்றார் எனக் கைவிடல் உண்டோ). The second speech limits the first: finding no benefit in an unreturned love does not make her able to give it up.

347 says griefs hold and do not let go of those who hold on to attachment. 359 gives the other case: for one who knows the support and lives so that supports fall away (சார்புகெட ஒழுகின்), the pains that were due do not come to cling. 347 states the bondage and 359 the way out, in the same language of things that cling.

1170 says that if her eyes could go where he is, as her mind does (உள்ளம்போன்று உள்வழிச் செல்கிற்பின்), they would not be swimming in tears. 1210 looks for a way round that limit: on Parimelazhagar's reading, since both of them look at the moon, her eyes meet his there (கண்ணினால் காண). Manakkudavar reads it differently, as a complaint that the moon will not set and let her sleep and see him in a dream.

410 makes book-learning the difference between people and beasts. 1012 says food, clothing and the rest are no different for any living being, and that the distinction of human beings is having shame (நாணுடைமை மாந்தர் சிறப்பு). The two verses give different answers, learning and shame, to what sets humans apart.

1145: as drinking is wanted more each time one gets drunk (களித்தொறும் கள்ளுண்டல் வேட்டற்றால்), love is sweeter each time it is exposed. 1288: his chest is as liquor is to those who have got drunk on it (களித்தார்க்குக் கள்ளற்றே), though it does shameful harm. Both take the drinker's returning appetite as the likeness for love; 1288 adds the harm and the shame that 1145 leaves out.

898 plays on குன்று (hill) and குன்ற (to diminish): if the hill-like intend diminishment, the seemingly permanent vanish. 965 uses the same play: even the hill-like (குன்றின் அனையாரும்) will diminish (குன்றுவர்) if they do a lowering thing as small as a kunri seed. In 898 the hill-like bring others low; in 965 they themselves can be brought low by their own act, so height gives power over others but no protection from one's own lapse.

802 says intimate liberty is a limb of friendship and that 'being உப்பு to it' (அதற்கு உப்பாதல்) is the duty of the worthy; Parimelazhagar reads this as being pleasant toward that liberty. 1328 uses உப்பு for the savour of union after a sulk, which Parimelazhagar again glosses as sweetness. In both, salt stands for the relish that makes something a close companion does, a liberty or a sulk, enjoyable and not an offence.

471 makes comparing strengths the test of whether to act. 250, in the chapter on compassion, uses the same comparison as a brake: when going against those weaker than oneself (தன்னின் மெலியார்மேல் செல்லுமிடத்து), one should think of oneself before the stronger (வலியார்முன் தன்னை நினைக்க). Being the stronger party permits action in 471, while 250 asks the stronger party to remember what that position feels like from below.

In 1119, the man tells the moon not to appear, as no one else should have her beauty. In 1210, the woman begs the moon to stay, since it's the only thing she may share with him. His moon is a rival to exclusive possession, and hers is the only link she has.

326 says Death, the eater of life, does not advance on the days of one who lives by not killing; 260 says all living beings fold their hands (கைகூப்பி) and worship the one who does not kill and refuses flesh. Both state what the non-killer receives in return, and both put it as a response of life itself: living beings honour him, and the taker of life leaves him alone.

309 says all that one has thought of is reached at once if one does not think of anger in the heart (உள்ளியதெல்லாம் உடனெய்தும்). 367 says the unfailing deed comes as one wishes (தான் வேண்டுமாற்றான் வரும்) once craving is cut. Each verse removes one passion, anger or craving, and promises that what one intends then arrives.

156 sets the one day's joy of those who retaliate (ஒருநாளை இன்பம்) against the lasting renown of those who forbear. 173 says those who want the other joy (மற்றின்பம்) will not do what is not aram out of desire for a small joy (சிற்றின்பம்). Both argue against a wrong by the shortness of the pleasure it buys, for retaliation in one verse and for coveting in the other.

661 locates firmness in action in the mind and sets other things aside. 600 says a person's real strength (உரம்) is abundance of spirit (உள்ள வெறுக்கை), and those without it are trees. Both place strength within the person; Parimelazhagar's note on 661 lists the outer things meant by 'மற்றைய' as the firmness of army, fort and allies.

Verse 65 names two sense pleasures a child gives: touching the child's body is joy to the body (உடற்கின்பம்) and hearing its words is joy to the ear (இன்பம் செவிக்கு). In 1101 the lover says the five senses, seeing, hearing, tasting, smelling and touching (கண்டுகேட்டு உண்டுயிர்த்து உற்றறியும்), all have their objects in one woman. Both list pleasures sense by sense and locate them in a single loved person, a child in one and a lover in the other.

819, on bad friendship, says the tie with those whose deeds are one thing and words another is bitter even in a dream (கனவினும் இன்னாது). In 1217 the lover who gives nothing in waking life hurts her in her dreams as well (கனவினால் ... பீழிப்பது). Both take the dream as the last place a person's unreliability should reach, and both find that it reaches there: one verse in the book of polity, the other in a lover's complaint.

1287 asks what use it is to sulk when one knows the sulk will prove false (பொய்த்தல் அறிந்து என் புலந்து), like those who jump into a stream knowing it will carry them off. 1260 asks whether those with hearts like fat put in fire (நிணம் தீயில் இட்டன்ன நெஞ்சினார்) can ever say they will hold out in a sulk. One image is of being swept away and the other of melting, and both conclude that the sulk cannot be sustained.

653 tells those who say 'ஆஅதும்' (we shall rise) to stop doing what dims their ஒளி. 962 says those who want சீர் together with பேராண்மை will not do 'சீரல்ல' even for the sake of சீர். 962 takes the harder case 653 leaves open: the dimming deed may itself be a route to fame, and it is still refused.

53 asks what is lacking if the wife has worth (இல்லதென் இல்லவள் மாண்பானால்) and what is there if she does not (உள்ளதென் ... மாணாக் கடை). 430 says those with understanding have everything, and those without it have nothing whatever they have (என்னுடையரேனும் இலர்). The same two-sided formula, one possession that makes all others count or not count, is applied to a wife's character in the home and to understanding in a ruler.

875 says that one without allies and facing two enemies should take one of them as a pleasing ally. 679 says that winning over ஒட்டார் is more urgent than favours to friends; Manakkudavar takes ஒட்டார் as one's enemies, Parimelazhagar as those not allied with one's enemy. On either reading both verses treat alliance as something to be made out of the hostile or uncommitted when one is pressed.

72 says the loveless keep everything for themselves, while the loving belong to others even in their bones (என்பும் உரியர் பிறர்க்கு). 251 describes the reverse movement: another's body (பிறிது ஊன்) taken to build one's own. Read together, the body is the measure in both: love gives it over, and the eater of flesh takes another's.
Here the town's talk is a misunderstanding she can rebut. In 1147, the talk has become manure for the love itself. Her stance towards gossip shifts from defence to using it.

852 ranks not harming a provoker as தலை, the best course. 203 uses the same ranking word: the head of all understanding (அறிவினுள் எல்லாம் தலை) is not to do evil even to those who hate you (செறுவார்க்கும்). Together they show the text treating non-retaliation as a matter of good sense as well as of virtue; Parimelazhagar on 852 explains that retaliating feeds the enmity while refraining lets it die out.

700 says the familiarity (கெழுதகைமை) that does improper things on the thought 'we are old associates' (பழையம் எனக்கருதி) brings ruin. 801 defines old friendship (பழைமை) as friendship that in no way cuts down the liberties of intimacy (கிழமையைக் கீழ்ந்திடா நட்பு). The liberty that defines friendship between equals is thus withdrawn where the other party is a king, as Parimelazhagar reads 700.

555 asks whether the tears of those who suffer under a ruler are not the weapon that wears away his wealth (கண்ணீர் அன்றே செல்வத்தைத் தேய்க்கும் படை). 1258 has the same form of question: are his humble words not the weapon that breaks our womanhood (பணிமொழி அன்றோ ... உடைக்கும் படை). In both a soft thing, tears or gentle speech, is named as the real weapon against something that looks strong.

868 says a man without qualities and with many faults comes to have no one with him (இனனிலனாம்). 525 gives the positive case: one who can give and speak pleasantly will be surrounded by kin in rows (அடுக்கிய சுற்றத்தால் சுற்றப்படும்). Both make a person's following a product of his character; 868 adds the military consequence of losing it.

649 treats wanting to say many things as the sign of someone unable to say a few well. 193 says spread-out talk on useless matters (பயனில பாரித்துரைக்கும் உரை) itself announces that the speaker lacks நயன். In both, length of speech is evidence against the speaker; 193 judges his character, 649 his skill.

295 sets the truthful speaker above those who practise austerity and giving. 48 says a household life that keeps others on their way and does not slip from virtue has more endurance than those who do penance (நோற்பாரின் நோன்மை உடைத்து). In both, the ascetic is the standard of comparison and an ordinary life rightly lived is placed above it.

839 says, with irony, that the friendship of fools is very sweet because parting from them brings no pain (பிரிவின்கண் பீழை தருவதொன்றில்). 812 asks what it matters whether one gains or loses (பெறினும் இழப்பினும் என்) the friendship of those who befriend when there is profit and leave when there is none. Both measure a worthless friendship by the same test: its loss costs nothing.

655 asks that one not do what will be regretted afterwards. 467 says to think and then resolve (எண்ணித் துணிக), and calls it a lapse to say 'we will think after resolving'. Both put the reflection before the act: 467 as a rule of planning, 655 as a rule about the purity of the deed.

757 calls அருள் a child born of love that is raised by the wealthy foster-mother called பொருள். 938 has gambling destroy both பொருள் and அருள். Parimelazhagar assigns the losses in 938 to separate causes (losing, winning, resentment), but 757 suggests a link between them: with the nurse gone, the child is harder to raise.

1160 speaks, with irony, of the many who agree to the hard thing, endure the parting and live on afterwards (அரிதாற்றி ... பிரிவாற்றிப் பின்இருந்து வாழ்வார் பலர்); Parimelazhagar glosses அரிது ஆற்றி as consenting to the parting. 1181 is the woman who did consent (நல்காமை நேர்ந்தேன்) and now cannot bear the result. Read together, 1181 shows the cost of the consent that 1160 doubted anyone could really give.

Both say that a living body can be dead in effect, and Manakkudavar on 9 also says such bodies lack life. The criterion is worship in chapter 1 and love in chapter 8, so the two chapters compete for what makes a person alive.

486 says the holding back of a person of energy is like a fighting ram stepping back in order to charge (பொருதகர் தாக்கற்குப் பேருந் தகைத்து). 827 says not to trust humble words from an enemy, because the bending of a bow means harm (வில்வணக்கம் தீங்கு குறித்தமையான்). Both use a drawing back that comes before a blow: 486 recommends it to oneself, and 827 teaches one to see it in an opponent.

440 says that if a ruler can enjoy what he loves without others knowing of his love (காதல் அறியாமை), his enemies' schemes come to nothing; 590 forbids showing favour to a spy where others can know of it. Both treat a ruler's visible attachments and rewards as information that others can use against him.

Verse 78 says a life with no love within is like a dried tree putting out shoots on hard ground (வற்றல் மரம் தளிர்த்தற்று), which Parimelazhagar takes as something that does not happen. In 1106 the lover says her touch makes his life sprout each time they meet (உறுதோறு உயிர் தளிர்ப்ப). The verb தளிர் carries both: life sprouts where love is, and 78 uses the same sprouting to mark what a loveless life cannot do.

1141 says life stays because the gossip has risen. 1263 says the woman still exists by longing for his return (வரல்நசைஇ இன்னும் உளேன்). Both verses name the one thing that keeps life from leaving; in 1141 it comes from outside, from the town, and in 1263 from her own hope.

188 asks what those whose way is to spread even the faults of people close to them (துன்னியார் குற்றமும் தூற்றும்) would do to strangers (என்னைகொல் ஏதிலார் மாட்டு). In 1165 the woman asks what those who can bring grief within friendship (நட்பினுள்) would become in enmity. Both argue from conduct toward intimates to what must follow toward others; in 1165 it is a lover's complaint, not a general teaching.

534 says the fearful have no fortress (அச்ச முடையார்க்கு அரணில்லை). 741 says a fort is of value both to those who march out and to those who, in fear, protect themselves (அஞ்சித் தற்போற்றுபவர்க்கும் பொருள்). The conflict holds if 534's first half is taken as a plain claim about forts and the fearful; Parimelazhagar's readings ease it, since he takes 534 as fear in the mind making a fort useless and 741 as the weaker side prudently taking refuge.

55 praises a wife who does not worship a god (தெய்வம் தொழாஅள்) and worships her husband, and credits her with power over the rain. 2 asks what use learning is if the learned do not worship the feet of the one of pure knowledge (நற்றாள் தொழாஅர் எனின்), with the same verb in the same negative form. Read literally, 55 commends for the wife the not-worshipping that the first chapter treats as making a person's attainments useless. Parimelazhagar removes the conflict by reading 'other gods' (பிற தெய்வம்) and making the husband her god; the tension depends on taking தெய்வம் தொழாஅள் at face value.

948 tells the healer to examine the disease, then its root (நோய்முதல்), then the means that subdue it (அது தணிக்கும் வாய்), as three separate things. 1102 first grants the ordinary rule, that the medicine is other than the disease, and then says love is the exception, where cause and remedy are the same person. The lover's verse marks love's sickness as a case the method of 948 does not cover.

684 counts presence (உரு) among the three things an envoy needs. 407 says the fine looks of one without fine, penetrating understanding are those of a well-made clay doll (மண்மாண் புனைபாவை). 407 supplies the limit on 684's உரு: appearance counts only in the union (செறிவு) with understanding and learning that 684 itself demands.

488 advises bearing with enemies when one meets them until their end is in view. 830 advises a friendly face toward enemies at a time when, as Parimelazhagar explains, they cannot be openly put aside. Both treat outward civility toward an enemy as a matter of timing and not of feeling.

On the commentators' reading, 37 treats the difference between rider and bearer as virtue made visible. In 972, birth is the same for all beings, and distinction comes from what one does, which still leaves open whether the palanquin bearer's lot is deserved.

71 asks whether there is a bolt that can shut love in (அன்பிற்கும் உண்டோ அடைக்குந்தாழ்), since the small tears of the loving make it known. 1138 says காமம் breaks through secrecy and appears in public. The Book of Virtue says of அன்பு what the Book of Love says of காமம்: neither can be kept hidden, and each publishes itself.

1301 has the friend urge the woman to hold back her embrace and sulk (புல்லாது இராப் புலத்தை) so they can watch his pain 'a little' (சிறிது). 1302 states the limit that word implies: sulking is like salt in right measure, and letting it run on (நீள விடல்) is like salt in excess. Parimelazhagar reads the சிறிது of 1301 as already pointing to this rule.

95 makes humility (பணிவு) the true ornament (அணி). 978 says greatness always bows (பணியுமாம்) while smallness adorns itself in self-admiration (அணியுமாம் தன்னை வியந்து). The same two roots are set against each other in 978: the small person's self-adornment is the false ornament, and the bowing 95 praises is what the great actually wear.

562 tells those who want lasting prosperity to raise the rod sharply but strike gently (கடிதோச்சி மெல்ல எறிக). 567 names what happens when the stroke is not gentle: punishment past the bound (கையிகந்த தண்டம்), with harsh words, is a file that wears down the king's strength. 562 gives the practice and 567 the cost of abandoning it; the 'long prosperity' (நெடிதாக்கம்) of one is the 'conquering strength' (அடுமுரண்) eroded in the other.

616 says effort creates prosperity and lack of effort brings in want (முயற்றின்மை இன்மை புகுத்திவிடும்). 1040 pictures the Land laughing at people who claim poverty while sitting idle (அசைஇ இருப்பார்). Both hold that such poverty comes from not working; 1040 states it as mockery from the land that would have paid them.

371 says tireless effort arises from a fate of gain and sloth arises from a fate of loss (போகூழால் தோன்றும் மடி). 618 says lacking good fortune (பொறியின்மை) is no one's disgrace, but lacking effort after learning what should be known is a disgrace (ஆள்வினை இன்மை பழி). If sloth itself is produced by fate, as 371 says on a plain reading, the line 618 draws between blameless fortune and blameworthy idleness is hard to hold.

130 has virtue looking for its chance and coming along the path to the restrained person; 594 has prosperity asking the way and going to the one of unwavering energy (ஆக்கம் அதர்வினாய்ச் செல்லும்). The same figure, a good that seeks out the person fit for it instead of being pursued, is used for virtue in the first book and for worldly gain in the second. The edition's text of 594 has lost its first letter (க்கம் for ஆக்கம்), but the reading is not in doubt.

861 says to avoid standing against the strong (வலியார்க்கு மாறேற்றல் ஓம்புக). 680 describes what that means for a weak party: those of small domain, fearing the trembling of their own side (உள்நடுங்கல் அஞ்சி), bow to the greater and accept terms if they can get them (குறைபெறின் கொள்வர் பெரியார்ப் பணிந்து). 861 gives the rule and 680 the settlement that follows from it.

35 defines virtue as what proceeds without slipping into four things, one of which is craving (அழுக்காறு அவா வெகுளி இன்னாச்சொல்). 366 says craving is what deceives a person (வஞ்சிப்பது அவா), and that fearing it is itself virtue (அஞ்சுவதோரும் அறனே). 366 takes one item from the list in 35 and gives the reason for singling it out: it works by deceit, so it needs constant watch.

444 says living so that those greater than oneself become one's own is the head of all strengths (வன்மையுள் எல்லாம் தலை). 897 gives the other side: a fully appointed life and great wealth count for nothing (என்னாம்) once the worthy great are angered. Together they make one's standing with the great, and not one's possessions, the deciding strength.

183 says that dying yields more of the gain the books of virtue speak of than living by backbiting and falsehood (பொய்த்துயிர் வாழ்தலின் சாதல்). 967 says that rather than live by following those who scorn you (வாழ்தலின்), it is better to be called ruined as you are. Both use the comparative 'than living thus' to say that a kind of life can cost more than its end, once for the slanderer's two faces and once for lost honour.

Verse 17 pictures the cloud not giving (எழிலி தான் நல்காதாகி விடின்) and the sea itself shrinking as a result. Verse 1010 says the brief want of the renowned rich has the nature of the rain-cloud gone dry (மாரி வறங்கூர்ந்தனையது). Both use the withholding cloud; 1010 turns it into a figure for a giver's temporary incapacity, with the suggestion that it is as general a loss and as passing.

193 says that useless talk at length shows the speaker to be without நயன், so the two faults go together. 197 separates them and ranks them: speech without நயன் may be let pass in the worthy, speech without use may not. Read together, 197 makes uselessness the graver of the two; Parimelazhagar draws the same ranking from சொல்லினும்.

1022 pairs effort with full knowledge (ஆள்வினையும் ஆன்ற அறிவும்) as the two things that extend a family. 618 uses the same pairing when it assigns blame: lacking fortune is no disgrace, but lacking effort after knowing what should be known (அறிவறிந்து ஆள்வினை இன்மை) is. In both verses knowledge and effort are named together as what a person can be held to, as against fortune.

832 defines the folly of all follies (பேதைமையுள் எல்லாம் பேதைமை) as setting one's love on what is not proper to one (கையல்லதன்கண் காதன்மை). 141 names one case of exactly that: the பேதைமை of desiring (பெட்டு ஒழுகும்) a woman who is another's. Read together, 141 is an instance of the general definition that 832 gives much later.

612 warns against abandoning a task midway (வினைக்கண் வினைகெடல் ஓம்பல்). 674 says the remainder of a task, like the remainder of an enmity, burns like the remainder of a fire (தீயெச்சம் போலத் தெறும்). 674 supplies a reason 612 does not give: the unfinished part is not inert but goes on doing damage.

759 calls wealth the sharpest steel (எஃகு) against enemies' pride. 985 says bowing is the weapon (படை) by which the worthy turn their opponents (மாற்றாரை மாற்றும் படை). Each names a non-military thing as the real weapon against foes: resources for the ruler, humility for the person of character.

874 says the world rests in the greatness of the person of character who conducts himself taking enmity as friendship (பண்புடையாளன் தகைமைக்கண் தங்கிற்று உலகு). 996 says the world exists by resting on those of character (பண்புடையார்ப் பட்டுண்டு உலகம்), and would otherwise sink into the earth. Both make பண்பு the thing the world stands on; 874, in the chapter on enmity, specifies it as the capacity to turn enemies into friends.

396 says a sand-well yields water as far as it is dug, and understanding as far as one has learned (தொட்டனைத்து... கற்றனைத்து); 595 says a water-flower's stem is as long as the water is deep, and a person's height as great as their inner drive (வெள்ளத்தனைய... உள்ளத்தனையது). Both use a water image and the same 'as much as' construction to state a strict proportion, one for learning and knowledge, the other for drive and stature.

32 says nothing brings more gain than virtue, and 644 uses the same ஊங்கு formula to put apt speech above both virtue and gain. This is either high rhetoric or a real rearrangement. Parimelazhagar makes apt speech a cause of virtue to avoid the clash.

Verse 71 says tears raise a public noise (பூசல் தரும்) about the love inside. In 1180 the woman says it is not hard for the town to get at the secret (மறை) of those like her whose eyes are beaten drums (அறைபறை கண்ணார்). In both the eyes make public what the heart holds, and both describe this as sound: a clamour in 71, a drum in 1180.

844 locates want of understanding in the pride (செருக்கு) of saying 'we are bright'. 978 says smallness adorns itself in admiration of itself (சிறுமை அணியுமாம் தன்னை வியந்து) while greatness bows. Both make self-admiration the identifying mark of the deficient state, one for understanding and one for stature.

344 says having nothing is natural to austerity (இயல்பாகும் நோன்பிற்கொன்று இன்மை). 378 looks at those who already have nothing through poverty and says they would renounce, but for what fate makes them undergo. Parimelazhagar makes the connection: they have already lost what a renouncer gives up, and still suffer because their intent differs. Having nothing is the condition of austerity in 344, and 378 shows it is not enough by itself.

719 and 728 share the phrase நல்லவையுள் நன்கு செலச் சொல்லு-. 728 says those who cannot speak tellingly in a good assembly are of no use though they have learned much; 719 tells those who can do so not to speak in a mean assembly even by forgetting (பொச்சாந்தும் சொல்லற்க). Together they set the limits: silence in a good assembly is a failure, and silence in a mean one is required.

The first line of 681 and of 992 is the same: அன்புடைமை ஆன்ற குடிப்பிறத்தல். 992 says these two are what is called courtesy (பண்புடைமை என்னும் வழக்கு); 681 lists them and adds a third, the qualities kings desire (வேந்தவாம் பண்புடைமை), as the nature of one who carries a message. The envoy's qualification is thus the book's general definition of courtesy with a courtly requirement added.

475 says a light load breaks the axle when there is too much of it (அப்பண்டம் சால மிகுத்துப் பெயின்). Parimelazhagar takes the verse as an indirect statement that a strong king who makes enemies of many because each is weak loses his strength when they combine. 873 says this outright: one who, alone, takes on the enmity of many (தமியனாய்ப் பல்லார் பகைகொள்பவன்) is more foolish than the mad.

1184: she thinks of him and what she speaks of is his merit (உரைப்பது அவர்திறம்), and still the pallor comes. 1298: her heart thinks of what pertains to him (அவர்திறம் உள்ளும்), judging that to scorn him would be a disgrace. The phrase அவர் திறம் with உள்ளுதல் appears in both; in 1184 it is her own loyal practice that goes unrewarded, and in 1298 it is something her heart does that she stands apart from.

760 makes wealth the route to the other two aims, virtue and pleasure. 31 makes virtue the source of distinction and wealth (சிறப்பு ஈனும் செல்வமும் ஈனும்). Each verse, speaking from within its own book, puts its own aim first as the one from which the others follow.

80 says the seat of life goes by way of love (அன்பின் வழியது உயிர்நிலை) and without it a body is bones wrapped in skin; 1013 says worth depends on shame as life depends on flesh. Both use the life-and-body relation to say a quality is what a thing lives by, love for the person in 80 and shame for சால்பு in 1013. Parimelazhagar notes a variant ஊணை ('food') in 1013, which Manakkudavar follows; the link rests on the reading ஊனை.

Both tell the injured not to return harm, but their reasons differ. In 314 the wrongdoer is shamed by kindness. In 852, on Parimelazhagar's reading, one's own position is improved. The same act is justified in moral terms in one book and in terms of advantage in another.

644 says to speak after knowing the திறன் of those concerned. 469 says that even in doing good there is error when it is done without knowing each person's character (அவரவர் பண்பறிந்து ஆற்றாக்கடை). Both make a good thing, a word or a deed, depend on fitting it to the particular person receiving it.

On Parimelazhagar's reading, 1010 says the brief want (சிறுதுனி) of the rich who have renown is like the rain cloud running dry (மாரி வறங்கூர்ந்தனையது). 219 says the poverty of a man of நயன் is just his not being able to do what he is used to doing. Both treat the giver's poverty as a loss to others, not to himself, and 1010 adds by its image that it passes.

778 says warriors who do not fear for their life when battle comes (உறின் உயிர் அஞ்சா மறவர்) do not lose their distinction even if their lord is angry. 690 says the envoy is one who, even if it brings his end (இறுதி பயப்பினும்), does not fall short and secures what is good for his lord (இறைவற்கு உறுதி). The envoy's office is given the soldier's standard, with both verses naming the lord (இறைவன்) as the one served.

26 says the great are those who do what is hard to do, and the small are those who cannot (செயற்கரிய செய்வார் பெரியர்). 489 uses the same phrase and adds a condition of time: hard deeds are to be done at the moment a rare opportunity arrives (செய்தற்கரிய செயல்). 26 places the ability in the person; 489 says it also depends on a moment that is itself hard to come by (எய்தற்கரியது).

231 ends 'ஊதியம் இல்லை உயிர்க்கு' and 31 ends 'ஆக்கம் எவனோ உயிர்க்கு': both use the figure of profit to a living being. 31 gives the place to virtue in general, which yields distinction and wealth; 231 gives it to renown that comes from giving. The shared formula shows 231 naming one particular form of the gain that 31 states broadly.

Verse 70 has onlookers explain a good son by asking what the father did as penance (என்நோற்றான்). Verse 265 says தவம் is striven for here because whatever is wanted is obtained as wanted (வேண்டிய வேண்டியாங்கு எய்தலால்). The onlookers' question in 70 assumes the doctrine 265 states, and it applies that doctrine to a son.

754 says wealth that came by knowing the right means and without wrong yields virtue and also pleasure (அறன்ஈனும் இன்பமும் ஈனும்). 39 says only what comes through virtue is pleasure (அறத்தான் வருவதே இன்பம்). 754 fits wealth into 39's rule: wealth produces real pleasure only when it was itself acquired without wrong.

123 says that if one knows and then restrains oneself in the proper way (அறிவறிந்து ஆற்றின் அடங்கப் பெறின்), that restraint is recognised and yields distinction; Parimelazhagar takes அறிவறிந்து as knowing that restraint is itself what knowledge is. 834 gives the negative: no fool is greater than one who has studied, understood and taught others but is not himself restrained (தானடங்காப் பேதை). Together they say knowledge is finished only when it turns into restraint.

736 calls foremost the land whose richness does not shrink even where ruin has come (கெட்ட இடத்தும் வளங்குன்றா). 955 says an old family does not part from its character even when what it has to give has fallen away (வழங்குவது உள்வீழ்ந்தக் கண்ணும் ... பண்பில் தலைப்பிரிதல் இன்று). Both use the same 'even when' construction to test excellence by what remains after loss, one for a land and one for a family.

1054 says asking from those who do not know concealing even in a dream is like giving (இரத்தலும் ஈதலே போலும்). 1061 takes the same givers, who give gladly without concealing and are dear as one's eyes (கரவாது உவந்தீயும் கண்ணன்னார்), and says not asking even of them is worth ten million times more (இரவாமை கோடி உறும்). 1061 limits the praise in 1054: the best case of asking still ranks below not asking.

451 says greatness fears small company (சிற்றினம் அஞ்சும் பெருமை) while smallness takes it for kin. 201 says those given to evil deeds do not fear them but the excellent do (தீவினையார் அஞ்சார் விழுமியார் அஞ்சுவர்). In both, what marks the better person is fear of the thing the worse person is at ease with, once about company and once about deeds.

370 says craving has a nature that is never filled (ஆரா இயற்கை அவா). 940 gives a picture of that: as the gambler loves the game more with each loss (இழத்தொறூஉம் காதலிக்கும்), a living being's love grows with each suffering (துன்பம் உழத்தொறூஉம் காதற்று உயிர்); Parimelazhagar takes this as love of the body. 940 shows why satisfying craving cannot end it, which is why 370 says it has to be given up.

229: eating alone to fill one's own store (தாமே தமியர் உணல்) is more bitter than begging. 1107: eating one's own after sharing it, in one's own house, is the model of sweetness, and the embrace is like it. Read together they give both halves of one judgement on eating: bitter when hoarded, sweet when shared.

760 says that for those who have made bright wealth in full, the other two, virtue and pleasure, are easy to have together (ஏனை இரண்டும் ஒருங்கு). 754 says the wealth that yields virtue and pleasure is wealth that came without wrong (தீதின்றி வந்த பொருள்). 754 supplies the condition; Parimelazhagar reads it into 760's ஒண்பொருள் as wealth that comes by the right way.

1299 asks who will be a companion in grief when one's own heart is not (தாமுடைய நெஞ்சந் துணையல் வழி). 1300 repeats the frame, தாமுடைய நெஞ்சம் தமரல் வழி, and draws the further step: then it is a small matter that strangers are not one's own. The pair moves from the loss of the nearest help to an inference about everyone else, and Parimelazhagar gives both to the man, where the first eight verses of the chapter are the woman's.

311 says the spotless hold to not hurting others even if it would bring wealth that gives distinction. 1016, on Parimelazhagar's reading, says the high take shame as their fence and do not want the wide world (வியன்ஞாலம் பேணலர்) where the two conflict. Both state a refusal of great gain at the price of a restraint; the other reading he reports, that they will not want the world without first having the fence of shame, gives the same result.

346 says one who cuts off the pride of saying 'I' and 'mine' (யான் எனது என்னும் செருக்கு) enters a world above the gods. 72 says the loveless keep everything for themselves (எல்லாம் தமக்குரியர்) while the loving belong to others even to their bones (என்பும் உரியர் பிறர்க்கு). The householder's love already loosens 'mine', and even the body as 'I', by giving it to others; renunciation does it by cutting the notion itself.

239 says land that has borne a body without renown (இசையிலா யாக்கை பொறுத்த நிலம்) will decline in its yield. 1003 says the appearance of men who cling to accumulation and do not want renown is a burden to the land (நிலக்குப் பொறை). Both make the person without renown a weight the earth carries; 239 adds the cost to the earth.

341 ties freedom from pain to having left the thing itself (நீங்கியான்). 629 says one who does not crave the pleasure in pleasure (இன்பத்துள் இன்பம் விழையாதான்) does not suffer the pain in pain; Parimelazhagar reads this as someone who goes on experiencing the pleasure without wanting it. The pairing shows the same result claimed for an inward letting go, without the outward leaving.

833 describes the fool by four negations. 865 describes the ideal enemy to have by a similar string: he does not look to the way, does not do what is fitting, does not look to blame, has no character (வழிநோக்கான் ... பழிநோக்கான் பண்பிலன்), and so is sweet to his foes. The same profile that 833 treats as a moral portrait is, in the chapter on enmity, a strategic weakness.
374 separates wealth and wisdom as different fates, and 400 goes further by calling learning the only true wealth. Read together, they redefine wealth.

224 says the unease of being asked lasts until the asker's face is glad. 228 names what follows as a pleasure in its own right, ஈத்துவக்கும் இன்பம், which Parimelazhagar explains as the joy the giver has from the receiver's rejoicing. 228 then uses that pleasure as a charge against those who hoard and lose.

434 calls one's own fault the only enemy that brings ruin. 448 shows the mechanism: without those who rebuke, no outside enemy is needed. Self-correction turns out to be something a person needs other people for.

1037 says that if ploughed soil is dried until a measure of dust (தொடிப்புழுதி) falls to a quarter (கஃசு), the crop thrives without even a handful of manure. 1038 says manuring is better than ploughing (ஏரினும் நன்றால் எருவிடுதல்). The two set tillage and manure against each other from opposite sides: thorough working of the soil can replace manure, yet as a rule manure counts for more than ploughing.

89 says poverty in the midst of wealth is the folly (மடமை) of not caring for guests. 841 says lack of understanding is the poverty of poverties (அறிவின்மை இன்மையுள் இன்மை) and that the world does not count other lack as lack. 841 states as a general principle what 89 shows in one case: the real want is a failure of understanding, whatever one owns.

In Parimelazhagar's reading, 471 says to act only if your side is stronger. 493 says the weak can win by choosing the ground. If so, the calculation of 471 must already have place in it, or 471's rule is too strict.

832 names as the worst folly a liking (காதன்மை) for what is not fit for one. 439 gives the matching instruction: do not set your desire on a deed that yields no good (நயவற்க நன்றி பயவா வினை). Both locate the error in the wanting, before any deed is done.

956 says those who mean to keep to a spotless line do not do what lacks worth (சால்பில செய்யார்); Parimelazhagar adds 'even in poverty'. 656 says one should not do what the worthy condemn (சான்றோர் பழிக்கும் வினை) even if one must see one's mother hungry. Both set a standard of worthy conduct above need, 656 naming the hardest case.

462 says nothing is hard to attain for those who act after examining a matter with chosen company and thinking it through themselves (தெரிந்த இனத்தொடு தேர்ந்தெண்ணி). 568 gives the negative case: the fortune of a king who does not think matters through with his circle (இனத்தாற்றி எண்ணாத வேந்தன்) and then rages will shrink. Both make deliberation with one's இனம் the condition of success, stated once as promise and once as warning.

985 says the strength of those who accomplish is bowing (பணிதல்), and that this is the weapon by which the worthy turn foes. 978 says greatness always bows (பணியுமாம் என்றும் பெருமை) while smallness adorns itself in self-admiration. Both attach bowing to the strong and not the weak; 985 adds that it has an effect on opponents.

492 says that even for those with fighting strength (முரண்சேர்ந்த மொய்ம்பினவர்க்கும்) the advantage of joining a fort (அரண்சேர்ந்தாம் ஆக்கம்) yields many gains. 741 says a fort is of value to those able to go on the offensive (ஆற்றுபவர்க்கும்) as well as to those who guard themselves in fear. Both deny that a fort is only for the weak: the chapter on place and the chapter on forts make the same point about the strong.

488 says to bear an enemy when you meet him until his final limit comes, and then his head goes down. 829 says to keep the false friend pleased and hold him in the appearance of friendship while it dies inwardly. Both advise outward accommodation of an enemy who cannot yet be opposed openly, in the chapter on timing and in the chapter on false friendship.

In 1216 the woman says that if there were no such thing as waking, her lover would not leave her in the dream (கனவினால் காதலர் நீங்கலர் மன்). In 1329 the man, in the middle of a lovers' quarrel, wishes the night would lengthen so that he can go on pleading (நீடுக மன்னோ இரா). Both wish away the end of the night and both close on the wistful particle மன்; hers is said of a dream meeting and his of a real one.

222 holds receiving to be bad whatever is said in its favour. 1061 says that not asking is worth a crore even from those dear as one's eyes who give gladly without hiding (கரவாது உவந்தீயும் கண்ணன்னார் கண்ணும் இரவாமை). Both refuse the best case that could be made for receiving: 222 the claim that it is a good path, 1061 the excellence of the giver.

The two verses have the same construction: an opinion is held only by those who lack an experience. In 66, 'the flute is sweet, the lute is sweet' is said by those who have not heard their own children's prattle (மழலைச்சொல் கேளாதவர்). In 1219 those who blame the man for giving nothing in waking life are those who have not seen a lover in dreams (கனவினால் காதலர்க் காணாதவர்). Parental love in the first book and a lover's dream in the third both discredit a judgment by pointing to what its holders have not known.

527 says crows do not hide food but call the others and eat, and that ஆக்கம் belongs only to those of that nature (அன்ன நீரார்க்கே). 166 gives the opposite disposition and result: one who grudges giving leaves his சுற்றம் without food or clothing. Both tie a household's kin and its prosperity to the attitude taken toward sharing.

739 praises land whose riches need no seeking. 1040 says the good woman called Land laughs (நிலமென்னும் நல்லாள் நகும்) at those who say 'we have nothing' and sit idle (அசைஇ இருப்பாரை). 1040 limits 739: the land has riches to give, but not to those who do nothing.

705 asks what use eyes are among the limbs if they cannot read a sign by a sign (என்ன பயத்தவோ கண்). 574 asks what eyes without measured kindly regard do, beyond seeming to be there in the face (உளபோல் முகத்தெவன் செய்யும் ... கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லாத கண்). Each denies the eye its name unless it does more than see, perceiving another's mind in 705 and looking kindly in 574.

207 treats one's evil deeds as an enemy ('வினைப்பகை') worse than any outward one. 434, advising the king, says fault itself is the enemy that brings ruin ('குற்றமே அற்றம் தரூஉம் பகை') and so guarding against fault should be one's aim. The two verses, one in the Book of Virtue and one in the Book of Wealth, both move the real enemy from outside to one's own conduct.

71 says love cannot be bolted in, because the small tears of the loving make it public (புன்கணீர் பூசல் தரும்). 1232 says her eyes, pale and running with tears (பசந்து பனிவாரும் கண்), seem to tell of the unkindness of the one she desired (நல்காமை சொல்லுவ போலும்). The same mechanism, tears that disclose, works in both; in 71 they reveal the weeper's love, in 1232 they also accuse the absent lover.

83 says the life of one who tends the arriving guest every day (வைகலும் ஓம்புவான்) does not suffer and go to ruin (பருவந்து பாழ்படுதல் இன்று). 227 says the disease called hunger rarely touches one accustomed to sharing his food (பாத்தூண் மரீஇயவனை). Both promise that habitual sharing of food protects the sharer from want, once for the host of guests and once for the giver to the poor.

406 says the unlearned can only be said to exist (உளரென்னும் மாத்திரையர்) and are otherwise like barren saline land. 574 says eyes without kindly regard only seem to be there in the face (உளபோல் முகத்து) and do nothing more. Both verses grant bare existence and deny any use, of unlearned persons in one case and of unkind eyes in the other.

755 tells one to refuse wealth that comes without grace and love. 1009 says what becomes of such wealth: bright wealth amassed by setting love aside and not looking to virtue (அன்பொரீஇ ... அறநோக்காது ஈட்டிய) is taken by others. 1009 supplies a consequence for the wealth 755 rejects.

421 names understanding as the tool that guards against ruin (அற்றங் காக்குங் கருவி). 781 asks what guard is as hard for hostile action to get past as friendship (வினைக்கரிய யாவுள காப்பு). The Book of Wealth offers two protections that are not walls or weapons, one within the person and one between persons, and praises each in the vocabulary of defence.

333 says wealth is by nature unstaying; 753 calls it the unfailing lamp that drives out darkness wherever one intends. The chapter on impermanence and the chapter on acquiring wealth describe the same thing in opposite terms.

1053 says there is a beauty even in asking while standing before those of unconcealing heart who know what is due (கடனறிவார் முன்நின்று இரப்பும்). 708 says that if one has people who look within and understand, it is enough to stand looking at their face (முகம்நோக்கி நிற்க அமையும்). Parimelazhagar reads 1053 the same way: standing before such people is enough and nothing need be said, which is why the asking keeps some grace.

130 praises the one who guards against anger and, having learned, is restrained (கற்றடங்கல் ஆற்றுவான்): virtue itself seeks him out. 834 names the one who has read, understood and taught but is not restrained (ஓதி உணர்ந்தும் ... தானடங்கா) the greatest of fools. Both treat learning and அடங்கல் as a pair in which the learning is judged by the restraint.

507 says trusting the ignorant with affection as the ground (காதன்மை கந்தா அறிவறியார்த் தேறுதல்) yields every kind of folly. 515 says work is not to be assigned to someone because he is dear (சிறந்தானென்று ஏவற்பாற்றன்று), only to one who knows, endures and can do it. Both exclude affection as a ground of appointment, one at the stage of trust and the other at the stage of assigning work.

985 says that bowing (பணிதல்) is the strength of those who accomplish and the weapon by which the worthy change their opponents (மாற்றாரை மாற்றும் படை). 827 says that an enemy's verbal bowing should not be accepted, since it points to harm as a bent bow does. Bowing is a means of working on an adversary in both; 985 praises it in the worthy, and 827 says that from an enemy it must not be taken as goodwill.

In 1311 the woman refuses his chest because all women 'feast on it in common with their eyes' (கண்ணின் பொதுஉண்பர்), a sulk with a stated ground. In 1321 she grants there is no fault at all and says his tenderness itself brings the sulk on; Parimelazhagar explains this as her thought that others too might receive that same tenderness. On his reading the jealousy of 1311 survives in 1321 with its ground removed.

755 says a gain of wealth that does not come with grace and love should be let go, not embraced (புல்லார் புரள விடல்). 113 says gain that comes from leaving fairness should be let go that very day even if it brings only good (அன்றே யொழிய விடல்). Both end on the same command, விடல், for gain acquired the wrong way, one naming love and grace as the test and the other fairness.
இன்மை, having nothing, is natural and right for austerity in 344. In 1041, poverty, the same word, is what nothing else can match for misery. The word changes value completely with who has chosen it.

402 compares the unlearned man's desire to speak (சொற்காமுறுதல், as Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar read it) to a woman without breasts desiring womanhood. 727 compares the learning of one who fears the assembly to a bright sword in the hand of a பேடி among enemies. Both use a figure of lacking what one's role requires, and they cover the two opposite failures: wanting to speak without learning, and having learning without the nerve to speak. Kalaignar reads 402 differently, as desiring to hear the unlearned man's words.

1053 says that even asking, standing before those of unconcealing heart who know their duty, has a certain beauty (இரப்பும் ஓர் ஏஎர் உடைத்து). 1066 says nothing is more degrading to the tongue than asking (இரவின் இளிவந்தது இல்), even for a cow's water. They conflict if 1066 is read as covering every act of asking; on a narrower reading 1053 speaks only of asking from the right giver, which 1066 does not mention.

894 says the unable doing harm to the able (ஆற்றுவார்க்கு ஆற்றாதார் இன்னா செயல்) is like beckoning Death with the hand. 250 asks one about to go against someone weaker (மெலியார்மேல் செல்லுமிடத்து) to think of oneself before the stronger (வலியார்முன்). Both reason from the weak facing the strong: 894 uses it as prudence in the Book of Wealth, 250 turns the same experience into a ground for compassion in the Book of Virtue.

59 says those whose home does not seek renown (புகழ்புரிந்த இல்) have no proud gait before those who deride them (இகழ்வார்முன்). 237 asks why those who cannot live with renown (புகழ்பட வாழாதார்) resent those who deride them (இகழ்வாரை நோவது எவன்) and not themselves. Both set புகழ் against இகழ்வார்: 59 says that without renown one has no answer to scorners, and 237 adds that the scorn is then one's own doing.

நிறை appears in 57 as a woman's inner guard, and here it's what anyone stands to lose without forbearance. The same inner discipline is asked of women as chastity and of people in general as character.

204 says not to plot another's ruin even by a lapse (சூழற்க), because அறம் will plot the ruin of the plotter (அறஞ்சூழும் சூழ்ந்தவன் கேடு). 176 says that one who plots wrongs for wealth (பொல்லாத சூழ) will perish (கெடும்). The shared verb சூழ் places the ruin at the stage of planning, before any act; 204 names the agent of that ruin.

1000 says great wealth got by a man without courtesy is like good milk turned by the fault of its vessel (கலந்தீமையால் திரிந்தற்று); 1006 says the man who neither uses nor gives is ஏதம் to பெருஞ்செல்வம். In both the wealth is good in itself and the holder is what spoils it, which is how Parimelazhagar reads 1006 (others take the wealth to be a misery to him).

98 says sweet speech free of smallness gives joy (இன்சொல் ... இன்பம் தரும்) here and hereafter. 911 says the sweet speech of women who desire wealth and not the man brings harm (இன்சொல் இழுக்குத் தரும்). The two predicates answer each other, and the condition in 98 (சிறுமையுள் நீங்கிய) marks the difference: what 98 promises holds only for sweet words that are not serving a mean purpose.

Both verses open with the command to learn. 391 says learn without flaw and then stand in keeping with it (கற்க கசடற ... நிற்க அதற்குத் தக); 725 says learn with measure so as to give a fearless reply (மாற்றங் கொடுத்தற் பொருட்டு). 391 gives learning its end in conduct, and 725 gives it a second end in public speech.

447 values supporters for their rebuking (இடிக்கும்) and says a ruler who has them cannot be ruined. 784 defines friendship by the same act: it is not for laughing but for going ahead to rebuke when one oversteps (மேற்சென்று இடித்தற் பொருட்டு). Rebuke is treated as the purpose of the bond in both statecraft and friendship.

130 says அறம் itself watches for the right moment and enters the path of one who has guarded against anger, learned, and is restrained (அறம் பார்க்கும் ஆற்றின் நுழைந்து); 204 says that if you plot another's ruin, அறம் plots the ruin of the plotter (அறஞ்சூழும் சூழ்ந்தவன் கேடு). In both verses virtue is an agent that acts on a person, seeking out the restrained and planning against the malicious.

In 1319 even his effort to appease her makes her angry (உணர்த்தினும் காயும்): 'you must be like this with others too'. 693 warns those who serve kings that once suspicion has arisen, clearing it is hard for anyone (கடுத்தபின் தேற்றுதல் யார்க்கும் அரிது). The court maxim and the bedroom scene describe the same trap: reassurance offered to a suspicious mind is taken as more evidence.

1022 says the family (குடி) lengthens through long-continued work that has both effort (ஆள்வினை) and mature knowledge. 604 states the reverse case: for those sunk in sloth, without worthy exertion (மாண்ட உஞற்றிலவர்), the family dies down and faults multiply (குடிமடிந்து குற்றம் பெருகும்). Together they make one claim from both sides: the fortunes of a குடி follow the exertion of its members.

521 says that honouring the old tie even when a man's means are gone (பற்றற்ற கண்ணும் பழைமை பாராட்டுதல்) is found among kin. 1047 says that one in poverty will be looked on as a stranger even by the mother who bore him (ஈன்ற தாயானும் பிறன்போல நோக்கப்படும்). The conflict holds if 1047 is read as Pope reads it, of poverty in general; the verse's own qualifier அறஞ்சாரா, poverty unconnected with virtue, which Parimelazhagar and Subramuniyaswami keep, narrows it and reduces the conflict.

584 puts the king's own kin (தம் சுற்றம்) among those a spy examines, alongside his enemies (வேண்டாதார்); 882 says not to fear enemies who are like a sword but to fear the tie with enemies who are like kin (கேள்போல் பகைவர்). The chapter on internal enmity explains why 584 does not exempt relatives from scrutiny.

963 says that in small and shrunken circumstances one must hold oneself high (சிறிய சுருக்கத்து வேண்டும் உயர்வு). 680 says those whose domain is small (உறைசிறியார்), fearing their own people's trembling, will bow to the greater and accept terms (கொள்வர் பெரியார்ப் பணிந்து). They conflict if 963's 'reduced state' includes weakness of position before a stronger party; if 963 is only about poverty and personal bearing, 680 is separate advice on statecraft.

476 says pushing on past the tip of the branch (இறந்து ஊக்கின்) ends one's life. 858 uses the same verb of hostility: leaning away from it is gain, and if one pushes on to excel in it (மிகல் ஊக்கின்), ruin pushes on in turn (ஊக்குமாம் கேடு). In both, the drive that the book elsewhere praises becomes the cause of ruin when it is carried past a limit.

1091 (the man): her kohl-lined eyes hold two looks, one that gives the sickness and one that is its cure (நோய்நோக்கு ... மருந்து). 1171 (the woman): her own eyes showed him to her and so she came to know an unabating sickness (தண்டாநோய்), and she asks why they weep. Eyes are the source of love's sickness in both, the other's eyes for the man and her own for the woman, and only his verse has a cure.

628, in the chapter on not being undone by trouble, says one who does not desire pleasure (இன்பம் விழையான்) and calls hardship natural does not come to sorrow (துன்பம் உறுதல் இலன்). 368 says those without craving have no sorrow. The renouncer's doctrine reappears as practical advice for a person at work in the world, where Parimelazhagar relates it to the pains of effort.

181 holds that not backbiting is still good in a man who otherwise does wrong (அல்ல செயினும் ... இனிது). 297 says that if one keeps to not lying, not doing the other virtues is good (அறம்பிற செய்யாமை செய்யாமை நன்று). Both single out one restraint of speech and weigh it against the whole of the rest of conduct, though 297 goes further and treats it as sufficient.

953 names a smile, giving, sweet words and not scorning (நகை ஈகை இன்சொல் இகழாமை) as the share of a true lineage. 92 takes three of these and ranks them: being sweet-spoken with a glad face (முகனமர்ந்து இன்சொலன்) is better than giving with a glad heart (அகனமர்ந்து ஈதல்). The list in 953 is flat; 92 shows the book elsewhere weighing its items against one another.

295 says one who speaks truth in accord with his heart is above those who practise austerity together with giving (தவத்தொடு தானஞ்செய்வாரின் தலை). 259 says not killing one creature and eating it is better than a thousand sacrifices. Both rank a plain restraint, not lying and not killing, above the religious practices that carry the most prestige.

513 places trust in one who has love, understanding, clarity and freedom from desire (அன்பறிவு தேற்றம் அவாவின்மை). 682 opens with the same pair, அன்பறிவு, and adds considered eloquence as the three things an envoy cannot lack. The two lists share a core of loyalty and knowledge and then differ by office: the officer handling affairs needs steadiness and no greed, the envoy needs speech.

568 says the fortune of a king who does not think things through with his circle and then rages in anger will shrink (எண்ணாத வேந்தன் ... சிறுகும் திரு). 554 says a king who acts without reflection (சூழாது) and bends the sceptre loses wealth and people. In both, the king's loss is traced to acting without deliberation, shown in anger in 568 and in injustice in 554.

506 treats having no attachment (பற்றிலர்) as a reason not to trust a person, since such a one does not fear blame. 350 tells the renouncer to hold to the one without attachment (பற்றற்றான்) in order to let attachment go. The same word is a disqualification in the chapter on choosing officers and the goal in the chapter on renunciation; the contexts differ, so this is a contrast of valuation across the books and not a contradiction.

501 names four tests, virtue, wealth, pleasure and fear for life (அறம்பொருள் இன்பம் உயிரச்சம்), by which a person is examined before being trusted (தேறப்படும்). 513 names four qualities, love, understanding, clarity and freedom from desire, in whoever has which trust lies (நன்குடையான் கட்டே தெளிவு). The first four are trials applied from outside (Parimelazhagar describes staged temptations); the second four are the traits such trials are meant to find.

723 says those who will die amid enemies are easy to find, and those who do not fear within an assembly are hard to find (அவையகத்து அஞ்சாதவர்). 872 says one may take on the enmity of those who plough with the bow but not of those who plough with the word (சொல்லேர் உழவர்). Both rank the word above the weapon, 723 by how rare the courage is and 872 by how dangerous the opponent is.

In adjacent chapters a ruler's eye is first the grace that spares and then the instrument that watches everyone, kin included (584). The Kural does not reconcile the two eyes, and 578 is the nearest it comes to a rule between them.

1026 defines நல்லாண்மை as making oneself fit to manage the house one was born into (இல்லாண்மை ஆக்கிக் கொளல்). 1133 uses the same word for what the lover had before (நல்லாண்மை பண்டுடையேன்) and has now exchanged for the palmyra horse. Set beside 1026's definition, the lover's loss is of the capacity that makes a man of use to his family, not only of pride.

351 traces birth to confusion and 361 traces it to craving, and both claim to be the root. Parimelazhagar makes them a sequence, with ignorance first and craving following, but the verses each say it singly.

850 condemns the one who denies what the world affirms. 140 says those who have not learned to conduct themselves in accord with the world (உலகத்தோடு ஒட்ட ஒழுகல்) lack understanding however much they have studied. Parimelazhagar takes 'the world' in both as the high-minded many, so both make their consensus a test that private cleverness does not override.

73 says the bond of the precious life with the body (ஆருயிர்க்கு என்போடு இயைந்த தொடர்பு) is the way that came to be joined with love, so embodiment is given a purpose. 345 says that for those undertaking to cut off births (பிறப்பறுக்கல் உற்றார்க்கு) the body itself is excess and other ties (தொடர்ப்பாடு) pointless. The value 73 gives the body-bond holds within the life of love; 345 marks where, for the renouncer, it stops holding.

In 733 the land bears the load that comes upon it (பொறை ... தாங்கி). In 990 the great earth will not bear its load (தாங்காது ... பொறை) if the worthy decline in worth. The same words describe a land's capacity to carry weight, and 990 makes that capacity depend on the character of its best people.

56 includes guarding the well-founded word, the couple's good name (தகைசான்ற சொற்காத்து), in its definition of the wife. 59 says those whose home does not seek renown (புகழ்புரிந்த இல் இலோர்க்கு) cannot walk with a proud gait before those who deride them. Parimelazhagar connects them directly, saying 59 states the fault that follows when that good name is not kept: the husband's standing in public depends on it.

774 shows a warrior who has thrown his spear at an elephant pulling out the spear lodged in his own body and laughing; 597 shows the elephant itself holding firm when struck by arrows, as the image of those who do not give way in ruin. In both, a wound taken is the occasion that shows firmness, and the Book of Wealth draws the general rule in 597 that the war chapter acts out in 774.

748 says a fort is where those who hold it keep their hold (பற்றாற்றி) and defeat even those strong enough to besiege them; Parimelazhagar notes that the smaller force does not just endure but wins. 493 says even those without strength become strong and win (ஆற்றாரும் ஆற்றி அடுப) if they know the place and act against foes while guarding themselves. 748 is 493's rule about place applied to the fort.

612 warns against letting a task perish in the middle of doing it (வினைக்கண் வினைகெடல் ஓம்பல்), because the world gives up on those who leave work unfinished. 473 describes how that happens: people start on enthusiasm without knowing their strength and break midway (இடைக்கண் முரிந்தார்). 612 demands finishing; 473 puts the remedy before the start, in measuring one's strength.

642 says ruin as well as gain comes from speech and asks for vigilance against slips. 128 gives the scale of the risk: if even one harmful word has its effect (ஒன்றானும் தீச்சொல்), the good turns to no good (நன்றாகாதாகி விடும்). 128 supplies the reason why 642 treats a lapse (சோர்வு), and not only deliberate bad speech, as the danger.

664 says saying is easy for anyone and doing as one has said is hard (சொல்லிய வண்ணம் செயல்). 779 takes the hardest case, a sworn vow in battle, and says the one who dies in the attempt cannot be blamed for failing. Death in the effort is accepted as having kept one's word, a limit on how literally 664's standard is applied.

562 asks for a light stroke after a stern show (மெல்ல எறிக); Manakkudavar takes this to mean the penalty should fall short of what the offence deserves. 550 says a king's punishing the cruel with death (கொலையிற் கொடியாரை வேந்தொறுத்தல்) is like weeding the young crop. The pairing marks where gentleness stops: for those 550 calls கொடியார், the book accepts the severest penalty.

501 says a man is to be trusted after being tested by virtue, wealth, pleasure and fear for life. 688 lists the faithful envoy's marks as purity, support, resolve and truthfulness (தூய்மை துணைமை துணிவுடைமை ... வாய்மை). Parimelazhagar explains தூய்மை as being clean in respect of wealth and pleasure and துணிவு as not holding back for fear of harm, which makes 688's qualities the passes of 501's tests.

228 speaks of the giver's joy, the pleasure of giving and being glad (ஈத்துவக்கும் இன்பம்), which hoarders do not know. 1057 speaks of the asker's joy, the heart glad within (உள்ளுள் உவப்பது), when the giving is free of scorn. The same verb உவ marks gladness on both sides of one act of giving.

822 uses women's minds as its example of something that changes (மகளிர் மனம்போல வேறுபடும்); Parimelazhagar takes this of women in general and supports it with a line from the Valaiyapathi. 974 takes single-minded women (ஒருமை மகளிர்) as its model of the constancy that greatness needs. On Parimelazhagar's general reading of 822 the two figures conflict; if 822's மகளிர் is limited to the courtesans of chapter 92, they do not.

Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar read நோநொந்து in 157 as grieving for the suffering that will come to the wrongdoers. 319 states the mechanism behind that expectation: if one does harm to others in the forenoon, harm comes to oneself in the afternoon of its own accord (தாமே வரும்). On the commentators' reading 157 presupposes 319: the injured person pities the offender because the offence will return on him, and for the same reason does not add a wrong of his own. Kalaignar instead takes the pain in 157 as the injured person's own.

444 calls greater people as support the chief of all strengths; 497 says no support is needed but fearlessness, if the thinking and place are right. Five chapters later, the book seems to qualify its own superlative.

837 says a fool's great wealth feeds strangers (ஏதிலார்) while his own go hungry. 1009 says wealth amassed by giving up love, denying oneself and ignoring virtue will be taken by others (கொள்வார் பிறர்). The miser and the fool arrive at the same result by opposite routes, one by holding wealth back and one by letting it go to the wrong people.

195 says that if people of fine nature (நீர்மையுடையார்) speak useless things, their distinction and the regard it earned leave them. 965 says even those like a hill will sink if they do a lowering thing the size of a kunri seed. Both hold that standing does not protect the eminent from a small lapse; 195 applies this to idle speech.

969 says those like the கவரிமா give up life when their honour is at stake (உயிர் நீப்பர் மானம் வரின்). 779 asks who could reproach as failures those who die so that what they vowed is not broken (இழைத்தது இகவாமைச் சாவார்). Dying to avoid going back on what one stands for appears as a matter of civil honour in 969 and as a soldier's vow in 779.

80 says the seat of life follows love, and that for those without it the body is bone wrapped in skin (என்புதோல் போர்த்த உடம்பு). 913 likens the false embrace (பொய்ம்மை முயக்கம்) of women who want wealth to embracing an unknown corpse in a dark room (ஏதில் பிணம்). 913 applies 80's premise to a particular case: a body offered without love is, for the one who holds it, a dead one.

760 says that for those who have made bright wealth in plenty (ஒண்பொருள் காழ்ப்ப இயற்றியார்க்கு) the other two, virtue and pleasure, come easily. 1009 uses the same word, ஒண்பொருள், for wealth amassed by dropping love, denying oneself and not looking to virtue, and says others will take it. So the promise of 760 fails when the two ends it names are given up in the earning; Parimelazhagar reads 760 as wealth that comes by the right way.

344 treats having nothing (ஒன்றின்மை) as the proper state of the vow. 1050 speaks of those who have nothing to enjoy (துப்புரவில்லார்) and yet do not fully renounce (துவரத் துறவாமை), calling them death to salt and gruel. Lacking things is therefore not the same as renouncing: poverty without the inner giving up is counted as a burden, not as austerity.

58 says women who 'obtain the one who obtained them' (பெற்றாற் பெறின்) gain great distinction in the world where the gods live (புத்தேளிர் வாழும் உலகு); Parimelazhagar supplies 'honour' and reads it as wives who revere their husbands. 50 says the man who lives on earth as he should is placed among the gods of the sky. The two adjacent chapters end on the same reward, one for the householder and one for the wife, each for fulfilling the household role.

954 says the well-born do not do things that diminish (குன்றுவ செய்தல் இலர்), whatever the gain. 965 uses the same word to say what follows if they do: even those like a hill sink (குன்றுவர்) if they do a diminishing thing (குன்றுவ) the size of a kundri seed. 954 gives the rule and 965 the cost of breaking it, at a scale far below crores.

Both verses use the act of putting wealth away (வை). In 226 feeding the destitute is the வைப்புழி, the place of deposit; in 228 the hard-eyed 'keep and lose' what they own (வைத்திழக்கும்). The chapter sets a store that holds beside a store that is lost.

907 gives greatness to the woman with shame over the submissive man's manhood (பெண்ணே பெருமை உடைத்து). 1137, a speech in the Book of Love, says nothing has more worth than womanhood that suffers a sea of desire and still does not mount the palmyra horse (மடலேறாப் பெண்ணின் பெருந்தக்கது இல்). In both, a woman's restraint is measured against a man's lack of it and ranked higher.

895 makes the king's anger inescapable for those under him; 899 says that if those of exalted resolve flare up (ஏந்திய கொள்கையார் சீறின்), the king himself (வேந்தனும்) breaks midway and loses his kingship. Within the chapter the pair sets up an order of power: the king who destroys others can himself be destroyed by the anger of the great. Parimelazhagar takes வேந்தன் in 899 as Indra.
100 calls harsh speech a foolish choice when sweet words are available. 184 ranks it above backbiting. The two together suggest a scale of speech: sweet, then harsh and open, then hidden.

In 1132 the man says his body and life, unable to bear it, will mount the palmyra horse, with shame set aside (நாணினை நீக்கி நிறுத்து). In 1297 the woman says she has forgotten shame through her heart's inability to forget him. Each sex is shown losing நாண் to love; the man sets it aside to act in public, and the woman finds it gone.

253 says the mind of one who has eaten a creature's body with relish does not turn to good (நன்னூக்காது), like the heart of one holding a weapon. 285 says a loving nature with அருள் in view (அருள்கருதி) is not found in those who, with goods in view (பொருள்கருதி), watch for another's lapse. In both, what the mind is fixed on, flesh or another's property, leaves no room for அருள்; Parimelazhagar glosses 253 the same way, as a mind that looks only to the meat.

1218 says that on waking he quickly becomes one who is in her heart (நெஞ்சத்தர் ஆவர்). 1249 tells her own heart that the lover is inside it (உள்ளத்தார் காதலவர்), so there is no one to go out looking for. Both use his dwelling in her heart to deny that he is absent; 1218 adds the dream so that both night and day are covered.

723 calls those who die amid enemies எளியர், easy to find. 762 says the hardness that does not fear wounds when the king falters is rare except in an old army (தொல்படைக்கல்லால் அரிது). If 723's first half is read as saying battle courage is common, the two disagree about how rare it is; if 762 is limited to courage in defeat and with reduced numbers, they do not.
389 asks the king to bear bitter words; 448 says what follows if no one speaks them: he falls with no enemy needed. Parimelazhagar's gloss on 389 uses the same idea of இடிக்கும் துணை.

36 says virtue, done without delay, is the companion that does not die when one dies (பொன்றுங்கால் பொன்றாத் துணை). 1299 says that in grief there is no companion if one's own heart is not one. Both verses ask what stays with a person when other support is gone; Book One answers virtue, and the lover's verse names the heart and finds it missing.

In 1262 the woman tells her friend that if she forgets him today (இன்று மறப்பின்), her beauty will leave her shoulders and her ornaments will slip off (கலங்கழியும் காரிகை நீத்து). In 1234 the beauty has faded and the bangles are slipping because her partner is gone (துணை நீங்கி). Read together, the bodily loss follows his absence whether she remembers or forgets, though in 1262 she holds that remembering is what prevents it.

232 makes giving the subject of all praise. 296 says there is no renown like not lying (பொய்யாமை அன்ன புகழில்லை). They conflict if both are read as naming the single greatest source of renown; Parimelazhagar's gloss on 296, that truthfulness is the cause of renown in this life, keeps the claim just as strong.

235 calls rare a death that is really a coming into existence. 780 says that if one can die so that the eyes of those who sustained one fill with tears, that death (சாக்காடு) is worth getting even by begging. The soldier's death in 780 is an instance, in the domain of war, of the death 235 says only the skilled achieve.

797 says leaving a fool's friendship is gain. 816 says that being a stranger to the wise (அறிவுடையார் ஏதின்மை) is ten million times better than close friendship with a fool (பேதை பெருங்கெழீஇ நட்பு); Pope and Subramuniyaswami render ஏதின்மை as enmity. Both verses put a fool's friendship below having no tie at all.

794 says the friendship of the well-born man who fears blame is worth getting even by giving (கொடுத்தும் கொளல்). 800 says the friendship of the ஒப்பிலார் is worth leaving even by giving something (ஒன்றீத்தும் ஒருவுக). The chapter uses the figure of payment in both directions, for acquiring a good friend and for getting free of a bad one.

838 likens a fool's possession to drunkenness added to derangement. 408 says fortune lodged with the unlearned is more painful than poverty lodged with the good (கல்லார்கண் பட்ட திரு). Both deny that wealth is a good independent of its holder; 838 gives the image and 408 the comparative judgment.

746 wants in a fort good men who help at the place where it would otherwise fall; Parimelazhagar glosses இடத்து as the point of destruction by those outside. 762 says the hardness that does not fear a wound when things give way and the force is reduced (உலைவிடத்து ஊறஞ்சா வன்கண்) is rare except in an ancient army. Both measure fighting men by what they do at the moment of collapse, in the fort and in the field.

1040 says the good woman called Land laughs on seeing those who sit idle saying 'we have nothing' (இலமென்று அசைஇ இருப்பாரை). 174 has the same words, இலமென்று, as the thought that does not move the self-controlled to covet. The plea of having nothing is refused twice: it excuses neither taking from others nor sitting idle.
382 lists fearlessness as a king's nature. 569 suggests that it also has a material condition: without prepared defences, even a king comes to fear.

Verse 9 calls a head that does not bow to the Lord's feet useless. Here a woman who does not worship a god is the one whom the rain obeys. Parimelazhagar's added 'other gods' softens the contrast, but the Tamil does not contain it.

1304 compares leaving a sulking lover unappeased to cutting an already withered creeper at its root (வாடிய வள்ளி முதல் அரிந்தற்று). 1030 says a family with no good man to prop it falls when trouble cuts it at the foot (இடுக்கண் கால் கொன்றிட வீழும்); Parimelazhagar takes this as an axe at the tree's base. Both picture a weakened plant that needed support and got the cut instead, once in love and once in the household.

Verse 74 says love gives birth (ஈனும்) to eagerness, and that gives birth to friendship, an unsought distinction (நாடாச் சிறப்பு). Verse 757 calls அருள் the child born of love (அன்பீன் குழவி), raised by the foster-mother wealth. Both use the figure of birth for what comes out of அன்பு, and together they give love two offspring, friendship in the home and grace toward all.

342 says that after renouncing, many things come about here (ஈண்டு இயற்பால பல), which Parimelazhagar takes as joys in this life. 369 says joy is unbroken even here (இன்பம் இடையறாது ஈண்டும்) once craving, the sorrow of sorrows, is gone. Both place the reward of letting go in this world (ஈண்டு), not only after death.

In 1081 his heart reels (மாலும் நெஞ்சு) because it cannot place her among goddess, peahen and woman. In 1112 he scolds the same heart for being confused at flowers (மலர்காணின் மையாத்தி நெஞ்சே), as if her eyes were like what many can see. The confusion moves from what she is to what could be compared with her, and by 1112 he treats it as the heart's error.

85 implies that the field of the host who feeds guests first yields without sowing. 545 says rain and harvest gather together (பெயலும் விளையுளும் தொக்கு) in the land of the king who wields the sceptre as he should. In both, right conduct is said to make the land fruitful, at the scale of one household's field and at the scale of a kingdom.

823 says that even after learning many good things it is hard for the unworthy to become good in heart (பலநல்ல கற்றக் கடைத்தும் மனநல்லர் ஆகுதல் மாணார்க்கு அரிது); Parimelazhagar applies this to enemies. 373 says that after much study a person's own understanding still prevails. The same limit on what books can change is stated once for understanding and once for the heart.

883 says to fear the enemy within, because at the moment of weakness (உலைவிடத்து) it cuts like the tool that cuts the potter's clay (மட்பகை). 821 says the friendship of those who join without inner accord (நேரா நிரந்தவர்) is an anvil (பட்டடை) for striking once they find the right opening (சீரிடம் காணின்). Both verses use a craftsman's tool for the hidden enemy and both place the blow at the moment that suits him.

571 says the world exists because the beauty called kindly regard exists (கண்ணோட்டம் ... உண்மையான் உண்டிவ் வுலகு). 1055 uses the same word and construction: asking goes on because the unconcealing exist (உண்மையால்). In both, a practice or the world itself is said to rest on the existence of a disposition in some people.

1109 lists sulking, reconciling and uniting (ஊடல் உணர்தல் புணர்தல்) as the rewards of those joined in love; 1267 shows the woman, before he has even returned, unable to choose between sulking and embracing and wondering whether to combine them. What 1109 states as a sequence of pleasures, 1267 shows as one impatient wish for all of them at once, which is how Parimelazhagar explains its place in this chapter.

271 says the five elements laugh inwardly (அகத்தே நகும்) at the hidden conduct of a man with a deceitful mind. 927 says those who drink and droop are seen through and always laughed at by their own town (உள்ளொற்றி உள்ளூர் நகப்படுவர்); Parimelazhagar takes கள்ளொற்றி as drinking in concealment. In both, concealed conduct has a witness that laughs, the elements within the body in 271 and the neighbours who infer what is going on in 927.

293: do not lie about what your heart knows, for after the lie your own heart will burn you (தன்நெஞ்சே தன்னைச் சுடும்). 1296: thinking alone, she finds her own heart is there to eat her. In both the tormentor is one's own heart and the setting is solitude with what one knows; 293 makes this the working of conscience, and 1296 gives it as the experience of the abandoned lover, with no fault of hers involved.

882 contrasts the enemy who is like a drawn sword (வாள்போல் பகைவர்) with the one who looks like kin, and fears the second. 828 says a weapon hides even within an enemy's hands folded in worship (தொழுதகையுள்ளும் படையொடுங்கும்), and his tears are the same. In 882 the visible sword is the safer one; 828 shows where the other sword is kept.

Parimelazhagar reads 961's இன்றி அமையா as things without which one would not survive, so the verse puts standing above life. 131 says conduct is to be guarded more than life (உயிரினும் ஓம்பப்படும்) because it gives excellence. The same ranking, a value kept ahead of survival, is made for honour in one chapter and for conduct in the other.

611 says one must not lose heart on the thought that a thing is hard (அருமை உடைத்தென்று அசாவாமை வேண்டும்), since effort gives the greatness needed. 537 says nothing is beyond doing as 'hard' (அரிய என்று ஆகாத இல்லை) when done with unforgetting care. Each denies that difficulty is a reason to give up, and each names its own remedy: effort in 611, sustained attention in 537.

124 says the stature of one who is restrained without shifting from his station (நிலையின் திரியாது அடங்கியான்) is far greater than a mountain's. 965 says even those like a hill will sink if they do a lowering thing as small as a kundri seed (குன்றின் அனையாரும் குன்றுவர்). The mountain stature of 124 holds only while the 'not shifting' holds; 965 states how little it takes to lose it.

85 asks whether one who feeds guests and eats what is left (விருந்தோம்பி மிச்சில் மிசைவான்) need even sow his field (வித்தும் இடல்வேண்டும் கொல்லோ); Parimelazhagar supplies that it will bear by itself. 1039 says that if the owner stays away and does not go to it (செல்லான் கிழவன் இருப்பின்), the land sulks like a wife. The conflict holds only if 85 is taken literally, as Parimelazhagar does, and not as a figure of praise; Kalaignar reads 85 quite differently, as asking whether such a host would hold back even his seed-grain.

Parimelazhagar reads 643 as speech that binds those who have accepted one as a friend (கேட்டார்ப் பிணிக்கும்) and makes even those who have not want friendship. 187 gives the failure of this skill: those who do not know how to make friends with pleasing talk (நகச்சொல்லி நட்பாடல் தேற்றாதவர்) part even their own kin with divisive talk. On that reading the two verses are the positive and negative of one ability, speech as what holds or breaks alliances.
