692 says that not desiring what kings desire (மன்னர் விழைப விழையாமை) brings lasting prosperity through those kings. 180 says not wanting others' goods yields victory, while coveting without thought yields destruction. The courtier's rule in Book 2 follows the same logic as 180: refraining from what belongs to another is what secures gain.

594 says gain asks the way and goes to one whose ஊக்கம் does not waver (அசைவிலா ஊக்கமுடையான் உழை). 473 says many who did not know their own strength set out on ஊக்கம் and broke midway (வலியறியார் ஊக்கத்தின் ஊக்கி இடைக்கண் முரிந்தார் பலர்). The same word names the quality praised in chapter 60 and the cause of failure here, so 473 limits 594: drive pays only when it is matched to a measured strength.

203 calls it the chief of all understanding to refrain from doing evil even to those who hate one ('செறுவார்க்கும் செய்யா விடல்'). 312 says that not hurting in return even one who has hurt you out of hatred ('கறுத்து இன்னா செய்த அக்கண்ணும்') is the settled stand of the stainless. The same rule is called knowledge (அறிவு) in the householder's chapter and purity (மாசற்றார் கோள்) in the ascetic's.

139 says that for people of good conduct it is not possible to speak evil with the mouth even by a slip (வழுக்கியும் வாயாற் சொலல்). 689 asks the same of the envoy in his own field: a firmness whose mouth does not let slip a word that brings blemish (வடுமாற்றம் வாய்சோரா). What Book 1 treats as a result of character, 689 makes a condition for carrying the king's word. (This edition prints வாய்சேரா; the commentaries read வாய்சோரா.)

Verse 63 reports the saying that one's children are one's wealth (தம்பொருள்). Verse 400 says learning is the imperishable wealth (கேடில் விழுச்செல்வம்) and that other things are not wealth (மாடல்ல). Both move the word for property from goods to something else, but 400 denies the title to everything other than learning, while 63 only reports what people say.

380 says fate is the strongest thing and gets ahead of any plan. 619 grants that a thing may not come about because of fate (தெய்வத்தான் ஆகாதெனினும்), and adds that effort still pays the wage of the body's labour (மெய்வருத்தக் கூலி தரும்). 619 accepts the limit that 380 states and marks out what remains for effort within it.

313 says that doing hurt, even to those who hated you though you did nothing to them (செய்யாமல் செற்றார்க்கும்), brings sorrow with no escape (உய்யா விழுமம்). 207 says people escape any enmity (உய்வர்) but the enmity of their own deeds follows and kills (வினைப்பகை வீயாது பின்சென்று அடும்). The shared root உய் shows the reasoning: an enemy can be survived, one's own retaliation cannot.

468 says effort without the right method fails whatever support it has (பலர் நின்று போற்றினும் பொத்துப்படும்). 640 says those without practical capacity leave things unfinished even after planning them in proper order (முறைப்படச் சூழ்ந்தும் முடிவிலவே செய்வர் திறப்பாடு இலாதவர்). The two are complementary failures: effort without method in 468, and method on paper without the ability to carry it out in 640.

799 says the friendship of those who abandon one in ruin burns the heart even to think of at the time of death (அடுங்காலை உள்ளினும்). 819 says the bond with those whose words and deeds differ is painful even in a dream (கனவினும் இன்னாது). Each verse extends the harm of a false friend beyond ordinary waking life, to the deathbed in one and to sleep in the other.

1302 gives the measure: a little sulking seasons, a little too long spoils. 1306 gives the two failures by name: without துனி and புலவி, love is like கனி and கருக்காய், which Manakkudavar reads as overripe fruit and unripe fruit. Together they make sulking a matter of degree, judged by taste, in both verses through a food image.
133 says conduct itself is lineage and lapse is low birth. 958 is less radical, since lapse leads people to doubt a man's birth, which keeps birth as the underlying fact while 133 dissolves it.

931 says not to want gambling even if you win, since what is won (வென்றதூஉம்) is like the hook a fish has swallowed. 1327 says that in a sulk the loser is the winner (தோற்றவர் வென்றார்). The two verses reverse the apparent result of a contest in opposite directions: the gambler's win is a loss that shows later, and the lover's loss is a win that shows later in union (கூடலிற் காணப்படும்).

In 1308 suffering is pointless when the other does not know or care that one suffers. In 1200 the woman tells her heart that reporting its great pain to one who is not close (உறாஅர்க்கு உறுநோய் உரைப்பாய்) is like trying to fill in the sea. Man and woman reach the same judgment from opposite sides of the couple.

1056 gives the good outcome of asking: meeting those without concealment ends the afflictions of want. 1068 gives the other outcome: the unsafe boat called asking splits when it strikes the rock called concealment (கரவென்னும் பார்தாக்க). Both make the result of asking turn on கரவு in the person asked, so 1068 states the risk that 1056 leaves out.

107 says people will remember (உள்ளுவர்) through seven births the friendship of those who wiped away their distress. 799 says the bond with those who abandoned one in ruin (கெடுங்காலைக் கைவிடுவார்) burns the heart even when thought of (உள்ளினும்) at the hour of death. Both are about how conduct in another's hard time is remembered: the helper for lives to come, the deserter up to the last moment.

570 says that a harsh sceptre over the unlearned is the only burden on the earth. 1003 uses the same phrase for hoarders. The same claim to being earth's one burden is made against a tyrant and against a hoarder.

1049 says one can even sleep in the midst of fire, but in want there is no closing the eyes (நெருப்பினுள் துஞ்சலும் ஆகும்). 896 says one burned by fire may yet survive, but those who go on offending the great will not (எரியால் சுடப்படினும் உய்வுண்டாம்). Both measure a non-physical danger by granting that fire can be endured and denying the same of the thing compared.

188 asks what people whose habit is to broadcast even the faults of those close to them (துன்னியார் குற்றமும் தூற்றும்) would do to strangers. 820 warns against the bond with those who are friendly in private and blame one in public. Both take the public exposure of an intimate as the mark of a person no one should be near.

227 promises that the one who shares his food will not meet hunger. 85 asks whether the field of one who feeds guests and eats what is left even needs sowing (வித்தும் இடல் வேண்டும் கொல்லோ). Both state as a rule that feeding others first secures one's own food.

1048 is a poor man's cry: will the want that as good as killed me yesterday come today too (நெருநலும் கொன்றது போலும் நிரப்பு)? 532 uses the same noun and verb in a simile, constant poverty killing understanding (நிச்ச நிரப்புக் கொன்றாங்கு). Both treat நிரப்பு as something that kills and that returns daily; Parimelazhagar glosses both with a man who fills his stomach each day only with great pain.

298 says outer purity comes by water and inner purity is seen through truthfulness (அகந்தூய்மை வாய்மையால் காணப்படும்). 455 says purity of mind comes resting on purity of company. The book thus gives inner purity two supports, one's own truthfulness and the people one keeps.

348 gives the prize only to those who renounce thoroughly (தீரத் துறந்தார்). 365 says those called 'freed' are those freed of craving, and the others are not freed in that way (மற்றையார் அற்றாக அற்றது இலர்), whatever else they have given up. 365 specifies what 348's 'thoroughly' requires: the giving up must reach craving, not only things.

285 describes those who, with goods in view, watch for another's lapse (பொச்சாப்புப் பார்ப்பார்), and denies them a loving nature. 1186 gives pallor the same posture: it watches for the weak moment (அற்றம் பார்க்கும்), which Parimelazhagar notes is a figurative use of 'watch'. The book's picture of the thief waiting for inattention is the picture the woman uses for what takes her colour.

758 praises acting with wealth in hand (கைத்து உண்டாக). 593 says those who hold steady energy as what is in their hand (ஊக்கம் ஒருவந்தம் கைத்துடையார்) do not grieve that they have lost their gains. The same word கைத்து is used for money in 758 and for drive in 593, which treats energy as the holding that matters when the money is gone.

427 defines those with understanding as those who know what is going to be (ஆவதறிவார்). 429 says those whose understanding guards against what is ahead (எதிரதாக் காக்கும் அறிவினார்) have no affliction that comes to shake them. 429 gives the use of the foresight that 427 only defines: knowing beforehand matters because it lets one guard beforehand.

788 defines friendship as removing a friend's distress on the spot (ஆங்கே இடுக்கண் களைவது), like the hand of a man whose garment slips. 908 says those who live as the woman of the fine brow wishes (நன்னுதலாள் பெட்டாங்கு ஒழுகுபவர்) do not see their friends' needs through (நட்டார் குறைமுடியார்). 908 names a condition under which the duty of 788 goes unmet: the man's actions are no longer his own to direct.

978 says greatness always bows (பணியுமாம் என்றும் பெருமை), and elsewhere the book calls bowing good for everyone. 903 names one bowing that brings shame: lowering oneself before one's wife (தாழ்ந்த இயல்பின்மை), which Parimelazhagar explains as arising from fear. The pair separates humility that comes from the absence of pride from submission that comes from fear.

1017 says those ruled by shame give up life for shame's sake and do not give up shame for life's sake (நாண்துறவார்). In 1297 the woman has forgotten shame because her heart cannot forget him, and Parimelazhagar glosses the shame as dearer to her than life, the valuation of 1017. The pairing sets the rule from the chapter on shame beside a speaker in the Book of Love who holds that rule and reports failing it; it is her confession, not a contrary teaching.

124 praises one who is restrained and does not shift from his station (நிலையின் திரியாது); 989 says those called the ஆழி of worth do not shift even when the age shifts (ஊழி பெயரினும் தாம் பெயரார்). Both measure a person by immovability, 124 against a mountain and 989 against the turning of an age.

856 says the life of one who declares it sweet to excel in hostility (இகலின் மிகல் இனிது என்பவன்) is close to failure and ruin. 307 says the ruin of one who takes anger to be a thing of worth (சினத்தைப் பொருளென்று கொண்டவன்) is as sure as the hand of one who strikes the ground. In both the fault is the valuing of the passion, and both attach certain or imminent ruin to it.

789 defines the height of friendship as a firm state of propping the other up (ஊன்றும் நிலை). 449 says those without the support of a prop (மதலையாம் சார்பு) have no standing (நிலை), as those without capital have no profit. 789 describes the supporter and 449 the one who needs supporting, in the chapter on a king's reliance on the great.

1283 says that though he disregards her and does only as he pleases, her eyes will not rest without seeing him (கொண்கனைக் காணாது அமையல கண்). 1244 says the eyes, wanting to see him (அவர்க் காணல் உற்று), eat her. Both make the eyes an appetite of their own that her judgment of him does not govern.

968 asks whether a life that tends the flesh is a medicine (மருந்தோ) once greatness has lost its dignity; Parimelazhagar takes this as a medicine against dying. 82 says that eating while the guest waits outside is not to be wanted even if the food were the medicine of deathlessness (சாவா மருந்தெனினும்). Both raise the idea of an immortality-medicine only to rank it below a duty, honour in one and hospitality in the other.

118 (with 115) calls not leaning to one side the ornament of the worthy (கோடாமை சான்றோர்க்கு அணி); 1014 calls shame the ornament of the worthy (அணியன்றோ நாணுடைமை சான்றோர்க்கு). The same phrase names two inner restraints, and neither is an outward decoration.

349 says the moment attachment ends births are cut off, and otherwise impermanence is what is seen (மற்று நிலையாமை காணப்படும்). 331 faults the understanding that takes the unlasting for lasting. 349 explains why the error in 331 matters: for one still attached, impermanence is the standing condition, and Parimelazhagar on 331 likewise ties the error to attachment and rebirth.

341's doubled யாதனின் யாதனின் ... அதனின் அதனின் allows release thing by thing: each thing left stops hurting. 343 demands that everything wanted be let go together (வேண்டிய வெல்லாம் ஒருங்கு). Parimelazhagar notices the difference under 341, calling giving up everything at once the chief way while granting that giving things up one by one still removes the pain each brings.
Here giving and austerity cannot last without rain. In 34, virtue is simply a spotless mind and everything else is noise. If virtue is only inward, the drought in 19 shouldn't threaten it.

658 warns that the gain of a forbidden deed turns to பீழை later. 177 says not to want gain that comes by coveting (வெஃகியாம் ஆக்கம்), because at the time of enjoying it the fruit is hard to make good (விளைவயின் மாண்டற்கு அரிதாம் பயன்). Both place the harm at the stage of the result and not at the stage of getting.

649 faults many words and praises a few faultless ones; the next verse faults those who cannot expound what they have learned so that others understand (உணர விரித்துரையாதார்). Manakkudavar reads the pair together: speak briefly, but also expand where it is needed. 650 keeps 649 from being taken as a rule of brevity alone.

351 says an inglorious birth comes from the delusion that takes what is not real for real (மருளானாம் மாணாப் பிறப்பு). 1002 ends with the same words: the delusion of thinking everything comes by wealth, and so hoarding without giving, produces an inglorious birth. The book of wealth applies the metaphysical formula to one concrete error, treating money as the thing that matters.

1316 has her treat remembering as proof of forgetting. In 1207 the woman, alone, says she does not know forgetting (மறப்பறியேன்) and that even remembering burns. The standard she holds him to in 1316, never having forgotten at all, is the one she claims for herself in separation.

117 says the low state of a person who stands fair is not held to be ruin (கெடுவாக வையாது). 988 says poverty is no disgrace (இன்மை இளிவன்று) for one who has the firmness called சால்பு. Both deny that poverty lowers a person of character; 117 says it for fairness in particular, 988 for worth as a whole.

606: even when the holdings of those who own the earth come to them (படியுடையார் பற்றமைந்தக் கண்ணும்), the slothful rarely reach an excellent fruit. 591: what makes one 'a possessor' is energy; do those without it possess even what they possess (உடையது உடையரோ)? Both deny that having things amounts to benefiting from them when the inner quality is missing. Parimelazhagar notes another reading of 606 in which the earth-owners' support, not their wealth, is what comes.

848 describes one who does not act when told and does not see for himself (ஏவவும் செய்கலான் தான் தேறான்), and calls that life a disease until it departs. 638 describes a king in the same two terms, one who destroys what the knowing say and does not know himself (அறிகொன்று அறியான்), and says the minister must still tell him what is sound. The same double failing appears in both; 848 gives the verdict on the person and 638 the duty of those beside him.

906 says that even if they live like the gods (இமையாரின் வாழினும்), men who fear their wife's bamboo-like shoulders (அமையார்தோள் அஞ்சுபவர்) have no dignity (பாடிலர்). In 1088 a lover exclaims that his might (பீடு), feared by enemies in battle, has broken before her bright forehead alone. Both show male standing giving way before a woman's bodily feature; the Book of Wealth counts it a disgrace, while in the Book of Love it is a lover's speech in the moment and carries no judgment.

Both use seven births. In 62 a child's character shields the parent, and in 107 memory of a helper persists. Parimelazhagar on 107 refers back to his explanation at 62, so he treats the phrase as one idea.

205 argues that wrongdoing won't cure poverty. 657 removes that premise: even when wealth does come through blame, the poverty of the worthy is better. Moral refusal doesn't depend on the prediction in 205.

789 places friendship's throne in supporting the friend without wavering wherever it is possible (ஒல்லும்வாய் ஊன்றும் நிலை). 818 says to let slip without a word the friendship of those who make difficult a task they could do (ஒல்லும் கருமம் உடற்றுபவர்). The same word for what lies within one's power sets the standard in 789 and identifies the friend who fails it in 818.

88 pictures people guarding their goods with pain (பரிந்தோம்பி) and still losing them. 376 says what is not allotted to one will not stay even if guarded with pain (பரியினும் ஆகாவாம் பாலல்ல), and what is one's own will not leave even if poured away (சொரியினும் போகா தம). The fate chapter gives a general ground for 88's observation: anxious guarding does not decide whether wealth stays, so spending it on guests risks nothing that guarding would have saved.

920 says double-minded women, liquor and dice are the companions of those whom Fortune has removed from herself (திருநீக்கப்பட்டார்). 936 says those covered by the goddess of misfortune named gambling (சூதென்னும் முகடி) do not eat their fill and suffer. Both verses describe a vice through the two sister goddesses: in 920 the vices attend the man Tiru has already left, in 936 one of them is Mugadi herself.

484 says the world comes to hand if one considers the time and acts by the place (இடத்தாற் செயின்). 497, in the next chapter, uses the same phrase: one needs no support but fearlessness if one thinks everything through and acts by the place (எண்ணி இடத்தால் செயின்). 484 names place as a second condition beside time, and the following chapter, with 497, takes it up as its own subject.

Both verses turn on the same phrase, 'the soft arms of the one they love' (தாம்வீழ்வார் மென்றோள்). In 1103 sleeping on them is set against the world of the lotus-eyed one; in 1325 being kept away from them (அகறலின்), though one is faultless, 'has a certain something' (ஆங்கொன்று உடைத்து). The repeated phrase shows the book's last chapter finding a pleasure in the very absence of what the first union praised.
Here only those at the Lord's feet cross the sea of births. In 38, on the commentators' reading, a daily good deed blocks the road of births, and God is not mentioned.

152 says bearing an excess done to you is good and forgetting it is better still (அதனை மறத்தல் அதனினும் நன்று). 314 ends on விடல்: do good and let it go. Parimelazhagar takes this விடல் as forgetting both the hurt and the good done in return, which would make 314 the fuller form of 152's advice; the Tamil itself says only 'do and leave'.

Verse 80 says that for those without love the body is only bones wrapped in skin (என்புதோல் போர்த்த உடம்பு). Verse 1020 says the movements of those with no shame within (நாண் அகத்தில்லார்) are like a wooden puppet feigning life by its string (மரப்பாவை ... உயிர்மருட்டியற்று). Both describe a moving body that lacks an inward quality as something without life in it, a frame of bone in one and a puppet in the other.

Verse 79 asks what all the outer parts can do (புறத்துறுப்பெல்லாம் எவன்செய்யும்) for those who lack love, the inner part (அகத்துறுப்பு). Verse 574 asks what eyes do (எவன் செய்யும்), beyond seeming to be in the face, when they have no கண்ணோட்டம். The same question in the same words is put to the whole body in 79 and to one organ in 574: a part is judged by the disposition it serves.

In 1312 she suspects his sneeze was a trick to get the customary 'live long' out of her. In 1317 she gives that blessing (வழுத்தினாள்) and at once takes it back (அழித்து அழுதாள்) with a new suspicion. One sneeze is read two ways in the chapter, as a stratagem and as proof of another woman.

502 places trust in one born in a good family (குடிப்பிறந்து), free of faults and with a shame that recoils from blemish. 681 makes birth in a fit family (ஆன்ற குடிப்பிறத்தல்) one of the envoy's three marks. Family is used in both as evidence about a person before he is given a charge, for trust in general in 502 and for the embassy in 681.

713 says those who take up speaking without knowing the assembly (அவையறியார்) do not know the kinds of speech and have no ability at all. 401 says holding forth in an assembly (கோட்டி கொளல்) without full learning is like playing dice with no marked board. Each names a different missing precondition for speaking in an assembly, knowledge of the hearers in 713 and knowledge of the books in 401, and each treats the speech that results as empty.

Verse 23 says the greatness of those who have discerned the two (இருமை வகைதெரிந்து) and taken on அறம் here stands highest in the world; Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar read the two as birth and release and the அறம் as renunciation. Verse 49 says that what is called அறம் is household life (அறன் எனப்பட்டதே இல்வாழ்க்கை). On the commentators' reading of 23 the two verses attach the word அறம், and the highest standing, to different lives. Kalaignar reads 23 as choosing good over bad in general, and on that reading there is no conflict.

864 says one who does not leave off anger (நீங்கான் வெகுளி) and has no நிறை is easy for anyone, at any time, anywhere. 305 says that if you would guard yourself, guard against anger, because unguarded anger kills oneself (தன்னையே கொல்லுஞ் சினம்). 305 states the self-destruction as an ethical fact; 864 shows how it works in a contest, by making the angry man open to any opponent.

121 ends அடங்காமை ஆரிருள் உய்த்து விடும், and 168 ends with envy, called a பாவி, which destroys fortune and தீயுழி உய்த்து விடும். The same closing verb phrase, 'drives and leaves one there', is used for lack of restraint and for envy, so the two vices are given the same power to deliver a person to a bad place.

749 places a fort's distinction in the actions by which enemies are brought down as soon as battle is joined (முனைமுகத்து); Parimelazhagar explains these as recognising the attack begun and choosing the acts that defeat it. 767 says an army is one that knows the way to bear the battle coming at it (தலைவந்த போர்தாங்கும் தன்மை அறிந்து) and advances. Both ask for trained response to the enemy's opening move, from the walls and in the field.

109 says that even harm like killing disappears when one recalls a single good the person once did (அவர் செய்த ஒன்று நன்று உள்ள). 807 says those whose bond has come by the way of love do not cut off love even when the friend does ruinous things (அழிவந்த செய்யினும் அன்பறார்). Both have the same 'even if they do grave harm' (செயினும்) clause; what outweighs the harm is a remembered favour in one and long affection in the other.

520 says that if the one doing the work does not bend, the world will not bend (கோடாமை கோடாது உலகு). 546 says victory comes from the king's sceptre, provided it does not bend (கோலதூஉங் கோடாதெனின்). கோடாமை, not bending, is the mark of the just sceptre, and 520 applies the same word to the officer, on whose straightness the world's straightness is made to depend.

437: the wealth of one who clings to it without doing what should be done with it (செயற்பால செய்யாது இவறியான்) perishes without lasting. 228 asks whether the hard-eyed who keep what they have and lose it (வைத்திழக்கும்) don't know the joy of giving. Both assume hoarded wealth is lost anyway; 228 adds what the hoarder missed in the meantime.

437 says wealth perishes when its owner does not do the things that ought to be done (செயற்பால செய்யாது ... கெடும்). 466 says one perishes by doing what is unfit and also by not doing what is fit (செய்தக்க செய்யாமை யானுங் கெடும்). The miser of 437 is a case of 466's second half: ruin by omission.

797 calls it gain to give up and leave the friendship of fools (பேதையார் கேண்மை ஒரீஇ விடல்). 839 uses the same phrase, பேதையார் கேண்மை, and says it is very sweet because there is no pain in parting from it. Read together, 839 is the ironic version of 797: the one good thing about such a friendship is the leaving of it.

Verse 19 says giving and austerity (தானம் தவம் இரண்டும்) will not stay in the world if the sky does not give. Verse 559 says that if the king acts with justice bent (முறைகோடி), the sky will not pour in season (ஒல்லாது வானம் பெயல்). Chapter 2 makes virtue depend on rain; 559 makes the rain depend in turn on a human virtue, the ruler's justice, so the dependence runs both ways.

980 says greatness covers others' exposure (அற்றம் மறைக்கும்) and smallness only speaks their faults. 1015 gives the feeling behind that conduct: being ashamed of another's disgrace as of one's own. One who feels the other's பழி in this way has no reason to tell it.

851 defines இகல் as the disease (நோய்) that spreads பகல், the ill nature of division, among all living beings. 886 takes the same division to its end inside one's own circle: if ஒன்றாமை arises among ஒன்றியார், escaping death (பொன்றாமை) is hard at any time. The general diagnosis of 851 becomes a specific warning about a ruler's own people; Parimelazhagar reads 886 of a king.

In 1081 the man cannot decide whether she is an அணங்கு, a choice peahen or a woman, and his heart reels (மாலும் என் நெஞ்சு). 918 says the embrace of deceiving women (மாய மகளிர் முயக்கு) is called an அணங்கு for those without discerning sense. The same word names a spirit that overpowers a man in both books: here it is a lover's wonder, there a warning, and Parimelazhagar glosses it in 918 as a divine woman who takes life through desire.

263 speaks of the others, householders on Parimelazhagar's reading, as having forgotten தவம் while they provide for renouncers. 48 says a household life that keeps others on their way and does not slip from virtue has more endurance than those who do penance (நோற்பாரின் நோன்மை உடைத்து); Parimelazhagar reads 'keeps on their way' as supporting ascetics. On 48's account the provider has not forgotten austerity: his life already contains more of it.

617 says the dark goddess of misfortune lives in sloth (மடியுளாள் மாமுகடி) and the lotus goddess lives in the effort of the one without sloth. 371 says sloth (மடி) and its opposite are themselves produced by the fate of loss and the fate of gain. In 617 fortune depends on whether one is slothful; 371 adds that whether one is slothful depends on fate.

112 says a fair person's wealth is a support to his posterity (எச்சத்திற்கு ஏமாப்பு). 171 states the reverse: if one covets others' goods without fairness (நடுவின்றி), the family perishes (குடிபொன்றி) and guilt comes at once. Both tie நடுவு to what happens to one's line, 112 as promise and 171 as warning.

304 counts the death of laughter and joy (நகையும் உவகையும்) as the harm that makes anger the worst enemy. 999 says that for those not capable of laughing (நகல்வல்லர் அல்லார்க்கு) the great world lies in darkness even by day. 999 describes the state that 304 says anger produces.

In 1143 the man says the gossip the town knows is like having obtained what he has not obtained (பெறாஅது பெற்றன்ன நீர்த்து). In 1213 the woman sees in dreams the man who gives nothing in waking life, and lives by it. Both take a substitute for union as if it were union: public talk for him, a dream for her.

1165: she asks what those who bring grief in friendship would do as enemies; Parimelazhagar says this is aimed, in a sulk, at the friend who has not sent a message. 805 advises that when friends do something hurtful (நோதக்க நட்டார் செயின்) it should be understood as folly or as great intimacy. 805 offers the charitable reading that her question refuses.

479 says the life of one who lives without knowing the measure (அளவறிந்து வாழாதான்) perishes. 947 says that one who eats a great deal without regard to the measure of his digestive fire (தீயளவன்றித் தெரியான் பெரிதுண்ணின்) gets disease without measure (நோய் அளவின்றிப் படும்). Ignoring a measure brings ruin of wealth in one verse and of health in the other. 479 is printed with a corrupted character in அளவறிந்து in this edition.

509 says to trust no one without examining them and, having examined, to trust what is to be trusted (தேறற்க யாரையும் தேராது). 825 says that those who are not at one with you in mind are not to be judged trustworthy by their words in any matter (சொல்லினால் தேறற்பாற்று அன்று). 825 adds to the rule of examination a statement of what cannot count as evidence.

435 says the life of one who does not guard before a fault arrives (வருமுன்னர்க் காவாதான்) perishes like straw before fire. 569 applies the same logic to war: the king who has not prepared his defence beforehand is overtaken when the battle arrives (செருவந்த போழ்தில்) and perishes. Both place the failure in the time before the danger, not in the moment of it.

Verse 78 likens the loveless life to a withered tree on hard ground. Verse 576 says those who have eyes and no kindly regard are like trees fixed in the soil (மண்ணோடியைந்த மரத்தனையர்). In both a person without the inward quality, அன்பு in one and கண்ணோட்டம் in the other, is reduced to a tree, alive in form and without response.
The earth is morally responsive in both: it yields less under a body without fame, and laughs at those who sit idle pleading poverty. Land is more than a backdrop to human conduct in the Kural.

569 says a king who has made no defence (சிறைசெய்யா வேந்தன்) will be seized by fear when war comes and quickly perish. 534 says that for the fearful there is no fort (அச்ச முடையார்க்கு அரணில்லை); Parimelazhagar explains that defences are no use to a frightened mind. One verse says lack of a fort produces fear, the other that fear cancels a fort, so the fort is necessary but not sufficient.

452 says water takes the nature of the land, and understanding the nature of one's company (இனத்தியல்பு). 959 says the sprout shows what lay in the ground (நிலத்தில் கிடந்தமை கால் காட்டும்) and speech shows the family one was born in. Both treat a person as carrying the mark of the ground they stand in, 452 for the company kept and 959 for birth.

Verse 77 says அறம் scorches what has no love as the sun scorches what has no bones (வெயில்போலக் காயுமே). Verse 204 says that if one plots another's ruin, அறம் plots the plotter's ruin (அறஞ்சூழும் சூழ்ந்தவன் கேடு). In both அறம் is an agent that acts against a person, and Parimelazhagar glosses it in both places as அறக்கடவுள், the god of virtue.

1308, which Parimelazhagar gives to the man during a sulk, asks what use suffering is where there is no lover who recognises that one suffers (நோதல் எவன் ... அஃதறியும் காதலர் இல்லா வழி). 1242 has the woman tell her heart that suffering is folly when he has no love (நோவது பேதைமை). Both speakers, from either side of the relationship, make pain depend for its point on the other's loving awareness of it.

655 tells one not to do deeds over which one will grieve, saying 'what have I done' (எற்றென்று இரங்குவ செய்யற்க). 535 uses the same verb, இரங்கு, for the grief of one who failed to guard in advance. The pairing shows regret following from omission in 535 as it follows from commission in 655.

Both open with the same words, மறைப்பேன்மன் ('I would hide it'), and both say the attempt fails: in 1161 the pain rises like spring water under baling, in 1253 desire shows itself without her intending it, like a sneeze (குறிப்பின்றித் தும்மல்போல்). Read together, one figure says concealment makes it grow and the other that it escapes her will altogether.

217 makes a tree the figure of a generous man's wealth: a tree that is medicine and does not fail ('மருந்தாகித் தப்பா மரம்'). 576 makes a tree the figure of people who have eyes but no kindly regard: they are like trees joined to the soil ('மண்ணோடு இயைந்த மரத்தனையர்'). The book uses the tree in two ways, for what gives to all who come to it and for what stands unmoved, so the image alone carries no fixed value.

1005 says those who neither give nor enjoy have nothing even with crores piled up (கோடியுண்டாயினும் இல்); 591 asks whether those without energy really have what they have. Both separate holding goods from having them, 1005 by the test of use and 591 by the test of the holder's drive.

353 says that for those who have left doubt and become clear (ஐயத்தின் நீங்கித் தெளிந்தார்க்கு) the sky is nearer than the earth. 702 says one who knows without doubt what is within another (ஐயப்படாஅது அகத்தது உணர்வானை) should be held equal to a god. In both, knowing free of doubt lifts a person toward the divine, once in the knowledge of reality and once in a courtier's reading of minds.

In Parimelazhagar's reading, the two make one argument across chapters: learning travels with the soul through births, while caste rank ends with the body. That is why 409 can rank learning over birth.

154 ties நிறை to forbearance: to keep நிறையுடைமை, live guarding பொறையுடைமை. 864 pairs the same two things in the negative, describing the man who does not leave off anger and has no நிறை (நீங்கான் வெகுளி நிறையிலன்) as easy prey for anyone. The commentators gloss நிறை differently in the two places (Parimelazhagar: சால்பு in 154; Pope, following him, has keeping secrets in 864; Manakkudavar on 154 has a conduct of self-guarding), but in both verses its presence goes with restraint of anger and its absence with unchecked anger.

903 calls a man's stooping before his wife (இல்லாள்கண் தாழ்ந்த) இயல்பின்மை, something against the natural order, which shames him among the good. 55 praises the wife who rises worshipping her husband (கொழுநன் தொழுதெழுவாள்). The two show that the book fixes the direction of deference in marriage: it is a merit in the wife and a disgrace in the husband.

931 opens with the same prohibition, வேண்டற்க: do not want gambling even if you win, because the winnings are like the hook a fish has swallowed. 177 says வேண்டற்க of the gain got by coveting, whose fruit turns out badly. Both warn against a gain that is real at the moment of taking and harmful afterwards.
Two images of bearing a load form a stack: five qualities are pillars carrying worth, and worth carries what the earth bears. The chapter's architecture rests the world on small daily dispositions.

308 asks for no anger even under harm like fire. 852, in the chapter on hostility in the Book of Wealth, says that even if someone does what cannot be borne, meaning division, not doing harm in return is best (இன்னா செய்யாமை தலை). The same advice, with the same 'even if ... செயினும்' form, is given as virtue in one book and as policy in the other.

892 warns that going on without cherishing the great (பெரியாரைப் பேணாது ஒழுகின்) brings, through them, ills that do not leave. 976 says the intent to cherish and win the great (பெரியாரைப் பேணிக் கொள்வேம் என்னும் நோக்கு) is simply absent from the minds of the small. The shared verb பேணு ties them: 976 names who it is that fails to cherish, 892 what the failure costs.

964 says people who have come down from their position (நிலையின் இழிந்தக் கடை) are like hair fallen from the head. 973 says those who are not low are not low even when placed low (கீழிருந்தும் கீழல்லார் கீழல்லவர்). They conflict if 964's நிலை means outward rank or station; on Parimelazhagar's reading it means the high standard the well-born hold themselves to, so the fall is their own doing and the verses agree.

190 asks what harm could come if people saw their own faults as they see strangers' faults (ஏதிலார் குற்றம்போல் தங்குற்றங் காண்கிற்பின்). 1285 says she cannot see her husband's fault when he is before her, as the eye cannot see the kohl-stick touching it. In both, what is nearest is what goes unseen; 190 treats this as a failing to correct, and 1285 as a fact about love.

885 says an inner enmity that comes in the form of kinship (உறல்முறையான் உட்பகை) brings many ills of a deadly kind (இறல்முறையான் ஏதம்) to the ruler. 735 defines a land as one without many factions, without ruinous inner enmity (பாழ்செய்யும் உட்பகை) and without murderous marauders who harass the king. The danger 885 describes for the king's person and household is, in 735, something whose absence is part of what makes a country a country.

800 says to leave the friendship of the unfit even at a cost. 818 says how to leave one kind of bad friend, those who make hard work of what they could do: without speaking of it, let the friendship slip (சொல்லாடார் சோர விடல்). 818 adds a manner of leaving to 800's instruction to leave.
Under Manakkudavar's reading of 1029 the two use the same verb, மறைத்தல்: greatness hides others' weakness, and so does the family's support. He bears the cost in his body.

446: against one who can conduct himself as having the worthy for his company (தக்கார் இனத்தனாய்), enemies have nothing left to do. 868 gives the reverse case: one with no good qualities and many faults is without company (இனன் இலன்), and that is a protection to his opponents. Both verses use the word இனம் and both make a ruler's exposure to enemies depend on who stands with him.

5 says the two kinds of deed do not attach (சேரா) to those devoted to the Lord's praise. 359 says the pains due to attach will not attach (சார்தரா சார்தரு நோய்) to one who knows the support and lives so that supports perish; Parimelazhagar takes these as the fruits of stored deeds still awaiting experience, and Manakkudavar takes சார்பு itself as the hold of deeds. Devotion in 5 and knowledge with practice in 359 are credited with the same effect on karma.

429 says those whose understanding guards against what is coming (எதிரதாக் காக்கும் அறிவினார்) meet no affliction that shakes them. 372 says a fate of loss makes a person foolish (பேதைப் படுக்கும் இழவூழ்); Parimelazhagar adds that this happens even to one who has understanding. The protection 429 promises rests on understanding, and 372 says understanding itself can be taken away by fate.

1017: those ruled by shame give up life for shame and do not give up shame for life (நாணால் உயிரைத் துறப்பர்). 1163 shows that ranking from inside: she drops neither love nor shame, and it is her life, the pole (உயிர் காவா), that takes the strain; Parimelazhagar adds that the life will snap.

171 says that coveting another's goods without fairness ruins the family (வெஃகின் குடிபொன்றி). 1043 names poverty itself a craving (நல்குரவு என்னும் நசை) and gives it the same effect on ancient descent. Read together, 1043 treats poverty as harmful to a lineage through the desire it breeds, the mechanism 171 states for covetousness.

654 says those of unshaken sight do nothing degrading even in distress (இடுக்கண் படினும்). 174 says those of 'புன்மையில் காட்சி' who have conquered the senses will not covet on the plea 'இலம்' (we have nothing). Both verses name a clear-sighted person (காட்சியவர்) and deny that need is an excuse; 174 applies it to coveting, 654 to action generally.

465 pictures a rash attack as planting the enemy in a bed where he will grow. 879, in a chapter on enemies, says to cut a thorn tree while it is young, since when hardened it wounds the hand that cuts it (இளைதாக முள்மரம் கொல்க). Both treat the enemy as a plant whose growth is the danger: 879 says to stop it early, 465 warns against tending it by one's own haste.

871 says enmity, a thing without good in it (பண்பிலதனை), is not to be wanted even in jest (நகையேயும் வேண்டற்பாற்று அன்று). 867 says the enmity of one who stays close and does unfitting things must certainly be got, even by paying for it (கொடுத்தும் கொளல்வேண்டும் மன்ற). The conflict holds if 871 is read as a rule about all enmity; Parimelazhagar narrows it to enmity that brings no benefit, which would leave room for 867.

158 says to defeat those who did wrong out of arrogance by one's own worthiness (தம் தகுதியான் வென்று விடல்), which Parimelazhagar reads as forbearance. 314 goes a step further: do them a kindness so that they feel shame. Both keep the vocabulary of contest (winning, punishing) while replacing retaliation, and 314 adds the active good that 158 leaves unstated.

332 says great wealth (பெருஞ்செல்வம்) arrives and leaves like a theatre crowd, with no exception stated. 112 says the wealth of a person of rectitude does not decay and is a support to his descendants (சிதைவின்றி எச்சத்திற்கு ஏமாப்பு உடைத்து). If 332 is read as a claim about all wealth, 112's durable wealth contradicts it; the conflict eases if 332 is taken, with Parimelazhagar, as wealth that stays only while its cause in good deeds lasts.

332 likens the coming of great wealth to a crowd gathering at a dance hall and its going to that crowd dispersing. 592 says possession of goods does not stay and slips away (பொருளுடைமை நில்லாது நீங்கிவிடும்), while possession of inner drive is real possession. The impermanence of wealth taught to the renouncer is restated in the Book of Wealth, where it becomes a reason to value energy and not a reason to withdraw.

994 praises people of நயன் whose doing good makes them useful (பயனுடையார்). 216 says wealth falling to one who has நயன் (நயனுடையான்) is like a fruit-bearing tree (பயன்மரம்) ripening in the middle of the town. 216 supplies the picture for 994: the person of நயன் is of பயன் to everyone within reach.
In 1093, the water poured into love's plot is her lowered glance. In 1147 the water is her mother's harsh words. What nourishes love moves from the most private gesture to the most hostile.

678 says to get one deed done by means of another, as one binds an elephant with a rutting elephant (யானையால் யானையாத் தற்று). Manakkudavar takes this as setting an enemy's own enemy against him. On that reading 875 is the case worked out: one who is alone with two enemies should take one of them as an ally (இன்துணையாக் கொள்க அவற்றின் ஒன்று). Parimelazhagar reads 678 more generally, as making a task in hand the means to another like it.

503 says hard learning and freedom from fault still leave some ignorance when one looks closely. 373 says that however many subtle books one studies, one's own inherent understanding still prevails (தன் உண்மை அறிவே மிகும்). Both set a limit on what study can change in a person, one in the chapter on choosing officers and one in the chapter on fate.

520: let the king look daily into the one doing his work (நாடோறும் நாடுக மன்னன்). 553: the king who does not look daily and do justice loses his land daily (நாடொறும் நாடி முறைசெய்யா மன்னவன் நாடொறும் நாடு கெடும்). The same phrase of daily examination is used for officers and for justice, and both tie the state of the land to that routine.

907 pairs நாண் and ஆண்மை: manhood that obeys a woman is worth less than womanhood with shame. In 1134 a lover says the fierce flood of desire carries off the raft made of shame and good manliness (நாணொடு நல்லாண்மை என்னும் புணை). Both treat shame and manliness as the two things a man loses together under a woman's hold; 907 states it as a judgment, 1134 as a lover's own complaint.

849 ends with the unseeing person continuing to see as he saw (தான்கண்டவாறு). 373 says that however many subtle books one studies, one's own underlying understanding prevails (தன் உண்மையறிவே மிகும்). Both hold that what is brought from outside, a teacher in 849 and books in 373, does not displace the understanding a person already has.

812 treats the friendship of those who leave when the gain ends (அறின் ஒரூஉம்) as a matter of indifference, gained or lost. 799 says that the friendship of those who abandon one in ruin (கெடுங்காலைக் கைவிடுவார்) burns the heart even when recalled at the hour of death (உள்ளினும் உள்ளஞ் சுடும்). Read together, losing such a friend is no loss, yet having trusted one is not painless.

887 says a family with inner enmity is not joined, though it joins like a casket and its lid (செப்பின் புணர்ச்சிபோல் கூடினும் கூடாதே). 786 says friendship that makes only the face smile is not friendship; friendship is what makes the heart within smile (நெஞ்சத்து அகநக). Both deny the name of union to a joining that is only on the surface, in the family and in friendship.

223 says not uttering the misery of 'I have nothing' (இலனென்னும் எவ்வம் உரையாமை), and giving, are found in one of good family; Pope takes the words as the giver's excuse, while Parimelazhagar first takes them as the asker's plea. 1070 says the asker's life leaves when the word is spoken (சொல்லாட); Parimelazhagar takes this as the concealer saying 'no'. On Pope's reading of 223 both verses are about the word of refusal, which the well-born never say and which 1070 says kills the hearer.

505 says a person's own deeds are the touchstone (கருமமே கட்டளைக் கல்) of greatness and smallness. 986 asks what the touchstone of worth is (சால்பிற்குக் கட்டளை யாதெனின்) and answers: accepting defeat even from those not one's equal. Both use the assayer's stone for testing people; 505 names the general test, deeds, and 986 picks one particular deed as the decisive one.

831 says folly is accepting harm and letting gain go. 925 gives a concrete case in drinking: handing over wealth to receive ignorance of one's own body (பொருள்கொடுத்து மெய்யறியாமை கொளல்), which it traces to கையறியாமை, not knowing what to do. The drinker's purchase is 831's exchange carried out literally.

44 says a life that fears blame and has பாத்தூண், food shared out, never sees its line fail (வழியெஞ்சல் எஞ்ஞான்றும் இல்). 227 uses the same compound: the one habituated to shared food (பாத்தூண் மரீஇயவனை) is hardly touched by the disease called hunger. Both attach a protective result to the same practice, one for the descendants and one for the sharer himself.

799 says the thought of false friends burns the heart (உள்ளஞ் சுடும்). 293 says that after a lie one's own heart burns one (தன்நெஞ்சே தன்னைச் சுடும்). In 293 the heart burns for one's own fault, in 799 for another's desertion, so the same inner fire is given two different causes.

617 says the lotus goddess lives in the effort of the unslothful (மடியிலான் தாளுளாள்); 594 says prosperity finds its own way to the person of unwavering energy. Both personify fortune as choosing where it lives by the person's exertion, and neither leaves it to chance.

203 calls refraining from harm even to enemies the height of understanding, and 261 defines austerity by harmlessness. Yet 264 advertises the power to crush foes. Parimelazhagar's 'enemies of virtue' and his comment that ascetics don't think of it are attempts to close this gap.

1243 asks the heart why it sits and suffers in thought (இருந்துள்ளி என் பரிதல்) when he has no pitying thought. 1296 says that when she sits alone and thinks (தனியே இருந்து நினைத்தக்கால்) her heart is there only to eat her (என்னைத் தினிய). Both describe sitting and remembering as self-inflicted harm, and each blames the heart for it.

647 says no one can easily defeat a fearless, unfaltering speaker in a contest (இகல் வெல்லல் யார்க்கும் அரிது). 872 gives the advice that follows for the other side: take on the enmity of those whose plough is the bow if you must, but not of those whose plough is the word (சொல்லேர் உழவர் பகை). Parimelazhagar takes the latter to be ministers, the people 647 describes.

1173 finds it laughable that the eyes looked of themselves and weep of themselves. 1176 goes a step further: it is sweet (ஓஒ இனிதே) that the eyes which gave her this sickness have fallen into it too (தாஅம் இதற்பட்டது). The sequence moves from mockery of her eyes to satisfaction at their suffering.

In 1263 she waits for the man who left wanting victory; in 1268, which Parimelazhagar assigns to the man away on the king's service, he wishes the king would engage and win (வினைகலந்து வென்றீக வேந்தன்) so that he can join his wife for the evening. On that reading the pair gives both ends of one separation: her longing for his return and his impatience for the work to finish.

139 says a person of conduct cannot speak evil even by a slip; 1044 says that even in the well-born, poverty brings the slackness from which degrading words are born (இற்பிறந்தார் கண்ணேயும் இன்மை இளிவந்த சொற்பிறக்கும் சோர்வு தரும்). 1044 names a condition, want, under which the slip of speech that 139 calls impossible does happen to good people.

714 uses a colour pair for intelligence: be bright (ஒள்ளியர்) before the bright, and take the colour of white plaster (வான்சுதை வண்ணம்) before the blank (வெளியார்). 844 uses the same pair: whiteness (வெண்மை) is the conceit that says 'we have brightness' (ஒண்மை உடையம் யாம்). Read together, the learned person of 714 puts on whiteness knowingly before those who, by 844, are white because they think themselves bright.

Verse 29 speaks of the anger (வெகுளி) of those who stand on the hill of good qualities; on Parimelazhagar's reading they are sages whose anger, though it lasts a moment, cannot be warded off by its target. Verse 310 says those who have renounced anger are the equals of renouncers (சினத்தைத் துறந்தார் துறந்தார் துணை), which makes freedom from anger the renouncer's mark. On Parimelazhagar's reading the book's model renouncer still gets angry, and dangerously. Kalaignar reads 29 as saying their anger does not stay even a moment, and on that reading the two verses agree.

41 makes the householder the support of the three, read by Parimelazhagar as the other orders, ascetics included. 263 asks, with கொல், whether 'the others' (மற்றையவர்கள்) have forgotten தவம் because they want to provide for the renounced (துறந்தார்க்குத் துப்புரவு வேண்டி); Parimelazhagar glosses 'the others' as householders. The Thavam chapter thus looks at the same arrangement from the ascetic side: the householder's support of renouncers is given as the reason he does no austerity himself.

948 tells the healer to look for the root of the disease (நோய்முதல்) before the remedy. 360 does this for suffering in general: when desire, anger and confusion perish even in name, the நோய் perishes. The chapter on true perception treats pain as chapter 95 treats illness, by naming causes and removing them.

791 says that for those who keep friendship there is no leaving once it is formed (வீடில்லை). 809 says the world wants (விழையும் உலகு) those who do not leave (விடாஅர்) the friendship of friends of unbroken long standing. What 791 gives as a reason for caution before befriending, 809 presents as what earns a person general regard.

394 describes the learned as people whose company others want again after it ends. 643 defines speech as what binds those who heard it and makes even those who did not hear want it (கேளாரும் வேட்ப). 643 gives the means, speech, for the effect 394 describes.

391 asks for two things in order: learn without flaw (கசடறக் கற்க), then stand in keeping with it (நிற்க அதற்குத் தக). 834 names the person who does the first and skips the second: one who has studied, understood and even taught others but is not himself restrained (தானடங்கா) is the greatest of fools. The pair shows that the second half of 391 is not an afterthought: learning without it is classed as folly.

179 says திரு, knowing the way (திறன் அறிந்து), goes to those who know virtue and do not covet. 594 says ஆக்கம் asks the way (அதர்வினாய்) and goes to the one of unwavering drive. In both, fortune is a traveller that seeks the person out; Book 1 gives non-coveting as what draws it and Book 2 gives energy.

1202 says thinking of the beloved brings no pain, and 1207 says even thinking burns. If Parimelazhagar is right that a man speaks 1202 and a woman 1207, then the chapter makes a pointed contrast between their experience of memory.
265 recommends austerity because it gets whatever one wants. 370 says the unchanging state comes from removing desire. The means is sold by appeal to the very thing the end abolishes.

1283 says her eyes will not rest without seeing her husband (கொண்கனைக் காணாது அமையல கண்) even though he does as he pleases; 1265 prays to see the same கொண்கன் until her eyes are full. Both make the eyes' need to see him the thing that must be satisfied before anything else can mend.

461 tells one to weigh what will be lost, what will be gained and the later yield, and then act (அழிவதூஉம் ஆவதூஉம் ... ஊதியமும் சூழ்ந்து செயல்). 676 has the same closing command and also three items, but different ones: what it takes to finish, the obstacles, and the great yield at completion (முடிவும் இடையூறும் ... படுபயனும் பார்த்துச் செயல்). 461 is an account of cost and return; 676 keeps the return and adds the course of the work itself.

943 says to eat knowing the measure once digestion is complete, as the way one who has a body can carry it long (நெடிதுய்க்கும் ஆறு). 479 says the life of one who does not live knowing the measure (அளவறிந்து வாழாதான்) seems to exist and then perishes; Parimelazhagar refers that measure to one's wealth. The same phrase governs both the stomach and the purse. (This edition prints 'அறவறிந்து' in 943; Parimelazhagar's gloss reads அளவு அறிந்து.)

128 says that if even one bad word has its effect, the good turns out not good (ஒன்றானும் தீச்சொல் ... நன்றாகாதாகி விடும்); Parimelazhagar takes this as the person's other merit turning bad. 965 says even hill-like people sink if they do a lowering thing the size of a kundri seed. Both hold that a single small lapse is enough to cancel a large standing good, in speech in one verse and in honour in the other.

510 speaks to the ruler: doubt of one already trusted brings trouble that does not end. 693 speaks to the courtier: guard against grave faults, because once suspicion has arisen it is hard for anyone to clear it (கடுத்தபின் தேற்றுதல் யார்க்கும் அரிது). The two verses describe the same event, a ruler's suspicion, as lasting damage from each side of the relationship.

1201 says love gives a joy that does not end even in recollection (உள்ளினும் தீரா). 1215 says that what she saw in waking was sweet then, and the dream too is sweet just while it is seen (கண்ட பொழுதே இனிது). Manakkudavar glosses both pleasures as lasting for that moment; Parimelazhagar takes her point to be that dream and waking are therefore equal for her. On either reading the woman's sweetness is tied to the moment of seeing, where the man's persists in thought.

1058 says that without askers the world would be puppets coming and going, which makes askers part of a living world; Manakkudavar draws the conclusion that asking is therefore not to be held low. 1062 says that if one must live even by begging, let the maker of the world wander and perish (பரந்து கெடுக உலகியற்றியான்). They conflict on whether a world that contains begging is as it should be; the conflict depends on reading 1058 as approval and not only as a remark about what givers need.

837 speaks of great wealth that has come to a fool (பெருஞ்செல்வம் உற்றக்கடை) and benefits the wrong people. 1000 says great wealth obtained by one without character (பண்பிலான் பெற்ற பெருஞ்செல்வம்) is like good milk spoiled by its vessel. Parimelazhagar notes on both verses that the verb marks wealth received and not made; both hold that the holder's defect ruins what the wealth could do.

970 says the world worships and praises the radiance of the honourable who do not live on in disgrace. 235 says that a ruin which is growth and a death which is existence (உளதாகும் சாக்காடு) are hard to reach except for the skilled. 235 gives the general idea that 970 applies: a death can leave a person present in fame.

694 says that in the presence of the great one should suppress whispering and shared smiles (செவிச்சொல்லும் சேர்ந்த நகையும் அவித்தொழுகல்). 715 calls the restraint of not speaking first among elders (முதுவருள் முந்து கிளவாச் செறிவு) the best of good things. Court and assembly get the same rule of holding speech back before superiors; 694 extends it to private asides and laughter, which Parimelazhagar says the king would take as aimed at himself.

866 says the enmity of a man of blind anger and excessive lust (காணாச் சினத்தான் கழிபெருங் காமத்தான்) is to be welcomed. 360 names the same two, with delusion, as what must perish for suffering to perish (காமம் வெகுளி மயக்கம்). What the chapter on true knowledge treats as obstacles to release, the chapter on enemies treats as what makes an opponent beatable; Parimelazhagar says such men destroy themselves.

Both look at a death through those left behind. 780's soldier dies so that his patron's eyes fill and such death is worth begging for, and 970's man of honour is worshipped by the world. Honour and the warrior ethic share one structure.

118 describes a balance that first makes itself level (சமன்செய்து) and then weighs (சீர்தூக்கும்). 561 says a king is one who examines a case fittingly (தக்காங்கு நாடி) and punishes in proportion (ஒத்தாங்கு ஒறுப்பது); Parimelazhagar glosses the examining as done 'standing in the middle' (நடுவாக நின்று). The two steps of the scale, being level and then measuring, match the two steps of just punishment.

255 says that if one eats flesh, அளறு (the mire, hell) will not open its mouth (அண்ணாத்தல் செய்யாது), which Parimelazhagar explains as not opening to let him out again. 835 says a fool can in one birth make the அளறு he will enter and sink in for seven (எழுமையும் தான் புக்கழுந்தும் அளறு). Both use the same rare word for a hell one makes for oneself and does not get out of.

963 asks for an upright bearing (உயர்வு) when one's means have shrunk. 988 says poverty is no disgrace (இன்மை ஒருவற்கு இளிவன்று) for one who has the firmness called worth (சால்பென்னும் திண்மை). 988 supplies the ground for 963's demand: want does not itself lower a person, so there is no reason to stoop in it.

1082 makes her answering glance an armed host (தானை). 1113, listing her beauties, calls her kohl-lined eyes spears (வேலுண்கண்). The eye as weapon is a fixed figure of the man's praise, used first as his alarm and later as a plain item of description.

478 says a small income does no harm if spending does not exceed it. 463 says those with understanding do not undertake a deed that loses the capital for the sake of gain (ஆக்கம் கருதி முதலிழக்கும் செய்வினை ஊக்கார்). Both put keeping what one has ahead of getting more: 478 for the regular flow of income and spending, 463 for a single venture.

308 says that even if someone does harm like the touch of massed flames (இணர்எரி தோய்வன்ன இன்னா செயினும்), not being angry is good, if one can manage it (புணரின்). 312 says that even when someone has done hurt in hatred, not doing hurt in return is the settled stand of the stainless (மறுத்தின்னா செய்யாமை). 308 governs the feeling and 312 the act that would follow from it; 308 alone concedes that it may not be possible.

On Parimelazhagar's reading, 87 scales the fruit of hospitality to the guest's worth (விருந்தின் துணைத்துணை). 221 says giving to those who have nothing (வறியார்க்கு ஒன்று ஈவதே ஈகை) is the only real giving, and all the rest is like a loan expecting return. One verse values the gift by the receiver's merit and the other by the receiver's need; the conflict depends on reading துணை in 87 as merit and on treating feeding a guest and giving as the same kind of act.

545 says rain and harvest gather in the land of the king who rules justly (பெயலும் விளையுளும் தொக்கு). 1034 says those who hold the grain bring many kings' umbrellas under their own. The dependence runs in both directions: in 545 good rule yields harvest, and in 1034 harvest yields the king's wider rule.

373 says that however many subtle books one studies, the understanding that is truly one's own still prevails (தன் உண்மையறிவே மிகும்). 262 says austerity too succeeds only for those who already have it. Both hold that a discipline taken up now, study or austerity, yields only according to what the person brings to it; Parimelazhagar refers both to what earlier births have fixed.

791: inquire first, since after befriending there is no leaving (நட்டபின் வீடில்லை). 467: think and then resolve on a task, and to say 'we will think after resolving' (துணிந்தபின் எண்ணுவம்) is a lapse. The same order of thought before an irreversible step is applied to friendship and to action.

428 makes fear of the right things the work of the knowing (அறிவார் தொழில்). 1075 says fear is the whole basis of proper behaviour among the base (அச்சமே கீழ்களது ஆசாரம்), which Parimelazhagar takes as fear of harm from the king. Together they show that fear in itself does not separate the wise from the low; what separates them is that the wise fear what deserves it and the base behave only for fear of being punished.
1051 tells one to ask of those worth asking and makes refusal their fault, not yours. 1035 presents a person who never needs the permission, and who is on the giving end of that same act.

94 asserts that sweet speakers do not fall into want, without saying how. 525 says one who can give and speak sweetly (கொடுத்தலும் இன்சொலும் ஆற்றின்) will be surrounded by layer on layer of kin (அடுக்கிய சுற்றத்தால் சுற்றப்படும்). 525 supplies a worldly mechanism for 94's promise: sweet speech gathers people around one, and a person so surrounded is not left destitute.

Verse 77 compares the loveless to a thing without bones (என்பிலது) dried by the sun; Kalaignar and Subramuniyaswami take it as a worm. Verse 80 says the body of those without love is bones wrapped in skin (என்புதோல் போர்த்த உடம்பு). The chapter uses bone twice for the loveless in opposite ways, once as what they lack and once as all they are.

344 says having nothing at all is natural to the vow (இயல்பாகும் நோன்பிற்கு ஒன்றின்மை) and that owning anything brings back confusion. 1036 says that if ploughmen fold their hands, even those who say 'we have given up what is desired' have no standing (விட்டேம் என்பார்க்கும் நிலை இல்லை). The renouncer's owning nothing rests on others who produce food.

188 describes people whose habit is to broadcast (தூற்றும்) the faults of those near them. 1076 likens the base to a beaten drum because they carry any secret they have heard to others (கேட்ட மறை பிறர்க்கு உய்த்துரைக்கலான்). 1076 places the habit of 188 in the Kural's portrait of the base person.

851 names the fault as பகல், splitting apart, and its chapter closes (860) by setting நகல் against இகல். 187 uses the same pair of roots: those who do not know how to make friends by நகச்சொல்லி will பகச்சொல்லி and separate even their kin. The chapter on backbiting already holds the contrast between dividing and laughing together that the chapter on hostility is built on.

228 speaks of a pleasure the hoarder never learns, ஈத்துவக்கும் இன்பம். 598, which Parimelazhagar applies to kings, says those without inner drive never reach the proud joy of saying 'we have been generous' (வள்ளியம் என்னும் செருக்கு). The pleasure of giving is missed through hardness in the one verse and through lack of energy in the other.

97 says speech that yields benefit and does not part from pleasantness (பயன்ஈன்று பண்பின் தலைப்பிரியாச் சொல்) produces நயன் and brings forth good (நன்றி). 194 says speech with no benefit and no pleasantness (பயன்சாராப் பண்பில்சொல்) is without நயன் and removes one from good (நன்மையின் நீக்கும்). The four terms பயன், பண்பு, நயன் and நன்மை recur in the negative, so 194 is 97 inverted; Parimelazhagar glosses பண்பு as sweetness and நயன் as justice in both.

119 says rectitude is the absence of crookedness in speech (சொற்கோட்டம்), provided there is none within (உட்கோட்டம்). 279 says the straight arrow is cruel and the bent lute (யாழ்கோடு) is good, so judge people by what their deeds do. Both use straight and bent to separate appearance from substance: 119 will not take straight words as proof without a straight mind, and 279 will not take outward shape as proof at all.

629: one who does not crave the pleasure within pleasure does not come to pain within pain (இன்பத்துள் இன்பம் விழையாதான்). 1166: the pleasure of love is a sea and its pain when it afflicts is larger still (துன்பம் அதனிற் பெரிது). The woman's experience fits the link between relishing pleasure and suffering pain that 629 states as a rule in the Book of Wealth.

42 names the householder as the support of those who have renounced (துறந்தார்க்கும் ... இல்வாழ்வான் என்பான் துணை), along with the destitute and the dead. 263 asks, with a wry கொல், whether the rest have forgotten தவம் out of a wish to provide for renouncers (துறந்தார்க்குத் துப்புரவு வேண்டி). It turns the duty stated in 42 into an explanation, or an excuse, for why householders do no austerity themselves.

488 says to bear with enemies on meeting them (செறுநரைக் காணின் சுமக்க), for when their end comes their head will go down; Parimelazhagar glosses சுமக்க as bowing. 680 has the small bow to the great to obtain terms. 488 adds what 680 does not say: that such bowing can be a way of waiting for the stronger side's fall.

400 gives the title of real wealth to learning. 241 gives it to grace (அருட்செல்வம் செல்வத்துள் செல்வம்), with the reason that wealth of goods is found even among the base. The same move appears in the Book of Virtue with a different winner, and 241's reason, who can hold it, differs from 400's, whether it can be lost.

1108 specifies 'two who desire' (வீழும் இருவர்க்கு இனிதே): the close embrace is sweet to both. 1196: love on one side only is painful, and like a carrying pole it is sweet on both ends (இருதலையானும் இனிது). Both make sweetness depend on the love being mutual, 1108 in fulfilment and 1196 from the woman who lacks it.

49 says what is called virtue is household life, and 'that too' (அஃதும்) is good if it is not something others blame (பிறன் பழிப்பது இல்லாயின்). Parimelazhagar takes அஃதும் as renunciation and the blame as false conduct in ascetics (Manakkudavar keeps it on household life). 280 says neither shaving nor growing the hair is needed if one drops what the world has blamed (உலகம் பழித்தது ஒழித்து விடின்). On Parimelazhagar's reading the chapter on false ascetics works out the condition 49 states in passing: the renouncer's standing rests on being free of blame.

195 says useless talk costs people of fine nature their distinction (சீர்மை சிறப்பொடு நீங்கும்). 957 says a fault in the well-born shows up high, like the spot on the moon (மதிக்கண் மறுப்போல் உயர்ந்து). 957 supplies a reason for 195: a fault that would pass unnoticed in others is conspicuous in those held high.

529 says those who were one's own and left will return to kinship when the cause of the discord is absent (அமராமைக் காரணம் இன்றி வரும்). 633 lists among a minister's abilities reuniting those who have parted (பிரிந்தார்ப் பொருத்தல்). 529 says how that reunion comes about: the ground of the estrangement has to be removed, which Parimelazhagar takes as a fault on the king's own side.

136 says the strong do not slacken in conduct, knowing the harm that comes of a lapse (இழுக்கத்தின் ஏதம் படுபாக்கறிந்து); 164 says people do no wrong out of envy, knowing the harm that comes of the wrong path (இழுக்காற்றின் ஏதம் படுபாக்கு அறிந்து). The second lines are nearly the same words, and both verses ground good behaviour in foreseeing consequences, which 136 counts as strength (உரவோர்).

1113 lists her features as metaphors: body a tender shoot (முறி), teeth pearls, and kohl-lined eyes that are spears (வேலுண்கண்). 1084 had already noticed the mismatch this list contains: her eyes, with a look that eats the life of those who see them, are at war (அமர்த்தன) with her gentle womanly nature. Read together, the spear in the inventory of soft things is the same contradiction 1084 names outright.

Verse 22 says that to state the measure of the greatness of renouncers (துறந்தார்) is like counting the dead of the world (இறந்தாரை எண்ணிக்கொண்டற்று). Verse 310 rhymes the same two words: those who exceed in anger (இறந்தார்) are like the dead, and those who have renounced anger are equal to renouncers (துறந்தார் துணை). In 22 the dead supply only a number too large to count; in 310 the same pairing sets renouncers and the dead as opposite ends, and extends the renouncer's standing to anyone who gives up anger.

791 says those devoted to friendship cannot leave a friend once made. 797 calls leaving a fool's friendship pure gain. Parimelazhagar's 800 offers a way out: leaving is for what one took on without knowing.

852, on hostility, says that even if someone does unbearable things intending division, not doing hurt in return out of hostility is the highest course (இகல்கருதி இன்னாசெய்யாமை தலை). 312 says not hurting in return (மறுத்தின்னா செய்யாமை) is the stand of the stainless. The same rule, in nearly the same words, is carried from personal purity into the politics of faction.

1036 says that if ploughmen fold their hands, even those who say 'we have given up desire' (விட்டேம் என்பார்) cannot keep their state. 263 assumes the same dependence: renouncers need others to supply their needs (துப்புரவு). Both verses note that renunciation rests on people who have not renounced.

95 says being humble and sweet-spoken (பணிவுடையன் இன்சொலன் ஆதல்) is a person's ornament, and nothing else is. 419 says a mouth that bows (வணங்கிய வாய்) is hard to come by without fine listening. 95 holds humble speech up for everyone, and 419 adds a condition: it has to be prepared for by listening.

Verse 76 says the ignorant hold that love supports only virtue, while it is the help (துணை) for மறம் as well; Kalaignar reads மறம் as valour, Parimelazhagar as the hostility that love removes. Verse 862 asks how a man without love (அன்பிலன்), without allies and without strength of his own can wear down an enemy's might. On Kalaignar's reading 862 is the case in point: in Book 2 love is listed first among the things a fighter needs.

616 says effort produces fortune. 594 says increase asks the way and goes to the one of unwavering drive (அதர்வினாய்ச் செல்லும் அசைவிலா ஊக்கமுடையானுழை). Both place the source of prosperity in the person's exertion, and 594 pictures it as prosperity doing the seeking. The first word of 594 is truncated in this edition (க்கம் for ஆக்கம்).

788 defines friendship by the moment of need: like the hand of a man whose garment slips, it removes distress there and then (ஆங்கே இடுக்கண் களைவது). 814 pictures the reverse, a horse that gives way in the battle itself (அமரகத்து). Both locate the test of a friend at the instant of crisis, one by the hand that acts unasked and one by the mount that fails.

714 tells the speaker to change with the audience, bright before the bright and blank before the blank. 425 says understanding is what does not open and close (மலர்தலும் கூம்பலும் இல்லது அறிவு). If 425's second half is read generally, as steadiness of bearing, the two disagree about whether the wise adapt their display; on Parimelazhagar's reading, where 425 is about constancy in friendship with the world, the conflict disappears.

495 shows a strong animal losing outside its own element: the crocodile out of water is killed by others. 500 gives the sharper case, where a jackal kills a fearless war elephant in mud where its feet sink (காலாழ் களரில் நரியடும்). Together they state both halves: one's own ground makes one win, and the wrong ground lets even a much weaker creature win.

573 asks what use an eye is without kindly regard (கண்என்னாம் கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லாத கண்), as a melody is no use that does not fit the song. 705 asks what use eyes are among the limbs if they cannot read another's sign (என்ன பயத்தவோ கண்). Both judge the eye by what it does for another person, kindness in one verse and understanding in the other, and not by sight.

48 says a household life that keeps others on their path (ஆற்றின் ஒழுக்கி) and does not slip from virtue has more endurance than those who do penance (நோற்பாரின் நோன்மை உடைத்து). 225 says the strength of the strong is enduring hunger, and that comes behind the strength of those who remove that hunger (மாற்றுவார் ஆற்றலின் பின்). Both rank the one who provides above the one who abstains, and both do it by granting the ascetic's own virtue, endurance, and awarding more of it to the provider.

284 speaks of காதல் grown in களவு and means desire for stealing, which ends in undying sorrow; in 1092 the man says the small look her eyes steal (கண் களவு கொள்ளும் சிறுநோக்கம்) is more than half of love's pleasure. The same word களவு is condemned as theft of goods in the book of virtue and prized as the stolen glance in the book of love, where it is a lover's speech and not a teaching about theft.

778 says the lord's anger does not reduce the standing or ardour (சீர்) of fearless warriors. 895 says those who have drawn the anger of a king of fierce might (வேந்து செறப்பட்டவர்) will not survive anywhere they go. Both use the verb செறு for the king's anger; 778 marks a case where it is harmless, anger at excess of loyal zeal, while 895 concerns those who offend the powerful, whom Parimelazhagar takes to be rival kings.

This is Parimelazhagar's own cross-reference. He cites 166 to read 135's simile: as the envious man's kin suffer, so do a man's kin when he lacks conduct. The commentary reads one verse by way of the other.

937 says time spent in the gaming hall ruins long-held wealth and character (பழகிய செல்வமும் பண்பும் கெடுக்கும்). 1043 says poverty destroys together one's ancient descent and one's தோல் (தொல்வரவும் தோலும் கெடுக்கும்), which Pope takes as dignity of speech. The two sentences have the same shape: an inherited standing and a personal quality lost at one stroke, with gambling as a cause and poverty as a cause.

509 orders examination first and commitment after. 791 says nothing ruins like befriending without inquiry, because for those who keep friendship there is no letting go once it is made (நட்டபின் வீடில்லை). Friendship follows the same sequence as appointment, and 791 states the reason the order matters: the commitment is hard to reverse.

641 sets the good of the tongue above every other good. 411 calls the wealth of the ear the wealth among wealths and the head of them all (செல்வத்துள் எல்லாம் தலை). The book gives the top place once to listening and once to speaking, in chapters addressed to the learner and to the minister.

723 says those who will die among enemies are easy to find and those who do not fear in an assembly are rare (பகையகத்துச் சாவார் எளியர் அரியர் அவையகத்து அஞ்சாதவர்). 690 asks the envoy to face death (இறுதி) while speaking in a hostile court. 723 separates the two kinds of courage and rates the second as rarer; the envoy of 690 needs both together, which indicates how much the verse asks.

264 credits austerity with the power to crush foes. On Parimelazhagar's reading of 305, the ascetic who uses this power in a curse loses his austerity and returns to the misery of births. The power is real, but using it destroys its source.

279 says the straight arrow is cruel and the bent lute is upright, so take people by the nature of their deeds (வினைபடு பாலால் கொளல்); 505 says one's own deeds are the touchstone of greatness and smallness (கருமமே கட்டளைக் கல்). The same rule appears as a test for ascetics in the book of virtue and as a test for choosing officers in the book of statecraft.

985 says that bowing is the strength of those who accomplish things and the weapon by which the worthy turn their opponents (பணிதல் ... மாற்றாரை மாற்றும் படை). 1258 calls her lover's lowly speech (பணிமொழி) the weapon that breaks her firmness. Humility as a படை is praised in the ethics of the worthy, and in the love poems the woman sees the same device used on her and calls its user a thief.

Harsh speech in 100 is merely a stupid choice of raw fruit. In 129 it leaves a scar that never heals. The first chapter on speech treats the speaker's loss, and this one treats the listener's lasting injury.

795 says to choose as friends those who can rebuke (இடித்து) and bring one to tears over a wrong. 448 says a king without those who rebuke him (இடிப்பாரை இல்லாத) perishes even with no one to ruin him. The rebuker counts as a safeguard both for the private person choosing friends and for the king choosing his support.

107 says the friendship of one who removed one's distress is remembered through seven births (எழுமை எழுபிறப்பும்). 398 says learning gained in one birth (ஒருமைக்கண்) is a protection through seven (எழுமையும்). The seven-birth span is the book's figure for what outlasts a single life, used here for a debt of gratitude and there for learning.

In 1162 she says she cannot hide this sickness, and that telling it to the one who caused it brings shame (உரைத்தலும் நாணுத் தரும்). In 1237 she asks her heart whether it can gain honour by telling him of her wasting shoulders. The two give opposite values to the same act of telling him, shame in one and possible honour (பாடு) in the other; in 1237 it is the heart and not she herself who would carry the word.

41 calls the householder the துணை who stands on the good path (நல்லாற்றின் நின்ற) for 'the three' (இயல்புடைய மூவர்), whom Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar take as the other three orders of life (Kalaignar instead reads parents, spouse and children). 1036 says that if the ploughmen's hands fold (கைம்மடங்கின்), even those who say 'we have let go of desire' (விட்டேம் என்பார்) have no standing (நிலை). On the older commentators' reading both verses make the renouncer's state depend on someone who stays in the world and produces: the householder in Book 1, the farmer in Book 2.

42 lists துவ்வாதவர், those who have nothing to eat or enjoy, among the people the householder supports. 226 says that ending the destroying hunger of those without means (அற்றார் அழிபசி தீர்த்தல்) is the place where a person who has gained wealth stores it (பொருள் வைப்புழி). 226 turns the duty stated in 42 into a claim about what wealth is for.

236 says: if you appear, appear with renown, and for those without it not appearing is better than appearing (தோன்றலின் தோன்றாமை நன்று). 1003 says the appearance (தோற்றம்) of men who cling to accumulation and do not want renown (இசை வேண்டா) is a burden to the land. Both judge a person's coming into the world by renown, and 1003 names the misers as a case of those who 'appear' without it.

10: the great sea of birth is swum by those who reach the Lord's feet and not by others (பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல் நீந்துவர்); Parimelazhagar supplies the feet as the raft. 1164: the sea of love exists and the raft to swim it does not (அது நீந்தும் ஏமப்புணை). The same structure of a sea crossed only with a support appears in the first chapter and in a separated woman's complaint.

In 1308 the man asks what use suffering is when there is no lover who knows 'this one is suffering' (அஃதறியும் காதலர் இல்லா வழி). In 1197 the woman asks whether Kaman fails to see her suffering. Both speakers treat pain as needing a witness, and each finds the one who ought to notice absent.

138 calls good conduct the seed of good (நன்றிக்கு வித்தாகும் நல்லொழுக்கம்) and says bad conduct always gives suffering; 361 calls craving the seed that produces unending birth for all beings (தவாஅப் பிறப்பீனும் வித்து). The seed figure is used for a cause whose yield comes later and keeps coming, once for a good crop and once for a bad one.

1255 says the dignity of not going after one who has turned away is unknown to the lovesick (செற்றார்பின் செல்லாப் பெருந்தகைமை). In 1298 her heart reasons the opposite way about where disgrace lies: it thinks that to scorn him would be a disgrace (எள்ளின் இளிவாம் என்று எண்ணி) and so keeps thinking of his side. 1298 shows the lovesick heart not merely ignorant of that dignity, as 1255 has it, but supplied with its own argument from honour for doing without it.

1255 says the dignity of not going after one who has turned away (செற்றார்பின் செல்லாப் பெருந்தகைமை) is something the lovesick cannot know. 1292 shows it: her heart goes to him (சேறி) though it has seen that he is not attached to her. 1255 gives the general statement and 1292 the instance, addressed to the heart that does the going.

428 says not fearing what should be feared is folly and fearing it is the work of the knowing (அஞ்சுவது அஞ்சல் அறிவார் தொழில்). 464 gives one such fear and what it does: fear of disgrace (இளிவென்னும் ஏதப்பாடு) keeps people from beginning what they have not made clear.
