The general rule of 428 is applied in 464 to the start of an undertaking.

935 says those who clung (இவறியார்) in pride to dice, gaming hall and skilled hand became people with nothing (இல்லாகியார்). 437 uses the same word of the miser: the wealth of one who clings (இவறியான்) without doing what should be done perishes. இவறுதல், holding on and not letting go, ends in loss in both verses, whether the thing held is money or the game.

613 says the standing of a benefactor rests on labour. 1035 says those whose way is to eat what their hands produce do not beg and give to those who beg without hiding anything (கைசெய்தூண் மாலையவர்). The farming chapter shows 613's general claim in one occupation: the person who works with his hands is the one in a position to give.
Both move the definition of being alive from body to relationship: 80 to love, 214 to knowing what is due. The body without these is bone and skin, or a corpse.

285 says a loving nature with அருள் in view (அருள்கருதி) is not found in those who, with goods in view (பொருள்கருதி), watch for another's lapse. 176 says one who stands on the path desiring அருள் (அருள்வெஃகி) perishes if he desires பொருள் (பொருள்வெஃகி) and plots wrongs. Both verses set அருள் and பொருள் as rival objects of one desire and say the second drives out the first.
அற்றார் are the destitute in 226, to be fed, and the freed in 365, to be revered. The same word for lacking marks both the most pitiable person and the most complete one.

In 1317 sneezing brings the charge that some woman is thinking of him. In 1318 he holds the sneeze back (தும்முச் செறுப்ப) and she weeps anyway: 'are you hiding from me that your people think of you?' (நுமர் உள்ளல் எம்மை மறைத்திரோ). The two verses close both exits: sneezing and not sneezing are both faults.

1106: his life sprouts afresh whenever he touches her. 1124: she is to his life what living is when they are together, and what dying is when she leaves (வாழ்தல் உயிர்க்கன்னள் ... சாதல் அதற்கன்னள்). Both tie his உயிர் to her presence; 1124 states the other half, which 1106's 'each time' (உறுதோறு) implies.

477 says to give knowing the measure, for that is the way of guarding wealth while bestowing it (அளவறிந்து ஈக அது பொருள் போற்றி வழங்கு நெறி). 943 says to eat knowing the measure once the last meal is digested, for that is the way to carry the body far (அளவறிந்து உண்க அஃது உடம்பு பெற்றான் நெடிதுய்க்கும் ஆறு). The two verses have the same build, a command to know the measure followed by 'that is the way', applied to wealth in one and the body in the other. Both verses are printed with அறவறிந்து in this edition; the reading அளவு is from Parimelazhagar's gloss.

520 tells the king to look daily (நாடோறும் நாடுக) into the one doing his work, since the world stays straight if he does; 582 makes constant, quick knowledge of everyone's affairs the king's own occupation (வேந்தன் தொழில்). Both treat continuous inquiry, not occasional inspection, as the core of rule; 582 widens the object from the king's officers to everyone.

130 says virtue watches for the right moment and comes by the path to the one who guards against anger and has learned restraint (அறம் பார்க்கும் ஆற்றின் நுழைந்து). 1018, as the commentators read it, has virtue ashamed to come near the shameless. Together they give the two directions of the same figure: virtue seeks out the restrained and shrinks from those without shame.

1291 opens the chapter with the woman asking her heart why it is not hers when his heart is his own (நீ எமக்கு ஆகாதது). 1300 closes it with the general form: when one's own heart is not one's kin (நெஞ்சம் தமரல் வழி), it is nothing that strangers are not. Parimelazhagar gives the first to the woman and the last to the man, so the chapter begins and ends with the same complaint from each side.
In Parimelazhagar's reasoning on 408, poverty doesn't ruin the good. 532 makes chronic poverty the very image of what destroys understanding. Either understanding survives poverty, or it doesn't.

924 says shame turns away from the drinker. In 1288 the speaker tells her lover that his chest is to her as liquor is to those who have enjoyed it, wanted even though it does harm that brings disgrace (இளித்தக்க இன்னா செயினும்). The simile in the Book of Love takes for granted what 924 teaches, that drink disgraces, and uses it to describe a desire that persists in spite of shame.

838 says a fool getting something into his hand is like a deranged man getting drunk (மையல் ஒருவன் களித்தற்று). 925 says paying out wealth to buy oblivion shows ignorance. 838 uses drunkenness as the image for what a fool does with property, and 925 describes drunkenness itself as a fool's use of property.

205 quotes the plea 'இலன் என்று' as an excuse for wrongdoing. 1040 quotes the same plea, 'இலமென்று', as an excuse for sitting idle, and says the good woman called Land laughs at those who make it. The book hears 'I have nothing' twice as a pretext, once for evil and once for sloth, and rejects it both times.

Here the texts' settled view exalts renouncers above all. In 49, on Parimelazhagar's reading, the thing called virtue is household life, and renunciation is good only if it is blameless. The book states both verdicts without reconciling them.

135 takes it as given that the envious have no gain (ஆக்கம்); 169 says the gain of the crooked-hearted and the ruin of the upright are things to be pondered (அவ்விய நெஞ்சத்தான் ஆக்கமும் ... நினைக்கப்படும்). 169 concedes that the case 135 calls non-existent can occur and needs explaining, which weakens the simile's premise; Parimelazhagar softens it by adding 'if they occur'.

466 says one is ruined by not doing what is fit to do (செய்தக்க செய்யாமை யானுங் கெடும்). 538 says what has been praised must be carefully done, and those who slight it and do not do it (செய்யாது இகழ்ந்தார்க்கு) have nothing through seven births. 538 takes the omission half of 466 and extends its cost beyond this life.

420 treats those without the ear's taste as people whose death and life are the same. 214 says only one who knows what is fitting truly lives (உயிர்வாழ்வான்), and anyone else is counted among the dead (செத்தாருள் வைக்கப்படும்). The book repeatedly denies real life to those who lack one defining quality; here the quality is listening, and in 214 it is knowing one's duty to others.

664: saying is easy for anyone; doing as one has said (சொல்லிய வண்ணம் செயல்) is hard. 819: the bond with those whose deed is one thing and word another (வினைவேறு சொல்வேறு பட்டார்) is bitter even in a dream. 664 states the gap between word and deed as a difficulty of execution; 819 judges the same gap in a friend as a fault of character.

525 names giving and pleasant speech as what surrounds a man with kin. 526 keeps giving, now great giving (பெருங்கொடை), and replaces pleasant speech with not cherishing anger (பேணான் வெகுளி), and raises the result to a following unmatched on earth. The pair is not a repetition: the second verse moves from a positive manner to the removal of what drives people away.

834 says no one is a greater fool than the person who has studied, understood and taught others and yet does not restrain himself (தானடங்கா). 175 says subtle and wide understanding is worth nothing if its owner covets and does வெறிய things. Both hold that learning which does not govern conduct does not count.

1297 says that, caught up with a foolish heart that cannot forget him, she has forgotten even shame (நாணும் மறந்தேன்). 1257 says she knows nothing of a thing called shame (நாண் என ஒன்றோ அறியலம்) when the one she cherishes does out of desire what she longs for. The two verses give the same loss of shame from two moments, separation in 1297 and reunion in 1257.

780 calls a death that brings tears to one's ruler's eyes worth begging for, in the chapter on martial pride. 723 calls those who die among enemies easy to find. The Kural holds both, and each chapter's supreme value is deflated by the other.

193 says that a man's spreading out useless matter in speech itself announces that he is without நயன் (நயனிலன் என்பது சொல்லும்). 959 says the words of the mouth show the family one comes from, as a sprout shows the soil. In both the speech testifies about the speaker; 193 makes the talk itself the subject of the verb 'says', which Parimelazhagar notes.

261 defines the form of tavam as two things: bearing the pain that comes to one (உற்றநோய் நோன்றல்) and doing no harm to living beings. 160 uses the same verb for both the faster and the one who endures harsh words (நோற்பார்). By 261's definition the person in 160 who bears abuse and does not retaliate already meets both parts of tavam, which explains how 160 can rank him ahead of those who fast.

113 says to give up at once gain that comes from leaving fairness (நடுவிகந்தாம் ஆக்கம்), even if it yields only good (நன்றே தரினும்). 328 says that, however great the gain that brings good (நன்றாகும் ஆக்கம் பெரிதெனினும்), gain that comes by killing (கொன்றாகும் ஆக்கம்) is lowest to the worthy. The same concession, 'even if it is good and large', is refused in both; only the forbidden means differs.

211 says duty-giving seeks no return (கைம்மாறு). 221, opening the next chapter, defines giving as giving to those who have nothing, and says everything else has the nature of 'குறியெதிர்ப்பை', a measured loan to be returned. 221 turns 211's point into a test: a gift that looks to a return is not giving.

1092 values the small look her eyes steal (கண்களவு கொள்ளும் சிறுநோக்கம்) at more than half of love; 1275 says her கள்ளம், her stealth, contains a medicine. Theft is the figure for her indirect signalling in both, at first meeting in 1092 and after reunion in 1275.

391 treats right conduct as what should follow flawless learning. 823, on false friends, says that even after studying many good things (பலநல்ல கற்றக் கடைத்தும்) it is hard for the unworthy (மாணார்) to become good at heart. It limits 391: study does not by itself produce the standing-by-it, which is why 391 has to command it separately.

412 allows the stomach only a little (சிறிது), and Parimelazhagar explains the word by saying heavy eating multiplies disease and desire. 946, in the chapter on medicine, says well-being stays with the one who eats knowing to stop short (இழிவறிந்து உண்பான்) and disease with the heavy eater (கழிபேர் இரையான்). The same restraint at the table is asked for in the name of listening in one verse and in the name of health in the other.

502 places trust in one born of good family, free of faults, with a shame that recoils from blemish (குடிப்பிறந்து ... வடுப்பரியும் நாணுடையான்). 794 says the friendship of one born of good family who is ashamed of blame on himself (குடிப்பிறந்து தன்கண் பழிநாணுவானை) should be had even at a price. The same two criteria, birth and shame, are used to choose a king's officer and to choose a friend.

986 says the touchstone of worth is accepting defeat (தோல்வி கொளல்) even from those who are not one's equal. In 1327 the man says that in a lovers' quarrel the one who loses has won (ஊடலில் தோற்றவர் வென்றார்), as the reunion shows. Both treat yielding as the better outcome; 1327 is a lover's remark about a sulk, while 986 states a test of character.

1147 makes the sickness of love a crop, manured by gossip and watered by a mother's words, that grows long (நீளும் இந்நோய்). 1227 makes the same இந்நோய் a flower that buds in the morning and opens in the evening. In both the woman describes her lovesickness as a plant with its own growth, fed in 1147 and timed in 1227.

334 says what shows itself as a 'day' (நாளென ஒன்றுபோற் காட்டி) is a blade that saws through life (உயிர் ஈரும் வாள்), for those who perceive it. 1221 has the parted woman tell the hour it is not evening (மாலையோ அல்லை) but a thing that eats the life of those once wed (உயிருண்ணும் வேலை; Parimelazhagar takes வேலை as a final hour, Manakkudavar and Kalaignar as a spear). Both unmask a unit of time as something that consumes life, one as a general truth of impermanence, the other as one lover's experience of separation.

1171: she asks why her eyes weep, since they showed him to her (தாம் காட்ட யாம் கண்டது). 1244: the eyes consume her in their wish to see him (அவர்க்காணல் உற்று). In both she speaks of her eyes as agents apart from herself, with wants of their own that she pays for.

752 reports that all scorn the poor and all honour the rich. 988 says lack is no disgrace to one who has the firmness called worth (இன்மை ஒருவற்கு இளிவன்று சால்பென்னும் திண்மை). 752 describes how the world behaves; 988 denies that the scorn is deserved where character is present, which Parimelazhagar's gloss on 752 (scorned 'even if they have every good') makes pointed.

135 pairs the same two words: as the envious have no ஆக்கம், so one without ஒழுக்கம் has no உயர்வு. 161 fuses them, asking that freedom from அழுக்காறு be taken as ஒழுக்காறு. The rhyme ஒழுக்கு/அழுக்காறு is used in both to set envy and conduct side by side.

524 says the fruit of having gained wealth is to live surrounded by one's kin (சுற்றத்தால் சுற்றப்பட ஒழுகல்). 837 says that when a fool gets great wealth, strangers eat their fill and his own people go hungry (ஏதிலார் ஆரத் தமர்பசிப்பர்). 837 shows the failure of exactly the use 524 names: wealth that does not reach one's own people has missed its purpose.

882 says do not fear enemies who are like swords, but fear the tie with enemies who are like kin (கேள்போல் பகைவர்). 1300 finds the same reversal inside one person: the heart that should be தமர், one's own people, is not, and beside that the distance of outsiders hardly counts. The lesson of the chapter on enmity within, that the danger is in what is closest, is applied in 1300 to the heart.

598 says those without drive never reach the pride of saying 'we are generous' (வள்ளியம் என்னும் செருக்கு). 1193 says the pride of saying 'we shall live' (வாழுநம் என்னும் செருக்கு) suits only those loved by the ones they love. The same construction makes a justified pride depend on a prior condition: inner drive in the one case, being loved in return in the other.

1304 says not appeasing one who sulks (ஊடியவரை உணராமை) is like cutting a withered creeper at the root. In 1319 he does appease her (தன்னை உணர்த்தினும்) and that too is a fault. Taken together, the man is blamed in chapter 131 for not doing what chapter 132 shows cannot be done to her satisfaction.

350 says to hold to the hold of the one who has none. 359 says that if one knows the support and lives so that supports perish (சார்புணர்ந்து சார்புகெட ஒழுகின்), the pains due to come will not come. The two are built alike on a repeated word, பற்று and சார்பு, and Parimelazhagar reads the சார்பு that is known as the true reality on which all rests, so 359 states the result of the practice 350 prescribes.

600 says those without inner drive are trees, and their being human in form is the only difference (மரம் மக்களாதலே வேறு). 1071 says the base resemble people exactly (மக்களே போல்வர்). Both treat the human shape as something that can be present without what makes a person, lacking drive in 600 and lacking character in 1071.

441 tells a ruler to choose, after weighing, the friendship of those who know virtue and are mature in understanding (கேண்மை ... தேர்ந்து கொளல்). 795 tells anyone to examine and take the friendship (நட்பு ஆய்ந்து கொளல்) of those able to make one weep, to rebuke, and to teach the right way. The same instruction, to select friends for their capacity to guide, is given for the king's advisers and for ordinary friendship.

737 names a strong fort (வல்லரண்) among the limbs (உறுப்பு) of a land, with its waters and hill. 381 names the fort (அரண்) and the people or land (குடி) as two of the six things a king must have, which Parimelazhagar calls his six limbs (அங்கம்). 737 nests one of the king's limbs inside another, which fits the order of the chapters: land, then fort.

527 praises the crow for not hiding (கரவா) its food and for calling others to eat. 1035 says those who live by eating what their own hands produce do not beg and give to those who ask without hiding (கரவாது). Not concealing what one has, கரவு being the book's word for the withholder's fault in chapters 106 and 107, is the shared mark of the crow and of the farmer.

724 joins two acts: convey your learning (செலச்சொல்லி) and take in what those more learned have. 424 joins the same two as its definition of understanding: say things so that they go in (செலச்சொல்லி) and see the subtle meaning in what others say (பிறர்வாய் நுண்பொருள் காண்பது). What 424 calls understanding, 724 presents as what a fearless speaker gains from an assembly.

939 names five things, among them learning (கல்வி), that 'அடையா' the one who takes to gaming. Parimelazhagar glosses this as 'do not come to him', but Pope's verse rendering and Kalaignar take the five as departing from him. On that second reading 939 conflicts with 400, which calls learning the wealth that cannot perish (கேடில் விழுச்செல்வம்); on Parimelazhagar's reading there is no conflict, since the gambler never acquires it.

624 likens the person who pulls through every obstruction to a draught ox (மடுத்தவாயெல்லாம் பகடன்னான்) and says the trouble he meets is itself troubled. 597 says the strong do not give way where things break down (சிதைவிடத்து ஒல்கார்), like an elephant standing firm under arrows. Both make the same claim through a working or fighting animal; the ox adds forward motion to the elephant's holding of ground.

768 says an army gains stature through its array (படைத்தகையால் பாடு பெறும்) even if it lacks striking power and endurance; Parimelazhagar takes படைத்தகை as splendour of appearance. 750 says a fort, whatever excellences it has, is as nothing with people who lack excellence in action (வினைமாட்சி இல்லார்கண் இல்லது). They conflict if 768's பாடு is read as real military worth; if it means only repute, 768 is a concession and 750 still stands.

Both verses address the moon with வாழி மதி. In 1118 the man tells it that it could have his love if it could shine like her face; Parimelazhagar hears the blessing as mockery. In 1210 the woman, left behind, asks it not to set so that her eyes may find the man who has gone without leaving her heart. The moon is a rival to be dismissed in the time of union and a helper to be begged in separation.

1039 compares the land to a wife (இல்லாள்) who sulks when her owner stays away. 1040 calls the land a good woman (நிலமென்னும் நல்லாள்) who laughs at those who sit idle pleading poverty. The chapter closes with two verses that make the land a woman who responds to how a man treats her, by sulking in one and by laughing in the other.

Chapter 57 tells the king not to be dreaded, and this chapter tells the courtier how to live with one who is. Both are realistic, and the Kural addresses each party without assuming the other has listened.

715 praises the restraint (செறிவு) of not speaking first among elders. 419 says a mouth that bows (வணங்கிய வாய்) is hard to have for those without fine listening. Both treat modest speech as a mark of what a person has learned, and 419 supplies the source 715 leaves unstated: the habit of listening.

716 says a slip (இழுக்கு) before those who have taken in wide learning is like faltering from one's footing on the path. 957 says a fault in the well-born shows up high, like the spot on the moon (மதிக்கண் மறுப்போல்). In both, the weight of a fault depends on where it is seen, the standing of the witnesses in 716 and of the person in 957, and not only on its size.

157 says that though others do you wrong, it is good to feel the pain and not do what is contrary to virtue (நோநொந்து அறனல்ல செய்யாமை). 261 defines தவம் by the same two parts: bearing pain, and causing none to living beings. The chapter on forbearance asks of the householder, in dealings with those who wrong him, what 261 gives as the whole form of austerity.

In 1180 the woman says the town easily learns the secret of those like her whose eyes are beaten drums (அறைபறை கண்ணார்). In 1232 the friend says her pale, weeping eyes seem to be telling of his unkindness. Both treat the eyes as announcing what she would keep hidden; the woman says it of herself and the friend says it to urge her to bear up, as Parimelazhagar frames it.

740 says a land's excellences bring no benefit (பயமின்று) without accord between it and its king. 558 says that under the sceptre of a king who does not do justice, having is more painful than not having (இன்மையின் இன்னாது உடைமை). 558 shows one way the wealth praised in this chapter turns useless or worse under the wrong ruler.

238 says it is a disgrace to leave no legacy of renown. 1004 asks what the man whom no one wants (நச்சப்படாதவன்) supposes will remain as his எச்சம்; Parimelazhagar explains that he is unwanted because he has never given. 1004 applies 238's standard to the miser and finds nothing left.

434 says fault itself is the enemy that brings one's end (குற்றமே அற்றம் தரூஉம் பகை). 165 says the same of one fault: envy suffices to ruin its holder without any ஒன்னார். The king's general rule in Book 2 has a specific case already stated in Book 1.

669: do with resolve the deed that yields joy (இன்பம் பயக்கும் வினை), even though pain comes close at first (துன்பம் உறவரினும்). 615: one who does not want pleasure but wants the work (இன்பம் விழையான் வினை விழைவான்) is a pillar who wipes away his kin's துன்பம். Both set இன்பம், துன்பம் and வினை against each other; 669 justifies bearing pain by the joy the deed yields, while 615 describes a doer who is not after pleasure at all and whose work removes others' pain.

98 says sweet speech that is clear of smallness (சிறுமையுள் நீங்கிய இன்சொல்) gives joy in the next life and this one; Parimelazhagar explains சிறுமை as causing pain to others by what the words mean. 291 defines truth as speech containing no harm at all (யாதொன்றும் தீமை இலாத சொலல்). Sweetness and truthfulness are both defined by the same test, the absence of harm to others, and not by sound or by literal accuracy. (This edition prints சிறுமையுவு in 98, a typo for சிறுமையுள்.)

303 says evils are born from anger (தீய பிறத்தல் அதனான் வரும்). 360 names anger (வெகுளி) with desire and confusion as the three whose very names must perish for pain to perish. What 303 says of anger as a source of evils, 360 places in a full account of the roots of suffering.

804 says that when friends act without asking, out of intimacy (கெழுதகையாற் கேளாது), it is welcomed. 788 compares friendship to the hand of a man whose garment slips, removing the distress there and then (ஆங்கே). The hand in 788 does not ask leave before acting; 804 states the same thing from the receiving side, that such unasked action is to be wanted and not resented.

1145: as drinking is wanted more each time one gets drunk (களித்தொறும் கள்ளுண்டல் வேட்டற்று), love is sweeter each time it is exposed. 1110: love is like finding one's ignorance each time one learns, each time he is close to her. Both say love grows by repetition and does not wear out; 1110 takes its likeness from knowledge and 1145 from drink, and they differ in what is repeated, union or exposure by gossip.

309 praises one who does not think of anger in the heart at all (உள்ளத்தால் உள்ளான் வெகுளி). 487 says the bright do not flare up outwardly on the spot but, watching for the time, burn within (காலம்பார்த்து உள்வேர்ப்பர்). They conflict if both describe how a wise person treats anger inwardly, one removing it and the other keeping it for later; the conflict lessens if 309 is for the ascetic, as Parimelazhagar reads it, and 487 for a ruler facing enemies.

Both verses use the phrase உடுப்பதூஉம் உண்பதூஉம். In 1079 the base man sees others' clothing and food and finds fault with them; in 166 the kin of one who envies what is given (கொடுப்பது அழுக்கறுப்பான்) perish without clothing or food. The pairing shows what is envied returning as what is lost.

1140: the ignorant laugh where she can see it (நகுப அறிவில்லார்), because they have not suffered what she has. 1173: she finds her own eyes' plight fit to be laughed at (நகத்தக்கது உடைத்து). Laughter at a lover's suffering comes from outsiders in one verse and from the sufferer herself in the other.

752 says everyone scorns those who have nothing (இல்லாரை எல்லாரும் எள்ளுவர்). 1046 gives a particular case: even when the poor understand a good matter well and say it, their words go slack (சொற்பொருள் சோர்வு படும்). The general contempt of 752 is shown reaching what a poor person says.

601 calls the family a lamp that does not dwindle (குடியென்னும் குன்றா விளக்கம்) which dies when the grime of sloth spreads over it (மடியென்னும் மாசூர). 753 calls wealth a lamp that does not fail (பொருளென்னும் பொய்யா விளக்கம்) which goes where its owner intends and cuts the darkness. The same 'X என்னும் ... விளக்கம்' figure is used twice in the Book of Wealth, and Parimelazhagar glosses both as a நந்தா விளக்கு; one lamp is shown dispelling darkness abroad, the other being put out from within.

277 says the world has people who look outwardly like the red kunri seed but are inwardly black like its tip (புறம் ... அகம்); 824 says to fear deceivers who smile sweetly with the face and are bitter within (முகத்தின் இனிய ... அகத்தின்னா வஞ்சர்). The same outside/inside split is described for the false ascetic and for the false friend.

267 says that for those able to endure, pain burning them makes them shine (ஒளிவிடும்), as gold shines the more it is heated. 630 says that if one takes what hurts as pleasure (இன்னாமை இன்பம் எனக்கொளின்), there comes a distinction even one's enemies admire. The ascetic's gain from pain in the first book has a worldly counterpart in the second: in both, pain borne in the right way adds to the person.

Chapters 97 and 99 give different answers to humiliation. 967 prefers being called dead to living behind those who scorn you, and 986 makes accepting defeat even from lesser people the touchstone of worth. The two make most sense as distinct ideals, honour and fullness of character, and not as one code.

1017 says the shame-bearing would give up life before shame. 1251 says that love's axe breaks the door barred by shame. The same supreme barrier falls in the book of love, and the whole book of love depends on that collapse.

417 says well-grounded listeners do not speak folly even when they have misunderstood (பிழைத்துணர்ந்தும்). 139 says that for those who have conduct, speaking evil even by a slip (வழுக்கியும்) is not possible. The same guarantee, speech that holds even under error, is attached to listening in the Book of Wealth and to conduct in the Book of Virtue.

716 says a slip (இழுக்கு) before those of wide learning is like falling from the path. 721 answers from the next chapter: those who know words and know the assembly do not slip before the capable (வல்லவை வாய்சோரார்). One verse gives the cost of the slip and the other says what prevents it.

784 says friendship exists to rebuke, openly and in advance. 818 says that with a certain kind of friend, say nothing and let it fade. Whether one rebukes turns out to depend on whether the friend is still worth the rebuke.

1075 says the base behave properly out of fear. 1078 says the base, like sugar-cane, are of use only when crushed (கொல்லப் பயன்படும் கீழ்). 1078 applies the rule of 1075 to giving: what fear does for their conduct, force does for their generosity.

970 sets disgrace against radiance: the world worships the ஒளி of those who will not live when இளி comes. 971 defines the same two words: one's ஒளி is abundance of aspiration, and one's இளி is saying 'we will live without it' (அஃதிறந்து வாழ்தும் எனல்). In both, disgrace is a way of going on living, and radiance belongs to those who refuse it.

772 prefers the failed throw at an elephant to the successful shot at a hare, and Manakkudavar takes it with 771 as saying the warrior should send the weak away and fight those who can oppose him. 861 advises the reverse: avoid meeting the strong (வலியார்க்கு மாறேற்றல் ஓம்புக) and keep up enmity against the weak (மெலியார்மேல் மேக பகை). The conflict holds if 772 is read as a rule for choosing opponents and 861 as Parimelazhagar reads it; it is the warrior's pride against the king's policy. Kalaignar's gloss of 861 turns it into fighting the strong, which would remove the conflict.

250 says: when you move against those weaker than you, think of yourself before those stronger (வலியார்முன் தன்னை நினைக்க). 539 says: when you grow strong in your own joy, think of those ruined by negligence (இகழ்ச்சியின் கெட்டாரை உள்ளுக). Both prescribe a deliberate act of recollection at the moment of feeling powerful, for the sake of compassion in 250 and of vigilance in 539.

Both verses use the formula 'the one called a householder' (இல்வாழ்வான் என்பான்). 41 defines him by what he supports: he is the steady help of the three on their good path. 147 defines him by what he refrains from: he lives the household life with aram (அறனியலான்) who does not desire the womanhood of one who belongs to another (பிறனியலாள் பெண்மை நயவாதவன்). Together they give a positive and a negative test for the same title.

1021 praises the resolve never to stop work once begun (கைதூவேன்). 612 gives the other side: guard against the work dying in mid-course (வினைக்கண் வினைகெடல் ஓம்பல்), since, in Parimelazhagar's reading, the world gives up on those who give up their unfinished work. The pair shows the same refusal to stop as honour in one verse and as a condition of the world's regard in the other.

670: whatever other firmness they have attained (எனைத்திட்பம் எய்தியக் கண்ணும்), the world does not want those who do not want firmness in action. 750: whatever excellences it has (எனைமாட்சித்து ஆகியக் கண்ணும்), a fort is nothing with those who lack excellence in action (வினைமாட்சி இல்லார்கண்). The two chapter-closing verses are built alike and make the same point, that other strengths count for nothing without the capacity to act, once of a minister and once of a fort's defenders.

92 says being sweet-spoken with a glad face is better than giving with a glad heart (அகன்அமர்ந்து ஈதலின் நன்றே). 295 says one who speaks truth in accord with his heart (மனத்தொடு வாய்மை மொழியின்) is above those who do austerity together with giving (தவத்தொடு தானஞ்செய்வாரின் தலை). Twice the book ranks a quality of speech above material giving, once for kindness and once for truthfulness.

81 says the whole point of keeping a home is to tend guests. 1211 applies that duty to a dream, which can be neither fed nor refused. A woman with an empty house is still measuring her situation in terms of the householder's virtue.

1212 makes everything depend on a condition: if her eyes would sleep when she begs them (யானிரப்பத் துஞ்சின்). 1179 says why the condition fails: her eyes do not sleep when he does not come and do not sleep when he does (வாராக்கால் துஞ்சா வரின்துஞ்சா). Set beside chapter 122, this shows that the dream which consoles her in the following verses is not available to her at will.

125 treats bowing (பணிதல்) as an excellence, a second wealth for the rich; 985 says bowing is the strength of those who get things done and the weapon by which the worthy turn opponents around (ஆற்றுவார் ஆற்றல் பணிதல்). The same act is valued as character in the Book of Virtue and as effective power in the Book of Wealth.

781 praises friendship as the best protection. 815 says the poor friendship of small people, which gives no safety even after it is made (செய்து ஏமம் சாரா), is better not had than had. The protection claimed in 781 belongs only to friendship with the right people; made with the wrong ones it guards nothing.

208 says the ruin of those who do evil is like a shadow that never leaves and rests at the foot (நிழல் ... அடி உறைந்தற்று). 319 puts the same inevitability in time: forenoon and afternoon (முற்பகல், பிற்பகல்). One verse uses space and the other the day's two halves to say that consequence is attached to the deed; the day figure also fits a shadow lengthening after noon, though the text does not say so.

289 says those who know nothing but stealth do what is beyond measure and perish right there (அளவல்ல செய்தாங்கே வீவர்). 947 says the one who eats beyond the measure of his fire gets disease beyond measure. Chapter 29 uses அளவு as a moral measure and chapter 95 as a bodily one, and in each case overstepping it brings its own penalty.

450 says abandoning one's tie with the good (நல்லார் தொடர் கைவிடல்) is ten times worse than the enmity of many. 800 says to hold close the friendship of the stainless (மருவுக மாசற்றார் கேண்மை) and to be rid of the friendship of the unfit even at a price. 800 gives the same instruction for friendship and adds its other half, which bonds to drop.

In both verses the woman rejects the idea of forgetting him, which Parimelazhagar says the friend had advised in each case. 1207 asks what she would become if she forgot (மறப்பின் எவனாவன்); 1262 answers concretely that if she forgot today (இன்று மறப்பின்) her beauty would go and the bangles slip from her arms. Remembering hurts, but both verses hold that forgetting would be worse.

207 says the enmity of deeds does not leave and follows behind to kill ('வீயாது பின்சென்று அடும்'). 208 gives the image for it: the ruin of evildoers is like a person's shadow that does not leave and stays at the foot ('வீயாது அடி உறைந்தற்று'). The repeated 'வீயாது' ties them, and both Manakkudavar and Parimelazhagar say 208 illustrates what 207 asserted.

768 allows an army without strength to gain stature from its bearing. 273 says one without strength putting on the form of the strong (வலியில் நிலைமையான் வல்லுருவம்) is like a cow grazing in a tiger's skin. On Parimelazhagar's reading of படைத்தகை as outward show, 768 credits what 273 mocks; 273 is about a false ascetic, so the conflict holds only if both are taken as claims about appearance without substance.

488 says to bear with enemies until their end comes (இறுவரை காணின்). 879 says to cut down a thorn tree while it is young, because once it has hardened it destroys the hand that cuts it (இளைதாக முள்மரம் கொல்க ... காழ்த்த இடத்து). 879 limits 488's patience: waiting serves when time works against the enemy, and not when the enemy is growing stronger.

782 uses the moon's phases for friendship: with the wise it fills like the crescent, with fools it shrinks like the moon after full. 1117 mentions the same cycle, a moon that shines only after filling its lost parts (அறுவாய் நிறைந்த), as a defect that her face does not share. The waxing that is a hopeful figure in 782 counts in 1117 as evidence of the moon's inconstancy.

847 says a person without understanding lets the precious மறை slip (அருமறை சோரும்) and so harms himself. Manakkudavar takes மறை as a secret let out to others, a reading Parimelazhagar reports and rejects. On that reading the verse meets 1076, where the base are like a beaten drum because they carry every மறை they hear to others; 1076 notes the harm to others, 847 the harm to the leaker.

773 makes help to a foe in trouble the cutting edge of valour; Parimelazhagar illustrates it with the king of Ayodhya telling his disarmed enemy to go and come back tomorrow. 987 asks what use worth (சால்பு) is if one does not do what is sweet even to those who did one harm (இன்னா செய்தார்க்கும் இனியவே). The ideal of the worthy person in the chapter on சால்பு appears here as the height of a soldier's manhood.

306 says anger, the fire that kills what it touches, burns even the safe raft called one's people (இனமென்னும் ஏமப் புணையைச் சுடும்). 568 shows this at court: the king who neglects his circle (இனம்) and then turns his anger on them (சினத்தாற்றிச் சீறின்) loses his fortune; Parimelazhagar adds that the frightened ministers leave him. The general warning in the book of virtue becomes a specific danger for a ruler.

271 says the five elements laugh within (பூதங்கள் ஐந்தும் அகத்தே நகும்) at the concealed conduct of a deceitful mind; 293 says that after a lie about what one's own heart knows, that heart itself burns one (தன்நெஞ்சே தன்னைச் சுடும்). Both place the witness to a hidden fault inside the person; 293 moves it from the body's elements, which only laugh, to the heart, which punishes.

1181 puts the consent on herself: நல்காமை நேர்ந்தேன், I agreed to his absence. 1189 names him as the one who brought her to agree (நயப்பித்தார்) and says let her body pale as it will if he stands well; Parimelazhagar reads நன்னிலையர் as free of fault, while Manakkudavar reads the condition as his suffering too. On Parimelazhagar's reading the two verses share out the responsibility and she keeps the cost.

386 says that if a king is easy to see and not harsh of speech, his land is spoken of above others (மீக்கூறும் மன்னன் நிலம்). 564 gives the reverse case: where people say 'our lord is harsh' (இறைகடியன்), the king quickly perishes. Both verses measure a reign by what is said about it.

The two verses share one sentence frame. 369: joy is unbroken if the sorrow of sorrows called craving perishes (அவாவென்னும் துன்பத்துள் துன்பங் கெடின்). 854: it yields the joy of joys if the sorrow of sorrows called hostility perishes (இகலென்னும் துன்பத்துள் துன்பங் கெடின்). The same title, sorrow of sorrows, is given to craving in the book of virtue and to hostility in the book of statecraft, each as the worst thing in its own field.

1045 says many sufferings arrive within the one affliction called poverty (நல்குரவு என்னும் இடும்பையுள் பல்குரைத் துன்பங்கள்). 1056 says that on seeing those free of the affliction of concealing, all the afflictions of poverty perish together (நிரப்பிடும்பை எல்லாம் ஒருங்கு கெடும்). The next chapter answers this verse in its own terms: the sufferings that come as a group also leave as a group.

696 tells the courtier to read the king's mood and consider the time (குறிப்பறிந்து காலங் கருதி) before speaking. 687 has the best envoy know what is due, consider the time (காலங் கருதி) and know the place before he speaks. The phrase காலங் கருதி is common to both, so the discipline for speaking to one's own king is the same as for speaking to another's.

660: wealth made by deceit is water kept in an unfired clay vessel. 1000: great wealth obtained by one without character is good milk spoiled by the fault of its vessel (கலந்தீமையால் திரிந்தற்று). Both use a faulty கலம் for wealth that cannot be kept, but the fault differs: in 660 it is how the wealth was made, in 1000 it is the holder's character.

Verse 74 derives friendship (நண்பு) from love by way of eagerness (ஆர்வம்) and calls it a distinction that is not sought (நாடா). Verse 785 says meeting and long acquaintance are not needed, because feeling itself (உணர்ச்சிதான்) gives the claim of friendship. The friendship chapter of Book 2 keeps the account given in Book 1: friendship comes from an inner disposition and not from arrangement or contact.

621 says to laugh when trouble comes (இடுக்கண் வருங்கால் நகுக), since nothing presses it back as well. 774 shows a warrior who, having thrown his spear at an elephant, pulls out the one lodged in his own body and laughs (மெய்வேல் பறியா நகும்). The battlefield verse acts out the advice of 621: the laugh comes at the moment of injury, and the injury is turned to use.

1166 says love's pain, when it afflicts, is greater than the sea (அதனிற் பெரிது). 1175 repeats the measure as an epithet, a love-sickness the sea cannot hold (கடலாற்றாக் காமநோய்), and goes on to assign blame for it to her eyes.

1180 (the woman): the town can easily learn the secret of those whose eyes are beaten drums. 1271 (the man): though she hides it, her kohl-lined eyes go beyond her control (கரப்பினும் கையிகந்து) and have something to tell. Both lovers say her eyes disclose what she means to conceal.

1033 describes everyone but the farmer as those who bow, eat and walk behind others (தொழுதுண்டு பின்செல்பவர்). 967 says it is better to be called ruined than to live by going behind those who do not accept one (ஒட்டார் பின்சென்று வாழ்தல்). Both treat 'going behind' another for a living as a lesser life; 967 judges it by honour, and 1033 names farming as the livelihood that avoids it.
The warrior of 774 pulls a spear from his own body and laughs. The warrior of 1088 has that same reputation and is broken by a forehead. The Kural's courage has no defence against this enemy.

283 says gain made by stealth perishes beyond measure even as it seems to grow (ஆவது போலக் கெடும்). 178 says the way to keep wealth from shrinking is not to covet another's goods. 283 gives the negative side of the same claim: what is added by taking another's property is not a lasting addition.

839 says the friendship of fools is very sweet (பெரிதினிது), because parting from it gives no pain. 1072 says the base are fortunate (திருவுடையர்), because their hearts have no distress. Both verses praise a bad thing for the absence of a pain that only something of value would cause.

Both verses use a flower's scent (நாற்றம்) for what is inside a person. In 650 the flower is fully open and gives no scent, like the learned person who cannot convey what he knows; in 1274 the scent is held inside a closed bud, like the unspoken meaning inside the girl's budding smile. The two uses mirror each other: an open display with nothing reaching others, and a closed one whose content the lover already perceives.

502 makes birth in a good family (குடிப்பிறந்து) a ground for trust alongside freedom from fault. 133 says having good conduct is itself good birth, and a lapse in conduct becomes low birth (ஒழுக்கம் உடைமை குடிமை இழுக்கம் இழிந்த பிறப்பாய் விடும்). On 133's definition, 502's first criterion cannot be checked apart from its second: family does not vouch for a person whose conduct fails.

762 says only a long-established army stays firm when it is reduced and the king is faltering. 955 says an old family (பழங்குடி) does not part from its nature even when its means of giving have shrunk. In both, age of standing is what keeps character intact under loss.
467 fixes the order, deliberate and then resolve, which supports Manakkudavar's reading of துணிவு here and sits uneasily with Parimelazhagar's action without regard to anything.

403 counts silence before the learned as the unlearned person's merit. 729 says those who have studied and understood yet fear an assembly of the good are lower than the unlearned (கல்லாதவரின் கடை). Silence is therefore not good in itself: it is right for the one with nothing to say and a failing in the one who has something.

504 lets the predominant side decide what a person is. 965 says even those like a hill are diminished if they do a lowering thing the size of a kundri seed (குன்றி அனைய செயின்). 965 names a kind of fault, the degrading act, that is not outweighed by the mass of a person's merits, which limits the simple weighing of 504.

139 says speaking evil things even by a slip is not possible for those who have conduct (வழுக்கியும் வாயாற் சொலல் ஒல்லாவே); 199 says those of stainless sight do not say meaningless things even in forgetfulness (பொச்சாந்தும் சொல்லார்). Both claim that a settled quality rules out even the accidental lapse of speech, and they trace that quality to conduct in one case and to clear understanding in the other.

In 1088, a warrior laments his strength being broken by her forehead, and takes it as defeat. In 1327, the man has worked out that losing is the way to win. The book's military imagery, which begins with injury, ends in a pleasantly ruined scoreboard.

334 presents each day as a blade cutting life, with no one exempted. 326 says Death, the eater of life, does not advance on the days (வாழ்நாள்மேல் செல்லாது) of one who lives by not killing. Read literally, 326 exempts the non-killer from the daily loss of life that 334 treats as universal; the conflict depends on taking 326 as a promise about lifespan and not as praise of the vow.

911 warns that the இன்சொல் of women who want a man's wealth brings him harm. In 1258 a woman calls the soft speech (பணிமொழி) of her lover, a 'thief of many deceptions' (பன்மாயக் கள்வன்), the weapon that breaks her womanly reserve (பெண்மை உடைக்கும் படை). Both treat gentle words as an instrument that undoes the hearer, though 1258 is a lover's complaint in the Book of Love, not a warning the book gives in its own voice.

692 says that not desiring what kings desire (மன்னர் விழைப விழையாமை) brings lasting prosperity through those same kings; Parimelazhagar takes விழைப as the enjoyments, adornment and precedence proper to a king. 179 says Fortune herself comes to the wise who, knowing virtue, do not covet (அறனறிந்து வெஃகா அறிவுடையார்ச் சேரும் ... திரு). Both make not-wanting the route by which wealth arrives, once as court prudence and once as virtue.

876 says that whether or not one has trusted the enemy before, in a time of ruin (அழிவின்கண்) one should neither join him nor break from him (தேறான் பகாஅன் விடல்); Parimelazhagar explains that joining lets him destroy from inside and breaking makes him add to the ruin. 691 tells those who serve quarrelsome kings to be like people warming at a fire, neither moving off nor coming close (அகலாது அணுகாது). Both prescribe a deliberate middle distance from a dangerous party, once toward an enemy and once toward one's own king.

64: gruel stirred by the small hands of one's own children is far sweeter than ambrosia (அமிழ்தினும் ஆற்ற இனிதே). 1106: her shoulders are made of ambrosia (அமிழ்தின் இயன்றன) because their touch revives his life. Parent and lover both reach for அமிழ்து to measure the nearness of someone of their own; the parent ranks the child's gruel above it and the lover equates her with it.

1195 asks what those we love can do for us if they do not love in return (தாம் காதல் கொள்ளாக் கடை). 1242 draws the conclusion and turns it on her own heart: since he has no love (காதல் அவரிலர் ஆக), its suffering is folly (நோவது பேதைமை). The first states the uselessness of one-sided love, the second names persisting in it as foolishness.

44 promises an unfailing line (வழி) to the life that fears blame (பழியஞ்சி) and shares its food; Parimelazhagar reads the fear of blame as applying to how the wealth is earned. 112 says the prosperity of the person of rectitude (செப்பம் உடையவன் ஆக்கம்) does not decay and is a security to those who come after (எச்சத்திற்கு ஏமாப்பு). In both, wealth held without wrong is what lasts into the next generation.

952 says the well-born do not slip (இழுக்கார்) in conduct, truthfulness and shame. 133 says having conduct is itself குடிமை and that a lapse (இழுக்கம்) turns into low birth (இழிந்த பிறப்பாய் விடும்). Read together, 952's claim is close to a definition: whoever slips has by 133 already left the class of the well-born, a point Parimelazhagar makes on 133 while keeping it within varna.

845 says one false claim to learning casts doubt on what one has mastered without flaw. 128 says that if even one bad word has its effect, the good comes to nothing (நன்றாகாதாகி விடும்). Both describe a single lapse spreading backward over what was sound, in knowledge and in speech.

ஏதிலர், the 'stranger', has been her word for him in the town's mouth, in 1129 and 1130. In 1300 the same word is used for a stranger, and now the one who isn't one's own is one's own heart. By the end, the outsider is inside.

117 says the world (உலகம்) will not count as ruin the low state (தாழ்வு) of one who stays in virtue by standing fair. 752 says everyone scorns those who have nothing (இல்லாரை எல்லாரும் எள்ளுவர்); Parimelazhagar adds 'even if they have every good quality'. They conflict if உலகம் in 117 means people in general; Parimelazhagar avoids this by reading உலகம் there as the high-minded (உயர்ந்தோர்).

174 says those of faultless vision who have conquered the senses (புலம்வென்ற புன்மையில் காட்சியவர்) will not covet, even thinking 'we have nothing'. 258 says those whose vision is free of fault do not eat flesh. Both attach an abstention that costs something, from another's goods or from meat, to காட்சி, and 174 adds the mastery of the senses that 258 leaves unstated.

712 says those who know how words work should discern the opening (இடைதெரிந்து), understand well and then speak; Parimelazhagar takes இடை as the receptive moment of the assembly. 687 asks the envoy to consider the time, which Parimelazhagar likewise glosses as the listener's receptive state (செவ்வி). Both make the listener's readiness a condition of speaking.

1083: 'I did not know before (பண்டறியேன்) what Death is; now I know'. 1226: the woman did not know (அறிந்ததிலேன்), while her husband had not left, that evening brings sickness. In both a lover says love has taught what was only a word before, the man at first sight and the woman in separation.

159 praises those who endure harsh words (இன்னாச்சொல்) from people who overstep. 389 says the world rests under the parasol of the king who has the character to bear words bitter to the ear (செவிகைப்பச் சொற்பொறுக்கும்). The same capacity is a private virtue in one verse and a quality of rule in the other. Parimelazhagar takes the bitter words of 389 to be the rebukes of advisers, so there the speaker means well, unlike the transgressors of 159.

279 warns against reading uprightness from shape, with the arrow and lute as examples; 667 says do not scorn on seeing someone's form (உருவுகண்டு எள்ளாமை), because the great chariot has its small linchpin. One verse guards against being impressed by form and the other against despising it, and both replace form with function.

95: humility and sweet speech are a person's ornament and nothing else is (அணியல்ல மற்றுப் பிற). 1089: what use are foreign ornaments (ஏதில தந்து அணி) to one who has a doe's artless look and modesty? Both deny that added adornment counts beside an inborn quality, 95 as a rule of conduct and 1089 as a lover's praise.

103 says help given by those who do not weigh the return (பயன்தூக்கார்) proves, when its worth is weighed (நயன்தூக்கின்), greater than the sea. 912 uses the same pair of words in the same order: the women weigh the gain (பயன்தூக்கி), and the man is to weigh their conduct (நயன்தூக்கி) and not join them. Weighing the return is what spoils a relationship in both verses, and weighing worth is the observer's proper response.

398 says the learning acquired in one birth protects through seven (எழுமையும் ஏமாப்புடைத்து). 356 says those who have learned here and seen the true thing (கற்றீண்டு மெய்ப்பொருள் கண்டார்) reach the path of not coming back here (மற்றீண்டு வாரா நெறி). Learning in the book of wealth is an asset carried across births; learning that ends in seeing the real is said to end the births themselves.

656 says that even if one must see the mother who bore one go hungry (ஈன்றாள் பசி காண்பான் ஆயினும்), one should not do what the worthy condemn. 174 says the thought of being without does not make the self-controlled covet. 656 pushes the same refusal to its hardest case, where the want is another's and not one's own.
Hunger is here the world's worst consequence of drought, a natural evil. In 225, relieving hunger outranks the ascetic's power to endure it, which turns this natural fact into a moral priority.

855 holds that the one who gives way before hostility cannot be beaten. In 1327 the man says that in a lovers' sulk the one who loses has won (ஊடலில் தோற்றவர் வென்றார்), as the reunion shows. The speaker in 1327 is a lover talking about play-quarrels, so this is the same pattern of winning by yielding in a different setting, not a doctrine shared with 855.

966 asks what is gained by going and standing behind those who scorn you (இகழ்வார் பின் சென்று நிலை). 1033 says only those who eat by their own ploughing truly live, and all others bow to eat and go behind (தொழுதுண்டு பின்செல்பவர்). Both use 'going behind' another as the picture of a dependent life, and 1033 names the livelihood that avoids it.

948 sets out an order of enquiry: look into the disease, then its root, then the means that subdue it, and act so that it works (நோய்நாடி நோய்முதல் நாடி ... வாய்நாடி). 504 has the same threefold நாடி for judging a person: examine the qualities, examine the faults, examine which predominates, and take that. Diagnosis of a patient and assessment of a candidate are given the same grammar of step-by-step examination before a decision.

895 says those who draw the anger of a king of fierce might (வெந்துப்பின் வேந்து செறப்பட்டவர்) cannot go on existing anywhere they go. 691 gives the working rule for those who serve such kings: like people warming at a fire, neither move off nor come close (அகலாது அணுகாது தீக்காய்வார் போல்க). 895 states the danger, and 691 the conduct that lives beside it.

306 calls one's people a safe raft (ஏமப் புணை) that anger burns. In 1164 the woman says the sea of love certainly exists and the safe raft to swim it (ஏமப் புணை) does not. The same phrase names what keeps a person afloat; in one verse a passion destroys it and in the other a passion leaves the speaker without one.

606 says the greatest possessions yield the slothful no excellent fruit (மாண்பயன் எய்தல் அரிது). 750 says a fort, whatever excellences it has, is as nothing with those who lack excellence in action (வினைமாட்சி இல்லார்கண் இல்லது அரண்). The two share the 'ஆகியக் கண்ணும் / அமைந்தக் கண்ணும்' concession: resources do not work without the action of those who hold them.

616 says effort makes fortune and lack of effort brings want in (முயற்றின்மை இன்மை புகுத்தி விடும்); Parimelazhagar applies it to kings. 1063 calls it hardness (வன்மை) to think poverty's affliction can be ended by begging, and Parimelazhagar explains that the proper path, effort, is being set aside. 1063 applies 616's rule to the poor man and names begging as the wrong substitute for effort.

1253 likens desire to a sneeze that appears without one's intending it; Parimelazhagar glosses that it cannot be held in. In 1318 the man does stifle a sneeze (தும்முச் செறுப்ப), and she weeps that he is hiding from her that his people are thinking of him. The sneeze is in both an involuntary sign of what is within, and 1318 shows that even suppressing it is read as a disclosure.

657 ranks the utter poverty of the worthy above blame-laden wealth. 988 says poverty (இன்மை) is no disgrace (இளிவன்று) to one who has the firmness called சால்பு. 988 supplies the ground for 657's ranking: for the சான்றோர் poverty carries no இளிவு, whereas the wealth in 657 carries பழி.

Verse 44 says that if a household life fears blame (பழியஞ்சி) and shares its food, its line (வழி) never fails. Verse 62 says that if one gets children in whom blame does not grow (பழிபிறங்கா), no evil touches one for seven births. In 44 the parent's freedom from blame secures the descendants; in 62 the descendants' freedom from blame secures the parent.

981 says that for those who know what is due (கடன் அறிந்து) and take on worth, every good thing is கடன்; Parimelazhagar glosses this as the good qualities being natural to them. 218 uses the same phrase, கடனறி காட்சியவர், for people who do not falter in ஒப்புரவு even in a season without means (இடனில் பருவத்தும்). 218 shows one concrete case of 981's general claim: a duty that is felt as one's own does not wait on circumstances.
Rain is the world's amrita in 11, and in 64 a child's messy gruel beats amrita. The same word is the top of two different scales: what sustains all life, and what is sweet to one parent.

536 says nothing equals unfailing vigilance toward everyone at all times (யார்மாட்டும் என்றும்). 582 says it is the king's work to know quickly everything that happens to everyone at all times (எல்லார்க்கும் எல்லாம் நிகழ்பவை எஞ்ஞான்றும்). The same universal scope appears in both, and 582 gives the general vigilance of 536 a concrete form in intelligence gathering.
Two pursuers that can't be evaded: the deed follows from behind (பின் சென்று) and fate arrives first (முந்துறும்). Together they close off escape in both directions.

143 counts the betrayer of a trusting household as no different from the dead (விளிந்தாரின் வேறல்லர்); 214 says only the one who knows what is fitting lives (உயிர்வாழ்வான்), and anyone else is placed among the dead (செத்தாருள் வைக்கப்படும்). In both, being alive is measured by conduct and not by breath, once for a wrong committed and once for a duty to others left undone.

370 says that giving up craving gives, in that very state (அந்நிலையே), a nature that does not shift (பேரா இயற்கை). 349 says the moment attachment ends (பற்றற்ற கண்ணே) it cuts off birth. Both make the result immediate on the cause ending, with no further step between.

345 says even the body is too much for one seeking to end birth. 627, in the book of wealth, says the great do not take trouble as trouble, knowing the body is a target for suffering (இலக்கம் உடம்பு இடும்பைக்கு). Both start from the body as a liability, but 627 uses that view to keep steady in worldly trouble while 345 uses it to argue for giving up every tie.

828 says a weapon hides within an enemy's folded hands, and his shed tears are the same (படையொடுங்கும் ... அழுத கண்ணீரும் அனைத்து). 555 calls the tears shed by the afflicted the weapon that wears away wealth (அழுத கண்ணீர் ... படை). Both join the same two words, tears and weapon: in 828 the tears conceal a weapon, and in 555 the tears are the weapon.

The two verses end with the same formula, 'அந்நலம்/பிறநலம் யா/எந்நலத்து உள்ளதூஉம் அன்று', used in opposite directions. In 641 the goodness of the tongue (நாநலம்) is not contained in any other goodness, which Parimelazhagar takes to mean it exceeds them all; in 982 every goodness other than the goodness of character (குணநலம்) is not counted among goodnesses at all. One chapter ranks eloquence highest for a minister, the other ranks character alone for the worthy.

777 says that for those who want fame that circles the earth and do not want life (வேண்டா உயிரார்), tying on the war-anklet is an adornment. 235 says a ruin that is growth and a death that is existence (உளதாகும் சாக்காடு) are possible only for the skilled, which Parimelazhagar explains by the body of fame outliving the body of flesh. 235 gives the reasoning for the warrior's choice in 777.

422 says understanding does not let one go wherever the mind has gone, but draws away from evil and directs toward good (தீதொரீஇ நன்றின்பால் உய்ப்பது). 787 says friendship removes one from what ruins and sets one on the path (அழிவினவை நீக்கி ஆறுய்த்து). The two verses use the same pair of actions and the same verb of steering (உய்); what understanding does for a person from inside, the friend does from outside.

968 questions the worth of a life that merely feeds the body (ஊன் ஓம்பும் வாழ்க்கை) when dignity is gone. 1017 says those governed by shame give up life for shame and do not give up shame for life (நாணால் உயிரைத் துறப்பர் ... நாண் துறவார்). The chapters on honour and on shame reach the same ordering of life and self-respect.

36 tells one to do virtue without saying 'we will see to it then' (அன்றறிவாம் என்னாது). 342's உண்டாகத் துறக்க is read by Parimelazhagar as 'renounce while there is time', i.e. in youth, so the joys last long; Manakkudavar instead reads it as 'if you want gain for your life'. On Parimelazhagar's reading the chapter on renunciation repeats, for renouncing, the earlier rule against postponing virtue.

1275 says the stealth with which she acted and withdrew (செய்திறந்த கள்ளம்) holds a medicine for great sorrow; 1279 states what she did (அஃதாண்டவள் செய்தது): she looked at her bangles, her shoulders and her feet. Parimelazhagar ties the two explicitly, taking 1279's அஃது to point back to 1275, so that the silent gesture is the 'stealth' and its meaning, going with him, is the cure.

222 says taking is bad even if it were called a good path (நல்லாறு எனினும் கொளல் தீது). 1054 says that asking from those who do not know concealment even in a dream is itself like giving (இரத்தலும் ஈதலே போலும்). They conflict if கொளல் is read, with Parimelazhagar, as accepting alms without exception; on Kalaignar's reading of கொளல் as taking goods from others by whatever fair means, the two address different acts.

939 says that clothing, wealth, food, lustre (ஒளி) and learning do not come near a man who takes to gaming. 921 says those devoted to liquor lose their ஒளி and are not feared. The adjoining chapters on drink and dice both count the loss of ஒளி, the standing that makes a man regarded, among the costs.
1130 insists he lives in her heart, so he has not gone anywhere. In 1184 her mind and words are full of him, but her skin has its own view. Her body undercuts what chapter 113 argues.

326 says Death, the eater of life (உயிருண்ணுங் கூற்று), does not advance on the days of one who lives by not killing. 255 gives hell a mouth (அண்ணாத்தல்), which on Parimelazhagar's reading has swallowed the eater of flesh and will not open again. In both the language of eating is turned on the human: the one who spares life is not eaten, and the one who eats is.

224 says being asked is unpleasant (இன்னாது இரக்கப் படுதல்) until one sees the asker's glad face. 1069 says the heart melts at the thought of asking. Taken together they say asking is painful on both sides, for the one asked in 224 and for the one who asks or contemplates it in 1069, and that only the gift ends the pain.

656 uses the mother who bore one (ஈன்றாள்) as the strongest pull toward wrongdoing for the sake of relief. 1047 says that one in poverty not joined with virtue (அறஞ்சாரா நல்குரவு) is looked on as a stranger even by the mother who bore him (ஈன்ற தாயானும்). The mother marks the limit case in both: 656 holds conduct firm against her need, while 1047 says poverty without virtue loses even her regard.

1252 says the thing called desire has no eye, that is no pity (கண்ணின்று), since it works her heart even at midnight. 1197 asks whether Kaman, who stays and acts on one person only, does not see her pain and misery (காணான்கொல்). The complaint moves from the feeling to the god, and both use sight as the test of his mercy.

1093 reports a wordless act and reads it: she looked, and having looked bowed her head (நோக்கினாள் நோக்கி இறைஞ்சினாள்), and that (அஃது) was water poured on their bond; 1279 reports that she looked at her bangles, her shoulders and her feet, and that (அஃது) is what she did there. Both verses consist of a sequence of looks followed by அஃது, leaving the meaning to be drawn from the gesture, at courtship in 1093 and at the threat of parting in 1279.

Verse 73 says the life's connection with the bone (என்போடு) goes with love. Verse 80 says the seat of life (உயிர்நிலை) follows love, and that for those without it the body is bone wrapped in skin (என்புதோல் போர்த்த உடம்பு). The chapter's last verse gives the negative of 73: take away the love and what remains of the union is the bone alone.

108 says a wrong done to you should be forgotten that very day (அன்றே மறப்பது). 113 says gain that comes from leaving fairness should be let go that very day (அன்றே ஒழிய விடல்). The shared அன்றே gives both the same urgency: neither a grievance nor an unfair gain is to be kept overnight.

139 makes the absence of evil speech a test of having conduct; 959 says that as a sprout shows the ground it lay in, the words from the mouth show the family of the one born in it (குலத்தில் பிறந்தார் வாய்ச்சொல்). Both treat what comes out of the mouth as the evidence of what a person is.

532 uses as its comparison that constant poverty kills understanding (அறிவினை நிச்ச நிரப்புக் கொன்றாங்கு). 1046 describes one form of it: even when the poor speak good matter well understood, their words and meaning go slack (சொற்பொருள் சோர்வு படும்); Parimelazhagar says nobody listens, so their learning yields nothing. Read together, the 'killing' of understanding in 532 includes its losing all effect in the world.

564 says the king of whom the painful words 'our lord is harsh' (இறைகடியன் என்றுரைக்கும் இன்னாச்சொல்) are spoken will quickly perish. 555 says the tears of those who cannot bear their affliction are the weapon that wears away wealth (செல்வத்தைத் தேய்க்கும் படை). In both, what destroys the ruler comes from the subjects' suffering, as speech in one verse and as tears in the other.

233 names renown as the one thing in the world that doesn't die. 331 calls taking what doesn't last for what lasts the lowest kind of knowledge. Chapter 34 never excepts fame, so fame's permanence is exactly what the later chapter puts in doubt.

Verse 27 says the world lies within the one who discerns the kinds of the five (ஐந்தின் வகைதெரிவான் கட்டே உலகு): taste, light, touch, sound and smell. Verse 354 says that even having gained the fivefold awareness (ஐயுணர்வு எய்தியக் கண்ணும்) is of no benefit to those without perception of the real (மெய்யுணர்வு). Verse 354 sets a limit on 27: command of the five is not the end, and without true perception it yields nothing.

285 says that a loving nature with grace in view (அருள்கருதி) is not found in those who, with goods in view (பொருள்கருதி), watch for another's unguarded moment. 914 opposes those who examine அருட்பொருள் to women for whom பொருள் is the only thing of value. In the chapter on theft and in this one, the same pair, aiming at grace or aiming at goods, sorts people into two kinds that do not mix.

34 says being spotless in mind is the whole of virtue (மனத்துக்கண் மாசிலன் ஆதல் அனைத்து அறன்). 317 makes the highest thing the absence of any mind-born ill toward anyone (மனத்தானாம் மாணா செய்யாமை தலை), in a chapter whose first two verses speak of the மாசற்றார். 317 gives 34's general claim a specific content: the unstained mind is one that harbours no hurt.

141 says the folly (பேதைமை) of desiring a woman who is another's (பிறன்பொருளாள்) is not found (இல்) in those who have seen aram and porul; 910 says the folly that comes of attachment to a woman (பெண்சேர்ந்தாம் பேதைமை) is never found (இல்) in those with a deliberating mind. Both end on 'பேதைமை ... இல்' and treat the lapse as a failure of understanding that knowledge excludes, once about another's wife in the Book of Virtue and once about subservience to one's own in the Book of Wealth.

844 says the claim to ஒண்மை is itself what வெண்மை is. 404 says that however good an unlearned person's ஒட்பம் may be, those with understanding do not accept it (கொள்ளார் அறிவுடையார்). 404 shows the other side of 844's self-assessment: the brightness one credits to oneself is not credited by those able to judge.

261 says the form of தவம் is just this: bearing one's own pain and doing no harm to living beings (உயிர்க்குறுகண் செய்யாமை அற்றே). 264 says crushing foes (ஒன்னார்த் தெறல்) and raising friends come through தவம், if one so intends. Read plainly, austerity defined by harmlessness is credited three verses later with the power to destroy. Parimelazhagar eases this by taking the foes as enemies of virtue and by reading எண்ணின் as implying that ascetics do not normally think of such things.

210 promises that the one who does no evil will not come to ruin. 117 says the world will not count as ruin ('கெடுவாக வையாது') the low state (தாழ்வு) of one who stays in virtue by standing fair. 117 allows that the upright may be brought low and changes what counts as 'கேடு', which limits how literally 210's promise can be taken.

469 says doing good can itself be a mistake if the character of the person is not taken into account. 987 asks what worth has achieved if it does not do what is sweet even to those who have done one harm (இன்னா செய்தார்க்கும் இனியவே செய்யாக்கால்), which makes the recipient's conduct irrelevant. The conflict holds if 469's நன்றாற்றல் is read as doing good in general, as Pope and Kalaignar take it; Parimelazhagar narrows it to a king's use of gifts and soft words toward other kings, and on that reading the two do not meet.

In 239 the land bears (பொறுத்த) a body without renown and yields less. 189 asks whether it is out of regard for virtue that the earth carries the weight (பொறை) of one who speaks ill of a person behind his back. Both picture the earth as bearing a moral load, and they differ in that 189's earth endures while 239's earth declines.

616: effort makes fortune (முயற்சி திருவினை ஆக்கும்) and lack of effort brings one into want. 371: unflagging effort arises from a fate of gain, and sloth from a fate of loss (ஆகூழால் தோன்றும் அசைவின்மை ... போகூழால் தோன்றும் மடி). 616 makes effort the cause of wealth; 371 makes fate the cause of effort, so on 371's account the causal chain in 616 starts one step earlier and is not in the person's hands.

157: though others do one wrong, not doing what is not aram is good (அறனல்ல செய்யாமை நன்று). 852: though someone does unbearable things intending division (பகல்கருதிப் பற்றா செயினும்), not doing harm with hostility in mind is the chief thing (இன்னாசெய்யாமை தலை). The 'even if they do ... not doing' structure and the refusal to answer in kind recur in the Book of Wealth's chapter on hostility, where the reason given is political prudence as well as virtue.

409 says the unlearned, though born high, do not have the worth (பாடு) of the learned born low. 133 says having conduct is good family, and lapse from it becomes low birth (இழிந்த பிறப்பாய் விடும்). Both make birth give way to something acquired, learning in 409 and conduct in 133.

769 names a resentment that will not leave (செல்லாத் துனி) among the things an army must be free of to win; Parimelazhagar says it arises from degrading treatment. 567 says harsh words and punishment beyond bounds are a file that wears down a king's conquering strength (அடுமுரண் தேய்க்கும் அரம்). 567 gives a cause on the king's side for the condition 769 warns of.
231 says the only profit for a life is to give and live with fame (இசை). 777 wants the same இசை, and pays for it with life itself. Giving and dying are two routes to one reward.

1223 says the evening that used to come budding with chill and looking wan (பனி அரும்பிப் பைதல்கொள் மாலை) now comes with revulsion budding and sorrow growing (துனி அரும்பித் துன்பம் வளர). 1227 says her sickness buds in the morning (காலை அரும்பி), swells through the day and opens in the evening. Both use அரும்பு, budding, for her pain, and together they give evening as both what brings the bud and when it opens.

983 lists five pillars that bear worth: அன்பு, நாண், ஒப்புரவு, கண்ணோட்டம், வாய்மை. 1013 singles out one of them: as all lives are fixed on the body (ஊனைக் குறித்த), சால்பு is fixed on the good called shame (நாண் என்னும் நன்மை குறித்தது). Read together, shame is one support among five in 983 and the seat of worth itself in 1013.

471 says to weigh one's own strength against the opponent's before acting (தன்வலியும் மாற்றான் வலியும் தூக்கிச் செயல்). 861 states what follows from that weighing when choosing an enemy: avoid opposing the stronger (வலியார்க்கு மாறேற்றல் ஓம்புக) and pursue enmity with the weaker (மெலியார்மேல் மேக பகை). 861 is 471's comparison turned into a rule.

614 says the generosity of a man without effort comes to nothing. 219 says that for a man of good feeling, being poor just is not being able to do the helpful things he would do (செயும்நீர செய்யாது அமைகலா வாறு). 219 shows the same blocked intention from the inside and without blame, so 614's scorn falls only on the case where the lack of means comes from not working.

824 says to fear deceivers who smile sweetly with the face while bitter within. 829 says that those who make much of you outwardly and despise you (மிகச்செய்து தம்மெள்ளுவார்) should be made to smile and be embraced within the friendship so that it dies (நகச்செய்து நட்பினுள் சாப்புல்லல்). The response 829 prescribes has the same form as the conduct 824 warns against; Parimelazhagar notes that it is allowed as royal policy although such doubleness is otherwise unfitting.

873 states the folly of standing alone (தமியனாய்) against many enemies. 875 gives the working rule for the smallest such case: with no ally and two enemies (தன்துணை இன்றால் பகையிரண்டால்), make one of them a pleasing ally (இன்துணையாக் கொள்க). 875 turns 873's condemnation into a remedy.

6 describes God as the one who quenched the five whose gates are the senses (பொறிவாயில் ஐந்தவித்தான்) and promises long life to those who keep to his path. 343 lays the same thing on the renouncer as a duty (அடல்வேண்டும் ஐந்தன் புலத்தை). The renouncer is asked to do what the invocation names as the mark of the Lord.

739 says lands that give riches only when sought are not lands (நாடல்ல நாட வளந்தரு நாடு); Parimelazhagar takes நாடுதல் as searching with toil. 1031 says ploughing is foremost even though one toils at it (உழந்தும் உழவே தலை). On Parimelazhagar's reading, 739 counts the need for toil against a land while 1031 honours the toil that produces its yield; if நாட means only that the inhabitants need not go looking elsewhere, the conflict fades.

695 treats the king's secret (மறை) as something to be heard only when he lets it go. 1076 says the base are like a beaten drum because they carry to others the secrets they have heard (தாம் கேட்ட மறை பிறர்க்கு உய்த்துரைக்கலான்). The two give the two ends of handling a secret: restraint in acquiring it in 695, and the failure to hold it in 1076.

221 says giving to those who have nothing is what giving is (வறியார்க்கொன்று ஈவதே ஈகை), and all other giving has the nature of a loan to be returned. 1077 says the base will not even shake a wet hand (ஈர்ங்கை விதிரார்) except for those whose bent fist would break their jaw; Parimelazhagar sums up that they give nothing to the weak and everything to those who hurt them. The base man's giving in 1077 is the reverse of 221's definition: it goes only to the strong.

152 says always bear with an excess done to you, and that forgetting it is better still (அதனை மறத்தல் அதனினும் நன்று). 303 uses the same verb for the anger itself: forget anger toward anyone (மறத்தல் வெகுளியை யார்மாட்டும்), since evils are born from it. One forgets the offence and the other the anger at it; 303 adds the reason.

Parimelazhagar reads 847 as a person who receives rare instruction and lets it run out without taking it in, harming himself. 418 says ears not pierced by listening are deaf even though they hear (கேட்பினுங் கேளாத் தகையவே). On that reading both describe teaching that reaches a person and does not enter; 847 adds that the loss is self-inflicted.

234 joins earthly renown (புகழ்) to honour in the gods' world (புத்தேள் உலகு). 966 names the same pair as the two things lost by following those who scorn you: it brings no renown and does not carry one to the gods' land (புகழ் இன்றால் புத்தேள் நாட்டு உய்யாதால்). In both verses renown here and the gods' world there are counted together, as gained in 234 and forfeited in 966.

395 calls the unlearned the lowest (கடையரே கல்லாதவர்). 729 uses the same word to put someone beneath them: those who have studied and understood and still fear an assembly of the good are lower than the unlearned (கல்லாதவரின் கடை). 729 thus limits 395's ranking, since learning that is not voiced does not lift a person above the bottom rank and, as Parimelazhagar explains, leaves them with only the labour of having studied.

696 opens with குறிப்பறிந்து, knowing the king's mood, as the first condition of speaking to him. 701 praises the one who looks and knows what is meant without its being said (கூறாமை நோக்கிக் குறிப்பறிவான்) as an ornament to the earth. The skill 696 names in passing is taken up as the subject of the next chapter, beginning with 701.

754 limits its promise to wealth that came without wrong (தீதின்றி வந்த பொருள்). 659 says what was taken making others weep leaves with weeping, while what came by good ways pays later even if lost (பிற்பயக்கும் நற்பாலவை). Both make the manner of acquisition decide what wealth yields.

167 says the fair goddess (செய்யவள்) grudges the envious man and shows him to her elder sister (தவ்வை). 617 names both sisters by residence: மாமுகடி lives in sloth, and தாமரையினாள் in the effort of the unslothful. The same pair of goddesses marks envy in Book 1 and sloth in Book 2 as conditions that hand a person over from fortune to misfortune.

These are the two 'at least this' verses: however much else is left unguarded, guard the tongue; however wrong the rest, don't desire another's wife. They show what the book treats as the last line of moral defence.

429 says those whose understanding guards against what is ahead have no affliction that comes to shake them (அதிர வருவதோர் நோய்). 435 says the life of one who does not guard before it comes (வருமுன்னர்க் காவாதான்) perishes like a straw-heap before fire. They are the positive and negative statements of one rule; 435 stands in the chapter on faults, where Parimelazhagar supplies 'fault' as what comes, while 429 speaks of harm in general.

220 speaks of a man selling himself ('ஒருவன் விற்றுக்கோள்') as a price worth paying for the ruin that benevolence brings. 1080 says the base are fit for one thing: when something befalls them, to sell themselves quickly ('விற்றற்கு உரியர் விரைந்து'). Self-sale is honourable in the first as the cost of giving and contemptible in the second as an escape from one's own trouble.

474 lists three failings that bring quick ruin: not living in accord (அமைந்தாங்கு ஒழுகான்), not knowing one's measure (அளவறியான்) and admiring oneself. 863 lists the traits of one who is easy for an enemy, and two of them match: he does not know (அறியான்) and does not fit in with others (அமைவிலன்). The chapter on what makes a good enemy to have describes, from the other side, the man 474 says will perish.

882 uses the verb of fear for kin-like enemies (அஞ்சுக கேள்போல் பகைவர் தொடர்பு). 824 uses it for deceivers who smile sweetly with the face and are bitter within (முகத்தின் இனிய நகாஅ அகத்தின்னா வஞ்சரை அஞ்சப்படும்). The chapter on false friendship and the chapter on inner enmity reach the same instruction: what is to be feared is hostility presented as closeness.

158 says to overcome those who do excessive wrong out of arrogance (மிகுதியான்) by one's own worthiness (தகுதியான் வென்றுவிடல்), which Parimelazhagar glosses as forbearance. 985 says the strength of the able is to bow (பணிதல்), and that this is the weapon by which the worthy change their opponents (மாற்றாரை மாற்றும் படை). Both describe yielding as the means of prevailing and use the vocabulary of contest, வெல்லல் and படை, for it.

862 asks how a man with no love, no worthy allies (ஆன்ற துணையிலன்) and no strength of his own can wear down an enemy's might. 449 states the principle: those without capital have no profit, and those without the prop of supporters (மதலையாஞ் சார்பிலார்) have no standing. 862 applies to a contest with an enemy what 449 says of a ruler's position in general.

137 says that from conduct people reach high standing and from a lapse they reach எய்தாப் பழி, which Parimelazhagar takes as blame that is not properly theirs, laid on them because the lapse makes it believable. 117 says the world will not count as ruin the low state of one who stays in the right by being fair (கெடுவாக வையாது உலகம்). In both the world's verdict follows character more than facts: it discounts the upright person's fall and charges the lapsed person with more than he did.

1005 says those who neither give nor enjoy have nothing even with crores piled up (அடுக்கிய கோடியுண்டாயினும் இல்), and treats this as the miser's own failing. 377 says even those who have gathered crores can enjoy them only as the apportioner has apportioned (வகுத்தான் வகுத்த வகையல்லால் ... துய்த்தல் அரிது). Both separate owning from enjoying; 377 places part of enjoyment outside the owner's choice, which limits the blame in 1005.

110 says there is escape (உய்வுண்டாம்) for other wrongs but none (உய்வில்லை) for killing gratitude. 896 says one burned by fire may survive (உய்வுண்டாம்), but those who go on offending the great will not (உய்யார்).
