The same உய்வு formula marks what each chapter treats as its unforgivable offence, so a reader should take 'only this has no escape' as the book's way of stressing gravity and not as a strict ranking.

275 says the concealed conduct of those who say 'we are free of attachment' brings many harms with the cry எற்றெற்று; 655 says do not do what will make you grieve saying எற்று ('what is this I have done'). The same exclamation of regret marks the test in both, in the renouncer's conduct and in the minister's action; Manakkudavar, however, takes the cry in 275 as other people's, not the doer's.

In 1250 she says that if she keeps in her heart the man who left without coming close (துறந்தாரை நெஞ்சத்து உடையேமா), she will lose still more beauty (இன்னும் இழத்தும் கவின்); Parimelazhagar frames this as a case for forgetting him. In 1262 she tells her friend that if she forgets him today, beauty will leave her and the bangles slip from her arms (இன்று மறப்பின் ... கலங்கழியும் காரிகை நீத்து). The two speeches give opposite accounts of whether remembering or forgetting costs her beauty; both are a speaker's words in the moment, and the conflict holds on Parimelazhagar's reading of the settings.

352 has darkness leave and joy arise for those who see truly. 243 says those whose hearts are joined with compassion do not enter the painful world joined with darkness (இருள்சேர்ந்த இன்னா உலகம்). 243's wording supports Parimelazhagar's reading of இருள் in 352 as a dark world of suffering, and shows the book promising escape from it by compassion as well as by knowledge.

1207 says she does not know how to forget, and that even remembering burns her heart (உள்ளினும் உள்ளம் சுடும்). 1250 says that holding him in her heart will cost her yet more beauty. Both count remembering him as a harm to herself, while 1207 adds that forgetting is not available to her.

50 places the person who lives rightly on earth (வையத்துள்) among the gods of the sky. 413 says those who have listening as food for the ear are, though on earth (நிலத்து), equal to the gods who are fed by oblations. Both verses set 'on earth' against the gods and say a human excellence closes the gap, right living in one case and learning by listening in the other.

438 says the miserliness called the clinging heart (பற்றுள்ளம் என்னும் இவறன்மை) is not to be counted among any others; Parimelazhagar takes this to mean it exceeds all other faults. 1002 names what lies behind it, the delusion (மருள்) that everything comes by wealth, so that one clings without giving (ஈயாது இவறும்), and gives its result as an inglorious birth. 1002 supplies a cause and a consequence for the fault 438 ranks.

251 asks how one who eats another's flesh to enlarge his own (தன்னூன் பெருக்கற்கு) can exercise அருள்; 968 asks whether a life that nurses the flesh (ஊன் ஓம்பும் வாழ்க்கை) is any medicine once dignity is lost. Both use ஊன், one's own flesh, for a body tended at the cost of something higher: அருள் in one verse, honour in the other.

189 wonders that the earth bears the backbiter's weight at all. 990 says that if the worthy decline in worth, the great earth will not bear its load (இருநிலந்தான் தாங்காது மன்னோ பொறை). Together they show the image used at both ends: the earth strains under the bad man, and is able to carry its load only while the worthy stay worthy.

Verse 24 calls the one who guards the five senses a seed (வித்து) for the ground called வரன், which Parimelazhagar takes as release. Verse 361 calls craving the seed (வித்து) that bears unceasing birth for all beings. The book uses the seed for both outcomes: restraint of the senses is sown toward release, and craving is what sprouts as rebirth.

956 says those resolved to live by their spotless lineage will not do unworthy things by taking to deceit (சலம் பற்றி). 660 uses the same word for wealth-making: securing wealth made by deceit (சலத்தால் பொருள் செய்து) is like keeping water in an unfired clay pot. 956 rules deceit out on grounds of family honour; 660 adds that its gains do not hold anyway.

186 says the one who tells another's blame (பிறன்பழி கூறுவான்) will have his own faults sorted through and told (தன்பழியுள்ளும் திறன்தெரிந்து கூறப்படும்). 319 says that hurt done to others in the forenoon comes back on oneself in the afternoon (பிற்பகல் தாமே வரும்). The same return of the deed appears for speech and for injury; in 186 the return is carried out by other people's tongues.
Here effort is fate's product. In 620, effort puts fate behind you. The tension is sharper than one between effort and fate as rivals, because 371 removes effort as an independent force.

515 requires for a task one who knows and endures and can carry it through (அறிந்தாற்றிச் செய்கிற்பாற்கு). 640 says that those without practical ability (திறப்பாடு இலாதவர்), though they plan in proper order, do things that never reach completion. 640 shows what 515's last requirement guards against: knowing is not enough without the capacity to finish.

1014 asks whether shame is not an ornament (அணி) to the worthy, and whether without it their proud walk is not a disease (அஃதின்றேல் பிணி). 575 has the same shape: kindly regard is the eye's ornament (அணிகலம்), and without it (அஃதின்றேல்) the eye is a sore (புண்). In both the missing virtue does not leave the thing plain but turns it into an affliction.

439 commands: never admire yourself (வியவற்க எஞ்ஞான்றும் தன்னை). 474 gives the outcome for one who doesn't live in accord with others, doesn't know his measure and admires himself (தன்னை வியந்தான்): he perishes quickly. Parimelazhagar connects them in his note on 439, saying that self-admiration keeps one from knowing place, time and strength.

Verse 67 says a father's good to his son is to make him sit foremost in the assembly; Parimelazhagar takes this as making him learned beyond the learned there. Verse 722 says those called learned among the learned (கற்றாருள் கற்றார்) are those who can make what they learned go home before the learned. 722 supplies what the front seat of 67 requires in practice: learning that can be delivered in front of that assembly.

120 asks traders to care for what belongs to others as for what is theirs (பிறவும் தமபோல் பேணி). 1015 says the world calls those who feel shame at others' blame and their own (பிறர்பழியும் தம்பழியும் நாணுவார்) the dwelling of shame; Parimelazhagar reads this as weighing the two alike. Both define a virtue, fairness in one and shame in the other, by removing the difference between oneself and others.

893 says: if you want ruin (கெடல்வேண்டின்), go ahead without listening and wrong those able to destroy. 922 says: do not drink, but if anyone will, let it be those who do not want the regard of the worthy (எண்ணப்பட வேண்டாதார்). Both forbid by an ironic permission addressed to whoever wants the bad result, once about offending the powerful and once about liquor.

999 says that for those not able to laugh (நகல் வல்லர் அல்லார்) the great world lies in darkness even by day; Parimelazhagar takes நகல் as mixing with others and being glad at heart. 523 says the life of one who does not mingle freely (அளவளாவு இல்லாதான்) is like a tank filling without a bank. On Parimelazhagar's reading both describe the cost of not mixing with people, as lost wealth in 523 and a darkened world in 999.

983 lists kindly regard (கண்ணோட்டம்) with love, shame, obligingness and truth as the five pillars that hold up worth (சால்பு). 572 gives it a wider load: the conduct of the world rests in it (கண்ணோட்டத் துள்ளது உலகியல்). The quality that is one support of personal character in 983 is the support of social life in 572.

294 says one who lives without falsehood in the heart (உள்ளத்தாற் பொய்யாது) is present in the hearts of all the world. 119 says rectitude is speech without bend, provided there is surely no bend within (உட்கோட்டம் இன்மை). In truthfulness and in impartiality alike, straight speech is counted only when the inside matches it.

910 says the folly that comes of attachment to a woman never exists in those whose hearts hold deliberation (எண்சேர்ந்த நெஞ்சத்து இடனுடையார்). 918 says the embrace of deceiving women is an affliction to those who lack examining understanding (ஆயும் அறிவினர் அல்லார்க்கு). The neighbouring chapters, on subservience to a wife and on courtesans, give the same safeguard: a mind that thinks the matter through.

760 says abundant wealth makes virtue and pleasure easy to get. 1002 calls it a delusion to hoard without giving on the thought that everything comes from wealth (பொருளானாம் எல்லாமென்று ஈயாது இவறும் மருள்), and says it leads to a low birth. 760's claim holds for wealth that is made and used; held back by a miser, the same belief is called delusion.

239 says the land's rich yield shrinks (வண்பயன் குன்றும்) under a person without renown. 560 says the yield of cows shrinks (ஆபயன் குன்றும்) if the guardian does not guard. The same phrase ties natural yield to human conduct, a private person's in 239 and the king's in 560.

In 1140 the woman says the unknowing laugh where she can see, because they have not undergone what she has (யாம்பட்ட தாம்படா ஆறு). In 1219 she says those who blame him for not being gracious in waking life are those who have not seen a lover in dreams (காதலர்க் காணாதவர்). Both explain the town's judgement by its lack of the lover's experience.

763 says a crowd of weak enemies is nothing to one strong fighter. 873 says one who, being alone, takes on the enmity of many is more foolish than the mad (தமியனாய்ப் பல்லார் பகைகொள்பவன்). 763 holds only where the one is a cobra and the many are rats; 873 is the warning for a lone person who assumes that.

126 says restraint of the five in one birth protects through seven; 835 says a fool can, by what he does in one birth (ஒருமைச் செயல்), make the mire he will sink in through seven (எழுமையும் தான்புக்கு அழுந்தும் அளறு). The one-birth and seven-births arithmetic runs in both directions: one life is enough to secure the next seven or to ruin them.

654: clear-sighted people do not do what is degrading even when trouble comes. 218: those of 'கடனறி காட்சி' do not falter in ஒப்புரவு even in a season without means (இடனில் பருவத்தும் ... ஒல்கார்). One verse says hardship does not make them do wrong, the other that it does not make them stop doing good; the two are the negative and positive halves of the same steadiness.

557 says that a king's lack of tender care (அளியின்மை) is to those who live under him what lack of rain is to the earth. 571 states the positive side: the world exists because kindly regard exists; Parimelazhagar reads this of kings. In both verses the ruler's kindness is treated as a condition of life for the people, not as an ornament only.

855 asks who would be inclined to overcome those able to lean away when hostility confronts them (இகலெதிர் சாய்ந்தொழுக வல்லாரை). 985 says the strength of the capable is to bow (பணிதல்), and that this is the weapon by which the worthy change their opponents (மாற்றாரை மாற்றும் படை). Both treat yielding as what disarms an opponent; 985 states it as a trait of the சான்றோர், 855 as a skill (வல்லார்), which Parimelazhagar says is hard for kings.

853 says that removing the painful disease of hostility gives a brightness that neither fails nor is flawed (தவலில்லாத் தாவில் விளக்கம்), which Parimelazhagar takes as lasting fame. 156 says those who punish have one day's pleasure while those who forbear have praise until the end (பொன்றுந் துணையும் புகழ்). Both make enduring renown the result of declining the quarrel, one in the householder's ethics and one in public life.

638 obliges the man at the king's side to tell him what is good, even if the king destroys wise counsel. 696 and 697 advise saying what is not disliked, in the way that he wants. The same courtier is told to be fearless and to be careful. Parimelazhagar narrows the gap by reading 'wanted' as also greatly beneficial.

709 says the eye itself tells enmity and friendship (கண்ணுரைக்கும்) to those who know its kinds; in 1271 the man tells her that though she hides it, her eyes have slipped her control and have something to say (உண்கண் உரைக்கல் உறுவது). The minister's skill of reading the eye in the book on statecraft is the lover's skill here, with the same verb உரை for what the eye does.

1246 tells the heart that when it sees the lover it cannot even sulk and then be reconciled (புலந்துணராய்), so its present anger is a false heat (பொய்க்காய்வு காய்தி). 1294 makes the same charge: the heart will not first raise a quarrel and then enjoy (துனிசெய்து துவ்வாய்), so no one will plan with it. In both the heart is accused of being incapable of the sulk it pretends to.
Both state a return of harm: 319 in morning and evening, 659 in the taking and the leaving. 659 restricts it to wealth and adds the positive half, that clean gains come back.

759 tells the reader bluntly to make wealth, for nothing cuts an enemy's pride so sharply. 1230 gives the cost of that advice from where it falls: a man whose nature has become wealth, and a woman who is dying of it. The separate books don't reconcile the claims.

769 says an army wins if it is free of dwindling, of resentment that does not leave, and of poverty (வறுமை). 759 says to make wealth because it is the sharpest weapon against foes. Parimelazhagar links them from both sides: under 769 he says desertion and want arise when the king does not pay, and under 759 that making wealth brings a large army.

425 says understanding is what has neither opening nor closing (மலர்தலும் கூம்பலும் இல்லது), which Parimelazhagar reads as steadiness in friendship with the high-minded, unlike a pond flower that opens and shuts. 782 says the friendship of the wise fills like the crescent moon and that of fools shrinks like the moon after full. Both verses judge attachment by a natural cycle; 782 praises the bond that grows, while 425 asks for one that does not swing in either direction.

In 775 a warrior whose glaring eye (விழித்த கண்) blinks when a spear is thrown counts that as running away. In 1082 the man looks, and her look answering his (நோக்கெதிர் நோக்குதல்) is like an army brought against him. Both treat meeting another's gaze as combat, one on the battlefield and one at first sight in love.

722 gives the title 'learned among the learned' to those who can convey their learning to the learned. 650 gives the reverse case: those who cannot unfold what they have learned so that others understand (கற்றது உணர விரித்துரையாதார்) are like flowers that bloom in clusters without scent. Together they treat communication as part of learning itself.

285 says அருள் with love is not found in one who watches to take another's goods; 251 asks how one who eats another creature's flesh to swell his own can hold to அருள் (எங்ஙனம் ஆளும் அருள்). Both test a claim to அருள் against a practice of taking from another for oneself, property in one case and the body in the other.

366 warns the renunciant to fear craving (அவா), because it deceives. In 1310, the sulking man names the same craving as what drives his heart to her. He uses the moral vocabulary correctly, with no intention of following it.

201 says the excellent fear the intoxication called evil deed (விழுமியார் அஞ்சுவர்); 1011 defines shame proper as shame on account of deeds (கருமத்தால் நாணுதல்). Fear and shame are given the same object, one's own wrong action, in two chapters, and Parimelazhagar glosses நாணுதல் elsewhere (433, 172) as அஞ்சுதல்.

1227 describes love's sickness as budding in the morning (காலை அரும்பி), swelling through the day and flowering at evening; 1274 places an unspoken meaning inside the bud of her smile (நகைமொக்குள்). Both use the bud for a feeling that is already there and has not yet opened, pain in the one and a hidden intention in the other.

733 defines a land as one that bears burdens arriving all at once and still agrees to give the king his whole due (இறையொருங்கு நேர்வது). 552 says that asking (இரவு) by one who stands with the sceptre is like a man standing with a spear saying 'hand it over'. The land's willingness to pay in 733 is not a licence for the king to demand: Manakkudavar reads 733's burdens as levies beyond the fixed due, which is the situation 552 condemns.

115 says loss and increase both occur, and the worthy keep the heart from bending because of them. 169 gives the hard case: the crooked-hearted prosper and the upright are ruined (செவ்வியான் கேடு), which calls for reflection. 169 shows the situation in which 115's advice is tested, when fortune seems to reward bending.

The verses share the words நினை and காய். In 1208 the woman says that however much she thinks of him he is not angry (எனைத்து நினைப்பினும் காயார்), and that this is all the honour he does her. In 1320 the man reports that when he merely sits thinking and looks at her she is angry (நினைத்திருந்து நோக்கினும் காயும்) and asks whom he is thinking of. The absent lover tolerates everything because he is not there to care, while the present one is questioned about every thought.

404 says that however good an unlearned person's brightness (ஒட்பம்) may be, those with understanding do not accept it. 423 says understanding is seeing the true substance of a thing from whoever's mouth it is heard (யார்யார்வாய்க் கேட்பினும்). If 404 means the wise set aside what the unlearned say even when it is good, it conflicts with 423's rule to judge the matter and not the speaker; on Parimelazhagar's reading, that they only decline to credit him with real brightness because an occasional hit is accidental, the conflict is smaller.

279: the arrow is straight but cruel, the lute bent but sweet, so judge by what a thing does (வினைபடு பாலால் கொளல்). 1084 sets a girl of womanly gentleness (பெண்டகைப் பேதை) against eyes that look as if they eat lives; Parimelazhagar takes அமர்த்தன as 'were at odds' with her nature. Both verses turn on a form that does not match its effect, one as a rule for judging ascetics and one as a lover's surprise.

610 gives the unslothful king the whole measured world. 606, in the same chapter, says that even when the wealth of earth-owners arrives the slothful get no excellent fruit from it. Together they separate two things: sloth does not only block gaining the world, it also empties the world of value when it is handed over.

262 says தவம் comes to those who already have தவம், and that for those without it taking it up is futile; Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar both read this as merit from earlier births. 273 pictures a person without strength (வலியில் நிலைமையான்) who takes on the form of the strong: a cow grazing in a tiger's skin. 273 shows what the futile undertaking of 262 looks like in practice. (The edition's text of 262 lacks the word அவம் at the start of the second line.)

530 says the king should attend to the reason for which a man who left has come back, wait, and accept him after thinking it over (இழைத்திருந்து எண்ணிக் கொளல்). 830 says that when an enemy turns friend, one should be friendly in face and withhold the heart (முகநட்டு அகநட்பு ஒரீஇ விடல்). Both deal with someone who comes over after having been apart and both withhold immediate trust, but 530 ends in acceptance of the kinsman while 830 ends in letting the former enemy go.

Both verses end with the identical line சொல்லின் தொகையறிந்த தூய்மையவர். 711 commands such people to know the assembly before speaking; 721 says that, having known the kinds (வகையறிந்து), they do not let their speech slip before the capable (வல்லவை வாய்சோரார்). The repeated line makes 721 the outcome of 711's instruction: knowing the assembly is what removes the fear that causes slips.

749 says a fort has its distinction from what is done in action (வினைமுகத்து வீறெய்தி) so that enemies fall at the front of battle. 750 says that whatever excellence a fort has, it is nothing with those who lack excellence in action (வினைமாட்சி இல்லார்கண் இல்லது). 750 turns 749's praise into a condition; Parimelazhagar says the two verses together show that a fort cannot do without its defenders.

356 speaks of those who learn and see the true thing; 357 adds the mind's own work: if the mind examines and knows with certainty what is (ஓர்த்து ... உள்ளது உணரின் ஒருதலையா), one need not think of birth again. Parimelazhagar reads the two as successive means, hearing instruction in 356 and reasoned examination in 357. The printed text here has உணரான், but Parimelazhagar's and Manakkudavar's glosses read உணரின், which the sense requires.

1016 says the high do not care for the wide world unless they have shame as their fence (நாண்வேலி). 1075 says the conduct of the base is fear (அச்சமே கீழ்களது ஆசாரம்), which Parimelazhagar takes as fear of harm from the king. Each verse names what keeps a kind of person within bounds: shame from inside for the high, fear from outside for the base.

517 tells the king to leave the task to the chosen man (அவன்கண் விடல்). 520, in the same chapter, tells the king to look into the one doing the work daily (நாடோறும் நாடுக), because the world stays straight only if he does. The delegation in 517 is therefore not a withdrawal of attention; Parimelazhagar's note on 520 says the checking should be done privately so that the man's standing is not damaged.

528 says that if the king looks at people not in common but according to rank (பொதுநோக்கான் வேந்தன் வரிசையா நோக்கின்), many will live looking to that. 972 says birth is alike for all, but distinction is not alike, because of the difference in what people do (சிறப்பொவ்வா செய்தொழில் வேற்றுமையான்). 972 gives a basis for the differential regard of 528: Parimelazhagar reads வரிசை there as each person's merit, and 972 locates such difference in conduct, not birth.

1311 gives her stated ground: every woman takes him in with her eyes (கண்ணின் பொது உண்பர்). 1313 shows the same worry applied to a trifle: a wreath must have been put on to be shown to another woman (ஒருத்தியைக் காட்டிய சூடினீர்). Her jealousy in both is about who sees him.
291 defines truthfulness as speech without harm; 200 demands use. Harmless idle talk passes the one test and fails the other, so the two chapters set different standards for speech.

1301 proposes not embracing (புல்லாது) in order to see his அல்லல்நோய். 1303 uses the same two words from the other side: leaving the one who sulks unembraced (புல்லா விடல்) is like giving அல்லல்நோய் to those already in distress (அலந்தாரை). Read together, the pain that 1301 treats as a brief test is the pain 1303 says must not be left standing.

840 treats the fool's mere entry (புகல்) into the company of the worthy as a defilement; Parimelazhagar adds that the assembly itself is lowered by it. 403 allows that even the unlearned are very good if they can stay silent before the learned (கற்றார்முன் சொல்லாதிருக்கப் பெறின்). 403 leaves a condition under which presence is acceptable, though its subject is the unlearned and 840's is the fool.

In 1135 the man says the girl with small bangles gave him (தந்தாள்) the palmyra horse and the grief that evening brings. In 1183 the woman says he took her grace and shame and gave in return (கைம்மாறா ... தந்து) sickness and pallor. Each lover describes the affliction as a gift from the other, and in both verses shame is part of what is lost.

Verse 62 has blameless children keep evil away through seven births (எழுபிறப்பும்). Verse 835 has the fool, in one birth's doing (ஒருமைச் செயல்), make the mire (அளறு) he sinks in for seven (எழுமையும்). The same seven-birth reckoning is applied in the opposite direction, once to a safeguard and once to a ruin made by oneself.

783 says that with people of character (பண்புடையாளர்) the bond grows sweeter with practice. 811 says that with those who lack character (பண்பிலார்), friendship is better shrinking than growing, even if they seem to drink one up with affection. The reward of long practice in 783 depends on பண்பு; without it, more closeness is worse.

510 says that doubting a man one has examined and trusted (தெளிந்தான்கண் ஐயுறவு) brings endless trouble. 514 says that even when tested in every way (எனைவகையான் தேறியக் கண்ணும்), many people turn different through the nature of the work (வினைவகையான் வேறாகும்). Read together, 514 limits 510: testing does not settle the matter, so the ban on doubt cannot mean a ban on watching how the man changes in office.

99 asks what could lead someone who knows the good that sweet words do to use harsh ones (வன்சொல்). 784 says friendship is not for laughing together but for going ahead to rebuke when a friend oversteps (மிகுதிக்கண் மேற்சென்று இடித்தற் பொருட்டு). The friendship chapter supplies a case where sharp words have a purpose, so 99's question is best read as aimed at needless harshness and not at every hard word.

447 asks who can ruin a ruler who keeps as his own those who will rebuke him (இடிக்குந் துணையாரை யாள்வாரை). 570 shows the opposite court: the harsh sceptre gathers the unlearned around it (கல்லார்ப் பிணிக்கும்), because, as Parimelazhagar says, such a ruler admits only those who will go along with him. The two verses together make a ruler's choice of companions a sign of the kind of rule he runs.

502 puts trust in one who has a shame that recoils from blemish (நாணுடையான்). 506 warns against trusting those who are cut off (அற்றார்), because they have no attachment and are not ashamed of blame (பற்றிலர் நாணார் பழி); Parimelazhagar takes அற்றார் as those without kin, Manakkudavar as those without conduct. The two verses are the positive and negative of one criterion, and 506 adds a cause: shame depends on having ties.

445 says counsellors must be chosen with care because the ruler sees by them. 639 states the cost of choosing badly: a minister at one's side who plots harm (பழுதெண்ணும் மந்திரி) is worse than seventy crore enemies. 639 shows what the care in 445 protects against.

In 1238 the man recalls that when he loosened the arms that embraced her, her forehead turned pale (பசந்தது ... பேதை நுதல்). In 1328 he recalls union so intense that her forehead sweated (நுதல் வெயர்ப்ப). Her forehead is the place where he reads both the first sign of separation and the fullness of union.

590 warns that a king who honours a spy so that others know of it (சிறப்பறிய) has himself let the secret out (புறப்படுத்தான் ஆகும் மறை); 663 says a deed should be done so that it shows only at the end, since showing midway brings lasting trouble (இடைக்கொட்கின்). In both the actor's own conduct, not an enemy's skill, is what exposes the undertaking.

739 says lands are those whose riches come without being sought (நாடா வளத்தன). 594 says prosperity itself asks the way and goes (ஆக்கம் அதர்வினாய்ச் செல்லும்) to the person of unwavering drive. Both picture wealth arriving unsought, but 594 makes it the result of the person's energy, where 739 makes it a property of the land.

1111 says she is more delicate than the anicham (நின்னினும் மென்னீரள்); 1289 says love itself is more delicate than a flower (மலரினும் மெல்லிது காமம்) and few catch its right moment. The same comparative, softer than a flower, is applied first to the beloved's body and later to the experience of love.

In 1188 the woman complains that people say only 'she has grown pale' and no one says 'he has left her' (துறந்தார் அவர் என்பார் இல்). In 1235 the wasted shoulders themselves declare his cruelty. One speech says the visible change brings talk about her alone, and the other says the same kind of change speaks against him; the difference is in who is reading the body, the town or the friend.

706 and 710 say the face and eyes can't but show what is within. 585 asks the spy to stand under suspicious eyes and let nothing spill. If the face always reveals, the spy's art should be impossible, and if the spy's art is possible, this chapter overclaims.

1305, on Parimelazhagar's reading, has the man find beauty in her sulk even though he is good and blameless. 1321 gives her side: he has no fault (இல்லை தவறு அவர்க்கு), yet the way he shows tenderness (அவர் அளிக்குமாறு) is what makes sulking possible. Both verses detach the sulk from any real offence.

327 says don't take another's life even if it costs your own. 550 says the king's killing of the cruel is like weeding. The book's sharpest split between Aram and Porul: an absolute rule meets the role of king. Parimelazhagar resolves it through caste duty, which the verses don't mention.

409 ranks the learned low-born over the unlearned high-born. 502 makes good birth the first condition for trust. The two can be squared, but the book's position on birth clearly depends on what is being asked.

757 says the child grace, born of love, is reared by the nurse called wealth (பொருளென்னும் செல்வச் செவிலி). 247 sets the two side by side: that world is not for those without grace, as this world is not for those without wealth. Both pair அருள் with பொருள்; 247 keeps them parallel, while 757 makes grace depend on wealth to grow.

Verse 68 says one's children's understanding (அறிவுடைமை) is sweet to all beings on the great earth (மன்னுயிர்க்கெல்லாம் இனிது); Parimelazhagar reads தம்மின் as 'more than to oneself', while Kalaignar and Subramuniyaswami take it as children who surpass their parents. Verse 399 says the learned love learning more on seeing that what delights them delights the world (தாமின்புறுவது உலகின்புறக் கண்டு). Both treat knowledge as a pleasure that is not private: the parent's pride in 68 and the scholar's delight in 399 are each measured against the world's share in it.

889 says that inner enmity, though as small as a split sesame seed (எட்பகவன்ன சிறுமைத்தே ஆயினும்), has ruin in it. 965 says even those like a hill will be lowered if they do a lowering thing the size of a kunri seed (குன்றி அனைய செயின்). Both use a tiny seed as the measure of something that brings down what is large, a family or kingdom in 889 and a person's standing in 965.

1170 regrets that her eyes cannot travel to where he is as her mind can. In 1214 the dream does the travelling: it seeks out the man who gives nothing in waking life and brings him (நல்காரை நாடித் தரற்கு), and so there is pleasure in the dream. Parimelazhagar spells it out: the dream goes to the country he went to, finds him and delivers him.

691 tells those who serve quarrelsome kings (இகல்வேந்தர்) to be like people warming at a fire, neither moving off nor closing in (அகலாது அணுகாது தீக்காய்வார் போல்க). In 1104 a lover asks where she got a fire that burns when he withdraws and is cool when he comes near (நீங்கின் தெறூஉம் குறுகுங்கால் தண்ணென்னும் தீ). The king's fire burns at close range and the lover's reverses that rule, so the court calls for a kept middle distance and the love speech for none.

432 calls honour that has passed beyond the fine a fault in a ruler. 1028 says that for one raising his family, idling and minding his மானம் brings ruin (மடிசெய்து மானங் கருதக் கெடும்). Both treat a misplaced sense of honour as a fault, one in the king and one in the head of a house.

376 says what is not one's portion will not stay however carefully it is guarded (பரியினும் ஆகாவாம் பாலல்ல), and what is one's own will not leave even if thrown out. 659 says all that is taken with others' tears leaves with tears, and what is of the good kind (நற்பாலவை) pays later even if lost. Both say some goods stay and some go whatever one does; 659 gives a test the person controls, the way the wealth was gained, where 376 gives only fate's allotment.

855 says no one sets out to defeat a person who can lean away from hostility. 874 goes a step further: the world rests in the greatness of the person of character who conducts himself taking enmity as friendship (பகை நட்பாக் கொண்டொழுகும்). 855 describes safety gained by not answering hostility; 874 describes actively turning the enemy into a friend and gives it a public value.

Verse 28 says the greatness of people whose word is full (நிறைமொழி மாந்தர்) is shown on earth by their மறைமொழி; Parimelazhagar explains நிறைமொழி as speech that produces its result whether spoken in grace or in anger. Verse 55 says that when the wife who worships her husband says 'rain', it rains (பெய்யெனப் பெய்யும் மழை). Both give a person's word power over the world as the proof of their standing, for the renouncer through austerity and for the wife through steadfastness at home.

276 ends 'வாழ்வாரின் வன்கணார் இல்': none are harder than those who live by posing as renouncers. 1198, spoken by the woman in separation, ends with the same words: none in the world are harder than those who go on living without a kind word from the one they love. The shared formula uses வன்கண் in two senses, the cruelty of the deceiver in 276 and the grim endurance of the one left behind in 1198.

1116 says the stars cannot distinguish the moon from her face. 1117 immediately denies that the two are alike: the moon fills out from loss and has a spot, and her face has none (மறுவுண்டோ). Parimelazhagar reads 1117 as mocking the stars for missing an obvious difference, so the second verse withdraws the equality the first seemed to grant.

341 says a person has no pain from each thing he has left (யாதனின் யாதனின் நீங்கியான் நோதல் அதனின் அதனின் இலன்), taking objects one by one. 368 says those without craving have no sorrow at all (அவாஇல்லார்க்கு இல்லாகுந் துன்பம்). 368 moves from the objects given up to the craving behind them, so the relief is complete instead of item by item.

420 asks what it matters whether they die or live, those மாக்கள் who know taste by the mouth and not by the ear. 1012 says food, clothing and the rest are no different for all living beings (ஊணுடை எச்சம் உயிர்க்கெல்லாம் வேறல்ல), and the distinction of மாந்தர் is having shame. Both verses treat eating as what humans share with every creature and put human worth elsewhere, in the ear's taste for one and in shame for the other.

854 offers இன்பத்துள் இன்பம், the joy of joys, as what follows when hostility goes. 629 uses the same two phrases differently: one who does not crave pleasure within pleasure (இன்பத்துள் இன்பம் விழையாதான்) does not feel pain within pain (துன்பத்துள் துன்பம் உறுதல் இலன்). Read together, the joy 854 promises is a result of removing a cause of suffering, and 629 warns against making such joy an object of desire.

133 makes conduct the thing that constitutes good family (ஒழுக்கம் உடைமை குடிமை); 951 says integrity and shame are found together by nature only in those born in a good house (இற்பிறந்தார் கண்அல்லது இல்லை இயல்பாக). If குடிமை in 133 means that conduct alone makes one well-born, 951 runs the other way and makes birth the source of the conduct. The conflict disappears on Parimelazhagar's reading of 133, where conduct only preserves or forfeits a rank that birth has already given.

336 says a person who was yesterday is not today (இன்றில்லை). 235 speaks of a death that is really existence (உளதாகும் சாக்காடு), possible only for the skilled, which Parimelazhagar explains as the body of fame surviving. The two verses use the same pair, உள and இல், in opposite directions: 336 for the plain fact of death and 235 for the rare death that leaves something that is.

651 sets வினைநலம் above துணைநலம்: support gives only ஆக்கம், good action gives all that is wanted. 455 says purity of mind and purity of action (செய்வினை தூய்மை) both come leaning on purity of company (இனந்தூய்மை தூவா வரும்). Read together, the action that 651 ranks above one's support is itself said to depend on the people one keeps.

860 says all ills come from hostility, and from friendly gladness (நகல்) comes 'the pride called good conduct' (நன்னயம் என்னும் செருக்கு). 180 has the same shape and the same closing phrase: coveting without thought yields destruction, and 'the pride called not-wanting' (வேண்டாமை என்னும் செருக்கு) yields victory. In both the verse sets a ruinous impulse against its absence and calls that absence a செருக்கு, which Parimelazhagar glosses in both places as wealth.

563 says a cruel-sceptred king who keeps doing what terrifies (வெருவந்த செய்தொழுகும் வெங்கோலன்) will certainly and quickly perish (ஒருவந்தம் ஒல்லைக் கெடும்). 548 says a king who is not easy of access and does not inquire and do justice will sink and perish of himself (தானே கெடும்). Neither verse needs an enemy to bring the king down: in both the misrule is itself the cause of the fall.

296 says not lying gives all the virtues (எல்லா அறமுந் தரும்); Parimelazhagar takes எய்யாமை as 'without wearying the body'. 297 then concludes that one who keeps steadily to not lying does well even without doing the other virtues (அறம்பிற செய்யாமை நன்று). The second verse depends on the first: the others can be left undone because this one already supplies them.

475 warns that even a cart loaded with peacock feathers breaks its axle if the load is piled too high (அச்சிறும்). 1115 says she has worn anicham flowers without removing the stalks (கால்களையாள்), so no good drums will sound for her waist; Parimelazhagar explains that the waist will break under the weight and get the funeral drum. Both make the lightest possible load the breaking one, as counsel on overreach in 475 and as playful hyperbole about her slenderness in 1115.

1260 asks whether those with hearts like fat in fire can say they will hold out in a sulk (புணர்ந்தூடி நிற்பேம் எனல்). 1294 tells the heart that it will not sulk first and enjoy afterwards, so no one will plan such things with it. Both say the intention to sulk cannot survive her own heart; 1294 adds that she will stop consulting it.

383 names three things that never leave a ruler: promptness, learning and resolve (தூங்காமை கல்வி துணிவுடைமை இம்மூன்றும்). 688 has the same frame for the envoy who repeats the king's message: purity, support and resolve, these three (தூய்மை துணைமை துணிவுடைமை இம்மூன்றின்). துணிவுடைமை is the term common to king and envoy; the other two differ with the office.

669 says to do with resolve the deed that yields joy even though pain comes thick at first (துன்பம் உறவரினும் ... இன்பம் பயக்கும் வினை): pain now, joy later. 630 goes a step further and has the person take the pain itself as joy (இன்னாமை இன்பம் எனக்கொளின்). Parimelazhagar reads the pain in both as the strain of effort.
464 says to avoid beginning what isn't clear. 469 adds that even with the deed and intent clear, the person is another thing to know. Clarity about the act is not clarity about the recipient.

529 says estranged kin return of themselves once the cause of discord is gone. 530 turns to one who left and has come back for a reason (காரணத்தின் வந்தானை) and tells the king to attend to it and accept him only after reflection (இழைத்திருந்து எண்ணிக் கொளல்). The pair separates two kinds of return, one that follows from the king's own correction and one prompted by the returner's interest, and prescribes welcome for the first and caution for the second.

1207 says that even as she remembers, her heart is burned (உள்ளம் சுடும்). 1159 describes the same burning as a property of love's sickness: fire burns only when touched, and cannot burn when one moves away as love does (விடிற்சுடல் ஆற்றுமோ தீ). 1159 gives the general paradox of a fire that burns at a distance, and 1207 shows it at work inside memory.

418 denies real hearing to ears that listening has not opened. 577 says those without kindly regard have no eyes (கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லவர் கண்ணிலர்), and those who have eyes do not lack it. The form of argument is the same, an organ is counted as present only when it is used for its higher purpose, applied to instruction in 418 and to kindness in 577.

1164 says the sea of love exists and the raft to cross it does not (காமக் கடல் ... ஏமப் புணை இல்). 1200 tells the heart to fill up the sea (கடலைச் செறாஅஅய்) instead of telling its pain to the unloving; Pope takes this sea as her own sorrow, while Parimelazhagar takes it as the sea that torments her. On Pope's reading the two verses share the sea as the measure of her grief, with crossing it and filling it both out of reach.

619 says that even if a thing cannot come about because of fate (தெய்வத்தான் ஆகாதெனினும்), effort pays the wage of the body's strain; 596 says a high aim keeps its worth even when it is thrust aside, which Parimelazhagar takes as being denied by fate. Both hold that what fate withholds in outcome does not cancel the value of the striving or the aim.

732 says a land yields greatly because ruin is rare there (அருங்கேட்டால் ஆற்ற விளைவது). 15 says rain is what ruins (கெடுப்பதூஉம்) and also what raises up the ruined. Parimelazhagar's list of the கேடு meant in 732 begins with too much rain and no rain, so 15 names the chief source of the ruin that 732 wants to be rare.

762 says the hardness that does not fear harm in a time of decline (தொலைவிடத்து) is found only in an old army (தொல்படை). 806 says those who keep to the bounds do not give up, even in decline (தொலைவிடத்தும்), the bond of those who stood by them of old (தொல்லைக்கண் நின்றார்). Both use the same two words to tie loyalty in bad times to length of standing, in an army and in friendship.

595 says a person's height rises with their spirit, as a lotus stem with the water. 473 says many have been broken by exactly that spirit, ஊக்கம், when it wasn't measured. One counts spirit as the measure and the other demands a measure for spirit.

439 ends 'நயவற்க நன்றி பயவா வினை', do not desire a deed that yields no good. 652 ends with the same phrase and extends it: one must always avoid a deed that yields neither renown nor good (புகழொடு நன்றி பயவா வினை). The rule is given in 439 as part of a ruler's guarding against faults and in 652, on Parimelazhagar's reading, as a rule for ministers.

Asking from the right person is like giving (1054), yet asking even water for a cow is the most degrading thing the tongue can do (1066). The chapters give opposite values to one act, and the difference of giver doesn't fully explain it, since 1061 refuses even the best givers.

988 calls சால்பு a firmness (திண்மை) that keeps poverty from being a disgrace. 1064 describes that firmness at work: the worth that will not consent to begging even when no means remain (இடமில்லாக் காலும் இரவொல்லாச் சால்பு) is too large for all space to hold. 1064 shows what the poor but worthy person of 988 does and does not do.

995 warns that இகழ்ச்சி, scorn, wounds even as a joke. 953 lists not scorning (இகழாமை) with a smile, giving and sweet words as the four marks of a true family. 953 names the trait as a mark of good birth, and 995 gives the reason for it.

1111 says she is more delicate than the anicham. 1115 pushes the claim to a comic limit: the unremoved stalks of that same flower (அனிச்சப்பூக் கால்களையாள்) are too heavy for her waist. The flower that was the standard of softness becomes a burden.

777 describes warriors who prefer fame (இசை) to life. 1017 says those ruled by shame give up life for shame and will not give up shame for life (நாணால் உயிரைத் துறப்பர்). Both rank a value above staying alive; in one it is public renown won in battle, in the other an inner restraint.

1066 says nothing shames the tongue more than begging, even water for a cow. 780 says this death is worth begging for, with the same root (இர-). Only something beyond the Kural's worst disgrace could justify the word.

915 calls the women பொதுநலத்தார், those whose favours are common to all, and says the wise will not touch them. In 1311 a wife tells her husband that all women feast on him in common with their eyes (கண்ணின் பொதுஉண்பர்), calls him பரத்த, and refuses his chest. The reproach of being 'common' is turned on the man there, and it is a sulking wife's charge in the Book of Love, not a judgement the book makes itself.

227 praises habitual shared eating (பாத்தூண்). In 1107 the man compares his beloved's embrace to living in one's own home and eating one's own food after sharing it (தமது பாத்து உண்டற்று). The lover's simile takes the householder's sharing of 227 as its standard of pleasure.

1128 says that since her lover is in her heart (நெஞ்சத்தார் காதலவராக) she fears eating anything hot, knowing it would burn him. 1249 uses almost the same opening, உள்ளத்தார் காதலவராக, to ask her heart whom it goes out looking for when he is within it. The playful premise of 1128, said to defend him, is used in 1249 to rebuke her own restless heart.

783 says friendship grows with practice and 785 says practice isn't needed. Parimelazhagar reconciles them by ranking three causes of friendship and placing shared feeling first, but the verses themselves sit in plain tension.

1188 says people say only 'she has grown pale' and no one says 'he left her' (துறந்தார் அவர் என்பார் இல்). In 1220 the townspeople do say he has left her in waking life (நனவினால் நம்நீத்தார் என்பர்), and she answers that they must not see him in dreams. These are speeches at different moments, but together they show her objecting both when the town blames only her and when it blames him.

347 says griefs hold and do not let go of those who hold attachment and do not let go (பற்றினைப் பற்றி விடாஅதவர்க்கு). 940 says that as a gambler loves the game more with each loss, the life grows more fond with each suffering it undergoes (துன்பம் உழத்தொறூஉம் காதற்று உயிர்); Parimelazhagar and Pope take the object of that fondness to be the body. 940 supplies what 347 leaves unexplained: suffering does not loosen the grip but tightens it.

1306 says love without துனி and புலவி is like fruit over-ripe or unripe (கனியும் கருக்காயும் அற்று), so some quarrel is needed. 1322 names the amount: only the 'small துனி' that arises in a sulk (ஊடலின் தோன்றும் சிறுதுனி), which leaves his tenderness greater even if it droops for a while. Parimelazhagar on 1306 takes துனி as the full-grown quarrel and புலவி as the young one, so 1322's சிறு marks the tolerable dose.

799 ends உள்ளினும் உள்ளஞ் சுடும்: even to think of the deserter's friendship burns the heart. 1207 ends with the same words in the mouth of the parted woman, for whom even remembering her lover burns. The phrase is used once for betrayal and once for separation in love; in both the pain comes from memory of a bond, not from a present injury.

738 lists five ornaments (அணி) of a land: freedom from disease (பிணியின்மை), wealth, yield, happiness and protection (ஏமம்). 734 defines a land by three absences: severe hunger, unceasing disease (ஓவாப் பிணி) and destructive enemies. The two lists match as positive and negative: yield answers hunger, பிணியின்மை answers disease, and ஏமம் answers the enemy, while 738 adds wealth and happiness.

140 makes accord with the world the test that learning must pass; 280 says neither shaving nor matted hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns (உலகம் பழித்தது ஒழித்துவிடின்). In both, the world's standard outranks a formal qualification, learning for the scholar and outward marks for the ascetic. Parimelazhagar takes உலகம் in both verses as the worthy and not people at large.

653 treats ஒளி as something the ambitious ('ஆஅதும் என்னுமவர்') must protect by refraining from certain deeds. 971 defines ஒளி as 'உள்ள வெறுக்கை', abundance of spirit, and இளி as saying one will live without it. Together they give ஒளி two sides: it is lost by what one does (653) and it consists in what one aspires to (971).

493 says even those without strength win (ஆற்றாரும் ஆற்றி அடுப) if they know the place and act against foes while guarding themselves (போற்றிச் செயின்). 878 says the enemy's pride dies when one knows the way, builds oneself up and guards oneself (வகையறிந்து தற்செய்து தற்காப்ப). Self-guarding plus knowledge is the common recipe; 878 generalises 493's 'place' to knowing the way of acting.

342 says if you want what renunciation brings, renounce while there is still something (உண்டாகத் துறக்க), which Parimelazhagar takes as 'while there is time'. 335 says to hurry to good deeds before the death rattle. On that reading the next chapter applies the same urgency to renouncing that 335 applies to good deeds.

211 says obligation wants no return, கைம்மாறு வேண்டா கடப்பாடு, and points to the rain, which the world cannot repay. 1183 uses the same word bitterly: as கைம்மாறு for the grace and modesty he took, he gave sickness and pallor. The word that names the return a good giver does not ask for is here the name of a bad bargain.

1206 says she lives by looking back at the days of union (உள்ள உளேன்). 1263 says she still lives by longing for his return (வரல் நசைஇ இன்னும் உளேன்). The same verb உளேன் is supported in one verse by the past and in the other by the expected future; Parimelazhagar on 1206 notes that the other supports, such as a messenger from him, are missing.

457 says goodness of mind gives gain (ஆக்கம்) and goodness of company gives all praise as well (இனநலம் எல்லாப் புகழும் தரும்). 651 has the same two-step form but says goodness of companions gives gain and goodness of action gives all that is wanted (துணைநலம் ஆக்கம் தரூஉம் வினைநலம் வேண்டிய எல்லாம் தரும்); Parimelazhagar there reads companions as giving wealth only. Company holds the higher place in 457 and the lower in 651, where one's own action outranks it.

712 asks the speaker in an assembly to discern the opening (இடைதெரிந்து), which Parimelazhagar glosses as the hearers' readiness to listen. 696 asks the same of one speaking to a king: know his mood and consider the time (குறிப்பறிந்து காலங் கருதி) and say it so that it is wanted. The timing rule is the same before an assembly and before a single ruler.

703 says to give whatever it takes from one's resources and secure those who read a sign by a sign (யாது கொடுத்தும் கொளல்). 794 says the friendship of one of good family who is ashamed of blame should be had even by giving (கொடுத்தும் கொளல்வேண்டும் நட்பு). The shared formula marks the two kinds of person the book thinks worth paying for, the perceptive adviser and the friend with a sense of shame.

649 says those who cannot say a few faultless words (மாசற்ற சில சொல்லல் தேற்றாதவர்) long to say many. 685 makes brevity the envoy's first mark: he speaks compactly (தொகச் சொல்லி), drops what is harsh, and speaks so as to please. 685 shows the positive skill whose absence 649 describes.

602 tells those who want their family to be a family (குடியைக் குடியாக வேண்டுபவர்) to live treating sloth as sloth, or killing it (மடியை மடியா ஒழுகல்). 1028 says those who build the family have no season to wait for, and that if they idle and think of their dignity it is ruined (மடிசெய்து மானங் கருதக் கெடும்). 1028 gives 602's rule its practical form: for the family-builder sloth shows up as waiting for the right time and standing on dignity.

293 says not to lie about what one's own heart knows, for the heart will burn the liar afterwards. 928 concerns one such lie, 'I have never been drunk' (களித்தறியேன்), about something the speaker's heart knows, and says that drink brings the hidden thing out. 293 gives the inner penalty for this kind of lie and 928 adds an outward one, exposure.

In 1133 the man says he once had shame and good manliness (நாணொடு நல்லாண்மை பண்டுடையேன்) and today has the palmyra horse. In 1254 the woman says she used to say she had restraint (நிறையுடையேன் என்பேன்மன்), yet her desire passes concealment and comes out in public. Each speaker sets a former self-possession against its loss to love; his loss is நாண் and ஆண்மை, hers is நிறை.

531 states the danger: slackness from the elation of great joy is worse than excessive anger. 539 gives the practice against it: when one grows strong in one's own joy (மகிழ்ச்சியின் மைந்துறும் போழ்து), call to mind those ruined by negligence (இகழ்ச்சியின் கெட்டாரை உள்ளுக).

1326 ranks sulking above union: ஊடல் is sweeter than புணர்தல் for love. 1330 calls sulking love's pleasure but adds that the pleasure of the sulk itself lies in being able to come together and embrace (கூடி முயங்கப் பெறின்). The closing verse makes the sulk's sweetness depend on the union that 1326 placed below it, as digestion has value for the next meal.

448 says a king without people who rebuke him will perish even with no one to ruin him (கெடுப்பாரிலானுங் கெடும்). 848 takes the case one step further: a person who has people to direct him and still does not act on it, and cannot work it out alone. 448 makes having correctors the safeguard; 848 shows the safeguard is useless to one who will not be corrected.

In 224 the giver watches the asker's face and is uneasy until it turns glad. In 90 the guest watches the host's face and wilts, like the anicham flower when smelled, if that face changes (முகந்திரிந்து நோக்க). The face is the measure of the exchange in both, read in opposite directions.

In 1136 the man's eyes will not close (படல் ஒல்லா) for the girl, so even at midnight (யாமத்தும்) he thinks of riding the palmyra horse. In 1252 the woman says desire, having no pity, rules her heart at its work even at midnight (யாமத்தும் ஆளும் தொழில்). Both use midnight, when all else rests, as the proof that love allows no rest.

952 lists three things the well-born keep: ஒழுக்கம், வாய்மை, நாண். 983 lists five pillars that hold up சால்பு: love, shame (நாண்), obligingness, kindly regard and truthfulness (வாய்மை). Two of the three marks of lineage reappear as supports of personal worth, so the same core is described once as inherited and once as a structure a person stands on.

1108, spoken in union, says the close embrace is sweet to two who desire each other (வீழும் இருவர்க்கு இனிதே). 1191, spoken in separation, says those loved by the ones they love (தாம்வீழ்வார் தம்வீழப் பெற்றவர்) have the stoneless fruit. Both place love's sweetness in the desire being mutual, using the same verb வீழ்; one says it from inside and the other from outside.

432 lists இவறல் as one of three faults in a ruler, beside excessive honour and excessive joy. 438, on Parimelazhagar's reading, takes it out of any such list as greater than the rest (எற்றுள்ளும் எண்ணப்படுவதொன்று அன்று). Manakkudavar reads 438 differently, as saying miserliness is not to be valued as anything, and on that reading the two verses simply agree.

Verse 13 says that if the sky proves false (விண் பொய்ப்பின்), hunger stays and torments the world (உள்நின்று உடற்றும் பசி), sea-girt though it is. Verse 734 defines a land as one that severe hunger (உறுபசி), unending disease and destructive enemies do not reach. Read together, the first mark of a proper country in the Book of Wealth rests on something no ruler supplies, the rain of chapter 2.

In 1209 the woman says her dear life is perishing (விளியும் என் இன்னுயிர்) as she thinks much on the lack of kindness of one who said they were not separate. In 1230 her life, which had not died till now (மாயா உயிர்), is dying in the dim evening as she thinks of the man whose nature is wealth (பொருள்மாலையாளரை உள்ளி). Both say that thinking of him is what wears her life away, and each names him by a reproach: his broken word in one, his preference for wealth in the other.

Verse 27 lists the five sense objects (சுவை ஒளி ஊறு ஓசை நாற்றம்) and says the world belongs to the one who discerns them. In 1101 the lover lists the same five as acts, seeing, hearing, tasting, smelling and touching (கண்டுகேட்டு உண்டுயிர்த்து உற்றறியும் ஐம்புலனும்), and says they are all found in this one woman (ஒண்தொடி கண்ணே உள). The same inventory serves the renouncer as a field to be understood and the lover as a field of enjoyment; the second is a speech in the moment and not a counter-teaching.

892 says disregard of the great brings unending trouble (பேரா இடும்பை); 450 says letting go the tie with the good (நல்லார் தொடர் கைவிடல்) is ten times worse than taking on the enmity of many. Both chapters on the great rank a bad relation to them above ordinary dangers, 450 by a number and 892 by permanence.

1125 and 1184 open with the same words, உள்ளுவன் மன்யான். The man in 1125 says he would remember her qualities if he ever forgot them, and he does not know forgetting; the woman in 1184 says she thinks of him and yet turns pale. The same claim of constant thought is his proof of love and her complaint that such thought gives no protection.

Here a pleasant word beats a gladly given gift. In 225, relieving hunger is a power above the ascetic's. A hungry person's view of 92 might differ, which suggests the ranking in 92 assumes someone who isn't in need.

793 and 794 screen friends by family. 972 says birth is equal for all living beings and only deeds make the difference. The chapter on choosing friends keeps a criterion that the chapter on greatness dissolves.

235 says a loss can be an increase. 117 says the world will not set down as ruin (கெடுவாக வையாது உலகம்) the low state of one who stays in virtue by standing fair. Both deny that the decline of a good person's fortunes is a real loss, 235 from the side of renown and 117 from the world's judgement.

218 says those who see what is due do not slacken in ஒப்புரவு even in a time without means (இடனில் பருவத்தும் ஒப்புரவிற்கு ஒல்கார்). 480 says ஒப்புரவு that does not weigh the limit of one's means (உளவரை தூக்காத) quickly destroys those means. The Book of Virtue praises not letting scarcity stop one's helpfulness, and the Book of Wealth, speaking of a ruler's resources, makes the weighing of means a condition of it.

842 says that when a person without understanding gives gladly, the cause is nothing but the receiver's தவம். 70 says a son's service to his father is to make people ask what the father did as penance (என்நோற்றான் கொல்) to have him. Both use the same figure, explaining a good by the stored merit of the one who benefits; 70 uses it as praise of the son and 842 to deny the giver any credit.
750 says a fort fails without capable people. In 766 four virtues are the army's ஏமம, and Parimelazhagar concludes that such men need no other fort. Read together, the people are the real wall.

602 states the negative condition for a family's standing: remove sloth. 1022 states the positive one: the family lengthens (நீளும் குடி) through long work in two things, effort and mature knowledge (ஆள்வினையும் ஆன்ற அறிவும்). Read together, absence of sloth is necessary but 1022 adds knowledge beside effort.

In 1263 she says he left desiring victory with his own resolve as companion (உரன் நசைஇ உள்ளம் துணையாகச் சென்றார்), and that she still lives by desiring his return (வரல் நசைஇ இன்னும் உளேன்). In 1230 thinking of the man given to wealth makes her life die. Both name him by the aim he left for, but in one speech the thought of him keeps her alive and in the other it kills; these are two moments of the same speaker, not a doctrine.

404 says native brightness without learning is not accepted by the wise. 636 says nothing over-subtle can stand before those who have keen native intelligence together with book-learning (மதிநுட்பம் நூலோடு உடையார்). 636 states positively what 404 implies: natural intelligence gains its force when joined to study.

724 says to make what one has learned go home before the learned (கற்றார்முன் கற்ற செலச்சொல்லி). 686 uses the same two terms for the envoy: having learned (கற்று), he speaks so that it goes home (செலச்சொல்லி). In both, learning is complete only when it can be delivered to a demanding audience, the assembly in 724 and a hostile court in 686.

291 defines truth (வாய்மை) not as reporting what happened but as speech with no harm in it at all (யாதொன்றும் தீமை இலாத சொலல்). 292 draws the consequence: even a falsehood stands in truth's place (பொய்மையும் வாய்மை யிடத்த) if it yields faultless good. Read together, the second verse is the first's definition applied to its hardest case.

405 says an unlearned person's standing gives way once he meets others and speaks (சொல்லாடச் சோர்வு படும்). 845 describes a further loss for one who has some real learning: by taking on what he has not learned, he puts even his genuine mastery in doubt (ஐயம் தரும்). 405 is the exposure of a claim; 845 is the damage the exposure does to what was true.

522 says that if a man gets kin whose love does not lapse (விருப்பறாச் சுற்றம் இயையின்), they give many gains (ஆக்கம் பலவும் தரும்). 884 says that if hidden enmity of unreformed mind appears, it gives many ills that turn his circle bad (இனமாணா ஏதம் பலவும் தரும்). The two verses have the same shape with opposite content, and Parimelazhagar notes that 'whose love does not lapse' in 522 is said to exclude the inner enmity of chapter 89: kin are an asset only on that condition.

144 asks what greatness comes to, however great a person is (எனைத்துணையர் ஆயினும் என்னாம்), if he enters another's home without weighing it even a millet's worth (தினைத்துணையும் தேரான்). 965 says even those like a hill (குன்றின் அனையார்) sink if they do a lowering deed as small as a kunri seed. Both hold that standing does not outweigh a degrading act; 965 gives the general rule and 144 one named act.

760 says that for those who have made abundant wealth the other two, virtue and pleasure, are easily had together (ஏனை இரண்டும் ஒருங்கு). 909 says that deeds of virtue, ample wealth and the other pursuits (அறவினையும் ஆன்ற பொருளும் பிறவினையும்) are all absent in those who do a woman's bidding; Parimelazhagar and Pope take பிறவினை as pleasure. Both use the three aims as the measure of a life: 760 shows how they are gained together, 909 a way they are lost together.

158 says one defeats the overbearing by one's own forbearing worth. 1327, spoken by the man in the Book of Love, says that in a lovers' quarrel the one who loses has won (ஊடலில் தோற்றவர் வென்றார்), as is seen in the union that follows. The paradox that giving way is the real victory appears in ethics and again, in a dramatised speech, in love; the second is a lover's remark and not a moral rule, but the shape of the thought is the same.

528 ends: many will live looking to that (அதுநோக்கி வாழ்வார் பலர்). 542 says the world lives looking to the sky and the people live looking to the king's sceptre (கோல்நோக்கி வாழுங் குடி). The phrase 'live looking to' makes the king's conduct something people depend on as they depend on rain; 528 uses it for his recognition of each person's worth.

276 says none are more hard-hearted than those who, unrenounced at heart, live by deceiving in the likeness of renouncers (துறந்தார்போல் வஞ்சித்து வாழ்வார்); 586 has the spy take the guise of renouncers (துறந்தார் படிவத்தராகி) to get into places and investigate. The conflict holds if 276 condemns the false ascetic guise as such; Parimelazhagar narrows 276 to cheating donors, and on that reading the spy's disguise in the king's service falls outside it.

338 pictures the body as a குடம்பை, shell or nest, that the bird leaves empty; 340 pictures it as a lodging (துச்சில்) where life stays as a tenant without a home of its own (புக்கில்). Both make the body a dwelling and life its occupant. 338 shows the departure, and 340 asks why there has to be one; Manakkudavar takes the permanent home to be liberation.

1057 says that on seeing those who give without scorn, the heart rejoices deep within (உள்ளம் உள்ளுள் உவப்பது உடைத்து). 1069 says that at the thought of asking the heart melts (உள்ளம் உருகும்), and at the thought of concealment even what remains is gone (உள்ளதூஉம் இன்றிக் கெடும்). Both follow the heart (உள்ளம்) through the act of asking; 1057 gives its state before a good giver and 1069 its state before a refusal. Parimelazhagar takes the heart in 1069 as the speaker's, while he reports others take it as the asker's.

1304 compares the unappeased sulker to a withered creeper (வாடிய வள்ளி) cut at the root. 1310 speaks of being left to dry up in the sulk (ஊடல் உணங்க விடுவார்). The wife's warning and the man's complaint use the same picture of a plant left without water; Parimelazhagar places 1310 in a sulk she does not answer.

509 gives the rule: trust no one without examining, then trust (தேறற்க யாரையும் தேராது). 530 applies examination to a man who was already one's own, left, and came back for a reason: he is to be received after reflection (எண்ணிக் கொளல்). Leaving resets the earlier trust, so the test of chapter 51 has to be done again.

11 says that the rain, sustaining the world, is to be known as ambrosia. 1192 uses the whole opening doctrine for one person's survival. The same dependence that the Kural gives to all life at its start reappears as a lover's condition.

415 says the words from the mouth of those with conduct (ஒழுக்கமுடையார் வாய்ச்சொல்) are like a staff where the ground is slippery (இழுக்கல் உடையுழி). 139 says of the same people (ஒழுக்கமுடையவர்க்கு) that speaking evil with the mouth, even by a slip (வழுக்கியும் வாயாற் சொலல்), is not possible. 139 gives the reason 415 needs: those who do not slip in what they say are the ones whose words can steady someone who is slipping.

429 says those whose understanding guards against what is coming (எதிரதாக் காக்கும் அறிவினார்) have no affliction that comes to shake them. 662 keeps that first rule (ஊறொரால்) but adds a second for when harm arrives anyway (உற்றபின் ஒல்காமை). 662 thus allows that foresight is not always enough; Parimelazhagar reads the second case as a task spoiled by fate.

In 1301 the friend wants the sulk kept up so that his suffering can be seen for a while. In 1329 the man himself wishes she would go on sulking (ஊடுக மன்னோ) and the night grow long so that he may keep pleading (யாம் இரப்ப). Both sides treat the sulk as something to prolong on purpose, hers to watch and his to beg.

143 says those who go on doing evil in the home of people who trust them (தெளிந்தாரில்) are 'no different from the dead' (விளிந்தாரின் வேறல்லர்); 926 uses the same construction for sleepers (துஞ்சினார் செத்தாரின் வேறல்லர்) and extends it to drinkers. Parimelazhagar explains 926 by the absence of awareness and 143 by the loss of aram, porul and inbam, so the same formula of living death is applied to a moral failure in one verse and to loss of consciousness in the other.

862 describes the man without love, allies or strength as unable to resist an enemy. 873 judges the man in that position who nevertheless provokes: one who, alone (தமியனாய்), takes on the enmity of many is more foolish than the mad. 862 gives the weak position seen by an attacker; 873 gives the advice that follows for the one who is in it.

Verse 80 says the seat of life (உயிர்நிலை) goes by way of love (அன்பின் வழியது). Verse 255 says உயிர்நிலை lies in not eating flesh (உண்ணாமை உள்ளது உயிர்நிலை); Parimelazhagar reads this as life's staying in the body resting on that virtue. The rare word உயிர்நிலை is used in both to make a moral quality, love or not eating flesh, the condition of being alive at all.

630 measures the reward by the enemy: a distinction one's foes desire or esteem (ஒன்னார் விழையும் சிறப்பு). 810 uses the same measure with the same verb: those who do not depart from their nature toward old friends are wanted even by those who do not want them (விழையார் விழையப்படுப). Each verse marks an unusual constancy, under pain or toward friends who have erred, by saying that even the hostile regard it.

756 names what is the king's wealth: what comes unowned, customs duty, and tribute from enemies (உறுபொருளும் உல்கு பொருளும் தன் ஒன்னார்த் தெறுபொருளும்). 552 treats a sceptre-holder's 'asking' (இரவு) of his people as highway robbery; Parimelazhagar notes that the word இரவு marks it as something other than the due tax. 756 shows the lawful sources against which 552's demand is measured.

514 observes that many who passed every test turn different through the work (வினைவகையான் வேறாகும் மாந்தர் பலர்). 520 tells the king to look into the one doing the work every day (நாடோறும் நாடுக மன்னன்). The chapter's closing instruction answers the problem 514 raises: since office changes people, examination has to continue after appointment.

45 says that if household life has love and virtue (அன்பும் அறனும்), that is its character and its fruit (பண்பும் பயனும்). 75 says the distinction reached by those who have had joy in this world is, 'they say', the result of a way of life settled in love (அன்புற்று அமர்ந்த வழக்கு); Parimelazhagar takes this as household life lived with love, rewarded with heaven. 75 spells out the பயன் that 45 only names.

1330 says the sulk's own pleasure comes if the lovers get to unite and embrace (பெறின்). 1304 states the other case: not reconciling one who has sulked (ஊடியவரை உணராமை) is like cutting a wilted creeper at the root. The conditional in 1330 is a real one, and 1304 shows what a sulk is when the condition fails.

887 uses the casket and its lid for a family that fits together outwardly while divided within. 277 uses the kunri seed for false ascetics, red on the outside (புறங்குன்றி கண்டனையர்) and black within like its tip. Each verse chooses an everyday object to show an outside that does not match the inside, one for kin and one for renouncers.

Verse 20 says no one's world can do without water (நீர்இன்று அமையாது உலகு), and that ஒழுக்கு cannot exist without the sky. Parimelazhagar takes ஒழுக்கு as the water's unbroken flow; Pope's verse rendering and Kalaignar take it as ordered conduct. Verse 542 states the first half as a given (வானோக்கி வாழும் உலகெல்லாம்) and sets the people's dependence on the sceptre beside it. On either reading of ஒழுக்கு, 542 treats the dependence 20 argues for as the standard case of something one cannot live without.

187 says those who do not know how to make friends by words that bring laughter (நகச்சொல்லி நட்பாடல் தேற்றாதவர்) will part even their own kin by words that divide (பகச்சொல்லிக் கேளிர்ப் பிரிப்பர்). 525 says one who can give and speak pleasantly will be surrounded by kin in layers (இன்சொலும் ஆற்றின் ... சுற்றத்தால் சுற்றப்படும்). The two state the same link between speech and keeping one's people, from its negative and positive sides, in the Book of Virtue and the Book of Wealth.

745 says a fort is hard to take, holds stored food (கொண்ட கூழ்த்து) and is easy for those inside to hold their position in (அகத்தார் நிலைக்கு எளிது). 499 says that even people with no good defences or standing (சிறைநலனும் சீரும் இலரெனினும்) are hard to take on in the land where they live (உறைநிலத்தோடு ஒட்டல் அரிது). 499 shows that the insiders' advantage of position, which 745 asks the fort to give, already belongs to home ground without walls.

918 says that for those without discerning understanding the embrace of deceiving women is an அணங்கு, which Parimelazhagar glosses as the touch of a spirit-woman who takes life through desire. In 1082 a lover says that her returning his look is like an attacking அணங்கு (தாக்கணங்கு) arriving with an army. The same figure of the woman as an afflicting spirit is a lover's praise in the Book of Love and a warning in 918.

889 says inner enmity carries ruin even when it is as small as a split sesame seed. 879 says to cut a thorn tree while it is young (இளைதாக), since grown hard it destroys the cutter's hand. The two neighbouring chapters, on open and on inner enmity, make the same point that hostility should be judged by what it will grow into; only 879 goes on to say what to do about it.

504 tells the ruler to examine a man's qualities, then his faults, and judge by what predominates (மிகை நாடி மிக்க கொளல்). 868 describes the result when the tally is all on one side: with no qualities and many faults (குணனிலனாய்க் குற்றம் பலவாயின்) he is left without companions, and that is a support to his opponents. The test used for choosing servants in 504 is applied by 868 to the ruler himself, with his enemies as the ones who benefit.

289 says those who know nothing but stealing do what is beyond measure and perish right there (அளவல்ல செய்தாங்கே வீவர்); 479 says the life of one who does not live knowing the measure seems to exist, then is not, and perishes without trace. Both make ignoring அளவு the cause of ruin, in the renouncer's conduct and in the management of means; Parimelazhagar reads அளவல்ல in 289 as wrong thoughts and not as excess of spending, so the likeness is of pattern, not of subject.

407 says good looks without understanding are worth what a clay doll's are. 667 says not to scorn anyone on seeing their form (உருவுகண்டு எள்ளாமை), since the great chariot has its small linchpin. Both deny that appearance measures a person, 407 for the handsome and empty, 667 for the slight and capable.
423 tells the individual to find the truth whoever is speaking. 589 turns the same refusal to trust a source into a state procedure, with independence and counting as its method.

1284 reports to her friend that her heart forgot the sulk and went to unite. 1294 gives the consequence: since the heart will not first sulk and then enjoy (துனிசெய்து துவ்வாய்), who will consult with it about such things again (நின்னொடு சூழ்வார் யார்). The report of the heart's desertion in one chapter becomes the quarrel with the heart in the next.

429 says those whose understanding guards against what is coming (எதிரதாக் காக்கும் அறிவினார்) have no affliction that arrives to shake them; 622 says that for the person of understanding (அறிவுடையான்) even a flood of suffering already present is ended by thinking. The pair gives understanding two jobs, forestalling trouble and dissolving the trouble that came anyway, which Parimelazhagar takes in 622 to be trouble from fate.
763 mocks the sea-roar of an army without heroes. 768 allows that an army without fight can still gain stature through its show. Noise is nothing in one and display is something in the other.

403 says even the unlearned are very good if they can keep from speaking before the learned (கற்றார்முன் சொல்லாதிருக்கப் பெறின்). 414 addresses the same person (கற்றிலனாயினும்) and tells him to listen (கேட்க). The silence that 403 only recommends as damage control becomes in 414 the means of gaining what he lacks.

1134: the fierce flood of love carries off the raft of shame and manliness (காமக் கடும்புனல் உய்க்கும்). 1287: why sulk knowing it will prove false, like those who leap into a stream knowing it will carry them off (உய்த்தல் அறிந்து புனல்பாய்பவர்). The same water and the same verb, உய்த்தல், are used by the man of his restraint in 1134 and by the woman of her sulk here.

873 says one who, being alone, takes on the enmity of many (பல்லார் பகை கொள்பவன்) is more wretched than the mad. 450 uses the same phrase as its measure: letting go the tie with the good is ten times worse than that (பல்லார் பகை கொளலிற் பத்தடுத்த தீமைத்து). Read together, what 873 treats as an extreme of folly becomes the smaller of two harms in 450.

1191 says those loved by the ones they love have 'obtained' (பெற்றவர் பெற்றாரே) love's stoneless fruit; Parimelazhagar ties the word to earlier good deeds. 1194 gives the negative: even those who are esteemed are கெழீஇயிலர் if the one they love does not love them, which Parimelazhagar glosses as lacking good deeds and Manakkudavar as being without what they desire. The pair states the same condition from both sides, and shows the commentators reading it as fortune and not merit.

Both verses use பொருள் in an unusual, moral sense alongside அருள். 246 says those who leave அருள் and do what should not be done have left பொருள் and forgotten (பொருள்நீங்கிப் பொச்சாந்தார்); 254 calls eating flesh பொருளல்லது. Parimelazhagar takes பொருள் in 254 as virtue (so that பொருளல்லது is sin) and in 246 as the lasting good one should have done.

42 makes the householder the support of those who have renounced (துறந்தார்க்கும் ... துணை); 276 says none are more hard-eyed than those who, unrenounced at heart, live by deceiving as if they had renounced (துறந்தார்போல் வஞ்சித்து வாழ்வார்). Parimelazhagar takes the deceived to be the givers, so the pairing shows what the false renouncer exploits: the duty of support that 42 lays on the householder.

82 says eating alone while the guest is outside (விருந்து புறத்ததாத் தானுண்டல்) is not to be desired even if the food were the medicine against death. 229 says eating by oneself alone (தாமே தமியர் உணல்) to fill up one's store is more bitter than begging. Both judge the solitary meal itself, one by setting it against the best imaginable food and the other against the worst condition.

261 gives the form of தவம் as bearing one's own pain and doing no harm to living beings (உயிர்க்குறுகண் செய்யாமை); 274 speaks of doing 'what is not it' (அல்லவை) under cover of தவம் and compares this to a hunter snaring birds. Read together, the hunter simile shows the hypocrite doing the very thing, harm to creatures, whose absence 261 makes the definition of austerity.

46 asks what a person who runs household life by the way of virtue would gain by going to the outside way (புறத்தாற்றில் போஒய்ப் பெறுவது எவன்). 342 says that after renouncing there are many things to be had here, and urges renouncing if one wants them (வேண்டின் ... துறக்க). The conflict depends on reading புறத்தாறு as the ascetic path, as Pope does: on that reading 46's rhetorical 'what is gained?' gets the answer 'much' in 342.

115 and 118 end with the same line, கோடாமை சான்றோர்க்கு அணி, 'not bending is the ornament of the worthy'. In 115 the bending is of the heart under loss and gain (நெஞ்சத்துக் கோடாமை); in 118 it is leaning to one side (ஒருபால் கோடாமை), like a balance. The repetition joins two sides of நடுவு: steadiness under one's own fortunes and impartiality between others.

585 ends with the spy's ability never to let anything spill (யாண்டும் உகாஅமை); 689 wants the bearer of a king's message to be a hard man whose mouth does not let slip a damaging word (the edition prints வாய்சேரா; Parimelazhagar reads வாய் சோரா). Both make control of what leaves the mouth under pressure the test of the king's agents abroad.

994 says the world honours the character (பண்பு) of those whose usefulness (பயன்) comes from doing good with fairness (நயனொடு நன்றி புரிந்த). 97 uses the same four words of speech: words that yield benefit (பயன்) and do not part from பண்பு produce நயன் and bring forth நன்றி. Parimelazhagar glosses நயன் as justice in both, so the cluster describes good speech in 97 and a good life in 994.

116 says that if one's heart leaves fairness and does wrong (நடுவொரீஇ அல்ல செயின்), one should know 'I will perish' (கெடுவல்யான்). 204 says do not plot another's ruin even by a lapse, for அறம் will plot the plotter's ruin (சூழ்ந்தவன் கேடு). Both say that harm intended for others returns as one's own ruin; 116 makes it the wrongdoer's own knowledge, 204 gives the agent as அறம்.

199 says what those of stainless sight will not say. 258 says those whose sight has parted from fault (செயிரின் தலைப்பிரிந்த காட்சியார்) will not eat flesh that has parted from life. The book repeatedly states a restraint as what people of clear காட்சி simply do not do; here the same form covers speech and diet.

240 says that to live without renown is not to live. 970 says the world worships and praises the radiance of those with honour who will not live when disgrace comes (இளிவரின் வாழாத மானம் உடையார்). 970 shows a person acting on 240's equation, and the result is the renown 240 demands.

791 grounds the need for inquiry on the claim that for those who keep friendship there is no leaving once it is formed (நட்டபின் வீடில்லை). 800 tells one to leave the friendship of the ஒப்பிலார், even by giving something (ஒன்றீத்தும் ஒருவுக), and Parimelazhagar takes this as the remedy for a friendship taken up unknowingly. If வீடில்லை is read as a flat 'there is no release', the two conflict; if it describes only what a true friend will not do, 800 is the exception the chapter allows.

872 says that even if you take on the enmity of those whose plough is the bow (வில்லேர் உழவர்), you should not take on that of those whose plough is the word (சொல்லேர் உழவர்). 129 says a wound burned by fire heals within, but the scar burned by the tongue (நாவினாற் சுட்ட வடு) does not. Both rank harm done by words above harm done by a physical instrument, one in statecraft and one in personal conduct.
