348 divides people the same way: those who have thoroughly renounced have reached the head, and the rest, confused, are caught in the net (மயங்கி வலைப்பட்டார் மற்றையவர்). 266 says those who do தவம் do their own work and the rest act in vain, caught in desire (ஆசையுட் பட்டு). Both use பட்டு / பட்டார், being caught, for everyone outside the ascetic's path; Parimelazhagar supplies 'the net of desire' in his gloss on 266.

900 says that even those with support beyond measure will not survive (உய்யார்) if those of the highest distinction are angered (சிறந்தமைந்த சீரார் செறின்). 29 says the anger (வெகுளி) of those standing on the hill of good qualities is hard to ward off (காத்தல் அரிது) even for a moment. The Book of Wealth applies to kings and their resources what the opening chapters said in praise of renouncers.

In 776 the warrior takes up his days (தன் நாளை எடுத்து) and files every day without a wound as wasted; in 1261 the wife marks off the days of his absence (நாளொற்றி) until her finger wears down. Both keep a ledger of days, the soldier's reckoned by wounds received and the waiting wife's by absence endured.

430 says those without understanding have nothing, whatever they possess (என்னுடைய ரேனும் இலர்). 534 says the heedless have no good (பொச்சாப் புடையார்க்கு நன்கு இல்லை), which Parimelazhagar reads as: even with every kind of wealth, they get no benefit from it. The same logic of having without having is applied to lack of understanding in one verse and to lack of vigilance in the other.

474 says the one who admires himself (தன்னை வியந்தான்) perishes quickly. 978 uses the same phrase to define smallness: greatness always bows, and smallness adorns itself in self-admiration (சிறுமை அணியுமாம் தன்னை வியந்து). In 978 self-admiration is a mark of character, and in 474 it is a miscalculation of strength with a practical result.

1272 says this girl has a great measure of womanly nature (பெண்நிறைந்த நீர்மை பெரிது), which Parimelazhagar takes as artlessness beyond the usual; 1280 says that telling love's sickness with the eyes and pleading is womanhood added to womanhood (பெண்ணினால் பெண்மை உடைத்து). The chapter's first observation about her is given its content at the end: her womanliness is her saying it with the eyes and not in words.

1087: the cloth over her firm breasts is the face-cloth on a rutting bull elephant (கடாஅக் களிற்றின்மேற் கட்படாம்). 24: the renouncer guards the five senses with the goad of firmness (உரனென்னும் தோட்டியான்), a goad being the elephant-driver's tool. Both draw on the dangerous elephant held in check; the ascetic chapter makes the senses the elephant, and the lover makes her covered breasts the elephant.

1170 wishes the eyes could travel to him as the heart does. Next, 1171 begins the attack on them. Parimelazhagar explicitly calls 1170 a preparation for this chapter, so what looks like a change of subject is a single thought.

213 says that in the world of the gods or here (புத்தேளுலகத்தும் ஈண்டும்) it is hard to find another good like ஒப்புரவு, doing one's part for others. 1103 asks whether the lotus-eyed one's world is as sweet as sleeping on the beloved's shoulders. Both measure an earthly thing against heaven and prefer it; in the Book of Virtue it is a duty, and here it is a lover's own claim about his pleasure.

Both verses name the ஒப்பிலார். 812 says it makes no difference whether their friendship is had or lost; 800 goes further and says to leave it even by giving something (ஒன்றீத்தும் ஒருவுக). Parimelazhagar explains the word differently in each place: here as those who fit with no one because they look only to their own gain, there as those who do not accord with the world.

494 says those who had planned (against you) lose their plan (எண்ணியார் எண்ணம் இழப்பர்) when you advance knowing the place and hold close to it. 440 says the enemies' scheme becomes void (ஏதில ஏதிலார் நூல்) when a ruler enjoys what he loves without letting the love be known. In both, the opponent's design is defeated before any fight by removing what it relied on: bad ground in one case, a known weakness in the other.

60 says the excellence of the home is called its blessing (மங்கலம்) and the gaining of good children (நன்மக்கட் பேறு) its fine ornament. 61, opening the next chapter, says that of all things to be gained we know none like the gaining of children who know what should be known (அறிவறிந்த மக்கட்பேறு). 61 picks up the word மக்கட்பேறு from 60 and specifies what makes the children 'good': their understanding.

424 says understanding sees the fine meaning in what others say (பிறர்வாய் நுண்பொருள்); Manakkudavar takes this as seeing what they mean without their spelling it out. 701 praises one who knows what is intended by looking, without its being said (கூறாமை நோக்கிக் குறிப்பறிவான்). 701 carries the second half of 424 one step further, from reading what lies within words to reading what is never put into words.

567 says harsh words and punishment beyond bounds are a file that wears down a king's conquering strength (அடுமுரண் தேய்க்கும் அரம்). 555 says the tears of the afflicted are a tool that wears down wealth (செல்வத்தைத் தேய்க்கும் படை). Both describe the effect of a king's cruelty as slow abrasion by a tool, using the same verb தேய்க்கும்.

784 says friendship isn't for laughter (நகுதல்). 860 makes நகல் the very source of good ways, which Parimelazhagar glosses as friendship. The same root gets very different valuations in the chapter on what friendship is for and the chapter on hostility.

The two ask the same question, what learning is worth, and answer differently. For 2, learning lacks fruit without worship, and for 140 it isn't understanding without fitting conduct in the world. One looks up and the other looks out.

274 has the hunter hidden in the bush as the image of evil done under cover of austerity; 828 says a weapon hides even in an enemy's hands folded in worship (தொழுதகை யுள்ளும் படையொடுங்கும்), and likewise in his tears. In both a gesture of piety is the cover for harm, once in ascetic life and once in false friendship.

In 1277 her bangles understood before she did that the lord of the cool shore had parted (தணந்தமை ... முன்னம் உணர்ந்த வளை). In 1233 her shoulders announce that he has parted, with the same word தணந்தமை. In 1277 the body is first to know of the parting, and in 1233 it is the one that tells others.

158 calls forbearance toward the arrogant a victory (வென்றுவிடல்). 986 says the touchstone of சால்பு is to accept defeat (தோல்வி ... கொளல்) even from those who are not one's equals. The same conduct toward an overbearing lesser person is named winning in one verse and taking a loss in the other; 986 adds that it has to be felt and accepted as a defeat, which guards against reading 158 as a way of scoring over the offender. Manakkudavar on 158 says explicitly that forbearing is not defeat but is itself the victory.

A scale of giving. In Parimelazhagar's reading of 1051 the worthiest give before anything is said, in 1078 the worthy give when told, and the base give when crushed. 1077 adds that the base give nothing to any who can't hurt them.

446 says enemies can do nothing against one who keeps the company of the worthy. 460 says there is no support greater than good company (நல்லினத்தின் ஊங்கும் துணையில்லை) and nothing that brings more affliction than bad company. 460 states as a general rule what 446 applies to a ruler facing enemies.

401 says holding forth in an assembly without full book-learning (நிரம்பிய நூலின்றிக் கோட்டி கொளல்) is like playing dice without a marked board. 728 says those who have learned many things are still of no use if they cannot speak well and tellingly in a good assembly. Together they give both halves: speech without learning has nothing to stand on, and learning without speech yields nothing.

891 makes not slighting the able the chief safeguard; 861 tells the ruler to avoid standing against the stronger (வலியார்க்கு மாறேற்றல் ஓம்புக). The chapter on enmity gives as a tactical rule what 891 gives as a rule of self-protection.

In 1319 the man reports that even when he tries to appease her she is angry (உணர்த்தினும் காயும்), saying he is like this with others too: a complaint that he is blamed without cause. In 1325 he grants the same situation, a man without fault (தவறிலர் ஆயினும்) kept from her arms, and finds something to enjoy in it. The groundless sulks listed in chapter 132 are re-read as a pleasure in chapter 133.

Fear and craving appear together in both verses with opposite roles. In 1075 fear is the whole conduct of the base (அச்சமே கீழ்களது ஆசாரம்), with a little more if there is something they crave (அவாவுண்டேல்); Parimelazhagar takes the fear as fear of punishment. In 366 fear is directed at craving itself and is called virtue. The pairing separates fear that serves craving from fear that guards against it.

In 1184 she thinks of him and speaks only of his merits (உள்ளுவன் ... உரைப்பது அவர்திறம்), and calls it deceit (கள்ளம்) that the pallor comes all the same. In 1250 she tells her heart that by keeping in it the man who left, she will lose still more beauty (இன்னும் இழத்தும் கவின்). 1250 states as cause and effect what 1184 finds baffling: the faithful thinking does not hold the pallor off.

721 says those who know the body of words and the kinds of assembly do not let their speech slip before the capable (வாய்சோரார்), which Parimelazhagar reads as not slipping out of fear. 647 lists the same qualities, able to speak, without slips, without fear (சொலல்வல்லன் சோர்விலன் அஞ்சான்), and says such a person is hard for anyone to defeat. 647 states the payoff of the fearlessness that 721 describes.

54 asks what is greater than a woman, if she has the firmness called கற்பு (கற்பென்னும் திண்மை உண்டாகப் பெறின்). 988 says poverty is no disgrace to a person, if he has the firmness called சால்பு (சால்பென்னும் திண்மை உண்டாகப் பெறின்). The second line is the same but for one word, so the book describes a woman's fidelity and a worthy person's character with the same term, திண்மை, a firmness that outweighs outward circumstances.

29 says the anger of those who stand on the hill of good qualities cannot be withstood even for a moment (கணமேயும் காத்தல் அரிது), on Parimelazhagar's and Pope's reading; Kalaignar takes it to mean their anger does not last a moment. On the first reading it agrees with 264 that renouncers hold a power to ruin those who oppose them, though 264 makes it a matter of intention (எண்ணின்) and 29 of anger.

835 calls the fool's destination an அளறு, a mire or hell, into which he enters and sinks (புக்கழுந்தும்). 919 calls the shoulders of women who draw no line the அளறு in which base men sink (பூரியர்கள் ஆழும் அளறு). 919 uses for one present indulgence the image that 835 uses for the result of a whole life of folly.

243 says those whose hearts are joined to அருள் do not enter the dark world of pain (அருள் சேர்ந்த நெஞ்சினார்க்கு இல்லை இருள் சேர்ந்த இன்னா உலகம் புகல்). 459 agrees that the next world comes from goodness of mind (மனநலத்தின் ஆகும் மறுமை) and adds that even this is made secure by goodness of company. The afterlife that 243 rests on the heart alone is given a second support in 459.

958 says that if lack of affection (நாரின்மை) shows in a man, people will doubt his lineage (குலத்தின்கண் ஐயப்படும்). 992 names having love and being born in a seasoned family (அன்புடைமை ஆன்ற குடிப்பிறத்தல்) as the two things that make up courtesy. 992 pairs love and birth as partners; 958 shows that when the first is missing the second is no longer believed.

Both verses use the millet's measure (தினைத்துணை). In 433 those who are ashamed of blame (பழிநாணுவார்) take a fault of a millet's size as large as a palmyra; in 144 the man entering another's home does not reflect even a millet's worth (தினைத்துணையும் தேரான்). The pair shows the same measure from opposite sides: the careful person enlarges the smallest fault, and the adulterer does not give the smallest thought.

190 wishes that people would see their own faults as they see a stranger's. 930 asks whether a drinker, when sober and seeing another man drunk, does not think of his own lapse when he drinks (உள்ளான்கொல் உண்டதன் சோர்வு). 930 is a concrete instance of the failure 190 names: the other man's fault is seen clearly and one's own identical fault is not.

990 says the earth cannot carry its burden (பொறை) once the worthy lose their worth. 572 says those without kindly regard are, by merely existing, a burden to the earth (நிலக்குப் பொறை). The same figure is used from two sides: the worthy are what lets the earth carry its load, and people without கண்ணோட்டம் are dead weight on it.

406 grants the unlearned existence only and compares them to land that yields nothing (பயவாக் களர்). 572 says the existence of those without kindly regard is a burden to the earth (உண்மை நிலக்குப் பொறை). Both reduce a person lacking a quality to mere existence and express it through land, as barren soil in one and as weight on the ground in the other.

1199 says that though the one she longs for gives nothing (நல்கார் எனினும்), even a word about him is sweet to her ear. 1208 measures what an ungiving lover leaves her more sharply: his whole gift (சிறப்பு) is that he does not object to being thought of. Parimelazhagar takes 1208 as scorn of the friend's promise that he will come and be kind, whereas Manakkudavar takes the not-being-angry as real grace.

24 praises the one who guards the five senses with the goad called firmness (உரனென்னும் தோட்டியான்); 273 likens one of strengthless nature (வலியில் நிலைமையான்) who takes the form of the strong to a cow grazing in a tiger's skin. Parimelazhagar reads the missing strength in 273 as the power to bring the mind under control, which is what 24 names as the mark of the real renouncer, so 273 shows the outward form of 24 without its substance.

642 says to guard against a lapse in speech (சொல்லின்கட் சோர்வு) because both gain and ruin come from it. 689 is that rule at the point where the stakes are the king's: the envoy must not let a word that discredits slip from his mouth (வாய்சோரா); Parimelazhagar adds that the slip in question would come from fear for himself. The verb சோர் is shared, and 689 names the hardness (வன்கண்) that prevents the lapse 642 warns of.

1238 says that when he loosened the embracing arms her forehead turned pale. 1240 says the pallor of her eyes itself came to distress (கண்ணின் பசப்போ பருவரல் எய்தின்றே) on seeing what the bright forehead had done (ஒண்ணுதல் செய்தது கண்டு). 1240 depends on 1238 for what the forehead did; Parimelazhagar explains that the eyes' pallor was abashed that the forehead had paled sooner than they did, at a smaller cause.

707 says nothing is as knowing as the face, since whether one is pleased or angry it gets there first (உவப்பினும் காயினும் தான்முந்துறும்). 830 advises that when an enemy turns friend one should befriend with the face and let go in the heart (முகநட்டு அகநட்பு ஒரீஇ விடல்). If the face always runs ahead of the mind, as 707 says, the control 830 recommends should not be possible; the two agree only if 707 describes the unguarded face.

187 treats speaking so that others laugh (நகச்சொல்லி) as the way friendship is made. 784 says friendship is not for laughing (நகுதற் பொருட்டன்று நட்டல்) but for going ahead to rebuke when the friend oversteps. 784 limits 187: pleasant talk may begin a friendship, but it is not what the friendship is for.

827 warns not to take an enemy's bowing words at face value, because a bow's bending signals harm (வில்வணக்கம் தீங்கு குறித்தமையான்); in 1276 the woman reads his unusually great tenderness (பெரிதாற்றிப் பெட்பக் கலத்தல்) as a sign of coming absence. The same inference, that excess of kindness points to its opposite, is advice about false friends in one book and a wife's reading of her husband in the other, though she alleges no enmity.

124 says the stature of one who is restrained without shifting from his position (நிலையின் திரியாது அடங்கியான்) is far greater than a mountain. 964 uses the same word for the opposite case: those who descend from their position (நிலையின் இழிந்த) are like hair off the head. Together they give the two ends of one scale, both measured by whether a person keeps to their நிலை.

The Kural keeps asking what eyes are for. 577 answers kindly regard, 393 learning, and 705 reading signs. Each makes the physical eye worthless by that chapter's standard, so 'real sight' is defined differently each time.

1121 calls her பணிமொழி, the woman of soft, low speech, in a verse about the sweetness of her kiss. In 1258 the woman uses the same word for his speech: the soft words (பணிமொழி) of that thief of many deceits are the weapon that breaks her womanly reserve. The quality he savours in her is the one she names in him as a weapon.

316 gives the rule: what one has perceived as painful, do not do to another (துன்னாமை வேண்டும் பிறன்கண் செயல்). 318 turns it into a question: one who knows what hurts his own life (தன்னுயிர்க்கு இன்னாமை தானறிவான்), why (என்கொலோ) does he hurt other lives? The second verse treats breaking the rule as something needing explanation; Parimelazhagar suggests delusion as the implied answer. (The edition's text of 318 has typos in its first line.)

405 says the unlearned person's self-regard gives way when he engages and speaks (சொல்லாடச் சோர்வு படும்); Parimelazhagar supplies that the talk is with a learned person. 1046 says that even when the poor speak of good matters well understood, their words go slack (சொற்பொருள் சோர்வு படும்). The same closing phrase marks two ways speech fails: in 405 for want of learning in the speaker, in 1046 for want of standing with the hearers, though the content is sound.

434 says fault itself is the enemy that brings ruin. 304 asks whether there is any other enemy (பகையும் உளவோ பிற) than anger, which kills laughter and joy. 304 applies to one named fault the claim 434 makes of fault in general: the real enemy is inside.

920 lists two-minded women (இருமனப் பெண்டிர்) with liquor and dice as the company of those fortune has left. 822 compares false friendship to women's minds that become other (வேறுபடும்). The divided or shifting female mind serves in both as the book's figure for a tie that cannot be relied on, and 920 suggests which women the figure has in view.

31 asks what gain is greater for a living being than virtue (அறத்தினூஉங்கு ஆக்கம் எவனோ உயிர்க்கு); 122 says there is no gain for a living being beyond restraint (ஆக்கம் அதனினூஉங்கு இல்லை உயிர்க்கு) and tells one to guard it as wealth. 122 reuses chapter 4's formula almost word for word and applies it to one particular virtue, so restraint is given the rank the earlier verse gave to virtue as a whole.

84 has the goddess of fortune (செய்யாள்) living in the home of the glad-faced host. 617 says she of the lotus (தாமரையினாள்) lives in the effort of the unslothful (மடியிலான் தாளுளாள்), and her dark sister in sloth. The same figure is given two different dwellings, generosity in the Book of Virtue and exertion in the Book of Wealth.

467 says to think and then resolve on a task, and that saying 'we will think after resolving' is a lapse. 668 takes up from that point: once the task has been seen without confusion (கலங்காது கண்ட), act without wavering (துளங்காது). Together they give a sequence in which doubt belongs before the decision and not after it.

207 says those who incur any enmity whatever survive it (எனைப்பகை உற்றாரும் உய்வர்), and only the enmity of one's own evil deeds follows and kills. 896 says those who keep offending the great do not survive (உய்யார்). If எனைப்பகை is taken literally as every human enmity, the two conflict; the conflict eases if 207's phrase is read as a rhetorical foil for the enmity of deeds, or if the harm in 896 is understood as itself the fruit of a wrong deed.

960 pairs நலம் with shame and குலம் with humility: want நலம், then want நாணுடைமை; want குலம், then want பணிவு toward all. 1019 uses the same pair in negative form: a lapse in principle burns one's குலம், and settled shamelessness burns one's நலம் (நலஞ்சுடும் நாணின்மை). The two verses share the குலம்/நலம் pairing and agree that நலம் depends on shame.

177 argues from the outcome: gain got by coveting does not turn out well when enjoyed. 113 says gain that comes from leaving fairness is to be given up that very day even if it brings only good (நன்றே தரினும்). 113 removes the dependence on outcome, so the prohibition would stand even where 177's prediction failed.

286 says those with hardened desire for stealing cannot stand and walk within அளவு (அளவின்கண் நின்றொழுகல் ஆற்றார்); 474 says the one who does not live in accord, does not know his measure (அளவறியான்) and admires himself perishes quickly. On Kalaignar's reading of அளவு in 286 as a limit one lives within, the two apply one idea, conduct kept inside a known measure, to the renouncer and to the king; Parimelazhagar instead takes அளவு in 286 as the reasoned measuring of the soul and its ends, on which reading the link is only verbal.

44 names பாத்தூண், shared food, as the mark of the householder's life. In 1107 the lover says the embrace of the woman is like staying in one's own home and eating one's own after sharing it (தம்மில் இருந்து தமது பாத்து உண்டற்று). The Book of Love takes the householder's sharing meal as a standard of pleasure, where 44 gives it as a duty with a reward; the comparison is the speaker's, not a teaching.

466 says one is ruined by doing what is not fit to do, and also by not doing what is fit (செய்தக்க செய்யாமை யானும் கெடும்). 510 says trusting someone unexamined and doubting someone already examined and trusted both bring unending trouble (தேரான் தெளிவும் தெளிந்தான்கண் ஐயுறவும்). Each verse sets an error of excess beside an error of defect and gives them the same result, once for action and once for trust.

Verse 21 says the settled view of the texts (பனுவல் துணிவு) sets the greatness of those who have renounced within their discipline (ஒழுக்கத்து நீத்தார் பெருமை) highest among excellent things. Verse 48 says the household life that keeps others on their path and does not slip from virtue has more endurance than those who do penance (நோற்பாரின் நோன்மை உடைத்து). If 48 is read as ranking the householder above the ascetic, as its plain wording allows, the two chapters give the first place to different lives; if 48 is read as praising only the householder's endurance, they do not collide.

1144 says love thrives by gossip and would droop without it. 1148 puts the same point as a rebuttal of those who expect gossip to end the affair: it is ghee on fire. 1148 gives the image and the opposing view that 1144's plain statement lacks.

303 says to forget anger toward anyone at all (யார்மாட்டும்), because every evil is born from it. 900 treats the anger of the most distinguished (சீரார் செறின்) as a force no support can save one from, and Parimelazhagar and Pope take these as people of great austerity. If they are ascetics, the chapter on not being angry would have them without anger; the conflict depends on that identification and on reading 900 as accepting such anger, where it may only be warning the offender of what follows.

1269 says one day passes like seven (ஒருநாள் எழுநாள்போல்) for those awaiting the return day; in 1278 she says he left only yesterday (நெருநற்று) and she has been pale for seven days (எழுநாளேம்). Both use seven days to measure how separation distorts time, stretching a day of waiting in 1269 and running ahead of the departure itself in 1278.

Both verses use the phrase மாசற்றார் கேண்மை, the bond of the stainless: 106 says do not forget it (மறவற்க), 800 says keep close to it (மருவுக). Each then adds a second command about a kind of friend, 106 never to abandon those who were a support in distress, 800 to drop the unsuitable (ஒப்பிலார்) even at a cost. The chapter on choosing friends repeats the gratitude chapter's rule and supplies its other half, whom to leave.

831 defines folly as taking up what harms and letting gain go (ஏதங்கொண்டு ஊதியம் போக விடல்). 422 defines understanding as the reverse movement: turning away from evil and steering toward good (தீதொரீஇ நன்றின்பால் உய்ப்பது). Read together, the two definitions are mirror images, so folly in 831 is not a lack of information but the wrong choice between two things in view.
112 promises that a fair person's wealth will last, and 117 allows that such a person may fall into low estate. The chapter keeps both. The second stops the first from being a simple reward promise.

212 says all the wealth produced by exertion ('தாளாற்றித் தந்த பொருள்') is for doing 'வேளாண்மை', benefaction. 613 says the proud distinction called benefaction ('வேளாண்மை என்னும் செருக்கு') rests in the quality called exertion ('தாளாண்மை'). The same two words are paired from opposite ends: in the Book of Virtue helping others is the purpose of earning, and in the Book of Wealth effort is the basis that makes helping possible.

360 says pain perishes when desire, anger and confusion perish down to their names (காமம் வெகுளி மயக்கம் ... நாமம் கெட); Parimelazhagar glosses the three as wanting, aversion and ignorance. 4 describes God as the one without wanting or not-wanting (வேண்டுதல் வேண்டாமை இலான்) and says those who reach his feet have no suffering. The state 360 sets as the goal is the nature 4 gives to the Lord, with the same result, the end of suffering.

The opening verse sets the world under a First One without reservation. In 1062, Valluvar curses whoever ordered the world so that people must beg to live. Read together, they show the book does not treat the world's source as beyond moral judgement.

397 says that for the learned any land is one's land and any town one's town (யாதானும் நாடாம் ஊராம்). 753 says the unfailing lamp called wealth goes to whatever country one has in mind (எண்ணிய தேயத்துச் சென்று) and cuts away the darkness there. Learning and wealth are each credited with making foreign places open to a person.

535: one who slipped by not guarding beforehand will grieve afterwards over his own error (முன்னுறக் காவாது ... பின்னூறு இரங்கிவிடும்). 1172: the eyes that looked without foresight now toil in misery (பைதல் உழப்பது). Parimelazhagar's comment on 1172 uses the same terms, that those who do not guard against what is coming can only bear it when it arrives.

452 uses water changing with the nature of the land it meets (நிலத்தியல்பால் நீர் திரிந்து) for understanding taking on the nature of one's company. In 1323 a lover calls the pair those joined as water with earth (நிலத்தொடு நீர் இயைந்தன்னார்), and Parimelazhagar explains that image by water taking on the land's nature. The same picture of water absorbed into soil is a caution about company in one place and a figure of union in the other.

435 says the life of one who does not guard before it comes will burn like straw. 442 tells the ruler to cherish and take as his own those whose nature is to remove the affliction that has come and to guard beforehand against what has not (உறாஅமை முற்காக்கும் பெற்றியார்). The foresight 435 demands of the ruler is, in 442, something he obtains through the people he keeps.

Both verses use the rare word சிறுதுனி for a brief bad spell in something good. In 1010 the short want of the renowned rich is like the rain-cloud going dry (மாரி வறங்கூர்ந்தனையது); in 1322 the small pain that sulking brings may make his good tenderness droop (நல்லளி வாடினும்), yet it gains worth (பாடு பெறும்). In each the dryness is temporary and belongs to a giver whose giving is not in doubt.

1109 counts sulking (ஊடல்) among the fruits of love. 1302 says sulking is like salt in the right amount, and letting it run a little long is like a little too much salt (சிறிது மிக்கற்றால் நீள விடல்). The later verse sets a limit on the first item of 1109's list: it is a gain only in measure.

426 makes accord with the world part of what understanding is. 850 says one who says 'it is not' of what the world says is (உலகத்தார் உண்டென்பது இல்லென்பான்) will be set down as a demon on earth. 850, in the chapter on shallow understanding, extends 426 from conduct to belief and states the cost of breaking with the world's view.
656 forbids what the worthy condemn even if one's mother is starving, the most extreme form of Manakkudavar's reading here, that being able to succeed doesn't excuse scorned means.

In 1247 the woman tells her heart to give up either desire or shame, since she cannot bear the two together (காமம் விடு ஒன்றோ நாண்விடு). 1132 is that choice made: the man keeps desire and puts shame aside (நாணினை நீக்கி) to ride the palmyra horse. Read together, 1247 states the dilemma and 1132 shows one way out of it.

759 says wealth is sharper than any steel against foes. 546 says it is not the spear that gives victory but the king's sceptre, if it does not bend (வேலன்று வென்றி தருவது). In both the literal weapon is set below something else, wealth in one and just rule in the other.

336 says this world has the 'greatness' that one who was here yesterday is not here today (நெருநல் உளனொருவன் இன்றில்லை). 233 says nothing in the world stands undying except high renown (புகழல்லால் பொன்றாது நிற்பதொன்றில்). 233 agrees with 336 about everything else and names one exception; the renouncer's chapter offers none.

798 uses ஆற்றறுப்பார் for friends who fail one in distress. 814 uses the same expression of the untrained horse that fails its rider in battle (அமரகத்து ஆற்றறுக்கும் கல்லாமா) and says solitude is better than such people as one's own. 814 supplies the picture for 798's word: support that holds until the moment it is needed.

784 gives rebuke as friendship's purpose. 795 turns it into a test for choosing friends: examine and take the friendship of those able to speak so that one weeps, to rebuke (இடித்து) and to teach what is proper. What 784 says a friend is for, 795 tells the reader to look for beforehand.

519 warns the king against taking amiss the familiarity of a hard-working officer (வினைக்கண் வினையுடையான் கேண்மை). 700, addressed to the courtier, says that familiarity which does improper things on the thought 'we are old associates' (பழையம் எனக்கருதிப் பண்பல்ல செய்யும் கெழுதகைமை) brings ruin. The king must tolerate the liberty and the servant must not presume on it; each verse limits the other.

652 says to avoid any action that yields neither renown nor good (புகழொடு நன்றி பயவா வினை), which makes renown one of the tests of an act. 962 says those who want renown together with great manliness will not do unworthy things even for renown (சீரினும் சீரல்ல செய்யார்). 962 therefore narrows 652's test: bringing fame does not by itself make an act fit to do.

167 says the fair goddess, grudging the envious man, shows him to her elder sister (தவ்வையைக் காட்டி விடும்). 936 names that sister, முகடி, as gambling itself, covering those who play. Envy hands a person over to misfortune; gambling, in 936, is misfortune under another name.

1045 states as plain fact that within the one suffering called poverty many sufferings arrive and settle (பல்குரைத் துன்பங்கள் சென்று படும்), and offers no remedy. 625 addresses exactly such piling up (அடுக்கி வரினும்) and says it fails against one who is not undone. Set side by side, 625's confidence is conditional on the person, while 1045 describes what the stacking is like for those in want.
233 says nothing is imperishable but high fame, and 1004 asks what the unwanted hoarder imagines will remain. Parimelazhagar's note supplies the link: fame rests only on the giver.

648 says the world listens readily to skilled, pleasing speakers. 1046 says the words of the poor go slack even when they speak good matter that they have understood well (நற்பொருள் நன்குணர்ந்து சொல்லினும் ... சோர்வு படும்). 1046 limits 648: how the world receives speech depends on the speaker's means as well as his skill.

567 calls harsh words and excessive punishment a file (அரம்) that wears down (தேய்க்கும்) the king's conquering strength. 888 says a family with enmity inside it wears away (தேயும்) like metal rubbed by a file (அரம்பொருத பொன்போல), its strength ground down. In both the file stands for slow loss of strength from within, by the king's own conduct in one and by a house's own members in the other.

615 describes one who does not want pleasure but wants the work (இன்பம் விழையான் வினைவிழைவான்) as the pillar who wipes away his kin's sorrows. 1029 looks at that same person from the inside: his body seems to hold nothing but suffering. 1029 states the cost of the role that 615 praises; Parimelazhagar takes the question as noting that pleasure never reaches him.

587 defines the spy as able to learn what was concealed and to hold what he has learned without doubt (ஐயப்பாடு இல்லதே); 702 ranks with a god the one who knows without doubt what is within another (ஐயப்படாஅது அகத்தது உணர்வானை). Both prize certain knowledge of what others hide, one gained by inquiry among informants and the other by reading a person's mind from signs.

Both use the phrase கொடியார் கொடுமை, 'the cruelty of the cruel one', for the absent man. In 1235 her shoulders, their old beauty faded, declare it; in 1169 she uses it as the measure the long nights exceed (கொடுமையின் தாம் கொடிய). 1169 moves the charge of cruelty from the man to the time itself.

656 says that even if one must see one's own mother hungry (ஈன்றாள் பசி காண்பான் ஆயினும்), one should not do what the worthy condemn. 1066 says that even asking water for a cow is degrading to the tongue (நாவிற்கு இளிவந்தது). Each picks the most sympathetic motive available, a hungry mother or a thirsty cow, and holds that it does not excuse the act.

1060 tells the asker not to be angry at a refusal, since the affliction of his own want is witness enough (நிரப்பிடும்பை தானேயும் சாலும் கரி); Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar take it as witness that means are hard to come by for anyone. 250 says that when going against someone weaker, think of yourself before those stronger (வலியார்முன் தன்னை நினைக்க). Both restrain a person by turning him to his own experience as evidence of the other's position.

212 says wealth is for benefaction, with 'தக்கார்க்கு' read by Manakkudavar and Kalaignar as the worthy who receive it and by Parimelazhagar as the worthy who own it. 1006 describes the failure of this purpose: one who neither enjoys his great wealth nor gives anything to the worthy ('தக்கார்க்கு ஒன்று ஈதல் இயல்பிலாதான்') is an affliction (ஏதம்) to it. 1006 uses 'தக்கார்க்கு' plainly of recipients, which supports the Manakkudavar reading of 212.

1023 has தெய்வம் tying up its garment (மடிதற்று) to go before the family-builder. 617 says the dark goddess lives in sloth (மடி) and the lotus goddess in the effort of the one without sloth (மடியிலான் தாள்). Both put divine favour on the side of the one who works; 1023's மடி (cloth) also echoes the மடி (sloth) that 617 and the chapter on sloth condemn.

In 271 the five elements laugh within at a hypocrite's hidden conduct; in 1040 the good woman called Land laughs (நிலமென்னும் நல்லாள் நகும்) at those who sit idle saying 'we have nothing'. In both a part of the material world is the one that laughs at a human pretence, and Parimelazhagar glosses the laugh in 1040 too as inward (தன்னுள்ளே).

747 says a fort is hard to seize by encircling, by assault without encircling, or by subversion (அறைப்படுத்தும்), which Parimelazhagar explains as undermining those inside through people they trust. 764 defines an army as one that does not break and cannot be subverted (அறைபோகாதாகி). The same word அறை marks treachery from within as a danger that fort and army must both be proof against, beside open force.

Two agents of the king, both ready for death, with opposite methods: the spy says nothing whatever is done to him (586), and the envoy says everything whatever may come (690). They share an unflinching eye: compare 585's கண்ணஞ்சாது with 686's கண் அஞ்சான்.

1108 praises the embrace with no gap. In 1187 the woman says she lay embracing, shifted a little (புடைபெயர்ந்தேன்), and at once pallor was on her thick enough to scoop up. The woman's verse gives a reason from her side why the unbroken embrace is the sweet one: the least separation brings the pallor of parting.

1173: the eyes looked hastily of themselves (கதுமெனத் தாம் நோக்கி) and now weep of themselves, which is laughable. 435: the life of one who does not guard before a fault comes is destroyed like straw before fire (வருமுன்னர்க் காவாதான்). Parimelazhagar explains the laughter in 1173 with that same phrase: it is laughable to those who guard before it comes.

508 and 510 share their closing line (தீரா இடும்பை தரும்) and their first fault, trusting without examining. 510 adds a second fault of equal weight: doubting one who has been trusted (தெளிந்தான்கண் ஐயுறவும்). Read after 508, 510 shows that the chapter's warning is not simply 'trust less': misplaced doubt is punished in the same words as misplaced trust.
225 favours giving over austerity, the commentators on 263 favour austerity over giving, and 295 now sets truth above both. The chapters rank a shifting set of virtues rather than a fixed ladder.

433 describes how those ashamed of blame weigh a small fault of their own. 957 says a fault in the well-born shows up raised high, like the spot on the moon (மதிக்கண் மறுப்போல் உயர்ந்து). 957 adds the public side: in a person of standing a small fault is seen large by others too.

1027 says that as in battle the load falls on the stout-hearted (வன்கண்ணர்), so among kin the burden (பொறை) falls on those able to carry it. 770 says an army has no existence without leaders, however many steady men it has (தலைமக்கள் இல்வழி இல்). 770 is the military fact that 1027 uses as its simile: numbers do not carry a force or a family, a few capable people do.

93 requires the glad face and the sweet word to come from within (முகத்தான் அமர்ந்து ... அகத்தானாம்). 786 says friendship that makes only the face smile is not friendship; friendship that makes the heart within smile is (முகநக ... நெஞ்சத்து அகநக). The same முகம்/அகம் pairing sets the test of genuineness for kind speech and for friendship.

483 names two conditions that make a hard deed possible, means and time (கருவியான் காலம் அறிந்து). 675 lists five things to think through before acting: resources, means, time, the deed and the place (பொருள் கருவி காலம் வினை இடன்). 675 keeps 483's pair and sets it inside a fuller list.

184: though you speak harshly to his face (சொல்லினும்), do not speak (சொல்லற்க) the heedless word behind his back. 197: let the worthy say what lacks நயன் if they must (சொல்லினுஞ் சொல்லுக), it is good that they not say what lacks use. The two neighbouring chapters use the same concessive move, granting a lesser fault of speech in order to isolate the one the chapter is about.

647 lists three things that make a person hard to beat in a contest: able to speak, free of lapses, unafraid (சொலல்வல்லன் சோர்விலன் அஞ்சான்). 686 defines the envoy with nearly the same set: learned, not afraid of hostile eyes (கண் அஞ்சான்), speaking so it goes home, and knowing what fits the time. The envoy chapter puts the general portrait of 647 into the one post where it is tested before an enemy.

183 says that it is better to die than to live by backbiting, because it is a false kind of life. In 1141 backbiting is what keeps someone else alive. The same act has a very different moral look from the side of its target.

578 forbids kindness that damages the work, and 580 praises kindness that swallows poison. Parimelazhagar resolves this by confining forbearance to wrongs against oneself, but the verses themselves don't state that limit.

653 tells those who mean to rise to leave off any deed that dims their lustre (ஒளிமாழ்கும் செய்வினை). 921 says those who live in love of liquor (கட்காதல் கொண்டொழுகுவார்) are never held in awe and lose their lustre (ஒளியிழப்பர்). 921 gives a named instance of the kind of act 653 warns against in general.

1109 names quarrel, making up and union together as rewards without ranking them. 1326 ranks them: as digesting is sweeter than eating, sulking is sweeter than union (புணர்தலின் ஊடல் இனிது). The later verse takes one item from 1109's list and gives it first place.

167 says the fair goddess grudges the envious man and shows him to her elder sister. 179 says திரு goes to those who know virtue and do not covet. The two neighbouring chapters use the goddess in opposite directions: she leaves the one who resents others' goods and comes to the one who does not want them.

239 says land that bears a body without renown declines in its blameless rich yield (வண்பயன் குன்றும்). 559 says the sky holds back rain when the king bends justice, and the next verse, 560, uses the same verb for cows' yield (ஆபயன் குன்றும்). In each, nature's yield falls in response to a human moral failing, an individual's in 239 and a ruler's in 559.

667: do not scorn anyone on seeing their form (உருவுகண்டு எள்ளாமை), for there are people like the linchpin (அச்சாணி) of a great rolling chariot. 1032: those who plough are the ஆணி of the world's people, because they bear all who cannot plough and take up other work. Both use the pin that holds the wheel for someone small in appearance on whom everything turns; 667 leaves the person unnamed and 1032 names the farmer. Parimelazhagar supplies the smallness in 667 from the simile.

761 says a conquering army, complete in its parts and unafraid of wounds, is the chief of all a king's wealth (வெறுக்கையுள் எல்லாம் தலை). 381 lists the six things a king must have and puts the army first (படைகுடி கூழ் ...). The placing in 381's list and the ranking in 761 agree.

773 says fierceness is called great manliness (பேராண்மை), and that helping a foe in distress (ஊராண்மை) is its edge. 1026 says good manliness (நல்லாண்மை) is making oneself the one who manages the house one was born in (இல்லாண்மை). Each verse takes ஆண்மை and coins a second compound that turns it toward care for others; Parimelazhagar notes that 'நல்' in 1026 is there to set it apart from the manliness of war.

175 asks what fine and wide understanding comes to (அஃகி அகன்ற அறிவு என்னாம்) if one covets and acts senselessly toward everyone. 315 asks whether anything comes of understanding (அறிவினான் ஆகுவதுண்டோ) if one does not guard against another's pain as one's own. Both test அறிவு by how its owner treats other people, in coveting and in causing hurt.

Both verses name a 'poverty within poverty' (இன்மையுள் இன்மை) and give different answers: in 153 it is turning away a guest, in 841 it is lack of understanding (அறிவின்மை), with other lack not counted as lack by the world. The same superlative formula serves hospitality in the Book of Virtue and intelligence in the Book of Wealth, which shows the formula working as emphasis within each chapter's topic.

1082 says her returning look is like an attacking spirit come with an army (தாக்கணங்கு தானைக்கொண் டன்னது): the look only wounds. 1091 finds two looks in her eyes (இருநோக்கு), one that gives the sickness and one that is its medicine (நோய்நோக்கு ... அந்நோய் மருந்து). The next chapter adds the healing side that 1082 leaves out.
225 places enduring hunger below removing it. 261 defines austerity as endurance plus not harming living things, so the austerity that 225 ranks low is not the fuller ideal of chapter 27.

962 refuses unworthy acts even when they would bring renown (சீரினும்). 113 says to let go at once of gain that departs from fairness even if it brings nothing but good (நன்றே தரினும் நடுவிகந்தாம் ஆக்கம்). Both have the form 'even if it yields the thing you want, not by this means', applied to fame in one and to profit in the other.

941 says the three humours counted by the learned, beginning with wind, cause disease whether they exceed or fall short (மிகினும் குறையினும்); Parimelazhagar refers the excess and shortfall to food and activity. 466 says one is ruined by doing what is unfit and also by not doing what is fit (செயக் கெடும் ... செய்யாமையானும் கெடும்). Both verses locate harm on two sides of a right amount, in the body and in action.

503 observes that even in those who have learned hard things and are free of fault, it is rare on examination to find no blankness (இன்மை அரிதே வெளிறு). 504 gives the rule that follows: examine the qualities and the faults and judge by what predominates (மிகைநாடி மிக்க கொளல்). Parimelazhagar on 504 makes the bridge explicit, saying no one in the world has only qualities or only faults.

658 says forbidden actions bring anguish even when they are accomplished. 931 says not to want gambling even if one wins (வென்றிடினும்), since the winnings are like the hook a fish has swallowed. The gambling verse gives an image for 658's claim: the success itself is what carries the harm.

In 1157 the woman asks whether the bangles slipping past her wrist do not proclaim (தூற்றாகொல்) that the lord of the shore has left her. In 1233 the shoulders that swelled on the day of union (மணந்தநாள் வீங்கிய தோள்) seem to announce fully that he has parted (தணந்தமை சால அறிவிப்ப போலும்). In both her body makes the separation public without her speaking; 1233 adds the contrast with how the same shoulders looked at union.

In 1146 the woman saw him one day only, and the gossip has spread like the serpent seizing the moon (திங்களைப் பாம்புகொண்டற்று), which Parimelazhagar glosses as spreading everywhere. 957 says a fault in the well-born shows high, like the spot on the moon in the sky (மதிக்கண் மறுப்போல்). Both use the moon as the thing whose blemish everyone sees: a brief event or a small fault becomes public because of where it sits.

904 says the man who fears his wife gets no distinction from his command of action (வினையாண்மை வீறெய்தல் இன்று). 1026 defines good manliness (நல்லாண்மை) as making the mastery of one's house one's own (இல்லாண்மை ஆக்கிக் கொளல்), which Parimelazhagar takes as leading one's family. Both build on ஆண்மை as mastery: the man of 904 has given up mastery at home, and his mastery of work earns no honour.

299 names not lying the one true lamp for the worthy (பொய்யா விளக்கே விளக்கு). 601 calls lineage an undimming lamp (குடியென்னும் குன்றா விளக்கம்) that nevertheless goes out when the grime of sloth covers it. The lamp figure marks what a person's standing depends on, and 601 adds that such a lamp can be put out by neglect.

1038 treats manure (எரு) and water (நீர்) as what makes a crop grow. In 1147 the woman says her love-sickness grows with the town's gossip as manure and her mother's words as water (கெளவை எருவாக அன்னைசொல் நீராக). The Book of Love takes the two inputs that 1038 gives as farming advice and uses them as a figure for what feeds her passion.

171 says that coveting another's goods without fairness makes the family perish and brings faults at once (குடிபொன்றிக் குற்றமும் ஆங்கே தரும்). 604 says of the slothful that the family dies down and faults multiply (குடிமடிந்து குற்றம் பெருகும்). The same double penalty, on the குடி and in குற்றம், is attached to greed in Book 1 and to sloth in Book 2.

In 1145 a lover says love grows sweeter each time it is exposed, as drinking is wanted more each time one is drunk (களித்தொறும் கள்ளுண்டல் வேட்டற்றால்). 940 has the same 'each time ... the more' construction with another vice, the dice, as the comparison (இழத்தொறூஉம் காதலிக்கும் சூதேபோல்). The lover uses the figure to praise his state, while 940 uses it to describe an attachment fed by its own losses.

88 says those who do not take up the sacrifice of tending guests guard their goods painfully (பரிந்தோம்பி) and end by saying 'we have no support' (பற்றற்றேம்). 228 asks whether the hard-eyed who store what they have and lose it (வைத்திழக்கும்) do not know the joy of giving. Both describe the same sequence of hoarding and then loss, and both set it against a use of wealth the hoarder never tried.

In 1182 the woman says pallor spreads and rides over her body with the pride (தகையால்) that he was the one who gave it. In 1240 the man says the pallor of her eyes felt distress (பருவரல்) on seeing what her forehead had done. Both give the pallor feelings of its own, pride in one and distress in the other, so that பசப்பு is spoken of as a party to the love and not only its symptom.

218 says those who see their duty do not slacken in ஒப்புரவு even in a season without means (இடனில் பருவத்தும்). 1064 says worth does not consent to asking even at a time without means (இடமில்லாக் காலும்). The same test, what a person does when resources are gone, is applied to giving in 218 and to asking in 1064: the good neither stop giving nor start begging.

157 says that though others do what is improper to one (திறனல்ல தற்பிறர் செய்யினும்), it is good not to do what is not aram. 312 says that even when someone has done harm out of hatred, not doing harm in return (மறுத்தின்னா செய்யாமை) is the settled principle of the stainless. The same rule appears in the householder's chapter on forbearance and in the ascetic's chapter on not harming, which makes it common to both ways of life.

697 says to speak what is wanted and never to say what has no use, even if asked (வினையில எஞ்ஞான்றும் கேட்பினும் சொல்லாவிடல்). 200 gives the general rule: say words that have use, do not say words that have none (சொல்லிற் பயனிலாச் சொல்). The court verse applies the household rule and tightens it, since here even the king's own request does not license useless talk.

355 makes seeing the true thing the definition of understanding. 857 says those of bitter understanding who hold to hostility do not see the true thing (மெய்ப்பொருள் காணார்); Parimelazhagar takes it there as the substance of the texts on right policy that bring success. The same phrase marks, in the book of wealth, what a mind bent on quarrel cannot perceive.

283 says gain made by stealth perishes beyond measure while seeming to grow (ஆவது போலக் கெடும்); 660 says making wealth by deceit (சலத்தால் பொருள்செய்து) and feeling secure in it is like keeping water in an unfired clay pot. The same claim, that wrongly got wealth looks held and is being lost, is made to the renouncer in one book and to the minister in the other.

490 says to be like the heron in the season for folding up (கூம்பும் பருவத்து), and like its strike when the moment is right. 126 says that one who can draw in the five senses like a tortoise (ஆமைபோல் ஐந்தடக்கல்) in one birth has protection for seven. Both teach restraint through an animal that draws itself in. The tortoise's withdrawal is the discipline itself, and the heron's is half of a pair that ends in a strike (குத்து).

233 says that apart from high renown nothing in the world stands without perishing (புகழல்லால் பொன்றாது நிற்பதொன்று இல்). 145 says the blame of the man who violates another's home also stands forever without dying (எஞ்ஞான்றும் விளியாது நிற்கும் பழி). Taken literally 145 names a second undying thing, so the pair shows the book treating lasting blame as the counterpart of lasting fame.

160 ranks those who fast behind those who bear harsh words; 295 says one who speaks truth in accord with his heart is above those who practise austerity together with giving (தவத்தொடு தானஞ்செய்வாரின் தலை). In both a virtue of everyday speech, enduring it in one case and keeping it truthful in the other, is placed above formal religious practice.

482 says that acting in accord with the season (பருவத்தோடு ஒட்ட ஒழுகல்) is the rope that keeps fortune from leaving. 1028 says those who raise their family have no season (குடிசெய்வார்க்கு இல்லை பருவம்), and that idling and thinking of one's dignity ruins it. The two conflict if பருவம் in 1028 means the right moment for action; Parimelazhagar instead takes it there as seasons of heat, rain and cold used as an excuse to put work off, which removes the conflict.

412 treats listening as food for the ear (செவிக்குணவு) and lets the stomach have a little (சிறிது) only when that food is absent. 420 turns the same ear-and-mouth pairing into a judgment: for those who know taste by the mouth and not by the ear (செவியிற் சுவையுணரா வாயுணர்வின் மாக்கள்), living and dying come to the same. The chapter's ranking of the two appetites starts as a rule for mealtimes and ends as a measure of a life.

1168: the night has put all living beings to sleep and, she says with pity (அளித்து), has no companion but her. 1222: she tells the evening it looks sad-eyed (புன்கண்ணை) and asks whether its partner is as hard as hers. In both she treats a time of day as a fellow sufferer and puts her own state onto it; Parimelazhagar says as much of 1222.

1011 ranks shame at one's deeds (கருமத்தால் நாணுதல்) as true shame and sets aside the shame of fair-browed women (திருநுதல் நல்லவர் நாண்) as another kind. 907 says a woman who has shame (நாணுடைப் பெண்) has more greatness than the manhood of one who lives doing a woman's bidding. So the woman's modesty that 1011 treats as the lesser kind still outranks, in 907, manhood that has given up command.

In 46 there's nothing to gain by leaving household life. Parimelazhagar on 176 calls household life a path toward renunciation, so leaving is the natural end. This commentator's way of ordering the stages conflicts with the plain force of 46.

826 says the words of the unreconciled are quickly seen through although they say good things as friends do. 828, in the same chapter, says a weapon can lie hidden in hands joined in worship (தொழுதகை யுள்ளும் படையொடுங்கும்) and in an enemy's tears. 828 limits the confidence of 826: the speech may give itself away, but gestures of submission and grief can still conceal the intent.

213 ranks ஒப்புரவு above anything to be had in the gods' world or this one. 222 says giving is good even if there were no higher world ('மேலுலகம் இல்லெனினும் ஈதலே நன்று'). Both detach the worth of helping others from heaven as a reward: in 213 heaven holds nothing better, and in 222 the good stands even without heaven.

237 tells those without renown to blame themselves and not their scorners. 1060 tells the asker not to be angry at a refusal, since the affliction of his own want is witness enough (நிரப்பிடும்பை தானேயும் சாலும் கரி). In both the grievance against another person is turned back to one's own condition.

1188 complains that the talk fixes on her pallor and not on his leaving. 1190 says it is good to get the name of pallor, provided they do not spread talk of his unkindness (நல்காமை தூற்றார் எனின்); Parimelazhagar sets it as her reply when the friend has blamed him. The complaint of 1188 should therefore not be read as a wish to have him blamed: in 1190 she accepts the very imbalance she resents.

495 gives the image: the crocodile wins in its own deep water. 499 states the human case without an image: even people with no fortress and no great standing (சிறைநலனும் சீரும் இலரெனினும்) are hard to engage on the land where they live (உறைநிலத்தோடு ஒட்டல் அரிது). 499 applies the crocodile's lesson to an invader's estimate of a weak-looking people.
Sweet words here must be free of deceit. In 292, even a falsehood counts as truth if it yields blameless good. What 91 excludes by definition, 292 may allow when the outcome justifies it.

489 says that when what is hard to get has come, one should at that very point do what is hard to do (இயைந்தக்கால் அந்நிலையே செய்தற்கரிய செயல்). 333 says wealth has the nature of not staying, and that on getting it one should at once do what stays (அதுபெற்றால் அற்குப ஆங்கே செயல்). Both reason from something that will not last, an opportunity in 489 and wealth in 333, to acting at once, and 333 turns the king's rule of timing toward lasting good.

864 says the man who cannot leave anger is easy for anyone to overcome. 526 gives the opposite case: no one on earth has more people at his side than one who gives greatly and does not cherish anger (பேணான் வெகுளி). Put together, anger decides whether a man stands with many around him or exposed to all.

408 says wealth is worse than poverty when it sits with the unlearned (வறுமையின் இன்னாதே). 558 says having is more painful than not having (இன்மையின் இன்னாது உடைமை) under a ruler who does no justice. Both invert the usual ranking of wealth over poverty under a stated condition: the holder's lack of learning in one, the king's injustice in the other.

106 says not to give up the friendship of those who were one's strength in sorrow (துன்பத்துள் துப்பாயார் நட்பு). 815 says the friendship of the small, which gives no safety (ஏமம்), is better not obtained at all. The same measure, support in trouble, decides in one verse which friends must be kept and in the other which should never be acquired.

204 says that if one plots another's ruin, virtue plots one's own. 319 states the return in terms of time: harm done to others in the forenoon brings harm to oneself in the afternoon, of itself ('பிற்பகல் தாமே வரும்'). 319's 'தாமே' leaves the return impersonal where 204 gives it an agent, and Parimelazhagar on 204 adds the same point about speed: virtue begins plotting at the very moment the plotter does.

In 1313 the man reports that even wearing a wreath makes her angry (காயும்): 'you wore it to show some woman'. In 1321 the woman says he has no fault (இல்லை தவறு அவர்க்கு), yet his way of showing tenderness can bring on a sulk. 1321 supplies from her mouth what the man's complaints in chapter 132 imply: the grounds are invented.

833 lists four absences as the fool's work: no shame, no inquiry, no tenderness, no care for anything (நாணாமை நாடாமை நாரின்மை யாதொன்றும் பேணாமை பேதை தொழில்). 428 defines folly as not fearing what should be feared and calls fearing it the work of the knowing (அறிவார் தொழில்). Both define folly as a missing response where one is due, and both set it out as a characteristic தொழில்.

1148 says that to think of putting out love with gossip is like thinking to put out fire with ghee (நெய்யால் எரி நுதுப்பேம்). 1260 asks whether those whose hearts are like fat put in fire (நிணம் தீயில் இட்டன்ன) can say they will hold out in a sulk. Both use fat meeting fire for love: in 1148 the fat feeds the fire, in 1260 the heart is the fat that melts.

100 says speaking unpleasant things when pleasant ones are available is like taking the unripe fruit when the ripe is there (கனிஇருப்பக் காய்கவர்ந்தற்று). 1306, a speech in the Book of Love, says that love without serious and light quarrels is like over-ripe fruit and unripe fruit (கனியும் கருக்காயும் அற்று). The ripe/unripe pair is used differently: in 100 the ripe fruit is simply the right choice, while the lover treats fruit that is too ripe and fruit that is too raw as two ways of missing the right point.

485 praises waiting for the right time. 671 says deliberation ends in reaching a resolve, and it is bad for that resolve to rest in delay (அத்துணிவு தாழ்ச்சியுள் தங்குதல் தீது). 671 marks the limit of 485: waiting that is fixed on the time (காலம் கருதி) is part of the plan, and holding back after the decision, for no such reason, is a fault.

944 instructs: know that the earlier meal is digested (அற்றது அறிந்து) and eat only when thoroughly hungry (துவரப் பசித்து). 1326 says the digesting of what was eaten is sweeter than eating (உணலினும் உண்டது அறல் இனிது), and so sulking is sweeter than union. The chapter on medicine states as a rule of health what the man uses as his simile; Parimelazhagar on 1326 draws the same line, that one who eats when hungry eats more and with more relish.

433 says those ashamed of blame treat a fault as small as a millet as if it were a palmyra (தினைத்துணையாங் குற்றம்... பனைத்துணையாக் கொள்வர்). 1282 uses the same two measures in the other direction: with love as large as a palmyra, even a millet of sulking over his fault is to be avoided. In 433 the small fault is magnified; in 1282 the small grievance is to be dropped.

615 makes the work-loving man a pillar that props his kin (துடைத்தூன்றும் தூண்). 1030 says a family with no good person to stand by and prop it (அடுத்தூன்றும் நல்லாள் இலாத குடி) falls when trouble cuts at its foot. 1030 states the cost of the absence of the figure 615 praises, with the same verb ஊன்று.

422 defines understanding as what does not let the mind go wherever it has gone, but turns it from evil toward good (தீதொரீஇ நன்றின்பால் உய்ப்பது அறிவு); 287 grants stealing the name அறிவு only with the qualifier கார், dark. By 422's definition the thief's skill fails as அறிவு, which explains why 287 marks it as darkened.

709 says the eye itself tells of enmity and friendship (பகைமையும் கேண்மையும் கண்ணுரைக்கும்) to those who know how to read it. 826 says an enemy's words are soon recognised even when they sound like a friend's. Both hold that hostility shows through the surface; 709 makes this depend on a skilled reader, a condition 826 leaves unstated.

473 says many who did not know their strength broke midway (இடைக்கண் முரிந்தார்). 899 uses the same figure for a king: if those of exalted resolve are angered, even the king breaks midway and loses his kingship (இடைமுரிந்து வேந்தனும் வேந்து கெடும்). Parimelazhagar reads 473 as starting something against those stronger than oneself, and 899 gives one such case, a ruler who misjudges the power of the great.

982 says the worthy have only the goodness of character (குணநலம்), and that other goodness is not counted among goodnesses; Parimelazhagar takes பிறநலம் to be the goodness of the bodily limbs. 79 asks what all the outer limbs (புறத்துறுப்பு) can do for those who lack love, the inner limb (அகத்துறுப்பு). Both verses rank an inner quality over the body's outward parts, one for worth and one for love.

805 advises that when friends do something painful, one should take it as either folly or great intimacy (பேதைமை ஒன்றோ பெருங்கிழமை என்றுணர்க). 580 describes people who drink poison they have seen poured. 805 supplies a way of construing a friend's injury that makes the conduct in 580 intelligible, though 580's own stated motive is the wish for நாகரிகம் and not a charitable reading of the giver.

1180 says it is not hard for the town to get the secret of those like her, whose eyes are beaten drums (அறைபறை கண்ணார்). 1254 says her desire goes past concealment into the public place (மன்று படும்). 1180 supplies a means by which the exposure described in 1254 happens: her own eyes announce it.

509 says trust no one without examining, and after examining, trust what is to be trusted (தேர்ந்தபின் தேறுக தேறும் பொருள்). 518 says that after examining a person's fitness for the work (வினைக்குரிமை நாடிய பின்றை), make him fully entitled to it (அதற்குரியனாகச் செயல்). 518 turns 509's second half into an act: the trust that follows examination is shown by handing over real authority.

539 advises thinking, when swollen with one's own joy, of those who were ruined by negligence (இகழ்ச்சியின் கெட்டாரை உள்ளுக). 935 supplies such a memory: those who took pride (தருக்கி) in the dice and came to nothing; Parimelazhagar reads them as kings of former times and names the Pandavas. 935 does for gambling what 539 asks a ruler to do in general.

456 says no deed fails to turn out well for those whose company is pure (இனந்தூயார்க்கு இல்லை நன்றாகா வினை), and Parimelazhagar gives the reason: their deeds are thought through with good company. 462 states that mechanism directly: nothing is hard to attain for those who act after examining the matter with chosen company (தெரிந்த இனத்தொடு தேர்ந்தெண்ணி).

472 says nothing fails for those who know what they can do and what must be known and proceed resting in that (ஒல்வது அறிவது அறிந்து ... செல்லாதது இல்). 462 says nothing is out of reach for those who act after examining the matter with chosen company and thinking it over themselves (தேர்ந்தெண்ணிச் செய்வார்க்கு அரும்பொருள் யாதொன்றும் இல்). The promise is the same in both and the condition differs: knowledge of one's own capacity in 472, counsel and deliberation in 462.

482 pictures fortune (திரு) as something that leaves unless tied, and names timely action as the rope (தீராமை ஆர்க்கும் கயிறு). 617 pictures her as living in the effort of the one without sloth (மடியிலான் தாளுளாள் தாமரையினாள்), with her dark elder sister living in sloth. Both treat fortune as a visitor kept by conduct, and they name different conduct: timing in 482, steady effort in 617.

1201 (the man, for Parimelazhagar) says love is sweeter than toddy because it gives great joy that does not end even when only thought of (உள்ளினும் தீராப் பெருமகிழ்). 1281, spoken by the woman, makes the same comparison: elation at a thought and delight at a sight belong to love and not to toddy (கள்ளுக்கு இல் காமத்திற்கு உண்டு). The pairing shows the same judgment given from both sides of the couple, built on the same verb உள்ளுதல்.

Both use ஒறுத்தல், punish. 314 says to punish wrongdoers by shaming them with kindness; 550 says that the king punishing the worst of them with death is simply weeding a crop. The word keeps its form while the ethics of person and state divide.

Verse 64 sets a child's messy gruel above amrita. In 1103 the lover asks whether the world of the lotus-eyed one (தாமரைக் கண்ணான் உலகு) can be sweeter (இனிதுகொல்) than sleeping on the soft arms of the one he loves; Parimelazhagar has him say this to a companion who reproved him. The same move, a heavenly standard of sweetness outdone by an intimate bodily one, appears in the parent's voice in Book 1 and in a lover's speech in Book 3.

625 says that though troubles come stacked (அடுக்கி வரினும்), those of one who is not undone (அழிவிலான்) are themselves in trouble. 989 says those called the shore of worth do not shift even if the age shifts (ஊழி பெயரினும் தாம் பெயரார்). Both define a person by not moving under pressure, one in the chapter on a king's undertakings and one in the chapter on character.

34 says all virtue comes to a stainless mind and the rest is noise. 829 teaches outward friendship with inward death. Parimelazhagar accepts the conflict openly and resolves it as a rule for enemies only, which is a substantive claim about how the books of the Kural relate.

1302 says a sulk is like salt in the right amount, and letting it run long (நீள விடல்) is like a little too much. 1330 makes the sulk love's pleasure only if embrace follows (கூடி முயங்கப் பெறின்). Parimelazhagar reads 1330's condition through this measure: the sulk must be ended at the right point, between a quarrel too ripe and one too young, and that is hard to judge.

1190 says being named for her pallor is good if people do not broadcast his unkindness (நல்காமை தூற்றார் எனின்). 1236 says the hurt is in hearing him called cruel (கொடியர் எனக்கூறல் நொந்து), more than in the slipping bangles. Both verses make the talk against him, and not her own disfigurement, the thing she cannot bear.

742 says a fort has clear water (மணிநீர்), open ground, a hill (மலை) and a forest of fine shade. 737 lists as limbs of a land the two waters (இருபுனல்), a well-placed hill (வாய்ந்த மலை), the water that comes from it, and a strong fort. The same features of the terrain, water and hill, are counted first as a land's resources and then as a fort's defences, and 737 already names the fort as part of the land.

605 treats sloth and its companions as something the ruin-bound choose and desire (காமக் கலன்). 371 says sloth itself arises from a fate of loss (போகூழால் தோன்றும் மடி). 371 puts a cause behind what 605 describes as a preference, which matches 605's own word கெடுநீரார், people whose nature is already to perish.

1137 speaks of suffering a love like the sea (கடலன்ன காமம் உழந்தும்) and praises womanhood that still does not mount the palmyra horse. 1166 uses the sea twice over: love's pleasure is a sea, and when it afflicts (அடுங்கால்) the pain is greater than that. The sea is the book's measure for love, and 1166 says the measure is exceeded.

1247 leaves open which of desire and shame is to go (காமம் விடு ஒன்றோ நாண் விடு). 1251, opening the next chapter, reports the outcome: the axe of desire breaks the door of restraint that shame had bolted (காமக் கணிச்சி உடைக்கும் ... நாணுத்தாழ் வீழ்த்த கதவு). The choice she offers her heart in 1247 is settled in 1251 by force, not by decision.

218: even at a time without means ('இடனில் பருவத்தும்'), those who see what is due do not slacken in ஒப்புரவு. 955: even when what they have to give has shrunk ('வழங்குவது உள்வீழ்ந்தக் கண்ணும்'), an old family does not part from its character. The Book of Virtue credits this constancy to insight into duty ('கடனறி காட்சி'), and the Book of Wealth credits it to lineage ('பழங்குடி').
The same satirical move rises in rank: they're like men, and then they're like gods. What makes them like the gods, acting as they please, is what makes them not like men.

1164 says the sea of love exists and there is no raft to swim it. 1167 continues the figure: she has swum the fierce flood (காமக் கடும்புனல் நீந்தி) and sees no shore (கரை காணேன்), and at midnight there is only herself. The second verse turns the missing raft into an actual, endless swim.

Both verses turn on the same play of உள்ளம் (mind) and உள்ளுதல் (to think): in 622 a flood of suffering perishes when the wise person thinks with the mind (உள்ளத்தின் உள்ளக் கெடும்), and in 309 all one has thought of is gained if one does not think anger in the mind (உள்ளத்தால் உள்ளான் வெகுளி எனின்). Read together they make a single act of thought decide the outcome, once by what is thought and once by what is left unthought.

In 1189, on Parimelazhagar's reading, she accepts the pallor so long as the man who persuaded her is held blameless. In 1236 her arms thin and her bangles slip, and what pains her is hearing him called cruel (அவரைக் கொடியர் எனக்கூறல் நொந்து). In both she ranks his good name above her own wasting.

In 1102 the man says that medicines for other ailments are things other than the ailment (பிணிக்கு மருந்து பிற), but she is herself the medicine for the sickness she causes (தன்நோய்க்குத் தானே மருந்து). In 1241 the woman, apart from him, asks her heart to think of any medicine at all (எனைத்தொன்றும் ... மருந்து) for her sickness. Read together, 1102 explains why her heart has nothing to offer: the only cure is the absent person who caused the illness.

982 denies that any goodness other than character counts for the worthy. 407 says the handsome looks (எழில்நலம்) of one without fine, penetrating understanding are those of a decorated clay doll (மண்மாண் புனைபாவை). Both dismiss outward நலம் that has nothing inside it, though 407 measures by understanding and 982 by character.

704 says those who grasp what is meant without being told and the rest are alike in limbs (உறுப்போ ரனையரால்) and yet different. 993 says likeness of limbs is not likeness among people (உறுப்பொத்தல் மக்களொப்பு அன்றால்), and true likeness is likeness of character. Both deny that the shared body makes people alike, with perception the dividing line in 704 and பண்பு in 993.

152 says always bear with excess against you (பொறுத்தல் இறப்பினை என்றும்); Parimelazhagar adds 'even when you are able to punish'. 579 is that case in the ruler, who has the power to punish and is asked to bear with those who harm him. 152 goes a step further than 579 by preferring forgetting the wrong to bearing it.

661: firmness in action is a person's firmness of mind (மனத்திட்பம்); everything else is something other (மற்றைய எல்லாம் பிற). 34: being spotless in mind (மனத்துக்கண் மாசிலன் ஆதல்) is all of virtue; the rest is noisy show (ஆகுல நீர பிற). The two verses have the same shape, reducing a whole domain to a state of mind and dismissing the remainder as 'பிற', once for virtue and once for effective action.

1162: she cannot hide the sickness, and telling it to the one who caused it brings shame (உரைத்தலும் நாணுத் தரும்). 1200: she tells her heart that it means to tell its pain to one who is not close (உறாஅர்க்கு உறுநோய் உரைப்பாய்) and might as well fill up the sea. Parimelazhagar reads both as about sending him word; 1200 adds futility to the shame that 1162 gives as the obstacle.

1309 limits the sweetness of sulking to those who love (வீழுநர் கண்ணே). 1323 asks whether any heaven matches sulking with those joined like water with earth (நிலத்தொடு நீர் இயைந்தன்னார் அகத்து). Both say the value of the sulk depends on the closeness of the two, and both use water to say it.

308 says that even if harm is done to you like the touch of massed flames (இணர்எரி தோய்வன்ன), not being angry is good if one can manage it. 267 says pain that burns (துன்பஞ் சுடச்சுட) makes those who can endure it shine like gold in fire. Both picture suffering as fire applied to a person; 308 asks only that it be borne without anger, and 267 says what the bearing produces.

1169: the nights that pass so long these days (நெடிய கழியும் இரா) are crueller than the cruel one's cruelty. 1269: for those who pine with a set day of return in mind, one day passes like seven (ஒருநாள் எழுநாள்போல்). Both say that time stretches for the one who waits.

In 1168 the night has put all living beings to sleep (மன்னுயிர் எல்லாம் துயிற்றி) and she alone is its companion, so her suffering is solitary. In 1229 she says that when evening spreads, bewildering the mind (மதிமருண்டு; Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar take this as her own mind), the whole town is bewildered and suffers (பதிமருண்டு பைதல் உழக்கும்). The two speeches picture the world around her in opposite ways, asleep and untouched in one and sharing her distress in the other.

339 presents death and birth as alternating like sleep and waking, which both Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar read as a cycle that keeps turning. 356 says those who have learned here and seen the true thing reach the path of not coming back here (மற்றீண்டு வாரா நெறி). 356 limits 339: the waking that follows each death is the rule only for those who have not seen the real.

611: do not flag saying 'it is hard' (அருமை உடைத்தென்று அசாவாமை), for effort will give the greatness (பெருமை முயற்சி தரும்). 26: those who do what is hard to do are great, those who cannot are small (செயற்கரிய செய்வார் பெரியர்). 26 defines greatness by hard deeds as if it were a fixed difference between people; 611 says the greatness needed is itself produced by trying.

843 says the fool harms himself beyond what an enemy could. 434 says one's own fault is the enemy that brings ruin (குற்றமே அற்றந் தரூஉம் பகை) and is therefore the thing to guard against. 434 gives the general principle of which 843 is the case of the person who cannot do the guarding.

153 says the strength within strength (வன்மையுள் வன்மை) is bearing with fools (மடவார்ப் பொறை); 444 says the chief of all strengths (வன்மையுள் எல்லாம் தலை) is to live so that those greater than oneself become one's own. Neither verse puts strength in force. One finds it in enduring those below one in understanding and the other in attaching oneself to those above.

471 tells one to weigh four strengths before acting: of the deed, oneself, the opponent and the allies (வினைவலி, தன்வலி, மாற்றான் வலி, துணைவலி ... தூக்கிச் செயல்). 675 gives a second checklist with the same closing command, five things to think through until the darkness clears: resources, means, time, the deed and the place (பொருள் கருவி காலம் வினை இடன் ... எண்ணிச் செயல்). Read together, 471 measures the parties to a contest and 675 adds the circumstances of the act, and only the deed (வினை) is on both lists.

1303 says that leaving unembraced those who have sulked (புலந்தாரைப் புல்லா விடல்) is like giving sharp pain to those already suffering (அலந்தாரை அல்லல்நோய் செய்தற்று). 1304 says that not appeasing those who sulk (ஊடியவரை உணராமை) is like cutting a withered creeper at the root (வாடிய வள்ளி முதல் அரிந்தற்று). The pair states one claim twice, once as added hurt and once as a finishing cut. Parimelazhagar takes both as the wife's taunt sending the man back to his other women.

1169 says the long nights now passing are crueller than the cruelty of the cruel one (கொடியார் கொடுமையின் தாம்கொடிய). 1224 says that where her lover is absent (காதலர் இல்வழி) evening comes like ஏதிலர், pitiless strangers or foes, on a killing ground (கொலைக்களத்து). Both make a stretch of time into a cruel agent set beside human cruelty, and 1224 names the condition: it is so only in his absence.

205 rules out poverty as a ground for evil deeds. 656 takes the hardest case: even if one must see the mother who bore one go hungry ('ஈன்றாள் பசி காண்பான் ஆயினும்'), one should not do what the worthy condemn. Parimelazhagar notes that 656 sets aside a general rule of the dharma texts allowing wrong to feed one's dependants, which shows how far 205's principle is taken.

644 says to speak knowing the திறன், which Parimelazhagar takes as the relative standing of speaker and hearers. 711 gives the method: those who know the stock of words should speak after knowing the assembly and examining (அவையறிந்து ஆராய்ந்து சொல்லுக). Chapter 72 works out as a practice what 644 states as a principle.

750 says a fort's excellences do not exist for those who lack excellence in action. 727 says the treatise learned by one who fears the assembly is like a bright sword in the hand of a பேடி amid enemies (பகையகத்துப் பேடிகை ஒள்வாள்). In both a good instrument, a fort or learning, is worth nothing in the hands of someone who cannot act when the test comes.

Both verses describe the same event: he is with her in sleep and gone on waking. In 1217 this is his cruelty; Parimelazhagar explains the torment as his being on her shoulder in the dream and vanishing when she wakes. In 1218 she tells it in his favour: asleep he is on her shoulder (தோள்மேலர்), and awake he hurries into her heart (நெஞ்சத்தர் ஆவர் விரைந்து), so he never leaves her at all. Parimelazhagar says 1218 is her defence of him after the friend had spoken against him.

339 says death is like sleep and birth is like waking from it, as an image of impermanence. 1216 wishes waking away altogether, for the sake of staying with her lover. If the two were read together, her wish would come close to a wish not to be reborn, though nothing in the verse says this.

786 says friendship in which only the face smiles is not friendship (முகநக நட்பது நட்பன்று), and that friendship in which the heart within smiles is. 824 says to fear deceivers who smile sweetly with the face and are bitter within (முகத்தின் இனிய நகாஅ அகத்தின்னா). The face and heart contrast that defines true friendship in 786 becomes in 824 the mark of a false friend to be feared.

50 says one who lives on earth (வையத்துள்) as one should is placed among the gods who dwell in the sky. 353 uses the same pair, earth and sky (வையத்தின் வானம்), and says the sky is the nearer of the two for one who is clear of doubt. The householder gets there by right living and the knower by certainty, and in both the sky is brought within reach of someone still on earth.

Verse 19 says austerity (தவம்) cannot last without rain. Verse 1036 gives the step in between: if the ploughmen's hands fold, those who say they have left desire have no standing (விட்டேம் என்பார்க்கும் நிலை இல்லை). The renouncer's practice rests on the farmer's food, and the farmer's on the sky.

224 speaks from the giver's side: being asked is painful (இன்னாது இரக்கப்படுதல்) until one sees the asker's glad face. 1052 speaks from the asker's side: asking is a pleasure if what is asked comes without suffering (துன்பம் உறாஅ வரின்). Each verse makes the pain or pleasure of one party depend on how the exchange goes for the other.

730 counts those who cannot voice their learning as equal to those who are not, though they exist. 214 says one who knows what is fitting truly lives and anyone else is placed among the dead (செத்தாருள் வைக்கப்படும்). Both apply the figure of a living person counted as dead or absent to someone who gives nothing to others, wealth in 214 and learning in 730; Parimelazhagar reads 730's இல்லார் as the dead.
