512 says the work should go to one who widens the sources of income (வாரி பெருக்கி) and increases the yield. 478 says that even if the channel of income is narrow (ஆகாறு அளவிட்டிதாயினும்) there is no ruin, as long as the channel of outgo is not wider (போகாறு அகலாக்கடை). 512 values enlarging income, and 478 adds that safety depends on the relation between the two channels and not on the size of the first.

302's first half says anger where it cannot take effect is bad, which Parimelazhagar explains as harm coming back from the stronger party. 895 states that harm at its extreme: those a king of fierce might is angry with (வேந்து செறப்பட்டவர்) will not survive wherever they go. The chapter on not offending the great fills in what 302 leaves as a bare 'bad'.

863 puts fear first among the traits that make a man easy for his enemy. 534 says the fearful have no fortress (அச்சமுடையார்க்கு அரணில்லை); Parimelazhagar explains that defences are of no use to one with fear in his mind. Both say that fear cancels whatever other protection a person has.

842 says that when a person without understanding gives gladly, the cause is nothing other than the receiver's தவம் (பெறுவான் தவம்). 270 says the have-nots are many because those who practise austerity are few. Both explain who gets and who lacks by austerity, and 842 shows the idea used in passing in the second book, as an accepted explanation.

In 1314 'more than anyone' is heard as implying other loves; in 1315 'we will not part in this birth' (இம்மைப் பிறப்பில் பிரியலம்) fills her eyes with tears, because she hears a parting in the next. Parimelazhagar describes the move in 1315: she takes a plain statement as a hinting one. Both verses turn a strong assurance into an offence by what it leaves unsaid.

584 defines the spy as one who examines everyone, beginning with those who do the king's work (வினைசெய்வார்); 514 observes that even people trusted after every test often turn different through the nature of the work (வினைவகையான் வேறாகும்). 514 supplies the reason for watching one's own appointed officers: the testing done before appointment does not settle how they behave afterwards.
Both use 'even by forgetting', 199 for the speech of the clear-sighted and 204 for plotting harm. The first describes an achieved nature, and the second commands what such a nature would be.

368 says there's no suffering for those without desire, the ascetic's freedom from anguish. 1072's base have that freedom, by not knowing what is good. The verse exposes a counterfeit of equanimity: peace of mind can't itself be the measure.

695 tells those who serve a king not to listen in on or press after anything when a secret (மறை) is in progress, and to hear it only when he releases it; 587 makes the ability to hear concealed things (மறைந்தவை கேட்க வற்றாகி) the definition of a spy. The pairing marks a boundary: prying into secrets is a skill the king directs at others, and a fault when his own attendants turn it on him.

1179: when he does not come the eyes do not sleep, and when he comes they do not sleep (வாராக்கால் துஞ்சா வரின் துஞ்சா). 1295: the heart fears not having him and, having him, fears parting (பெறாஅமை அஞ்சும் பெறின் பிரிவு அஞ்சும்). The same two-sided bind is said of the eyes and of the heart, and Parimelazhagar explains 1179 by the fear of parting that 1295 names.

880 states the cost of not breaking the pride of one's enemies (செயிர்ப்பவர் செம்மல் சிதைக்கலாதார்): one cannot be counted as living. 759 names the instrument for that task: wealth, the sharpest steel for cutting the pride of foes (செறுநர் செருக்கறுக்கும் எஃகு). One verse gives the necessity and the other the means.

Verse 73 treats the joining of life and body (என்போடு இயைந்த தொடர்பு) as something fitted to love. Verse 338 says the friendship between body and life (உடம்பொடு உயிரிடை நட்பு) is like a bird flying off and leaving its குடம்பை alone. The pairing sets a limit on 73: the bond that exists for love's sake is, in the chapter on impermanence, one the life will abandon.

1113 praises her as bamboo-shouldered (வேய்த்தோளவட்கு). 906, in the chapter on men ruled by their wives, says those who fear the wife's bamboo-like shoulders (அமையார்தோள் அஞ்சுபவர்) have no standing even if they live like the gods. The same stock epithet of beauty is admired in the Book of Love and named in the Book of Wealth as the thing an unmanned husband fears.

230 says nothing is more bitter than dying, yet even dying is sweet when giving is not possible (ஈதல் இயையாக் கடை). 1070 says the asker's life goes at the word of refusal (சொல்லாடப் போஒம் உயிர்) and asks where the concealer's life hides (யாங்கொளிக்கும் கொல்லோ). 230 gives the giver's view that life without giving is not worth keeping; 1070 puts that standard to the one who can give and refuses, and wonders that his life stays.

1141 says that because gossip has risen the precious life holds on (அலரெழ ஆருயிர் நிற்கும்). 1213 says the woman's life exists because she sees in dreams the one who gives nothing in waking life (காண்டலின் உண்டென் உயிர்). In each a lover's life is kept going by something that only stands in for the beloved: the town's talk in one, a dream in the other.

152 says always to bear with an excess done to one, and that forgetting it is better still (பொறுத்தல் இறப்பினை என்றும் அதனை மறத்தல் அதனினும் நன்று). 487 says the bright do not flare up outwardly at once but, watching for the time, burn within (காலம் பார்த்து உள்வேர்ப்பர்). Both hold back the outward response, and they differ on what happens inside: 152 wants the wrong forgotten, 487 wants the anger kept. The conflict holds if both are read as general advice; 152 belongs to the householder's virtues and Parimelazhagar takes 487 as addressed to kings facing enemies.

Wood is used twice for those without inner quality. The courtesy chapter's man is a tree in 997, and the shameless man here a wooden puppet. The puppet is worse, since it has been shaped to look alive.
In 18, even the gods' worship depends on rain. Here rain answers to a woman who bypasses the gods. Together the two verses invert the expected order of gods, rain and humans.

208 uses a simile of something that cannot fail to happen: ruin stays with the evildoer as his shadow stays at his foot. 307 does the same for anger: the ruin of one who treats anger as a thing of worth is like the hand of one who strikes the ground, which cannot miss ('கை பிழையாதற்று'). Both verses take 'கேடு' as their subject and end on a simile of certainty, one for evil deeds and one for anger.

197 lets the worthy say even what lacks நயன் but holds that they should not say what lacks use (பயனில சொல்லாமை நன்று). 697 tells one who serves a king to say what is wanted and never to say what is without use even if asked (வினையில எஞ்ஞான்றும் கேட்பினும் சொல்லாவிடல்); Parimelazhagar glosses வினையில as matters without benefit. The rule against useless speech is kept as firmly at court as in private ethics, and neither verse lets circumstances excuse it.

706 says the face shows what is strongest in the heart, as crystal shows what is next to it (நெஞ்சம் கடுத்தது காட்டும் முகம்); 277 says there are people red outside and black inside. 277 limits 706: the face may betray a passing feeling to a skilled reader, but a settled outward appearance can be the opposite of the inside.

In 1170 her heart goes to where he is, and she wishes her eyes could follow (உள்ளம்போன்று உள்வழிச் செல்கிற்பின்); in 1264 her heart rises thinking of his return (வரவுள்ளி). Both make the heart the part of her that moves toward him while she stays put; on Manakkudavar's reading of 1264 it even climbs to do the seeing her eyes cannot.

732 asks that ruin be rare (அருங்கேடு) so that the land yields abundantly. 736 goes a step further: the foremost land does not know ruin, and its richness does not shrink even where ruin has come (கெட்ட இடத்தும் வளங்குன்றா). 732 states the ordinary standard and 736 the highest one.

In 1258 the woman says the soft speech (பணிமொழி) of her deceiving lover is the weapon that breaks her womanly reserve (பெண்மை உடைக்கும் படை). In 1228 the herdsman's flute is a weapon that kills (கொல்லும் படை). Both call a gentle sound a படை, one because it draws her to him and the other because it announces the evening without him.

72: the loveless belong wholly to themselves, and the loving belong to others even in their bones (அன்பிலார் எல்லாம் தமக்குரியர்). 1291: his heart is for him (அவர்நெஞ்சு அவர்க்காதல்), so why, heart, are you not for me (நீ எமக்கு ஆகாதது). The woman's complaint is 72's distinction seen from the inside: the one who loves no longer owns her own heart, and the one who does not love keeps his.

1111 opens the chapter by ranking her above the anicham in softness. 1120 closes it by making the anicham and swan's down hurt her feet like the nerunji fruit, a thorn (மாதர் அடிக்கு நெருஞ்சிப் பழம்). The flower moves from being less soft than she is to being painful to her. Parimelazhagar sets the verse in a refusal to take her on a desert elopement.

485 says those who aim at the world wait, unshaken, with their mind on the time (காலம் கருதி இருப்பர் கலங்காது). 672 says to take one's time over what should be done slowly (தூங்குக தூங்கிச் செயற்பால) and not to delay what should be done without delay. Both treat waiting as a decision that fits some tasks, and 672 adds the second half that 485 leaves out.

1011 mentions the other shame, that of women, without describing it. In 1251 a woman in the Book of Love describes it from inside: shame is the bolt (நாணுத்தாழ்) on the door of her restraint, which the axe of desire breaks. This is a speech in character, but it shows what the shame 1011 calls பிற is: a guard on conduct in love, not a recoil from a wrong deed.

417 says those whose wide listening rests on their own close inquiry (இழைத்துணர்ந்து ஈண்டிய கேள்வியவர்) do not speak folly even when they have misunderstood (பிழைத்துணர்ந்தும் பேதைமை சொல்லார்). 199 says those of stainless vision, free of delusion (மருள்தீர்ந்த மாசறு காட்சியவர்), do not say empty things even in forgetfulness (பொச்சாந்தும் சொல்லார்). The two verses have the same shape, a kind of person whose speech stays sound even when the mind lapses, and they credit it to different sources: listening in one, clear vision in the other.

1285 gives the image: the eye does not see the stick that is lining it, and she does not see his blame when she sees him (பழிகாணேன் கண்ட இடத்து). 1286 states the other half that the image implies: when she does not see him she sees nothing but his faults (காணாக்கால் காணேன் தவறல்லவை). Parimelazhagar's gloss on 1285 already supplies this, saying the eye has seen the stick at every other time.

893 states as irony what 861 states as a plain command: offending those with the power to destroy (அடல்வேண்டின் ஆற்றுபவர்) is a way to seek one's own ruin, and 861 says to avoid opposing the stronger (வலியார்க்கு மாறேற்றல் ஓம்புக).

754 says wealth that comes without wrong and with knowledge of the means (தீதின்றி வந்த பொருள்) yields both அறன் and இன்பம். 173 says the small joy got by coveting is refused by those who want the other joy. Together they show the choice in 173 is not between wealth and joy: wealth rightly got delivers the joy that coveting forfeits.

392 makes numbers and letters the eyes of the living. 445 says a king goes about with his counsellors as his eyes (சூழ்வார் கண்ணாக) and so must choose them with care. Both treat sight as something acquired from outside oneself, through learning in one case and through chosen advisers in the other.

782 contrasts friendships that grow and friendships that wane according to the kind of person. 811 says that with people without character, however ardent they look, it is better for the friendship to shrink than to grow (பெருகலிற் குன்றல் இனிது). The waning that 782 observes in bad friendships is in 811 what one should want for them.

790 says friendship looks shabby (புல்லென்னும்) even when friends dress it up in words (புனையினும்) such as 'they are this to us and we are that to them'. 978 says greatness always bows while smallness adorns itself in self-admiration (அணியுமாம் தன்னை வியந்து). In both, the verbal ornament is the sign of the lesser thing: real friendship, like real greatness, does not advertise itself.

201 makes fear of evil deeds the mark of the excellent. 244 says that for one who sustains living beings and practises அருள் there are no deeds his own life need fear ('தன்னுயிர் அஞ்சும் வினை இல்'). The fear 201 commends is aimed at one's own possible deeds, and 244 names the condition under which nothing of that kind remains to be feared.

1307 names the one pain within sulking: the thought of whether union will be delayed or not (புணர்வது நீடுவது அன்றுகொல்). 1329 wishes for that delay, asking that she keep sulking and the night grow long (ஊடுக ... நீடுக). Parimelazhagar gives both to the man, 1307 during a sulk and 1329 after one has ended well, so the delay feared in the moment is desired in retrospect.

877 says not to let softness show before enemies (மேவற்க மென்மை பகைவர் அகத்து); Parimelazhagar takes மென்மை as lack of strength, which enemies watch for. 440 says that if a ruler can enjoy what he loves without that love being known (காதல் அறியாமை), his enemies' designs come to nothing (ஏதில ஏதிலார் நூல்). In both, what an enemy can use is what he is allowed to learn about one's inner state, weakness in one verse and desire in the other.

575 says that without kindly regard the eye is perceived as a wound (புண்ணென்று உணரப்படும்); 257 says flesh would not be eaten if people perceived it as another creature's wound (புண்ணது உணர்வார்). Both use புண் with உணர் to strip something of its usual standing, and both are about compassion: the eye without it is a sore, and food seen with it is a sore.

731 sets unfailing yield and worthy people (தக்கார்) side by side as marks of a land. 239 says land that bears a body without renown (இசையிலா யாக்கை பொறுத்த நிலம்) declines in its blameless rich produce (வண்பயன் குன்றும்). 239 makes a causal claim where 731 only lists: the land's yield depends on the quality of the people it carries.

231 says that apart from living with renown through giving there is no profit for a living being (அது அல்லது ஊதியம் இல்லை உயிர்க்கு). 122 says no gain for a living being is greater than restraint (ஆக்கம் அதனினூஉங்கு இல்லை உயிர்க்கு). Read literally the two exclusive claims cannot both hold; the conflict disappears if each is taken as the emphasis its own chapter gives its subject.

302 says anger is bad where it cannot take effect, and where it can, nothing is worse (செல்லிடத்தும் இல்அதனின் தீய பிற); Parimelazhagar reads the two places as the stronger and the weaker. 861 advises avoiding opposition to the strong and pressing enmity against the weak (மெலியார்மேல் மேக பகை). They conflict if 302 is taken as a rule for everyone; if the anger chapter is addressed to ascetics, as Parimelazhagar holds, and 861 to a king, they are advice for different people.

978 says greatness always bows and smallness adorns itself in admiration of itself (சிறுமை அணியுமாம் தன்னை வியந்து). 1074 says the base man, on seeing those worse than himself, outdoes them and swaggers (மிகப்பட்டுச் செம்மாக்கும்); this follows Parimelazhagar's reading of அகப்பட்டி as those of looser conduct, while Manakkudavar reads the word quite differently. On Parimelazhagar's reading 1074 shows where the self-admiration of 978 finds its material: in comparison with someone lower.

881 says the nature of one's own people is bad if it does harm (தமர்நீரும் இன்னாவாம் இன்னா செயின்). 522 says kin whose affection does not lapse (விருப்பறாச் சுற்றம்) yield many gains that keep branching; Parimelazhagar notes that this wording is chosen to exclude inner enmity. The condition written into 522 is the case 881 describes, so each verse marks the limit of the other.

In 1187 she lay embracing him, shifted a little (புடைபெயர்ந்தேன்), and at once the pallor was thick enough to scoop up. In 1239 the man recalls that a cool breeze cutting between them in the embrace (முயக்கிடைத் தண்வளி போழ) was enough to pale her eyes. Both verses, from the two partners, set the threshold of separation at the smallest physical gap.

165 says envy is enough for the envious: it brings ruin even when enemies fail (ஒன்னார் வழுக்கியும் கேடீன்பது). 448 says a king without people who rebuke him perishes even with no one to ruin him (கெடுப்பார் இலானும் கெடும்). Both describe ruin that needs no outside enemy, once in a private vice and once in a ruler's unguarded state.

813 sets friends who weigh what will come to them (உறுவது சீர்தூக்கும் நட்பு) beside 'those who take what they get' (பெறுவது கொள்வார்), whom Parimelazhagar identifies as courtesans, and thieves. 912 describes those women directly: they weigh the profit and then speak of character (பயன்தூக்கிப் பண்புரைக்கும்). The later chapter spells out the comparison 813 makes in a phrase, with the same verb தூக்கு for the calculating look.

710 says the measuring rod (அளக்குங்கோல்) of those who call themselves subtle is nothing but the eye. 796 says ruin has one benefit: it is a rod that measures one's people to full length (கிளைஞரை நீட்டி அளப்பதோர் கோல்). The book uses the measuring rod twice for gauging other people, the eye taking a present reading of a mind in 710 and adversity testing loyalty over time in 796.

Both use கெழுதகைமை, the privilege of old intimacy. 803 asks what good long friendship is unless such liberties are accepted as if your own. 700 says to take such liberties with a king brings ruin. Friendship and power apply opposite rules to the same bond.

206: one who does not want afflicting things to overpower him ('நோய்ப்பால தன்னை அடல் வேண்டாதான்') should not do evil to others. 320: all pains rest on those who caused pain, so those who want freedom from pain cause none ('நோய் செய்யார் நோயின்மை வேண்டுபவர்'). The claim and its form (நோய், வேண்டு-) are nearly the same, stated once for the householder in the chapter on fearing evil deeds and once among the ascetic virtues.

In 1124 the man says her leaving is death to his life (சாதல் அதற்கன்னள் நீங்கும் இடத்து). In 1151 the reply to his announced journey is that news of his quick return should be told to those who will be alive then (வாழ்வார்க் குரை); Parimelazhagar gives the line to her friend, Manakkudavar to the woman. Each side says that separation is not survivable, he at a brief parting after a meeting and her side when he leaves on a long journey.

142 says that among all who stand outside virtue (அறன்கடை நின்றாருள் எல்லாம்) none is a greater fool than the one who stands at another's door (பிறன்கடை); 150 says that even one who does not keep to virtue and does wrong (அறன்வரையான் அல்ல செயினும்) does well not to desire another's woman. Both verses rank within the class of the non-virtuous, and both put this one offence at the bottom, 142 by naming the worst case and 150 by naming the one abstention still worth having.

863 lists fear and ignorance among the weaknesses that make a man easy prey (அஞ்சும் அறியான்). 869 keeps just those two and states them from the other side: joy does not go far from those who fight if they get enemies who are without understanding and afraid (அறிவிலா அஞ்சும் பகைவர்ப் பெறின்). The chapter moves from describing the weak enemy to stating what the attacker gains from him.

In 1144 the man says his love thrives through gossip (கவ்வையால் கவ்விது காமம்) and without it would lose its nature and go slack. In 1147 the woman says the town's gossip is manure and her mother's words water to 'this sickness' (நீளும் இந்நோய்). Both say gossip feeds love; he calls what grows காமம் and welcomes it, she calls it நோய்.

196 calls the habitual idle talker chaff, a husk with nothing in it. 406 says the unlearned can only be said to exist and are like barren saline land that yields nothing (பயவாக் களரனையர்). Both take a farming image of something that looks like the useful thing and gives no yield, and both turn on பயன், what a person produces.

960 asks for humility toward all (யார்க்கும் பணிவு) from anyone who wants to keep a lineage. 963, in the next chapter, limits when bowing is called for: in abundance one must bow (பெருக்கத்து வேண்டும் பணிதல்), but in reduced circumstances one must stand high (சுருக்கத்து வேண்டும் உயர்வு). The humility of 960 is thus not meant to cover bending under want.

114 says whether people were worthy or not is seen from their எச்சம்; 1004 asks what எச்சம் the unwanted man imagines for himself. Parimelazhagar takes the word as offspring in 114 and as what remains after death, i.e. renown, in 1004, so the pairing shows the same test of a life by what it leaves, applied with two senses of the word.

151 says bearing with those who scorn us is the foremost thing (பொறுத்தல் தலை). 579, in the chapter on kindly regard in the Book of Wealth, says that showing regard and bearing (கண்ணோடிப் பொறுத்தாற்றும் பண்பே தலை) even with those whose nature is to hurt us is the foremost quality. The same ranking, with the same words பொறுத்தல் and தலை, is given for the householder and again for the ruler.

Verse 67 makes it the father's gift that the son sits ahead in the assembly (அவையத்து முந்தி இருப்ப). Verse 715 says the best of good things is the restraint of not speaking first among elders (முதுவருள் முந்து கிளவாச் செறிவு). The shared root முந்து shows the limit: standing first in the assembly is the goal, but being first to speak before one's seniors is what the book warns against.

240 uses the formula வாழ்வாரே வாழ்வார் for those who live without blame. 1033 uses the same formula for those who live by eating what they plough (உழுதுண்டு வாழ்வாரே வாழ்வார்), with all others following and bowing for their food. The phrase 'they alone live' is awarded on two different grounds, a good name in 240 and self-reliance in 1033.

1261 shows the woman's finger worn (தேய்ந்த விரல்) from marking the days since he left (அவர்சென்ற நாளொற்றி); 1269 says that for those pining with the return day in mind (வருநாள்வைத்து ஏங்குபவர்க்கு) one day passes like seven. 1269 gives the felt arithmetic behind 1261's tally: the days she counts are each lived as many.

287 calls stealing a dark knowledge (களவென்னும் காரறி வாண்மை) that is not found in those set on the strength called அளவு; 175 asks what a fine and wide understanding (அஃகி அகன்ற அறிவு) comes to if, coveting, one acts senselessly toward everyone. Both deny that cleverness in the service of taking others' goods counts as real understanding.

429 gives the positive case: those whose understanding guards against what is coming (எதிரதாக் காக்கும் அறிவினார்) meet no affliction that shakes them. 535 gives the negative: one who did not guard beforehand later grieves over his own fault (தன்பிழை பின்னூறு இரங்கி விடும்). Together they show foresight treated as part of understanding and its absence as heedlessness.

In 1128 his presence in her heart is something she protects, to the point of avoiding hot food. In 1205 the same presence is a complaint: he keeps her out of his own heart and yet is not ashamed to come into hers without pause (எம்நெஞ்சத்து ஓவா வரல்). The later verse adds what 1128 leaves out, the question whether the dwelling is mutual.
371 says sloth (மடி) arises from a fate of loss. This chapter treats the same மடி as a thing one can depose at will. The tension is direct, and neither chapter acknowledges the other.

Two reports of what the world does. 752 says everyone despises those with nothing. 841 says the world doesn't count lack of wealth as lack. Both can't be plain observation, so at least one of them is the Kural speaking for how the world ought to judge.

746 says a fort has every needed thing and good men who help at the critical place (இடத்துதவும் நல்லாள்). 1030 says a family with no good man to stand by and prop it (அடுத்தூன்றும் நல்லாள் இலாத குடி) falls when trouble cuts at its foot. The same word நல்லாள் names the person on whom a fort and a family each depend at the moment of danger; goods alone hold up neither.

860 says இகலான் ஆம் இன்னாத எல்லாம்: every painful thing arises from hostility. 303 says to forget anger toward anyone, because the birth of evils comes from it (தீய பிறத்தல் அதனான் வரும்). The Book of Virtue makes anger the source of evils and the Book of Wealth makes hostility the source, with nearly the same construction.

186 warns the teller of others' faults that his own will be told. 980 says greatness covers another's weakness while smallness only tells faults (சிறுமைதான் குற்றமே கூறிவிடும்). 186 gives the consequence of the habit and 980 gives its diagnosis: fault-telling is what smallness does.

563 says a king of cruel sceptre who goes on doing what terrifies will certainly and quickly perish (ஒருவந்தம் ஒல்லைக் கெடும்). 556 says kings endure through just rule (மன்னர்க்கு மன்னுதல் செங்கோன்மை) and without it their lustre does not endure. Both tie how long a king lasts to how he rules; Parimelazhagar takes what endures in 556 to be the king's fame.

551 compares the oppressive king to murderers and finds him worse. 552 compares the king who demands wealth to a man standing with a spear saying 'hand it over' (வேலொடு நின்றான் இடுவென்றது). Together the two opening verses of the chapter set the unjust ruler beside common criminals, first the killer and then the robber.

1041 says nothing hurts like poverty. 657 chooses extreme poverty over tainted wealth. The chapter on poverty doesn't withdraw this, so the choice is made in full knowledge of what the poverty will be.

770 says an army does not exist without leaders. 1030 says a family with no good person to prop it (அடுத்தூன்றும் நல்லாள் இலாத குடி) falls when trouble cuts at its foot. Both make a group's survival depend on a capable person at its head, in the army and in the household.

587 requires the spy to be free of doubt about what he has learned (அறிந்தவை ஐயப்பாடு இல்லதே); 588 tells the king to check even such a report (தந்த பொருளையும்) through another spy. The spy's certainty is a quality of the source and not a warrant for the king, who is to keep doubting until reports agree.

967, on honour, says it is better to be called ruined as one stands than to live by going behind those who are hostile to one (ஒட்டார்பின் சென்று வாழ்தலின்). 680 says the small will bow to the great and take what terms they can. The conflict depends on reading 967's ஒட்டார் as covering a stronger enemy; Parimelazhagar limits it to following scorners for a living, but he also remarks on 680 that bowing is not the wish of those with honour, which is why the verse says 'they will accept' as a report of worldly practice.

1088: his might (பீடு), feared even by enemies in battle, has broken (உடைந்ததே) before her bright forehead alone. 1258: the woman says the soft words of that deceiving thief are the weapon that breaks her womanly firmness (பெண்மை உடைக்கும் படை). Each lover uses the language of war and breaking for the loss of the quality they prized in themselves, his strength and her restraint.

265: austerity is practised here because whatever is wanted is obtained as it is wanted (வேண்டிய வேண்டியாங்கு எய்தலால்). 1105: her shoulders are like each desired thing at the moment of desiring it (வேட்ட பொழுதின் அவையவை போலுமே). Both describe desire met exactly as it arises, promised to the ascetic through தவம் and claimed by the lover in her embrace.

413 makes listeners equal to the oblation-fed (ஆன்றாரோடொப்பர்). 702 says one who knows without doubt what is inside another (அகத்தது உணர்வான்) should be taken as equal to a god (தெய்வத்தோடொப்பக் கொளல்). In both, a human being is ranked with the gods for a faculty of taking in what others carry: their teaching in one, their unspoken thought in the other.

675 says to act after thinking through resources, means, time, deed and place (காலம் ... இடனொடு ... எண்ணிச் செயல்). 687 uses the same terms for speech: consider the time, know the place, think it through and then speak (காலங் கருதி இடனறிந்து எண்ணி உரைப்பான்). The envoy's speech is planned by the same checklist the book gives for any deed.

101 says that for help given without any prior help (செய்யாமல் செய்த உதவி) even earth and heaven are hardly a match (ஆற்றல் அரிது). 211 says obligation wants no return (கைம்மாறு வேண்டா) and asks what the world does for the rain in exchange (என் ஆற்றுங் கொல்லோ). The same verb ஆற்று marks both: one verse looks from the receiver who cannot repay, the other from the giver who does not ask to be repaid.

432 lists 'மாணா உவகை' among a ruler's faults; Parimelazhagar takes it as joy beyond measure. 531 says why such joy is dangerous: the slackness that comes from the elation of great joy (சிறந்த உவகை மகிழ்ச்சியிற் சோர்வு) is worse than excessive anger. 531 supplies the mechanism for the fault 432 only names.

122 tells one to guard restraint as பொருள், wealth, since nothing is a greater gain; 363 says there is no fine wealth (விழுச்செல்வம்) here like not wanting, and nothing equal to it there either. Both verses count an inner holding-back as the real wealth and both use the 'nothing equals it' form, once for the householder's restraint and once for the renouncer's freedom from craving.
270 explains poverty as too little austerity, which is something people could change. 377 says enjoyment is only as the apportioner apportioned. The same fact gets a moral cause and a fatal one.

all_proposals.note: Verse 11 says the world keeps going because the rain stands unfailing (வான்நின்று உலகம் வழங்கி வருதலால்) and so rain should be understood as amrita. Verse 542 opens with the same fact, வானோக்கி வாழும் உலகெல்லாம், and uses it as the measure of how subjects depend on the king's sceptre. The Book of Wealth takes the rain chapter's claim as settled and builds its account of rule on it.

Verse 11 gives rain the name அமிழ்தம் because the world's life continues through it. In 1106 the lover says her shoulders must be made of amrita (அமிழ்தின் இயன்றன தோள்) because his life puts out new shoots at each touch (உயிர் தளிர்ப்ப). Both verses award the word for the same reason, that the thing keeps life going, once for the whole world and once in a lover's speech about himself.

Verse 13 says that if the sky proves false (விண் பொய்ப்பின்), hunger stays and torments the world (உள்நின்று உடற்றும் பசி), sea-girt though it is. Verse 734 defines a land as one that severe hunger (உறுபசி), unending disease and destructive enemies do not reach. Read together, the first mark of a proper country in the Book of Wealth rests on something no ruler supplies, the rain of chapter 2.

Verse 14 says ploughmen will not plough with the plough (ஏரின் உழாஅர் உழவர்) when the yield of the rain-cloud shrinks. Verse 1031 says the world, however it whirls about, goes behind the plough (ஏர்ப் பின்னது உலகம்). The two make a chain: the world follows the plough, and the plough waits on the rain.

Verse 14 says ploughing stops when the rain's bounty declines. Verse 1036 says that if the ploughmen's hands fold (உழவினார் கைம்மடங்கின்), even those who say they have given up desire cannot hold their state. Verse 14 names one cause that would fold those hands, so the failure of rain reaches as far as the renouncer.

Verse 15 says it is rain that ruins (கெடுப்பதூஉம்) and rain again that stands by the ruined and lifts them (எடுப்பதூஉம்); Parimelazhagar explains that it ruins by not falling. In 1102 the lover says that for other diseases the medicine is something else, but she is herself the medicine for the sickness she causes (தன்நோய்க்குத் தானே மருந்து). The pattern of one thing being both the harm and the only remedy appears for rain and the world and, in a lover's speech, for the beloved.

Verse 16 says that unless drops fall from the sky (விசும்பின் துளிவீழின் அல்லால்) not even the tip of green grass can be seen. Verse 557 says that what lack of drops (துளியின்மை) is to the earth, the king's lack of tender regard (அளியின்மை) is to those who live under him. Verse 16 supplies the picture that 557's comparison assumes: without the king's அளி, the people are the bare ground.

Verse 211 asks what the world does for the rain-cloud in return (மாரிமாட்டு என் ஆற்றுங் கொல்லோ உலகு) and makes it the model of duty that wants no repayment. Verse 17 says even the long sea loses its nature if the cloud, having taken from it (தடிந்து, as Parimelazhagar reads it), does not give back. On that reading the cloud is not a pure giver: it returns what it drew from the sea, and the sea suffers if it withholds. Manakkudavar takes தடிந்து as lightning flashing, and on his reading the qualification falls away.

Verse 17 pictures the cloud not giving (எழிலி தான் நல்காதாகி விடின்) and the sea itself shrinking as a result. Verse 1010 says the brief want of the renowned rich has the nature of the rain-cloud gone dry (மாரி வறங்கூர்ந்தனையது). Both use the withholding cloud; 1010 turns it into a figure for a giver's temporary incapacity, with the suggestion that it is as general a loss and as passing.

Verse 18 says that if the sky dries up (வானம் வறக்குமேல்), festival and worship for the gods will not go on here (சிறப்பொடு பூசனை செல்லாது). Verse 560 says that if the guardian does not guard (காவலன் காவான் எனின்), the cows' yield shrinks and those of the six duties forget their book (நூல் மறப்பர்). Both say religious practice has a material precondition that can fail; chapter 2 names the rain and chapter 56 names the king.

Verse 19 says giving and austerity (தானம் தவம் இரண்டும்) will not stay in the world if the sky does not give. Verse 559 says that if the king acts with justice bent (முறைகோடி), the sky will not pour in season (ஒல்லாது வானம் பெயல்). Chapter 2 makes virtue depend on rain; 559 makes the rain depend in turn on a human virtue, the ruler's justice, so the dependence runs both ways.

Verse 19 says austerity (தவம்) cannot last without rain. Verse 1036 gives the step in between: if the ploughmen's hands fold, those who say they have left desire have no standing (விட்டேம் என்பார்க்கும் நிலை இல்லை). The renouncer's practice rests on the farmer's food, and the farmer's on the sky.

Verse 20 says no one's world can do without water (நீர்இன்று அமையாது உலகு), and that ஒழுக்கு cannot exist without the sky. Parimelazhagar takes ஒழுக்கு as the water's unbroken flow; Pope's verse rendering and Kalaignar take it as ordered conduct. Verse 542 states the first half as a given (வானோக்கி வாழும் உலகெல்லாம்) and sets the people's dependence on the sceptre beside it. On either reading of ஒழுக்கு, 542 treats the dependence 20 argues for as the standard case of something one cannot live without.

Verse 20 ends the chapter by saying nothing in the world, for anyone, holds without the sky. Verse 55 says that for the wife who rises worshipping her husband, it rains when she says 'rain' (பெய்யெனப் பெய்யும் மழை). Three chapters after rain is made the condition of everything, the rain is said to answer to one person's steadfastness.

Verse 21 says the settled view of the texts (பனுவல் துணிவு) sets the greatness of those who have renounced within their discipline (ஒழுக்கத்து நீத்தார் பெருமை) highest among excellent things. Verse 48 says the household life that keeps others on their path and does not slip from virtue has more endurance than those who do penance (நோற்பாரின் நோன்மை உடைத்து). If 48 is read as ranking the householder above the ascetic, as its plain wording allows, the two chapters give the first place to different lives; if 48 is read as praising only the householder's endurance, they do not collide.

Verse 21 rests its claim on பனுவல் துணிவு, the settled conclusion of the texts. Verse 533 uses the same appeal: that the heedless have no fame is the conclusion of authors of every school (எப்பால் நூலோர்க்கும் துணிவு). These are two places where the Kural, which usually argues from observation, cites the agreement of the books as its ground.

Verse 22 says that to state the measure of the greatness of renouncers (துறந்தார்) is like counting the dead of the world (இறந்தாரை எண்ணிக்கொண்டற்று). Verse 310 rhymes the same two words: those who exceed in anger (இறந்தார்) are like the dead, and those who have renounced anger are equal to renouncers (துறந்தார் துணை). In 22 the dead supply only a number too large to count; in 310 the same pairing sets renouncers and the dead as opposite ends, and extends the renouncer's standing to anyone who gives up anger.

Verse 23 says the greatness of those who have discerned the two (இருமை வகைதெரிந்து) and taken on அறம் here stands highest in the world; Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar read the two as birth and release and the அறம் as renunciation. Verse 49 says that what is called அறம் is household life (அறன் எனப்பட்டதே இல்வாழ்க்கை). On the commentators' reading of 23 the two verses attach the word அறம், and the highest standing, to different lives. Kalaignar reads 23 as choosing good over bad in general, and on that reading there is no conflict.

Verse 23, as Parimelazhagar reads it, praises above all those who take up renunciation in this birth after weighing birth against release. Verse 46 asks what one who conducts household life in the way of virtue would gain by going off on the outside path (புறத்தாற்றில் போஒய்ப் பெறுவது எவன்). If the outside path is the ascetic's, as Pope takes it, 46 denies that the step 23 praises adds anything for a good householder.

Verse 24 says one who guards the five with the goad of firmness (உரனென்னும் தோட்டியான் ஓரைந்தும் காப்பான்) is a seed for the best of grounds; the goad implies the senses are elephants, as Parimelazhagar notes. Verse 126 says that drawing in the five like a tortoise in one birth (ஆமைபோல் ஐந்தடக்கல்) protects through seven. The same claim is made in the renouncer's chapter and in the householder's chapter on restraint, with different pictures of the senses: a strong animal to be driven, and limbs to be pulled in.

Verse 24 calls the one who guards the five senses a seed (வித்து) for the ground called வரன், which Parimelazhagar takes as release. Verse 361 calls craving the seed (வித்து) that bears unceasing birth for all beings. The book uses the seed for both outcomes: restraint of the senses is sown toward release, and craving is what sprouts as rebirth.

Verse 25 says Indra, king of those in the wide sky, is witness enough (இந்திரனே சாலுங் கரி) to the power of one who has quenched the five. Verse 899 says that if those of exalted vows flare up, even the வேந்தன் breaks midway and loses his kingship; Parimelazhagar reads the வேந்தன் there as Indra. On his reading 899 states outright the event that 25 only points to, a king of gods brought down by an ascetic's power.

Verse 25 speaks of the power of ஐந்தவித்தான், one who has quenched the five. Verse 6 uses the same phrase for the Lord (பொறிவாயில் ஐந்தவித்தான்) whose path of conduct gives long life to those who keep it. The renouncer of chapter 3 is described in the words chapter 1 uses for the one whose feet are to be reached.

Verse 25 offers Indra as its witness, using the word கரி. Verse 245 says those who hold to அருள் have no distress, and the wide earth where the wind moves is the witness (மல்லன்மா ஞாலங் கரி). In both verses a claim about an inner quality is supported by pointing to a single witness on a cosmic scale, the king of heaven for the ascetic's power and the whole earth for compassion.

Verse 26 says those who do what is hard to do (செயற்கரிய செய்வார்) are great and those who cannot are small. Verse 975 says those who have greatness will carry out in the proper way deeds that are hard (அருமை உடைய செயல்). Chapter 3 says it of renouncers, and Parimelazhagar takes the hard things to be restraint of the senses; chapter 98 says it of greatness in worldly life. The test of greatness is the same in both books.

Verse 26 divides people by whether they can do what is hard to do. Verse 664 says saying is easy for anyone and doing as one has said is hard (அரியவாம் சொல்லிய வண்ணம் செயல்). The chapter on firmness in action applies the renouncer's standard to statecraft and names what is hard in a deed: carrying it out as announced.

Verse 27 says the world lies within the one who discerns the kinds of the five (ஐந்தின் வகைதெரிவான் கட்டே உலகு): taste, light, touch, sound and smell. Verse 354 says that even having gained the fivefold awareness (ஐயுணர்வு எய்தியக் கண்ணும்) is of no benefit to those without perception of the real (மெய்யுணர்வு). Verse 354 sets a limit on 27: command of the five is not the end, and without true perception it yields nothing.

Verse 27 lists the five sense objects (சுவை ஒளி ஊறு ஓசை நாற்றம்) and says the world belongs to the one who discerns them. In 1101 the lover lists the same five as acts, seeing, hearing, tasting, smelling and touching (கண்டுகேட்டு உண்டுயிர்த்து உற்றறியும் ஐம்புலனும்), and says they are all found in this one woman (ஒண்தொடி கண்ணே உள). The same inventory serves the renouncer as a field to be understood and the lover as a field of enjoyment; the second is a speech in the moment and not a counter-teaching.

Verse 28 says the greatness of people whose word is full (நிறைமொழி மாந்தர்) is shown on earth by their மறைமொழி; Parimelazhagar explains நிறைமொழி as speech that produces its result whether spoken in grace or in anger. Verse 55 says that when the wife who worships her husband says 'rain', it rains (பெய்யெனப் பெய்யும் மழை). Both give a person's word power over the world as the proof of their standing, for the renouncer through austerity and for the wife through steadfastness at home.

Verse 29 speaks of the anger (வெகுளி) of those who stand on the hill of good qualities; on Parimelazhagar's reading they are sages whose anger, though it lasts a moment, cannot be warded off by its target. Verse 310 says those who have renounced anger are the equals of renouncers (சினத்தைத் துறந்தார் துறந்தார் துணை), which makes freedom from anger the renouncer's mark. On Parimelazhagar's reading the book's model renouncer still gets angry, and dangerously. Kalaignar reads 29 as saying their anger does not stay even a moment, and on that reading the two verses agree.

Verse 29 puts the virtuous on a hill (குணமென்னும் குன்றேறி நின்றார்) and warns of their anger. Verse 898 calls such people hill-like (குன்றன்னார்) and says that if they think ill of someone (Parimelazhagar's reading of குன்ற மதிப்பின்), those who seemed fixed on the earth perish with their line. The Book of Wealth returns to the same figure and turns chapter 3's remark into advice for kings not to offend them.

Verse 30 says those called அந்தணர் are the virtuous (அறவோர்), because they live clothed in cool kindness toward every living being (எவ்வுயிர்க்கும் செந்தண்மை பூண்டொழுகலான்). Verse 134 says a பார்ப்பான் can relearn the Veda he forgot, but his birth is ruined when conduct declines (பிறப்பொழுக்கங் குன்றக் கெடும்). Both tie the title to how one lives: 30 by defining it through kindness, 134 by saying the birth is lost with conduct.

Verse 30 defines அந்தணர் by conduct, as those who practise kindness to all beings; Parimelazhagar applies it to renouncers. Verse 543 speaks of the book of the அந்தணர் (அந்தணர் நூல்), which Parimelazhagar takes as the Veda, and says the king's sceptre stands as the ground of it and of virtue. The word is used in 543 in its ordinary sense for a group with a scripture, so a reader should not carry 30's definition into every use of the word in the book.

41 calls the householder the துணை who stands on the good path (நல்லாற்றின் நின்ற) for 'the three' (இயல்புடைய மூவர்), whom Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar take as the other three orders of life (Kalaignar instead reads parents, spouse and children). 1036 says that if the ploughmen's hands fold (கைம்மடங்கின்), even those who say 'we have let go of desire' (விட்டேம் என்பார்) have no standing (நிலை). On the older commentators' reading both verses make the renouncer's state depend on someone who stays in the world and produces: the householder in Book 1, the farmer in Book 2.

41 makes the householder the support of the three, read by Parimelazhagar as the other orders, ascetics included. 263 asks, with கொல், whether 'the others' (மற்றையவர்கள்) have forgotten தவம் because they want to provide for the renounced (துறந்தார்க்குத் துப்புரவு வேண்டி); Parimelazhagar glosses 'the others' as householders. The Thavam chapter thus looks at the same arrangement from the ascetic side: the householder's support of renouncers is given as the reason he does no austerity himself.

41 names the householder the support of 'the three of proper nature' (இயல்புடைய மூவர்); 42 repeats the frame இல்வாழ்வான் என்பான் துணை and adds three more: துறந்தார், துவ்வாதவர், இறந்தார். Parimelazhagar takes these as the abandoned, the poor and those who died with no one of their own, so the pair moves from the recognised orders to people with no claim on anyone. Pope and Kalaignar read துறந்தார் as ascetics, which would make 42 overlap 41 rather than extend it.

42 lists துவ்வாதவர், those who have nothing to eat or enjoy, among the people the householder supports. 226 says that ending the destroying hunger of those without means (அற்றார் அழிபசி தீர்த்தல்) is the place where a person who has gained wealth stores it (பொருள் வைப்புழி). 226 turns the duty stated in 42 into a claim about what wealth is for.

43 lists five quarters to be tended (ஐம்புலத்தாறு ஓம்பல்): ancestors, gods, guests (விருந்து), kin and oneself, and calls this the chief thing (தலை). 81 says that all of staying, guarding one's goods and living at home (இருந்தோம்பி இல்வாழ்வதெல்லாம்) is for the sake of tending guests and doing them good (விருந்தோம்பி வேளாண்மை செய்தற் பொருட்டு). One of the five items of 43 is taken up, with the same verb ஓம்பு, and made the purpose of the whole household.

43 puts kin (ஒக்கல்) among the five the householder must tend. 524, in the chapters on kingship, says that living so as to be surrounded by one's kin (சுற்றத்தால் சுற்றப்பட ஒழுகல்) is the fruit of having gained wealth. The household duty of Book 1 reappears in Book 2 as the point of a ruler's prosperity.

44 says a life that fears blame and has பாத்தூண், food shared out, never sees its line fail (வழியெஞ்சல் எஞ்ஞான்றும் இல்). 227 uses the same compound: the one habituated to shared food (பாத்தூண் மரீஇயவனை) is hardly touched by the disease called hunger. Both attach a protective result to the same practice, one for the descendants and one for the sharer himself.

44 promises an unfailing line (வழி) to the life that fears blame (பழியஞ்சி) and shares its food; Parimelazhagar reads the fear of blame as applying to how the wealth is earned. 112 says the prosperity of the person of rectitude (செப்பம் உடையவன் ஆக்கம்) does not decay and is a security to those who come after (எச்சத்திற்கு ஏமாப்பு). In both, wealth held without wrong is what lasts into the next generation.

44 names பாத்தூண், shared food, as the mark of the householder's life. In 1107 the lover says the embrace of the woman is like staying in one's own home and eating one's own after sharing it (தம்மில் இருந்து தமது பாத்து உண்டற்று). The Book of Love takes the householder's sharing meal as a standard of pleasure, where 44 gives it as a duty with a reward; the comparison is the speaker's, not a teaching.

45 says that if household life has love and virtue (அன்பும் அறனும்), that is its character and its fruit (பண்பும் பயனும்). 75 says the distinction reached by those who have had joy in this world is, 'they say', the result of a way of life settled in love (அன்புற்று அமர்ந்த வழக்கு); Parimelazhagar takes this as household life lived with love, rewarded with heaven. 75 spells out the பயன் that 45 only names.

46 asks what one who conducts household life in the way of virtue would gain by going to the outside way (புறத்தாற்றில் போஒய்ப் பெறுவது எவன்); Parimelazhagar and Pope take the outside way as renunciation. 348 says those who have renounced completely (தீரத் துறந்தார்) have reached the head, and the rest (மற்றையவர்) are confused and caught in the net. If புறத்தாறு is renunciation and the question in 46 is rhetorical, 46 denies the gain that 348 reserves for renouncers alone; if புறத்தாறு means only ways outside virtue, the conflict disappears.

47 says the one who lives household life according to its nature is first among all who strive (முயல்வாருள் எல்லாம் தலை). 266 says those who do தவம் are doing their own work and the rest (மற்றல்லார்), caught in desire, do what is futile (அவஞ்செய்வார்). On Parimelazhagar's reading of 47, where the strivers are those working to leave the senses, the householder is ranked above ascetics, while 266 counts everyone but the ascetic as wasting effort. Manakkudavar reads முயல்வார் as those who strive for wealth, and on that reading the two do not collide.

48 says a household life that keeps others on their path (ஆற்றின் ஒழுக்கி) and does not slip from virtue has more endurance than those who do penance (நோற்பாரின் நோன்மை உடைத்து). 225 says the strength of the strong is enduring hunger, and that comes behind the strength of those who remove that hunger (மாற்றுவார் ஆற்றலின் பின்). Both rank the one who provides above the one who abstains, and both do it by granting the ascetic's own virtue, endurance, and awarding more of it to the provider.

48 gives household life more நோன்மை than those who do penance (நோற்பார்). 160 says those who fast as penance (உண்ணாது நோற்பார்) are great, but behind those who bear the harsh words others speak (இன்னாச்சொல் நோற்பாரின் பின்), using the same verb நோல் for both. The same comparison is made in the chapter on forbearance: an everyday virtue practised among people is placed above formal austerity.

49 says what is called virtue is household life, and 'that too' (அஃதும்) is good if it is not something others blame (பிறன் பழிப்பது இல்லாயின்). Parimelazhagar takes அஃதும் as renunciation and the blame as false conduct in ascetics (Manakkudavar keeps it on household life). 280 says neither shaving nor growing the hair is needed if one drops what the world has blamed (உலகம் பழித்தது ஒழித்து விடின்). On Parimelazhagar's reading the chapter on false ascetics works out the condition 49 states in passing: the renouncer's standing rests on being free of blame.

44 opens with பழியஞ்சி: the household life that fears blame and shares its food keeps its line. 49 calls household life virtue itself, then adds that it is good if there is nothing others blame (பிறன் பழிப்பது இல்லாயின்). On Manakkudavar's reading, where அஃதும் still refers to household life, 49 makes absence of blame the condition on the chapter's whole praise of the householder, which 44 had already built into its description.

50 says one who lives on earth as one should (வாழ்வாங்கு வாழ்பவன்) will be placed among the gods who dwell in the sky (தெய்வத்துள் வைக்கப்படும்). 388 says the king who does justice and protects will be set apart as இறை for the people (இறையென்று வைக்கப்படும்). The same passive, வைக்கப்படும், is used for both: a human being who fully does the duty of his station, householder or ruler, is ranked as divine by others. This edition prints 50's third word corruptly (வான்உநற்யும் for வானுறையும்).

50 places the person who lives rightly on earth (வையத்துள்) among the gods of the sky. 413 says those who have listening as food for the ear are, though on earth (நிலத்து), equal to the gods who are fed by oblations. Both verses set 'on earth' against the gods and say a human excellence closes the gap, right living in one case and learning by listening in the other.

51 defines the companion of life as the wife who has the qualities the home needs and is வளத்தக்காள், fitted to the means of the man who took her; Parimelazhagar glosses this as spending in line with his income. 478 says that even if the channel of income is narrow there is no ruin, so long as the channel of outgo is not wider (போகாறு அகலாக் கடை). The rule 478 gives a king for his treasury is the one 51 builds into the definition of a good wife.

52 says that if excellence of the home (மனைமாட்சி) is not in the wife, the life is nothing, whatever excellence it has (எனைமாட்சித் தாயினும் இல்). 750 says that whatever excellence a fort has (எனைமாட்சித் தாகியக் கண்ணும்), it is as nothing in those who lack excellence in action (வினைமாட்சி இல்லார்கண் இல்லது). The two share the phrase and the argument: the outward assets of a home or a fortress count for nothing without the quality of the person inside who runs it.

53 asks what is lacking if the wife has worth (இல்லதென் இல்லவள் மாண்பானால்) and what is there if she does not (உள்ளதென் ... மாணாக் கடை). 430 says those with understanding have everything, and those without it have nothing whatever they have (என்னுடையரேனும் இலர்). The same two-sided formula, one possession that makes all others count or not count, is applied to a wife's character in the home and to understanding in a ruler.

54 asks what is greater than a woman, if she has the firmness called கற்பு (கற்பென்னும் திண்மை உண்டாகப் பெறின்). 988 says poverty is no disgrace to a person, if he has the firmness called சால்பு (சால்பென்னும் திண்மை உண்டாகப் பெறின்). The second line is the same but for one word, so the book describes a woman's fidelity and a worthy person's character with the same term, திண்மை, a firmness that outweighs outward circumstances.

55 says that when the wife who worships no god but rises worshipping her husband says 'rain', it rains (பெய்யெனப் பெய்யும் மழை). 545 says rain and harvest together (பெயலும் விளையுளும் தொக்கு) belong to the land of the king who wields the sceptre as he should. In both, rain answers to a person keeping faith with a role, the wife in the house and the king over the land; 559 gives the reverse case, where the sky withholds rain from an unjust king.

55 praises a wife who does not worship a god (தெய்வம் தொழாஅள்) and worships her husband, and credits her with power over the rain. 2 asks what use learning is if the learned do not worship the feet of the one of pure knowledge (நற்றாள் தொழாஅர் எனின்), with the same verb in the same negative form. Read literally, 55 commends for the wife the not-worshipping that the first chapter treats as making a person's attainments useless. Parimelazhagar removes the conflict by reading 'other gods' (பிற தெய்வம்) and making the husband her god; the tension depends on taking தெய்வம் தொழாஅள் at face value.

56 defines the woman as one who guards herself (தற்காத்து), cares for her husband and guards the good name (சொற்காத்து) without flagging. 57 asks what guarding by confinement (சிறைகாக்கும் காப்பு) can do, and says the guard women keep by their own நிறை is the chief one. 57 explains why 56 makes her the subject of the verb 'guard': the guarding that counts cannot be done by anyone else.

56 includes guarding the well-founded word, the couple's good name (தகைசான்ற சொற்காத்து), in its definition of the wife. 59 says those whose home does not seek renown (புகழ்புரிந்த இல் இலோர்க்கு) cannot walk with a proud gait before those who deride them. Parimelazhagar connects them directly, saying 59 states the fault that follows when that good name is not kept: the husband's standing in public depends on it.

57 says guarding women by confinement achieves nothing and the guard kept by their own steadfastness (நிறைகாக்கும் காப்பு) is chief. 974 says greatness, like single-minded women (ஒருமை மகளிரே போல), exists only if one keeps hold of oneself (தன்னைத்தான் கொண்டொழுகின்). The self-guarding wife of 57 becomes, in Book 2, the model for how anyone keeps greatness: it cannot be conferred or enforced from outside.

57 treats நிறை as a guard that women themselves keep and sets it above any confinement. In 1251 the woman in love says the axe of desire breaks the door called நிறை, bolted with the bar of shame (நிறையென்னும் நாணுத்தாழ் வீழ்த்த கதவு). Both picture நிறை as a barrier held from the inside; the Book of Love speaker reports it giving way under desire, which is her experience in the moment and not a retraction of 57.

58 says women who 'obtain the one who obtained them' (பெற்றாற் பெறின்) gain great distinction in the world where the gods live (புத்தேளிர் வாழும் உலகு); Parimelazhagar supplies 'honour' and reads it as wives who revere their husbands. 50 says the man who lives on earth as he should is placed among the gods of the sky. The two adjacent chapters end on the same reward, one for the householder and one for the wife, each for fulfilling the household role.

59 says those whose home does not seek renown (புகழ்புரிந்த இல்) have no proud gait before those who deride them (இகழ்வார்முன்). 237 asks why those who cannot live with renown (புகழ்பட வாழாதார்) resent those who deride them (இகழ்வாரை நோவது எவன்) and not themselves. Both set புகழ் against இகழ்வார்: 59 says that without renown one has no answer to scorners, and 237 adds that the scorn is then one's own doing.

59 says that without a home that seeks renown there is no walking with a bull's (Parimelazhagar: lion's) proud gait, ஏறுபோல் பீடு நடை. 1014 says shame is an ornament to the worthy, and without it their பீடு நடை is a disease. The proud walk appears twice as something that must be earned by an inner or domestic quality, the household's good name in one verse and a sense of shame in the other.

60 says the excellence of the home is called its blessing (மங்கலம்) and the gaining of good children (நன்மக்கட் பேறு) its fine ornament. 61, opening the next chapter, says that of all things to be gained we know none like the gaining of children who know what should be known (அறிவறிந்த மக்கட்பேறு). 61 picks up the word மக்கட்பேறு from 60 and specifies what makes the children 'good': their understanding.

Verse 60 calls good children (நன்மக்கட் பேறு) the ornament of a home's excellence. Verse 61 raises the same பேறு to the top of everything one can gain and specifies the children as அறிவறிந்த, those who know what should be known. Read together, the chapter on children opens by taking up the last word of the chapter on the wife and narrowing 'good' to 'knowing'.

Verse 61 says that among all things gained (பெறுமவற்றுள்) 'we' know of nothing to set beside knowing children. Verse 162 says that among excellent gains (விழுப்பேற்றின்) nothing equals (அஃதொப்பது இல்லை) being free of envy. The two top rankings conflict only if each superlative is read literally as a ranking across all gains; read as each chapter's idiom of praise they do not.

Both verses rank their subject first by the author's own witness in the first person plural: 61 has யாமறிவது இல்லை ('we know of none') for knowing children, 300 has யாமெய்யாக் கண்டவற்றுள் இல்லை ('among what we have seen as true there is none') for truthfulness. The pairing shows the same rare device, the poet's 'we', used to vouch for a household good and for a virtue of speech.

Verse 62 says evils will not touch a person in all seven births (எழுபிறப்பும் தீயவை தீண்டா) if they get children of character who bring no blame. Verse 398 says the learning gained in one birth is a protection in seven (எழுமையும் ஏமாப்புடைத்து). Both name a good of this life whose protection outlasts it by seven births: in one case one's children, in the other one's own learning.

Verse 62 has blameless children keep evil away through seven births (எழுபிறப்பும்). Verse 835 has the fool, in one birth's doing (ஒருமைச் செயல்), make the mire (அளறு) he sinks in for seven (எழுமையும்). The same seven-birth reckoning is applied in the opposite direction, once to a safeguard and once to a ruin made by oneself.

Verse 44 says that if a household life fears blame (பழியஞ்சி) and shares its food, its line (வழி) never fails. Verse 62 says that if one gets children in whom blame does not grow (பழிபிறங்கா), no evil touches one for seven births. In 44 the parent's freedom from blame secures the descendants; in 62 the descendants' freedom from blame secures the parent.

Verse 63 says people call their children their wealth (தம்பொருள் என்ப தம் மக்கள்), and ties that wealth to deeds (வினையான் வரும்). Verse 114 says whether people are worthy or not is seen from their எச்சம், what they leave behind, which Parimelazhagar takes as their offspring and Kalaignar as the name they leave. On Parimelazhagar's reading the pair makes children both a person's property and the evidence by which that person is judged.

Verse 63 reports the saying that one's children are one's wealth (தம்பொருள்). Verse 400 says learning is the imperishable wealth (கேடில் விழுச்செல்வம்) and that other things are not wealth (மாடல்ல). Both move the word for property from goods to something else, but 400 denies the title to everything other than learning, while 63 only reports what people say.

Verse 64 says the gruel (கூழ்) stirred by one's children's small hands is far sweeter than amrita. Verse 1065 says that though it is gruel thin as clear water (தெண்ணீர் அடுபுற்கை), nothing is sweeter than eating what one's own effort brought (தாள் தந்தது). In both the plainest food is the sweetest because of whose hands stand behind it, the child's in one and one's own labour in the other.

Verse 64 ranks gruel handled by one's children above amrita (அமிழ்தினும் ஆற்ற இனிதே). Verse 82 says that even the medicine of deathlessness (சாவா மருந்து) is not to be wanted if eaten alone while a guest stays outside. Both use the divine food as the measure and then place a household relation above it, the child at the meal in 64 and the guest at the door in 82.

Verse 64 sets a child's messy gruel above amrita. In 1103 the lover asks whether the world of the lotus-eyed one (தாமரைக் கண்ணான் உலகு) can be sweeter (இனிதுகொல்) than sleeping on the soft arms of the one he loves; Parimelazhagar has him say this to a companion who reproved him. The same move, a heavenly standard of sweetness outdone by an intimate bodily one, appears in the parent's voice in Book 1 and in a lover's speech in Book 3.

Verse 65 names two sense pleasures a child gives: touching the child's body is joy to the body (உடற்கின்பம்) and hearing its words is joy to the ear (இன்பம் செவிக்கு). In 1101 the lover says the five senses, seeing, hearing, tasting, smelling and touching (கண்டுகேட்டு உண்டுயிர்த்து உற்றறியும்), all have their objects in one woman. Both list pleasures sense by sense and locate them in a single loved person, a child in one and a lover in the other.

Verse 66 says only those who have not heard their own children's prattle call the flute (குழல்) and the lute sweet. In 1228 the woman left alone says the herdsman's flute (ஆயன் குழல்) is now a messenger of the burning evening and a weapon that kills; Parimelazhagar notes that it had been sweet to her before. In both the flute stands for accepted sweetness, and in both that sweetness is made to depend on the hearer's situation.

Verse 67 states what a father does for a son (தந்தை மகற்காற்றும் நன்றி): he makes him sit at the front of the assembly. Verse 70 states the son's help in return (மகன் தந்தைக்கு ஆற்றும் உதவி): that people ask what penance his father did to get him. The two are built as a matching pair, and the son's return is paid in public speech, in the same assembly where the father placed him.

Verse 67 makes it the father's gift that the son sits ahead in the assembly (அவையத்து முந்தி இருப்ப). Verse 715 says the best of good things is the restraint of not speaking first among elders (முதுவருள் முந்து கிளவாச் செறிவு). The shared root முந்து shows the limit: standing first in the assembly is the goal, but being first to speak before one's seniors is what the book warns against.

Verse 67 says a father's good to his son is to make him sit foremost in the assembly; Parimelazhagar takes this as making him learned beyond the learned there. Verse 722 says those called learned among the learned (கற்றாருள் கற்றார்) are those who can make what they learned go home before the learned. 722 supplies what the front seat of 67 requires in practice: learning that can be delivered in front of that assembly.

Verse 68 says one's children's understanding (அறிவுடைமை) is sweet to all beings on the great earth (மன்னுயிர்க்கெல்லாம் இனிது); Parimelazhagar reads தம்மின் as 'more than to oneself', while Kalaignar and Subramuniyaswami take it as children who surpass their parents. Verse 399 says the learned love learning more on seeing that what delights them delights the world (தாமின்புறுவது உலகின்புறக் கண்டு). Both treat knowledge as a pleasure that is not private: the parent's pride in 68 and the scholar's delight in 399 are each measured against the world's share in it.

Verse 69 says a mother rejoices more than at the hour of birth when she hears her son called சான்றோன். Verse 923 says drunken joy is painful even before the mother who bore one (ஈன்றாள் முகத்தேயும் இன்னாது), and asks what it must then be before the சான்றோர். Both verses set the mother beside the worthy as the two audiences of a son's conduct; 923 shows that her gladness in 69 is not unconditional, though Parimelazhagar calls her one who is pleased whatever he does.

Verse 69 has the mother's joy grow when she hears others call her son worthy (சான்றோன் எனக் கேட்ட தாய்). Verse 1047 says one in poverty unconnected with virtue (அறஞ்சாரா நல்குரவு) is looked on as a stranger even by the mother who bore him (ஈன்ற தாயானும் பிறன்போல நோக்கப்படும்). In both the mother's regard follows the son's standing, rising with his name in 69 and withdrawn in 1047.

Verse 69 says what gladdens a mother most is hearing her son called சான்றோன். Verse 656 says that even if one must see one's mother hungry (ஈன்றாள் பசி காண்பான் ஆயினும்), one should not do the deed the சான்றோர் condemn. Read with 69, the rule of 656 does not set the mother against the worthy: the judgment of the worthy that 656 obeys is the judgment the mother of 69 most wants to hear.

Verse 70 defines the son's help to his father as the saying 'what penance did this one's father do?' (இவன் தந்தை என்நோற்றான் கொல்). Verse 67 defines the father's good to the son as making him sit foremost in the assembly. The pair closes a circle: the father's gift is the son's standing, and the son's gift is the credit that standing reflects back on the father.

Verse 70 has onlookers explain a good son by asking what the father did as penance (என்நோற்றான்). Verse 265 says தவம் is striven for here because whatever is wanted is obtained as wanted (வேண்டிய வேண்டியாங்கு எய்தலால்). The onlookers' question in 70 assumes the doctrine 265 states, and it applies that doctrine to a son.

Verse 71 asks whether there is any bolt that shuts love in (அன்பிற்கும் உண்டோ அடைக்குந்தாழ்), since the tears of the loving give it away. In 1251 the woman says the axe of desire breaks the door of restraint that is fastened with the bolt of shame (நாணுத்தாழ் வீழ்த்த கதவு). The same figure of a bolt that cannot hold is used for household affection (அன்பு) in Book 1 and for a lover's desire (காமம்) in Book 3.

Verse 71 says the small tears (புன்கணீர்) of the loving proclaim their love; Parimelazhagar specifies tears shed at the suffering of those they love. Verse 828 says a weapon lies hidden in an enemy's worshipping hands, and that the tears an enemy has wept are the same (ஒன்னார் அழுத கண்ணீரும் அனைத்து). Tears are evidence of love in 71 only when they come from the loving; 828 warns that tears as such prove nothing.

Verse 71 says tears raise a public noise (பூசல் தரும்) about the love inside. In 1180 the woman says it is not hard for the town to get at the secret (மறை) of those like her whose eyes are beaten drums (அறைபறை கண்ணார்). In both the eyes make public what the heart holds, and both describe this as sound: a clamour in 71, a drum in 1180.

Verse 72 says the loveless belong to themselves in everything (எல்லாம் தமக்குரியர்) while the loving belong to others (பிறர்க்கு) even in their bones. Verse 1009 says wealth piled up by putting love aside (அன்பொரீஇ), denying oneself and ignoring virtue will be taken by others (கொள்வார் பிறர்). 1009 gives the outcome of the stance in 72: what the loveless keep for themselves ends with பிறர் anyway.

Verse 72 says those who have love belong to others even in their bones (என்பும் உரியர் பிறர்க்கு). Verse 220 says that if ruin comes through ஒப்புரவு, that ruin is worth buying even by selling oneself (விற்றுக்கோள் தக்கது). Both carry giving past one's goods to one's own person, 72 as a description of love and 220 as the price of duty to the community.

Verse 73 says the tie of the life with the body (ஆருயிர்க்கு என்போடு இயைந்த தொடர்பு) is, they say, a matter of being joined with love (அன்போடு இயைந்த வழக்கு); Parimelazhagar takes embodiment as the result of a course meant for joining with love. In 1122 the lover says the bond between him and the woman is what the bond between body and life is (உடம்பொடு உயிரிடை என்ன). 73 explains the union of body and life by love, and the lover in 1122 measures his love by that union.

Verse 73 treats the joining of life and body (என்போடு இயைந்த தொடர்பு) as something fitted to love. Verse 338 says the friendship between body and life (உடம்பொடு உயிரிடை நட்பு) is like a bird flying off and leaving its குடம்பை alone. The pairing sets a limit on 73: the bond that exists for love's sake is, in the chapter on impermanence, one the life will abandon.

Verse 73 says the life's connection with the bone (என்போடு) goes with love. Verse 80 says the seat of life (உயிர்நிலை) follows love, and that for those without it the body is bone wrapped in skin (என்புதோல் போர்த்த உடம்பு). The chapter's last verse gives the negative of 73: take away the love and what remains of the union is the bone alone.

Verse 74 says love gives birth (ஈனும்) to eagerness, and that gives birth to friendship, an unsought distinction (நாடாச் சிறப்பு). Verse 757 calls அருள் the child born of love (அன்பீன் குழவி), raised by the foster-mother wealth. Both use the figure of birth for what comes out of அன்பு, and together they give love two offspring, friendship in the home and grace toward all.

Verse 74 derives friendship (நண்பு) from love by way of eagerness (ஆர்வம்) and calls it a distinction that is not sought (நாடா). Verse 785 says meeting and long acquaintance are not needed, because feeling itself (உணர்ச்சிதான்) gives the claim of friendship. The friendship chapter of Book 2 keeps the account given in Book 1: friendship comes from an inner disposition and not from arrangement or contact.

Verse 45 says that if household life has love and virtue (அன்பும் அறனும்), that is its character and its fruit (பண்பும் பயனும்). Verse 75 says the distinction reached by those who have had joy in the world (வையகத்து இன்புற்றார் எய்தும் சிறப்பு) is, they say, the result of a life settled in love (அன்புற்று அமர்ந்த வழக்கு); Parimelazhagar reads the distinction as heaven after household joy. 75 spells out the 'fruit' that 45 only names, and credits it to love.

Verse 39 says only what comes through virtue is joy (அறத்தான் வருவதே இன்பம்) and everything else lies outside it. Verse 75 traces the joy and distinction people reach in the world to a life settled in love (அன்புற்று அமர்ந்த வழக்கு). Set side by side, 75 adds love to the source that 39 confines to அறம், which agrees with verse 45's coupling of the two.

Verse 76 says the ignorant hold that love supports only virtue, while it is the help (துணை) for மறம் as well; Kalaignar reads மறம் as valour, Parimelazhagar as the hostility that love removes. Verse 862 asks how a man without love (அன்பிலன்), without allies and without strength of his own can wear down an enemy's might. On Kalaignar's reading 862 is the case in point: in Book 2 love is listed first among the things a fighter needs.

Verse 76 says love is the ally not only of virtue but of மறம்; the link holds on the reading, Kalaignar's, that மறம் is valour. Verse 773 says fierceness is called great manhood (பேராண்மை), and that helping a foe in trouble (ஊராண்மை) is its cutting edge (எஃகு). Both refuse to keep kindness and martial courage in separate compartments.

Verse 77 says அறம் scorches what has no love as the sun scorches what has no bones (வெயில்போலக் காயுமே). Verse 204 says that if one plots another's ruin, அறம் plots the plotter's ruin (அறஞ்சூழும் சூழ்ந்தவன் கேடு). In both அறம் is an agent that acts against a person, and Parimelazhagar glosses it in both places as அறக்கடவுள், the god of virtue.

Verse 77 has அறம் burn the loveless. Verse 130 has அறம் watch for its moment (செவ்வி அறம்பார்க்கும்) and enter by the path to the one who has guarded against anger and learned restraint. The two show the same personified virtue in both directions: it seeks out the self-governed and dries up the loveless.

Verse 77 compares the loveless to a thing without bones (என்பிலது) dried by the sun; Kalaignar and Subramuniyaswami take it as a worm. Verse 80 says the body of those without love is bones wrapped in skin (என்புதோல் போர்த்த உடம்பு). The chapter uses bone twice for the loveless in opposite ways, once as what they lack and once as all they are.

Verse 78 says a life with no love within is like a dried tree putting out shoots on hard ground (வற்றல் மரம் தளிர்த்தற்று), which Parimelazhagar takes as something that does not happen. In 1106 the lover says her touch makes his life sprout each time they meet (உறுதோறு உயிர் தளிர்ப்ப). The verb தளிர் carries both: life sprouts where love is, and 78 uses the same sprouting to mark what a loveless life cannot do.

Verse 78 likens the loveless life to a withered tree on hard ground. Verse 576 says those who have eyes and no kindly regard are like trees fixed in the soil (மண்ணோடியைந்த மரத்தனையர்). In both a person without the inward quality, அன்பு in one and கண்ணோட்டம் in the other, is reduced to a tree, alive in form and without response.

Verse 79 asks what all the outer parts can do (புறத்துறுப்பெல்லாம் எவன்செய்யும்) for those who lack love, the inner part (அகத்துறுப்பு). Verse 574 asks what eyes do (எவன் செய்யும்), beyond seeming to be in the face, when they have no கண்ணோட்டம். The same question in the same words is put to the whole body in 79 and to one organ in 574: a part is judged by the disposition it serves.

Verse 79 says the outer limbs are of no use without the inner limb, love. Verse 407 says the fine looks (எழில்நலம்) of one without subtle, penetrating understanding are like those of a well-made clay doll (மண்மாண் புனைபாவை). Both set a complete exterior against a missing interior, love in Book 1 and understanding in Book 2.

Verse 80 says the seat of life (உயிர்நிலை) goes by way of love (அன்பின் வழியது). Verse 255 says உயிர்நிலை lies in not eating flesh (உண்ணாமை உள்ளது உயிர்நிலை); Parimelazhagar reads this as life's staying in the body resting on that virtue. The rare word உயிர்நிலை is used in both to make a moral quality, love or not eating flesh, the condition of being alive at all.

Verse 80 says that for those without love the body is only bones wrapped in skin (என்புதோல் போர்த்த உடம்பு). Verse 1020 says the movements of those with no shame within (நாண் அகத்தில்லார்) are like a wooden puppet feigning life by its string (மரப்பாவை ... உயிர்மருட்டியற்று). Both describe a moving body that lacks an inward quality as something without life in it, a frame of bone in one and a puppet in the other.

81 says all of staying at home and guarding one's goods (இருந்தோம்பி இல்வாழ்வதெல்லாம்) is for tending guests and doing them good; 212 says all the wealth produced by effort (தாளாற்றித் தந்த பொருளெல்லாம்) is for doing good to the deserving. Both end on the identical line வேளாண்மை செய்தற் பொருட்டு, so the household and earned wealth are given the same single purpose in two chapters.

81 makes the guest the purpose of the whole household life (இல்வாழ்வதெல்லாம் ... விருந்தோம்பி). 43 lists the guest (விருந்து) as one of five the householder must tend, alongside ancestors, gods, kin and oneself (ஐம்புலத்தாறு ஓம்பல் தலை). Read together, 81's 'all' is the hospitality chapter's emphasis on one duty that 43 sets among five.

82 says eating alone while the guest is outside (விருந்து புறத்ததாத் தானுண்டல்) is not to be desired even if the food were the medicine against death. 229 says eating by oneself alone (தாமே தமியர் உணல்) to fill up one's store is more bitter than begging. Both judge the solitary meal itself, one by setting it against the best imaginable food and the other against the worst condition.

82 uses the deathless medicine (சாவா மருந்து, which Parimelazhagar glosses as அமிழ்தம்) as the best food there could be, and says even that should not be eaten with the guest shut out. 64 says gruel stirred by one's children's small hands is far sweeter than அமிழ்து. In both the nectar is the benchmark that a human tie outranks: the food's worth depends on who is at the meal.

83 says the life of one who tends the arriving guest every day (வைகலும் ஓம்புவான்) does not suffer and go to ruin (பருவந்து பாழ்படுதல் இன்று). 227 says the disease called hunger rarely touches one accustomed to sharing his food (பாத்தூண் மரீஇயவனை). Both promise that habitual sharing of food protects the sharer from want, once for the host of guests and once for the giver to the poor.

83 says daily hospitality never brings a household to ruin (பாழ்படுதல் இன்று), which Parimelazhagar takes to mean the host's goods are not used up. 480 says helpfulness that does not weigh the extent of what one has (உளவரை தூக்காத ஒப்புரவாண்மை) quickly ends one's wealth (வல்லைக் கெடும்). The Book of Wealth thus attaches a condition of measure to the kind of promise 83 makes without one.

In 84 the fair goddess (செய்யாள்) dwells with a glad heart in the house of one who tends guests with a glad face. In 167 the same goddess (செய்யவள்) cannot bear the envious man and shows him to her elder sister (தவ்வையைக் காட்டி விடும்). Fortune is pictured as a person who stays or leaves according to how the householder regards other people: welcome keeps her, envy sends her away.

84 has the goddess of fortune (செய்யாள்) living in the home of the glad-faced host. 617 says she of the lotus (தாமரையினாள்) lives in the effort of the unslothful (மடியிலான் தாளுளாள்), and her dark sister in sloth. The same figure is given two different dwellings, generosity in the Book of Virtue and exertion in the Book of Wealth.

84 pairs அகனமர்ந்து (with a glad heart, said of the goddess) with முகனமர்ந்து (with a glad face, said of the host). 92 reuses the same two words: sweet speech with a glad face (முகனமர்ந்து இன்சொலன்) is better than giving with a glad heart (அகனமர்ந்து ஈதல்). The repeated formula ties the hospitality chapter to the next one, and in both it is the visible face that the verse singles out.

85 asks whether one who feeds guests and eats what is left (விருந்தோம்பி மிச்சில் மிசைவான்) need even sow his field (வித்தும் இடல்வேண்டும் கொல்லோ); Parimelazhagar supplies that it will bear by itself. 1039 says that if the owner stays away and does not go to it (செல்லான் கிழவன் இருப்பின்), the land sulks like a wife. The conflict holds only if 85 is taken literally, as Parimelazhagar does, and not as a figure of praise; Kalaignar reads 85 quite differently, as asking whether such a host would hold back even his seed-grain.

85 implies that the field of the host who feeds guests first yields without sowing. 545 says rain and harvest gather together (பெயலும் விளையுளும் தொக்கு) in the land of the king who wields the sceptre as he should. In both, right conduct is said to make the land fruitful, at the scale of one household's field and at the scale of a kingdom.

86 says one who tends the departing guest and watches for the next (வருவிருந்து பார்த்திருப்பான்) will be a good guest to those in the sky (வானத்தவர்க்கு). 50 says one who lives on earth as one should (வாழ்வாங்கு வாழ்பவன்) will be placed among the gods who dwell in the sky (வான்உறையும் தெய்வத்துள்). 86 names one specific practice that earns what 50 promises the householder in general, and turns it into a reciprocity: the host becomes the guest. (This edition prints நல்வருந்து in 86 and உநற்யும் in 50; both are typos.)
