87 says the fruit of the sacrifice of hospitality has no fixed measure and is as great as the guest (விருந்தின் துணைத்துணை), which Parimelazhagar takes as the guest's worth. 105 says help is not bounded by the help itself but by the worth of those it was done for (செயப்பட்டார் சால்பின் வரைத்து); Parimelazhagar reads 105 as being about help given in return. The same rule of measuring an act by its recipient and not its size appears in hospitality and in gratitude.

On Parimelazhagar's reading, 87 scales the fruit of hospitality to the guest's worth (விருந்தின் துணைத்துணை). 221 says giving to those who have nothing (வறியார்க்கு ஒன்று ஈவதே ஈகை) is the only real giving, and all the rest is like a loan expecting return. One verse values the gift by the receiver's merit and the other by the receiver's need; the conflict depends on reading துணை in 87 as merit and on treating feeding a guest and giving as the same kind of act.

87 calls hospitality a வேள்வி (sacrifice) whose fruit has no fixed measure; Parimelazhagar notes it is one of the five great sacrifices. 259 says not taking a life and eating it is better than pouring oblations in a thousand sacrifices (அவிசொரிந்து ஆயிரம் வேட்டலின்). In both verses the ritual word is used to rank an ethical practice: one is named a sacrifice, the other is set above a thousand of them.

88 says those who do not take up the sacrifice of tending guests guard their goods painfully (பரிந்தோம்பி) and end by saying 'we have no support' (பற்றற்றேம்). 228 asks whether the hard-eyed who store what they have and lose it (வைத்திழக்கும்) do not know the joy of giving. Both describe the same sequence of hoarding and then loss, and both set it against a use of wealth the hoarder never tried.

88 pictures people guarding their goods with pain (பரிந்தோம்பி) and still losing them. 376 says what is not allotted to one will not stay even if guarded with pain (பரியினும் ஆகாவாம் பாலல்ல), and what is one's own will not leave even if poured away (சொரியினும் போகா தம). The fate chapter gives a general ground for 88's observation: anxious guarding does not decide whether wealth stays, so spending it on guests risks nothing that guarding would have saved.

89 calls the folly that neglects hospitality 'poverty within having' (உடைமையுள் இன்மை) and says it is found among fools (மடவார்கண்). 153 calls turning away a guest 'the poverty of poverties' (இன்மையுள் இன்மை விருந்தொரால்) and then names bearing with fools (மடவார்ப் பொறை) the strength of strengths. The forbearance chapter reuses both the formula and the word மடவார், with inhospitality as its standard example of the worst lack. (This edition misprints the first word of 153.)

89 says poverty in the midst of wealth is the folly (மடமை) of not caring for guests. 841 says lack of understanding is the poverty of poverties (அறிவின்மை இன்மையுள் இன்மை) and that the world does not count other lack as lack. 841 states as a general principle what 89 shows in one case: the real want is a failure of understanding, whatever one owns.

89 says the inhospitable fool is poor while possessing (உடைமையுள் இன்மை). 1005 says those who neither give nor enjoy have nothing even with crores piled up (அடுக்கிய கோடி உண்டாயினும் இல்). Both verses, in the Book of Virtue and the Book of Wealth, deny that unused wealth counts as having.

90 says the anicham flower wilts when merely smelled (மோப்பக் குழையும் அனிச்சம்) and a guest wilts at a look from a changed face. In 1111 the man addresses the anicham, grants its delicate nature (நன்னீரை) and says the woman he loves is more delicate still (நின்னினும் மென்னீரள்). The flower is the book's standard of fragility in both places; 90 applies it to a guest's feelings and the lover to a woman's person, each claiming something more delicate than the flower.

90 says a guest wilts when looked at with an altered face (முகந்திரிந்து நோக்க). 707 says nothing is as knowing as the face, since whether one is pleased or angry it gets there first (உவப்பினும் காயினும் தான்முந்துறும்). 707 explains why 90's guest is hurt before a word is spoken: the face has already reported the host's mind.

90 gives the negative case: a face that turns (முகந்திரிந்து) and looks makes the guest wilt. 93 gives the positive rule in nearly the same terms: with a glad face, looking sweetly (முகத்தான் அமர்ந்து இனிது நோக்கி), then sweet words from the heart. The last verse of the hospitality chapter and the third of the next share the face-and-look sequence; Parimelazhagar on 90 also lists the glad face, the sweet word and the good deed as successive stages of welcome.

91 defines sweet words (இன்சொல்) as words mixed with tenderness and free of deceit (ஈரம் அளைஇப் படிறு இலவாம்). 911 says the இன்சொல் of women who want a man's wealth and not out of love (அன்பின் விழையார் பொருள்விழையும்) will bring him harm (இழுக்குத் தரும்). 911 uses the same word for speech that fails both of 91's tests, which shows the definition in 91 is doing real work: pleasant sound without love is not what chapter 10 praises.

91 says sweet words are the speech of those who have seen the செம்பொருள் (செம்பொருள் கண்டார் வாய்ச்சொல்), which Parimelazhagar glosses here as those who know virtue. 358 defines understanding as seeing the செம்பொருள் so that the folly of birth departs (செம்பொருள் காண்பது அறிவு). The same phrase links ordinary kind speech to the insight the renunciation chapters describe, though the commentator gives the word a more modest sense in 91.

92 says being sweet-spoken with a glad face is better than giving with a glad heart (அகன்அமர்ந்து ஈதலின் நன்றே). 295 says one who speaks truth in accord with his heart (மனத்தொடு வாய்மை மொழியின்) is above those who do austerity together with giving (தவத்தொடு தானஞ்செய்வாரின் தலை). Twice the book ranks a quality of speech above material giving, once for kindness and once for truthfulness.

92 ranks sweet speech with a glad face above glad-hearted giving. 387 says the world answers to the word of one able to give with sweet words and protect (இன்சொலால் ஈத்தளிக்க வல்லார்க்கு); 525 likewise joins கொடுத்தலும் இன்சொலும். Where the Book of Wealth describes what actually wins people, the two are combined and not ranked, so 92's comparison reads as a statement about relative worth, not advice to speak kindly in place of giving.

93 says virtue lies in sweet words that come from within (அகத்தானாம் இன்சொலினதே அறம்), after a glad face and a kind look. 34 says being spotless in mind is the whole of virtue and the rest is noisy show (ஆகுல நீர பிற); Parimelazhagar counts speech and outward guise among that rest. 93's word அகத்தானாம் is what keeps sweet speech on the right side of 34's line: it counts as virtue because it issues from the mind.

93 requires the glad face and the sweet word to come from within (முகத்தான் அமர்ந்து ... அகத்தானாம்). 786 says friendship that makes only the face smile is not friendship; friendship that makes the heart within smile is (முகநக ... நெஞ்சத்து அகநக). The same முகம்/அகம் pairing sets the test of genuineness for kind speech and for friendship.

93 places virtue in a glad face followed by sweet words from within (அகத்தானாம்). 824 warns that deceivers who smile sweetly with the face and are bitter within (முகத்தின் இனிய நகாஅ அகத்தின்னா வஞ்சரை) are to be feared. 824 describes the counterfeit of 93's first half, so the outward signs 93 begins with cannot by themselves be taken as proof of the inner part.

94 says want that brings suffering (துன்புறூஉம் துவ்வாமை) does not come to those whose sweet speech gives joy to everyone. 566 says that if a ruler is harsh of speech and without kindly regard (கடுஞ்சொல்லன் கண்ணிலன்), his long-standing wealth perishes on the spot. The two verses state the same link between speech and prosperity from opposite sides, for anyone in the Book of Virtue and for a king in the Book of Wealth.

94 asserts that sweet speakers do not fall into want, without saying how. 525 says one who can give and speak sweetly (கொடுத்தலும் இன்சொலும் ஆற்றின்) will be surrounded by layer on layer of kin (அடுக்கிய சுற்றத்தால் சுற்றப்படும்). 525 supplies a worldly mechanism for 94's promise: sweet speech gathers people around one, and a person so surrounded is not left destitute.

95 says being humble and sweet-spoken (பணிவுடையன் இன்சொலன் ஆதல்) is a person's ornament and nothing else is. 125 says bowing (பணிதல்) is good for everyone and for the rich it is a further wealth (செல்வர்க்கே செல்வம் தகைத்து). Both treat humility as an added possession, an ornament in one verse and wealth in the other, and 125 says who gains most from it.

95 makes humility (பணிவு) the true ornament (அணி). 978 says greatness always bows (பணியுமாம்) while smallness adorns itself in self-admiration (அணியுமாம் தன்னை வியந்து). The same two roots are set against each other in 978: the small person's self-adornment is the false ornament, and the bowing 95 praises is what the great actually wear.

95 says humility and sweet speech are a person's ornament and other things are not (அணியல்ல மற்றுப் பிற). 1014 asks whether shame is not the ornament of the worthy (அணிஅன்றோ நாணுடைமை சான்றோர்க்கு), and 575 names kindly regard as the eye's ornament. The exclusive wording of 95 is therefore the chapter's emphasis: other chapters award the same title to other inner qualities, while agreeing with 95 (as Parimelazhagar reads it) that bodily ornaments are not meant.

96 says that if one seeks out good things and says them sweetly (நல்லவை நாடி இனிய சொலின்), what is not virtue wears away and virtue grows. 128 says that if even one harmful word has its effect (ஒன்றானும் தீச்சொல் பொருட்பயன் உண்டாயின்), what was good turns out not good. Together they give speech power over one's stock of virtue in both directions: good words build it and a single bad word undoes it.

35 defines virtue as what proceeds without slipping into four things, the last being painful speech (இன்னாச்சொல்). 96 says virtue grows and its opposite wears away when one speaks good things sweetly (அல்லவை தேய அறம்பெருகும்). 35 only requires avoiding harsh words; 96 adds that the positive practice of sweet, well-chosen speech actively increases virtue.

97 says speech that yields benefit and does not part from pleasantness (பயன்ஈன்று பண்பின் தலைப்பிரியாச் சொல்) produces நயன் and brings forth good (நன்றி). 194 says speech with no benefit and no pleasantness (பயன்சாராப் பண்பில்சொல்) is without நயன் and removes one from good (நன்மையின் நீக்கும்). The four terms பயன், பண்பு, நயன் and நன்மை recur in the negative, so 194 is 97 inverted; Parimelazhagar glosses பண்பு as sweetness and நயன் as justice in both.

97 asks for speech that has both benefit (பயன்) and pleasantness (பண்பு), and credits it with producing நயன். 197 says the worthy may say what lacks நயன் if they must, but should not say what lacks பயன் (நயனில சொல்லினும் சொல்லுக ... பயனில சொல்லாமை நன்று). 197 thus ranks the qualities 97 holds together: use is the one that cannot be given up. Parimelazhagar takes நயன் in 197 as justice; Subramuniyaswami takes it as pleasantness, which makes the limit on chapter 10 more direct.

98 says sweet speech that is clear of smallness (சிறுமையுள் நீங்கிய இன்சொல்) gives joy in the next life and this one; Parimelazhagar explains சிறுமை as causing pain to others by what the words mean. 291 defines truth as speech containing no harm at all (யாதொன்றும் தீமை இலாத சொலல்). Sweetness and truthfulness are both defined by the same test, the absence of harm to others, and not by sound or by literal accuracy. (This edition prints சிறுமையுவு in 98, a typo for சிறுமையுள்.)

98 says sweet speech free of smallness gives joy (இன்சொல் ... இன்பம் தரும்) here and hereafter. 911 says the sweet speech of women who desire wealth and not the man brings harm (இன்சொல் இழுக்குத் தரும்). The two predicates answer each other, and the condition in 98 (சிறுமையுள் நீங்கிய) marks the difference: what 98 promises holds only for sweet words that are not serving a mean purpose.

99 asks why one who sees how sweetly sweet words yield (இன்சொல் இனிதீன்றல் காண்பான்) would use harsh words (எவன்கொலோ வன்சொல் வழங்குவது); Parimelazhagar takes it as one who has felt the pleasure of others' kind words to himself. 318 asks why one who knows what is painful to his own life does painful things to other lives (என்கொலோ மன்னுயிர்க்கு இன்னா செயல்). The two rhetorical questions have the same form and the same argument from one's own experience to the treatment of others, applied to words in 99 and to harm in general in 318. (The first line of 318 is misprinted in this edition, but the verse is recoverable.)

99 asks what could lead someone who knows the good that sweet words do to use harsh ones (வன்சொல்). 784 says friendship is not for laughing together but for going ahead to rebuke when a friend oversteps (மிகுதிக்கண் மேற்சென்று இடித்தற் பொருட்டு). The friendship chapter supplies a case where sharp words have a purpose, so 99's question is best read as aimed at needless harshness and not at every hard word.

100 says speaking unpleasant things when pleasant ones are available is like taking the unripe fruit when the ripe is there (கனிஇருப்பக் காய்கவர்ந்தற்று). 1306, a speech in the Book of Love, says that love without serious and light quarrels is like over-ripe fruit and unripe fruit (கனியும் கருக்காயும் அற்று). The ripe/unripe pair is used differently: in 100 the ripe fruit is simply the right choice, while the lover treats fruit that is too ripe and fruit that is too raw as two ways of missing the right point.

100 pictures someone who has ripe fruit at hand and takes the unripe: unpleasant words chosen while pleasant ones exist (இனிய உளவாக இன்னாத கூறல்). 831 defines folly as taking hold of harm and letting gain go (ஏதங்கொண்டு ஊதியம் போக விடல்). Harsh speech in 100 is an instance of exactly the choice 831 names as folly, which fits the chapter's closing argument that harsh words are a bad bargain for the speaker as well as wrong.

101 says that for help given without any prior help (செய்யாமல் செய்த உதவி) even earth and heaven are hardly a match (ஆற்றல் அரிது). 211 says obligation wants no return (கைம்மாறு வேண்டா) and asks what the world does for the rain in exchange (என் ஆற்றுங் கொல்லோ). The same verb ஆற்று marks both: one verse looks from the receiver who cannot repay, the other from the giver who does not ask to be repaid.

Both open with செய்யாமல், 'without (the other) having done anything first'. 101 applies it to help: unprompted help is beyond repayment. 313 applies it to hatred: even toward those who hate you though you did nothing (செய்யாமல் செற்றார்க்கும்), doing hurt brings sorrow with no escape. Read together, the unprovoked good creates a boundless debt while the unprovoked wrong still gives no licence to retaliate.

102 says help done at the time of need (காலத்தினால் செய்த நன்றி), though small, is greater than the earth. 788 makes that timeliness the definition of friendship: it removes distress there and then (ஆங்கே இடுக்கண் களைவது), like the hand going to a slipping garment. 102 values the help by its moment; 788 says what kind of helper acts in that moment.

103 praises help from those who do not weigh the return (பயன்தூக்கார்), calling its good greater than the sea. 813 uses the same weighing verb for the opposite case: friends who weigh what they will get (உறுவது சீர்தூக்கும் நட்பு) are put level with thieves. The pair shows the book judging help and friendship by one test, whether the giver was calculating.

103 sets apart help given without weighing its return (பயன்தூக்கார் செய்த உதவி). 221 says only giving to those who have nothing is giving, and everything else has the nature of a loan expecting return (குறியெதிர்ப்பை நீரது). Both separate real help from exchange, 103 from the side of gratitude and 221 from the side of the giver.

The two verses share a frame almost word for word: தினைத்துணை ... பனைத்துணையாக் கொள்வர். In 104 those who understand its fruit (பயன்தெரிவார்) take a millet-sized good done to them as palmyra-sized; in 433 those ashamed of blame (பழிநாணுவார்) take a millet-sized fault of their own as palmyra-sized. The same magnifying habit is recommended for others' kindness and for one's own faults.

104 uses millet and palmyra (தினைத்துணை, பனைத்துணை) for how a small good should be valued. 1282, a lover's speech in the Book of Love, reuses the pair: when love comes full as a palmyra (பனைத்துணையும் காமம் நிறைய வரின்) there should be not even a millet of sulking (தினைத்துணையும் ஊடாமை). The measure-pair moves from ethics to love, there contrasting two quantities where 104 converts one into the other.

104 says a millet of good is taken as a palmyra by those who know its worth. 109 says even harm like killing (கொன்றன்ன இன்னா) vanishes when one thinks of a single good the person did (ஒன்று நன்று உள்ளக் கெடும்). Parimelazhagar connects them in his note on 109: because the small good is held as large, that one good can cancel the later harm.

105 says help is not bounded by the help itself; its measure is the worth of the one helped (செயப்பட்டார் சால்பின் வரைத்து). 87 says the fruit of hospitality has no fixed size; it is as great as the guest (விருந்தின் துணைத்துணை). Both verses move the measure of an act of giving from the gift to the character of the person who receives it.

Both verses use the phrase மாசற்றார் கேண்மை, the bond of the stainless: 106 says do not forget it (மறவற்க), 800 says keep close to it (மருவுக). Each then adds a second command about a kind of friend, 106 never to abandon those who were a support in distress, 800 to drop the unsuitable (ஒப்பிலார்) even at a cost. The chapter on choosing friends repeats the gratitude chapter's rule and supplies its other half, whom to leave.

106 commands: do not abandon (துறவற்க) the friendship of those who were a support in distress. 806 states it as a description: those who keep within the bounds will not abandon (துறவார்) the tie of long-standing friends even in ruin (தொலைவிடத்தும்). The same verb is used in both, with the direction reversed: 106 is loyalty owed for help received in one's own trouble, 806 loyalty kept when trouble comes.

107 says people will remember (உள்ளுவர்) through seven births the friendship of those who wiped away their distress. 799 says the bond with those who abandoned one in ruin (கெடுங்காலைக் கைவிடுவார்) burns the heart even when thought of (உள்ளினும்) at the hour of death. Both are about how conduct in another's hard time is remembered: the helper for lives to come, the deserter up to the last moment.

107 says the friendship of one who removed one's distress is remembered through seven births (எழுமை எழுபிறப்பும்). 398 says learning gained in one birth (ஒருமைக்கண்) is a protection through seven (எழுமையும்). The seven-birth span is the book's figure for what outlasts a single life, used here for a debt of gratitude and there for learning.

108 says it is good to forget what is not good that very day (நன்றல்லது அன்றே மறப்பது நன்று). 152 says bear with a wrong, and forgetting it is better still (அதனை மறத்தல் அதனினும் நன்று). Both put forgetting an injury above merely tolerating it; 108 pairs it with the opposite duty of never forgetting a good.

108 says a wrong done to you should be forgotten that very day (அன்றே மறப்பது). 113 says gain that comes from leaving fairness should be let go that very day (அன்றே ஒழிய விடல்). The shared அன்றே gives both the same urgency: neither a grievance nor an unfair gain is to be kept overnight.

109 says that even harm like killing disappears when one recalls a single good the person once did (அவர் செய்த ஒன்று நன்று உள்ள). 807 says those whose bond has come by the way of love do not cut off love even when the friend does ruinous things (அழிவந்த செய்யினும் அன்பறார்). Both have the same 'even if they do grave harm' (செயினும்) clause; what outweighs the harm is a remembered favour in one and long affection in the other.

110 says those who kill any good may have an escape (உய்வுண்டாம்), but there is none for one who kills a good done to him (செய்ந்நன்றி கொன்ற மகற்கு). 207 has the same shape: those who incur any enmity (எனைப்பகை உற்றாரும்) escape (உய்வர்), but the enmity of one's deeds follows and kills. Both use 'everything else can be survived' to single out one thing, ingratitude in 110 and evil deeds in general in 207.

110 says there is escape (உய்வுண்டாம்) for other wrongs but none (உய்வில்லை) for killing gratitude. 896 says one burned by fire may survive (உய்வுண்டாம்), but those who go on offending the great will not (உய்யார்). The same உய்வு formula marks what each chapter treats as its unforgivable offence, so a reader should take 'only this has no escape' as the book's way of stressing gravity and not as a strict ranking.

111 says the virtue called தகுதி is good if one keeps to what is due in each case (பகுதியால் பாற்பட்டு ஒழுக); Parimelazhagar takes பகுதி as enemy, stranger and friend. 541 defines a king's justice (முறை) as inquiring, showing favour to no one (யார்மாட்டும் கண்ணோடாது) and acting after consideration. The householder's impartiality of 111 reappears as the procedure of the ruler's court.

111 asks that fairness be kept alike across the divisions of people, on Parimelazhagar's reading toward enemy, stranger and friend. 528 says a king should not look on all in common (பொதுநோக்கான்) but according to rank or merit (வரிசையா நோக்கின்), and many will then stay by him. Together they show that impartiality in 111 does not mean identical treatment: one may not favour by relationship, but one should distinguish by desert.

112 says the wealth of a person of rectitude (செப்பம் உடையவன் ஆக்கம்) does not decay and is a security to his descendants. 169 admits the opposite case occurs: the prosperity of the crooked-hearted and the ruin of the upright (செவ்வியான் கேடு) are things to be pondered (நினைக்கப்படும்). 169 thus limits 112 to the usual course of things; Parimelazhagar explains the exceptions by deeds of earlier births.

112 says a fair person's wealth is a support to his posterity (எச்சத்திற்கு ஏமாப்பு). 171 states the reverse: if one covets others' goods without fairness (நடுவின்றி), the family perishes (குடிபொன்றி) and guilt comes at once. Both tie நடுவு to what happens to one's line, 112 as promise and 171 as warning.

112 says the wealth of the fair person does not decay and secures those who come after (எச்சம்). 44 says that if a household fears blame and shares its food, its line never fails (வழியெஞ்சல் எஞ்ஞான்றும் இல்); Parimelazhagar reads the fear of blame as applying to how the wealth is earned. Both promise continuity of the family to blameless livelihood, with 44 adding sharing as a condition.

113 says to give up at once gain that comes from leaving fairness (நடுவிகந்தாம் ஆக்கம்), even if it yields only good (நன்றே தரினும்). 328 says that, however great the gain that brings good (நன்றாகும் ஆக்கம் பெரிதெனினும்), gain that comes by killing (கொன்றாகும் ஆக்கம்) is lowest to the worthy. The same concession, 'even if it is good and large', is refused in both; only the forbidden means differs.

113 says to abandon gain got by departing from fairness even if it brings good. 657 says the extreme poverty of the worthy (சான்றோர் கழிநல்குரவு) is better than wealth gained by taking on blame (பழிமலைந்து எய்திய ஆக்கம்). 657 names the price that 113 leaves unstated: giving up such gain may mean poverty, and the book accepts that.

114 says whether people are worthy or not is seen by their எச்சம், what they leave behind; Parimelazhagar takes this as having or lacking good children. 456 says those pure of mind have a good எச்சம் (எச்சம் நன்றாகும்), which he again reads as offspring. The two run the same link in opposite directions: 456 from character to legacy, 114 from legacy back to character.

114 makes எச்சம் the evidence of whether someone was fair. 238 speaks of 'the எச்சம் called renown' (இசையென்னும் எச்சம்) and calls it a disgrace not to leave it. 238 supports reading the legacy in 114 as reputation, which is how Kalaignar takes it, against Parimelazhagar's reading of children.

115 says loss and increase are not absent from life (கேடும் பெருக்கமும் இல்லல்ல), and that not bending in the heart (நெஞ்சத்துக் கோடாமை) is the ornament of the worthy. 379 asks why those who take good as good when it comes grieve when the opposite comes (அன்றாங்கால் அல்லற்படுவது எவன்). Both ask for the same response to gain and loss; Parimelazhagar grounds both in the working of past deeds.

115 says loss and increase both occur, and the worthy keep the heart from bending because of them. 169 gives the hard case: the crooked-hearted prosper and the upright are ruined (செவ்வியான் கேடு), which calls for reflection. 169 shows the situation in which 115's advice is tested, when fortune seems to reward bending.

115 and 118 end with the same line, கோடாமை சான்றோர்க்கு அணி, 'not bending is the ornament of the worthy'. In 115 the bending is of the heart under loss and gain (நெஞ்சத்துக் கோடாமை); in 118 it is leaning to one side (ஒருபால் கோடாமை), like a balance. The repetition joins two sides of நடுவு: steadiness under one's own fortunes and impartiality between others.

116 says that if one's heart leaves fairness and does wrong (நடுவொரீஇ அல்ல செயின்), one should know 'I will perish' (கெடுவல்யான்). 204 says do not plot another's ruin even by a lapse, for அறம் will plot the plotter's ruin (சூழ்ந்தவன் கேடு). Both say that harm intended for others returns as one's own ruin; 116 makes it the wrongdoer's own knowledge, 204 gives the agent as அறம்.

116 locates the departure from fairness in the heart (தன் நெஞ்சம்), and Parimelazhagar reads செயின் as covering even the thought of doing wrong. 282 says outright that merely thinking in the mind (உள்ளத்தால் உள்ளலும்) of taking another's goods by stealth is wrong. 282 supports that reading of 116: the fault begins with the intention, before any act.

117 says the world (உலகம்) will not count as ruin the low state (தாழ்வு) of one who stays in virtue by standing fair. 752 says everyone scorns those who have nothing (இல்லாரை எல்லாரும் எள்ளுவர்); Parimelazhagar adds 'even if they have every good quality'. They conflict if உலகம் in 117 means people in general; Parimelazhagar avoids this by reading உலகம் there as the high-minded (உயர்ந்தோர்).

117 says the low state of a person who stands fair is not held to be ruin (கெடுவாக வையாது). 988 says poverty is no disgrace (இன்மை இளிவன்று) for one who has the firmness called சால்பு. Both deny that poverty lowers a person of character; 117 says it for fairness in particular, 988 for worth as a whole.

118 compares the worthy to the balance beam (சீர்தூக்கும் கோல்) that levels itself and then weighs, not leaning to a side (கோடாமை). 546 says it is the king's sceptre (கோல்), not his spear, that gives victory, if it does not bend (கோடாது). கோல் and கோடுதல் carry the same idea in both: the weighing beam of the private person and the sceptre of the ruler are good only while straight.

118 describes a balance that first makes itself level (சமன்செய்து) and then weighs (சீர்தூக்கும்). 561 says a king is one who examines a case fittingly (தக்காங்கு நாடி) and punishes in proportion (ஒத்தாங்கு ஒறுப்பது); Parimelazhagar glosses the examining as done 'standing in the middle' (நடுவாக நின்று). The two steps of the scale, being level and then measuring, match the two steps of just punishment.

119 says rectitude is the absence of crookedness in speech (சொற்கோட்டம்), provided there is none within (உட்கோட்டம்). 279 says the straight arrow is cruel and the bent lute (யாழ்கோடு) is good, so judge people by what their deeds do. Both use straight and bent to separate appearance from substance: 119 will not take straight words as proof without a straight mind, and 279 will not take outward shape as proof at all.

119 makes unbent speech count as rectitude only if the mind too is unbent (உட்கோட்டம் இன்மை பெறின்). 295 praises one who speaks truth together with the mind (மனத்தொடு வாய்மை மொழியின்) above those who do austerity and give. Both attach the same condition to good speech, agreement between word and mind, in the fields of fairness and of truthfulness.

120 says true trade for traders is to look after others' things as their own (பிறவும் தமபோல்). 315 asks what use understanding is if one does not guard against another's pain as one's own (பிறிதின்நோய் தந்நோய்போல்). The same 'as one's own' (தம்போல்) test is applied to goods in the market and to suffering in the chapter on not hurting.

120 asks traders to care for what belongs to others as for what is theirs (பிறவும் தமபோல் பேணி). 1015 says the world calls those who feel shame at others' blame and their own (பிறர்பழியும் தம்பழியும் நாணுவார்) the dwelling of shame; Parimelazhagar reads this as weighing the two alike. Both define a virtue, fairness in one and shame in the other, by removing the difference between oneself and others.

121 says lack of restraint drives one into thick darkness (ஆரிருள் உய்த்து விடும்); 243 says those whose hearts hold அருள் do not enter the painful world joined with darkness (இருள்சேர்ந்த இன்னா உலகம்). Both use darkness as the place a moral failing leads to, which Parimelazhagar glosses in both verses as a hell; the pairing shows the same destination attached to two different virtues, restraint in the householder's section and அருள் in the ascetic's.

121 ends அடங்காமை ஆரிருள் உய்த்து விடும், and 168 ends with envy, called a பாவி, which destroys fortune and தீயுழி உய்த்து விடும். The same closing verb phrase, 'drives and leaves one there', is used for lack of restraint and for envy, so the two vices are given the same power to deliver a person to a bad place.

121 says restraint brings one among the immortals (அமரருள் உய்க்கும்); 50 says one who lives on earth as one should will be placed among the gods who dwell in the sky (தெய்வத்துள் வைக்கப்படும்). Both promise a place among the gods to a person living an ordinary household life well, without renunciation, and 121 names restraint as the quality that does it.

31 asks what gain is greater for a living being than virtue (அறத்தினூஉங்கு ஆக்கம் எவனோ உயிர்க்கு); 122 says there is no gain for a living being beyond restraint (ஆக்கம் அதனினூஉங்கு இல்லை உயிர்க்கு) and tells one to guard it as wealth. 122 reuses chapter 4's formula almost word for word and applies it to one particular virtue, so restraint is given the rank the earlier verse gave to virtue as a whole.

122 tells one to guard restraint as பொருள், wealth, since nothing is a greater gain; 363 says there is no fine wealth (விழுச்செல்வம்) here like not wanting, and nothing equal to it there either. Both verses count an inner holding-back as the real wealth and both use the 'nothing equals it' form, once for the householder's restraint and once for the renouncer's freedom from craving.

123 says that if one knows and then restrains oneself in the proper way (அறிவறிந்து ஆற்றின் அடங்கப் பெறின்), that restraint is recognised and yields distinction; Parimelazhagar takes அறிவறிந்து as knowing that restraint is itself what knowledge is. 834 gives the negative: no fool is greater than one who has studied, understood and taught others but is not himself restrained (தானடங்காப் பேதை). Together they say knowledge is finished only when it turns into restraint.

123 calls restraint செறிவு and says that, recognised, it yields distinction; 715 calls not speaking first among elders a செறிவு and ranks it the best of good things (முந்து கிளவாச் செறிவு). The shared word shows the general restraint of chapter 13 turning up in the assembly as a concrete act, holding back one's speech before those who know more.

124 says the stature of one who is restrained without shifting from his station (நிலையின் திரியாது அடங்கியான்) is far greater than a mountain's. 965 says even those like a hill will sink if they do a lowering thing as small as a kundri seed (குன்றின் அனையாரும் குன்றுவர்). The mountain stature of 124 holds only while the 'not shifting' holds; 965 states how little it takes to lose it.

124 praises one who is restrained and does not shift from his station (நிலையின் திரியாது); 989 says those called the ஆழி of worth do not shift even when the age shifts (ஊழி பெயரினும் தாம் பெயரார்). Both measure a person by immovability, 124 against a mountain and 989 against the turning of an age.

29 speaks of those who have climbed and stand on the hill called good qualities (குணமென்னும் குன்றேறி நின்றார்), whom Parimelazhagar takes to be ascetics; 124 says the restrained person's stature is greater than a mountain (மலையினும் மாணப் பெரிது), and Parimelazhagar reads நிலை there as the householder's state. On his readings the renouncer stands on a hill while the householder who stays restrained in his own station is said to overtop one.

125 says bowing (பணிதல்) is good for everyone and is a further wealth for the wealthy; 963 says bowing is needed in abundance (பெருக்கத்து வேண்டும் பணிதல்) and standing tall is needed in shrunken circumstances. 963 keeps 125's point about the rich and adds the other half: when one has little, the same concern for character calls for not stooping.

125 says bowing is good for all and especially fine in the wealthy; 978 says greatness always bows (பணியுமாம் என்றும் பெருமை) while smallness adorns itself in self-admiration. Both make humility the mark of those who have most reason for pride, wealth in one verse and greatness in the other.

125 treats bowing (பணிதல்) as an excellence, a second wealth for the rich; 985 says bowing is the strength of those who get things done and the weapon by which the worthy turn opponents around (ஆற்றுவார் ஆற்றல் பணிதல்). The same act is valued as character in the Book of Virtue and as effective power in the Book of Wealth.

126 says that drawing in the five like a tortoise in one birth is a protection through seven (ஒருமையுள் ... எழுமையும் ஏமாப்புடைத்து); 398 says the learning one gains in one birth is a protection through seven (ஒருமைக்கண் ... எழுமையும் ஏமாப்புடைத்து). The closing formula is identical, so sense-restraint and learning are set side by side as the two acquisitions that carry across births.

126 says restraint of the five in one birth protects through seven; 835 says a fool can, by what he does in one birth (ஒருமைச் செயல்), make the mire he will sink in through seven (எழுமையும் தான்புக்கு அழுந்தும் அளறு). The one-birth and seven-births arithmetic runs in both directions: one life is enough to secure the next seven or to ruin them.

126 pictures restraint as a tortoise drawing in its five (ஆமைபோல் ஐந்தடக்கல்); 24 pictures it as guarding the five with the goad of firmness (உரனென்னும் தோட்டியான் ஓரைந்தும் காப்பான்), which Parimelazhagar explains as driving five elephants. The two animal figures show two sides of the same control: the senses as limbs to be withdrawn from danger and as strong beasts to be steered.

127 says whatever else they fail to guard, let them guard the tongue, or they will grieve through a fault of speech (நாகாக்க காவாக்கால் சோகாப்பர்); 305 says if you would guard yourself, guard against anger, or anger will kill you (சினங்காக்க காவாக்கால் தன்னையே கொல்லும்). The sentence frame காக்க / காவாக்கால் is the same, and in both the harm of the unguarded thing falls on the person who failed to guard it.

127 warns that an unguarded tongue brings grief through a fault of speech (சொல்லிழுக்கு); 642 tells the minister to guard against any lapse in speech (காத்தோம்பல் சொல்லின்கட் சோர்வு) because both gain and ruin come from it (ஆக்கமும் கேடும்). 642 carries the rule into statecraft and adds what 127 leaves out: speech is guarded not only because it can harm but because gain comes by it too.

128 says that if even one bad word has its effect, the good turns out not good (ஒன்றானும் தீச்சொல் ... நன்றாகாதாகி விடும்); Parimelazhagar takes this as the person's other merit turning bad. 965 says even hill-like people sink if they do a lowering thing the size of a kundri seed. Both hold that a single small lapse is enough to cancel a large standing good, in speech in one verse and in honour in the other.

128 says one harmful word undoes a person's good; 109 says that even a hurt as bad as killing vanishes when one thinks of a single good the person did (அவர்செய்த ஒன்று நன்று உள்ளக் கெடும்). The 'one outweighs all' logic is used in opposite directions: in judging one's own speech one bad instance spoils everything, and in judging someone who has helped you one good instance clears everything.

129 says a wound burned by fire heals within but a scar burned by the tongue does not (தீயினாற் சுட்ட புண் உள்ளாறும்); 896 says one burned by fire may still survive, but those who go on offending the great will not (எரியால் சுடப்படினும் உய்வுண்டாம்). Both use a burn as the injury one can recover from, in order to mark something worse: a spoken wound in 129 and the anger of the great in 896.

129 sets a fire-burn, which heals, against the tongue's scar, which does not; 1049 says one can even sleep in the middle of fire but cannot close an eye in the middle of poverty (நெருப்பினுள் துஞ்சலும் ஆகும்). The book repeatedly takes fire as the measure of bearable pain and places a non-physical hurt beyond it.

129 says the scar left by the tongue never heals; 159 says those who bear the harsh words from the mouths of people who exceed all bounds (இறந்தார்வாய் இன்னாச்சொல் நோற்கிற்பவர்) are as pure as renouncers. 129 gives the reason 159's praise is so high: what the forbearing person takes without retaliation is the one kind of wound the book says does not close.

130 says அறம் itself watches for the right moment and enters the path of one who has guarded against anger, learned, and is restrained (அறம் பார்க்கும் ஆற்றின் நுழைந்து); 204 says that if you plot another's ruin, அறம் plots the ruin of the plotter (அறஞ்சூழும் சூழ்ந்தவன் கேடு). In both verses virtue is an agent that acts on a person, seeking out the restrained and planning against the malicious.

130 has virtue looking for its chance and coming along the path to the restrained person; 594 has prosperity asking the way and going to the one of unwavering energy (ஆக்கம் அதர்வினாய்ச் செல்லும்). The same figure, a good that seeks out the person fit for it instead of being pursued, is used for virtue in the first book and for worldly gain in the second. The edition's text of 594 has lost its first letter (க்கம் for ஆக்கம்), but the reading is not in doubt.

131 says conduct is to be guarded more than life because it gives excellence (ஒழுக்கம் உயிரினும் ஓம்பப்படும்); 1017 says those ruled by shame will give up life for shame and will not give up shame for life (நாணால் உயிரைத் துறப்பர்). Both place a quality of character above life itself; 1017 states as what such people actually do what 131 states as a rule.

131 ranks conduct above one's own life; 327 says do not do the deed that takes another's life even if your own life should go (தன்னுயிர் நீப்பினும் செய்யற்க). The 'more than life' ranking is applied to conduct in general in one verse and to the single act of not killing in the other.

132 says guard conduct with effort, for however much one sifts and examines, it alone is the help (தெரிந்தோம்பித் தேரினும் அஃதே துணை); 242 says hold to அருள், for by whatever many ways one examines, it alone is the help (பல்லாற்றால் தேரினும் அஃதே துணை). The closing words are the same, with the exclusive அஃதே, applied to conduct in the householder's section and to அருள் in the ascetic's; read together, each stage of life is told that its own central virtue is what survives every inquiry.

133 says having conduct is what good family is, and a lapse becomes low birth (ஒழுக்கம் உடைமை குடிமை இழுக்கம் இழிந்த பிறப்பாய் விடும்); 972 says birth is alike for all living beings and distinction differs by the difference in what they do (பிறப்பொக்கும் ... செய்தொழில் வேற்றுமையான்). Both move rank from birth to action. Parimelazhagar reads 133 inside the system of வருணம், as conduct proper to each class, which is narrower than the bare Tamil.

133 makes conduct the thing that constitutes good family (ஒழுக்கம் உடைமை குடிமை); 951 says integrity and shame are found together by nature only in those born in a good house (இற்பிறந்தார் கண்அல்லது இல்லை இயல்பாக). If குடிமை in 133 means that conduct alone makes one well-born, 951 runs the other way and makes birth the source of the conduct. The conflict disappears on Parimelazhagar's reading of 133, where conduct only preserves or forfeits a rank that birth has already given.

133 says a lapse from conduct turns into low birth; 1019 says a lapse in கொள்கை burns one's lineage (குலஞ்சுடும் கொள்கை பிழைப்பின்), and Parimelazhagar glosses கொள்கை there as ஒழுக்கம். Both say family standing is lost through the individual's failure in conduct, one calling the result a low birth and the other a burning.

134 says a Brahmin can relearn the Veda he has forgotten, but his birth is ruined when conduct declines (பார்ப்பான் பிறப்பொழுக்கம் குன்றக் கெடும்); 30 says those called அந்தணர் are the virtuous, because they live clothed in kindness to all beings (செந்தண்மை பூண்டொழுகலான்). Both tie the title to how the person lives and not to learning or descent. Parimelazhagar takes அந்தணர் in 30 to mean renouncers, so on his reading the two verses concern different people.

134 treats forgetting the Veda (மறப்பினும் ஓத்துக் கொளலாகும்) as a loss that can be made good; 560 lists among the effects of a king who does not protect that those of the six occupations forget their books (அறுதொழிலோர் நூல்மறப்பர்). The same forgetting appears as a private, repairable lapse in 134 and as a sign of public ruin in 560, while 134 keeps conduct as the loss that cannot be repaired.

135 argues by comparison: as there is no gain in the envious, there is no elevation in one without conduct (அழுக்காறுடையான்கண் ஆக்கம் போன்று இல்லை). 170 states the premise on its own: none have grown great through envy (அழுக்கற்று அகன்றாரும் இல்லை). 135 takes chapter 17's claim as already known and builds its point about conduct on it.

135 takes it as given that the envious have no gain (ஆக்கம்); 169 says the gain of the crooked-hearted and the ruin of the upright are things to be pondered (அவ்விய நெஞ்சத்தான் ஆக்கமும் ... நினைக்கப்படும்). 169 concedes that the case 135 calls non-existent can occur and needs explaining, which weakens the simile's premise; Parimelazhagar softens it by adding 'if they occur'.

136 says the strong do not slacken in conduct, knowing the harm that comes of a lapse (இழுக்கத்தின் ஏதம் படுபாக்கறிந்து); 164 says people do no wrong out of envy, knowing the harm that comes of the wrong path (இழுக்காற்றின் ஏதம் படுபாக்கு அறிந்து). The second lines are nearly the same words, and both verses ground good behaviour in foreseeing consequences, which 136 counts as strength (உரவோர்).

137 says that from conduct people reach high standing and from a lapse they reach எய்தாப் பழி, which Parimelazhagar takes as blame that is not properly theirs, laid on them because the lapse makes it believable. 117 says the world will not count as ruin the low state of one who stays in the right by being fair (கெடுவாக வையாது உலகம்). In both the world's verdict follows character more than facts: it discounts the upright person's fall and charges the lapsed person with more than he did.

138 calls good conduct the seed of good (நன்றிக்கு வித்தாகும் நல்லொழுக்கம்) and says bad conduct always gives suffering; 361 calls craving the seed that produces unending birth for all beings (தவாஅப் பிறப்பீனும் வித்து). The seed figure is used for a cause whose yield comes later and keeps coming, once for a good crop and once for a bad one.

139 says speaking evil things even by a slip is not possible for those who have conduct (வழுக்கியும் வாயாற் சொலல் ஒல்லாவே); 199 says those of stainless sight do not say meaningless things even in forgetfulness (பொச்சாந்தும் சொல்லார்). Both claim that a settled quality rules out even the accidental lapse of speech, and they trace that quality to conduct in one case and to clear understanding in the other.

139 says a person of conduct cannot speak evil even by a slip; 1044 says that even in the well-born, poverty brings the slackness from which degrading words are born (இற்பிறந்தார் கண்ணேயும் இன்மை இளிவந்த சொற்பிறக்கும் சோர்வு தரும்). 1044 names a condition, want, under which the slip of speech that 139 calls impossible does happen to good people.

139 makes the absence of evil speech a test of having conduct; 959 says that as a sprout shows the ground it lay in, the words from the mouth show the family of the one born in it (குலத்தில் பிறந்தார் வாய்ச்சொல்). Both treat what comes out of the mouth as the evidence of what a person is.

140 says those who have not learned to live in accord with the world (உலகத்தோடு ஒட்ட ஒழுகல்) lack understanding, however much they have studied; 426 says that to live with the world as the world lives is understanding (உலகத்தோடு அவ்வது உறைவது அறிவு). 140 states negatively in the first book what 426 states positively in the second, and both define அறிவு by fit with the world and not by study.

140 says much study without the ability to live in accord with the world is not understanding; 637 tells the minister that even after knowing the method of doing a thing, he must act knowing the way of the world (உலகத்து இயற்கை அறிந்து செயல்). 637 applies 140's ranking of worldly fit over book-knowledge to practical statecraft; Parimelazhagar glosses செயற்கை there as methods learned from treatises.

140 makes accord with the world the test that learning must pass; 280 says neither shaving nor matted hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns (உலகம் பழித்தது ஒழித்துவிடின்). In both, the world's standard outranks a formal qualification, learning for the scholar and outward marks for the ascetic. Parimelazhagar takes உலகம் in both verses as the worthy and not people at large.

141 says the folly (பேதைமை) of desiring a woman who is another's (பிறன்பொருளாள்) is not found (இல்) in those who have seen aram and porul; 910 says the folly that comes of attachment to a woman (பெண்சேர்ந்தாம் பேதைமை) is never found (இல்) in those with a deliberating mind. Both end on 'பேதைமை ... இல்' and treat the lapse as a failure of understanding that knowledge excludes, once about another's wife in the Book of Virtue and once about subservience to one's own in the Book of Wealth.

832 defines the folly of all follies (பேதைமையுள் எல்லாம் பேதைமை) as setting one's love on what is not proper to one (கையல்லதன்கண் காதன்மை). 141 names one case of exactly that: the பேதைமை of desiring (பெட்டு ஒழுகும்) a woman who is another's. Read together, 141 is an instance of the general definition that 832 gives much later.

142 says that among all who stand outside virtue (அறன்கடை நின்றாருள் எல்லாம்) none is a greater fool than the one who stands at another's door (பிறன்கடை); 150 says that even one who does not keep to virtue and does wrong (அறன்வரையான் அல்ல செயினும்) does well not to desire another's woman. Both verses rank within the class of the non-virtuous, and both put this one offence at the bottom, 142 by naming the worst case and 150 by naming the one abstention still worth having.

143 says those who go on doing evil in the home of people who trust them (தெளிந்தாரில்) are 'no different from the dead' (விளிந்தாரின் வேறல்லர்); 926 uses the same construction for sleepers (துஞ்சினார் செத்தாரின் வேறல்லர்) and extends it to drinkers. Parimelazhagar explains 926 by the absence of awareness and 143 by the loss of aram, porul and inbam, so the same formula of living death is applied to a moral failure in one verse and to loss of consciousness in the other.

143 counts the betrayer of a trusting household as no different from the dead (விளிந்தாரின் வேறல்லர்); 214 says only the one who knows what is fitting lives (உயிர்வாழ்வான்), and anyone else is placed among the dead (செத்தாருள் வைக்கப்படும்). In both, being alive is measured by conduct and not by breath, once for a wrong committed and once for a duty to others left undone.

144 asks what greatness comes to, however great a person is (எனைத்துணையர் ஆயினும் என்னாம்), if he enters another's home without weighing it even a millet's worth (தினைத்துணையும் தேரான்). 965 says even those like a hill (குன்றின் அனையார்) sink if they do a lowering deed as small as a kunri seed. Both hold that standing does not outweigh a degrading act; 965 gives the general rule and 144 one named act.

Both verses use the millet's measure (தினைத்துணை). In 433 those who are ashamed of blame (பழிநாணுவார்) take a fault of a millet's size as large as a palmyra; in 144 the man entering another's home does not reflect even a millet's worth (தினைத்துணையும் தேரான்). The pair shows the same measure from opposite sides: the careful person enlarges the smallest fault, and the adulterer does not give the smallest thought.

145 says one who crosses into another's home thinking it easy (எளிதென இல்லிறப்பான்) gets blame that stands forever without dying (விளியாது நிற்கும் பழி). 284 says a love grown strong in theft (களவின்கண் கன்றிய காதல்) yields at harvest a distress that does not die (வீயா விழுமம்). The same logic, a desire for what is another's that looks light at the start and has a permanent result, is applied to another's wife and to another's goods.

233 says that apart from high renown nothing in the world stands without perishing (புகழல்லால் பொன்றாது நிற்பதொன்று இல்). 145 says the blame of the man who violates another's home also stands forever without dying (எஞ்ஞான்றும் விளியாது நிற்கும் பழி). Taken literally 145 names a second undying thing, so the pair shows the book treating lasting blame as the counterpart of lasting fame.

146 lists four things that never leave the man who crosses into another's home: enmity, sin, fear and blame (பகை பாவம் அச்சம் பழி). 171 says that one who covets another's good property without fairness finds his family ruined and fault brought on at once (குடிபொன்றிக் குற்றமும் ஆங்கே தரும்). Coveting another's wife and coveting another's goods are both given immediate, compound consequences; Parimelazhagar reads the பழி of 146 as blame on the family (குடிப்பழி), which brings it closer to the குடி of 171.

Both verses use the formula 'the one called a householder' (இல்வாழ்வான் என்பான்). 41 defines him by what he supports: he is the steady help of the three on their good path. 147 defines him by what he refrains from: he lives the household life with aram (அறனியலான்) who does not desire the womanhood of one who belongs to another (பிறனியலாள் பெண்மை நயவாதவன்). Together they give a positive and a negative test for the same title.

49 says that what is called aram is household life, and that it is good if there is nothing in it that another blames (பிறன்பழிப்பது இல்லாயின்). 147 says the householder living by aram is the one who does not desire another's woman. 147 can be read as naming a specific condition under which the household life of 49 stays free of others' blame; chapter 15 itself (145, 146) names பழி as the result of the offence.

Both verses redefine பேராண்மை, great manliness. 773 says people call fierceness (தறுகண்) great manliness, and that help given when something befalls the foe (ஊராண்மை) is its edge. 148 gives the name to not looking at another's wife (பிறன்மனை நோக்காத பேராண்மை). In both, the word for martial valour is moved toward restraint; Parimelazhagar on 148 says it is called 'great' because the inner enemy, desire, is harder to subdue than outer enemies.

1026 says what is called good manliness (நல்லாண்மை) is making oneself able to govern the house one was born into (இல்லாண்மை); 148 calls not looking at another man's home or wife (பிறன்மனை) great manliness (பேராண்மை). Both locate ஆண்மை in the household and not on the battlefield: one in building up one's own house, the other in leaving another's alone.

148 praises not even looking at (நோக்காத) another's wife; Parimelazhagar glosses this as not taking her into the mind. 282 says that even thinking in the heart (உள்ளத்தால் உள்ளலும்) of taking another's goods (பிறன்பொருளை) by stealth is wrong. In both chapters the prohibition is moved back from the act to the look or the thought, for another's wife and for another's property.

149 says those entitled to good (நலக்குரியார்) are those who do not touch the shoulders of a woman who belongs to another (பிறர்க்குரியாள் தோள் தோயாதார்). 916 says those who would spread their own good (தந்நலம் பாரிப்பார்) do not touch (தோயார்) the shoulders of women who spread a base charm to all. The same phrase for sexual union, தோள் தோய்தல், and the same word நலம் are used for the two forbidden unions, with another's wife and with courtesans, and in both abstaining is tied to one's own நலம்.

The two verses share a construction. 150: even if one does not keep to aram and does what is not aram (அறன்வரையான் அல்ல செயினும்), it is good not to desire another's woman. 181: even if one does not speak of aram and does what is not aram (அறங்கூறான் அல்ல செயினும்), it is pleasing to be called one who does not backbite. Each chapter picks out its own abstention as the one that still counts for a person who otherwise fails at virtue.

150 says not desiring another's woman is good even in one who practises no aram and does wrong; 297 says that if one can keep to not lying, then not doing the other virtues (அறம்பிற செய்யாமை) is still good. Both isolate a single restraint and say it holds its value without the rest of virtue. Set side by side, the book makes this kind of claim for more than one virtue, so each is better read as emphasis than as a ranking.

151 holds up the earth that supports those who dig into it (அகழ்வாரைத் தாங்கும் நிலம்) as the model for bearing with those who scorn us. 189 asks whether it is out of regard for aram that the earth bears the weight (வையம் ... பொறை) of the man who watches for someone's absence and speaks mean words. Both make the earth the bearer of people who abuse; 151 offers it as an example to follow, and 189 uses it to express wonder that the slanderer is tolerated at all.

In 151 the earth holds up (தாங்கும்) even those who dig into it. In 990, if the worthy decline in their worthiness, the great earth itself will not bear its load (இருநிலந்தான் தாங்காது மன்னோ பொறை). The earth's bearing, which 151 treats as unconditional toward those who injure it, is in 990 made to depend on the character of the சான்றோர், and the word பொறை, burden, is the same word that names the forbearance of chapter 16.

151 says bearing with those who scorn us is the foremost thing (பொறுத்தல் தலை). 579, in the chapter on kindly regard in the Book of Wealth, says that showing regard and bearing (கண்ணோடிப் பொறுத்தாற்றும் பண்பே தலை) even with those whose nature is to hurt us is the foremost quality. The same ranking, with the same words பொறுத்தல் and தலை, is given for the householder and again for the ruler.

152 says to bear excess always, and that forgetting it is better still (அதனை மறத்தல் அதனினும் நன்று). 108 says it is not good to forget a good done, and that it is good to forget what is not good that very day (நன்றல்லது அன்றே மறப்பது நன்று). Both end on forgetting a wrong as the good thing; 108 adds the contrast that kindness must not be forgotten and specifies 'that very day', which Parimelazhagar also reads into 152 (அப்பொழுதே மறத்தல்).

Parimelazhagar reads 152 as telling one to bear a wrong even when one is able to punish it (தாம் ஒறுத்தற்கு இயன்ற காலத்தும்). 301 states that condition outright: only the one who holds back anger where it can take effect (செல்லிடத்துக் காப்பான்) truly holds it back, and where it cannot, it makes no difference. 301 supplies the reason the commentator's condition matters: forbearance toward those one cannot hurt is not yet forbearance.

152 says to bear transgression always (என்றும்) and better still to forget it. 488, advising a king on timing, says: on seeing enemies, bear them (சுமக்க); when their end is seen to have come, the head goes down (கிழக்காம் தலை). In 488 the bearing is temporary and is kept in mind until the moment to act, where 152 asks for a bearing with no end that passes into forgetting. The Book of Wealth thus limits to a tactic what the Book of Virtue states without condition.

153 says the poverty within poverty is turning away a guest (இன்மையுள் இன்மை விருந்தொரால்); 89 says the poverty within having (உடைமையுள் இன்மை) is the folly of not tending guests, found in fools (மடவார்). The two share the paradox of a 'poverty' that is really inhospitality, and the word மடவார்: in 89 the fools are those who neglect guests, and in 153 they are the people one must bear with.

Both verses name a 'poverty within poverty' (இன்மையுள் இன்மை) and give different answers: in 153 it is turning away a guest, in 841 it is lack of understanding (அறிவின்மை), with other lack not counted as lack by the world. The same superlative formula serves hospitality in the Book of Virtue and intelligence in the Book of Wealth, which shows the formula working as emphasis within each chapter's topic.

153 says the strength within strength (வன்மையுள் வன்மை) is bearing with fools (மடவார்ப் பொறை); 444 says the chief of all strengths (வன்மையுள் எல்லாம் தலை) is to live so that those greater than oneself become one's own. Neither verse puts strength in force. One finds it in enduring those below one in understanding and the other in attaching oneself to those above.

154 says that one who wants நிறையுடைமை never to leave should guard forbearance; Parimelazhagar glosses நிறை here as சால்பு. 987 asks what use சால்பு is if one does not do pleasing things even to those who have done one harm (இன்னாசெய்தார்க்கும் இனியவே செய்யாக்கால்). On Parimelazhagar's reading the two say the same thing from both ends: forbearance keeps சால்பு in place, and சால்பு that does not show in the treatment of offenders is worth nothing.

154 ties நிறை to forbearance: to keep நிறையுடைமை, live guarding பொறையுடைமை. 864 pairs the same two things in the negative, describing the man who does not leave off anger and has no நிறை (நீங்கான் வெகுளி நிறையிலன்) as easy prey for anyone. The commentators gloss நிறை differently in the two places (Parimelazhagar: சால்பு in 154; Pope, following him, has keeping secrets in 864; Manakkudavar on 154 has a conduct of self-guarding), but in both verses its presence goes with restraint of anger and its absence with unchecked anger.

155 says the wise do not count as anything those who punish in return (ஒறுத்தாரை ஒன்றாக வையார்) and keep those who forbear like stored gold. 314 keeps the word ஒறுத்தல் and gives it a new content: the way to punish those who have done harm is to shame them by doing them good (அவர்நாண நன்னயஞ் செய்து விடல்). 314 thus shows the only form of 'punishing' that 155's judgment leaves open. (The Parimelazhagar text displayed for 314 in this edition belongs to 315.)

155 says those who punish (ஒறுத்தார்) are not counted as anything. 549 says that guarding the people and removing wrongdoing (குற்றம் கடிதல்) is no stain on a king but his work (வடுவன்று வேந்தன் தொழில்). Parimelazhagar restricts 155 to a harm done to oneself, and 549 concerns a ruler acting for his subjects, so 549 marks the limit of 155: the low regard for punishing applies to personal retaliation and not to the office of justice.

156 sets the one day's joy of those who retaliate (ஒருநாளை இன்பம்) against the lasting renown of those who forbear. 173 says those who want the other joy (மற்றின்பம்) will not do what is not aram out of desire for a small joy (சிற்றின்பம்). Both argue against a wrong by the shortness of the pleasure it buys, for retaliation in one verse and for coveting in the other.

156 grants the retaliator one day's pleasure and gives the forbearing renown to the end. 856 says that the life of one who says it is sweet (இனிது) to prevail in hostility is close to failure and ruin (தவலும் கெடலும் நணித்து). Both admit that getting the better of an opponent tastes sweet and both say the sweetness is brief; the verse in the Book of Wealth names ruin where the verse in the Book of Virtue names only the loss of lasting fame.

156 says those who forbear have renown until the end (பொன்றுந் துணையும் புகழ்), against one day's pleasure for those who retaliate; 145 says the man who violates another's home thinking it easy gets blame that never dies (விளியாது நிற்கும் பழி). The adjacent chapters use the same accounting, a brief gratification weighed against a permanent reputation, with புகழ் on one side and பழி on the other. Manakkudavar takes பொன்றுந் துணையும் as until the person's own death, Parimelazhagar as until the world ends.

157 says that though others do what is improper to one (திறனல்ல தற்பிறர் செய்யினும்), it is good not to do what is not aram. 312 says that even when someone has done harm out of hatred, not doing harm in return (மறுத்தின்னா செய்யாமை) is the settled principle of the stainless. The same rule appears in the householder's chapter on forbearance and in the ascetic's chapter on not harming, which makes it common to both ways of life.

157: though others do one wrong, not doing what is not aram is good (அறனல்ல செய்யாமை நன்று). 852: though someone does unbearable things intending division (பகல்கருதிப் பற்றா செயினும்), not doing harm with hostility in mind is the chief thing (இன்னாசெய்யாமை தலை). The 'even if they do ... not doing' structure and the refusal to answer in kind recur in the Book of Wealth's chapter on hostility, where the reason given is political prudence as well as virtue.

Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar read நோநொந்து in 157 as grieving for the suffering that will come to the wrongdoers. 319 states the mechanism behind that expectation: if one does harm to others in the forenoon, harm comes to oneself in the afternoon of its own accord (தாமே வரும்). On the commentators' reading 157 presupposes 319: the injured person pities the offender because the offence will return on him, and for the same reason does not add a wrong of his own. Kalaignar instead takes the pain in 157 as the injured person's own.

158 says to overcome those who do excessive wrong out of arrogance (மிகுதியான்) by one's own worthiness (தகுதியான் வென்றுவிடல்), which Parimelazhagar glosses as forbearance. 985 says the strength of the able is to bow (பணிதல்), and that this is the weapon by which the worthy change their opponents (மாற்றாரை மாற்றும் படை). Both describe yielding as the means of prevailing and use the vocabulary of contest, வெல்லல் and படை, for it.

158 calls forbearance toward the arrogant a victory (வென்றுவிடல்). 986 says the touchstone of சால்பு is to accept defeat (தோல்வி ... கொளல்) even from those who are not one's equals. The same conduct toward an overbearing lesser person is named winning in one verse and taking a loss in the other; 986 adds that it has to be felt and accepted as a defeat, which guards against reading 158 as a way of scoring over the offender. Manakkudavar on 158 says explicitly that forbearing is not defeat but is itself the victory.

158 says one defeats the overbearing by one's own forbearing worth. 1327, spoken by the man in the Book of Love, says that in a lovers' quarrel the one who loses has won (ஊடலில் தோற்றவர் வென்றார்), as is seen in the union that follows. The paradox that giving way is the real victory appears in ethics and again, in a dramatised speech, in love; the second is a lover's remark and not a moral rule, but the shape of the thought is the same.

Both verses play on இறந்தார் and துறந்தார். 310: those who go beyond bounds in anger (இறந்தார்) are like the dead, and those who have renounced anger are equal to renouncers (துறந்தார் துணை). 159: those who endure harsh words from the mouths of those who go beyond bounds (இறந்தார்வாய் இன்னாச்சொல்) have the purity of renouncers (துறந்தாரின் தூய்மை). In both, a householder's control over anger, his own or his response to another's, earns the standing of renunciation.

159 says those who endure (நோற்கிற்பவர்) the harsh words of transgressors are as pure as renouncers. 48 says a household life that keeps others on their path and does not slip from aram has more endurance than those who do penance (நோற்பாரின் நோன்மை உடைத்து). Both apply the ascetic's verb நோல் to the householder and set him level with or above the ascetic; Parimelazhagar on 159 adds that these are people who remain in household life.

159 praises those who endure harsh words (இன்னாச்சொல்) from people who overstep. 389 says the world rests under the parasol of the king who has the character to bear words bitter to the ear (செவிகைப்பச் சொற்பொறுக்கும்). The same capacity is a private virtue in one verse and a quality of rule in the other. Parimelazhagar takes the bitter words of 389 to be the rebukes of advisers, so there the speaker means well, unlike the transgressors of 159.

The two verses have the same build. 160: those who endure without eating (உண்ணாது நோற்பார்) are great, but behind those who endure others' harsh words (நோற்பாரின் பின்). 225: the strength of the strong is enduring hunger, and it comes behind the strength of those who remove that hunger (மாற்றுவார் ஆற்றலின் பின்). Each grants the faster his greatness and then places a household virtue, forbearance in one and giving in the other, ahead of him with the same closing word பின்.

261 defines the form of tavam as two things: bearing the pain that comes to one (உற்றநோய் நோன்றல்) and doing no harm to living beings. 160 uses the same verb for both the faster and the one who endures harsh words (நோற்பார்). By 261's definition the person in 160 who bears abuse and does not retaliate already meets both parts of tavam, which explains how 160 can rank him ahead of those who fast.

160 ranks those who fast behind those who bear harsh words; 295 says one who speaks truth in accord with his heart is above those who practise austerity together with giving (தவத்தொடு தானஞ்செய்வாரின் தலை). In both a virtue of everyday speech, enduring it in one case and keeping it truthful in the other, is placed above formal religious practice.

35 defines அறம் as what proceeds without slipping into four things, with அழுக்காறு named first. 161 takes that first item and tells a person to hold a heart without envy (அழுக்காறு இலாத இயல்பு) as his own ஒழுக்காறு, rule of conduct. Together they show envy treated as a matter of conduct to be kept, and not only as a feeling.

135 pairs the same two words: as the envious have no ஆக்கம், so one without ஒழுக்கம் has no உயர்வு. 161 fuses them, asking that freedom from அழுக்காறு be taken as ஒழுக்காறு. The rhyme ஒழுக்கு/அழுக்காறு is used in both to set envy and conduct side by side.

162 says that among excellent gains (விழுப்பேற்றின்) nothing equals being free of envy toward anyone (அஃதொப்பது இல்லை). 363 says there is no excellent wealth (விழுச்செல்வம்) like வேண்டாமை, here or there (அஃதொப்பது இல்). The same formula ranks an absence, of envy in the householder book and of wanting in the ascetic book, above every positive possession.

61 says that of all that can be gained (பெறுமவற்றுள்) the speaker knows none like children who know what should be known (மக்கட்பேறு). 162 uses the same vocabulary of பேறு for a gain that is purely inward: அழுக்காற்றின் அன்மை. Read together they show the book using 'the best of gains' for different goods in different chapters, so neither superlative should be taken as an exclusive ranking.

163 says the one who does not cherish another's prosperity (பிறனாக்கம் பேணாது) and envies it is called one who wants neither அறன் nor ஆக்கம். 1079 shows the same reaction in the கீழ்: on seeing others clothed and fed (உடுப்பதூஉம் உண்பதூஉம் காணின்) he is quick to find a fault in them. The later verse gives the behaviour that the earlier one judges.

141 says the folly of desiring a woman who is another's (பிறன்பொருளாள்) is not found in those who have seen அறம் and பொருள். 163 says the envier of பிறனாக்கம் is one who wants neither அறன் nor ஆக்கம். In adjacent chapters a wrong attitude to what is another's is measured against the same pair, virtue and wealth.

The second line of 136 is almost the second line of 164: இழுக்கத்தின் ஏதம் படுபாக்கு அறிந்து against இழுக்காற்றின் ஏதம் படுபாக்கு அறிந்து. In 136 the strong (உரவோர்) do not slacken in ஒழுக்கம்; in 164 people do no wrong out of envy (அழுக்காற்றின் அல்லவை செய்யார்). The repeated line gives the same ground for both restraints: knowing the harm that follows a lapse.

165 says envy is enough for the envious: it brings ruin even when enemies fail (ஒன்னார் வழுக்கியும் கேடீன்பது). 448 says a king without people who rebuke him perishes even with no one to ruin him (கெடுப்பார் இலானும் கெடும்). Both describe ruin that needs no outside enemy, once in a private vice and once in a ruler's unguarded state.

434 says fault itself is the enemy that brings one's end (குற்றமே அற்றம் தரூஉம் பகை). 165 says the same of one fault: envy suffices to ruin its holder without any ஒன்னார். The king's general rule in Book 2 has a specific case already stated in Book 1.

304 asks whether there is any other enemy than anger (சினத்தின் பகையும் உளவோ பிற), which kills smile and joy. 165 says the envious need no enemy since envy itself brings ruin. Two of the four things 35 excludes from virtue, anger and envy, are each described as the person's own enemy.

Both verses use the phrase உடுப்பதூஉம் உண்பதூஉம். In 1079 the base man sees others' clothing and food and finds fault with them; in 166 the kin of one who envies what is given (கொடுப்பது அழுக்கறுப்பான்) perish without clothing or food. The pairing shows what is envied returning as what is lost.

527 says crows do not hide food but call the others and eat, and that ஆக்கம் belongs only to those of that nature (அன்ன நீரார்க்கே). 166 gives the opposite disposition and result: one who grudges giving leaves his சுற்றம் without food or clothing. Both tie a household's kin and its prosperity to the attitude taken toward sharing.

167 says the fair goddess (செய்யவள்) grudges the envious man and shows him to her elder sister (தவ்வை). 617 names both sisters by residence: மாமுகடி lives in sloth, and தாமரையினாள் in the effort of the unslothful. The same pair of goddesses marks envy in Book 1 and sloth in Book 2 as conditions that hand a person over from fortune to misfortune.

84 says செய்யாள் dwells with a glad heart (அகனமர்ந்து) in the home of one who tends guests with a glad face. 167 has the same goddess grudge (அவ்வித்து) the envious man and pass him to her elder sister. She stays with the one who is glad to give to others and leaves the one who resents their good.

168 calls envy அழுக்காறு என ஒரு பாவி, which destroys fortune (திரு) and drives one to the bad place (தீயுழி). 1042 uses the same construction for poverty, இன்மை என ஒரு பாவி, which comes with both the next world and this one lost. Parimelazhagar reads 168 as a loss in both worlds too, so the two personified 'sinners' are given the same double effect.

169 says the prosperity of the crooked-hearted (அவ்விய நெஞ்சத்தான் ஆக்கம்) and the ruin of the upright (செவ்வியான் கேடு) will be pondered, which treats them as things that occur. 170 says none have grown great by envying (அழுக்கற்று அகன்றாரும் இல்லை) and none free of it have lost increase. The conflict holds if 169 is read as admitting real cases; Parimelazhagar removes it by supplying 'if they exist' and having the wise look for another cause.

117 says the world will not set down as ruin (கெடுவாக வையாது) the low state of one who stays in what is right through fairness. 169 lists the ruin of the upright (செவ்வியான் கேடு) as something to be pondered. 117 limits how that கேடு should be counted: the upright person's decline is not regarded as real ruin.

375 says that in making wealth good things can all turn bad and bad things good (நல்லவை எல்லாஅந் தீயவாம் தீயவும் நல்லவாம்), in the chapter on ஊழ். 169 leaves the envious man's prosperity and the upright man's ruin as a puzzle to be thought about (நினைக்கப்படும்). The fate chapter supplies one answer the book offers to that puzzle; Parimelazhagar's note on 169 likewise points to earlier deeds.

135 takes it as given that there is no ஆக்கம் in the envious (அழுக்காறுடையான்கண் ஆக்கம் ... இல்லை) and uses that as the comparison for conduct. 170 states the same as a rule with no exceptions: none have grown great through envy, and none without it have fallen away from பெருக்கம். The chapter on conduct relies on what the chapter on envy concludes.

171 says that coveting another's goods without fairness makes the family perish and brings faults at once (குடிபொன்றிக் குற்றமும் ஆங்கே தரும்). 604 says of the slothful that the family dies down and faults multiply (குடிமடிந்து குற்றம் பெருகும்). The same double penalty, on the குடி and in குற்றம், is attached to greed in Book 1 and to sloth in Book 2.

112 says the wealth of one who has rectitude (செப்பம் உடையவன் ஆக்கம்) does not decay and is a security for his descendants (எச்சத்திற்கு ஏமாப்பு). 171 gives the reverse case: coveting நடுவின்றி destroys the குடி. Both measure fairness about property by what happens to the family line and not only to the person.

172 says those ashamed of unfairness (நடுவன்மை நாணுபவர்) will not do blameworthy things out of desire for the gain to be had (படுபயன் வெஃகி). 113 gives the instruction that goes with it: gain that comes from leaving fairness (நடுவிகந்தாம் ஆக்கம்) is to be dropped that very day, even if it brings only good. 172 describes the character and 113 the rule it follows.

164 says people do no wrong out of envy because they know the harm that comes of the wrong path (ஏதம் படுபாக்கு அறிந்து). 172 says people do nothing blameworthy out of coveting because they are ashamed of unfairness (நாணுபவர்). The neighbouring chapters use the same sentence shape, ending in செய்யார், with knowledge of consequences as the check in one and shame in the other.

173 says those who want the other joy (மற்றின்பம்) will not do what is not அறன் out of desire for a small joy (சிற்றின்பம்). 39 says only what comes through virtue is joy (அறத்தான் வருவதே இன்பம்) and all else lies outside it. 39 supplies the content of 173's 'other joy', and Parimelazhagar glosses it that way, as the lasting joy that comes by virtue; Pope instead takes it as the joy of heaven.

754 says wealth that comes without wrong and with knowledge of the means (தீதின்றி வந்த பொருள்) yields both அறன் and இன்பம். 173 says the small joy got by coveting is refused by those who want the other joy. Together they show the choice in 173 is not between wealth and joy: wealth rightly got delivers the joy that coveting forfeits.

174 says those of faultless sight who have conquered the senses will not covet on the thought 'we have nothing' (இலமென்று வெஃகுதல் செய்யார்). 205 forbids doing evil on the same plea (இலன் என்று தீயவை செய்யற்க) and adds that doing so makes one poor again. Both name poverty as the excuse and reject it; 205 gives the consequence that 174 leaves unstated.

1040 says the good woman called Land laughs on seeing those who sit idle saying 'we have nothing' (இலமென்று அசைஇ இருப்பாரை). 174 has the same words, இலமென்று, as the thought that does not move the self-controlled to covet. The plea of having nothing is refused twice: it excuses neither taking from others nor sitting idle.

656 says that even if one must see the mother who bore one go hungry (ஈன்றாள் பசி காண்பான் ஆயினும்), one should not do what the worthy condemn. 174 says the thought of being without does not make the self-controlled covet. 656 pushes the same refusal to its hardest case, where the want is another's and not one's own.

175 asks what fine and wide understanding comes to (அஃகி அகன்ற அறிவு என்னாம்) if one covets and acts senselessly toward everyone. 315 asks whether anything comes of understanding (அறிவினான் ஆகுவதுண்டோ) if one does not guard against another's pain as one's own. Both test அறிவு by how its owner treats other people, in coveting and in causing hurt.

834 says no one is a greater fool than the person who has studied, understood and taught others and yet does not restrain himself (தானடங்கா). 175 says subtle and wide understanding is worth nothing if its owner covets and does வெறிய things. Both hold that learning which does not govern conduct does not count.

285 says a loving nature with அருள் in view (அருள்கருதி) is not found in those who, with goods in view (பொருள்கருதி), watch for another's lapse. 176 says one who stands on the path desiring அருள் (அருள்வெஃகி) perishes if he desires பொருள் (பொருள்வெஃகி) and plots wrongs. Both verses set அருள் and பொருள் as rival objects of one desire and say the second drives out the first.

204 says not to plot another's ruin even by a lapse (சூழற்க), because அறம் will plot the ruin of the plotter (அறஞ்சூழும் சூழ்ந்தவன் கேடு). 176 says that one who plots wrongs for wealth (பொல்லாத சூழ) will perish (கெடும்). The shared verb சூழ் places the ruin at the stage of planning, before any act; 204 names the agent of that ruin.

177 says not to want gain that comes by coveting, since at its ripening (விளைவயின்) the fruit is hard to make good. 284 says the love grown strong in stealth yields, at its ripening (விளைவின்கண்), a sorrow that does not die. Coveting in the householder book and theft in the ascetic book are both judged by the harvest image, where the gain looks sound until it ripens.

931 opens with the same prohibition, வேண்டற்க: do not want gambling even if you win, because the winnings are like the hook a fish has swallowed. 177 says வேண்டற்க of the gain got by coveting, whose fruit turns out badly. Both warn against a gain that is real at the moment of taking and harmful afterwards.

177 argues from the outcome: gain got by coveting does not turn out well when enjoyed. 113 says gain that comes from leaving fairness is to be given up that very day even if it brings only good (நன்றே தரினும்). 113 removes the dependence on outcome, so the prohibition would stand even where 177's prediction failed.

178 asks what keeps wealth from shrinking (அஃகாமை செல்வத்திற்கு யாதெனின்) and answers: not coveting what is in another's hand. 112 says the wealth of one who has rectitude does not decay (சிதைவின்றி) and protects his descendants. Both make fairness about others' property the condition for one's own wealth lasting.

283 says gain made by stealth perishes beyond measure even as it seems to grow (ஆவது போலக் கெடும்). 178 says the way to keep wealth from shrinking is not to covet another's goods. 283 gives the negative side of the same claim: what is added by taking another's property is not a lasting addition.

179 says திரு, knowing the way (திறன் அறிந்து), goes to those who know virtue and do not covet. 594 says ஆக்கம் asks the way (அதர்வினாய்) and goes to the one of unwavering drive. In both, fortune is a traveller that seeks the person out; Book 1 gives non-coveting as what draws it and Book 2 gives energy.

130 says அறம் itself watches for the right moment (செவ்வி) and enters by the path of one who has guarded against anger and learned restraint. 179 says திரு knows the fitting way and reaches the one who does not covet. Each has a personified good coming unsought to a person defined by a restraint.

167 says the fair goddess grudges the envious man and shows him to her elder sister. 179 says திரு goes to those who know virtue and do not covet. The two neighbouring chapters use the goddess in opposite directions: she leaves the one who resents others' goods and comes to the one who does not want them.

180 says the pride called not-wanting (வேண்டாமை என்னுஞ் செருக்கு) yields victory, where Parimelazhagar glosses செருக்கு as wealth. 363 says there is no excellent wealth like வேண்டாமை in this world or the other. The word moves from not wanting another's goods in the householder chapter to not wanting anything in the renunciation chapter, and is counted a possession in both.

692 says that not desiring what kings desire (மன்னர் விழைப விழையாமை) brings lasting prosperity through those kings. 180 says not wanting others' goods yields victory, while coveting without thought yields destruction.
