The courtier's rule in Book 2 follows the same logic as 180: refraining from what belongs to another is what secures gain.

181 says that even of a man who does not speak of virtue and does wrong (அறங்கூறான் அல்ல செயினும்), it is pleasing to hear 'he does not backbite'. 150 uses the same frame, அறன்வரையான் அல்ல செயினும், and says it is good that he not desire another man's wife. The pairing shows the book using one formula to mark two abstentions as a floor that still counts in a person who has otherwise let virtue go.

181 holds that not backbiting is still good in a man who otherwise does wrong (அல்ல செயினும் ... இனிது). 297 says that if one keeps to not lying, not doing the other virtues is good (அறம்பிற செய்யாமை செய்யாமை நன்று). Both single out one restraint of speech and weigh it against the whole of the rest of conduct, though 297 goes further and treats it as sufficient.

182 condemns running a person down behind his back and then smiling falsely at him (புறனழீஇப் பொய்த்து நகை). 824 warns one to fear the deceivers who smile sweetly with the face and are bitter within (முகத்தின் இனிய நகாஅ அகத்தின்னா வஞ்சரை). The false smile is judged from the doer's side in the Book of Virtue and from the victim's side in the chapter on false friendship.

182 calls it worse than denying virtue to slander someone when absent and smile at him when present. 820 tells one not to come near those who are friendly in the house and blame you in the assembly (மனைக்கெழீஇ மன்றில் பழிப்பார்). 820 turns the moral verdict of 182 into practical advice about which friendships to refuse.

183 says that dying yields more of the gain the books of virtue speak of than living by backbiting and falsehood (பொய்த்துயிர் வாழ்தலின் சாதல்). 967 says that rather than live by following those who scorn you (வாழ்தலின்), it is better to be called ruined as you are. Both use the comparative 'than living thus' to say that a kind of life can cost more than its end, once for the slanderer's two faces and once for lost honour.

183 ranks death above a life kept up by backbiting and pretence. 230 says nothing is more bitter than death (சாதலின் இன்னாத தில்லை), yet even it is sweet when one cannot give. Each verse measures a fault or lack by setting death beside it and finding death the better; the pairing shows how the book uses that comparison for both a wrong done and a good left undone.

184 concedes speaking without kindly regard to a person's face (கண்ணின்று கண்ணறச் சொல்லினும்) and forbids only the word said in his absence that does not look to what follows (முன்னின்று பின்நோக்காச் சொல்). 795 goes further and tells one to seek out friends able to speak so that one weeps and to rebuke (அழச்சொல்லி ... இடித்து). What 184 merely tolerates, hard speech face to face, 795 treats as a mark of the friend worth choosing.

184: though you speak harshly to his face (சொல்லினும்), do not speak (சொல்லற்க) the heedless word behind his back. 197: let the worthy say what lacks நயன் if they must (சொல்லினுஞ் சொல்லுக), it is good that they not say what lacks use. The two neighbouring chapters use the same concessive move, granting a lesser fault of speech in order to isolate the one the chapter is about.

185 says that a man's heart does not really speak virtue is seen from the meanness of his backbiting (புறஞ்சொல்லும் புன்மையாற் காணப்படும்). 193 says that expansive talk of useless things itself declares the speaker to be without நயன் (நயனிலன் என்பது சொல்லும்). In both a kind of speech is treated as evidence about the speaker, whatever he professes.

34 says that being spotless in the mind is the whole of virtue and the rest is noise (மனத்துக்கண் மாசிலன் ஆதல் ... ஆகுல நீர பிற). 185 applies this to a case: a man may say virtue is good, but his backbiting shows it is not said from the heart (அறஞ்சொல்லும் நெஞ்சத்தான் அன்மை). 185 gives a test by which the outward show that 34 dismisses can be detected.

185 reads a man's inner lack of virtue from his backbiting. 959 says that as the sprout shows what lies in the soil, the words of the mouth show the family one is born in (காட்டும் குலத்தில் பிறந்தார் வாய்ச்சொல்). Both treat speech as the visible sign of something hidden, the heart in one case and lineage in the other.

186 says the one who tells another's blame (பிறன்பழி கூறுவான்) will have his own faults sorted through and told (தன்பழியுள்ளும் திறன்தெரிந்து கூறப்படும்). 319 says that hurt done to others in the forenoon comes back on oneself in the afternoon (பிற்பகல் தாமே வரும்). The same return of the deed appears for speech and for injury; in 186 the return is carried out by other people's tongues.

186 warns the teller of others' faults that his own will be told. 980 says greatness covers another's weakness while smallness only tells faults (சிறுமைதான் குற்றமே கூறிவிடும்). 186 gives the consequence of the habit and 980 gives its diagnosis: fault-telling is what smallness does.

187 says those who do not know how to make friends by words that bring laughter (நகச்சொல்லி நட்பாடல் தேற்றாதவர்) will part even their own kin by words that divide (பகச்சொல்லிக் கேளிர்ப் பிரிப்பர்). 525 says one who can give and speak pleasantly will be surrounded by kin in layers (இன்சொலும் ஆற்றின் ... சுற்றத்தால் சுற்றப்படும்). The two state the same link between speech and keeping one's people, from its negative and positive sides, in the Book of Virtue and the Book of Wealth.

187 treats speaking so that others laugh (நகச்சொல்லி) as the way friendship is made. 784 says friendship is not for laughing (நகுதற் பொருட்டன்று நட்டல்) but for going ahead to rebuke when the friend oversteps. 784 limits 187: pleasant talk may begin a friendship, but it is not what the friendship is for.

187 blames those who divide their own kin by divisive talk (கேளிர்ப் பிரிப்பர்). 633 lists dividing (பிரித்தல்) among a minister's abilities, together with keeping his own side and rejoining those who have parted; Parimelazhagar takes the dividing to be of the enemy's allies. The same act is a fault when turned on one's own people and a skill of statecraft when turned on opponents.

188 asks what those whose way is to spread even the faults of people close to them (துன்னியார் குற்றமும் தூற்றும்) would do to strangers (என்னைகொல் ஏதிலார் மாட்டு). In 1165 the woman asks what those who can bring grief within friendship (நட்பினுள்) would become in enmity. Both argue from conduct toward intimates to what must follow toward others; in 1165 it is a lover's complaint, not a general teaching.

188 describes people whose habit is to broadcast (தூற்றும்) the faults of those near them. 1076 likens the base to a beaten drum because they carry any secret they have heard to others (கேட்ட மறை பிறர்க்கு உய்த்துரைக்கலான்). 1076 places the habit of 188 in the Kural's portrait of the base person.

151 makes the earth that holds up those who dig into it (அகழ்வாரைத் தாங்கும் நிலம்) the model of bearing with those who scorn you. 189 asks whether it is with an eye to virtue that the earth bears the weight (பொறை) of the man who watches for someone's absence to speak mean words. 189 turns the earlier image on the backbiter: he is carried only because the earth is forbearing; Parimelazhagar reads it as the earth taking this bearing to be its virtue.

189 speaks of the backbiter as a weight the earth bears (வையம் ... பொறை). 572 says the existence of those without kindly regard is a burden to the earth (நிலக்குப் பொறை). The figure of a person as dead weight on the ground is used in both for someone who fails others in ordinary dealings, by malicious speech in one and by lack of regard in the other.

189 wonders that the earth bears the backbiter's weight at all. 990 says that if the worthy decline in worth, the great earth will not bear its load (இருநிலந்தான் தாங்காது மன்னோ பொறை). Together they show the image used at both ends: the earth strains under the bad man, and is able to carry its load only while the worthy stay worthy.

190 asks what harm could come to living beings if people saw their own faults as they see those of strangers (தங்குற்றங் காண்கிற்பின்). 436 asks what fault could attach to a ruler who first removes his own fault and then looks at others' (தன்குற்றம் நீக்கிப் பிறர்குற்றங் காண்கிற்பின்). Both use the same conditional காண்கிற்பின் and the same order of self before others, as an ethic for everyone and as a rule for the king who must judge.

190 wishes that people would see their own faults as they see a stranger's. 930 asks whether a drinker, when sober and seeing another man drunk, does not think of his own lapse when he drinks (உள்ளான்கொல் உண்டதன் சோர்வு). 930 is a concrete instance of the failure 190 names: the other man's fault is seen clearly and one's own identical fault is not.

193 says that a man's spreading out useless matter in speech itself announces that he is without நயன் (நயனிலன் என்பது சொல்லும்). 959 says the words of the mouth show the family one comes from, as a sprout shows the soil. In both the speech testifies about the speaker; 193 makes the talk itself the subject of the verb 'says', which Parimelazhagar notes.

97 says the word that yields use and does not part from good quality (பயன்ஈன்று பண்பின் தலைப்பிரியாச் சொல்) produces நயன் and brings good (நயன் ஈன்று நன்றி பயக்கும்). 194 says words without use and without quality (பயன்சாராப் பண்பில்சொல்), spoken among many, are without நயன் and remove one from good (நயன்சாரா நன்மையின் நீக்கும்). The four terms பயன், பண்பு, நயன் and நன்மை/நன்றி recur in the same roles, so 194 reads as the negative image of 97.

195 says that if people of fine nature (நீர்மையுடையார்) speak useless things, their distinction and the regard it earned leave them. 965 says even those like a hill will sink if they do a lowering thing the size of a kunri seed. Both hold that standing does not protect the eminent from a small lapse; 195 applies this to idle speech.

195 says useless talk costs people of fine nature their distinction (சீர்மை சிறப்பொடு நீங்கும்). 957 says a fault in the well-born shows up high, like the spot on the moon (மதிக்கண் மறுப்போல் உயர்ந்து). 957 supplies a reason for 195: a fault that would pass unnoticed in others is conspicuous in those held high.

196 says not to call the man who keeps up useless talk a man (மகன் எனல்) but chaff among people (மக்கட் பதடி). 1071 says the base look just like human beings (மக்களே போல்வர் கயவர்). Both separate the human form from being fully a person; 196 gives one specific ground for the distinction, and Parimelazhagar explains the chaff as lacking the kernel of understanding.

196 calls the habitual idle talker chaff, a husk with nothing in it. 406 says the unlearned can only be said to exist and are like barren saline land that yields nothing (பயவாக் களரனையர்). Both take a farming image of something that looks like the useful thing and gives no yield, and both turn on பயன், what a person produces.

197 lets the worthy say even what lacks நயன் but holds that they should not say what lacks use (பயனில சொல்லாமை நன்று). 697 tells one who serves a king to say what is wanted and never to say what is without use even if asked (வினையில எஞ்ஞான்றும் கேட்பினும் சொல்லாவிடல்); Parimelazhagar glosses வினையில as matters without benefit. The rule against useless speech is kept as firmly at court as in private ethics, and neither verse lets circumstances excuse it.

193 says that useless talk at length shows the speaker to be without நயன், so the two faults go together. 197 separates them and ranks them: speech without நயன் may be let pass in the worthy, speech without use may not. Read together, 197 makes uselessness the graver of the two; Parimelazhagar draws the same ranking from சொல்லினும்.

199 says those of stainless sight, freed from delusion (மருள்தீர்ந்த மாசறு காட்சியவர்), do not say meaningless things even by forgetfulness. 352 uses nearly the same phrase, மருள்நீங்கி மாசறு காட்சியவர்க்கு, for those to whom darkness departs and joy comes; Parimelazhagar takes it there as the true knowledge that ends birth. The phrase that names the liberated knower in the chapter on realisation is used in 199 to describe how such a person speaks.

199: those of clear sight do not say meaningless things even in forgetfulness (பொச்சாந்தும் சொல்லார்). 139: for those who have conduct, saying evil things with the mouth even by a slip is not possible (வழுக்கியும் வாயாற் சொலல் ஒல்லா). Both claim that a settled quality rules out even accidental bad speech, with knowledge as the ground in one and conduct in the other.

199 says what those of stainless sight will not say. 258 says those whose sight has parted from fault (செயிரின் தலைப்பிரிந்த காட்சியார்) will not eat flesh that has parted from life. The book repeatedly states a restraint as what people of clear காட்சி simply do not do; here the same form covers speech and diet.

200 says to speak, among words, those that have use and not those that have none (சொல்லுக சொல்லிற் பயனுடைய). 645 says to speak a word after knowing there is no other word that can defeat it (சொல்லுக சொல்லைப் பிறிதோர்சொல்). Both open with சொல்லுக and play on repeated சொல்; the test for a word is use in the Book of Virtue and whether it can be beaten in the minister's chapter on eloquence.

201 says those practised in evil do not fear 'தீவினை என்னும் செருக்கு' while the excellent (விழுமியார்) do. 428 gives the general rule in the chapter on understanding: not fearing what is to be feared (அஞ்சுவது அஞ்சாமை) is folly, and fearing it is 'அறிவார் தொழில்'. Read together, the fear in 201 is a working of knowledge and not timidity; Parimelazhagar on 428 lists sin, blame and ruin among the things to be feared.

Both end on the phrase 'என்னும் செருக்கு'. In 201 it is 'தீவினை என்னும் செருக்கு', which Parimelazhagar glosses as a delusion (மயக்கம்) and Manakkudavar as an exhilaration (களிப்பு) that the good fear; in 180 it is 'வேண்டாமை என்னும் செருக்கு', the pride of not wanting, which yields victory (விறல்). The same word names a heady state to be dreaded in one verse and a state worth having in the other, depending on what it rests on.

201 makes fear of evil deeds the mark of the excellent. 244 says that for one who sustains living beings and practises அருள் there are no deeds his own life need fear ('தன்னுயிர் அஞ்சும் வினை இல்'). The fear 201 commends is aimed at one's own possible deeds, and 244 names the condition under which nothing of that kind remains to be feared.

202 says evil deeds are to be feared more than fire ('தீயினும் அஞ்சப்படும்') because they yield evil. 129 sets fire against the tongue: a wound burned by fire heals, the scar burned by the tongue does not ('ஆறாதே நாவினாற் சுட்ட வடு'). In both, fire is the harm that ends, used to measure a harm that lasts; Parimelazhagar on 202 makes this explicit, saying fire cannot follow one into another time, place or body.

202 ranks evil deeds above fire as a thing to fear. 896, in the Book of Wealth, says one burned by fire may still survive ('எரியால் சுடப்படினும் உய்வுண்டாம்') but those who keep wronging the great will not. The same comparison, fire as the survivable danger, is applied once to one's own deeds and once to the anger of the powerful.

203 calls it the chief of all understanding to refrain from doing evil even to those who hate one ('செறுவார்க்கும் செய்யா விடல்'). 312 says that not hurting in return even one who has hurt you out of hatred ('கறுத்து இன்னா செய்த அக்கண்ணும்') is the settled stand of the stainless. The same rule is called knowledge (அறிவு) in the householder's chapter and purity (மாசற்றார் கோள்) in the ascetic's.

203 puts non-retaliation at the head of understanding ('அறிவினுள் எல்லாம் தலை'). 315 asks what understanding achieves at all ('அறிவினான் ஆகுவது உண்டோ') if one does not guard another's pain as one's own. 315 supplies a reason 203 leaves unstated: understanding is measured by how one treats others' pain, so harming even an enemy shows a failure of it.

203 asks only for restraint: do no evil even to enemies. 987 asks what worth (சால்பு) is good for if it does not do pleasant things even to those who did one harm ('இன்னா செய்தார்க்கும் இனியவே செய்யாக்கால்'). The Book of Wealth's ideal of the சான்றோர் goes one step beyond the householder's rule, from not returning harm to returning good.

In 204 அறம் is an agent that plots the ruin of anyone who plots another's ('அறம் சூழும் சூழ்ந்தவன் கேடு'). In 130 அறம் is again an agent, this time watching for the right moment to come to the man who has guarded against anger and learned restraint ('செவ்வி அறம் பார்க்கும்'). Parimelazhagar reads both as அறக்கடவுள்; the pair shows the same personified virtue seeking out a person for ruin in one case and for favour in the other.

204 forbids even contemplating another's ruin, even by a lapse ('மறந்தும் பிறன்கேடு சூழற்க'). 282 says that even to think in the heart of stealing another's goods is wrong ('உள்ளத்தால் உள்ளலும் தீதே'). Both place the fault at the thought, before any act, one for harm and one for theft.

204 says that if one plots another's ruin, virtue plots one's own. 319 states the return in terms of time: harm done to others in the forenoon brings harm to oneself in the afternoon, of itself ('பிற்பகல் தாமே வரும்'). 319's 'தாமே' leaves the return impersonal where 204 gives it an agent, and Parimelazhagar on 204 adds the same point about speed: virtue begins plotting at the very moment the plotter does.

205 forbids doing evil on the plea 'I have nothing' ('இலன் என்று'), since it only makes one poor again. 174 says those of faultless sight who have mastered the senses will not covet on the thought 'we have nothing' ('இலமென்று'). The same excuse is refused in both; 205 answers it with the consequence, 174 with the kind of person who never offers it.

205 rules out poverty as a ground for evil deeds. 656 takes the hardest case: even if one must see the mother who bore one go hungry ('ஈன்றாள் பசி காண்பான் ஆயினும்'), one should not do what the worthy condemn. Parimelazhagar notes that 656 sets aside a general rule of the dharma texts allowing wrong to feed one's dependants, which shows how far 205's principle is taken.

205 quotes the plea 'இலன் என்று' as an excuse for wrongdoing. 1040 quotes the same plea, 'இலமென்று', as an excuse for sitting idle, and says the good woman called Land laughs at those who make it. The book hears 'I have nothing' twice as a pretext, once for evil and once for sloth, and rejects it both times.

206: one who does not want afflicting things to overpower him ('நோய்ப்பால தன்னை அடல் வேண்டாதான்') should not do evil to others. 320: all pains rest on those who caused pain, so those who want freedom from pain cause none ('நோய் செய்யார் நோயின்மை வேண்டுபவர்'). The claim and its form (நோய், வேண்டு-) are nearly the same, stated once for the householder in the chapter on fearing evil deeds and once among the ascetic virtues.

206 gives a self-regarding reason for not harming others: the harm comes back on oneself. 316 gives a different ground: what one has oneself perceived as painful ('இன்னா எனத் தான் உணர்ந்தவை') one must not do to another. 206 alone could read as prudence; 316 shows the book also rests the same rule on knowing the other's pain from one's own.

207: whatever enmity people incur they survive ('உய்வர்'), but the enmity of deeds does not leave and follows to kill. 110: those who destroy any other good have an escape ('உய்வுண்டாம்'), but there is none ('உய்வில்லை') for one who destroys a kindness done to him. Both use the same figure, everything else can be escaped except this, to single out one thing: evil deeds in general in 207, ingratitude in 110.

207 treats one's evil deeds as an enemy ('வினைப்பகை') worse than any outward one. 434, advising the king, says fault itself is the enemy that brings ruin ('குற்றமே அற்றம் தரூஉம் பகை') and so guarding against fault should be one's aim. The two verses, one in the Book of Virtue and one in the Book of Wealth, both move the real enemy from outside to one's own conduct.

207 says the enmity of deeds does not leave and follows behind to kill ('வீயாது பின்சென்று அடும்'). 208 gives the image for it: the ruin of evildoers is like a person's shadow that does not leave and stays at the foot ('வீயாது அடி உறைந்தற்று'). The repeated 'வீயாது' ties them, and both Manakkudavar and Parimelazhagar say 208 illustrates what 207 asserted.

208: the ruin of those who did evil is like a shadow that never leaves a person. 36: virtue done now is, at the time one perishes, a companion that does not perish ('பொன்றுங்கால் பொன்றாத் துணை'). Both say a person's deeds stay with him; the good deed stays as a companion and the evil deed's ruin as a shadow at his heel.

208 uses a simile of something that cannot fail to happen: ruin stays with the evildoer as his shadow stays at his foot. 307 does the same for anger: the ruin of one who treats anger as a thing of worth is like the hand of one who strikes the ground, which cannot miss ('கை பிழையாதற்று'). Both verses take 'கேடு' as their subject and end on a simile of certainty, one for evil deeds and one for anger.

209: if a person loves himself ('தன்னைத்தான் காதலன் ஆயின்'), let him not go near evil deeds, however small. 305: if you would guard yourself ('தன்னைத்தான் காக்கின்'), guard against anger, or anger will kill you yourself. Both open with the same conditional about one's own self and argue from self-interest, one against evil deeds and one against anger.

209 assumes that doing evil is acting against oneself: one who loves himself stays away from it. 843 says the suffering that those without understanding inflict on themselves is hard even for their enemies ('செறுவார்க்கும்') to inflict. 843 describes the person who fails 209's test, and Parimelazhagar's comment there names poverty, blame and sin as what such people bring on themselves.

210 says that one who does not stray aside and do evil is 'அருங்கேடன்', a person for whom ruin is rare or, in Parimelazhagar's gloss, absent. 169 admits that the upright man's ruin ('செவ்வியான் கேடும்') and the crooked-hearted man's prosperity occur and must be thought about ('நினைக்கப்படும்'). They conflict if 210 is read, with Parimelazhagar and Kalaignar, as promising no ruin at all in this life; Parimelazhagar resolves 169 by referring such cases to deeds of earlier births.

210 promises that the one who does no evil will not come to ruin. 117 says the world will not count as ruin ('கெடுவாக வையாது') the low state (தாழ்வு) of one who stays in virtue by standing fair. 117 allows that the upright may be brought low and changes what counts as 'கேடு', which limits how literally 210's promise can be taken.

210: know ('அறிக') that one who does not turn aside to do evil has no ruin. 116: if one's heart leaves what is fair and does wrong, let one know ('அறிக') 'I shall perish' ('கெடுவல் யான்'). They state the same law from its two sides with the same imperative, 210 for the one who keeps straight and 116 for the one who leaves the middle.

211 says obligation (கடப்பாடு) wants no return, and asks what the world does for the rain in exchange ('என் ஆற்றுங் கொல்லோ'). 101, on gratitude, says that for help given when none was given first, earth and heaven together are hardly repayment ('ஆற்றல் அரிது'). The giver's side and the receiver's side meet: the giver asks for nothing, and the receiver is told that nothing would be enough.

211 uses the rain cloud (மாரி) as the model of one who gives to the world and gets nothing back. 1010 uses it again: the short-lived want of the renowned rich is like the rain cloud running dry ('மாரி வறங்கூர்ந்தனையது'). The same figure covers both the giving and its interruption; Parimelazhagar on 1010 takes the simile to imply that such poverty passes quickly and the giving resumes.

211 says duty-giving seeks no return (கைம்மாறு). 221, opening the next chapter, defines giving as giving to those who have nothing, and says everything else has the nature of 'குறியெதிர்ப்பை', a measured loan to be returned. 221 turns 211's point into a test: a gift that looks to a return is not giving.

212 says all the wealth produced by exertion ('தாளாற்றித் தந்த பொருள்') is for doing 'வேளாண்மை', benefaction. 613 says the proud distinction called benefaction ('வேளாண்மை என்னும் செருக்கு') rests in the quality called exertion ('தாளாண்மை'). The same two words are paired from opposite ends: in the Book of Virtue helping others is the purpose of earning, and in the Book of Wealth effort is the basis that makes helping possible.

212 ends 'வேளாண்மை செய்தற் பொருட்டு': earned wealth exists for the sake of benefaction. 81 ends on the same words: all of staying at home and keeping a household is for the sake of tending guests and doing them good. The household in 81 and wealth in 212 are given the same purpose in the same formula.

212 says wealth is for benefaction, with 'தக்கார்க்கு' read by Manakkudavar and Kalaignar as the worthy who receive it and by Parimelazhagar as the worthy who own it. 1006 describes the failure of this purpose: one who neither enjoys his great wealth nor gives anything to the worthy ('தக்கார்க்கு ஒன்று ஈதல் இயல்பிலாதான்') is an affliction (ஏதம்) to it. 1006 uses 'தக்கார்க்கு' plainly of recipients, which supports the Manakkudavar reading of 212.

213: neither in the world of the gods nor here ('புத்தேள் உலகத்தும் ஈண்டும்') is it easy to find another good like ஒப்புரவு. 363: there is no excellent wealth here like not wanting, and nothing there equals it either ('ஈண்டில்லை ஆண்டும் அஃதொப்பது இல்'). The same two-world formula crowns benevolence in the householder's section and desirelessness in the renouncer's; taken literally the two superlatives compete, and the pairing shows each section naming its own highest good.

213 ranks ஒப்புரவு above anything to be had in the gods' world or this one. 222 says giving is good even if there were no higher world ('மேலுலகம் இல்லெனினும் ஈதலே நன்று'). Both detach the worth of helping others from heaven as a reward: in 213 heaven holds nothing better, and in 222 the good stands even without heaven.

214: only one who knows what is fitting (ஒத்தது) lives, and anyone else is placed among the dead ('செத்தாருள் வைக்கப்படும்'). 1001: one who has piled up great wealth and does not use it is dead ('செத்தான்'), with nothing left for him to do. 1001 gives a concrete case of 214's verdict in the chapter on useless wealth: the hoarder is the man who does not know ஒப்புரவு.

214 defines who truly lives ('உயிர்வாழ்வான்') by knowing and doing what is fitting toward others. 240 defines it by reputation: those who live without blame are the ones who live, and those who live without renown do not ('வாழாதவர்'). Both redefine being alive by a social measure and count the rest as not living; the chapters on benevolence, giving and renown run in sequence.

Parimelazhagar reads 'ஒத்தது' in 214 as the way of the world (உலகநடை): one who knows and follows it lives. 140 says those who have not learned to conduct themselves in accord with the world ('உலகத்தோடு ஒட்ட ஒழுகல்') lack understanding however much they have studied. On that reading both make accord with the world the test of a person, of being alive in 214 and of having understanding in 140; Manakkudavar instead takes ஒத்தது as ஒப்புரவு itself.

215: the wealth of the greatly wise man is like the village drinking tank filled with water ('ஊருணி நீர்நிறைந்தற்று'). 523: the life of one who does not mingle with his kin is like a tank filling with water without a bank ('குளவளாக் கோடின்றி நீர்நிறைந்தற்று'). The same phrase 'நீர்நிறைந்தற்று' is used both ways: a full tank that the village drinks from, and a full tank that holds nothing because the man is cut off from his people.

216: wealth that comes to a man of நயன் is like a fruit-bearing tree ripening inside the town ('பயன்மரம் உள்ளூர்ப் பழுத்தற்று'). 1008: the wealth of a man no one seeks out is like a poison tree ripening in the middle of the town ('நடுவூருள் நச்சுமரம் பழுத்தற்று'). The second is the first image reversed, a tree in the same place whose fruit no one can use; Manakkudavar reads 'நயனுடையான்' in 216 as one whom others desire, the exact opposite of 1008's 'நச்சப்படாதவன்'.

217 makes a tree the figure of a generous man's wealth: a tree that is medicine and does not fail ('மருந்தாகித் தப்பா மரம்'). 576 makes a tree the figure of people who have eyes but no kindly regard: they are like trees joined to the soil ('மண்ணோடு இயைந்த மரத்தனையர்'). The book uses the tree in two ways, for what gives to all who come to it and for what stands unmoved, so the image alone carries no fixed value.

218: even at a time without means ('இடனில் பருவத்தும்'), those who see what is due do not slacken in ஒப்புரவு. 955: even when what they have to give has shrunk ('வழங்குவது உள்வீழ்ந்தக் கண்ணும்'), an old family does not part from its character. The Book of Virtue credits this constancy to insight into duty ('கடனறி காட்சி'), and the Book of Wealth credits it to lineage ('பழங்குடி').

219: poverty, for a man of நயன், is being unable to do the things he is disposed to do ('செயும் நீர செய்யாது அமைகலா ஆறு'); Parimelazhagar adds that it is not the loss of his own enjoyments. 230: nothing is more bitter than dying, yet even that is sweet when giving is not possible ('ஈதல் இயையாக் கடை'). 230 pushes 219's point further: for such a person the inability to give is worse than death.

219 redefines poverty for the benevolent man: it is not lacking goods but being unable to do good with them. 89 redefines it from the other side: poverty in the midst of having ('உடைமையுள் இன்மை') is the folly of not tending guests. In both verses poverty is measured by what one does for others and not by what one holds.

220: if ruin comes through ஒப்புரவு, that ruin is worth getting even by selling oneself ('விற்றுக்கோள் தக்கது உடைத்து'). 780: a death at which the eyes of one's lord fill with tears is worth getting even by begging ('இரந்துகோள் தக்கது உடைத்து'). The same closing formula takes something normally shunned, ruin or death, and declares it worth a degrading price, once for the benefactor and once for the soldier.

220 says ruin brought on by ஒப்புரவு is worth buying with oneself, and 218 says the dutiful do not slacken even without means. 480, in the chapter on knowing one's strength, warns that benevolence that does not weigh the limit of what one has ('உளவரை தூக்காத ஒப்புரவாண்மை') quickly ends one's wealth; Parimelazhagar comments that even ஒப்புரவு should not be overdone. They conflict if 220 is read as endorsing giving past one's means; on Manakkudavar's reading of 220, which treats the loss as a trade that pays later, the conflict is over whether that loss is a loss at all.

220 speaks of a man selling himself ('ஒருவன் விற்றுக்கோள்') as a price worth paying for the ruin that benevolence brings. 1080 says the base are fit for one thing: when something befalls them, to sell themselves quickly ('விற்றற்கு உரியர் விரைந்து'). Self-sale is honourable in the first as the cost of giving and contemptible in the second as an escape from one's own trouble.

221 says only giving to those who have nothing (வறியார்க்கு ஒன்று ஈவதே) is giving, and every other gift has the nature of குறியெதிர்ப்பை, a loan to be returned in the same measure. 211 says obligation wants no return (கைம்மாறு வேண்டா கடப்பாடு) and asks what the world gives back to the rain. Read together, the rain is the model of the giver whom 221 defines by exclusion: one whose recipient cannot repay.

221 restricts ஈகை to gifts to the destitute and classes 'all the rest' (மற்றெல்லாம்) as exchange. 212 says all wealth earned by effort exists for வேளாண்மை toward the deserving (தக்கார்க்கு), with no mention of need. The conflict holds if 221's 'all the rest' is taken to cover help to the worthy who are not poor; Parimelazhagar avoids it by treating ஒப்புரவு and ஈகை as separate virtues and limiting 'the rest' to gifts made to the non-poor with a benefit in view.

221 sets true giving against gifts that carry a measured return (குறியெதிர்ப்பை). 103, in the chapter on gratitude, says help done by those who do not weigh the return (பயன்தூக்கார் செய்த உதவி) is larger than the sea when its goodness is weighed. The same test, absence of calculation, is applied once from the giver's side and once from the receiver's.

222 says taking is bad even if it were called a good path (நல்லாறு எனினும் கொளல் தீது). 1054 says that asking from those who do not know concealment even in a dream is itself like giving (இரத்தலும் ஈதலே போலும்). They conflict if கொளல் is read, with Parimelazhagar, as accepting alms without exception; on Kalaignar's reading of கொளல் as taking goods from others by whatever fair means, the two address different acts.

222 holds receiving to be bad whatever is said in its favour. 1061 says that not asking is worth a crore even from those dear as one's eyes who give gladly without hiding (கரவாது உவந்தீயும் கண்ணன்னார் கண்ணும் இரவாமை). Both refuse the best case that could be made for receiving: 222 the claim that it is a good path, 1061 the excellence of the giver.

223 says that not uttering the misery of 'I have nothing' (இலன் என்னும் எவ்வம் உரையாமை) and giving are found only in one of good family (குலனுடையான் கண்ணே). 955 says an old family does not part from its nature even when what it can give has shrunk (வழங்குவது உள்வீழ்ந்தக் கண்ணும்). The chapter on giving and the chapter on lineage make the same claim: generosity that outlasts means is the mark of birth.

On Parimelazhagar's first reading, 223 says the well-born do not speak to others the beggar's degrading word 'I am poor'. 1044 says that even in the well-born (இற்பிறந்தார் கண்ணேயும்) poverty produces the lapse from which degrading words are born (இளிவந்த சொற்பிறக்கும் சோர்வு). The conflict depends on that reading of 223; if 'இலன்' is the giver's refusal to an asker, as Pope takes it, the two speak of different utterances.

Both verses turn on the quoted plea 'I have nothing': 223 has இலன் என்னும் எவ்வம், 205 has இலன் என்று தீயவை செய்யற்க. In 205 the plea is an excuse for doing evil and is answered with the warning that one will have nothing all over again; in 223 it is a plea the well-born do not voice. In both the book refuses to let want serve as a reason.

224 gives the giver's side: being asked is painful (இன்னாது இரக்கப்படுதல்) until one sees the asker's glad face (இன்முகம்). 1057 gives the asker's side: on seeing those who give without scorn or contempt, the heart rejoices deep within (உள்ளுள் உவப்பது உடைத்து). The two describe one moment from both ends, and the asker's gladness in 1057 is what ends the giver's discomfort in 224.

In 224 the giver watches the asker's face and is uneasy until it turns glad. In 90 the guest watches the host's face and wilts, like the anicham flower when smelled, if that face changes (முகந்திரிந்து நோக்க). The face is the measure of the exchange in both, read in opposite directions.

224 says the unease of being asked lasts until the asker's face is glad. 228 names what follows as a pleasure in its own right, ஈத்துவக்கும் இன்பம், which Parimelazhagar explains as the joy the giver has from the receiver's rejoicing. 228 then uses that pleasure as a charge against those who hoard and lose.

225 says the strength of the strong is enduring hunger, and that it comes after (பின்) the strength of those who remove hunger. 160 says those who fast in penance are great, but after (பின்) those who endure others' harsh words. The same construction is used twice to rank fasting below a virtue practised among other people.

225 places the ascetic's endurance of hunger behind the power of the one who relieves it. 48 says the household life that keeps others on their way without slipping from virtue has more endurance than those who do penance (நோற்பாரின் நோன்மை உடைத்து). Both rank the householder's provision above the austerity it supports.

225 ranks relieving hunger above bearing it. 263 asks whether the others have forgotten austerity out of a wish to provide for those who have renounced (துறந்தார்க்குத் துப்புரவு வேண்டி); Parimelazhagar takes 'the others' as householders. Read with 225, the verse from the austerity chapter concedes that the renouncer's fast depends on someone else's giving.

226 says that removing the ruinous hunger of the destitute (அற்றார் அழிபசி தீர்த்தல்) is the place where one who has gained wealth stores it (பெற்றான் பொருள் வைப்புழி). 333 says wealth by nature does not stay, so on gaining it (அது பெற்றால்) one should at once do what stays (அற்குப). 226 supplies the concrete act for 333's general rule.

Both verses use the act of putting wealth away (வை). In 226 feeding the destitute is the வைப்புழி, the place of deposit; in 228 the hard-eyed 'keep and lose' what they own (வைத்திழக்கும்). The chapter sets a store that holds beside a store that is lost.

227 says the evil disease called hunger hardly touches one accustomed to shared eating (பாத்தூண் மரீஇயவனை). 44 uses the same word: if a life fears blame and has பாத்தூண், its line never fails. The same practice is given a reward for the person in 227 and for the lineage in 44.

227 promises that the one who shares his food will not meet hunger. 85 asks whether the field of one who feeds guests and eats what is left even needs sowing (வித்தும் இடல் வேண்டும் கொல்லோ). Both state as a rule that feeding others first secures one's own food.

227 praises habitual shared eating (பாத்தூண்). In 1107 the man compares his beloved's embrace to living in one's own home and eating one's own food after sharing it (தமது பாத்து உண்டற்று). The lover's simile takes the householder's sharing of 227 as its standard of pleasure.

228 asks whether the hard-eyed who keep what they have and lose it (வைத்திழக்கும்) do not know the joy of giving. 88 says those who do not take up the sacrifice of tending guests guard their goods with care and end by saying 'we have no support' (பரிந்தோம்பிப் பற்றற்றேம் என்பர்); Parimelazhagar reads this as losing what was guarded. Both describe the same course: keeping, then loss.

228 speaks of a pleasure the hoarder never learns, ஈத்துவக்கும் இன்பம். 598, which Parimelazhagar applies to kings, says those without inner drive never reach the proud joy of saying 'we have been generous' (வள்ளியம் என்னும் செருக்கு). The pleasure of giving is missed through hardness in the one verse and through lack of energy in the other.

228 says only that the hoarder keeps his goods and loses them. 1009 says how: bright wealth gathered by giving up love, denying oneself and ignoring virtue is taken by others (கொள்வார் பிறர்). The later verse fills in the 'losing' of 228.

229 says that eating alone (தாமே தமியர் உணல்) in order to fill one's store is more bitter than begging. 82 says that eating by oneself while the guest is outside is not to be wished even if the food were the medicine of deathlessness (சாவா மருந்தெனினும்). Both condemn the solitary meal, one by ranking it below begging and one by refusing it even at the highest value.

229 condemns those who eat alone to build up their own wealth. 527 says crows do not hide their food but call and eat (காக்கை கரவா கரைந்துண்ணும்), and that gain belongs only to those of that nature. The rule against eating alone appears in the ethics of giving in 229 and as advice on keeping kin and prosperity in 527.

230 says nothing is more bitter than dying, yet even that is sweet when giving is not possible (ஈதல் இயையாக் கடை). 219 says the poverty of a person of நயன் consists in being unable to do the things he would do (செயும் நீர செய்யாது அமைகலா ஆறு). 219 defines the condition, and 230 says how the giver values it: below death.

230 holds death sweet for one who can no longer give. 968 asks whether a life of tending the flesh is any medicine once greatness has lost its dignity (பீடழிய வந்த இடத்து). In both a life is not worth keeping once the thing that gave it worth is gone: giving in 230, honour in 968.

1041 says that the only thing as painful as poverty is poverty itself (இன்மையின் இன்மையே இன்னாதது). 230 opens by saying nothing is more painful than death (சாதலின் இன்னாதது இல்லை), then reverses it for the person who cannot give. Taken together, 230's second half brings it into line with 1041: the want that stops giving is placed above death in bitterness.

231 says that apart from living with renown through giving there is no profit for a living being (அது அல்லது ஊதியம் இல்லை உயிர்க்கு). 122 says no gain for a living being is greater than restraint (ஆக்கம் அதனினூஉங்கு இல்லை உயிர்க்கு). Read literally the two exclusive claims cannot both hold; the conflict disappears if each is taken as the emphasis its own chapter gives its subject.

231 ends 'ஊதியம் இல்லை உயிர்க்கு' and 31 ends 'ஆக்கம் எவனோ உயிர்க்கு': both use the figure of profit to a living being. 31 gives the place to virtue in general, which yields distinction and wealth; 231 gives it to renown that comes from giving. The shared formula shows 231 naming one particular form of the gain that 31 states broadly.

232 says that everything speakers say comes to rest as praise on those who give to those who ask (இரப்பார்க்கு ஒன்று ஈவார்மேல் நிற்கும் புகழ்). 1059 asks what standing givers would have if there were none who wished to ask and receive (இரந்துகோள் மேவார் இலாஅக் கடை); Parimelazhagar takes தோற்றம் there as renown. The giver's fame in 232 therefore depends on the asker.

232 makes giving the subject of all praise. 296 says there is no renown like not lying (பொய்யாமை அன்ன புகழில்லை). They conflict if both are read as naming the single greatest source of renown; Parimelazhagar's gloss on 296, that truthfulness is the cause of renown in this life, keeps the claim just as strong.

232 says the world's speech settles as praise on the giver. 387 says that for one able to give and protect with sweet words (இன்சொலால் ஈத்தளிக்க வல்லார்க்கு), this world is as his own word would have it. In the chapter on kingship the same giving that earns the world's words in 232 earns its compliance.

233 says that nothing in the world stands without perishing (பொன்றாது நிற்பது) except high renown. 36 calls virtue the companion that does not perish when one perishes (பொன்றுங்கால் பொன்றாத் துணை). The same word marks two different survivals: renown remains in the world (உலகத்து), and virtue goes with the person who dies.

233 says only renown stands undying. 156 says those who punish have a day's pleasure, while those who forbear have renown பொன்றுந் துணையும், which Pope and Parimelazhagar take as until the world ends. 156 measures a virtue's reward by the lasting quality that 233 attributes to renown, and gives it a source other than giving.

233 says renown is the one thing that stands undying (பொன்றாது நிற்பது). 145 says the man who enters another's home thinking it easy gets blame that stands without ever dying (எஞ்ஞான்றும் விளியாது நிற்கும் பழி). Blame is given the same permanence as renown, which strains 233's 'nothing else' if that phrase is read strictly.

234 says that if a person achieves far-reaching renown within the earth's bounds (நிலவரை நீள்புகழ் ஆற்றின்), the world of the gods will not honour the புலவர், whom Parimelazhagar takes to be the sages who have reached it. 50 says one who lives on earth as life should be lived (வையத்துள் வாழ்வாங்கு வாழ்பவன்) will be placed among the gods who dwell in the sky. Both let a life lived on earth earn standing in heaven, and 234 goes further by ranking it above heaven's own.

234 joins earthly renown (புகழ்) to honour in the gods' world (புத்தேள் உலகு). 966 names the same pair as the two things lost by following those who scorn you: it brings no renown and does not carry one to the gods' land (புகழ் இன்றால் புத்தேள் நாட்டு உய்யாதால்). In both verses renown here and the gods' world there are counted together, as gained in 234 and forfeited in 966.

235, as Parimelazhagar reads it, speaks of a loss that is growth for the body of renown and a death in which that body comes to exist (நத்தம் போல் கேடும் உளதாகும் சாக்காடும்). 220 says that if ruin comes through ஒப்புரவு, that ruin (கேடு) is worth buying even by selling oneself. Both hold that there is a கேடு worth choosing.

235 calls rare a death that is really a coming into existence. 780 says that if one can die so that the eyes of those who sustained one fill with tears, that death (சாக்காடு) is worth getting even by begging. The soldier's death in 780 is an instance, in the domain of war, of the death 235 says only the skilled achieve.

235 says a loss can be an increase. 117 says the world will not set down as ruin (கெடுவாக வையாது உலகம்) the low state of one who stays in virtue by standing fair. Both deny that the decline of a good person's fortunes is a real loss, 235 from the side of renown and 117 from the world's judgement.

236 says: if you appear, appear with renown, and for those without it not appearing is better than appearing (தோன்றலின் தோன்றாமை நன்று). 1003 says the appearance (தோற்றம்) of men who cling to accumulation and do not want renown (இசை வேண்டா) is a burden to the land. Both judge a person's coming into the world by renown, and 1003 names the misers as a case of those who 'appear' without it.

Parimelazhagar reads 236 as: if born human, be born with the qualities that lead to renown. 972 says birth is alike for all living beings (பிறப்பொக்கும் எல்லா உயிர்க்கும்) and distinction differs through the difference in what they do. On the birth reading, 972 limits 236: no one is born with renown, so the 'appearing with renown' has to be made by deeds.

On Parimelazhagar's reading of தோன்றுதல் as birth, 236 treats being born with renown as good and not being born as only the better alternative for those without it. 362 says that if one wants anything it should be not to be born (வேண்டுங்கால் வேண்டும் பிறவாமை), with no exception. The conflict depends on the birth reading; on Kalaignar's reading, where 236 is about entering a field of activity, the two do not meet.

237 asks why those who cannot live with renown resent the people who scorn them (இகழ்வாரை) and not themselves. 59 says those whose home does not seek renown (புகழ்புரிந்த இல் இலோர்க்கு) cannot walk with a bull's proud gait before those who scorn them (இகழ்வார் முன்). Both pair lack of renown with scorners, and both place the cause with the one scorned.

237 tells those without renown to blame themselves and not their scorners. 1060 tells the asker not to be angry at a refusal, since the affliction of his own want is witness enough (நிரப்பிடும்பை தானேயும் சாலும் கரி). In both the grievance against another person is turned back to one's own condition.

238 calls renown an எச்சம், a thing left behind, and says it is a disgrace not to obtain it (இசை என்னும் எச்சம் பெறாஅவிடின்). 114 says whether people are worthy or unworthy is seen by their எச்சம் (அவரவர் எச்சத்தாற் காணப்படும்), which Pope and Parimelazhagar take as offspring. The shared word shows 238 treating renown as a kind of offspring, the thing by which a person is judged afterwards.

238 says it is a disgrace to leave no legacy of renown. 1004 asks what the man whom no one wants (நச்சப்படாதவன்) supposes will remain as his எச்சம்; Parimelazhagar explains that he is unwanted because he has never given. 1004 applies 238's standard to the miser and finds nothing left.

239 says land that has borne a body without renown (இசையிலா யாக்கை பொறுத்த நிலம்) will decline in its yield. 1003 says the appearance of men who cling to accumulation and do not want renown is a burden to the land (நிலக்குப் பொறை). Both make the person without renown a weight the earth carries; 239 adds the cost to the earth.

239 says the land's rich yield shrinks (வண்பயன் குன்றும்) under a person without renown. 560 says the yield of cows shrinks (ஆபயன் குன்றும்) if the guardian does not guard. The same phrase ties natural yield to human conduct, a private person's in 239 and the king's in 560.

In 239 the land bears (பொறுத்த) a body without renown and yields less. 189 asks whether it is out of regard for virtue that the earth carries the weight (பொறை) of one who speaks ill of a person behind his back. Both picture the earth as bearing a moral load, and they differ in that 189's earth endures while 239's earth declines.

240 says those who live without blame are the ones who live, and those who live without renown are the ones who do not (வாழாதவர்). 214 says one who knows what is fitting truly lives (உயிர்வாழ்வான்) and anyone else is placed among the dead (செத்தாருள் வைக்கப்படும்). Both redefine being alive by a moral test, and the tests are neighbours: ஒப்புரவு in 214 and the renown it earns in 240.

240 uses the formula வாழ்வாரே வாழ்வார் for those who live without blame. 1033 uses the same formula for those who live by eating what they plough (உழுதுண்டு வாழ்வாரே வாழ்வார்), with all others following and bowing for their food. The phrase 'they alone live' is awarded on two different grounds, a good name in 240 and self-reliance in 1033.

240 says that to live without renown is not to live. 970 says the world worships and praises the radiance of those with honour who will not live when disgrace comes (இளிவரின் வாழாத மானம் உடையார்). 970 shows a person acting on 240's equation, and the result is the renown 240 demands.

251 asks how one who eats another's flesh to enlarge his own (தன்னூன் பெருக்கற்கு) can exercise அருள்; 968 asks whether a life that nurses the flesh (ஊன் ஓம்பும் வாழ்க்கை) is any medicine once dignity is lost. Both use ஊன், one's own flesh, for a body tended at the cost of something higher: அருள் in one verse, honour in the other.

72 says the loveless keep everything for themselves, while the loving belong to others even in their bones (என்பும் உரியர் பிறர்க்கு). 251 describes the reverse movement: another's body (பிறிது ஊன்) taken to build one's own. Read together, the body is the measure in both: love gives it over, and the eater of flesh takes another's.

315 asks what understanding has achieved if one does not guard another's pain as one's own (பிறிதின்நோய் தந்நோய்போல்). 251 sets the same pair, self and other (தன் ஊன் / பிறிது ஊன்), the wrong way round: the other's flesh serves one's own. 315 gives the general test that 251's rhetorical question about அருள் applies to eating.

Both verses explain அருள் by putting it beside பொருள்: 247 says that world is not for those without அருள் just as this world is not for those without wealth, and 252 says holding அருள் (அருளாட்சி) is not for flesh-eaters just as holding wealth (பொருளாட்சி) is not for those who do not guard it. 252 takes the comparison one step on: அருள், like wealth, is something that can be lost through carelessness.

252 takes it as given that holding wealth is not for those who do not look after it (பொருளாட்சி போற்றாதார்க்கு இல்லை). 376 says what is not one's portion will not stay however anxiously it is guarded, and what is one's own will not leave even if carried out and poured away (பரியினும் ஆகாவாம் ... சொரியினும் போகா தம). The conflict holds if ஆட்சி is read as possession, as Manakkudavar and Pope read it; Parimelazhagar reads it as getting the benefit of wealth, which softens it.

253 says the mind of one who has eaten a creature's body with relish does not turn to good (நன்னூக்காது), like the heart of one holding a weapon. 285 says a loving nature with அருள் in view (அருள்கருதி) is not found in those who, with goods in view (பொருள்கருதி), watch for another's lapse. In both, what the mind is fixed on, flesh or another's property, leaves no room for அருள்; Parimelazhagar glosses 253 the same way, as a mind that looks only to the meat.

The two verses open with almost the same words. 321: if asked what virtuous action is, it is not killing, and killing brings every other kind of deed (அறவினை யாதெனின் கொல்லாமை கோறல்). 254, as Parimelazhagar construes it, defines அருள் and its opposite by the same pair, கொல்லாமை and கோறல், and then adds that eating that flesh is not பொருள். The chapter on meat borrows the non-killing chapter's definition and extends it from the killer to the eater. (The edition's text of 254 has lost its first letter; it should begin அருளல்லது.)

Both verses use பொருள் in an unusual, moral sense alongside அருள். 246 says those who leave அருள் and do what should not be done have left பொருள் and forgotten (பொருள்நீங்கிப் பொச்சாந்தார்); 254 calls eating flesh பொருளல்லது. Parimelazhagar takes பொருள் in 254 as virtue (so that பொருளல்லது is sin) and in 246 as the lasting good one should have done.

Both verses say where உயிர்நிலை, the standing or seat of life, lies. 80: it follows the way of love (அன்பின் வழியது உயிர்நிலை), and without love a body is bone wrapped in skin. 255: it lies in not eating flesh (உண்ணாமை உள்ளது உயிர்நிலை). Parimelazhagar takes the phrase in 255 to mean creatures' lives staying in their bodies; either way, both verses make life's hold on the body depend on a virtue.

255 says that if one eats flesh, அளறு (the mire, hell) will not open its mouth (அண்ணாத்தல் செய்யாது), which Parimelazhagar explains as not opening to let him out again. 835 says a fool can in one birth make the அளறு he will enter and sink in for seven (எழுமையும் தான் புக்கழுந்தும் அளறு). Both use the same rare word for a hell one makes for oneself and does not get out of.

326 says Death, the eater of life (உயிருண்ணுங் கூற்று), does not advance on the days of one who lives by not killing. 255 gives hell a mouth (அண்ணாத்தல்), which on Parimelazhagar's reading has swallowed the eater of flesh and will not open again. In both the language of eating is turned on the human: the one who spares life is not eaten, and the one who eats is.

329 says people whose work is killing (கொலைவினையர்) are of base occupation in the eyes of those who discern baseness. 256 argues that no one would supply flesh for a price (விலைப்பொருட்டால்) if the world did not kill, or on Manakkudavar's reading கொள்ளாது did not buy, for the sake of eating. 256 moves the blame that 329 puts on the slaughterer back to the eater whose demand creates the trade; Parimelazhagar says it answers the claim that the eater has no share in the killing.

1059 asks what distinction givers could have if there were none who wished to ask and receive (இரந்துகோள் மேவார் இலாஅக் கடை). 256 says none would bring flesh to sell if the world did not kill for eating. Both reason from a counterfactual about one party to the existence of the other: askers make givers possible, and eaters make sellers of flesh possible.

The two verses end with the same conditional: புண்ணது உணர்வார்ப் பெறின் (257) and வாளது உணர்வார்ப் பெறின் (334), 'if one could find people who perceive it as that'. 334 says what shows itself as a day is a blade sawing through life; 257 says meat is another creature's wound. In both the argument is a re-seeing of a familiar thing, and the phrasing admits that those who see it so are rare.

575 says that without kindly regard the eye is perceived as a wound (புண்ணென்று உணரப்படும்); 257 says flesh would not be eaten if people perceived it as another creature's wound (புண்ணது உணர்வார்). Both use புண் with உணர் to strip something of its usual standing, and both are about compassion: the eye without it is a sore, and food seen with it is a sore.

199: those of stainless vision, freed from delusion (மருள்தீர்ந்த மாசறு காட்சியவர்), do not say meaningless things even by a lapse. 258: those whose vision has parted from fault (செயிரின் தலைப்பிரிந்த காட்சியார்) do not eat flesh that has parted from life. The same figure, the person of clear காட்சி who simply does not do the thing, is used for speech and for food; restraint is presented as a consequence of seeing clearly, not of a rule.

174 says those of faultless vision who have conquered the senses (புலம்வென்ற புன்மையில் காட்சியவர்) will not covet, even thinking 'we have nothing'. 258 says those whose vision is free of fault do not eat flesh. Both attach an abstention that costs something, from another's goods or from meat, to காட்சி, and 174 adds the mastery of the senses that 258 leaves unstated.

259 says not taking a creature's life and eating it is better than pouring oblations in a thousand sacrifices (அவிசொரிந்து ஆயிரம் வேட்டலின்). 87 calls the tending of guests a வேள்வி and says its fruit is measured by the guest's worth. The Kural keeps the word for sacrifice while relocating its value: an ethical act is named as the sacrifice in 87 and ranked above the ritual in 259.

328 says that however great the gain said to bring good, gain that comes by killing is the lowest for the worthy (கொன்றாகும் ஆக்கங் கடை). Parimelazhagar takes this to be about killing in sacrifice for the gods, which householders are told brings great reward. On that reading it makes the same judgement as 259, which sets abstaining from one killing above a thousand sacrifices; the Tamil of 328 itself does not mention sacrifice.

295 says one who speaks truth in accord with his heart is above those who practise austerity together with giving (தவத்தொடு தானஞ்செய்வாரின் தலை). 259 says not killing one creature and eating it is better than a thousand sacrifices. Both rank a plain restraint, not lying and not killing, above the religious practices that carry the most prestige.

The two verses close with the same picture: எல்லா உயிருந் தொழும் (260) and மன்னுயிரெல்லாந் தொழும் (268), all living beings worship him. In 260 it is the one who does not kill and has refused flesh; in 268 it is the one who has fully gained his own life (தன்னுயிர் தான் அறப் பெற்றான்), whom Parimelazhagar identifies with the doer of தவம். The neighbouring chapters give the same honour to non-killing and to austerity.

326 says Death, the eater of life, does not advance on the days of one who lives by not killing; 260 says all living beings fold their hands (கைகூப்பி) and worship the one who does not kill and refuses flesh. Both state what the non-killer receives in return, and both put it as a response of life itself: living beings honour him, and the taker of life leaves him alone.

261 gives the form of தவம் as two things: bearing the pain that comes and doing no harm to living beings (உயிர்க்குறுகண் செய்யாமை). 984 says நோன்மை, austerity, has the goodness of not killing (கொல்லா நலத்தது நோன்மை). A verse in the second book, written to define சால்பு, repeats the definition of austerity by its restraint toward other lives and not by its hardships.

261 calls bearing the pain that comes (உற்றநோய் நோன்றல்) the form of தவம்; Parimelazhagar takes the pain to be that of fasting and similar observances. 160 uses the same verb, நோல், to rank kinds of bearing: those who fast (உண்ணாது நோற்பார்) are great, but only after those who bear the harsh words of others. So within the endurance that 261 names, 160 puts the householder's patience under insult above the ascetic's fast.

157 says that though others do you wrong, it is good to feel the pain and not do what is contrary to virtue (நோநொந்து அறனல்ல செய்யாமை). 261 defines தவம் by the same two parts: bearing pain, and causing none to living beings. The chapter on forbearance asks of the householder, in dealings with those who wrong him, what 261 gives as the whole form of austerity.

262 says தவம் comes to those who already have தவம், and that for those without it taking it up is futile; Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar both read this as merit from earlier births. 273 pictures a person without strength (வலியில் நிலைமையான்) who takes on the form of the strong: a cow grazing in a tiger's skin. 273 shows what the futile undertaking of 262 looks like in practice. (The edition's text of 262 lacks the word அவம் at the start of the second line.)

373 says that however many subtle books one studies, the understanding that is truly one's own still prevails (தன் உண்மையறிவே மிகும்). 262 says austerity too succeeds only for those who already have it. Both hold that a discipline taken up now, study or austerity, yields only according to what the person brings to it; Parimelazhagar refers both to what earlier births have fixed.

262 says that for those without தவம், undertaking it is futile. 620 says those who toil on without flagging or delay will see the back even of fate (ஊழையும் உப்பக்கம் காண்பர்). If the தவம் one must already have is merit from former births, as Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar read it, then 262 makes present effort useless without a prior endowment, which is what 620 denies. On Kalaignar's reading, where it means present firmness and self-control, the conflict disappears.

42 names the householder as the support of those who have renounced (துறந்தார்க்கும் ... இல்வாழ்வான் என்பான் துணை), along with the destitute and the dead. 263 asks, with a wry கொல், whether the rest have forgotten தவம் out of a wish to provide for renouncers (துறந்தார்க்குத் துப்புரவு வேண்டி). It turns the duty stated in 42 into an explanation, or an excuse, for why householders do no austerity themselves.

263 speaks of the others, householders on Parimelazhagar's reading, as having forgotten தவம் while they provide for renouncers. 48 says a household life that keeps others on their way and does not slip from virtue has more endurance than those who do penance (நோற்பாரின் நோன்மை உடைத்து); Parimelazhagar reads 'keeps on their way' as supporting ascetics. On 48's account the provider has not forgotten austerity: his life already contains more of it.

1036 says that if ploughmen fold their hands, even those who say 'we have given up desire' (விட்டேம் என்பார்) cannot keep their state. 263 assumes the same dependence: renouncers need others to supply their needs (துப்புரவு). Both verses note that renunciation rests on people who have not renounced.

261 says the form of தவம் is just this: bearing one's own pain and doing no harm to living beings (உயிர்க்குறுகண் செய்யாமை அற்றே). 264 says crushing foes (ஒன்னார்த் தெறல்) and raising friends come through தவம், if one so intends. Read plainly, austerity defined by harmlessness is credited three verses later with the power to destroy. Parimelazhagar eases this by taking the foes as enemies of virtue and by reading எண்ணின் as implying that ascetics do not normally think of such things.

899 says that if those of exalted resolve flare up (ஏந்திய கொள்கையார் சீறின்), even the king breaks midway and loses his rule. Parimelazhagar reads them as people of high vows, and Pope likewise. This is the power of 264, ஒன்னார்த் தெறல் through austerity, seen from the side of the king who must not provoke it.

29 says the anger of those who stand on the hill of good qualities cannot be withstood even for a moment (கணமேயும் காத்தல் அரிது), on Parimelazhagar's and Pope's reading; Kalaignar takes it to mean their anger does not last a moment. On the first reading it agrees with 264 that renouncers hold a power to ruin those who oppose them, though 264 makes it a matter of intention (எண்ணின்) and 29 of anger.

The two verses share a formula: வேண்டிய வேண்டியாங்கு எய்தலால் (265), what is wanted is obtained as it is wanted, and எண்ணிய எண்ணியாங்கு எய்துப (666), what is thought of is obtained as it was thought. 265 gives this as the reason austerity is striven for; 666 makes it depend on the planner's firmness (திண்ணியர் ஆகப் பெறின்). The promise made for austerity in the book of virtue is made for resolute action in the book of statecraft.

265 says austerity is practised because through it whatever is wanted is obtained as wanted. 362 says that if one must want, one should want not to be born, and that this comes by wanting not to want (வேண்டாமை வேண்ட வரும்). 362 narrows what the வேண்டிய of 265 should be; Parimelazhagar reads 265 itself as referring to results in the next life and release, while Manakkudavar takes it to include enjoyments.

309 says all one has thought of comes together at once if one never thinks of anger in the heart (உள்ளிய தெல்லாம் உடனெய்தும்). 265 says what is wanted is obtained as wanted through austerity. Both promise the fulfilment of wishes as the fruit of an inner discipline; Parimelazhagar reads 309 too as addressed to one doing தவம்.

266 says those who do தவம் are doing their own work (தங்கருமம்), and the rest, caught in desire, do what is futile (அவம்). 46 asks what one would gain by going off along the outside way if one conducts household life in the way of virtue (புறத்தாற்றில் போஒய்ப் பெறுவதெவன்). If the 'rest' of 266 means everyone who is not an ascetic, as Parimelazhagar's gloss of தவம் செய்வார் as renouncers suggests, the virtuous householder of 46 is among those doing futile work, and the verses disagree about whether his life is enough.

348 divides people the same way: those who have thoroughly renounced have reached the head, and the rest, confused, are caught in the net (மயங்கி வலைப்பட்டார் மற்றையவர்). 266 says those who do தவம் do their own work and the rest act in vain, caught in desire (ஆசையுட் பட்டு). Both use பட்டு / பட்டார், being caught, for everyone outside the ascetic's path; Parimelazhagar supplies 'the net of desire' in his gloss on 266.

267 says that for those able to endure, pain burning them makes them shine (ஒளிவிடும்), as gold shines the more it is heated. 630 says that if one takes what hurts as pleasure (இன்னாமை இன்பம் எனக்கொளின்), there comes a distinction even one's enemies admire. The ascetic's gain from pain in the first book has a worldly counterpart in the second: in both, pain borne in the right way adds to the person.

308 says that even if harm is done to you like the touch of massed flames (இணர்எரி தோய்வன்ன), not being angry is good if one can manage it. 267 says pain that burns (துன்பஞ் சுடச்சுட) makes those who can endure it shine like gold in fire. Both picture suffering as fire applied to a person; 308 asks only that it be borne without anger, and 267 says what the bearing produces.

346 says one who cuts off the pride of 'I' and 'mine' (யான் எனது என்னும் செருக்கு) enters a world above the gods'. 268 says all other beings worship the one who தன்னுயிர் தான் அறப் பெற்றான். Manakkudavar takes அற as 'ceasing': one in whom the notion that his life is himself has ended, and Kalaignar reads it similarly, which makes the verse the same claim as 346. Parimelazhagar instead reads it as fully possessing one's own life, where the agreement is weaker.

326 says Death, the eater of life, does not advance on the days of one who lives by not killing (செல்லாது உயிருண்ணுங் கூற்று). 269 says even leaping past Death (கூற்றம் குதித்தலும்) becomes possible for those who have attained the power of austerity. Since 261 and 984 make non-killing the core of austerity, the two verses give the same exemption from கூற்று to what is largely the same practice.

620 says those who toil on without flagging will see the back even of fate (ஊழையும் உப்பக்கம் காண்பர்); 269 says even getting past Death (கூற்றம் குதித்தலும்) is within reach of those with the power of austerity. Each uses the particle உம், 'even', to name the one thing thought unbeatable and then says sustained effort beats it: labour in the book of statecraft, austerity in the book of virtue. (The edition's text of 269 ends with a stray letter, தலைப்பட்டவர்க்குல்.)

842 says that when a person without understanding gives gladly, the cause is nothing other than the receiver's தவம் (பெறுவான் தவம்). 270 says the have-nots are many because those who practise austerity are few. Both explain who gets and who lacks by austerity, and 842 shows the idea used in passing in the second book, as an accepted explanation.

616 says effort creates prosperity and the absence of effort brings in want (முயற்றின்மை இன்மை புகுத்தி விடும்). 270 says the have-nots (இலர்) are many because few practise austerity (நோற்பார் சிலர்). Both trace poverty to something people fail to do, but they name different things: present exertion in the chapter on labour, and austerity here, which the commentators take to bear fruit across births.

271 says the five elements laugh within (பூதங்கள் ஐந்தும் அகத்தே நகும்) at the concealed conduct of a deceitful mind; 293 says that after a lie about what one's own heart knows, that heart itself burns one (தன்நெஞ்சே தன்னைச் சுடும்). Both place the witness to a hidden fault inside the person; 293 moves it from the body's elements, which only laugh, to the heart, which punishes.

In 271 the five elements laugh within at a hypocrite's hidden conduct; in 1040 the good woman called Land laughs (நிலமென்னும் நல்லாள் நகும்) at those who sit idle saying 'we have nothing'. In both a part of the material world is the one that laughs at a human pretence, and Parimelazhagar glosses the laugh in 1040 too as inward (தன்னுள்ளே).

272 asks what a sky-high appearance can do if one's heart sinks into what it itself knows to be a fault (தன்னெஞ்சம் தான்அறி குற்றம்); 293 forbids lying about what one's own heart knows (தன்நெஞ் சறிவது), because that heart will burn one. Both make the person's own knowing heart the judge that outward success cannot get past, once for ascetic show and once for speech.

34 says being spotless in mind is the whole of virtue and the rest is noisy show (ஆகுல நீர பிற); 272 says a sky-high appearance (வானுயர் தோற்றம்) does nothing when the heart is in known fault. 272 applies the general rule of 34 to the specific case of the ascetic's appearance.

24 praises the one who guards the five senses with the goad called firmness (உரனென்னும் தோட்டியான்); 273 likens one of strengthless nature (வலியில் நிலைமையான்) who takes the form of the strong to a cow grazing in a tiger's skin. Parimelazhagar reads the missing strength in 273 as the power to bring the mind under control, which is what 24 names as the mark of the real renouncer, so 273 shows the outward form of 24 without its substance.

274 condemns hiding in austerity to do what is not austerity (தவமறைந்து அல்லவை செய்தல்), like a hunter hiding in a bush to snare birds; 586 defines the good spy as one who takes the guise of renouncers (துறந்தார் படிவத்த ராகி), goes in, examines, and never slips. The same disguise that the book of virtue treats as predation is, in the book of statecraft, a tool of the king's work; the two verses judge it by different standards without either mentioning the other.

274 has the hunter hidden in the bush as the image of evil done under cover of austerity; 828 says a weapon hides even in an enemy's hands folded in worship (தொழுதகை யுள்ளும் படையொடுங்கும்), and likewise in his tears. In both a gesture of piety is the cover for harm, once in ascetic life and once in false friendship.

261 gives the form of தவம் as bearing one's own pain and doing no harm to living beings (உயிர்க்குறுகண் செய்யாமை); 274 speaks of doing 'what is not it' (அல்லவை) under cover of தவம் and compares this to a hunter snaring birds. Read together, the hunter simile shows the hypocrite doing the very thing, harm to creatures, whose absence 261 makes the definition of austerity.

275 says the concealed conduct of those who say 'we are free of attachment' brings many harms with the cry எற்றெற்று; 655 says do not do what will make you grieve saying எற்று ('what is this I have done'). The same exclamation of regret marks the test in both, in the renouncer's conduct and in the minister's action; Manakkudavar, however, takes the cry in 275 as other people's, not the doer's.

42 makes the householder the support of those who have renounced (துறந்தார்க்கும் ... துணை); 276 says none are more hard-eyed than those who, unrenounced at heart, live by deceiving as if they had renounced (துறந்தார்போல் வஞ்சித்து வாழ்வார்). Parimelazhagar takes the deceived to be the givers, so the pairing shows what the false renouncer exploits: the duty of support that 42 lays on the householder.

276 ends 'வாழ்வாரின் வன்கணார் இல்': none are harder than those who live by posing as renouncers. 1198, spoken by the woman in separation, ends with the same words: none in the world are harder than those who go on living without a kind word from the one they love. The shared formula uses வன்கண் in two senses, the cruelty of the deceiver in 276 and the grim endurance of the one left behind in 1198.

277 says the world has people who look outwardly like the red kunri seed but are inwardly black like its tip (புறம் ... அகம்); 824 says to fear deceivers who smile sweetly with the face and are bitter within (முகத்தின் இனிய ... அகத்தின்னா வஞ்சர்). The same outside/inside split is described for the false ascetic and for the false friend.

706 says the face shows what is strongest in the heart, as crystal shows what is next to it (நெஞ்சம் கடுத்தது காட்டும் முகம்); 277 says there are people red outside and black inside. 277 limits 706: the face may betray a passing feeling to a skilled reader, but a settled outward appearance can be the opposite of the inside.

277 uses the kunri seed for its two colours, red body and black tip; 965 uses it for its size, saying even those like a hill sink if they do a lowering thing as small as a kunri (குன்றி அனைய). The same seed serves both verses as a figure for a small dark flaw in something that otherwise looks fine, by colour in one and by measure in the other.

278 says many with stain in the mind (மனத்தது மாசாக) bathe like the eminent and go about concealed; 298 says outer purity comes by water and inner purity is seen through truthfulness (அகந்தூய்மை வாய்மையால்). 298 states the principle that explains 278: bathing reaches only the outside, so it can serve as a cover.

34 says the whole of virtue is to be without stain in the mind (மனத்துக்கண் மாசிலன் ஆதல்) and the rest is noisy show; 278 describes people who keep the stain in the mind (மனத்தது மாசாக) and supply the show by ritual bathing. The shared word மாசு makes 278 the negative case of 34.

279 says the straight arrow is cruel and the bent lute is upright, so take people by the nature of their deeds (வினைபடு பாலால் கொளல்); 505 says one's own deeds are the touchstone of greatness and smallness (கருமமே கட்டளைக் கல்). The same rule appears as a test for ascetics in the book of virtue and as a test for choosing officers in the book of statecraft.

279 warns against reading uprightness from shape, with the arrow and lute as examples; 667 says do not scorn on seeing someone's form (உருவுகண்டு எள்ளாமை), because the great chariot has its small linchpin. One verse guards against being impressed by form and the other against despising it, and both replace form with function.

279 says the arrow, though straight, is cruel, and the lute, though bent, is good; 827 says do not accept the bowing speech of enemies, since the bending of a bow means harm (வில்வணக்கம் தீங்கு குறித்தமையான்). Both draw on archery to show that shape does not tell intent, and between them neither straightness nor bending is a reliable sign: the bent lute is harmless, the bent bow is not.

280 says neither shaving nor growing the hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns (உலகம் பழித்தது ஒழித்து விடின்); 49 says household life is what is called virtue, and it too is good if it has nothing others blame (பிறன்பழிப்ப தில்லாயின்). Both ways of life are put to the same test, absence of what others rightly blame, and the badge of the way of life is not the test.

34 reduces virtue to a stainless mind and calls all else noisy show; 280 says the ascetic's marks, shaven head or long hair (மழித்தலும் நீட்டலும்), are not needed if blameworthy conduct is dropped. 280 names the specific outward signs that fall under what 34 dismisses.

281 tells one who wants not to be scorned to guard his heart from stealing anything at all (கள்ளாமை காக்க தன் நெஞ்சு); 178 says that what keeps one's wealth from shrinking is not coveting the goods in another's hand (வெஃகாமை ... பிறன்கைப் பொருள்). Each gives restraint toward others' property as the means to something one wants for oneself, standing in 281 and one's own wealth in 178; Parimelazhagar reads 281 differently, as about one esteemed for not despising release.

282 says even thinking in the mind (உள்ளத்தால் உள்ளலும்) of taking another's goods by stealth is wrong; 317 says the highest thing is not to do, with the mind (மனத்தானாம்), anything ill to anyone at any time in any degree. Both place the fault at the level of intention before any act, for theft in one and for harm in general in the other.

282 forbids the thought 'we will steal another's goods by stealth'; 204 forbids plotting another's ruin even in forgetfulness (மறந்தும் பிறன்கேடு சூழற்க), and adds that virtue then plots the plotter's ruin. Both treat the plan against another person (பிறன்) as already the offence; 204 supplies the consequence that 282 leaves unstated.

283 says gain made by stealth perishes beyond measure while seeming to grow (ஆவது போலக் கெடும்); 660 says making wealth by deceit (சலத்தால் பொருள்செய்து) and feeling secure in it is like keeping water in an unfired clay pot. The same claim, that wrongly got wealth looks held and is being lost, is made to the renouncer in one book and to the minister in the other.

283 says stolen gain perishes even as it seems to grow; 659 says all that is taken with others' tears leaves with tears, while what comes rightly pays later even if lost (இழப்பினும் பிற்பயக்கும்). 659 adds the other half that 283 lacks: wrong gain that seems to grow is lost, and right gain that seems lost returns.

283 says stolen gain perishes while seeming to increase (ஆவது போல); 479 says the life of one who does not live knowing the measure perishes while seeming to exist (உளபோல இல்லாகி). Both describe a ruin hidden behind an appearance of prosperity and both tie it to அளவு, measure: 283's gain perishes 'beyond measure' (அளவிறந்து) and 479's spender ignores it.

284 says intense desire for stealing gives undying sorrow at its ripening (விளைவின்கண் வீயா விழுமம்); 177 says do not want gain that comes by coveting, for at its ripening (விளைவயின்) the fruit is hard to make good. Both use the harvest word விளைவு to separate how wrongful taking looks at the start from what it yields, for the renouncer's theft and the householder's coveting.

368 says those without craving have no sorrow, and where craving exists sorrow comes on and on without fail (தவாஅது மேன்மேல் வரும்); 284 says desire hardened in stealing (கன்றிய காதல்) yields sorrow that does not die (வீயா விழுமம்). 284 is the general law of 368 applied to one desire, with the same stress on sorrow that does not end.

284 speaks of காதல் grown in களவு and means desire for stealing, which ends in undying sorrow; in 1092 the man says the small look her eyes steal (கண் களவு கொள்ளும் சிறுநோக்கம்) is more than half of love's pleasure. The same word களவு is condemned as theft of goods in the book of virtue and prized as the stolen glance in the book of love, where it is a lover's speech and not a teaching about theft.

285 says a loving nature that has அருள் in view is not found in those who, with goods in view, watch for another's lapse (பொருள்கருதிப் பொச்சாப்புப் பார்ப்பார்); 176 says one who stands on the path desiring அருள் perishes if, desiring பொருள், he plots wrongs. Both set அருள் against பொருள் taken from others as aims that cannot be held together; 176 says it of the householder, as Parimelazhagar reads it, and 285 of the renouncer.

285 opposes having அருள் in view to having பொருள் in view; 757 says the child அருள், born of அன்பு, is reared by the wealthy foster-mother பொருள். 757 limits how far 285 can be taken: the opposition holds for goods taken from others by watching for their lapses, not for wealth as such, which 757 makes the support of the same அருள் and அன்பு that 285 names.

285 says அருள் with love is not found in one who watches to take another's goods; 251 asks how one who eats another creature's flesh to swell his own can hold to அருள் (எங்ஙனம் ஆளும் அருள்). Both test a claim to அருள் against a practice of taking from another for oneself, property in one case and the body in the other.

286 says those with hardened desire for stealing cannot stand and walk within அளவு (அளவின்கண் நின்றொழுகல் ஆற்றார்); 474 says the one who does not live in accord, does not know his measure (அளவறியான்) and admires himself perishes quickly.
