On Kalaignar's reading of அளவு in 286 as a limit one lives within, the two apply one idea, conduct kept inside a known measure, to the renouncer and to the king; Parimelazhagar instead takes அளவு in 286 as the reasoned measuring of the soul and its ends, on which reading the link is only verbal.

287 calls stealing a dark knowledge (களவென்னும் காரறி வாண்மை) that is not found in those set on the strength called அளவு; 175 asks what a fine and wide understanding (அஃகி அகன்ற அறிவு) comes to if, coveting, one acts senselessly toward everyone. Both deny that cleverness in the service of taking others' goods counts as real understanding.

422 defines understanding as what does not let the mind go wherever it has gone, but turns it from evil toward good (தீதொரீஇ நன்றின்பால் உய்ப்பது அறிவு); 287 grants stealing the name அறிவு only with the qualifier கார், dark. By 422's definition the thief's skill fails as அறிவு, which explains why 287 marks it as darkened.

34 locates virtue in the mind being without stain; 288 says virtue stands in the heart of those who know அளவு just as concealment stands in the heart of those who know stealing (நெஞ்சத்து அறம் ... நெஞ்சில் கரவு). 288 adds to 34 that the heart is occupied either way: what one practises, measure or theft, decides whether virtue or deceit takes up residence there.

289 says those who know nothing but stealing do what is beyond measure and perish right there (அளவல்ல செய்தாங்கே வீவர்); 479 says the life of one who does not live knowing the measure seems to exist, then is not, and perishes without trace. Both make ignoring அளவு the cause of ruin, in the renouncer's conduct and in the management of means; Parimelazhagar reads அளவல்ல in 289 as wrong thoughts and not as excess of spending, so the likeness is of pattern, not of subject.

290 says that for those who steal the உயிர்நிலை fails, while for those who do not steal the world of the gods does not fail; 255 says உயிர்நிலை rests in not eating flesh, and that hell will not open its mouth for one who eats it. Both verses hang உயிர்நிலை, the standing of life in the body on Parimelazhagar's gloss, on one abstention and pair it with a fate after death; Manakkudavar reads the word in 290 as release itself.

290 gives the two outcomes of stealing and not stealing: loss of உயிர்நிலை, and the world of the gods (புத்தேள் உலகு) not failing; 121 gives the two outcomes of restraint and its lack: a place among the immortals (அமரருள்) and thick darkness. Each closes or opens its chapter with the same two-sided reward and penalty attached to a single virtue.

291 defines truth (வாய்மை) not as reporting what happened but as speech with no harm in it at all (யாதொன்றும் தீமை இலாத சொலல்). 292 draws the consequence: even a falsehood stands in truth's place (பொய்மையும் வாய்மை யிடத்த) if it yields faultless good. Read together, the second verse is the first's definition applied to its hardest case.

Both verses use the same question-and-answer frame, எனப்படுவது யாதெனின் யாதொன்றும்: 291 answers that truth is speech with no harm at all, 324 that the good path is the way that keeps in view not killing anything at all. The shared frame shows truthfulness and the good path being defined by the same test, the absence of injury to another.

292 lets a falsehood count as truth when it yields faultless good (புரைதீர்ந்த நன்மை பயக்கும் எனின்). 323 ranks not killing as the one good and puts not lying behind it (அதன் பின்சாரப் பொய்யாமை நன்று). The ranking explains the exception: Parimelazhagar's example for 292 is a lie that saves a creature from death, which is the case where the second virtue gives way to the first.

292 makes good results decisive: a falsehood that yields faultless good (நன்மை பயக்கும் எனின்) counts as truth. 113 says gain got by leaving fairness is to be dropped that very day even if it yields nothing but good (நன்றே தரினும்). The conflict holds only if both are read as answers to whether a good outcome can license a breach of a norm; 113 is about gain and 292 about speech, and 292's புரைதீர்ந்த (free of fault) may already exclude what 113 forbids.

293 forbids lying about what one's own heart knows (தன்நெஞ்சு அறிவது) because that heart will burn one afterwards. 272 asks what a sky-high appearance achieves if one's heart sinks into a fault it knows (தன்னெஞ்சம் தான்அறி குற்றம்). Both make the heart the witness that cannot be deceived, once against the liar and once against the false ascetic.

In 129 a burn from fire heals inside but the scar burned by the tongue (நாவினாற் சுட்ட வடு) does not; in 293 the liar's own heart burns him (தன்நெஞ்சே தன்னைச் சுடும்). Both use burning for the lasting damage of speech: the harsh word burns the hearer, the false word burns the speaker.

294 says one who lives without falsehood in the heart (உள்ளத்தாற் பொய்யாது) is present in the hearts of all the world. 119 says rectitude is speech without bend, provided there is surely no bend within (உட்கோட்டம் இன்மை). In truthfulness and in impartiality alike, straight speech is counted only when the inside matches it.

295 puts one who speaks truth in accord with the mind (மனத்தொடு வாய்மை மொழியின்) above those who do austerity together with giving. 160 calls those who fast great, but behind those who bear others' harsh words (இன்னாச்சொல் நோற்பாரின் பின்). Both rank an everyday discipline of speech, speaking it truly or enduring it, over formal austerity.

295 ranks truthful speech above austerity with giving (தவத்தொடு தானஞ்செய்வாரின் தலை); 259 says not killing and eating one creature is better than pouring oblations in a thousand sacrifices (அவிசொரிந் தாயிரம் வேட்டலின்). The same comparison is made twice: a plain restraint outranks the prestigious religious act.

295 sets the truthful speaker above those who practise austerity and giving. 48 says a household life that keeps others on their way and does not slip from virtue has more endurance than those who do penance (நோற்பாரின் நோன்மை உடைத்து). In both, the ascetic is the standard of comparison and an ordinary life rightly lived is placed above it.

296 says there is no renown like not lying (பொய்யாமை அன்ன புகழில்லை). 232 says all that speakers speak is praise resting on those who give to those who ask (இரப்பார்க்கொன்று ஈவார்மேல் நிற்கும் புகழ்). They conflict if both are read as naming the chief ground of renown, truthfulness in one and giving in the other; if 296 is only a chapter's praise of its own virtue the conflict softens.

296 says not lying gives all the virtues (எல்லா அறமுந் தரும்); Parimelazhagar takes எய்யாமை as 'without wearying the body'. 297 then concludes that one who keeps steadily to not lying does well even without doing the other virtues (அறம்பிற செய்யாமை நன்று). The second verse depends on the first: the others can be left undone because this one already supplies them.

297 says that if one keeps to not lying, not doing other virtues is good (அறம்பிற செய்யாமை செய்யாமை நன்று). 150 says that even if one does not hold to virtue and does wrong, not desiring another's wife is good (அறன்வரையான் அல்ல செயினும் ... நயவாமை நன்று). Both single out one restraint as worth having even when the rest of virtue is absent.

297 allows that one who never lies may leave the other virtues undone. 181 says that though a man does not speak of virtue and does wrong, it is pleasing to hear it said that he does not backbite (அறங்கூறான் அல்ல செயினும் ... புறங்கூறான் என்றல் இனிது). The concession 'even without the rest of virtue' is made for two different restraints of the tongue.

298 says outer purity comes by water and inner purity is seen through truth (அகந்தூய்மை வாய்மையால் காணப்படும்). 364 defines purity (தூஉய்மை) as the absence of craving and says that comes by wanting வாய்மை. The later verse gives the inner purity of 298 a content, freedom from desire, and keeps truth as its source.

298 grants that water produces outer purity (புறந்தூய்மை நீரான் அமையும்) and assigns inner purity to truth. 278 describes many who bathe as though distinguished while their minds hold dirt (மனத்தது மாசாக ... நீராடி) and live concealed. 278 shows the limit 298 implies: bathing cleans only the outside, and can serve as a cover for the lack of the other purity.

299 says that for the worthy the only lamp is the unfailing lamp (பொய்யா விளக்கே), which in this chapter is not lying. 753 uses the same phrase for wealth: பொருளென்னும் பொய்யா விளக்கம் goes to any land one thinks of and cuts the darkness. The Book of Virtue denies the name of lamp to everything but truthfulness, and the Book of Wealth gives the same title to money.

299 names not lying the one true lamp for the worthy (பொய்யா விளக்கே விளக்கு). 601 calls lineage an undimming lamp (குடியென்னும் குன்றா விளக்கம்) that nevertheless goes out when the grime of sloth covers it. The lamp figure marks what a person's standing depends on, and 601 adds that such a lamp can be put out by neglect.

300 says that among all the things we have seen as true there is nothing whatever better than truthfulness (எனைத்தொன்றும் வாய்மையின் நல்ல பிற இல்லை). 323 says the one good is not killing and that not lying is good behind it (அதன் பின்சாரப் பொய்யாமை நன்று). On the plain reading the two verses rank the same pair of virtues in opposite order.

300 speaks in the first person plural: 'among what we have seen as true' (யாமெய்யாக் கண்டவற்றுள்) nothing is better than truthfulness. 61 uses the same voice: 'of all that can be gained we know of nothing' (யாமறிவது இல்லை) like children who know what should be known. In both the author steps forward with 'we' to vouch for a superlative, which the Kural seldom does.

301 says only one who holds back anger where it can take effect (செல்லிடத்துக் காப்பான்) truly holds it back; Parimelazhagar takes this as anger at those weaker. 250 gives the means: when going against one weaker than yourself (தன்னின் மெலியார்மேல் செல்லுமிடத்து), think of yourself standing before the stronger. 301 says where restraint counts, and 250 supplies the thought that makes it possible.

301 counts restraint of anger only where the anger could have its way. 153 says the strength of strengths is bearing with fools (வன்மையுள் வன்மை மடவார்ப் பொறை). Both locate the real test of forbearance where one has the upper hand and nothing outside compels it.

302 says anger is bad where it cannot take effect, and where it can, nothing is worse (செல்லிடத்தும் இல்அதனின் தீய பிற); Parimelazhagar reads the two places as the stronger and the weaker. 861 advises avoiding opposition to the strong and pressing enmity against the weak (மெலியார்மேல் மேக பகை). They conflict if 302 is taken as a rule for everyone; if the anger chapter is addressed to ascetics, as Parimelazhagar holds, and 861 to a king, they are advice for different people.

302's first half says anger where it cannot take effect is bad, which Parimelazhagar explains as harm coming back from the stronger party. 895 states that harm at its extreme: those a king of fierce might is angry with (வேந்து செறப்பட்டவர்) will not survive wherever they go. The chapter on not offending the great fills in what 302 leaves as a bare 'bad'.

152 says always bear with an excess done to you, and that forgetting it is better still (அதனை மறத்தல் அதனினும் நன்று). 303 uses the same verb for the anger itself: forget anger toward anyone (மறத்தல் வெகுளியை யார்மாட்டும்), since evils are born from it. One forgets the offence and the other the anger at it; 303 adds the reason.

303 says evils are born from anger (தீய பிறத்தல் அதனான் வரும்). 360 names anger (வெகுளி) with desire and confusion as the three whose very names must perish for pain to perish. What 303 says of anger as a source of evils, 360 places in a full account of the roots of suffering.

304 asks whether there is any other enemy than anger, which kills the smile and the joy (சினத்தின் பகையும் உளவோ பிற). 165 says envy is enough for the envious: even if enemies fail, it brings ruin (ஒன்னார் வழுக்கியும் கேடீன்பது). Both treat an inner fault as an enemy that needs no outside enemy to finish the work.

304 counts the death of laughter and joy (நகையும் உவகையும்) as the harm that makes anger the worst enemy. 999 says that for those not capable of laughing (நகல்வல்லர் அல்லார்க்கு) the great world lies in darkness even by day. 999 describes the state that 304 says anger produces.

305 and 127 are built on the same turn, காக்க ... காவாக்கால்: guard against anger, or it is yourself that anger kills; guard the tongue whatever else you leave unguarded, or you will suffer from the fault of your words. In both, the thing to be guarded is something of one's own, and the one who fails to guard it is the one harmed.

305 says one who would guard himself (தன்னைத்தான் காக்கின்) must guard against anger. 209 says one who loves himself (தன்னைத்தான் காதலனாயின்) should not go near evil deeds, however small. Both argue from self-interest alone: the restraint is recommended as self-protection, not as a duty to others.

306 says anger, the fire that kills what it adjoins (சேர்ந்தாரைக் கொல்லி), burns even the safe raft of one's own people (இனமென்னும் ஏமப் புணை). 526 says no one on earth has more people around him than one who gives greatly and does not cherish anger (பேணான் வெகுளி). The two give the loss and the gain of the same fact: kin stay with the one who is free of anger.

306 calls one's people a safe raft (ஏமப் புணை) that anger burns. In 1164 the woman says the sea of love certainly exists and the safe raft to swim it (ஏமப் புணை) does not. The same phrase names what keeps a person afloat; in one verse a passion destroys it and in the other a passion leaves the speaker without one.

307 says the ruin of one who takes anger for a thing of worth is as sure as the hand of one who strikes the ground, which cannot miss (நிலத்தறைந்தான் கைபிழையாதற்று). 208 says the ruin of evildoers is like a shadow that stays at one's foot and never leaves (நிழல்தன்னை வீயாது அடிஉறைந்தற்று). Both use a plain physical certainty to say the consequence cannot be escaped; Kalaignar reads 307 as adding that the striking hand is what gets hurt.

308 says that even if someone does harm like the touch of massed flames (இணர்எரி தோய்வன்ன இன்னா செயினும்), not being angry is good, if one can manage it (புணரின்). 312 says that even when someone has done hurt in hatred, not doing hurt in return is the settled stand of the stainless (மறுத்தின்னா செய்யாமை). 308 governs the feeling and 312 the act that would follow from it; 308 alone concedes that it may not be possible.

308 asks for no anger even under harm like fire. 852, in the chapter on hostility in the Book of Wealth, says that even if someone does what cannot be borne, meaning division, not doing harm in return is best (இன்னா செய்யாமை தலை). The same advice, with the same 'even if ... செயினும்' form, is given as virtue in one book and as policy in the other.

309 says all one has thought of is gained at once (உள்ளியதெல்லாம் உடனெய்தும்) if one never thinks of anger in the heart. 540 says gaining what one has thought of is easy (உள்ளியது எய்தல் எளிது) if one can keep thinking of it. Both promise the same result in nearly the same words and set a condition on the mind: one removes a thought, the other holds one.

265 says austerity is striven for here because whatever is wanted is obtained as wanted (வேண்டிய வேண்டியாங்கு எய்தலால்). 309 says all that is thought of is obtained if anger is never thought of; Parimelazhagar takes its subject to be the one doing austerity. On that reading 309 names the condition under which the promise of 265 holds.

309 praises one who does not think of anger in the heart at all (உள்ளத்தால் உள்ளான் வெகுளி). 487 says the bright do not flare up outwardly on the spot but, watching for the time, burn within (காலம்பார்த்து உள்வேர்ப்பர்). They conflict if both describe how a wise person treats anger inwardly, one removing it and the other keeping it for later; the conflict lessens if 309 is for the ascetic, as Parimelazhagar reads it, and 487 for a ruler facing enemies.

310 plays on இறந்தார் and துறந்தார்: those who go beyond bounds in anger are like the dead, and those who have renounced anger are the equals of the renounced. 159 uses the same two words: those who bear harsh words from the mouths of இறந்தார் (those who overstep) have the purity of துறந்தார். In both, a householder's control over anger is measured against the renouncer and found equal.

310 makes giving up anger the mark that puts one level with renouncers (சினத்தைத் துறந்தார் துறந்தார் துணை). 29, in the chapter on the greatness of renouncers, speaks of the anger of those who stand on the hill of good qualities (குன்றேறி நின்றார் வெகுளி). On Pope's and Parimelazhagar's reading of 29, that this anger cannot be withstood even for a moment, the great renouncers do get angry; on the other reading, that they cannot keep anger even for a moment, the two verses agree.

311 says the stainless hold to not hurting others even if it would bring wealth that yields eminence (சிறப்பீனும் செல்வம் பெறினும்). 328 says that however great the gain that brings good, gain that comes by killing is the lowest for the worthy (கொன்றாகும் ஆக்கங் கடை). Adjacent chapters use the same concessive form to refuse the same trade, once for hurt and once for killing; Parimelazhagar narrows both, to yogic powers in 311 and to sacrifice in 328.

113 tells one to let go, that very day, of gain that comes from leaving fairness even if it brings only good (நன்றே தரினும் நடுவிகந்தாம் ஆக்கத்தை). 311 refuses wealth that would require hurting others (பிறர்க்கு இன்னா செய்யாமை). Both grant that the gain is real and still rule out the means, one in the householder's ethics and one in the renouncer's.

755, in the chapter on making wealth, says wealth that does not come with grace and love (அருளொடும் அன்பொடும் வாராப் பொருளாக்கம்) should be let go and not embraced. 311 makes not hurting others the settled stand of the stainless even at the cost of wealth. The condition that 311 states for the pure is repeated in the Book of Wealth as a rule for acquisition itself.

312 says that even when someone in hatred has done hurt (கறுத்து இன்னா செய்த அக்கண்ணும்), not hurting back is the stand of the stainless. 157 says that though others do what is improper to you, it is good to feel the pain and not do what is contrary to virtue (நோநொந்து அறனல்ல செய்யாமை நன்று). The forbearance chapter states for the householder what 312 states as a renouncer's resolve; Parimelazhagar reads the pain in 157 as pity for the wrongdoer.

852, on hostility, says that even if someone does unbearable things intending division, not doing hurt in return out of hostility is the highest course (இகல்கருதி இன்னாசெய்யாமை தலை). 312 says not hurting in return (மறுத்தின்னா செய்யாமை) is the stand of the stainless. The same rule, in nearly the same words, is carried from personal purity into the politics of faction.

313 says that doing hurt, even to those who hated you though you did nothing to them (செய்யாமல் செற்றார்க்கும்), brings sorrow with no escape (உய்யா விழுமம்). 207 says people escape any enmity (உய்வர்) but the enmity of their own deeds follows and kills (வினைப்பகை வீயாது பின்சென்று அடும்). The shared root உய் shows the reasoning: an enemy can be survived, one's own retaliation cannot.

314 defines punishing those who hurt you as doing them good so that they are ashamed (அவர்நாண நன்னயஞ் செய்து விடல்). 987 asks what worth (சால்பு) has achieved if one does not do sweet things even to those who did harm (இன்னாசெய்தார்க்கும் இனியவே செய்யாக்கால்). Both open on the same words, இன்னாசெய்தார்; the Book of Virtue gives it as a method, the Book of Wealth as the test of character.

158 says to defeat those who did wrong out of arrogance by one's own worthiness (தம் தகுதியான் வென்று விடல்), which Parimelazhagar reads as forbearance. 314 goes a step further: do them a kindness so that they feel shame. Both keep the vocabulary of contest (winning, punishing) while replacing retaliation, and 314 adds the active good that 158 leaves unstated.

152 says bearing an excess done to you is good and forgetting it is better still (அதனை மறத்தல் அதனினும் நன்று). 314 ends on விடல்: do good and let it go. Parimelazhagar takes this விடல் as forgetting both the hurt and the good done in return, which would make 314 the fuller form of 152's advice; the Tamil itself says only 'do and leave'.

315 asks what understanding achieves (அறிவினான் ஆகுவதுண்டோ) if one does not guard against another's pain as one's own. 203 says the chief of all understanding (அறிவினுள் எல்லாந் தலை) is not doing harm even to those who hate you. Read together they define அறிவு by non-harm: 203 positively, 315 by denying that anything else called understanding is of use.

315 asks for another's pain to be guarded against like one's own (பிறிதின்நோய் தந்நோய்போல்). 1015 says the world calls those who feel shame for others' disgrace and their own alike (பிறர்பழியும் தம்பழியும் நாணுவார்) the dwelling of shame. The same extension of a self-regarding feeling to others is made for pain in the Book of Virtue and for disgrace in the Book of Wealth.

120 says true trade for traders is caring for others' goods as their own (பிறவும் தமபோல் செயின்). 315 says understanding is useless unless another's pain is guarded like one's own (தந்நோய்போல்). The 'as one's own' measure is applied to goods in fair dealing and to suffering in non-harm.

316 says what one has perceived as painful (இன்னா எனத்தான் உணர்ந்தவை) one must not come near doing to another. 250 gives a way to perceive it: when going against the weaker, think of yourself before the stronger (வலியார்முன் தன்னை நினைக்க). 316 states the rule from one's own experience of pain; 250 supplies the act of imagination for the moment one has the upper hand.

317 calls it the highest thing not to do ill of any degree, at any time, to anyone, where the ill arises from the mind (மனத்தானாம் மாணா). 282 says even thinking in the heart of stealing another's goods is wrong (உள்ளத்தால் உள்ளலும் தீதே). Both locate the fault in the mind before any act; Manakkudavar reads 317 as 'even with the mind', while Parimelazhagar takes it as ill done with intent.

34 says being spotless in mind is the whole of virtue (மனத்துக்கண் மாசிலன் ஆதல் அனைத்து அறன்). 317 makes the highest thing the absence of any mind-born ill toward anyone (மனத்தானாம் மாணா செய்யாமை தலை), in a chapter whose first two verses speak of the மாசற்றார். 317 gives 34's general claim a specific content: the unstained mind is one that harbours no hurt.

316 gives the rule: what one has perceived as painful, do not do to another (துன்னாமை வேண்டும் பிறன்கண் செயல்). 318 turns it into a question: one who knows what hurts his own life (தன்னுயிர்க்கு இன்னாமை தானறிவான்), why (என்கொலோ) does he hurt other lives? The second verse treats breaking the rule as something needing explanation; Parimelazhagar suggests delusion as the implied answer. (The edition's text of 318 has typos in its first line.)

209 says that if a person loves himself (தன்னைத்தான் காதலனாயின்) he should not come near evil deeds, however small. 318 asks why one who knows what hurts his own life does hurt to other lives. Both reason from self-regard, by different routes: 209 from the doer's own interest, 318 from the doer's own knowledge of pain.

319 says that if you do hurt to others in the forenoon, hurt comes to you in the afternoon of itself (தாமே வரும்). 204 says do not plot another's ruin, for virtue plots the ruin of the plotter (அறஞ்சூழும் சூழ்ந்தவன் கேடு). Both make the return of harm automatic and close in time; 204 names அறம் as the agent where 319 leaves it as coming by itself.

208 says the ruin of those who do evil is like a shadow that never leaves and rests at the foot (நிழல் ... அடி உறைந்தற்று). 319 puts the same inevitability in time: forenoon and afternoon (முற்பகல், பிற்பகல்). One verse uses space and the other the day's two halves to say that consequence is attached to the deed; the day figure also fits a shadow lengthening after noon, though the text does not say so.

320 says all pains rest on those who caused pain, so those who want freedom from pain cause none (நோய்செய்யார் நோயின்மை வேண்டுபவர்). 206 says one who does not want afflicting things to overpower him (நோய்ப்பால தன்னை அடல் வேண்டாதான்) should not do evil to others. The two verses give the same prudential argument in the same vocabulary of நோய், one closing the renouncer's chapter on non-harm and one in the householder's chapter on fearing evil deeds.

320 says all pains fall on those who caused pain (நோயெல்லாம் நோய்செய்தார் மேலவாம்). 169 admits that the crooked-hearted prosper and the upright meet ruin, and says only that this is to be pondered (நினைக்கப் படும்). 169 concedes cases that 320's rule does not show on its face; Manakkudavar's reading of 320, that present pain comes from hurt done earlier, and Parimelazhagar's of 169, that such cases are to be examined for causes, are the way the commentators reconcile them.

331 calls lowest the paltry understanding that takes what does not last for lasting (நில்லாதவற்றை நிலையின என்றுணரும்). 351 says a joyless birth comes from the confusion that takes what is not real for real (பொருளல்லவற்றைப் பொருளென்று உணரும் மருள்). The two verses are built on the same sentence frame; 331 applies the misperception to duration and 351 to reality, and 351 adds the consequence, rebirth.

349 says the moment attachment ends births are cut off, and otherwise impermanence is what is seen (மற்று நிலையாமை காணப்படும்). 331 faults the understanding that takes the unlasting for lasting. 349 explains why the error in 331 matters: for one still attached, impermanence is the standing condition, and Parimelazhagar on 331 likewise ties the error to attachment and rebirth.

332 likens the coming of great wealth to a crowd gathering at a dance hall and its going to that crowd dispersing. 592 says possession of goods does not stay and slips away (பொருளுடைமை நில்லாது நீங்கிவிடும்), while possession of inner drive is real possession. The impermanence of wealth taught to the renouncer is restated in the Book of Wealth, where it becomes a reason to value energy and not a reason to withdraw.

332 says great wealth (பெருஞ்செல்வம்) arrives and leaves like a theatre crowd, with no exception stated. 112 says the wealth of a person of rectitude does not decay and is a support to his descendants (சிதைவின்றி எச்சத்திற்கு ஏமாப்பு உடைத்து). If 332 is read as a claim about all wealth, 112's durable wealth contradicts it; the conflict eases if 332 is taken, with Parimelazhagar, as wealth that stays only while its cause in good deeds lasts.

376 says what is not one's portion will not stay however it is guarded, and what is one's own will not go even if thrown out (பரியினும் ஆகாவாம் பாலல்ல ... சொரியினும் போகா தம). 332 says wealth comes and goes like a crowd at a show. 376 puts a cause behind 332's picture: coming and going follow one's allotted portion; Parimelazhagar reads 332 the same way, the crowd coming for the dance and leaving when it ends.

333 says wealth by nature does not stay, so on getting it one should at once do what stays (அது பெற்றால் அற்குப ஆங்கே செயல்). 226 says removing the ruinous hunger of the destitute is where one who has got wealth should deposit it (பெற்றான் பொருள்வைப்புழி). 226 names a concrete instance of the lasting thing 333 leaves open; Parimelazhagar glosses 333's lasting things as worship and giving done without looking for return.

437 says the wealth of the miser who does not do with it what should be done (செயற்பால செய்யாது) perishes without anything surviving. 333 says wealth does not stay and should be turned at once into what does. The Book of Wealth gives the same instruction negatively: unused wealth is simply lost.

334 says what shows itself as a 'day' is a blade sawing through life (உயிர் ஈரும் வாள்), for those who perceive it. 38 says doing good so that no day falls wasted (வீழ்நாள் படாஅமை) becomes a stone that blocks the road of one's days (வாழ்நாள் வழியடைக்கும் கல்), which Parimelazhagar takes as blocking further embodied life. Both count life in days; 38 says how the days that 334 shows being cut away can be used so that the counting stops.

334 presents each day as a blade cutting life, with no one exempted. 326 says Death, the eater of life, does not advance on the days (வாழ்நாள்மேல் செல்லாது) of one who lives by not killing. Read literally, 326 exempts the non-killer from the daily loss of life that 334 treats as universal; the conflict depends on taking 326 as a promise about lifespan and not as praise of the vow.

335 says good deeds must be hurried to before the hiccup rises and stops the tongue (நாச்செற்று விக்குள்மேல் வாராமுன்). 36 says do virtue without saying 'we will see to it then' (அன்றறிவாம் என்னாது), for it is the undying companion when one dies (பொன்றுங்கால் பொன்றாத் துணை). Both forbid postponing virtue to the deathbed; 335 gives the physical reason, that at that hour one cannot even speak.

342 says if you want what renunciation brings, renounce while there is still something (உண்டாகத் துறக்க), which Parimelazhagar takes as 'while there is time'. 335 says to hurry to good deeds before the death rattle. On that reading the next chapter applies the same urgency to renouncing that 335 applies to good deeds.

336 says this world has the 'greatness' that one who was here yesterday is not here today (நெருநல் உளனொருவன் இன்றில்லை). 233 says nothing in the world stands undying except high renown (புகழல்லால் பொன்றாது நிற்பதொன்றில்). 233 agrees with 336 about everything else and names one exception; the renouncer's chapter offers none.

336 says a person who was yesterday is not today (இன்றில்லை). 235 speaks of a death that is really existence (உளதாகும் சாக்காடு), possible only for the skilled, which Parimelazhagar explains as the body of fame surviving. The two verses use the same pair, உள and இல், in opposite directions: 336 for the plain fact of death and 235 for the rare death that leaves something that is.

338 says the friendship between body and life (உடம்பொடு உயிரிடை நட்பு) is like a bird flying off and leaving its shell or nest (குடம்பை) behind. In 1122 the lover says the bond between him and the girl is whatever the bond between body and life is (உடம்பொடு உயிரிடை என்ன மற்றன்ன ... நட்பு). The same phrase is used with opposite force: the lover uses it for closeness, and 338 has already said that this bond ends in desertion; Parimelazhagar notes that 1122 is spoken in fear of parting.

73 reports that the bond of life with the body (ஆருயிர்க்கு என்போடு இயைந்த தொடர்பு) is the way of being joined with love. 338 calls the same bond a நட்பு that ends as a bird leaves its shell. 73 gives the union a purpose, a life lived in love; 338 gives its term. Read together, the body is a temporary partner that exists for something.

338 pictures the body as a குடம்பை, shell or nest, that the bird leaves empty; 340 pictures it as a lodging (துச்சில்) where life stays as a tenant without a home of its own (புக்கில்). Both make the body a dwelling and life its occupant. 338 shows the departure, and 340 asks why there has to be one; Manakkudavar takes the permanent home to be liberation.

339 says death is like falling asleep and birth like waking from sleep (உறங்குவது போலுஞ் சாக்காடு). 926 says those asleep are no different from the dead (துஞ்சினார் செத்தாரின் வேறல்லர்), in order to say drinkers are always eating poison. The same equation of sleep and death runs both ways: 339 makes death as ordinary as sleep, 926 makes sleep, and so stupor, as bad as death; Parimelazhagar says the likeness in 926 is the absence of awareness.

339 presents death and birth as alternating like sleep and waking, which both Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar read as a cycle that keeps turning. 356 says those who have learned here and seen the true thing reach the path of not coming back here (மற்றீண்டு வாரா நெறி). 356 limits 339: the waking that follows each death is the rule only for those who have not seen the real.

340 asks whether the life that has stayed as a lodger in the body (உடம்பினுள் துச்சில் இருந்த உயிர்க்கு) has not found a permanent home. 345 says that for those set on cutting off births even the body is excess (உடம்பும் மிகை). 340 says the body is not life's own house; the chapter on renunciation draws the conclusion, that the seeker treats the body itself as one possession too many.

341 says that whatever one has left (யாதனின் நீங்கியான்), from that one has no pain (நோதல் இலன்). 626, in the chapter on not being undone by trouble, asks whether those who never guarded wealth saying 'we have got it' (பெற்றேமென்று ஓம்புதல் தேற்றாதவர்) would grieve saying 'we have lost it' (அற்றேமென்று). The renouncer's rule reappears in the book of wealth as a habit of mind for someone who still owns things.

341 ties freedom from pain to having left the thing itself (நீங்கியான்). 629 says one who does not crave the pleasure in pleasure (இன்பத்துள் இன்பம் விழையாதான்) does not suffer the pain in pain; Parimelazhagar reads this as someone who goes on experiencing the pleasure without wanting it. The pairing shows the same result claimed for an inward letting go, without the outward leaving.

341's doubled யாதனின் யாதனின் ... அதனின் அதனின் allows release thing by thing: each thing left stops hurting. 343 demands that everything wanted be let go together (வேண்டிய வெல்லாம் ஒருங்கு). Parimelazhagar notices the difference under 341, calling giving up everything at once the chief way while granting that giving things up one by one still removes the pain each brings.

342 says that after renouncing, many things come about here (ஈண்டு இயற்பால பல), which Parimelazhagar takes as joys in this life. 369 says joy is unbroken even here (இன்பம் இடையறாது ஈண்டும்) once craving, the sorrow of sorrows, is gone. Both place the reward of letting go in this world (ஈண்டு), not only after death.

46 asks what a person who runs household life by the way of virtue would gain by going to the outside way (புறத்தாற்றில் போஒய்ப் பெறுவது எவன்). 342 says that after renouncing there are many things to be had here, and urges renouncing if one wants them (வேண்டின் ... துறக்க). The conflict depends on reading புறத்தாறு as the ascetic path, as Pope does: on that reading 46's rhetorical 'what is gained?' gets the answer 'much' in 342.

36 tells one to do virtue without saying 'we will see to it then' (அன்றறிவாம் என்னாது). 342's உண்டாகத் துறக்க is read by Parimelazhagar as 'renounce while there is time', i.e. in youth, so the joys last long; Manakkudavar instead reads it as 'if you want gain for your life'. On Parimelazhagar's reading the chapter on renunciation repeats, for renouncing, the earlier rule against postponing virtue.

126, in the householder's chapter on restraint, speaks of drawing in the five like a tortoise (ஆமைபோல் ஐந்தடக்கல்), which protects through seven births. 343 uses a harder verb for the renouncer: the field of the five must be killed or crushed (அடல்வேண்டும் ஐந்தன் புலத்தை), and every wanted thing dropped at once. Read together they show two degrees of the same discipline, withdrawal that can be reversed and destruction that cannot.

6 describes God as the one who quenched the five whose gates are the senses (பொறிவாயில் ஐந்தவித்தான்) and promises long life to those who keep to his path. 343 lays the same thing on the renouncer as a duty (அடல்வேண்டும் ஐந்தன் புலத்தை). The renouncer is asked to do what the invocation names as the mark of the Lord.

343 says the field of the five senses must be crushed. In 1101 the lover lists the same five, seeing, hearing, tasting, smelling and touching (கண்டுகேட்டு உண்டுயிர்த்து உற்றறியும் ஐம்புலனும்), and says all are found in this one woman. This is a lover's speech and not a teaching, but the shared catalogue shows the Book of Love celebrating exactly what the chapter on renunciation tells the ascetic to destroy.

344 says having nothing at all is natural to the vow (இயல்பாகும் நோன்பிற்கு ஒன்றின்மை) and that owning anything brings back confusion. 1036 says that if ploughmen fold their hands, even those who say 'we have given up what is desired' have no standing (விட்டேம் என்பார்க்கும் நிலை இல்லை). The renouncer's owning nothing rests on others who produce food.

344 makes possessionlessness the nature of austerity. 263 asks whether the others have forgotten austerity out of a wish to provide for those who have renounced (துறந்தார்க்குத் துப்புரவு வேண்டி). The pairing shows that the ascetic's having nothing is sustained by householders who keep possessions in order to give.

344 treats having nothing (ஒன்றின்மை) as the proper state of the vow. 1050 speaks of those who have nothing to enjoy (துப்புரவில்லார்) and yet do not fully renounce (துவரத் துறவாமை), calling them death to salt and gruel. Lacking things is therefore not the same as renouncing: poverty without the inner giving up is counted as a burden, not as austerity.

340 calls the life a lodger in the body (உடம்பினுள் துச்சில் இருந்த உயிர்) and asks whether it has found no home of its own. 345 draws the consequence for those set on cutting off births: even the body is surplus (உடம்பும் மிகை), so further ties make no sense. The chapter on impermanence states the body's temporary status; this verse turns it into a reason to drop attachment.

73 says the bond of the precious life with the body (ஆருயிர்க்கு என்போடு இயைந்த தொடர்பு) is the way that came to be joined with love, so embodiment is given a purpose. 345 says that for those undertaking to cut off births (பிறப்பறுக்கல் உற்றார்க்கு) the body itself is excess and other ties (தொடர்ப்பாடு) pointless. The value 73 gives the body-bond holds within the life of love; 345 marks where, for the renouncer, it stops holding.

345 says even the body is too much for one seeking to end birth. 627, in the book of wealth, says the great do not take trouble as trouble, knowing the body is a target for suffering (இலக்கம் உடம்பு இடும்பைக்கு). Both start from the body as a liability, but 627 uses that view to keep steady in worldly trouble while 345 uses it to argue for giving up every tie.

346 says one who cuts off the pride of saying 'I' and 'mine' (யான் எனது என்னும் செருக்கு) enters a world above the gods. 72 says the loveless keep everything for themselves (எல்லாம் தமக்குரியர்) while the loving belong to others even to their bones (என்பும் உரியர் பிறர்க்கு). The householder's love already loosens 'mine', and even the body as 'I', by giving it to others; renunciation does it by cutting the notion itself.

50 says one who lives on earth as life should be lived will be placed among the gods who dwell in the sky (வானுறையும் தெய்வத்துள் வைக்கப்படும்). 346 promises the one who ends 'I' and 'mine' a world higher than the gods' (வானோர்க்கு உயர்ந்த உலகம்). Set side by side the two verses give a scale: the good householder reaches the gods, the renouncer goes beyond them.

347 says griefs hold and do not let go of those who hold attachment and do not let go (பற்றினைப் பற்றி விடாஅதவர்க்கு). 940 says that as a gambler loves the game more with each loss, the life grows more fond with each suffering it undergoes (துன்பம் உழத்தொறூஉம் காதற்று உயிர்); Parimelazhagar and Pope take the object of that fondness to be the body. 940 supplies what 347 leaves unexplained: suffering does not loosen the grip but tightens it.

347 uses பற்று for attachment in general and says its holders are held by griefs. 438, on a ruler's faults, names miserliness as 'the clinging heart' (பற்றுள்ளம் என்னும் இவறன்மை) and says it is not to be counted with any other fault. The same word and the same refusal to let go appear in the domain of wealth, where Parimelazhagar glosses it as not releasing goods when they ought to be released.

348 says those who have thoroughly renounced have reached the goal and the rest, confused, are caught in the net (மயங்கி வலைப்பட்டார் மற்றையவர்). 266 says those who do austerity do their own work and the rest, caught in desire, do what is futile (மற்றல்லார் அவஞ்செய்வார் ஆசையுட் பட்டு). Both divide people in two with the same 'caught' (பட்டு/பட்டார்), and 266 names the net as desire.

348 gives the prize only to those who renounce thoroughly (தீரத் துறந்தார்). 365 says those called 'freed' are those freed of craving, and the others are not freed in that way (மற்றையார் அற்றாக அற்றது இலர்), whatever else they have given up. 365 specifies what 348's 'thoroughly' requires: the giving up must reach craving, not only things.

348 sets those who have fully renounced above everyone else. 276 says none are harder-hearted than those who have not renounced in the heart (நெஞ்சின் துறவார்) and live by deceiving as though they had (துறந்தார்போல் வஞ்சித்து). The praise in 348 therefore applies to renunciation of the heart; the outward form without it is placed among the worst.

361 says craving is the seed that yields unceasing birth for all beings (தவாஅப் பிறப்பீனும் வித்து). 349 says the moment attachment is cut off, that cuts off birth (பற்றற்ற கண்ணே பிறப்பறுக்கும்). One verse names the cause and the other states what follows when the cause is removed; Parimelazhagar makes the same cause-and-effect point under 349.

331 calls it the lowest understanding to take what does not last for lasting (நில்லாதவற்றை நிலையின என்றுணரும்). 349 says that where attachment is not cut, impermanence is what is seen (மற்று நிலையாமை காணப்படும்), which Parimelazhagar reads as the round of being born and dying. The impermanence that chapter 34 asks the reader to recognise becomes, in 349, what the attached person goes on undergoing.

4 says those who reach the feet of the one without wanting or not-wanting (வேண்டுதல் வேண்டாமை இலான்) have no suffering anywhere. 350 tells one to cling to the clinging of the one without clinging (பற்றற்றான் பற்றினை), in order to let clinging go. The invocation's promise becomes a method here, and Parimelazhagar notes that பற்றற்றான் is used in keeping with the invocation chapter.

350 uses attachment to end attachment: cling to that clinging so that clinging is let go (பற்றுக பற்று விடற்கு). 362 uses desire the same way: if you must want, want not being born, and that comes by wanting not-wanting (வேண்டாமை வேண்ட வரும்). Both verses accept that the thing to be removed has to be turned on itself as the means.

350 says to hold to the hold of the one who has none. 359 says that if one knows the support and lives so that supports perish (சார்புணர்ந்து சார்புகெட ஒழுகின்), the pains due to come will not come. The two are built alike on a repeated word, பற்று and சார்பு, and Parimelazhagar reads the சார்பு that is known as the true reality on which all rests, so 359 states the result of the practice 350 prescribes.

351 says an inglorious birth comes from the delusion that takes what is not real for real (மருளானாம் மாணாப் பிறப்பு). 1002 ends with the same words: the delusion of thinking everything comes by wealth, and so hoarding without giving, produces an inglorious birth. The book of wealth applies the metaphysical formula to one concrete error, treating money as the thing that matters.

351 speaks of perceiving as real what is not real (பொருளல்லவற்றைப் பொருளென்று உணரும்). 331 has the same construction for time: perceiving as lasting what does not last (நில்லாதவற்றை நிலையின என்றுணரும்), which it calls the lowest of understandings. The two verses name the same mistake of perception, once about duration and once about reality, and 351 adds its cost: rebirth.

352 says that for those of stainless sight who have left delusion (மருள்நீங்கி மாசறு காட்சியவர்க்கு) darkness goes and joy comes. 199 uses nearly the same phrase (மருள்தீர்ந்த மாசறு காட்சியவர்) for people who do not say meaningless things even by a slip. The person who in 352 attains release is recognised in ordinary life, in 199, by how they speak.

5 says the two kinds of deed joined with darkness (இருள்சேர் இருவினை) do not attach to those devoted to the Lord's praise; Parimelazhagar glosses the darkness as delusion. 352 says darkness leaves (இருள்நீங்கி) those whose sight is free of delusion; Manakkudavar takes this darkness as ignorance, while Parimelazhagar takes it as hell and so as birth. The same darkness is removed in 5 by devotion and in 352 by clear seeing.

352 has darkness leave and joy arise for those who see truly. 243 says those whose hearts are joined with compassion do not enter the painful world joined with darkness (இருள்சேர்ந்த இன்னா உலகம்). 243's wording supports Parimelazhagar's reading of இருள் in 352 as a dark world of suffering, and shows the book promising escape from it by compassion as well as by knowledge.

353 says that for those who have left doubt and become clear (ஐயத்தின் நீங்கித் தெளிந்தார்க்கு) the sky is nearer than the earth. 702 says one who knows without doubt what is within another (ஐயப்படாஅது அகத்தது உணர்வானை) should be held equal to a god. In both, knowing free of doubt lifts a person toward the divine, once in the knowledge of reality and once in a courtier's reading of minds.

50 says one who lives on earth (வையத்துள்) as one should is placed among the gods who dwell in the sky. 353 uses the same pair, earth and sky (வையத்தின் வானம்), and says the sky is the nearer of the two for one who is clear of doubt. The householder gets there by right living and the knower by certainty, and in both the sky is brought within reach of someone still on earth.

27 says the world lies within one who discerns the kinds of the five: taste, light, touch, sound and smell (ஐந்தின் வகைதெரிவான் கட்டே உலகு). 354 says that even when the fivefold awareness is attained (ஐயுணர்வு எய்தியக் கண்ணும்) there is no benefit for those without perception of the real. Mastery of the five, praised in 27, is declared insufficient by itself in 354.

126 says that drawing in the five like a tortoise in one birth is a protection for seven. 354 says the attained fivefold awareness yields no fruit without true perception; Parimelazhagar reads ஐயுணர்வு as the mind withdrawn from the senses and held under control, and the missing fruit as release, while Manakkudavar reads it as knowing all that the five senses can know. On Parimelazhagar's reading sense-restraint earns protection across births, as 126 says, but not the end of birth.

2 asks what learning has achieved (கற்றதனால் ஆய பயனென்கொல்) if the learned do not bow at the feet of the one of pure knowledge. 354 says command of the five senses has no benefit (பயமின்றே) for those without perception of the real. Both verses grant an attainment and then deny its fruit when the final step is missing, learning without worship in one and discipline without insight in the other.

355 and 423 differ in a single phrase. 423: whatever is heard from whoever's mouth (யார்யார்வாய்க் கேட்பினும்), seeing the true thing in it is understanding; 355: whatever a thing is and of whatever nature (எத்தன்மைத் தாயினும்), seeing the true thing in it is understanding. Parimelazhagar reads மெய்ப்பொருள் in 423 as the real worth of what is said and in 355 as the reality left when the world's imposed notions are removed, so one formula serves practical judgment and knowledge of reality.

355 defines understanding as seeing the true thing (மெய்ப்பொருள் காண்பது) in anything. 249 uses that act as a comparison: virtue done by one without compassion is like an unclear person seeing the true thing (தெருளாதான் மெய்ப்பொருள் கண்டற்று). 249 assumes what 355 states, that seeing the real needs a clear mind, and treats the claim of someone muddled to have seen it as empty.

355 makes seeing the true thing the definition of understanding. 857 says those of bitter understanding who hold to hostility do not see the true thing (மெய்ப்பொருள் காணார்); Parimelazhagar takes it there as the substance of the texts on right policy that bring success. The same phrase marks, in the book of wealth, what a mind bent on quarrel cannot perceive.

398 says the learning acquired in one birth protects through seven (எழுமையும் ஏமாப்புடைத்து). 356 says those who have learned here and seen the true thing (கற்றீண்டு மெய்ப்பொருள் கண்டார்) reach the path of not coming back here (மற்றீண்டு வாரா நெறி). Learning in the book of wealth is an asset carried across births; learning that ends in seeing the real is said to end the births themselves.

356 joins learning to seeing: those who have learned and seen the true thing reach the path of no return. 373 says that however many subtle books one studies, one's own native understanding still prevails (தன் உண்மை யறிவே மிகும்). Study by itself does not guarantee the seeing, which is why 356 names both steps.

2 asks what use learning is to those who do not bow at the feet of the one of pure knowledge. 356 gives learning its use: those who learn here and see the true thing (கற்றீண்டு மெய்ப்பொருள் கண்டார்) gain the path of no return. Both measure learning by whether it reaches what is ultimate, named as the Lord in 2 and as the true thing in 356.

356 speaks of those who learn and see the true thing; 357 adds the mind's own work: if the mind examines and knows with certainty what is (ஓர்த்து ... உள்ளது உணரின் ஒருதலையா), one need not think of birth again. Parimelazhagar reads the two as successive means, hearing instruction in 356 and reasoned examination in 357. The printed text here has உணரான், but Parimelazhagar's and Manakkudavar's glosses read உணரின், which the sense requires.

358 defines understanding as seeing the செம்பொருள் (செம்பொருள் காண்பது அறிவு), which Parimelazhagar explains as the changeless first reality. 91 says sweet words come from the mouths of those who have seen the செம்பொருள் (செம்பொருள் கண்டார் வாய்ச்சொல்), where Parimelazhagar takes the word as virtue. The same phrase names the seer of final truth in one place and the source of kind, honest speech in the other.

351 says a joyless birth comes from the delusion (மருள்) that takes the unreal for real. 358 goes a step further and calls birth itself a folly (பிறப்பென்னும் பேதைமை); Parimelazhagar explains this as naming the effect in place of its cause. The chapter moves from delusion as the cause of birth to birth and delusion spoken of as one thing, removed together by seeing the real.

358 speaks of 'the folly called birth' departing when the real is seen. 835, in the chapter on folly in the book of wealth, says a fool can in one birth's doing make the mire he will sink into for seven (எழுமையும் தான்புக் கழுந்தும் அளறு). Both tie பேதைமை to the chain of births, 358 as its root and 835 through the fool's deeds.

5 says the two kinds of deed do not attach (சேரா) to those devoted to the Lord's praise. 359 says the pains due to attach will not attach (சார்தரா சார்தரு நோய்) to one who knows the support and lives so that supports perish; Parimelazhagar takes these as the fruits of stored deeds still awaiting experience, and Manakkudavar takes சார்பு itself as the hold of deeds. Devotion in 5 and knowledge with practice in 359 are credited with the same effect on karma.

347 says griefs hold and do not let go of those who hold on to attachment. 359 gives the other case: for one who knows the support and lives so that supports fall away (சார்புகெட ஒழுகின்), the pains that were due do not come to cling. 347 states the bondage and 359 the way out, in the same language of things that cling.

360 says pain perishes when desire, anger and confusion perish down to their names (காமம் வெகுளி மயக்கம் ... நாமம் கெட); Parimelazhagar glosses the three as wanting, aversion and ignorance. 4 describes God as the one without wanting or not-wanting (வேண்டுதல் வேண்டாமை இலான்) and says those who reach his feet have no suffering. The state 360 sets as the goal is the nature 4 gives to the Lord, with the same result, the end of suffering.

35 defines virtue as conduct that avoids four things: envy, craving, anger and harsh speech (அழுக்காறு அவா வெகுளி இன்னாச்சொல்). 360 names three, desire, anger and confusion, and asks that even their names be gone. Craving and anger are on both lists; the early verse asks that conduct not slip into them, the later one that they be destroyed at the root, with confusion added as the one that knowledge removes.

360 lists desire, anger and confusion as what must perish for pain to end. 431 lists three faults whose absence gives a ruler's prosperity its dignity: arrogance, anger and smallness (செருக்கும் சினமும் சிறுமையும்), which Parimelazhagar glosses as pride, anger and lust. A similar triad, sharing anger and, on that gloss, desire, is the obstacle to release in one book and to good rule in the other.

361 calls craving (அவா) the seed (வித்து) that yields unfailing birth (தவாஅப் பிறப்பு ஈனும்) for all beings at all times. 349 says the moment attachment ends it cuts off birth (பற்றற்ற கண்ணே பிறப்பறுக்கும்). The two state one causal claim from both ends: craving produces birth, and its ending stops birth.

361 uses வித்து for craving, the seed from which birth keeps growing. 24 uses the same word for the person who guards the five senses with the goad of firmness: he is a seed for the ground called வரன் (வரனென்னும் வைப்பிற்கோர் வித்து), which Parimelazhagar takes as the ground of release. The seed figure is used for both outcomes, rebirth from craving and release from restraint of the senses.

362 says that if one must want, one should want not to be born, and that this comes by wanting not-wanting (வேண்டாமை வேண்ட வரும்). 350 says to cling to the clinging of the one without clinging in order to let clinging go (பற்றுக ... பற்று விடற்கு). Both turn the fault against itself: wanting and clinging are given a single object whose effect is to end them.

265 says austerity is pursued here because whatever is wanted is obtained as wanted (வேண்டிய வேண்டியாங்கு எய்தலால்). 362 narrows what is worth wanting to one thing, not being born (வேண்டுங்கால் வேண்டும் பிறவாமை), and says it is reached by wanting not to want. Read together, 362 limits the open promise of 265 to a single proper wish.

180, on not coveting others' goods, says the pride called not-wanting yields victory (விறல்ஈனும் வேண்டாமை என்னுஞ் செருக்கு); Parimelazhagar glosses செருக்கு there as wealth. 363 says there is no fine wealth like not-wanting (வேண்டாமை அன்ன விழுச்செல்வம்) here or there. The householder's restraint toward another's property becomes, in the renouncer's chapter, not wanting anything at all, and in both it is counted as a possession.

363 says nothing here (ஈண்டு) or there (ஆண்டும்) equals not-wanting. 213 says that in the world of the gods and here (புத்தேளுலகத்தும் ஈண்டும்) it is hard to find another good like ஒப்புரவு, doing what is due to others. The same two-world formula ranks a different thing highest in each setting: giving to the world in the householder's book, wanting nothing in the renouncer's.

Both verses use விழுச்செல்வம், fine wealth, for something that is not goods. 400 says learning is the imperishable fine wealth and other things are not wealth (மாடல்ல மற்றையவை); 363 says no fine wealth is like not-wanting. The pairing shows the book repeatedly moving the word wealth away from property, to learning in one place and to the absence of want in another.

298 says outer purity comes by water and inner purity is seen through truth (அகந்தூய்மை வாய்மையால் காணப்படும்). 364 says purity is the absence of craving (தூஉய்மை என்பது அவாவின்மை) and that this comes by wanting வாய்மை. 364 puts a step between the two terms of 298: truth leads to freedom from craving, and that is what purity is. Manakkudavar reads வாய்மை in 364 as truthful speech, as in 298; Parimelazhagar reads it as the true reality.

34 says being spotless in mind is the whole of virtue (மனத்துக்கண் மாசிலன் ஆதல் அனைத்து அறன்). 364 defines purity as the absence of craving (அவாவின்மை). Taken together, 364 names the stain that 34 leaves unnamed.

365 says those called freed (அற்றவர்) are those freed of craving, and the rest (மற்றையார்) are not freed in that way. 348 says those who have renounced completely (தீரத் துறந்தார்) have arrived, and the rest (மற்றையவர்) are confused and caught in the net. Both divide people into two groups with no middle, and both make completeness the test.

275 warns that the hidden conduct of those who say 'we are free of attachment' (பற்றற்றேம் என்பார்) brings many harms. 365 says who may rightly be called freed (அற்றவர் என்பார்): only those freed of craving. 275 shows the claim made falsely; 365 gives the inner criterion that the claim has to meet.

35 defines virtue as what proceeds without slipping into four things, one of which is craving (அழுக்காறு அவா வெகுளி இன்னாச்சொல்). 366 says craving is what deceives a person (வஞ்சிப்பது அவா), and that fearing it is itself virtue (அஞ்சுவதோரும் அறனே). 366 takes one item from the list in 35 and gives the reason for singling it out: it works by deceit, so it needs constant watch.

428 says fearing what should be feared is the work of the knowing (அஞ்சுவது அஞ்சல் அறிவார் தொழில்) and leaves the object open. 366 names an object, craving, and calls the fear of it virtue (அஞ்சுவதோரும் அறனே). The general rule about right fear in the book of statecraft gets a specific content in the renouncer's chapter.

Fear and craving appear together in both verses with opposite roles. In 1075 fear is the whole conduct of the base (அச்சமே கீழ்களது ஆசாரம்), with a little more if there is something they crave (அவாவுண்டேல்); Parimelazhagar takes the fear as fear of punishment. In 366 fear is directed at craving itself and is called virtue. The pairing separates fear that serves craving from fear that guards against it.

266 says those who do austerity do their own work, and the others, caught in desire, do what is futile (அவஞ்செய்வார் ஆசையுட் பட்டு). 367 says that if craving is cut off thoroughly, the deed that does not fail (தவாவினை) comes in the way one wishes. They state the same link from opposite sides: desire makes action futile, and its removal makes action unfailing.

309 says all that one has thought of is reached at once if one does not think of anger in the heart (உள்ளியதெல்லாம் உடனெய்தும்). 367 says the unfailing deed comes as one wishes (தான் வேண்டுமாற்றான் வரும்) once craving is cut. Each verse removes one passion, anger or craving, and promises that what one intends then arrives.

341 says a person has no pain from each thing he has left (யாதனின் யாதனின் நீங்கியான் நோதல் அதனின் அதனின் இலன்), taking objects one by one. 368 says those without craving have no sorrow at all (அவாஇல்லார்க்கு இல்லாகுந் துன்பம்). 368 moves from the objects given up to the craving behind them, so the relief is complete instead of item by item.

347 says sorrows hold and do not let go of those who hold attachment and do not let go (பற்றி விடாஅ இடும்பைகள்). 368 says that where craving exists sorrow keeps coming without fail, one after another (தவாஅது மேன்மேல் வரும்). Both describe suffering as continuing for as long as its cause is kept.

628, in the chapter on not being undone by trouble, says one who does not desire pleasure (இன்பம் விழையான்) and calls hardship natural does not come to sorrow (துன்பம் உறுதல் இலன்). 368 says those without craving have no sorrow. The renouncer's doctrine reappears as practical advice for a person at work in the world, where Parimelazhagar relates it to the pains of effort.

The two verses share one sentence frame. 369: joy is unbroken if the sorrow of sorrows called craving perishes (அவாவென்னும் துன்பத்துள் துன்பங் கெடின்). 854: it yields the joy of joys if the sorrow of sorrows called hostility perishes (இகலென்னும் துன்பத்துள் துன்பங் கெடின்). The same title, sorrow of sorrows, is given to craving in the book of virtue and to hostility in the book of statecraft, each as the worst thing in its own field.

370 says craving has a nature that is never filled (ஆரா இயற்கை அவா). 940 gives a picture of that: as the gambler loves the game more with each loss (இழத்தொறூஉம் காதலிக்கும்), a living being's love grows with each suffering (துன்பம் உழத்தொறூஉம் காதற்று உயிர்); Parimelazhagar takes this as love of the body. 940 shows why satisfying craving cannot end it, which is why 370 says it has to be given up.

370 says that giving up craving gives, in that very state (அந்நிலையே), a nature that does not shift (பேரா இயற்கை). 349 says the moment attachment ends (பற்றற்ற கண்ணே) it cuts off birth. Both make the result immediate on the cause ending, with no further step between.

371 says tireless effort arises from a fate of gain and sloth arises from a fate of loss (போகூழால் தோன்றும் மடி). 618 says lacking good fortune (பொறியின்மை) is no one's disgrace, but lacking effort after learning what should be known is a disgrace (ஆள்வினை இன்மை பழி). If sloth itself is produced by fate, as 371 says on a plain reading, the line 618 draws between blameless fortune and blameworthy idleness is hard to hold.

594 says prosperity asks the way and goes to the one whose energy does not flag (அசைவிலா ஊக்கமுடையான்). 371 uses the same word, அசைவின்மை, and says it arises from a fate of gain (ஆகூழால் தோன்றும்). 594 presents unflagging energy as what draws fortune; 371 puts a favourable fate behind that energy.

617 says the dark goddess of misfortune lives in sloth (மடியுளாள் மாமுகடி) and the lotus goddess lives in the effort of the one without sloth. 371 says sloth (மடி) and its opposite are themselves produced by the fate of loss and the fate of gain. In 617 fortune depends on whether one is slothful; 371 adds that whether one is slothful depends on fate.

372 says a fate of loss makes a person foolish and a fate of gain, when it arrives, widens understanding (அறிவகற்றும் ஆகலூழ் உற்றக் கடை). 859 says that when gain is coming a person does not look at hostility (இகல்காணான் ஆக்கம் வருங்கால்), and to bring ruin on himself he looks to excel at it. In both, approaching gain or ruin shows first as a change in the person's own judgement.

429 says those whose understanding guards against what is coming (எதிரதாக் காக்கும் அறிவினார்) meet no affliction that shakes them. 372 says a fate of loss makes a person foolish (பேதைப் படுக்கும் இழவூழ்); Parimelazhagar adds that this happens even to one who has understanding. The protection 429 promises rests on understanding, and 372 says understanding itself can be taken away by fate.

396 says understanding wells up in people to the extent they have learned (கற்றனைத்து ஊறும் அறிவு), like water in a sand well. 373 says that however many subtle books a person studies, the understanding that is truly his own still prevails (தன் உண்மையறிவே மிகும்). On the reading that உண்மையறிவு is a fixed native understanding, which Parimelazhagar ties to fate, study does not decide how much a person understands, and the two conflict. Parimelazhagar notes the conflict himself under 396 and resolves it by saying 396 holds where fate does not oppose.

373 separates understanding gained from books (நூல்பல கற்பினும்) from a person's own understanding (தன் உண்மையறிவு) and says the second prevails. 636 names the same pair, natural acuteness together with books (மதிநுட்பம் நூலோடு), and says no subtle scheme can stand before a minister who has both. 373 ranks the two; 636 shows the best case, where both are present.

823 says that even after learning many good things it is hard for the unworthy to become good in heart (பலநல்ல கற்றக் கடைத்தும் மனநல்லர் ஆகுதல் மாணார்க்கு அரிது); Parimelazhagar applies this to enemies. 373 says that after much study a person's own understanding still prevails. The same limit on what books can change is stated once for understanding and once for the heart.

374 says the world's nature is of two separate kinds: being wealthy is one thing and being clear-minded is another (திருவேறு தெள்ளியராதலும் வேறு). 430 says those with understanding have everything (அறிவுடையார் எல்லாம் உடையார்). If 'everything' in 430 includes wealth, as Parimelazhagar explains it by saying wealth is made and kept by understanding, the two conflict; under 374 he says the opposite, that understanding is not even a contributing cause of wealth. If 430 only means that understanding outweighs possessions, there is no conflict.

374 states as a general fact that wealth and clear understanding are separate lots. 408 judges one result of that: wealth lodged with the unlearned is more painful than poverty lodged with the good (கல்லார்கண் பட்ட திரு). 408 takes for granted the mismatch that 374 explains.

169 says the prosperity of the crooked-hearted and the ruin of the upright are things to be pondered (நினைக்கப்படும்), and gives no answer; Parimelazhagar says the wise look for the earlier deed behind it. 374 notes a like mismatch between wealth and understanding and gives it as the two-fold nature of the world. One verse separates wealth from goodness and the other separates it from wisdom.

483 asks whether anything is hard for one who acts with the right means and knowing the time (கருவியான் காலம் அறிந்து செயின்). 375 says that in making wealth all that is good turns bad and bad turns good (நல்லவை எல்லாஅந் தீயவாம்); Parimelazhagar takes the good and bad things to be time, place, means and action, reversed by fate. On that reading the favourable conditions 483 relies on do not secure the result, and the two conflict. Kalaignar reads 375 differently, as good and bad deeds turning out contrary to intent.

376 says what is not one's portion will not stay however carefully it is guarded (பரியினும் ஆகாவாம் பாலல்ல), and what is one's own will not leave even if thrown out. 659 says all that is taken with others' tears leaves with tears, and what is of the good kind (நற்பாலவை) pays later even if lost. Both say some goods stay and some go whatever one does; 659 gives a test the person controls, the way the wealth was gained, where 376 gives only fate's allotment.

1005 says those who neither give nor enjoy have nothing even with crores piled up (அடுக்கிய கோடியுண்டாயினும் இல்), and treats this as the miser's own failing. 377 says even those who have gathered crores can enjoy them only as the apportioner has apportioned (வகுத்தான் வகுத்த வகையல்லால் ... துய்த்தல் அரிது). Both separate owning from enjoying; 377 places part of enjoyment outside the owner's choice, which limits the blame in 1005.

385 lists the king's skills with wealth: creating, gathering, guarding and apportioning what is guarded (காத்த வகுத்தலும்). 377 uses the same verb for the one who apportions each person's enjoyment (வகுத்தான் வகுத்த வகை), whom Parimelazhagar glosses as தெய்வம். The pairing sets the human apportioner of the state's wealth beside the apportioner who decides what even the gatherer of crores may enjoy.

377 and 1062 are two places where the book puts a personal agent behind people's lots: the apportioner (வகுத்தான்) in 377 and the one who made the world (உலகியற்றியான்) in 1062. 377 states his allotment as a fact that limits enjoyment. 1062 says that if he meant some to live even by begging, may he wander and perish (பரந்து கெடுக). One verse accepts the allotment and the other curses its author for one kind of lot.

Both verses begin with the same people, those without means of enjoyment (துப்புரவு இல்லார்), and both speak of their renouncing. 1050 says that their not renouncing fully (துவரத் துறவாமை) makes them death to others' salt and gruel. 378 says they would renounce if what they are due to undergo passed without afflicting them (உறற்பால ஊட்டா கழியுமெனின்). 378 gives the reason for the failure 1050 complains of: fate still makes them live through what is due. Kalaignar reads 378 differently, as renouncing when troubling feelings fall away.

344 says having nothing is natural to austerity (இயல்பாகும் நோன்பிற்கொன்று இன்மை). 378 looks at those who already have nothing through poverty and says they would renounce, but for what fate makes them undergo. Parimelazhagar makes the connection: they have already lost what a renouncer gives up, and still suffer because their intent differs. Having nothing is the condition of austerity in 344, and 378 shows it is not enough by itself.

379 asks why those who see things as good when good comes should grieve (அல்லற்படுவது எவன்) when it does not. 626 asks whether those who never clutched at wealth saying 'we have got it' would grieve (அல்லற்படுபவோ) saying 'we have lost it'. Both are rhetorical questions with the same verb and the same symmetry between gain and loss. 626 adds the practical point that grief at loss depends on how one held the gain.

115 says loss and increase are not absent from life, and that not bending in the heart (நெஞ்சத்துக் கோடாமை) is the ornament of the worthy. 379 asks why one who accepts the good should grieve at its opposite. Both ask for the same response to both turns of fortune, and Parimelazhagar refers both verses to the results of earlier deeds.

629 says one who does not desire the pleasure within pleasure does not suffer the pain within pain (இன்பத்துள் இன்பம் விழையாதான் துன்பத்துள் துன்பம் உறுதல் இலன்). 379 asks why people who take the good as good (நல்லவாக் காண்பவர்) suffer when the bad comes. 629 supplies an answer to that question: the suffering follows from the relish, and ends with it.

380 asks what is stronger than fate, since even when one devises another course it gets there first (மற்றொன்று சூழினுந் தான்முந்துறும்). 620 says those who labour on without flagging or delay will see even fate's back (ஊழையும் உப்பக்கம் காண்பர்). On a plain reading 620 says effort can defeat fate and 380 says nothing can, so they conflict. Parimelazhagar softens 620 to mean that fate cannot be averted in one or two attempts, so those who try repeatedly reach the result.

Both verses end with the same phrase, தான் முந்துறும். In 380 it is fate that gets ahead of whatever a person plans against it. In 1023 it is தெய்வம் that tucks up its garment and goes ahead of the one who says 'I will raise my family' (குடிசெய்வல்). The same power that outruns human planning in the chapter on fate is shown going in front of human resolve in the chapter on raising one's family.

380 says fate is the strongest thing and gets ahead of any plan. 619 grants that a thing may not come about because of fate (தெய்வத்தான் ஆகாதெனினும்), and adds that effort still pays the wage of the body's labour (மெய்வருத்தக் கூலி தரும்). 619 accepts the limit that 380 states and marks out what remains for effort within it.

391 asks for two things in order: learn without flaw (கசடறக் கற்க), then stand in keeping with it (நிற்க அதற்குத் தக). 834 names the person who does the first and skips the second: one who has studied, understood and even taught others but is not himself restrained (தானடங்கா) is the greatest of fools. The pair shows that the second half of 391 is not an afterthought: learning without it is classed as folly.

391 says to stand in keeping with what one has learned. 140 says those who have not learned to live in accord with the world (உலகத்தோடு ஒட்ட ஒழுகல் கல்லார்) are without understanding even though they have studied much (பலகற்றும்). Both measure learning by the conduct that follows it, and 140 turns the verb 'learn' itself toward conduct.

391 treats right conduct as what should follow flawless learning. 823, on false friends, says that even after studying many good things (பலநல்ல கற்றக் கடைத்தும்) it is hard for the unworthy (மாணார்) to become good at heart. It limits 391: study does not by itself produce the standing-by-it, which is why 391 has to command it separately.

392 calls numbers and letters, 'these two' (இவ்விரண்டும்), the eyes of living beings. 581 calls spies and the respected treatise, 'these two' (இவையிரண்டும்), the king's eyes (மன்னவன் கண்). The same two-eyes figure is used for every person and then for the ruler, and in both one eye is book knowledge; the king's second eye is live report.

392 makes numbers and letters the eyes of the living. 445 says a king goes about with his counsellors as his eyes (சூழ்வார் கண்ணாக) and so must choose them with care. Both treat sight as something acquired from outside oneself, through learning in one case and through chosen advisers in the other.

393 says only the learned have eyes; the unlearned have two sores on the face (முகத்திரண்டு புண்ணுடையர்). 575 says kindly regard is the eye's ornament and without it the eye is recognised as a sore (புண்ணென்று உணரப்படும்). The same eye-or-sore figure is applied to two different things, learning and kindly regard, so the book gives two separate tests for whether an eye is an eye.

393 denies real eyes to the unlearned. 418 says ears not pierced by listening (கேள்வியால் தோட்கப்படாத செவி) are of a deaf kind even though they hear. The next chapter repeats the pattern for the other sense: an organ counts only when it has been trained by learning or listening.

394 says the work of the learned is to meet so that others are glad and to part so that others think of them (உள்ளப் பிரிதல்). 839 says, ironically, that friendship with fools is very sweet because parting from them (பிரிவின்கண்) brings no pain at all. Both judge a person by what the parting leaves behind; the fool is the case where it leaves nothing.

394 describes the learned as people whose company others want again after it ends. 643 defines speech as what binds those who heard it and makes even those who did not hear want it (கேளாரும் வேட்ப). 643 gives the means, speech, for the effect 394 describes.

395 uses the poor standing before the rich (உடையார்முன் இல்லார்போல்) as its figure for the learner, and on Parimelazhagar's reading those who learned standing so are foremost while those who would not are lowest. 1066 says nothing is more degrading to the tongue than asking (இரவின் இளிவந்தது இல்), even asking water for a cow. Read together, the posture the book calls degrading when the object is goods is the one it honours when the object is learning.

395 praises learning in the stance of one who lacks before one who has. 724 tells even the learned to state what they have learned before the learned and take more from those who know more (மிக்காருள் மிக்க கொளல்). The asking stance of 395 is thus not only for beginners; it continues among the learned.

396 says understanding wells up in proportion to what one has learned (கற்றனைத்து ஊறும் அறிவு), as a sand-well gives water as far as it is dug. 373 says that however many subtle books one studies, one's own real understanding still prevails (தன் உண்மையறிவே மிகும்). If உண்மையறிவு is read with Parimelazhagar and Pope as the understanding fate has allotted, 373 caps what study can add, against 396's open-ended proportion.

396 says understanding grows with each bit of learning. 1110, a lover's speech, uses as its comparison that with each thing known one sees one's earlier not-knowing (அறிதோறு அறியாமை கண்டற்று). The comparison carries a view of learning that adds to 396: what increases with learning includes the awareness of how much was not known.

396 uses spring water in a dug sand-well (மணற்கேணி ... ஊறும்) for understanding that rises the more one learns. 1161 has a woman say that the pain she would hide rises like spring water for those who bale it out (இறைப்பவர்க்கு ஊற்றுநீர் போல மிகும்). The same image of a spring that gives more the more it is drawn serves for knowledge in one place and for love's pain in the other.

397 says that for the learned any land is one's land and any town one's town (யாதானும் நாடாம் ஊராம்). 753 says the unfailing lamp called wealth goes to whatever country one has in mind (எண்ணிய தேயத்துச் சென்று) and cuts away the darkness there. Learning and wealth are each credited with making foreign places open to a person.

398 says learning acquired in one birth is a protection in seven (எழுமையும் ஏமாப்புடைத்து). 126 ends with the same words: drawing in the five senses like a tortoise in one birth is a protection in seven. The shared formula puts learning beside sense-restraint as the two things said to carry over as a safeguard.

398 says what is learned in one span protects through seven. 835 says a fool can, in one span's doing (ஒருமைச் செயல்), make the mire he will sink in for seven (எழுமையும்). The same one-to-seven reckoning is run in the opposite direction, with folly in the place of learning.

398 has learning protect a person across seven births. 356 says those who have learned here and seen the true thing (கற்றீண்டு மெய்ப்பொருள் கண்டார்) reach the path of not coming back here. 356 takes learning one step past 398: joined to seeing the real, it ends the births that 398 says it guards.

399 says the learned, seeing the world take delight in what delights themselves, love it more; Parimelazhagar takes 'it' to be learning. 68 says one's children's understanding is sweeter to all living beings than to oneself (தம்மின் ... மன்னுயிர்க்கெல்லாம் இனிது). Both treat knowledge as a good whose pleasure is shared by the world and not kept by its holder.

399 assumes the learned person's learning gives the world joy. 650 says those who cannot unfold what they have learned so that others grasp it (கற்றது உணர விரித்துரையாதார்) are like a cluster of flowers in bloom without scent. It adds the condition 399 leaves unstated: the world's delight depends on being able to convey the learning.

400 says learning is the imperishable, excellent wealth and other things are not wealth (மாடல்ல மற்றையவை). 411 says the wealth of the ear is the wealth among wealths and the head of them all (செல்வத்துளெல்லாம் தலை). Adjacent chapters use the same 'true wealth' figure for study and then for listening, without ranking the two against each other.

400 calls learning wealth that cannot be destroyed (கேடில்) and denies the name to the rest. 592 says possession of inner drive is possession, while possession of goods does not stay and slips away (நில்லாது நீங்கிவிடும்). Both set an inner possession against goods on the ground of permanence.

400 gives the title of real wealth to learning. 241 gives it to grace (அருட்செல்வம் செல்வத்துள் செல்வம்), with the reason that wealth of goods is found even among the base. The same move appears in the Book of Virtue with a different winner, and 241's reason, who can hold it, differs from 400's, whether it can be lost.

401 says holding forth in an assembly without full book-learning (நிரம்பிய நூலின்றிக் கோட்டி கொளல்) is like playing dice without a marked board. 728 says those who have learned many things are still of no use if they cannot speak well and tellingly in a good assembly. Together they give both halves: speech without learning has nothing to stand on, and learning without speech yields nothing.

402 compares the unlearned man's desire to speak (சொற்காமுறுதல், as Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar read it) to a woman without breasts desiring womanhood. 727 compares the learning of one who fears the assembly to a bright sword in the hand of a பேடி among enemies. Both use a figure of lacking what one's role requires, and they cover the two opposite failures: wanting to speak without learning, and having learning without the nerve to speak. Kalaignar reads 402 differently, as desiring to hear the unlearned man's words.

403 says even the unlearned are very good if they can keep from speaking before the learned (கற்றார்முன் சொல்லாதிருக்கப் பெறின்). 715 says the best of all good things is the restraint of not speaking first among elders (முதுவருள் முந்து கிளவாச் செறிவு). 715 turns the rule 403 gives the unlearned into a general virtue of the assembly that binds capable speakers too.

403 counts silence before the learned as the unlearned person's merit. 729 says those who have studied and understood yet fear an assembly of the good are lower than the unlearned (கல்லாதவரின் கடை). Silence is therefore not good in itself: it is right for the one with nothing to say and a failing in the one who has something.

404 says that however good an unlearned person's brightness (ஒட்பம்) may be, those with understanding do not accept it. 423 says understanding is seeing the true substance of a thing from whoever's mouth it is heard (யார்யார்வாய்க் கேட்பினும்).
