610 gives the unslothful king the whole measured world. 606, in the same chapter, says that even when the wealth of earth-owners arrives the slothful get no excellent fruit from it. Together they separate two things: sloth does not only block gaining the world, it also empties the world of value when it is handed over.

611: do not flag saying 'it is hard' (அருமை உடைத்தென்று அசாவாமை), for effort will give the greatness (பெருமை முயற்சி தரும்). 26: those who do what is hard to do are great, those who cannot are small (செயற்கரிய செய்வார் பெரியர்). 26 defines greatness by hard deeds as if it were a fixed difference between people; 611 says the greatness needed is itself produced by trying.

611 answers the thought 'this is hard' with effort. 537 says nothing is impossible on the ground of being hard (அரியஎன்று ஆகாத இல்லை) if done with the tool of unforgetting care (பொச்சாவாக் கருவியால்). The same objection is met in two chapters with two different instruments, exertion and vigilance.

612: guard against the work failing in the doing, because the world has left those who left the work's need undone (வினைக்குறை தீர்ந்தாரின் தீர்ந்தன்று உலகு), on Parimelazhagar's reading; Manakkudavar takes the second line the other way, that the world does not leave those who finish. 670: whatever other firmness they have, the world does not want those who do not want firmness in action (வேண்டாரை வேண்டாது உலகு). Both make the world's regard answer in kind to how a person treats the task.

612 warns against abandoning a task midway (வினைக்கண் வினைகெடல் ஓம்பல்). 674 says the remainder of a task, like the remainder of an enmity, burns like the remainder of a fire (தீயெச்சம் போலத் தெறும்). 674 supplies a reason 612 does not give: the unfinished part is not inert but goes on doing damage.

613: the distinction called helping others rests in the quality called effort (தாளாண்மை ... வேளாண்மை). 212: all the wealth brought in by exertion is for doing help to the deserving (தாளாற்றித் தந்த பொருளெல்லாம் தக்கார்க்கு வேளாண்மை செய்தற் பொருட்டு). The same pair of words, தாள் and வேளாண்மை, is joined in the Book of Virtue as purpose and in the Book of Wealth as precondition: effort exists for giving, and giving depends on effort.

613 calls generosity a pride (செருக்கு) that stays only with effort. 598 says those without inner drive do not reach the pride of saying 'we have been generous' (வள்ளியம் என்னுஞ் செருக்கு). Both use செருக்கு approvingly for the giver's satisfaction and both make it unavailable to the inert; one names the missing thing as drive, the other as labour.

613 says the standing of a benefactor rests on labour. 1035 says those whose way is to eat what their hands produce do not beg and give to those who beg without hiding anything (கைசெய்தூண் மாலையவர்). The farming chapter shows 613's general claim in one occupation: the person who works with his hands is the one in a position to give.

614: the helpfulness of one without effort fails like a sword being wielded in the hand of a பேடி (பேடிகை வாளாண்மை). 727: the treatise learned by one who fears the assembly is a bright sword in the hand of a பேடி among enemies (பகையகத்துப் பேடிகை ஒள்வாள்). The same figure is used for two unused capacities, the will to give without the labour that funds it, and learning without the nerve to speak; Parimelazhagar explains 614 as fear making the sword useless, as poverty makes the intention useless.

614 says the generosity of a man without effort comes to nothing. 219 says that for a man of good feeling, being poor just is not being able to do the helpful things he would do (செயும்நீர செய்யாது அமைகலா வாறு). 219 shows the same blocked intention from the inside and without blame, so 614's scorn falls only on the case where the lack of means comes from not working.

615: one who does not want pleasure and wants the work (இன்பம் விழையான் வினைவிழைவான்) is a pillar that wipes away his kin's sorrow and holds them up. 628: one who does not want pleasure (இன்பம் விழையான்) and calls hardship natural does not come to sorrow. The same opening phrase carries two results in adjoining chapters: not seeking pleasure spares the man himself in 628 and, joined to love of work, relieves others in 615.

615 makes the work-loving man a pillar that props his kin (துடைத்தூன்றும் தூண்). 1030 says a family with no good person to stand by and prop it (அடுத்தூன்றும் நல்லாள் இலாத குடி) falls when trouble cuts at its foot. 1030 states the cost of the absence of the figure 615 praises, with the same verb ஊன்று.

615 praises the one who wants the work (வினைவிழைவான்) and not pleasure. 901 says those who desire the wife do not reach the excellent fruit, and that this is the very thing those who desire action do not want (வினைவிழையார் வேண்டாப் பொருளும் அது). Both set the desire for action against a desire for enjoyment and use nearly the same word for the man of action.

616: effort makes fortune (முயற்சி திருவினை ஆக்கும்) and lack of effort brings one into want. 371: unflagging effort arises from a fate of gain, and sloth from a fate of loss (ஆகூழால் தோன்றும் அசைவின்மை ... போகூழால் தோன்றும் மடி). 616 makes effort the cause of wealth; 371 makes fate the cause of effort, so on 371's account the causal chain in 616 starts one step earlier and is not in the person's hands.

616 says effort produces fortune. 594 says increase asks the way and goes to the one of unwavering drive (அதர்வினாய்ச் செல்லும் அசைவிலா ஊக்கமுடையானுழை). Both place the source of prosperity in the person's exertion, and 594 pictures it as prosperity doing the seeking. The first word of 594 is truncated in this edition (க்கம் for ஆக்கம்).

617: they say the dark Mugadi lives in sloth and the lotus goddess lives in the effort of the unslothful (மடியுளாள் மாமுகடி ... தாளுளாள் தாமரையினாள்). 167: the fair goddess, grudging the envious man, shows him to her elder sister (செய்யவள் தவ்வையைக் காட்டி விடும்). Both use the paired sisters of fortune and misfortune, and each names a different trait that decides which sister a person gets: envy in the Book of Virtue, sloth in the Book of Wealth.

617 houses Mugadi in a man's sloth. 936 says those covered by the Mugadi called gambling (சூதென்னும் முகடியான் மூடப்பட்டார்) do not fill their bellies and suffer. The rare name முகடி appears in both; in 617 she resides in a habit, in 936 a habit is itself called by her name.

617 says the lotus goddess dwells in the effort of the man without sloth (தாளுளாள்). 84 says the fair goddess dwells gladly in the house of one who tends good guests with a glad face (செய்யாள் உறையும்). Both say where Fortune lives, and the addresses differ: a person's labour in one, a hospitable home in the other.

618: lacking good fortune is no blame to anyone; knowing what should be known and not exerting oneself is the blame (பொறியின்மை யார்க்கும் பழியன்று ... ஆள்வினை இன்மை பழி). 371 says sloth itself arises from a fate of loss (போகூழால் தோன்றும் மடி). If 371 is read as saying fate causes a person's lack of effort, then the lack of effort 618 blames is a case of the ill fortune 618 excuses; the conflict depends on that causal reading of 371.

618 separates what is no disgrace (having no luck) from what is (not working). 988 says want is no disgrace to a person who has the firmness called worth (இன்மை ஒருவற்கு இளிவன்று). Both refuse to count an outward lack as shame and move the test to something in the person, effort in one and character in the other.

619: even if a thing cannot come about through the divine (தெய்வத்தான் ஆகாதெனினும்), effort gives the wage of the body's toil. 1023: for one who says 'I will build up my family', the divine girds its cloth and goes ahead of him (தெய்வம் மடிதற்றுத் தான்முந்துறும்). 619 treats தெய்வம் as a possible obstacle that effort partly outlasts; 1023 treats it as an ally that effort enlists, so the two give different pictures of how the same power stands to the one who works.

619 promises effort a return equal to the labour (மெய்வருத்தக் கூலி) even against the divine order. 377 says that even those who have amassed crores can enjoy them only in the way the apportioner has apportioned (வகுத்தான் வகுத்த வகையல்லால் ... துய்த்தல் அரிது). 377 limits what 619 leaves open: the wage may be earned and still not be enjoyed.

620: those who labour on without faltering and without delay will see even fate's back (ஊழையும் உப்பக்கம் காண்பர்). 380: what is stronger than fate? Even if one devises something else, it gets there first (மற்றொன்று சூழினுந் தான்முந்துறும்). Taken as general claims they conflict, one saying fate can be outlasted and the other that nothing overtakes it; Parimelazhagar softens 620 by saying fate can be turned back only by trying many times, not at once.

620 ends 'தாழாது உஞற்றுபவர்', those who labour without delay, and says they see fate's back. 1024 ends with the same phrase, 'தம்குடியைத் தாழாது உஞற்றுபவர்க்கு', and says that for them the outcome arrives by itself without deliberation (சூழாமல் தானே முடிவெய்தும்). The same people are described twice, once as defeating an opposing power and once as finding the result come unsought.

620 says persistent labour gets past fate. 269 says that for those who have reached the power of austerity even leaping past Death becomes possible (கூற்றம் குதித்தலும் கைகூடும்). Each takes the limit usually held to be unbeatable in its own sphere and says sustained discipline can cross it, in worldly action and in ascetic practice. The last word of 269 is misprinted in this edition (பட்டவர்க்குல்).

621 says to laugh when trouble comes (இடுக்கண் வருங்கால் நகுக), since nothing presses it back as well. 774 shows a warrior who, having thrown his spear at an elephant, pulls out the one lodged in his own body and laughs (மெய்வேல் பறியா நகும்). The battlefield verse acts out the advice of 621: the laugh comes at the moment of injury, and the injury is turned to use.

Both verses turn on the same play of உள்ளம் (mind) and உள்ளுதல் (to think): in 622 a flood of suffering perishes when the wise person thinks with the mind (உள்ளத்தின் உள்ளக் கெடும்), and in 309 all one has thought of is gained if one does not think anger in the mind (உள்ளத்தால் உள்ளான் வெகுளி எனின்). Read together they make a single act of thought decide the outcome, once by what is thought and once by what is left unthought.

429 says those whose understanding guards against what is coming (எதிரதாக் காக்கும் அறிவினார்) have no affliction that arrives to shake them; 622 says that for the person of understanding (அறிவுடையான்) even a flood of suffering already present is ended by thinking. The pair gives understanding two jobs, forestalling trouble and dissolving the trouble that came anyway, which Parimelazhagar takes in 622 to be trouble from fate.

623 says those who do not suffer at suffering (இடும்பைக்கு இடும்பை படாஅதவர்) make suffering itself suffer; Parimelazhagar places this in the middle of an undertaking. 261 makes bearing the pain that comes (உற்றநோய் நோன்றல்) half of the form of தவம். The same endurance is a means to finishing work in one book and the definition of austerity in the other.

624 likens the person who pulls through every obstruction to a draught ox (மடுத்தவாயெல்லாம் பகடன்னான்) and says the trouble he meets is itself troubled. 597 says the strong do not give way where things break down (சிதைவிடத்து ஒல்கார்), like an elephant standing firm under arrows. Both make the same claim through a working or fighting animal; the ox adds forward motion to the elephant's holding of ground.

624 says trouble is troubled by one who hauls on like an ox through every blocked place. 620 carries the claim to its limit: those who labour on without flagging (தாழாது உஞற்றுபவர்) see the back even of fate (ஊழையும் உப்பக்கம் காண்பர்). What 624 says of obstacles in the road, 620 says of the power behind them.

625 says that though troubles come stacked (அடுக்கி வரினும்), those of one who is not undone (அழிவிலான்) are themselves in trouble. 989 says those called the shore of worth do not shift even if the age shifts (ஊழி பெயரினும் தாம் பெயரார்). Both define a person by not moving under pressure, one in the chapter on a king's undertakings and one in the chapter on character.

1045 states as plain fact that within the one suffering called poverty many sufferings arrive and settle (பல்குரைத் துன்பங்கள் சென்று படும்), and offers no remedy. 625 addresses exactly such piling up (அடுக்கி வரினும்) and says it fails against one who is not undone. Set side by side, 625's confidence is conditional on the person, while 1045 describes what the stacking is like for those in want.

626 asks whether those who never clutched at wealth saying 'we have got it' (பெற்றேமென்று ஓம்புதல் தேற்றாதவர்) would grieve saying 'we have lost it'. 379 asks why those who see good things as good when they come grieve when the opposite comes (அல்லற் படுவது எவன்). Both use the same verb of grieving in a rhetorical question and locate grief at loss in one's attitude at the time of gain; 379 puts it under fate, 626 under steadiness in trouble.

626 says those who did not cling when they had wealth will not lament 'அற்றேம்'. 593 says those who hold steady energy as their cash in hand (ஊக்கம் ஒருவந்தம் கைத்துடையார்) do not fret 'ஆக்கம் இழந்தேம்'. Both quote the cry of loss in order to deny it, but for different reasons: in 626 the wealth was never held tightly, in 593 something else is counted as the real holding.

341 gives the renouncer's rule: from whatever one has moved away, from that one has no pain (யாதனின் நீங்கியான் நோதல் அதனின் இலன்). 626 applies a milder version within worldly life: one need not give wealth up, only not hoard it (ஓம்புதல் தேற்றாதவர்), to be free of grief at its loss.

627 says the high-minded know the body is a target for suffering (இலக்கம் உடம்பு இடும்பைக்கு) and so do not take trouble as distress. 1029 asks whether the body of one who shields his family from harm is a vessel for suffering alone (இடும்பைக்கே கொள்கலம் கொல்லோ ... உடம்பு). The two share the figure of the body as the place where இடும்பை lands; 627 makes it a general truth to be accepted, 1029 a question raised by one person's burden.

Both verses open with the same words, இன்பம் விழையான் (one who does not desire pleasure). In 628 he also holds that suffering is natural (இடும்பை இயல்பென்பான்) and so does not come to pain; in 615 he desires the work instead (வினை விழைவான்) and becomes a pillar that wipes away his kin's sorrow. 615 extends the benefit of 628 from the person himself to those who depend on him.

628 says one who does not desire pleasure and takes suffering as natural does not come to pain (துன்பம் உறுதல் இலன்). 368 says those without craving have no sorrow (அவா இல்லார்க்கு இல்லாகும் துன்பம்), and where craving exists sorrow keeps coming. The logic that absence of wanting removes pain appears in the renunciation chapters as a path to release and here as equipment for a person at work in the world.

629 says one who does not crave pleasure in the midst of pleasure does not suffer in the midst of pain. 115 says loss and increase are both part of life and that not letting the heart bend (நெஞ்சத்துக் கோடாமை) is the ornament of the worthy. Both ask for the same evenness across good and bad turns; 115 treats it as fairness of mind, 629 as protection against pain.

629 makes freedom from pain depend on not desiring pleasure when it is present (இன்பத்துள் இன்பம் விழையாதான்). 4 describes the Lord as one without wanting or not-wanting (வேண்டுதல் வேண்டாமை இலான்) and says those who reach his feet never have இடும்பை. The same link between having no pull toward or away from things and having no suffering appears as a divine attribute in Book 1 and as a human discipline here.

669 says to do with resolve the deed that yields joy even though pain comes thick at first (துன்பம் உறவரினும் ... இன்பம் பயக்கும் வினை): pain now, joy later. 630 goes a step further and has the person take the pain itself as joy (இன்னாமை இன்பம் எனக்கொளின்). Parimelazhagar reads the pain in both as the strain of effort.

630 says that taking what hurts as pleasure brings a distinction (சிறப்பு) even enemies esteem. 267 says that for those able to endure, pain as it burns makes them shine like gold in fire (துன்பம் சுடச்சுட ... ஒளிவிடும்). In both, pain rightly borne produces visible excellence; 267 says it of austerity, 630 of worldly effort.

630 measures the reward by the enemy: a distinction one's foes desire or esteem (ஒன்னார் விழையும் சிறப்பு). 810 uses the same measure with the same verb: those who do not depart from their nature toward old friends are wanted even by those who do not want them (விழையார் விழையப்படுப). Each verse marks an unusual constancy, under pain or toward friends who have erred, by saying that even the hostile regard it.

The two verses end with the same formula, 'அந்நலம்/பிறநலம் யா/எந்நலத்து உள்ளதூஉம் அன்று', used in opposite directions. In 641 the goodness of the tongue (நாநலம்) is not contained in any other goodness, which Parimelazhagar takes to mean it exceeds them all; in 982 every goodness other than the goodness of character (குணநலம்) is not counted among goodnesses at all. One chapter ranks eloquence highest for a minister, the other ranks character alone for the worthy.

641 sets the good of the tongue above every other good. 411 calls the wealth of the ear the wealth among wealths and the head of them all (செல்வத்துள் எல்லாம் தலை). The book gives the top place once to listening and once to speaking, in chapters addressed to the learner and to the minister.

642 says that since gain and ruin come from speech, one must guard against a lapse in it (காத்தோம்பல் சொல்லின்கண் சோர்வு). 127 says whatever else one fails to guard, guard the tongue (நாகாக்க), or one will grieve through a fault of speech (சொல்லிழுக்கு). The same instruction is given to the householder for his own sake and to the minister for the state's sake, as Parimelazhagar's gloss on 642 makes explicit.

642 says ruin as well as gain comes from speech and asks for vigilance against slips. 128 gives the scale of the risk: if even one harmful word has its effect (ஒன்றானும் தீச்சொல்), the good turns to no good (நன்றாகாதாகி விடும்). 128 supplies the reason why 642 treats a lapse (சோர்வு), and not only deliberate bad speech, as the danger.

Parimelazhagar reads 643 as speech that binds those who have accepted one as a friend (கேட்டார்ப் பிணிக்கும்) and makes even those who have not want friendship. 187 gives the failure of this skill: those who do not know how to make friends with pleasing talk (நகச்சொல்லி நட்பாடல் தேற்றாதவர்) part even their own kin with divisive talk. On that reading the two verses are the positive and negative of one ability, speech as what holds or breaks alliances.

On the plainer reading that Manakkudavar follows, 643 defines speech as what holds those who hear it and makes those who have not heard want to. 394 says the work of the learned is to meet so that others are glad and to part so that others think of them (உவப்பத் தலைக்கூடி உள்ளப் பிரிதல்). Both judge a person's words by the wish for more that they leave behind.

644 says to speak knowing the திறன், which Parimelazhagar takes as the relative standing of speaker and hearers. 711 gives the method: those who know the stock of words should speak after knowing the assembly and examining (அவையறிந்து ஆராய்ந்து சொல்லுக). Chapter 72 works out as a practice what 644 states as a principle.

644 asks for speech fitted to its hearers and says no virtue or gain exceeds it. 696 applies this to a single hearer, the king: know his mood, consider the time, and say what is needed in a way he will want (குறிப்பறிந்து காலம் கருதி ... வேட்பச் சொலல்). The general rule for a minister's speech becomes a specific rule for speech to power.

644 says to speak after knowing the திறன் of those concerned. 469 says that even in doing good there is error when it is done without knowing each person's character (அவரவர் பண்பறிந்து ஆற்றாக்கடை). Both make a good thing, a word or a deed, depend on fitting it to the particular person receiving it.

645 says to speak a word only after knowing that no other word can defeat it (வெல்லுஞ்சொல் இன்மை அறிந்து). 467 says to think and then commit to a task, and that saying 'we will think after committing' is a fault (எண்ணித் துணிக). Both put the testing before the irreversible step; 645 applies to an utterance the rule 467 gives for action.

646 gives a two-sided rule: speak so that others want to hear, and take the value from what others say (பிறர்சொல் பயன்கோடல்). 424 defines understanding with the same two sides: say things so they go in easily (செலச்சொல்லி) and see the subtle meaning in what comes from others' mouths (பிறர்வாய் நுண்பொருள் காண்பது). The minister's practice in 646 is what 424 calls அறிவு itself.

646 pairs speaking well with drawing the benefit from others' words. 724 sets that pair in the assembly of the learned: make what you have learned go home to them (கற்ற செலச்சொல்லி) and take what is more from those who know more (மிக்காருள் மிக்க கொளல்). 724 adds what 646 leaves open, that listening is how the speaker's own knowledge grows.

647 lists three things that make a person hard to beat in a contest: able to speak, free of lapses, unafraid (சொலல்வல்லன் சோர்விலன் அஞ்சான்). 686 defines the envoy with nearly the same set: learned, not afraid of hostile eyes (கண் அஞ்சான்), speaking so it goes home, and knowing what fits the time. The envoy chapter puts the general portrait of 647 into the one post where it is tested before an enemy.

647 says no one can easily defeat a fearless, unfaltering speaker in a contest (இகல் வெல்லல் யார்க்கும் அரிது). 872 gives the advice that follows for the other side: take on the enmity of those whose plough is the bow if you must, but not of those whose plough is the word (சொல்லேர் உழவர் பகை). Parimelazhagar takes the latter to be ministers, the people 647 describes.

648 says the world quickly takes up what is asked of it when it finds people who can speak in order and sweetly (நிரந்தினிது சொல்லுதல் வல்லார்). 387 says that for a king able to give and protect with sweet words, this world is as he sees it by his own word (தன்சொலால் தான் கண்டனைத்து). Both say the world follows pleasant speech; 387 joins giving to it, 648 orderly arrangement.

648 says the world listens readily to skilled, pleasing speakers. 1046 says the words of the poor go slack even when they speak good matter that they have understood well (நற்பொருள் நன்குணர்ந்து சொல்லினும் ... சோர்வு படும்). 1046 limits 648: how the world receives speech depends on the speaker's means as well as his skill.

649 says those who cannot say a few faultless words (மாசற்ற சில சொல்லல் தேற்றாதவர்) long to say many. 685 makes brevity the envoy's first mark: he speaks compactly (தொகச் சொல்லி), drops what is harsh, and speaks so as to please. 685 shows the positive skill whose absence 649 describes.

649 treats wanting to say many things as the sign of someone unable to say a few well. 193 says spread-out talk on useless matters (பயனில பாரித்துரைக்கும் உரை) itself announces that the speaker lacks நயன். In both, length of speech is evidence against the speaker; 193 judges his character, 649 his skill.

649 faults many words and praises a few faultless ones; the next verse faults those who cannot expound what they have learned so that others understand (உணர விரித்துரையாதார்). Manakkudavar reads the pair together: speak briefly, but also expand where it is needed. 650 keeps 649 from being taken as a rule of brevity alone.

650 likens those who cannot unfold their learning so that others grasp it to flowers that bloom in a cluster and give no scent (நாறா மலர்). 728 says the same without the image: though they have learned many things, those who cannot speak well and tellingly in a good assembly are of no use (பயமிலரே). Both hold that learning counts only when it can be communicated; Parimelazhagar's gloss on 728 gives fear as the cause, while 650 concerns the ability to explain.

Both verses use a flower's scent (நாற்றம்) for what is inside a person. In 650 the flower is fully open and gives no scent, like the learned person who cannot convey what he knows; in 1274 the scent is held inside a closed bud, like the unspoken meaning inside the girl's budding smile. The two uses mirror each other: an open display with nothing reaching others, and a closed one whose content the lover already perceives.

651 says the goodness of support (துணைநலம்) gives ஆக்கம், while the goodness of action (வினைநலம்) gives 'வேண்டிய எல்லாம்'. 457 uses the same frame, மனநலம் giving ஆக்கம் and இனநலம் giving 'எல்லாப் புகழும்'. In both, one good yields prosperity and a second yields everything, but the lesser term in 651 (companions) is close to the greater term in 457 (company), so the two rankings are worth reading together.

651 sets வினைநலம் above துணைநலம்: support gives only ஆக்கம், good action gives all that is wanted. 455 says purity of mind and purity of action (செய்வினை தூய்மை) both come leaning on purity of company (இனந்தூய்மை தூவா வரும்). Read together, the action that 651 ranks above one's support is itself said to depend on the people one keeps.

652 says one must always shun 'புகழொடு நன்றி பயவா வினை', action that yields neither renown nor good. 439, among the faults a ruler must guard against, says 'நயவற்க நன்றி பயவா வினை': do not set your heart on action that yields no good. The same phrase appears as a minister's rule of action and as a ruler's rule of desire, with 652 adding புகழ் and 'என்றும்'.

653 tells those who say 'ஆஅதும்' (we shall rise) to stop doing what dims their ஒளி. 962 says those who want சீர் together with பேராண்மை will not do 'சீரல்ல' even for the sake of சீர். 962 takes the harder case 653 leaves open: the dimming deed may itself be a route to fame, and it is still refused.

653 treats ஒளி as something the ambitious ('ஆஅதும் என்னுமவர்') must protect by refraining from certain deeds. 971 defines ஒளி as 'உள்ள வெறுக்கை', abundance of spirit, and இளி as saying one will live without it. Together they give ஒளி two sides: it is lost by what one does (653) and it consists in what one aspires to (971).

654: those of 'நடுக்கற்ற காட்சி' will not do degrading things (இளிவந்த செய்யார்) even when in trouble. 699: those of 'துளக்கற்ற காட்சி' will not do unacceptable things (கொள்ளாத செய்யார்) on the thought that they are in the king's favour. The same figure of unshaken sight, with the same 'செய்யார்', is tested once by distress and once by favour, so steadiness is shown under both pressure and licence.

654 says those of unshaken sight do nothing degrading even in distress (இடுக்கண் படினும்). 174 says those of 'புன்மையில் காட்சி' who have conquered the senses will not covet on the plea 'இலம்' (we have nothing). Both verses name a clear-sighted person (காட்சியவர்) and deny that need is an excuse; 174 applies it to coveting, 654 to action generally.

654: clear-sighted people do not do what is degrading even when trouble comes. 218: those of 'கடனறி காட்சி' do not falter in ஒப்புரவு even in a season without means (இடனில் பருவத்தும் ... ஒல்கார்). One verse says hardship does not make them do wrong, the other that it does not make them stop doing good; the two are the negative and positive halves of the same steadiness.

655 says not to do things one will lament with 'எற்று' (what have I done), using இரங்குவ. 535 describes the person who slipped by not guarding beforehand and afterwards 'இரங்கி விடும்' over his own error. 535 shows the regret 655 warns of and locates its cause in the failure to guard in advance. The second half of 655 is read differently by the commentators (Parimelazhagar: do not go on lamenting; Kalaignar: do not repeat the deed), and this link rests only on the first half.

655 asks that one not do what will be regretted afterwards. 467 says to think and then resolve (எண்ணித் துணிக), and calls it a lapse to say 'we will think after resolving'. Both put the reflection before the act: 467 as a rule of planning, 655 as a rule about the purity of the deed.

656: even if one sees one's own mother hungry (ஈன்றாள் பசி காண்பான் ஆயினும்), do not do what the worthy condemn. 327: even if one's own life must go (தன்னுயிர் நீப்பினும்), do not do the deed that takes another's life. Both use 'செய்யற்க' with an extreme concession, one in the chapter on not killing and one in the chapter on a minister's clean action, showing the book's habit of stating a prohibition at its hardest case.

656 forbids the blameworthy deed even when the need is a mother's hunger. 961 says to give up things that would diminish one (குன்ற வருப விடல்) even if they are indispensable (இன்றி அமையாச் சிறப்பின ஆயினும்). Both deny that necessity licenses a degrading act; 961 states the principle abstractly under honour, 656 gives it a concrete and painful instance.

656 uses the mother who bore one (ஈன்றாள்) as the strongest pull toward wrongdoing for the sake of relief. 1047 says that one in poverty not joined with virtue (அறஞ்சாரா நல்குரவு) is looked on as a stranger even by the mother who bore him (ஈன்ற தாயானும்). The mother marks the limit case in both: 656 holds conduct firm against her need, while 1047 says poverty without virtue loses even her regard.

657: the extreme poverty of the worthy (சான்றோர் கழிநல்குரவு) is better than wealth got by taking on blame (பழிமலைந்து எய்திய ஆக்கம்). 408: wealth lodged with the unlearned (கல்லார்கண் பட்ட திரு) is more painful than poverty lodged with the good (நல்லார்கண் பட்ட வறுமை). The same comparison of good people's poverty with bad people's wealth is made from each side, once about how wealth was got and once about who holds it.

657 ranks the utter poverty of the worthy above blame-laden wealth. 988 says poverty (இன்மை) is no disgrace (இளிவன்று) to one who has the firmness called சால்பு. 988 supplies the ground for 657's ranking: for the சான்றோர் poverty carries no இளிவு, whereas the wealth in 657 carries பழி.

658: forbidden deeds done without shunning them bring anguish even if they succeed (முடிந்தாலும் பீழை தரும்). 113: give up at once gain that comes from leaving fairness, even if it brings nothing but good (நன்றே தரினும்). Both concede success in advance and still reject the act, so the objection is not that such means fail.

658 says forbidden actions bring anguish even when they are accomplished. 931 says not to want gambling even if one wins (வென்றிடினும்), since the winnings are like the hook a fish has swallowed. The gambling verse gives an image for 658's claim: the success itself is what carries the harm.

658 warns that the gain of a forbidden deed turns to பீழை later. 177 says not to want gain that comes by coveting (வெஃகியாம் ஆக்கம்), because at the time of enjoying it the fruit is hard to make good (விளைவயின் மாண்டற்கு அரிதாம் பயன்). Both place the harm at the stage of the result and not at the stage of getting.

659: everything taken by making others weep leaves with weeping (அழக் கொண்ட எல்லாம் அழப்போம்). 555: the tears of those who weep under oppression they cannot bear (அழுத கண்ணீர்) are the weapon that wears away wealth (செல்வத்தைத் தேய்க்கும் படை). 555 applies the same idea to a king and names the tears themselves as the agent of the loss that 659 only states.

659 says what is taken with tears goes with tears. 283 says gain made by stealth (களவினால் ஆகிய ஆக்கம்) perishes beyond measure even while it seems to grow (ஆவது போலக் கெடும்). Both hold that wrongly got wealth does not stay; 283 adds that it looks like growth first.

The second half of 659 says what comes from good ways (நற்பாலவை) yields later even if it is lost (இழப்பினும் பிற்பயக்கும்). 112 says the wealth of a person of rectitude (செப்பம் உடையவன் ஆக்கம்) does not decay and is a security for those who come after (எச்சத்திற்கு ஏமாப்பு). Both give rightly got wealth a benefit that outlasts the moment, 659 for the person later and 112 for descendants.

660 compares making wealth by deceit (சலத்தால் பொருள்செய்து) and securing oneself with it to pouring water into a pot of unfired clay (பசுமண் கலத்துள் நீர்). 755 says accumulation of wealth that does not come with அருள் and அன்பு should be let go. Parimelazhagar, commenting on 755, explains the reason with this same image of water in an unfired pot, so he reads the two verses as one teaching: 660 gives the image and 755 the rule for a king's revenue.

660: wealth made by deceit is water kept in an unfired clay vessel. 1000: great wealth obtained by one without character is good milk spoiled by the fault of its vessel (கலந்தீமையால் திரிந்தற்று). Both use a faulty கலம் for wealth that cannot be kept, but the fault differs: in 660 it is how the wealth was made, in 1000 it is the holder's character.

661: firmness in action is a person's firmness of mind (மனத்திட்பம்); everything else is something other (மற்றைய எல்லாம் பிற). 34: being spotless in mind (மனத்துக்கண் மாசிலன் ஆதல்) is all of virtue; the rest is noisy show (ஆகுல நீர பிற). The two verses have the same shape, reducing a whole domain to a state of mind and dismissing the remainder as 'பிற', once for virtue and once for effective action.

661 locates firmness in action in the mind and sets other things aside. 600 says a person's real strength (உரம்) is abundance of spirit (உள்ள வெறுக்கை), and those without it are trees. Both place strength within the person; Parimelazhagar's note on 661 lists the outer things meant by 'மற்றைய' as the firmness of army, fort and allies.

662 gives two rules as the way of those who have studied the matter: avoid harm (ஊறொரால்) and do not give way once it has come (உற்றபின் ஒல்காமை). 442 tells a king to cherish those who remove the trouble that has come (உற்றநோய் நீக்கி) and guard beforehand against what has not (உறாஅமை முற்காக்கும்). The same before-and-after pair appears as the doer's own discipline in 662 and as the quality to look for in advisers in 442.

429 says those whose understanding guards against what is coming (எதிரதாக் காக்கும் அறிவினார்) have no affliction that comes to shake them. 662 keeps that first rule (ஊறொரால்) but adds a second for when harm arrives anyway (உற்றபின் ஒல்காமை). 662 thus allows that foresight is not always enough; Parimelazhagar reads the second case as a task spoiled by fate.

663: the right way to act is so that the deed becomes known only at its end (கடைக்கொட்க); if it becomes known midway (இடைக்கொட்கின்) it brings trouble that cannot be undone. 590: do not honour a spy where others can know it (சிறப்பறிய ... செய்யற்க); if the king does, he has himself let out the secret (புறப்படுத்தான் ஆகும் மறை). Both treat premature disclosure as a self-inflicted failure, in a minister's undertaking and in a king's use of spies.

664: saying is easy for anyone; doing as one has said (சொல்லிய வண்ணம் செயல்) is hard. 819: the bond with those whose deed is one thing and word another (வினைவேறு சொல்வேறு பட்டார்) is bitter even in a dream. 664 states the gap between word and deed as a difficulty of execution; 819 judges the same gap in a friend as a fault of character.

664 contrasts easy speech with the difficulty of doing what was said. 640 says those without practical capacity (திறப்பாடு இலாதவர்) leave things unfinished even after planning them in proper order (முறைப்படச் சூழ்ந்தும் முடிவிலவே செய்வர்). Both mark the distance between an account of the deed and the deed; Parimelazhagar reads 'சொல்லுதல்' in 664 as stating in order how a task will be done, which brings it close to 640's planning.

666: those who have planned obtain what they planned as they planned it (எண்ணிய எண்ணியாங்கு எய்துப), if they are firm (திண்ணியர்). 540: it is easy to obtain what one has thought of (உள்ளியது எய்தல் எளிது), if one can keep thinking of what one thought of (உள்ளியது உள்ளப் பெறின்). Both make attainment conditional with 'பெறின்' on a quality of mind, firmness in one and unforgetting attention in the other.

666 uses the formula 'எண்ணிய எண்ணியாங்கு எய்துப' for what the firm obtain. 265 uses the matching formula 'வேண்டிய வேண்டியாங்கு எய்தலால்' for what தவம் obtains, as the reason austerity is practised here. The repeated wording gives firmness in worldly action the same promise that the first book gives austerity; Parimelazhagar places 265's fruits in the next life.

666: what one has thought of is obtained as thought, if one is firm. 309: all one has thought of is obtained at once (உள்ளிய தெல்லாம் உடனெய்தும்), if one does not think of anger in the heart. The same promise is attached to two different inner conditions, one positive (firmness) and one negative (absence of anger).

667: do not scorn anyone on seeing their form (உருவுகண்டு எள்ளாமை), for there are people like the linchpin (அச்சாணி) of a great rolling chariot. 1032: those who plough are the ஆணி of the world's people, because they bear all who cannot plough and take up other work. Both use the pin that holds the wheel for someone small in appearance on whom everything turns; 667 leaves the person unnamed and 1032 names the farmer. Parimelazhagar supplies the smallness in 667 from the simile.

667 says not to judge by form (உரு), because the small-looking may be the linchpin. 279 says the arrow is straight but cruel and the lute bent but good, so people are to be taken by the nature of their deeds (வினைபடு பாலால் கொளல்). Both refuse appearance as the measure and point to function, 279 in the context of false ascetics and 667 in the context of capable agents.

668: in a task one has seen clearly and decided on (கலங்காது கண்ட வினை), act without wavering and without delay (தூக்கங் கடிந்து). 671, opening the next chapter, says deliberation ends in reaching resolve (துணிவு) and it is bad for that resolve to rest in delay (தாழ்ச்சியுள் தங்குதல் தீது). The same rule closes the chapter on firmness and opens the chapter on method: once the thinking is done, delay is the fault.

467 says to think and then resolve on a task, and that saying 'we will think after resolving' is a lapse. 668 takes up from that point: once the task has been seen without confusion (கலங்காது கண்ட), act without wavering (துளங்காது). Together they give a sequence in which doubt belongs before the decision and not after it.

669: do with resolve the deed that yields joy (இன்பம் பயக்கும் வினை), even though pain comes close at first (துன்பம் உறவரினும்). 615: one who does not want pleasure but wants the work (இன்பம் விழையான் வினை விழைவான்) is a pillar who wipes away his kin's துன்பம். Both set இன்பம், துன்பம் and வினை against each other; 669 justifies bearing pain by the joy the deed yields, while 615 describes a doer who is not after pleasure at all and whose work removes others' pain.

669 says to carry through the worthwhile deed despite the pain it brings at first. 611 says one must not slacken on the thought that a thing is hard (அருமை உடைத்தென்று அசாவாமை), since effort gives the greatness needed. Both refuse the difficulty of a task as a reason to hold back; 611 speaks of effort and 669 of resolve (துணிவு).

670: whatever other firmness they have attained (எனைத்திட்பம் எய்தியக் கண்ணும்), the world does not want those who do not want firmness in action. 750: whatever excellences it has (எனைமாட்சித்து ஆகியக் கண்ணும்), a fort is nothing with those who lack excellence in action (வினைமாட்சி இல்லார்கண்). The two chapter-closing verses are built alike and make the same point, that other strengths count for nothing without the capacity to act, once of a minister and once of a fort's defenders.

467 says to think and then resolve (எண்ணித் துணிக) and calls it a lapse to say 'we will think after resolving'. 671 takes up where that ends: deliberation's end is reaching resolve (சூழ்ச்சி முடிவு துணிவெய்தல்), and the fault now is letting that resolve sit in delay (தாழ்ச்சியுள் தங்குதல் தீது). Read together they bracket the moment of decision: no acting before it, no lingering after it.

668, in the chapter on firmness in action, says to carry out a deed seen with an unconfused mind without wavering and with delay driven off (தூக்கங் கடிந்து செயல்). 671 makes the same claim from the side of method: resolve that stays in delay (தாழ்ச்சி) is a fault. The pairing shows the book treating promptness after decision both as a trait of character and as a rule of procedure.

671 calls it a fault when a resolved deed lingers in delay (தாழ்ச்சியுள் தங்குதல் தீது). 672 immediately limits this: there are deeds to be done slowly, and over those one should take time (தூங்குக தூங்கிச் செயற்பால); only the deed that must be done without delay must not be slept on. Delay is therefore wrong by the nature of the task, not in itself.

383 lists தூங்காமை, not delaying, among three things that never leave a ruler. 672 uses the same verb to say தூங்குக for some tasks and தூங்கற்க for others. Parimelazhagar makes the connection himself, saying that what 383 stated as தூங்காமை is here divided into its cases.

490 says to be like the heron in the season for folding up (கூம்பும் பருவத்து) and like its strike when the moment is right (சீர்த்த இடத்து). 672 gives the same double instruction without the image: take time over what is to be done slowly, and do not delay what must not be delayed. Both hold that waiting and speed are each correct in their place.

33 tells one to do deeds of virtue by whatever means are possible (ஒல்லும் வகையான்) and wherever they can go (செல்லும்வாய் எல்லாம் செயல்). 673 uses the same pair of words for statecraft: wherever it is possible the deed is good (ஒல்லும்வாய் எல்லாம் வினைநன்றே), and where it is not, act by looking for the way that will go (செல்லும்வாய் நோக்கிச் செயல்). The same formula of the possible and the passable serves virtue in Book 1 and policy in Book 2. (The first word of 673 is misprinted in this edition; the commentaries read ஒல்லும்.)

485 says those who have the world in mind wait, unshaken, with their mind on the time (காலம் கருதி இருப்பர்). Manakkudavar reads the second half of 673 in that sense: when the deed is not possible, keep it in mind and act on seeing the place where it becomes possible. Parimelazhagar reads 673 differently, as open force where one is stronger and one of the other three expedients where one is not, so the link holds on Manakkudavar's reading.

879 says to cut a thorn tree while it is young, because grown hard it wounds the hand that cuts (கைகொல்லும் காழ்த்த இடத்து). 674 says what is left over (எச்சம்) of an enmity, like what is left of a fire, scorches later (தீயெச்சம் போலத் தெறும்). Both hold that an enemy not dealt with completely grows; one uses a tree and the other an ember.

612 warns against letting a task die in the doing, on the ground that the world leaves those who leave work unfinished (வினைக்குறை தீர்ந்தாரின் தீர்ந்தன்று உலகு). 674 gives a different ground for the same rule: the unfinished remainder of a task (வினை ... எச்சம்) is not inert but, like the remnant of a fire, comes back to destroy. 612 names the social cost of unfinished work and 674 the danger in the remainder itself.

631 defines the minister as one excellent in means, time, manner of doing and the hard deed itself (கருவியும் காலமும் செய்கையும் செய்யும் அருவினையும்). 675 lists resources, means, time, deed and place (பொருள் கருவி காலம் வினை இடனொடு ஐந்தும்) as what must be thought through before acting. The lists overlap in கருவி, காலம் and வினை, so 675 reads as the minister's competence of 631 turned into a procedure, with resources and place added.

471 says to weigh four strengths before acting: of the deed, oneself, the opponent and the allies (தூக்கிச் செயல்). 675 gives a second checklist of five ending in the same way (எண்ணிச் செயல்). Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar gloss each of the five in 675 as two-sided, one's own and the enemy's, which is the comparison 471 asks for, applied item by item.

461 says to act after considering what will be lost, what will come of it, and the gain it yields later (அழிவதூஉம் ஆவதூஉம் ... ஊதியமும் சூழ்ந்து செயல்). 676 says to act after looking at the completion, the hindrance, and the large yield once it is finished (முடிவும் இடையூறும் ... படுபயனும் பார்த்துச் செயல்). Both are a three-part weighing of cost against return placed before action; Parimelazhagar reads முடிவு in 676 as the effort needed to finish, which brings it close to 461's 'what is lost'.

462 says nothing is hard to attain for those who act after examining a matter with chosen company (தெரிந்த இனத்தொடு) and thinking it over themselves. 677 narrows whose counsel counts for a particular task: the one who knows that deed from inside (அவ்வினை உள்ளறிவான்), whom Parimelazhagar takes to be someone who has done it before. General consultation in 462 becomes, in 677, learning the mind of the person with experience of the task.

678 says to get one deed done by means of another, as one binds an elephant with a rutting elephant (யானையால் யானையாத் தற்று). Manakkudavar takes this as setting an enemy's own enemy against him. On that reading 875 is the case worked out: one who is alone with two enemies should take one of them as an ally (இன்துணையாக் கொள்க அவற்றின் ஒன்று). Parimelazhagar reads 678 more generally, as making a task in hand the means to another like it.

Both verses explain how a deed (வினை) is made easy through an elephant scene. In 758 one who acts with wealth in hand is like a man watching an elephant fight from a hilltop (குன்றேறி யானைப் போர் கண்டற்று), safe above the danger; in 678 one deed is used on another as a tame elephant is used to bind a wild one. The elephant stands in each for the dangerous size of the undertaking, handled once from a distance and once by using its own kind.

633 lists three abilities of a minister side by side: dividing, keeping one's own close, and joining those who had separated (பிரித்தலும் பேணிக் கொளலும் பிரிந்தார்ப் பொருத்தலும்). 679 ranks two such tasks: bringing the unallied over (ஒட்டாரை ஒட்டிக் கொளல்) is more urgent (விரைந்ததே) than doing good to friends. What 633 gives as a list of skills, 679 puts in order of urgency.

875 says that one without allies and facing two enemies should take one of them as a pleasing ally. 679 says that winning over ஒட்டார் is more urgent than favours to friends; Manakkudavar takes ஒட்டார் as one's enemies, Parimelazhagar as those not allied with one's enemy. On either reading both verses treat alliance as something to be made out of the hostile or uncommitted when one is pressed.

874 says the world rests in the greatness of the person of character who lives treating enmity as friendship (பகைநட்பாக் கொண்டொழுகும்). 679 states the same move as a priority in conducting a task: making the ஒட்டார் one's own comes before kindness to friends. 874 praises it as character (பண்பு) while 679 prescribes it as urgent policy.

861 says to avoid standing against the strong (வலியார்க்கு மாறேற்றல் ஓம்புக). 680 describes what that means for a weak party: those of small domain, fearing the trembling of their own side (உள்நடுங்கல் அஞ்சி), bow to the greater and accept terms if they can get them (குறைபெறின் கொள்வர் பெரியார்ப் பணிந்து). 861 gives the rule and 680 the settlement that follows from it.

488 says to bear with enemies on meeting them (செறுநரைக் காணின் சுமக்க), for when their end comes their head will go down; Parimelazhagar glosses சுமக்க as bowing. 680 has the small bow to the great to obtain terms. 488 adds what 680 does not say: that such bowing can be a way of waiting for the stronger side's fall.

967, on honour, says it is better to be called ruined as one stands than to live by going behind those who are hostile to one (ஒட்டார்பின் சென்று வாழ்தலின்). 680 says the small will bow to the great and take what terms they can. The conflict depends on reading 967's ஒட்டார் as covering a stronger enemy; Parimelazhagar limits it to following scorners for a living, but he also remarks on 680 that bowing is not the wish of those with honour, which is why the verse says 'they will accept' as a report of worldly practice.

The first line of 681 and of 992 is the same: அன்புடைமை ஆன்ற குடிப்பிறத்தல். 992 says these two are what is called courtesy (பண்புடைமை என்னும் வழக்கு); 681 lists them and adds a third, the qualities kings desire (வேந்தவாம் பண்புடைமை), as the nature of one who carries a message. The envoy's qualification is thus the book's general definition of courtesy with a courtly requirement added.

681 asks of the envoy 'qualities that kings desire' (வேந்தவாம் பண்புடைமை) without saying what they are. Manakkudavar glosses the phrase as not desiring what the king desires, which is the content of 692 (மன்னர் விழைப விழையாமை), and Parimelazhagar says this quality is obtained from the following chapter on conduct around kings. 692 therefore supplies, on the commentators' reading, what 681 leaves unstated.

502 places trust in one born in a good family (குடிப்பிறந்து), free of faults and with a shame that recoils from blemish. 681 makes birth in a fit family (ஆன்ற குடிப்பிறத்தல்) one of the envoy's three marks. Family is used in both as evidence about a person before he is given a charge, for trust in general in 502 and for the embassy in 681.

513 says trust belongs with one who has love, understanding, clarity and freedom from desire (அன்பறிவு தேற்றம் அவாவின்மை). 682 opens with the same two words and names the envoy's indispensable three as love, understanding and considered skill in speech (அன்பறிவு ஆராய்ந்த சொல்வன்மை). The envoy starts from the same base as any trusted officer, and what is particular to his office is speech; Parimelazhagar glosses அன்பு in both verses as love for the king.

722 says those who can make what they have learned go home before the learned are called learned among the learned (கற்றாருள் கற்றார்). 683 uses the same construction for the envoy: he must be strong in the treatises among those who know treatises (நூலாருள் நூல்வல்லன்). Both measure learning by standing among the learned, not against the unlearned.

683 sets two groups side by side: among spear-bearers (வேலாருள்) the envoy speaks of victory, and among treatise-knowers (நூலாருள்) he is master of the treatise. 727 pairs the same two things as a simile: the treatise learned by one who fears the assembly is a bright sword in the hand of a பேடி among enemies. In both the treatise is treated as the speaker's weapon, and 727 adds that it is useless without the nerve to use it.

636 asks what subtle scheme can stand before those who have keen intelligence together with the treatises (மதிநுட்பம் நூலோடு உடையார்க்கு). 684 requires of the envoy understanding and well-examined learning (அறிவு ... ஆராய்ந்த கல்வி) held together. Parimelazhagar glosses the first term in each verse as natural intelligence and the second as acquired learning, so both verses ask for the two in combination, for the minister and for the envoy.

684 counts presence (உரு) among the three things an envoy needs. 407 says the fine looks of one without fine, penetrating understanding are those of a well-made clay doll (மண்மாண் புனைபாவை). 407 supplies the limit on 684's உரு: appearance counts only in the union (செறிவு) with understanding and learning that 684 itself demands.

667 says not to scorn anyone on seeing their form (உருவுகண்டு எள்ளாமை வேண்டும்), since there are people like the linchpin of a great chariot. 684 makes form (உரு) a requirement for going on an embassy. The two can stand together if 667 is about judging capacity for work and 684 about the first impression at a foreign court, but 667 limits how far 684's criterion should be carried beyond that office.

649 says those who cannot say a few faultless words long to say many (பலசொல்லக் காமுறுவர் ... சிலசொல்லல் தேற்றாதவர்). 685 begins its description of the envoy with speaking in gathered, brief form (தொகச் சொல்லி). Brevity is treated in both as the mark of command of speech, and 685 makes it a working requirement of the envoy.

696 tells one who serves a king to say what is needed and not disliked, in a way that is wanted (வெறுப்பில வேண்டுப வேட்பச் சொலல்). 685 has the envoy remove what offends and speak so as to please (தூவாத நீக்கி நகச்சொல்லி) while securing good for his own side. The same manner of speech is prescribed toward one's own king in 696 and toward a foreign king in 685; in both the pleasing manner serves what has to be said.

585 describes the spy as one who does not fear the eye (கண்ணஞ்சாது) and never lets anything out. 686 describes the envoy as கண் அஞ்சான், one who does not fear the eye. Parimelazhagar glosses both as not flinching from an angry, searching look. The king's two agents abroad share this mark, though the spy must stay silent under the look and the envoy must go on speaking.

647 says one who is able in speech, makes no slip and has no fear (சொலல்வல்லன் சோர்விலன் அஞ்சான்) is hard for anyone to defeat. 686 gives the envoy the same combination: he speaks so that it goes home (செலச்சொல்லி) and does not fear (அஞ்சான்), with learning and a sense of timing added. 647 states the general claim about speech and 686 applies it to the embassy.

724 says to make what one has learned go home before the learned (கற்றார்முன் கற்ற செலச்சொல்லி). 686 uses the same two terms for the envoy: having learned (கற்று), he speaks so that it goes home (செலச்சொல்லி). In both, learning is complete only when it can be delivered to a demanding audience, the assembly in 724 and a hostile court in 686.

696 tells the courtier to read the king's mood and consider the time (குறிப்பறிந்து காலங் கருதி) before speaking. 687 has the best envoy know what is due, consider the time (காலங் கருதி) and know the place before he speaks. The phrase காலங் கருதி is common to both, so the discipline for speaking to one's own king is the same as for speaking to another's.

675 says to act after thinking through resources, means, time, deed and place (காலம் ... இடனொடு ... எண்ணிச் செயல்). 687 uses the same terms for speech: consider the time, know the place, think it through and then speak (காலங் கருதி இடனறிந்து எண்ணி உரைப்பான்). The envoy's speech is planned by the same checklist the book gives for any deed.

712 says those who know how words work should discern the opening (இடைதெரிந்து), understand well and then speak; Parimelazhagar takes இடை as the receptive moment of the assembly. 687 asks the envoy to consider the time, which Parimelazhagar likewise glosses as the listener's receptive state (செவ்வி). Both make the listener's readiness a condition of speaking.

501 says a man is to be trusted after being tested by virtue, wealth, pleasure and fear for life. 688 lists the faithful envoy's marks as purity, support, resolve and truthfulness (தூய்மை துணைமை துணிவுடைமை ... வாய்மை). Parimelazhagar explains தூய்மை as being clean in respect of wealth and pleasure and துணிவு as not holding back for fear of harm, which makes 688's qualities the passes of 501's tests.

298 says outer purity comes by water and inner purity is seen through truth (அகந்தூய்மை வாய்மையால் காணப்படும்). 688 names தூய்மை first among the envoy's marks and then requires வாய்மை along with all three. 298 gives the reason the two words belong together: truthfulness is how inner purity shows.

383 names three things that never leave a ruler: promptness, learning and resolve (தூங்காமை கல்வி துணிவுடைமை இம்மூன்றும்). 688 has the same frame for the envoy who repeats the king's message: purity, support and resolve, these three (தூய்மை துணைமை துணிவுடைமை இம்மூன்றின்). துணிவுடைமை is the term common to king and envoy; the other two differ with the office.

139 says that for people of good conduct it is not possible to speak evil with the mouth even by a slip (வழுக்கியும் வாயாற் சொலல்). 689 asks the same of the envoy in his own field: a firmness whose mouth does not let slip a word that brings blemish (வடுமாற்றம் வாய்சோரா). What Book 1 treats as a result of character, 689 makes a condition for carrying the king's word. (This edition prints வாய்சேரா; the commentaries read வாய்சோரா.)

642 says to guard against a lapse in speech (சொல்லின்கட் சோர்வு) because both gain and ruin come from it. 689 is that rule at the point where the stakes are the king's: the envoy must not let a word that discredits slip from his mouth (வாய்சோரா); Parimelazhagar adds that the slip in question would come from fear for himself. The verb சோர் is shared, and 689 names the hardness (வன்கண்) that prevents the lapse 642 warns of.

778 says warriors who do not fear for their life when battle comes (உறின் உயிர் அஞ்சா மறவர்) do not lose their distinction even if their lord is angry. 690 says the envoy is one who, even if it brings his end (இறுதி பயப்பினும்), does not fall short and secures what is good for his lord (இறைவற்கு உறுதி). The envoy's office is given the soldier's standard, with both verses naming the lord (இறைவன்) as the one served.

638 says that even if the king destroys good counsel and knows nothing himself, the one at his side owes it to him to say what is good for him (உறுதி ... கூறல் கடன்). 690 says the envoy secures the lord's good (உறுதி) even at the cost of his own life. Both use உறுதி for the king's real interest and hold the servant to it under threat, from his own king in 638 and from a foreign one in 690.

723 says those who will die among enemies are easy to find and those who do not fear in an assembly are rare (பகையகத்துச் சாவார் எளியர் அரியர் அவையகத்து அஞ்சாதவர்). 690 asks the envoy to face death (இறுதி) while speaking in a hostile court. 723 separates the two kinds of courage and rates the second as rarer; the envoy of 690 needs both together, which indicates how much the verse asks.

691 tells those who serve quarrelsome kings (இகல்வேந்தர்) to be like people warming at a fire, neither moving off nor closing in (அகலாது அணுகாது தீக்காய்வார் போல்க). In 1104 a lover asks where she got a fire that burns when he withdraws and is cool when he comes near (நீங்கின் தெறூஉம் குறுகுங்கால் தண்ணென்னும் தீ). The king's fire burns at close range and the lover's reverses that rule, so the court calls for a kept middle distance and the love speech for none.

691 compares the king to a fire one warms at from a measured distance. 896 says one burned by fire may still survive, but those who go on offending the great will not (எரியால் சுடப்படினும் உய்வுண்டாம் உய்யார் பெரியார்ப் பிழைத்தொழுகுவார்). Read together, the fire in 691 understates the danger: 896 ranks the offended great above fire, though Parimelazhagar takes its பெரியார் as those great in austerity, not kings.

692 says that not desiring what kings desire (மன்னர் விழைப விழையாமை) brings lasting prosperity through those same kings; Parimelazhagar takes விழைப as the enjoyments, adornment and precedence proper to a king. 179 says Fortune herself comes to the wise who, knowing virtue, do not covet (அறனறிந்து வெஃகா அறிவுடையார்ச் சேரும் ... திரு). Both make not-wanting the route by which wealth arrives, once as court prudence and once as virtue.

693 warns the servant that once suspicion has arisen it is hard for anyone to clear it (கடுத்தபின் தேற்றுதல் யார்க்கும் அரிது), so grave faults must be guarded against beforehand. 510 addresses the ruler: doubting one who has been examined and trusted (தெளிந்தான்கண் ஐயுறவும்) brings trouble that does not end. The pair shows the same suspicion from both sides: the book counts it a fault in the king, yet tells the minister to plan as if it cannot be undone.

693 says those who would guard themselves should guard against the gravest things (போற்றின் அரியவை போற்றல்), which Parimelazhagar reads as faults a king cannot forgive. 891 says not slighting the power of those able to act is the chief of all the guarding done by those who guard themselves (போற்றுவார் போற்றலுள் எல்லாம் தலை). Both use போற்றல் for self-protection and locate its first object in one's dealings with the powerful.

694 says that in the presence of the great one should suppress whispering and shared smiles (செவிச்சொல்லும் சேர்ந்த நகையும் அவித்தொழுகல்). 715 calls the restraint of not speaking first among elders (முதுவருள் முந்து கிளவாச் செறிவு) the best of good things. Court and assembly get the same rule of holding speech back before superiors; 694 extends it to private asides and laughter, which Parimelazhagar says the king would take as aimed at himself.

695 forbids the courtier to listen in on anything or press for it, and lets him hear a secret only when it is released (எப்பொருளும் ஓரார் தொடரார் ... விட்டக்கால் கேட்க மறை). 587 defines the spy as one able to hear what has been concealed (மறைந்தவை கேட்கவற்றாகி). Hearing hidden things is therefore not wrong in itself in this book: it is the spy's work directed outward, and what 695 bars is turning it on one's own king.

695 treats the king's secret (மறை) as something to be heard only when he lets it go. 1076 says the base are like a beaten drum because they carry to others the secrets they have heard (தாம் கேட்ட மறை பிறர்க்கு உய்த்துரைக்கலான்). The two give the two ends of handling a secret: restraint in acquiring it in 695, and the failure to hold it in 1076.

696 tells the minister to know the king's mood and consider the time (குறிப்பறிந்து காலங் கருதி) before speaking. 687 ranks highest the envoy who knows what is due, considers the time and knows the place (கடனறிந்து காலங் கருதி இடனறிந்து). The phrase காலங் கருதி is common to both, so the same discipline of timed speech is asked of the man at his own king's side and of the man sent to a foreign court.

696 limits what the minister says to things not disliked (வெறுப்பில) and said so that they are wanted (வேட்பச் சொலல்). 638 says that even if the king destroys good counsel and knows nothing himself, the one at his side is bound to tell him what is sound (உறுதி உழையிருந்தான் கூறல் கடன்). They conflict if வெறுப்பில is read, with Parimelazhagar, as matters the king will not reject; if it means only an inoffensive manner, 696 governs how to say what 638 obliges one to say.

696 opens with குறிப்பறிந்து, knowing the king's mood, as the first condition of speaking to him. 701 praises the one who looks and knows what is meant without its being said (கூறாமை நோக்கிக் குறிப்பறிவான்) as an ornament to the earth. The skill 696 names in passing is taken up as the subject of the next chapter, beginning with 701.

697 says to speak what is wanted and never to say what has no use, even if asked (வினையில எஞ்ஞான்றும் கேட்பினும் சொல்லாவிடல்). 200 gives the general rule: say words that have use, do not say words that have none (சொல்லிற் பயனிலாச் சொல்). The court verse applies the household rule and tightens it, since here even the king's own request does not license useless talk.

698 says not to belittle the king as younger or as a relative, but to act in keeping with the light that rests on him (நின்ற ஒளியோடு ஒழுகப்படும்). 388 says a king who does justice and protects is set apart for the people as இறை (மக்கட்கு இறையென்று வைக்கப்படும்). Parimelazhagar reads the ஒளி of 698 as the king's godlike quality, so 388 supplies its ground: the standing comes from the office of protecting, which is why age and kinship do not touch it.

698 forbids belittling a king on the grounds of youth or kinship (இளையர் இனமுறையர் என்றிகழார்). 667 says one must not scorn by outward form, since the great rolling chariot depends on its linchpin (உருவுகண்டு எள்ளாமை வேண்டும்). Both reject judging a person by a surface measure, whether age, family relation or size, and point instead to the function he carries.

699 says those of unshaken vision (துளக்கற்ற காட்சியவர்) will not do what is unacceptable on the thought that they are in favour. 654 says those of untrembling vision (நடுக்கற்ற காட்சியவர்) will not do what is degrading even when caught in trouble (இடுக்கண் படினும் இளிவந்த செய்யார்). The same formula is used for opposite pressures, so that steadiness is tested by favour in 699 as it is by hardship in 654.

700 says the familiarity (கெழுதகைமை) that does improper things on the thought 'we are old associates' (பழையம் எனக்கருதி) brings ruin. 801 defines old friendship (பழைமை) as friendship that in no way cuts down the liberties of intimacy (கிழமையைக் கீழ்ந்திடா நட்பு). The liberty that defines friendship between equals is thus withdrawn where the other party is a king, as Parimelazhagar reads 700.

700 says intimacy that does what is improper brings ruin (பண்பல்ல செய்யும் கெழுதகைமை கேடு தரும்). 805 says that when friends do something hurtful one should understand it as folly or as great intimacy (பேதைமை ஒன்றோ பெருங்கிழமை என்றுணர்க நோதக்க நட்டார் செயின்). The conflict holds on Manakkudavar's gloss of 700, which speaks of the nature of friendship in general; on Parimelazhagar's, 700 concerns a king and the two verses address different relationships.

701 praises the one who knows what is meant by looking, without its being said (கூறாமை நோக்கிக் குறிப்பறிவான்). 1100, in the love chapter that has the same title குறிப்பறிதல், says that when eyes agree with eyes in their look, spoken words have no use (வாய்ச்சொற்கள் என்ன பயனும் இல). Reading without speech is a minister's rare skill in 701 and the ordinary condition of two lovers in 1100.

702 says one who knows without doubt what is within another (ஐயப்படாஅது அகத்தது உணர்வானை) should be held equal to a god. 587 defines a spy as one able to hear what is concealed and to be without doubt about what he has learned (அறிந்தவை ஐயப்பாடு இல்லதே ஒற்று). Both set the same standard, hidden things known with certainty; the spy reaches it through informants and the sign-reader by perception alone.

702 says the one who knows another's mind without doubt is to be taken as equal to a god (தெய்வத்தோ டொப்பக் கொளல்). 388 says the king who does justice and protects is set down as இறை for the people (இறையென்று வைக்கப்படும்). In both a human being is ranked with the divine for a capacity he exercises, and Parimelazhagar notes in each case that he is still a man by birth.

703 says to give whatever it takes from one's resources and secure those who read a sign by a sign (யாது கொடுத்தும் கொளல்). 794 says the friendship of one of good family who is ashamed of blame should be had even by giving (கொடுத்தும் கொளல்வேண்டும் நட்பு). The shared formula marks the two kinds of person the book thinks worth paying for, the perceptive adviser and the friend with a sense of shame.

703 urges the king to pay any price for those who read signs. 445 says that since counsellors serve as the ruler's eyes (சூழ்வார் கண்ணாக ஒழுகலான்), he must choose them with care. 445 gives the reason behind 703: the king sees through his advisers, so an adviser who can read what is unsaid is worth what Parimelazhagar lists as wealth, land, elephants and horses.

704 says those who grasp what is meant without being told and the rest are alike in limbs (உறுப்போ ரனையரால்) and yet different. 993 says likeness of limbs is not likeness among people (உறுப்பொத்தல் மக்களொப்பு அன்றால்), and true likeness is likeness of character. Both deny that the shared body makes people alike, with perception the dividing line in 704 and பண்பு in 993.

704 says readers of the unspoken and others share the same limbs but are different (வேறு). 1071 says the base look just like people (மக்களே போல்வர் கயவர்), a resemblance the speaker has seen nowhere else. The same figure of outward human likeness hiding an inner difference serves a point about intelligence in 704 and about moral baseness in 1071.

704 stops at saying that those who cannot grasp the unspoken are 'different' (வேறு) from those who can. 410 says others stand to those who have studied the shining books as beasts stand to people (விலங்கொடு மக்கள் அனையர்). Parimelazhagar glosses the வேறு of 704 with this very comparison, the idea being that they are animals, so 410 states outright what 704 leaves implied.

705 asks what use eyes are among the limbs if they cannot read a sign by a sign (என்ன பயத்தவோ கண்). 574 asks what eyes without measured kindly regard do, beyond seeming to be there in the face (உளபோல் முகத்தெவன் செய்யும் ... கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லாத கண்). Each denies the eye its name unless it does more than see, perceiving another's mind in 705 and looking kindly in 574.

705 says eyes that cannot read another's meaning are of no use. 393 says only the learned have eyes, and the unlearned have two sores in the face (முகத்திரண்டு புண்ணுடையர் கல்லாதவர்). In both the physical eye is treated as worthless without a trained capacity behind it, learning in one and the reading of signs in the other.

706 says that as crystal shows what is next to it, the face shows what is strong in the heart (நெஞ்சம் கடுத்தது காட்டும் முகம்). 824 warns against deceivers who smile sweetly with the face while bitter within (முகத்தின் இனிய நகாஅ அகத்தின்னா வஞ்சரை). They conflict if 706 is read as holding of every face; Parimelazhagar's gloss, that the face shows what is in excess (மிக்கது) in the heart, leaves room for feeling that is kept under control.

706 says the face shows what fills the heart, as crystal shows what is beside it. 959 says the sprout shows what lay in the ground, and the spoken word shows the lineage of the one born in it (நிலத்தில் கிடந்தமை கால்காட்டும்). Both rest on காட்டும்: something visible discloses a hidden source, mood in the face and family in speech.

706 likens the face to crystal (பளிங்கு) that shows what is next to it. In 1273 a man says something shows through a young woman's beauty like the thread that shows in strung gems (மணியில் திகழ்தரு நூல்போல்). Both use a clear stone that lets something else be seen through it for an inner state appearing on the surface, as a rule about faces in 706 and as one lover's observation in the chapter on making signs known.

707 says nothing is as knowing as the face, since whether one is pleased or angry it gets there first (உவப்பினும் காயினும் தான்முந்துறும்). 830 advises that when an enemy turns friend one should befriend with the face and let go in the heart (முகநட்டு அகநட்பு ஒரீஇ விடல்). If the face always runs ahead of the mind, as 707 says, the control 830 recommends should not be possible; the two agree only if 707 describes the unguarded face.

707 says the face is ahead of the person in showing pleasure or anger (தான் முந்துறும்). In 1277 a woman says her bangles knew before she did that her lover had left (நம்மினும் முன்னம் உணர்ந்த வளை). Both give the body a knowledge that arrives before the mind's own, a general observation in 707 and a lover's remark on her thinning arms in 1277.

708 says that if one has people who look within and understand what has happened, it is enough to stand looking them in the face (முகம்நோக்கி நிற்க அமையும்). 1100 says that once eyes agree with eyes, spoken words are of no use. Both make speech unnecessary between the right pair; Parimelazhagar adds for 708 that going on to speak would lessen both parties, a concern for dignity the love verse does not have.

709 says the eye will tell enmity and friendship, if one has people who understand the kinds of look (கண்ணின் வகைமை உணர்வார்ப் பெறின்). In 1097 a lover reasons that harsh little words without anger and looks like an enemy's (செற்றார்போல் நோக்கும்) are the signs of those who are close while seeming strangers. The love verse shows why 709 needs its condition: a hostile look can mean attachment, so the eye tells only those who know its kinds.

709 says the eye itself declares enmity and friendship to those who can read it. 828 says a weapon is hidden even in an enemy's hands folded in worship, and the tears his eyes shed are the same (ஒன்னார் அழுதகண்ணீரும் அனைத்து). On the reading that the eye cannot conceal, which Parimelazhagar states under 710, the weeping eye of 828 should not be able to deceive; 828 holds that it does.

710 says the measuring rod (அளக்குங்கோல்) of those who call themselves subtle is nothing but the eye. 796 says ruin has one benefit: it is a rod that measures one's people to full length (கிளைஞரை நீட்டி அளப்பதோர் கோல்). The book uses the measuring rod twice for gauging other people, the eye taking a present reading of a mind in 710 and adversity testing loyalty over time in 796.

711 tells those who know the body of words (சொல்லின் தொகையறிந்த) to speak after knowing the assembly (அவையறிந்து ஆராய்ந்து சொல்லுக). 644 gives the same command in the chapter on eloquence, திறனறிந்து சொல்லுக, which Parimelazhagar takes as knowing one's own and the hearers' capacities, and adds that no virtue or gain exceeds it. The pair shows the audience rule stated once as a rule of speech and once as a rule of the court.

Both verses end with the identical line சொல்லின் தொகையறிந்த தூய்மையவர். 711 commands such people to know the assembly before speaking; 721 says that, having known the kinds (வகையறிந்து), they do not let their speech slip before the capable (வல்லவை வாய்சோரார்). The repeated line makes 721 the outcome of 711's instruction: knowing the assembly is what removes the fear that causes slips.

712 asks the speaker in an assembly to discern the opening (இடைதெரிந்து), which Parimelazhagar glosses as the hearers' readiness to listen. 696 asks the same of one speaking to a king: know his mood and consider the time (குறிப்பறிந்து காலங் கருதி) and say it so that it is wanted. The timing rule is the same before an assembly and before a single ruler.

712 says to discern the opening and understand clearly before speaking (இடைதெரிந்து நன்குணர்ந்து சொல்லுக). 687 ranks highest the envoy who considers the time, knows the place and speaks after thinking it through (காலங் கருதி இடனறிந்து எண்ணி உரைப்பான்). Both make the moment, not only the content, part of speaking well; Parimelazhagar glosses both with the same word, செவ்வி.

713 says those who take up speaking without knowing the assembly (அவையறியார்) do not know the kinds of speech and have no ability at all. 401 says holding forth in an assembly (கோட்டி கொளல்) without full learning is like playing dice with no marked board. Each names a different missing precondition for speaking in an assembly, knowledge of the hearers in 713 and knowledge of the books in 401, and each treats the speech that results as empty.

714 uses a colour pair for intelligence: be bright (ஒள்ளியர்) before the bright, and take the colour of white plaster (வான்சுதை வண்ணம்) before the blank (வெளியார்). 844 uses the same pair: whiteness (வெண்மை) is the conceit that says 'we have brightness' (ஒண்மை உடையம் யாம்). Read together, the learned person of 714 puts on whiteness knowingly before those who, by 844, are white because they think themselves bright.

714 tells the speaker to change with the audience, bright before the bright and blank before the blank. 425 says understanding is what does not open and close (மலர்தலும் கூம்பலும் இல்லது அறிவு). If 425's second half is read generally, as steadiness of bearing, the two disagree about whether the wise adapt their display; on Parimelazhagar's reading, where 425 is about constancy in friendship with the world, the conflict disappears.

715 calls the restraint of not speaking first among elders (முதுவருள் முந்து கிளவாச் செறிவு) the best of good things. 403 says even the unlearned are very good if they can stay silent before the learned (கற்றார்முன் சொல்லாதிருக்கப் பெறின்). 403 asks silence of those with nothing to say; 715 asks those who do have something to say only to hold back from going first, which Parimelazhagar notes still allows speaking with or after the elders.

715 praises the restraint (செறிவு) of not speaking first among elders. 419 says a mouth that bows (வணங்கிய வாய்) is hard to have for those without fine listening. Both treat modest speech as a mark of what a person has learned, and 419 supplies the source 715 leaves unstated: the habit of listening.

716 says a slip (இழுக்கு) before those who have taken in wide learning is like faltering from one's footing on the path. 957 says a fault in the well-born shows up high, like the spot on the moon (மதிக்கண் மறுப்போல்). In both, the weight of a fault depends on where it is seen, the standing of the witnesses in 716 and of the person in 957, and not only on its size.

642 gives the general rule: since gain and ruin come from speech, guard against a lapse in it (சொல்லின்கட் சோர்வு). 716 applies it to one setting, a slip before the widely learned, and measures the damage by comparing it to falling from the path (ஆற்றின் நிலைதளர்ந்தற்று), which Parimelazhagar reads as a renouncer's lapse from the good path.

717 says the learning of those who have studied and understood shines among those able to examine words without fault (சொல்தெரிதல் வல்லார் அகத்து). 404 says the wise do not accept an unlearned person's brightness (ஒட்பம்), however good it is. The same expert hearers decide both cases: before them real learning becomes visible and untaught cleverness is not accepted.

718 compares speaking before people of understanding to pouring water on a bed where the crop is already growing (பாத்தியுள் நீர் சொரிந்தற்று). In 1093 the man says her glance and lowered head were water poured on the growing bond between them (யாப்பினுள் அட்டிய நீர்). Both use irrigation for a response that makes something already alive grow, learning in one and love in the other; 1093 is a lover's speech, not a teaching.

718 and 720 are the chapter's two liquid images. Words before those who understand are water poured on a growing bed; words before those not of one's own kind are nectar spilled in a dirty yard (அங்கணத்துள் உக்க அமிழ்து). The second limits the first: the worth of what is poured does not save it, and nectar, which is worth more than water, is lost where water in the right bed is not.

719 and 728 share the phrase நல்லவையுள் நன்கு செலச் சொல்லு-. 728 says those who cannot speak tellingly in a good assembly are of no use though they have learned much; 719 tells those who can do so not to speak in a mean assembly even by forgetting (பொச்சாந்தும் சொல்லற்க). Together they set the limits: silence in a good assembly is a failure, and silence in a mean one is required.

719 forbids speaking good things in a mean assembly. 849 gives a reason in another chapter: one who shows something to a person who does not see becomes himself unseeing (காணாதான் காட்டுவான் தான்காணான்), while that person goes on seeing as he saw. Parimelazhagar makes the same point on 719, that both assemblies would then look down on the speaker.

720 says holding forth before those not of one's kind is like nectar spilled in a dirty yard (அங்கணத்துள் உக்க அமிழ்து). 1000 says great wealth in the hands of one without courtesy is like good milk spoiled by the fault of its vessel (கலந்தீமையால் திரிந்தற்று). Both describe a fine liquid ruined by where it lands, and so place the loss in the receiver and not in the thing given.

720 and 401 both use the phrase கோட்டி கொளல், holding forth in a gathering. 401 condemns it when the speaker lacks full learning (நிரம்பிய நூலின்றி); 720 condemns it when the hearers are not of the speaker's kind (தங்கணத்தார் அல்லார்முன்). The two verses cover the two ways the same act fails, from the speaker's side and from the audience's.

721 says those who know the body of words and the kinds of assembly do not let their speech slip before the capable (வாய்சோரார்), which Parimelazhagar reads as not slipping out of fear. 647 lists the same qualities, able to speak, without slips, without fear (சொலல்வல்லன் சோர்விலன் அஞ்சான்), and says such a person is hard for anyone to defeat. 647 states the payoff of the fearlessness that 721 describes.

716 says a slip (இழுக்கு) before those of wide learning is like falling from the path. 721 answers from the next chapter: those who know words and know the assembly do not slip before the capable (வல்லவை வாய்சோரார்). One verse gives the cost of the slip and the other says what prevents it.

722 says those who make what they have learned go home before the learned (கற்ற செலச் சொல்லுவார்) are called learned among the learned. 424 defines understanding with the same verb: saying things so that they go in easily (எண்பொருளவாகச் செலச்சொல்லி) and seeing the subtle meaning in what others say.
