339 says death is like falling asleep and birth like waking from sleep. 926 says sleepers are no different from the dead (துஞ்சினார் செத்தாரின் வேறல்லர்), and likewise those who drink are always eating poison (நஞ்சுண்பார்). The likeness of sleep and death that 339 uses to describe the passage between lives is used in 926 as a premise: as the sleeper is for that time as good as dead, the drinker is as good as poisoned. Parimelazhagar says the shared ground is the absence of awareness.

271 says the five elements laugh inwardly (அகத்தே நகும்) at the hidden conduct of a man with a deceitful mind. 927 says those who drink and droop are seen through and always laughed at by their own town (உள்ளொற்றி உள்ளூர் நகப்படுவர்); Parimelazhagar takes கள்ளொற்றி as drinking in concealment. In both, concealed conduct has a witness that laughs, the elements within the body in 271 and the neighbours who infer what is going on in 927.

928 tells the drinker to stop saying he has never been drunk, because what he hid in his heart shows all the more at that moment (ஒளித்ததூஉம் ஆங்கே மிகும்). In 1161 a woman says she would hide her pain, but like spring water for those who draw it, it increases (ஊற்றுநீர் போல மிகும்). Both end on மிகும்: the attempt to conceal an inner state is answered by its overflowing, in drink and in love.

293 says not to lie about what one's own heart knows, for the heart will burn the liar afterwards. 928 concerns one such lie, 'I have never been drunk' (களித்தறியேன்), about something the speaker's heart knows, and says that drink brings the hidden thing out. 293 gives the inner penalty for this kind of lie and 928 adds an outward one, exposure.

849 says one who tries to show something to a man who does not see ends up unseeing himself, while the other goes on seeing as he saw. 929 says showing reasons to a drunk man (களித்தானைக் காரணம் காட்டுதல்) is like searching with a flame for someone sunk under water. Both use காட்டு, showing, for instruction that cannot reach its hearer; 849 says it rebounds on the one who shows, 929 only that the light goes out.

190 asks what harm could come to living beings if people saw their own faults as they see those of strangers. 930 gives a case: a drinker, while sober, sees another man drunk, and the verse asks whether he does not think of the lapse of his own drinking (உள்ளான்கொல் உண்டதன் சோர்வு). Parimelazhagar reads it as 'it seems he does not', which makes 930 an instance of the failure 190 describes.

539 says: when you are swelling with your own joy, think of (உள்ளுக) those who were ruined by negligence. 930 asks whether the sober drinker, seeing a drunk man, does not think of (உள்ளான்கொல்) his own slackness when drunk. Both ask a person to read his own condition in someone else's ruin, and both place the reflection at the moment when it is hardest or most needed.

931 forbids wanting gambling even when one wins (வேண்டற்க வென்றிடினும்), because the winnings are like the hook's metal a fish swallows (தூண்டிற்பொன்). 177 opens with the same வேண்டற்க and forbids the gain of coveting (வெஃகியாம் ஆக்கம்) because its fruit is hard to make good when it ripens (விளைவயின் மாண்டற்கு அரிதாம் பயன்). Both judge a gain by what it does to the gainer afterwards, in dice and in coveting.

113 says to let go, that very day, of gain that comes from leaving fairness even if it yields only good (நன்றே தரினும்). 931 uses the same concession, 'even if you win' (வென்றிடினும்), and still refuses the gain, calling it a swallowed hook. In both the apparent success of a wrong source is conceded and set aside.

932 asks whether gamblers, who get one and lose a hundred (ஒன்றெய்தி நூறிழக்கும்), can have any way to live well. 463 says those with understanding do not take up a deed that loses the capital for the sake of a gain (ஆக்கம் கருதி முதலிழக்கும் செய்வினை). The gambler is the plain case of the trade 463 rules out in the planning of any undertaking.

931 compares what is won to the hook's metal swallowed by a fish; 932 then counts the cost: one gained, a hundred lost. Parimelazhagar ties them, reading the 'one' of 932 as that hook-bait, which keeps the player at the table in the hope of more.

933 says that if one keeps calling the rolling dice-throw (உருளாயம்), wealth and its income (பொருளாயம்) go and fall outside (புறமே படும்); Parimelazhagar takes 'outside' as into enemies' hands. 1009 says the wealth a miser gathered without love, self-regard or virtue is taken by others (கொள்வார் பிறர்). The gambler and the hoarder, by opposite habits, both end with their wealth in strangers' hands.

385 defines a king as one able to create sources of wealth, gather it, guard it and apportion it (இயற்றலும் ஈட்டலும் காத்தலும்). 933, which Parimelazhagar reads of a king, says both the gathered wealth and its sources (பொருள் ஆயம்) leave him if he keeps at the dice. One habit undoes the gathering and the guarding that 385 makes the mark of rule.

934 says nothing gives poverty like gambling, which does many small harms and ruins standing (சிறுமை பலசெய்து சீரழிக்கும்). 1045 says that within the one affliction called poverty many sufferings arrive (பல்குரைத் துன்பங்கள் சென்று படும்). Read together they form a chain: gambling brings harms on the way to poverty, and poverty then brings its own.

935 says those who clung (இவறியார்) in pride to dice, gaming hall and skilled hand became people with nothing (இல்லாகியார்). 437 uses the same word of the miser: the wealth of one who clings (இவறியான்) without doing what should be done perishes. இவறுதல், holding on and not letting go, ends in loss in both verses, whether the thing held is money or the game.

539 advises thinking, when swollen with one's own joy, of those who were ruined by negligence (இகழ்ச்சியின் கெட்டாரை உள்ளுக). 935 supplies such a memory: those who took pride (தருக்கி) in the dice and came to nothing; Parimelazhagar reads them as kings of former times and names the Pandavas. 935 does for gambling what 539 asks a ruler to do in general.

936 calls gambling முகடி, the goddess of misfortune, and says those she covers (மூடப்பட்டார்) will not fill their bellies and will suffer. 617 says the same goddess (மாமுகடி) lives in sloth, and the lotus goddess in the effort of the one without sloth. The book gives misfortune a residence twice: in idleness and in the dice.

167 says the fair goddess, grudging the envious man, shows him to her elder sister (தவ்வையைக் காட்டி விடும்). 936 names that sister, முகடி, as gambling itself, covering those who play. Envy hands a person over to misfortune; gambling, in 936, is misfortune under another name.

937 says time spent in the gaming hall ruins long-held wealth and character (பழகிய செல்வமும் பண்பும் கெடுக்கும்). 1043 says poverty destroys together one's ancient descent and one's தோல் (தொல்வரவும் தோலும் கெடுக்கும்), which Pope takes as dignity of speech. The two sentences have the same shape: an inherited standing and a personal quality lost at one stroke, with gambling as a cause and poverty as a cause.

938 lists what gambling does: it destroys wealth (பொருள் கெடுத்து), makes one take up lying, destroys compassion (அருள் கெடுத்து) and drives one through misery. 248 ranks two of these losses: those without wealth may flower again one day (பூப்பர் ஒருகால்), but those without அருள் are finished. By 248's measure the third item in 938's list is graver than the first.

757 calls அருள் a child born of love that is raised by the wealthy foster-mother called பொருள். 938 has gambling destroy both பொருள் and அருள். Parimelazhagar assigns the losses in 938 to separate causes (losing, winning, resentment), but 757 suggests a link between them: with the nurse gone, the child is harder to raise.

939 names five things, among them learning (கல்வி), that 'அடையா' the one who takes to gaming. Parimelazhagar glosses this as 'do not come to him', but Pope's verse rendering and Kalaignar take the five as departing from him. On that second reading 939 conflicts with 400, which calls learning the wealth that cannot perish (கேடில் விழுச்செல்வம்); on Parimelazhagar's reading there is no conflict, since the gambler never acquires it.

166 says the kin of one who envies a gift perish without anything to wear or eat (உடுப்பதூஉம் உண்பதூஉம் இன்றி). 939 begins its list of what gaming keeps away with the same pair, clothing and food (உடை ... ஊண்). Envy and gambling are both measured by the loss of the plainest necessities.

370 says craving has a nature that is never filled (ஆரா இயற்கை), and that giving it up yields a nature that does not shift. 940 shows that unfilled nature at work: the game is loved more with every loss (இழத்தொறூஉம் காதலிக்கும்), and the living being's love grows with every suffering (துன்பம் உழத்தொறூஉம் காதற்று உயிர்). That the love is for the body is Parimelazhagar's and Pope's supply; Kalaignar takes it as love of life.

In 1145 a lover says love grows sweeter each time it is exposed, as drinking is wanted more each time one is drunk (களித்தொறும் கள்ளுண்டல் வேட்டற்றால்). 940 has the same 'each time ... the more' construction with another vice, the dice, as the comparison (இழத்தொறூஉம் காதலிக்கும் சூதேபோல்). The lover uses the figure to praise his state, while 940 uses it to describe an attachment fed by its own losses.

941 says the three humours counted by the learned, beginning with wind, cause disease whether they exceed or fall short (மிகினும் குறையினும்); Parimelazhagar refers the excess and shortfall to food and activity. 466 says one is ruined by doing what is unfit and also by not doing what is fit (செயக் கெடும் ... செய்யாமையானும் கெடும்). Both verses locate harm on two sides of a right amount, in the body and in action.

942 says the body needs no medicine if one eats after making sure that what was eaten has been digested (அருந்தியது அற்றது போற்றி உணின்). In 1326 a lover says that digesting what was eaten is sweeter than eating (உணலினும் உண்டது அறல் இனிது), and likens sulking before union to it. The lover's figure takes for granted the rule that 942 states as medicine, and turns it from health to pleasure.

943 says to eat knowing the measure once digestion is complete, as the way one who has a body can carry it long (நெடிதுய்க்கும் ஆறு). 479 says the life of one who does not live knowing the measure (அளவறிந்து வாழாதான்) seems to exist and then perishes; Parimelazhagar refers that measure to one's wealth. The same phrase governs both the stomach and the purse. (This edition prints 'அறவறிந்து' in 943; Parimelazhagar's gloss reads அளவு அறிந்து.)

943 treats keeping the body going for long as a goal and gives the means. 968 asks whether a life of nursing the flesh (ஊன் ஓம்பும் வாழ்க்கை) is any medicine (மருந்தோ) once one's greatness has lost its dignity. The chapter on honour sets a limit to the chapter on medicine: prolonging the body is not worth having at that price.

943 speaks of 'one who has gained a body' (உடம்பு பெற்றான்) and how to make it last; Parimelazhagar adds that a human body is hard to gain. 345 says that for those set on cutting off births even the body is excess (உடம்பும் மிகை). The two address different people, householder and renouncer, and 345 marks where 943's care for the body stops applying.

946 says disease stays with the one of very great feed (கழிபேர் இரையான்), as pleasure stays with the one who eats knowing to stop short (இழிவறிந்து உண்பான்). 420 asks what it matters whether those live or die who know taste only by the mouth and not by the ear, and calls them மாக்கள். Both verses use a word with an animal sense for the person ruled by the mouth: இரை, feed, and மாக்கள்.

947 says that if one eats greatly without discerning the measure of the fire within (தீயளவு), disease arises without measure (நோயளவின்றிப் படும்). 475 says even a cart loaded with peacock feathers breaks its axle if they are piled too high (சால மிகுத்துப் பெயின்). In both a fixed capacity, the digestive fire or the axle, is what excess breaks, whatever the quality of the load.

289 says those who know nothing but stealth do what is beyond measure and perish right there (அளவல்ல செய்தாங்கே வீவர்). 947 says the one who eats beyond the measure of his fire gets disease beyond measure. Chapter 29 uses அளவு as a moral measure and chapter 95 as a bodily one, and in each case overstepping it brings its own penalty.

948 sets out an order of enquiry: look into the disease, then its root, then the means that subdue it, and act so that it works (நோய்நாடி நோய்முதல் நாடி ... வாய்நாடி). 504 has the same threefold நாடி for judging a person: examine the qualities, examine the faults, examine which predominates, and take that. Diagnosis of a patient and assessment of a candidate are given the same grammar of step-by-step examination before a decision.

948 tells the healer to look for the root of the disease (நோய்முதல்) before the remedy. 360 does this for suffering in general: when desire, anger and confusion perish even in name, the நோய் perishes. The chapter on true perception treats pain as chapter 95 treats illness, by naming causes and removing them.

949 says the learned healer should act after considering the patient's measure, the illness's measure and the time (உற்றான் அளவும் பிணியளவும் காலமும் ... கருதிச் செயல்). 471 says to act after weighing the strength of the deed, one's own, the opponent's and the allies' (தூக்கிச் செயல்). Both end in செயல் after a list of things to be sized up against each other: the patient's capacity against the disease, as one's own strength against the enemy's.

516 tells a ruler to examine the doer, examine the deed, and act in keeping with the time (காலத்தோடு எய்த உணர்ந்து செயல்). 949 gives the healer a matching three: the patient, the illness and the time. Person, matter and moment are the terms of judgement in delegation and in treatment alike.

637 says that even when one knows the method of doing a thing, one should act knowing how the world goes (செயற்கை அறிந்தக் கடைத்தும் உலகத்து இயற்கை அறிந்து செயல்); Parimelazhagar glosses the method as what the treatises teach. 949 addresses the one who has learned (கற்றான்) and still requires him to consider this patient, this illness and this moment. Both hold that book learning has to be fitted to the particular case.

950 divides medicine into four parts: the patient (உற்றவன்), the healer, the medicine and the attendant. In 1102 a lover first states the ordinary rule, that the remedy for an illness is something other than it (பிணிக்கு மருந்து பிற), and then says that for the illness she causes she is herself the medicine (தானே மருந்து). The lover's point depends on the separation of roles that 950 lays out, and collapses cause and cure into one person.

951 says integrity and shame together are found 'naturally' (இயல்பாக) only in those born to a good house (இற்பிறந்தார் கண் அல்லது இல்லை). 972 says birth is alike for all living beings (பிறப்பொக்கும் எல்லா உயிர்க்கும்) and that distinction differs only by what people do (செய்தொழில் வேற்றுமையான்). The conflict holds if 972's பிறப்பு is taken to deny any inborn difference of character; Parimelazhagar softens it by reading 972 as the common nature of birth, leaving room for family.

951 claims that uprightness and shame (செப்பமும் நாணும்) come naturally to the well-born. 502 turns the same pair of ideas into a hiring test: trust goes to one who is குடிப்பிறந்து, free of fault, and has the shame that shrinks from a blemish (வடுப்பரியும் நாணுடையான்). The chapter on lineage states a belief; the chapter on choosing officers applies it, but adds freedom from fault as a separate check, so birth alone is not treated as enough.

952 says the well-born do not slip (இழுக்கார்) in conduct, truthfulness and shame. 133 says having conduct is itself குடிமை and that a lapse (இழுக்கம்) turns into low birth (இழிந்த பிறப்பாய் விடும்). Read together, 952's claim is close to a definition: whoever slips has by 133 already left the class of the well-born, a point Parimelazhagar makes on 133 while keeping it within varna.

952 lists three things the well-born keep: ஒழுக்கம், வாய்மை, நாண். 983 lists five pillars that hold up சால்பு: love, shame (நாண்), obligingness, kindly regard and truthfulness (வாய்மை). Two of the three marks of lineage reappear as supports of personal worth, so the same core is described once as inherited and once as a structure a person stands on.

953 names a smile, giving, sweet words and not scorning (நகை ஈகை இன்சொல் இகழாமை) as the share of a true lineage. 92 takes three of these and ranks them: being sweet-spoken with a glad face (முகனமர்ந்து இன்சொலன்) is better than giving with a glad heart (அகனமர்ந்து ஈதல்). The list in 953 is flat; 92 shows the book elsewhere weighing its items against one another.

953 puts giving and not scorning (ஈகை ... இகழாமை) side by side among the marks of a good family; Parimelazhagar takes all four as the way one meets the poor who come. 1057 gives the receiver's side: on seeing those who give without scorn or contempt (இகழ்ந்தெள்ளாது ஈவார்), the asker's heart rejoices within. The pairing shows why 'not scorning' sits next to 'giving' in the list.

954 says the well-born will not do diminishing things (குன்றுவ) even if they get crores piled up (அடுக்கிய கோடி பெறினும்). 311 says the stainless hold to not hurting others even if it would bring wealth that gives distinction (சிறப்பீனும் செல்வம் பெறினும்). Both use the same 'even if they gained' (பெறினும்) form to set a fixed refusal against a large reward, once for family standing and once for non-harm.

954 says the well-born do not do things that diminish (குன்றுவ செய்தல் இலர்), whatever the gain. 965 uses the same word to say what follows if they do: even those like a hill sink (குன்றுவர்) if they do a diminishing thing (குன்றுவ) the size of a kundri seed. 954 gives the rule and 965 the cost of breaking it, at a scale far below crores.

954 says no amount of wealth makes the well-born do what lowers them. 657 says the extreme poverty of the worthy (சான்றோர் கழிநல்குரவு) ranks above gain reached by taking on blame (பழிமலைந்து எய்திய ஆக்கம்). Both rank standing above wealth; 657 states the comparison outright, in the context of a minister's clean action.

955 says an old family does not part from its character (பண்பில் தலைப்பிரிதல் இன்று) even when what it has to give has shrunk (வழங்குவது உள்வீழ்ந்தக் கண்ணும்). 223 says that giving without uttering the misery of 'I have nothing' (இலன் என்னும் எவ்வம் உரையாமை ஈதல்) is found only in one who has lineage (குலனுடையான் கண்ணே). The chapter on giving and the chapter on lineage make the same claim from two directions.

955 says an old family keeps its character when its means of giving fall away. 218 says those who see what is due (கடனறி காட்சியவர்) do not falter in ஒப்புரவு even in a season without means (இடனில் பருவத்தும்). The same constancy under shrinking resources is credited to lineage in one verse and to understanding of duty in the other.

955 says an ancient family (பழங்குடி) does not part from its character when its means shrink. 1043 says poverty destroys together one's ancient descent and one's speech (தொல்வரவும் தோலும் கெடுக்கும்). They conflict if 1043 is read as plain poverty undoing lineage; the conflict eases on Parimelazhagar's reading, which stresses that 1043 calls poverty a craving (நசை), so it is the wanting, not the lack, that ruins.

956 says those resolved to live by their spotless lineage will not do unworthy things by taking to deceit (சலம் பற்றி). 660 uses the same word for wealth-making: securing wealth made by deceit (சலத்தால் பொருள் செய்து) is like keeping water in an unfired clay pot. 956 rules deceit out on grounds of family honour; 660 adds that its gains do not hold anyway.

956 says those who mean to keep to a spotless line do not do what lacks worth (சால்பில செய்யார்); Parimelazhagar adds 'even in poverty'. 656 says one should not do what the worthy condemn (சான்றோர் பழிக்கும் வினை) even if one must see one's mother hungry. Both set a standard of worthy conduct above need, 656 naming the hardest case.

957 says a fault in the well-born shows up raised high, like the mark on the moon in the sky (மதிக்கண் மறுப்போல் உயர்ந்து). 433 says those ashamed of blame take a fault the size of a millet seed as the size of a palmyra (தினைத்துணை ... பனைத்துணை). 957 describes how the world sees a small fault in a prominent person; 433 describes the same enlargement done inwardly by the person, before the world does it.

957 uses the mark on the moon (மதிக்கண் மறு) as a figure for a fault that everyone sees because of where it sits. In 1117 the lover asks whether his beloved's face has a mark (மறு உண்டோ) as the bright full moon has. This is a lover's praise, not teaching, but both verses rely on the same fact: the moon's brightness is what makes its blemish known.

958 says that if lack of affection (நாரின்மை) shows in a man, people will doubt his lineage (குலத்தின்கண் ஐயப்படும்). 992 names having love and being born in a seasoned family (அன்புடைமை ஆன்ற குடிப்பிறத்தல்) as the two things that make up courtesy. 992 pairs love and birth as partners; 958 shows that when the first is missing the second is no longer believed.

959 says speech shows a person's lineage as a sprout shows the ground (குலத்தில் பிறந்தார் வாய்ச்சொல் காட்டும்). 1044 says that even in those of good birth (இற்பிறந்தார் கண்ணேயும்) poverty brings the slackness from which degrading words are born (இளிவந்த சொற்பிறக்கும் சோர்வு). So the sign 959 relies on can be distorted by want: low words do not always mean low birth.

959 says the sprout shows what lay in the ground (நிலத்தில் கிடந்தமை கால் காட்டும்), and speech shows the family. 452 says water changes with the nature of the ground (நிலத்தியல்பால் நீர் திரிந்தற்று), and a person's understanding takes the nature of their company. Both use soil as the hidden source that marks what comes out of it, but one source is birth and the other is chosen company, which gives two different accounts of where character comes from.

959 treats the words from a person's mouth (வாய்ச்சொல்) as evidence of lineage. 139 says that for those who have conduct, speaking evil with the mouth is not possible even by a slip (வழுக்கியும் வாயாற் சொலல்). Both make speech a reliable outward sign of something settled within, lineage in one and conduct in the other.

960 pairs நலம் with shame and குலம் with humility: want நலம், then want நாணுடைமை; want குலம், then want பணிவு toward all. 1019 uses the same pair in negative form: a lapse in principle burns one's குலம், and settled shamelessness burns one's நலம் (நலஞ்சுடும் நாணின்மை). The two verses share the குலம்/நலம் pairing and agree that நலம் depends on shame.

960 says one who wants lineage must want humility toward everyone (யார்க்கும் பணிவு). 125 says bowing is good for all (எல்லார்க்கும் நன்றாம் பணிதல்) and is a further wealth for the rich. Both make humility general, and each singles out the highly placed, by family or by wealth, as those it most becomes.

960 asks for humility toward all (யார்க்கும் பணிவு) from anyone who wants to keep a lineage. 963, in the next chapter, limits when bowing is called for: in abundance one must bow (பெருக்கத்து வேண்டும் பணிதல்), but in reduced circumstances one must stand high (சுருக்கத்து வேண்டும் உயர்வு). The humility of 960 is thus not meant to cover bending under want.

961 says to give up things that would diminish one (குன்ற வருப விடல்) even if they are of a kind one cannot do without (இன்றி அமையாச் சிறப்பின ஆயினும்). 656 gives a concrete instance: even if you must watch your mother go hungry (ஈன்றாள் பசி காண்பான் ஆயினும்), do not do what the worthy condemn. Both state a refusal that holds against necessity, one for honour and one for clean action.

961 tells one to drop whatever lowers one's standing, however necessary. 1028 says those raising their family have no proper season, and that if they idle and stand on honour (மடிசெய்து மானம் கருத) it will be ruined; Parimelazhagar takes the thing ruined to be the family. Honour kept by declining work is here a cause of loss, which limits how far 961's 'give it up' can be taken.

Parimelazhagar reads 961's இன்றி அமையா as things without which one would not survive, so the verse puts standing above life. 131 says conduct is to be guarded more than life (உயிரினும் ஓம்பப்படும்) because it gives excellence. The same ranking, a value kept ahead of survival, is made for honour in one chapter and for conduct in the other.

652 says to avoid any action that yields neither renown nor good (புகழொடு நன்றி பயவா வினை), which makes renown one of the tests of an act. 962 says those who want renown together with great manliness will not do unworthy things even for renown (சீரினும் சீரல்ல செய்யார்). 962 therefore narrows 652's test: bringing fame does not by itself make an act fit to do.

962 refuses unworthy acts even when they would bring renown (சீரினும்). 113 says to let go at once of gain that departs from fairness even if it brings nothing but good (நன்றே தரினும் நடுவிகந்தாம் ஆக்கம்). Both have the form 'even if it yields the thing you want, not by this means', applied to fame in one and to profit in the other.

963's first half says that in abundance one must bow (பெருக்கத்து வேண்டும் பணிதல்). 125 says bowing is good for all and for the rich it is a wealth of its own (செல்வர்க்கே செல்வம் தகைத்து). Both attach humility especially to prosperity; 963 then adds the opposite duty for hard times, which 125 does not address.

963 says that in small and shrunken circumstances one must hold oneself high (சிறிய சுருக்கத்து வேண்டும் உயர்வு). 680 says those whose domain is small (உறைசிறியார்), fearing their own people's trembling, will bow to the greater and accept terms (கொள்வர் பெரியார்ப் பணிந்து). They conflict if 963's 'reduced state' includes weakness of position before a stronger party; if 963 is only about poverty and personal bearing, 680 is separate advice on statecraft.

963 asks for an upright bearing (உயர்வு) when one's means have shrunk. 988 says poverty is no disgrace (இன்மை ஒருவற்கு இளிவன்று) for one who has the firmness called worth (சால்பென்னும் திண்மை). 988 supplies the ground for 963's demand: want does not itself lower a person, so there is no reason to stoop in it.

964 says people who have come down from their position (நிலையின் இழிந்தக் கடை) are like hair fallen from the head. 973 says those who are not low are not low even when placed low (கீழிருந்தும் கீழல்லார் கீழல்லவர்). They conflict if 964's நிலை means outward rank or station; on Parimelazhagar's reading it means the high standard the well-born hold themselves to, so the fall is their own doing and the verses agree.

124 says the stature of one who is restrained without shifting from his position (நிலையின் திரியாது அடங்கியான்) is far greater than a mountain. 964 uses the same word for the opposite case: those who descend from their position (நிலையின் இழிந்த) are like hair off the head. Together they give the two ends of one scale, both measured by whether a person keeps to their நிலை.

965 uses the kundri seed (குன்றி) for the smallest measure: a lowering act of that size brings down people like hills. 277 uses the same seed for its two colours: people red outside like the kundri and black within like its tip (புறங்குன்றி ... முக்கிற் கரியார்). The seed serves once as a unit of smallness and once as a figure of a fair surface with a dark spot, and in both verses the small dark thing is what counts.

965 sets a hill against a kundri seed: the hill-like sink through a lowering act the size of the seed (குன்றி அனைய செயின்). 433 sets a millet seed against a palmyra: those ashamed of blame treat a millet-sized fault as palm-sized. Both use a pair of extreme sizes to say that for people of standing a small fault is not small, 965 as an outcome and 433 as an attitude.

965 plays on குன்று: those like a hill (குன்றின் அனையார்) will dwindle (குன்றுவர்). 898 has the same play: if those like a hill (குன்றன்னார்) intend ruin (குன்ற மதிப்பின்), those who seemed established perish with their line. Parimelazhagar takes 898's hill-like ones to be ascetics, so the same figure marks people who can be brought low in 965 and people who bring others low in 898.

966 asks what is gained by going and standing behind those who scorn you (இகழ்வார் பின் சென்று நிலை). 1033 says only those who eat by their own ploughing truly live, and all others bow to eat and go behind (தொழுதுண்டு பின்செல்பவர்). Both use 'going behind' another as the picture of a dependent life, and 1033 names the livelihood that avoids it.

966 says standing in the train of those who scorn you brings neither renown nor the gods' land. 1053 says that even asking has a certain beauty (ஏஎர் உடைத்து) when one stands before those of unconcealing heart who know what is due (கரப்பிலா நெஞ்சின் கடனறிவார் முன்நின்று). What 966 rejects is therefore not dependence as such but dependence on people who despise the one who comes to them.

967 says that being called ruined, in that very state, is better than living by following those who do not accept you (வாழ்தலின் ... கெட்டான் எனப்படுதல் நன்று). 183 says dying yields more of what virtue promises than staying alive by backbiting and falsehood (பொய்த்துயிர் வாழ்தலின் சாதல்). Both use the form 'than living this way, death is better', for dishonourable dependence in one and for dishonest speech in the other.

967 prefers being called ruined to a life got by following those who reject you. 230 says nothing is more bitter than dying, yet even that is sweet when giving is out of reach (ஈதல் இயையாக் கடை). In both, a life that cannot be lived on one's own terms, without honour or without the power to give, is ranked below death.

968 asks whether a life that tends the flesh is a medicine (மருந்தோ) once greatness has lost its dignity; Parimelazhagar takes this as a medicine against dying. 82 says that eating while the guest waits outside is not to be wanted even if the food were the medicine of deathlessness (சாவா மருந்தெனினும்). Both raise the idea of an immortality-medicine only to rank it below a duty, honour in one and hospitality in the other.

968 questions the worth of a life that merely feeds the body (ஊன் ஓம்பும் வாழ்க்கை) when dignity is gone. 1017 says those governed by shame give up life for shame and do not give up shame for life (நாணால் உயிரைத் துறப்பர் ... நாண் துறவார்). The chapters on honour and on shame reach the same ordering of life and self-respect.

969 likens the honourable to the கவரிமா that will not live once it loses its hair (மயிர் நீப்பின் வாழா). 964 likens people fallen from their position to hair that has fallen from the head (தலையின் இழிந்த மயிர்). The chapter uses hair twice: in 964 the fallen person is the worthless hair, and in 969 the loss of a hair is the loss the animal will not outlive.

969 says those like the கவரிமா give up life when their honour is at stake (உயிர் நீப்பர் மானம் வரின்). 779 asks who could reproach as failures those who die so that what they vowed is not broken (இழைத்தது இகவாமைச் சாவார்). Dying to avoid going back on what one stands for appears as a matter of civil honour in 969 and as a soldier's vow in 779.

970 sets disgrace against radiance: the world worships the ஒளி of those who will not live when இளி comes. 971 defines the same two words: one's ஒளி is abundance of aspiration, and one's இளி is saying 'we will live without it' (அஃதிறந்து வாழ்தும் எனல்). In both, disgrace is a way of going on living, and radiance belongs to those who refuse it.

970 says the world worships and praises the radiance of the honourable who do not live on in disgrace. 235 says that a ruin which is growth and a death which is existence (உளதாகும் சாக்காடு) are hard to reach except for the skilled. 235 gives the general idea that 970 applies: a death can leave a person present in fame.

970 praises those who will not live when disgrace comes (இளிவரின் வாழாத). 240 says those who live free of blame are the ones who live, and those who live without renown are the ones who do not (இசையொழிய வாழ்வாரே வாழாதவர்). Both deny that survival under disgrace counts as living; 970 adds that the world honours those who act on this.

981 says that for those who know what is due (கடன் அறிந்து) and take on worth, every good thing is கடன்; Parimelazhagar glosses this as the good qualities being natural to them. 218 uses the same phrase, கடனறி காட்சியவர், for people who do not falter in ஒப்புரவு even in a season without means (இடனில் பருவத்தும்). 218 shows one concrete case of 981's general claim: a duty that is felt as one's own does not wait on circumstances.

981 makes all good things the கடன் of those who take on சான்றாண்மை. 802 names one such item with the same words, சான்றோர் கடன்: being 'as salt' (உப்பாதல்) to the liberties a friend takes. The pair shows the general statement being filled in by a specific obligation in the domain of friendship.

982 says the worthy have only the goodness of character (குணநலம்), and that other goodness is not counted among goodnesses; Parimelazhagar takes பிறநலம் to be the goodness of the bodily limbs. 79 asks what all the outer limbs (புறத்துறுப்பு) can do for those who lack love, the inner limb (அகத்துறுப்பு). Both verses rank an inner quality over the body's outward parts, one for worth and one for love.

982 denies that any goodness other than character counts for the worthy. 407 says the handsome looks (எழில்நலம்) of one without fine, penetrating understanding are those of a decorated clay doll (மண்மாண் புனைபாவை). Both dismiss outward நலம் that has nothing inside it, though 407 measures by understanding and 982 by character.

983 lists five pillars that bear worth: அன்பு, நாண், ஒப்புரவு, கண்ணோட்டம், வாய்மை. 1013 singles out one of them: as all lives are fixed on the body (ஊனைக் குறித்த), சால்பு is fixed on the good called shame (நாண் என்னும் நன்மை குறித்தது). Read together, shame is one support among five in 983 and the seat of worth itself in 1013.

983 names நாண் and வாய்மை among the five supports of சால்பு. 952 says those of good birth do not slip in three things: ஒழுக்கம், வாய்மை and நாண். Two of the items recur, so the lists of what holds up worth and what marks good family overlap in truthfulness and shame.

983 calls its five qualities the pillar planted to bear worth (சால்பு ஊன்றிய தூண்). 615 calls the man who wants the work and not pleasure a pillar that wipes away his kin's troubles and props them (துடைத்து ஊன்றும் தூண்). The same figure, with the same verb ஊன்று, is used once for qualities holding up a character and once for a person holding up a family.

984 says சால்பு lies in the goodness of not telling others' faults (பிறர் தீமை சொல்லா நலம்). 980, in the preceding chapter, says greatness covers another's weakness (அற்றம் மறைக்கும்) while smallness tells only faults (குற்றமே கூறிவிடும்). The same test, what one does with another person's faults, is applied to பெருமை in one chapter and to சால்பு in the next.

The first half of 984 says austerity (நோன்மை) lies in the goodness of not killing. 261 defines the form of தவம் as bearing one's own pain and doing no harm to living beings (உயிர்க்கு உறுகண் செய்யாமை). 984 takes over that definition from the Book of Virtue and sets not speaking of others' faults beside it as the matching mark of worth.

985 says the strength of those who accomplish is bowing (பணிதல்), and that this is the weapon by which the worthy turn foes. 978 says greatness always bows (பணியுமாம் என்றும் பெருமை) while smallness adorns itself in self-admiration. Both attach bowing to the strong and not the weak; 985 adds that it has an effect on opponents.

985 and 225 open with the same words, ஆற்றுவார் ஆற்றல். 225 says the strength of the strong is enduring hunger, and ranks it behind the strength of those who relieve hunger (மாற்றுவார்); 985 says it is bowing, the weapon that turns foes (மாற்றாரை மாற்றும்). In both the formula redefines strength as a kind of restraint, and both play on மாற்று.

985 presents bowing as the weapon (படை) with which the worthy change their opponents. 827 warns not to accept bowing in an enemy's words (சொல்வணக்கம் ஒன்னார்கண் கொள்ளற்க), because the bending of a bow means harm. Read from the receiving side, 827 limits 985: humility can disarm a foe, and a foe's humility can also be the drawn bow.

986 says the touchstone of worth is accepting defeat (தோல்வி கொளல்) even from those who are not one's equal. In 1327 the man says that in a lovers' quarrel the one who loses has won (ஊடலில் தோற்றவர் வென்றார்), as the reunion shows. Both treat yielding as the better outcome; 1327 is a lover's remark about a sulk, while 986 states a test of character.

986 asks what the கட்டளை of worth is; Parimelazhagar explains it as the touchstone for the gold of worth, and answers: accepting defeat from one's inferiors. 505 says a person's own deeds are the touchstone (கட்டளைக் கல்) of greatness and smallness alike. 505 gives the general rule of testing people by what they do, and 986 names the particular act that tests worth.

987 asks what worth has brought if one does not do what is sweet even to those who did one harm (இன்னா செய்தார்க்கும் இனியவே செய்யாக்கால்). 314 begins with the same words, இன்னா செய்தாரை, and says the way to punish them is to shame them by doing them good (நன்னயஞ் செய்து விடல்). 314 gives this as a rule of non-harming; 987 makes it the thing without which சால்பு has no use.

987 says worth is useless unless it does good even to those who did harm. 998, in the next chapter, says failing in courtesy even toward those who act without friendship or kindness (நயமில செய்வார்க்கும்) is lowness (கடை). Both verses use the particle 'even to' (-க்கும்) to extend the virtue to hostile people, one for சால்பு and one for பண்பு.

988 says poverty is no disgrace (இன்மை இளிவன்று) to one who has the firmness called worth. 1044 says that even in the well-born, poverty (இன்மை) produces the slackness from which demeaning words arise (இளிவந்த சொல்). They conflict if 1044's 'even' is taken to reach people of character generally; if சால்பு is a firmness beyond good birth, 988 states the exception.

988 says want does not disgrace a person of firm worth. 657 says the extreme poverty of the worthy (சான்றோர் கழிநல்குரவு) ranks above wealth gained by taking on blame. Both refuse to measure the சான்றோர் by their means; 657 adds the comparison with ill-gotten gain.

988 calls சால்பு a firmness (திண்மை) that keeps poverty from being a disgrace. 1064 describes that firmness at work: the worth that will not consent to begging even when no means remain (இடமில்லாக் காலும் இரவொல்லாச் சால்பு) is too large for all space to hold. 1064 shows what the poor but worthy person of 988 does and does not do.

989 says those called the ஆழி of worth will not shift (பெயரார்) even if the age shifts. 124 says the stature of one who is restrained and does not turn from his station (நிலையின் திரியாது) is greater than a mountain. Both praise immovability and measure it against the largest fixed things, the world-age in one and the mountain in the other.

989 speaks of the ஆழி of worth; Parimelazhagar takes worth as a sea and ஆழி as its shore, the people who hold firm when other seas leave their bounds at the end of an age. 8 calls God அறவாழி, which Parimelazhagar reads as a sea of virtue, and sets it against the other seas (பிறவாழி) that are hard to swim. The word ஆழி joined to a virtue appears in both, as the sea itself in 8 and, on Parimelazhagar's reading, as its boundary in 989.

990 says that if the worthy decline in worth, the great earth will not bear its load (இருநிலம் தாங்காது பொறை). 996 says the world exists by resting on people of courtesy (பண்புடையார்ப் பட்டு உண்டு உலகம்) and would otherwise enter the earth and perish. The two neighbouring chapters each end their argument with the same claim, that the world's continuance depends on a few people of character.

990 says the earth cannot carry its burden (பொறை) once the worthy lose their worth. 572 says those without kindly regard are, by merely existing, a burden to the earth (நிலக்குப் பொறை). The same figure is used from two sides: the worthy are what lets the earth carry its load, and people without கண்ணோட்டம் are dead weight on it.

991 says courtesy is easily reached by being accessible to everyone (யார்மாட்டும் எண்பதத்தால்). 386 says the land of a king who is easy to see (காட்சிக்கு எளியன்) and not harsh in speech is praised above others. Accessibility is a requirement of kingship in 386 and the entry to பண்புடைமை for anyone in 991.

991 and 548 share the word எண்பதம், easy access. In 548 a king who is not accessible (எண்பதத்தான் ஓரா) and does not examine and do justice falls and perishes by himself; in 991 being accessible to all makes courtesy easy to attain. The quality whose absence ruins a ruler is the one whose presence makes a person courteous.

992 and 681 share a line almost word for word: அன்புடைமை ஆன்ற குடிப்பிறத்தல். In 992 these two are the way called courtesy (பண்புடைமை என்னும் வழக்கு); in 681 they are, with qualities kings desire (வேந்தவாம் பண்புடைமை), the nature of an envoy. The envoy's qualifications are thus built from the same two sources 992 gives for courtesy in general.

992 pairs love with birth in a seasoned family as the two sources of courtesy. 958 says that if lack of affection (நாரின்மை) shows in a person of good standing, his lineage is doubted. Both tie affection to good family, so that in 958 its absence counts as evidence against the birth.

993 says likeness of limbs (உறுப்பொத்தல்) is not likeness among people; the likeness that counts is likeness of character (பண்பொத்தல்). 1071 says the base look exactly like people (மக்களே போல்வர்), and that the speaker has seen no resemblance so close. 1071 is the ironic application of 993: the bodily likeness is complete, and it settles nothing.

993 denies that sharing limbs makes people alike. 704 says those who grasp what is meant without its being said and the rest are alike in limbs yet different (உறுப்போரனையரால் வேறு). Both use உறுப்பு for the likeness that does not count; the difference that does is character in 993 and perceptiveness in 704.

994 says the world honours the character (பண்பு) of those whose usefulness (பயன்) comes from doing good with fairness (நயனொடு நன்றி புரிந்த). 97 uses the same four words of speech: words that yield benefit (பயன்) and do not part from பண்பு produce நயன் and bring forth நன்றி. Parimelazhagar glosses நயன் as justice in both, so the cluster describes good speech in 97 and a good life in 994.

994 praises people of நயன் whose doing good makes them useful (பயனுடையார்). 216 says wealth falling to one who has நயன் (நயனுடையான்) is like a fruit-bearing tree (பயன்மரம்) ripening in the middle of the town. 216 supplies the picture for 994: the person of நயன் is of பயன் to everyone within reach.

995 says scorn hurts even in jest (நகையுள்ளும் இன்னாது இகழ்ச்சி), and that those who know how others feel keep courtesy even in enmity. 871 says enmity, a thing without பண்பு, should not be wanted even in jest (நகையேயும்). Both refuse the excuse of play for something hurtful, and both bring பகை and பண்பு together.

995 says courtesy is present even in enmity (பகையுள்ளும் பண்புள) in those who understand others. 874 says the world rests in the greatness of the person of courtesy who treats enmity as friendship (பகை நட்பாக் கொண்டொழுகும் பண்புடையாளன்). 874 takes the step beyond 995, from staying courteous toward an enemy to turning him into a friend; Parimelazhagar reads 874 as a matter of policy.

995 warns that இகழ்ச்சி, scorn, wounds even as a joke. 953 lists not scorning (இகழாமை) with a smile, giving and sweet words as the four marks of a true family. 953 names the trait as a mark of good birth, and 995 gives the reason for it.

996 says the world exists by resting on people of courtesy (பண்புடையார்ப் பட்டு உண்டு உலகம்). 874 says the world rests in the greatness of the பண்புடையாளன் who treats enmity as friendship (தகைமைக்கண் தங்கிற்று உலகு). Both make the world depend on the person of பண்பு, the general claim in 996 and a specific case in the chapter on enmity.

996 says the world continues because of people of courtesy, and would otherwise perish. 571 says this world exists because the great beauty called kindly regard exists (கண்ணோட்டம் ... உண்மையான் உண்டு இவ்வுலகு). The two verses use the same construction, 'because of X the world is', for two closely related qualities.

997 says those without human courtesy (மக்கட்பண்பு) are like trees (மரம் போல்வர்), though sharp as a file. 600 says those without abundance of inner drive are trees, different only in having human form (மரம் மக்களாதலே வேறு). The tree stands in both for a person who lacks the defining human quality, which is courtesy in one verse and drive in the other.

997 likens the clever but discourteous to trees. 576 says those who have eyes and do not extend kindly regard are like trees fixed in the soil (மண்ணோடு இயைந்த மரத்தனையர்). In both the comparison is to something that has the equipment, a sharp mind or eyes, and does not respond to other people.

998 calls it lowness (கடை) to fail in courtesy even toward those who act without friendship or kindness. 579 calls it the highest thing (தலை) to extend kindly regard and bear with even those whose nature is to hurt (ஒறுத்தாற்றும் பண்பினார் கண்ணும்). The verses mark the two ends of the same scale: good conduct toward the hostile is தலை, and its failure is கடை.

998 requires courtesy even toward those who do unfriendly, unkind things. 852 says that even if someone does what one cannot bear, intending division (பகல் கருதிப் பற்றா செயினும்), it is best not to do harm in return out of hostility. 852 gives the minimum, no retaliation, and 998 asks for more, that courtesy itself not lapse.

999 says that for those not able to laugh (நகல் வல்லர் அல்லார்) the great world lies in darkness even by day; Parimelazhagar takes நகல் as mixing with others and being glad at heart. 523 says the life of one who does not mingle freely (அளவளாவு இல்லாதான்) is like a tank filling without a bank. On Parimelazhagar's reading both describe the cost of not mixing with people, as lost wealth in 523 and a darkened world in 999.

999 says the world is dark at midday to those who cannot laugh. 304 asks whether there is any enemy other than anger, which kills both the smile and joy (நகையும் உவகையும் கொல்லும்). 304 names one thing that removes நகை, and 999 says what a life without it is like.

1000 says great wealth obtained by one without courtesy is like good milk spoiled by the fault of its vessel (கலந்தீமையால் திரிந்தற்று). 1008 says the wealth of a man nobody seeks out is a poison tree bearing fruit in the middle of the village (நச்சு மரம் பழுத்தற்று). Both say a good thing is made useless or harmful by the character of its holder; Parimelazhagar reads 1000 as wealth that benefits no one.

1000 gives the bad case: wealth with a person without பண்பு is milk turned in a tainted vessel. 216 gives the good case: wealth falling to a person of நயன் is a fruit tree ripening in the middle of town. Together they show that the Kural judges wealth by who holds it, with a paired image for each outcome.

1000 uses a vessel (கலம்) whose fault spoils the milk poured into it, for wealth held by a person without courtesy. 660 uses an unfired clay pot (பசுமண் கலம்) that cannot hold the water poured in, for wealth made by deceit. Both figure wealth as a liquid and the fault as the container, the owner's character in 1000 and the means of earning in 660.

1001 calls the man who stores up great wealth and does not use it dead (செத்தான்); 214 says whoever does not know and do what is fitting (ஒத்தது அறிவான்) is 'placed among the dead' (செத்தாருள் வைக்கப்படும்). Both use death as a verdict on a living person, once for failing to use wealth and once for failing in ஒப்புரவு, so the hoarder falls under both.

229 says eating alone in order to fill up one's store (நிரப்பிய தாமே தமியர் உணல்) is more bitter than begging; 1001 takes the case one step further, the man who does not even eat it (அஃதுண்ணான்), and calls him dead. Read together they grade the misuse of wealth: unshared use is wretched, no use at all is not living.

The two verses end with the same line, மருளானாம் மாணாப் பிறப்பு. In 351 the delusion (மருள்) is taking what is not real for real (பொருளல்லவற்றைப் பொருளென்று); in 1002 it is holding that everything comes by wealth (பொருளானாம் எல்லாம்) and so clinging without giving. The pairing shows the miser's belief treated as a case of the same error about பொருள், with the same result in birth; Parimelazhagar glosses the birth in 1002 as a ghost's and in 351 as a joyless one.

751 says nothing but wealth makes people of no account into people of account (பொருளல்லது இல்லை பொருள்). 1002 names nearly the same thought, பொருளானாம் எல்லாம், as what the miser thinks, and says that when it leads to not giving (ஈயாது இவறும்) it is delusion. The chapter on making wealth is thus limited here: the claim holds only for wealth that is given and used.

Both end in நிலக்குப் பொறை, a burden to the earth: in 572 it is the existence (உண்மை) of those without kindly regard, in 1003 the appearance (தோற்றம்) of men who cling to accumulation and do not want renown (இசை வேண்டா). The same sentence is passed on two kinds of people who are of no use to others.

239 says land that bears a body without renown (இசையிலா யாக்கை பொறுத்த நிலம்) declines in its yield; 1003 says those who hoard and do not want இசை are a burden to the land. 239 states a consequence for the land of the weight 1003 names, and both rest on பொறு, the earth's bearing.

236 says: if you appear, appear with renown; for those without it not appearing is better (தோன்றலின் தோன்றாமை நன்று). 1003 calls the தோற்றம் of hoarders who do not want renown a burden to the earth, and Manakkudavar reads it as saying it is better they were not born. The chapter on useless wealth applies the rule of the chapter on renown to the miser.

238 calls renown the legacy (இசையென்னும் எச்சம்) and says failing to get it is a reproach. 1004 asks what the man wanted by no one (நச்சப்படாதவன்) supposes his எச்சம் will be. On Parimelazhagar's reading of 1004, renown stays only with the giver, so the question applies 238 to the miser and finds he has nothing to leave.

114 says whether people were worthy or not is seen from their எச்சம்; 1004 asks what எச்சம் the unwanted man imagines for himself. Parimelazhagar takes the word as offspring in 114 and as what remains after death, i.e. renown, in 1004, so the pairing shows the same test of a life by what it leaves, applied with two senses of the word.

89 defines poverty in the midst of having (உடைமையுள் இன்மை) as the folly of neglecting guests; 1005 says those who neither give nor enjoy have nothing even with piled-up crores (கோடி உண்டாயினும் இல்). Both say that possession without giving counts as not having, once in the household setting and once for wealth at large.

377 says even those who have amassed crores cannot enjoy them except as the apportioner has apportioned (கோடி தொகுத்தார்க்கும் துய்த்தல் அரிது). 1005 treats not enjoying and not giving (கொடுப்பதூஉம் துய்ப்பதூஉம் இல்லார்) as the person's own lack. The chapter on fate adds that the failure to enjoy one's crores may not be wholly in one's hands, which limits how far 1005's judgment can be read as blame.

430 says those without understanding have nothing, whatever they have (என்னுடையரேனும் இலர்); 1005 says the same of those who neither give nor enjoy, even with crores. The same form of argument, that owning is not having unless some further quality is present, is used for understanding in one place and for use and giving in the other.

212 says all wealth won by effort is for doing வேளாண்மை, with தக்கார் in the picture (Parimelazhagar takes it as wealth of the worthy owner, others as help to the worthy). 1006 describes the man who does not use his wealth and has no habit of giving to the deserving (தக்கார்க்கொன்று ஈதல் இயல்பிலாதான்) as ஏதம் to great wealth. 212 gives the purpose of wealth and 1006 the case where that purpose is defeated; Parimelazhagar says the man is a disease to the wealth because he makes it not what it is for.

1000 says great wealth got by a man without courtesy is like good milk turned by the fault of its vessel (கலந்தீமையால் திரிந்தற்று); 1006 says the man who neither uses nor gives is ஏதம் to பெருஞ்செல்வம். In both the wealth is good in itself and the holder is what spoils it, which is how Parimelazhagar reads 1006 (others take the wealth to be a misery to him).

226 says ending the ruinous hunger of the destitute (அற்றார் அழிபசி தீர்த்தல்) is the place where one who has got wealth stores it. 1007 says the wealth of one who does nothing for the destitute (அற்றார்க்கொன்று ஆற்றாதான்) is like a very beautiful woman growing old alone. 226 says where wealth is kept safe; 1007 shows what happens to wealth kept anywhere else: it passes its time unused.

1039 says land whose owner stays away sulks like a wife (இல்லாளின் ஊடிவிடும்); 1007 likens ungiven wealth to a beautiful woman who ages alone (தமியள் மூத்தற்று). Both picture a good left unattended as a woman without her partner, for farmland in one verse and for money in the other; Parimelazhagar notes for 1007 that the wealth itself loses its fruit.

216 says wealth with a man of நயன் is like a fruit tree ripening in the middle of the town (பயன்மரம் உள்ளூர்ப் பழுத்தற்று); 1008 says the wealth of the man no one wants is a poison tree ripening in the middle of the town (நடுவூருள் நச்சுமரம் பழுத்தற்று). The image is the same and only the tree differs, so the two verses read as a deliberate pair: the place and the ripeness are equal, and the owner decides whether anyone can eat.

760 says that for those who have made bright wealth in plenty (ஒண்பொருள் காழ்ப்ப இயற்றியார்க்கு) the other two, virtue and pleasure, come easily. 1009 uses the same word, ஒண்பொருள், for wealth amassed by dropping love, denying oneself and not looking to virtue, and says others will take it. So the promise of 760 fails when the two ends it names are given up in the earning; Parimelazhagar reads 760 as wealth that comes by the right way.

755 says wealth-making that does not come with அருள் and அன்பு should be let go; 1009 says wealth gathered by abandoning அன்பு and ignoring அறம் ends with others. The first gives the rule in the chapter on making wealth, and the second gives the outcome when the rule is ignored.

837 says that when a fool gets great wealth, strangers are filled and his own people go hungry (ஏதிலார் ஆரத் தமர் பசிப்பர்); 1009 says the miser's wealth is taken by others (கொள்வார் பிறர்), which Parimelazhagar reads as not even reaching his own line. Folly and miserliness arrive at the same result by opposite routes, one by careless spending and one by spending nothing.

On Parimelazhagar's reading, 1010 says the brief want (சிறுதுனி) of the rich who have renown is like the rain cloud running dry (மாரி வறங்கூர்ந்தனையது). 219 says the poverty of a man of நயன் is just his not being able to do what he is used to doing. Both treat the giver's poverty as a loss to others, not to himself, and 1010 adds by its image that it passes.

211 uses மாரி as the model of giving that asks no return; 1010 uses மாரி for the renowned rich in a lean spell. The same figure is carried from the chapter on ஒப்புரவு into the chapter on useless wealth, where it marks by contrast what the miser's wealth never is.

Manakkudavar reads 1010 differently: the renowned rich, in a small displeasure (சிறுதுனி), not giving is like the rains failing. On that reading 17 is the fuller statement of the image: even the sea loses its nature if the cloud takes from it and does not give back (எழிலி தான் நல்காதாகி விடின்). The link depends on Manakkudavar's reading and not on Parimelazhagar's.

201 says the excellent fear the intoxication called evil deed (விழுமியார் அஞ்சுவர்); 1011 defines shame proper as shame on account of deeds (கருமத்தால் நாணுதல்). Fear and shame are given the same object, one's own wrong action, in two chapters, and Parimelazhagar glosses நாணுதல் elsewhere (433, 172) as அஞ்சுதல்.

1011 sets aside the modesty of bright-browed women (திருநுதல் நல்லவர் நாணு) as something other than the shame it means. 907 says a woman who has shame (நாணுடைப் பெண்) has more greatness than the manhood of one who does a woman's bidding, which Parimelazhagar glosses as a man without shame. So the shame 1011 puts second is still ranked above a man's lack of the first kind.

1011 mentions the other shame, that of women, without describing it. In 1251 a woman in the Book of Love describes it from inside: shame is the bolt (நாணுத்தாழ்) on the door of her restraint, which the axe of desire breaks. This is a speech in character, but it shows what the shame 1011 calls பிற is: a guard on conduct in love, not a recoil from a wrong deed.

972 says birth is alike for all living beings and distinction differs by the work they do (பிறப்பொக்கும் எல்லா உயிர்க்கும் சிறப்பொவ்வா); 1012 says food, clothing and the rest are no different for all beings and the distinction of people is having shame (உயிர்க்கெல்லாம் வேறல்ல ... மாந்தர் சிறப்பு). Both have the form 'common to all, சிறப்பு from one thing', and they name different things: deeds in one, shame in the other.

993 says likeness of limbs is not likeness among people; the likeness that counts is of character (பண்பொத்தல்). 1012 says the bodily needs are shared by all and shame is what sets people apart. Both refuse to take what is physically common as the measure of a human being.

410 says the unlearned stand to the learned as beasts stand to people; 1012 says what all beings share is food and clothing and what marks people is shame. Each chapter claims its own quality as the line that divides the human from the rest, learning in 410 and shame in 1012.

983 lists shame (நாண்) as one of five pillars that hold up சால்பு, with love, ஒப்புரவு, kindly regard and truthfulness. 1013 says சால்பு is fixed on the good called shame as all lives are fixed on the body (ஊனைக் குறித்த உயிரெல்லாம்). The chapter on shame makes one of the five the seat of the whole; Manakkudavar says other qualities are needed but this one cannot be done without.

80 says the seat of life goes by way of love (அன்பின் வழியது உயிர்நிலை) and without it a body is bones wrapped in skin; 1013 says worth depends on shame as life depends on flesh. Both use the life-and-body relation to say a quality is what a thing lives by, love for the person in 80 and shame for சால்பு in 1013. Parimelazhagar notes a variant ஊணை ('food') in 1013, which Manakkudavar follows; the link rests on the reading ஊனை.

Both verses turn on பீடு நடை, the proud walk. 59 says those whose home does not seek renown cannot walk it before people who scorn them; 1014 says that for the worthy without shame the proud walk is a disease (பிணி), which Parimelazhagar takes as painful to those who see it. The gait is earned by something behind it, the household's good name in one verse and shame in the other.

575 says kindly regard is the eye's ornament and without it the eye is known as a sore (அணிகலம் ... அஃதின்றேல் புண்); 1014 says shame is the ornament of the worthy and without it the proud walk is a disease (அணி ... அஃதின்றேல் பிணி). The two share one construction: a thing without its ornament is not plain but a bodily affliction.

118 (with 115) calls not leaning to one side the ornament of the worthy (கோடாமை சான்றோர்க்கு அணி); 1014 calls shame the ornament of the worthy (அணியன்றோ நாணுடைமை சான்றோர்க்கு). The same phrase names two inner restraints, and neither is an outward decoration.

315 asks what understanding is worth if one does not guard against another's pain as one's own (பிறிதின்நோய் தந்நோய்போல்); 1015 says the world calls those who are ashamed at others' disgrace and their own alike (பிறர்பழியும் தம்பழியும்) the home of shame. The move of treating another's case as one's own is made for pain in one verse and for disgrace in the other.

980 says greatness covers others' exposure (அற்றம் மறைக்கும்) and smallness only speaks their faults. 1015 gives the feeling behind that conduct: being ashamed of another's disgrace as of one's own. One who feels the other's பழி in this way has no reason to tell it.

1015 praises one who feels shame even for others' disgrace; 1018 describes one who does not feel shame at what makes others ashamed (பிறர் நாணத்தக்கது தான் நாணான்). The two set out the ends of a scale inside the chapter: shame that extends beyond oneself, and shame that fails even for one's own act.

311 says the spotless hold to not hurting others even if it would bring wealth that gives distinction. 1016, on Parimelazhagar's reading, says the high take shame as their fence and do not want the wide world (வியன்ஞாலம் பேணலர்) where the two conflict. Both state a refusal of great gain at the price of a restraint; the other reading he reports, that they will not want the world without first having the fence of shame, gives the same result.

57 says confinement does little to guard women and the guard kept by their own firmness (நிறைகாக்கும் காப்பு) is best; 1016 says the high have shame for their fence (நாண்வேலி). In both the effective guard is a quality inside the person and not an outer barrier, for a wife's fidelity in one and for the conduct of the high in the other.

421 calls understanding an inner fortress enemies cannot destroy (உள்ளழிக்கலாகா அரண்); 1016 calls shame a fence (வேலி), which Parimelazhagar explains as keeping blame and sin from entering. Both give an inner quality the work of a defensive structure, one against ruin and one against disgrace.

969 says those like the yak that will not live once its hair is lost give up life when honour is at stake (உயிர்நீப்பர் மானம் வரின்); 1017 says those ruled by shame give up life for shame and not shame for life (நாணால் உயிரைத் துறப்பர்). The chapters on honour and shame make the same ranking of life below the quality, in adjoining parts of the book.

131 says conduct is to be guarded more than life (உயிரினும் ஓம்பப்படும்) because it gives excellence; 1017 says shame is not given up for the sake of life. The same comparison with life is used for conduct in the Book of Virtue and for shame here.

In 1132 a lover says his body and life, unable to bear more, will mount the palmyra horse after setting shame aside (நாணினை நீக்கி நிறுத்து). 1017 says those ruled by shame will not give up shame for life's sake (உயிர்ப்பொருட்டால் நாண்துறவார்). The same choice between shame and life is posed in love and resolved the other way; this is a lover's speech in a chapter about abandoning shame, so it shows the pressure 1017 has in view and is not a rival teaching.

924 says Shame, the good woman, turns her back (நாண்என்னும் நல்லாள் புறங்கொடுக்கும்) on the drinker; 1018 says that if a man is not ashamed of what shames others, it is a thing virtue would be ashamed of (அறம் நாணத்தக்கது), which Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar both read as virtue leaving or not approaching him. In both a personified quality withdraws from the shameless person, shame herself in one and virtue in the other.

130 says virtue watches for the right moment and comes by the path to the one who guards against anger and has learned restraint (அறம் பார்க்கும் ஆற்றின் நுழைந்து). 1018, as the commentators read it, has virtue ashamed to come near the shameless. Together they give the two directions of the same figure: virtue seeks out the restrained and shrinks from those without shame.

204 says that if one plots another's ruin, அறம் plots the plotter's ruin; 1018 says that if one is not ashamed, அறம் is ashamed. In both, virtue is an agent that answers the person's act in the terms of that act, with a penalty in 204 and with withdrawal in 1018.

960 says: if you want நலம், want shame; if you want குலம், want humility toward all. 1019 says a lapse in principle burns the குலம் and settled shamelessness burns the நலம். Both pair the same two goods and tie நலம் to shame, one as advice and one as warning; Parimelazhagar takes நலம் in 1019 to cover every good, from birth and learning to conduct.

133 says having conduct is good family and a lapse becomes low birth (இழுக்கம் இழிந்த பிறப்பாய் விடும்); the first half of 1019 says the same, that a lapse in கொள்கை burns the குலம். 1019 then sets shamelessness beside it as destroying more, and Parimelazhagar draws the conclusion that loss of shame is worse than loss of conduct.

952 says the well-born do not slip in three things: conduct, truthfulness and shame (ஒழுக்கமும் வாய்மையும் நாணும்). 1019 says what happens when two of those three fail: a lapse in conduct burns the family, and shamelessness that stays burns every good. The chapter on good family gives the mark and 1019 gives the cost of losing it.

Both use the wooden puppet (மரப்பாவை). In 1058 the wide world without anyone who asks would be puppets going and coming (சென்றுவந்தற்று); in 1020 the movement of those with no shame within is a puppet feigning life by its string (நாணால் உயிர் மருட்டியற்று). The image marks motion without what makes it human, which is giving and receiving in one verse and shame in the other; 1020 also plays on நாண், shame and string.

407 says the good looks of one without fine, penetrating understanding are those of a well-decorated clay doll (மண்மாண் புனைபாவை); 1020 says the shameless move like a wooden puppet. Both use a பாவை for a person who has the outward form without the inner quality, appearance without understanding in 407 and movement without shame in 1020.

80 says that without love a body is bones wrapped in skin; 1020 says that without shame within (நாண் அகத்தில்லார்) a person's movement is a puppet's and only imitates life. Each chapter names its quality as what makes a body a living person, and Manakkudavar reads 1020 as saying the shameless are not people.

1021 says no greatness has more dignity (பீடு) than that of the one who says 'I will not stay my hand' (கைதூவேன்) from the work. 611 says not to slacken at a task's difficulty because effort itself gives greatness (பெருமை முயற்சி தரும்). Both locate பெருமை in persistence rather than in rank or result; 1021 applies it to the work of raising one's family.

1021 praises the resolve never to stop work once begun (கைதூவேன்). 612 gives the other side: guard against the work dying in mid-course (வினைக்கண் வினைகெடல் ஓம்பல்), since, in Parimelazhagar's reading, the world gives up on those who give up their unfinished work. The pair shows the same refusal to stop as honour in one verse and as a condition of the world's regard in the other.

1022 says the family (குடி) lengthens through long-continued work that has both effort (ஆள்வினை) and mature knowledge. 604 states the reverse case: for those sunk in sloth, without worthy exertion (மாண்ட உஞற்றிலவர்), the family dies down and faults multiply (குடிமடிந்து குற்றம் பெருகும்). Together they make one claim from both sides: the fortunes of a குடி follow the exertion of its members.

1022 pairs effort with full knowledge (ஆள்வினையும் ஆன்ற அறிவும்) as the two things that extend a family. 618 uses the same pairing when it assigns blame: lacking fortune is no disgrace, but lacking effort after knowing what should be known (அறிவறிந்து ஆள்வினை இன்மை) is. In both verses knowledge and effort are named together as what a person can be held to, as against fortune.

1023 says that for one who resolves 'I will raise my family', தெய்வம் itself tucks up its cloth and goes in front. 619 allows that தெய்வம் may make an end unattainable (தெய்வத்தான் ஆகாதெனினும்) and promises only that effort pays the wage of the body's strain. Read together, 619 limits 1023: divine help is not guaranteed to effort in general, and 1023 claims it specifically for the one working for his குடி.

Both verses end on the phrase தான் முந்துறும், 'itself goes ahead'. In 380 it is fate (ஊழ்) that arrives first, whatever other course a person devises; in 1023 it is தெய்வம் that girds itself and goes ahead of the person who undertakes to raise his family. The shared phrase shows the same power pictured once as outrunning human plans and once as running in front to help them.

1023 has தெய்வம் tying up its garment (மடிதற்று) to go before the family-builder. 617 says the dark goddess lives in sloth (மடி) and the lotus goddess in the effort of the one without sloth (மடியிலான் தாள்). Both put divine favour on the side of the one who works; 1023's மடி (cloth) also echoes the மடி (sloth) that 617 and the chapter on sloth condemn.

The two verses share the phrase தாழாது உஞற்றுபவர், 'those who strive without delay'. 620 says such people will see even fate's back; 1024 says that for those who strive so for their family, the work reaches its end by itself without their planning it (சூழாமல் தானே முடிவெய்தும்). 1024 applies 620's general claim to the family and states its result in a stronger form.

467 says to resolve on a task only after thinking it through (எண்ணித் துணிக கருமம்), and calls thinking afterwards a lapse. 1024 says that for those who work promptly for their family the end is reached 'without deliberating' (சூழாமல்). The conflict holds on Parimelazhagar's reading, where the doer need not work out how to complete the task; Manakkudavar reads it as the result arriving before one has even thought of it, which is praise of merit rather than a rule against planning.

525 says one who gives and speaks sweetly will be surrounded by layers of kin (சுற்றத்தால் சுற்றப்படும்). 1025 uses the same play on சுற்றம்/சுற்றும்: the world gathers as kin (சுற்றமாச் சுற்றும் உலகு) around one who lives raising his family without fault. 1025 widens the circle from one's kin to the world and changes its cause from giving to blameless work for the குடி.

544 says the world stands embracing the feet of the king who rules embracing his people (குடிதழீஇ ... அடிதழீஇ நிற்கும் உலகு). 1025 says the world circles as kin the man who lives building up his family without fault. The same pattern appears in kingship and in the household: whoever takes care of his குடி finds the world attaching itself to him.

773 says fierceness is called great manliness (பேராண்மை), and that helping a foe in distress (ஊராண்மை) is its edge. 1026 says good manliness (நல்லாண்மை) is making oneself the one who manages the house one was born in (இல்லாண்மை). Each verse takes ஆண்மை and coins a second compound that turns it toward care for others; Parimelazhagar notes that 'நல்' in 1026 is there to set it apart from the manliness of war.

148 calls not looking at another man's wife great manliness (பேராண்மை). 1026 defines good manliness (நல்லாண்மை) as taking on the governance of one's own family. In both, the word for manly strength is given a domestic meaning: restraint in 148, responsibility in 1026.

1027 says that as in battle the load falls on the stout-hearted (வன்கண்ணர்), so among kin the burden (பொறை) falls on those able to carry it. 770 says an army has no existence without leaders, however many steady men it has (தலைமக்கள் இல்வழி இல்). 770 is the military fact that 1027 uses as its simile: numbers do not carry a force or a family, a few capable people do.

481 says kings who want to win need the right time, as the crow beats the owl only by day. 1028 says those who raise their family have no season (பருவம் இல்லை). Parimelazhagar himself cites 481 here and reads 1028 as denying that the rule of waiting for the time applies to this work, where putting it off for weather or season is only sloth (மடி).

961 tells one to give up even indispensable things if they diminish one, and its chapter places மானம் above life. 1028 says that if the family-builder idles and thinks of மானம் (மானங் கருத), the family is ruined. The conflict holds if மானம் means the same honour in both, as in Pope's rendering; Parimelazhagar narrows it in 1028 to a resentful pride ('why should I alone suffer?'), which removes the conflict.

627 says the great, knowing the body is a target for suffering (இலக்கம் உடம்பு இடும்பைக்கு), do not treat trouble as distress. 1029 asks whether the body of the man who shields his family from harm is a vessel for suffering alone (இடும்பைக்கே கொள்கலம் கொல்லோ). Both make the body the place where இடும்பை lands; 627 says it of everyone, 1029 of the one who takes on his family's troubles as well.

615 describes one who does not want pleasure but wants the work (இன்பம் விழையான் வினைவிழைவான்) as the pillar who wipes away his kin's sorrows. 1029 looks at that same person from the inside: his body seems to hold nothing but suffering. 1029 states the cost of the role that 615 praises; Parimelazhagar takes the question as noting that pleasure never reaches him.

1030 says a family with no good man to stand by and prop it (அடுத்தூன்றும் நல்லாள்) falls when trouble cuts at its foot. 615 calls the man who loves work a pillar who wipes away his kin's troubles and props them (துடைத்தூன்றும் தூண்). Both use the verb ஊன்று, to prop: 615 shows the prop in place and 1030 shows the family without it, which the commentators picture as a tree felled.

449 says those without a supporting prop (மதலையாஞ் சார்பு) have no standing (நிலை), as those without capital have no profit; it is said of a ruler who lacks great men beside him. 1030 says a family without a good man to prop it falls under trouble. The same structural image, a thing that stands only while something holds it up, is applied to a king in 449 and to a family in 1030.

1031 says the world, wherever it turns, comes behind the plough (ஏர்ப் பின்னது உலகம்), so farming is foremost. 14 says ploughmen will not plough with the plough (ஏரின் உழாஅர் உழவர்) if the rain's bounty declines. 14 puts a condition under 1031: the world depends on the plough, and the plough depends on the rain.

1032 calls those who plough the linchpin (ஆணி) of the world's people, because they carry all who go to other work. 667 says not to scorn people for their appearance, since some are like the linchpin of a great rolling chariot (அச்சாணி அன்னார்). The image is the same in both: a small part that keeps the whole vehicle from falling apart, used in 667 for the unimpressive but essential person and in 1032 for the farmer.

42 says the householder is the support (துணை) of renouncers, the destitute and the dead. 1032 says the ploughmen bear (பொறுத்து) everyone who does not plough. Both verses identify one group whose ordinary work holds up all the others: the householder in the Book of Virtue, the farmer in the Book of Wealth.

1033 says only those who plough and eat (உழுதுண்டு) truly live, while the rest eat by bowing to others. 1065 says nothing is sweeter than eating what one's own effort brought (தாள் தந்தது), even if it is thin gruel. Both value food by whether one's own labour produced it, 1033 as independence and 1065 as sweetness.

1033 describes everyone but the farmer as those who bow, eat and walk behind others (தொழுதுண்டு பின்செல்பவர்). 967 says it is better to be called ruined than to live by going behind those who do not accept one (ஒட்டார் பின்சென்று வாழ்தல்). Both treat 'going behind' another for a living as a lesser life; 967 judges it by honour, and 1033 names farming as the livelihood that avoids it.

389 says the world rests under the umbrella (கவிகை) of a king who can bear bitter words. 1034 says those who have the shade of grain will see the shade of many umbrellas come under their own umbrella (தங்குடைக்கீழ்), which Parimelazhagar takes as their own king's. Both use the royal umbrella's shade for dominion, but 389 credits the king's character and 1034 credits the farmers' harvest.

545 says rain and harvest gather in the land of the king who rules justly (பெயலும் விளையுளும் தொக்கு). 1034 says those who hold the grain bring many kings' umbrellas under their own. The dependence runs in both directions: in 545 good rule yields harvest, and in 1034 harvest yields the king's wider rule.

1061 says that not begging (இரவாமை), even from those who give gladly without concealing (கரவாது), is worth ten million times more. 1035 says those whose way is to eat what their own hands produce do not beg (இரவார்) and give to askers without concealing (கரவாது ஈவர்). 1035 names the livelihood that makes the ideal of 1061 possible, and puts the farmer on the giving side of the same exchange.

613 says the proud distinction of helping others (வேளாண்மை) rests on the quality of labour (தாளாண்மை). 1035 says those who live by the work of their hands (கைசெய்தூண்) are the ones who give to those who ask. Both make giving depend on one's own labour: 613 as a principle, 1035 in the person of the cultivator.

19 says neither giving nor austerity (தானம் தவம்) will stay in the world if the sky does not give. 1036 says that if the farmers' hands fold (கைம்மடங்கின்), even those who say 'we have given up desire' cannot keep their state. Both make the ascetic life depend on a material source, the rain in 19 and the farmer in 1036, and with verse 14 they form a chain from rain to plough to renouncer.

263 asks whether the others have forgotten austerity out of a wish to provide for those who have renounced (துறந்தார்க்குத் துப்புரவு வேண்டி). 1036 says that without the farmer's work the renouncer cannot hold his state (நிலை). Both say renunciation is carried by people who do not renounce; 1036 identifies the farmer as the one it finally rests on.

1037 says that if ploughed soil is dried until a measure of dust (தொடிப்புழுதி) falls to a quarter (கஃசு), the crop thrives without even a handful of manure. 1038 says manuring is better than ploughing (ஏரினும் நன்றால் எருவிடுதல்). The two set tillage and manure against each other from opposite sides: thorough working of the soil can replace manure, yet as a rule manure counts for more than ploughing.

1038 lists the stages of raising a crop, including the point after weeding (கட்டபின்), and ranks guarding above watering. 550 says a king punishing the cruel with death is like weeding the young crop (பைங்கூழ் களைகட்டதனொடு நேர்). 550 borrows for kingship one of the farmer's tasks that 1038 gives literally; in both, removing what harms the crop is part of tending it.

1038 treats manure (எரு) and water (நீர்) as what makes a crop grow. In 1147 the woman says her love-sickness grows with the town's gossip as manure and her mother's words as water (கெளவை எருவாக அன்னைசொல் நீராக). The Book of Love takes the two inputs that 1038 gives as farming advice and uses them as a figure for what feeds her passion.

1039 says that if the owner (கிழவன்) stays away and does not go to it, the land turns against him and sulks like a wife. 553 says the king who does not look into things and do justice every day loses his land day by day (நாடொறும் நாடு கெடும்). In both, land is lost through the owner's or ruler's lack of personal attention; Parimelazhagar reads 1039 too as requiring a daily visit.

1039 describes neglected land with the Book of Love's words for a lovers' sulk: it resents and sulks like a wife (புலந்து ... ஊடி விடும்). 1304, in the chapter on sulking, says that not appeasing one who has sulked (ஊடியவரை உணராமை) is like cutting a withered creeper at the root. The figures run in opposite directions: the land is compared to a sulking woman in 1039, and the neglected sulking woman to a plant in 1304.

1039 compares the land to a wife (இல்லாள்) who sulks when her owner stays away. 1040 calls the land a good woman (நிலமென்னும் நல்லாள்) who laughs at those who sit idle pleading poverty. The chapter closes with two verses that make the land a woman who responds to how a man treats her, by sulking in one and by laughing in the other.

271 says the five elements laugh inwardly (அகத்தே நகும்) at the false conduct of the deceitful-minded. 1040 says the good woman called Land laughs (நகும்) on seeing those who say 'we have nothing' and sit idle.
