In both verses a part of the natural world laughs at a person's self-deception; Parimelazhagar adds that the Land too laughs to herself.

205 says not to do evil on the plea 'I have nothing' (இலன் என்று), because doing so makes one poor again. 1040 has the Land laugh at those who say 'we have nothing' (இலமென்று) and sit idle. The same plea of poverty is rejected as an excuse in both, for wrongdoing in 205 and for idleness in 1040.

616 says effort creates prosperity and lack of effort brings in want (முயற்றின்மை இன்மை புகுத்திவிடும்). 1040 pictures the Land laughing at people who claim poverty while sitting idle (அசைஇ இருப்பார்). Both hold that such poverty comes from not working; 1040 states it as mockery from the land that would have paid them.

1041 says nothing is as painful as poverty except poverty itself (இன்மையின் இன்னாதது ... இன்மையே). 558 uses the same phrase to name an exception: under the rod of a king who does not do justice, having is more painful than not having (இன்மையின் இன்னாது உடைமை). The pairing shows the book allowing one condition in which poverty's first place in pain is lost.

1041 puts material want beyond comparison as a source of pain. 841 says lack of understanding is the lack among lacks (இன்மையுள் இன்மை) and that the world does not count any other lack as lack (பிறிதின்மை இன்மையா வையாது). They conflict if both are read as ranking the worst kind of want; the conflict eases if 1041 ranks pain felt and 841 ranks what the world counts as real deprivation.

Both verses personify an evil with the same phrase, 'என ஒரு பாவி': envy in 168, poverty in 1042. Each then names a double loss: envy destroys fortune and leads to the evil place (திருச்செற்றுத் தீயுழி உய்த்து விடும்), and poverty comes with both the next life and this one gone (மறுமையும் இம்மையும் இன்றி). Parimelazhagar himself points from 1042 back to 168 for the phrase.

247 divides the two worlds: this world is not for those without wealth (பொருளில்லார்க்கு இவ்வுலகம் இல்லாகி), as that world is not for those without அருள். 1042 goes further and says poverty costs both worlds (மறுமையும் இம்மையும் இன்றி). Parimelazhagar explains the loss of the next world by the poor person's inability to give.

1043 says poverty, called a craving (நசை), destroys ancient descent and தோல் together (தொல்வரவும் தோலும் கெடுக்கும்). 955 says an old family does not part from its character even when what it can give has shrunk (வழங்குவது உள்வீழ்ந்தக் கண்ணும் பழங்குடி பண்பில் தலைப்பிரிதல் இன்று). They conflict if தொல்வரவு is read as the family's inherited standing and character, which Parimelazhagar's gloss (poverty brings acts and words the family's elders never had) supports; 955 speaks of reduced means, 1043 of want that has become craving.

171 says that coveting another's goods without fairness ruins the family (வெஃகின் குடிபொன்றி). 1043 names poverty itself a craving (நல்குரவு என்னும் நசை) and gives it the same effect on ancient descent. Read together, 1043 treats poverty as harmful to a lineage through the desire it breeds, the mechanism 171 states for covetousness.

223 says that not uttering the misery of 'I have nothing' (இலனென்னும் எவ்வம் உரையாமை) is found only in one of good family (குலனுடையான் கண்ணே). 1044 says poverty produces, even in the well-born (இற்பிறந்தார் கண்ணேயும்), the lapse from which degrading words are born; Parimelazhagar takes those words to be the request 'give to me'. 1044 thus limits 223: birth does not fully protect against the speech 223 says the well-born avoid.

959 says the words from the mouth show the lineage one is born into (குலத்தில் பிறந்தார் வாய்ச்சொல்), as a sprout shows the soil. 1044 says poverty brings even the well-born to degrading words (இளிவந்த சொற்பிறக்கும் சோர்வு). The pairing shows a case where speech stops being a reliable sign of birth.

1045 says many sufferings arrive within the one affliction called poverty (நல்குரவு என்னும் இடும்பையுள் பல்குரைத் துன்பங்கள்). 1056 says that on seeing those free of the affliction of concealing, all the afflictions of poverty perish together (நிரப்பிடும்பை எல்லாம் ஒருங்கு கெடும்). The next chapter answers this verse in its own terms: the sufferings that come as a group also leave as a group.

1046 says that even when the poor speak good matter they have understood well, their words lose their force (நல்கூர்ந்தார் சொற்பொருள் சோர்வு படும்). 752 says everyone scorns those who have nothing (இல்லாரை எல்லாரும் எள்ளுவர்). 1046 is the particular case of 752 for speech: the hearers' disregard, not the content, empties the words; Parimelazhagar says no one listens for fear of having to help.

532 says in a simile that constant poverty kills understanding (அறிவினை நிச்ச நிரப்புக் கொன்றாங்கு). 1046 grants the poor person full understanding (நன்குணர்ந்து சொல்லினும்) and places the loss in how the words are received. The two give different accounts of what poverty does to a knowing person: one says it destroys the knowledge, the other that it leaves the knowledge and removes its audience.

1047 says the person in poverty unconnected with virtue (அறஞ்சாரா நல்குரவு) is looked on as a stranger even by his own mother. 117 says the world does not count as ruin the low state of one who stays in virtue (நன்றிக்கண் தங்கியான் தாழ்வு). The qualifier அறஞ்சாரா in 1047 marks the boundary 117 draws: estrangement follows poverty without virtue, while poverty with virtue is not held against a person.

Both verses use the mother who bore one as the limiting case. 656 says do not do what the worthy condemn even if you must see your mother hungry (ஈன்றாள் பசிகாண்பான் ஆயினும்). 1047 says poverty apart from virtue makes even that mother look on one as a stranger (ஈன்ற தாயானும் பிறன்போல நோக்கப்படும்). On Kalaignar's reading of 1047, as a man who leaves virtue because of poverty, the two fit closely: the wrong done to feed her would lose her regard.

1048 is a poor man's cry: will the want that as good as killed me yesterday come today too (நெருநலும் கொன்றது போலும் நிரப்பு)? 532 uses the same noun and verb in a simile, constant poverty killing understanding (நிச்ச நிரப்புக் கொன்றாங்கு). Both treat நிரப்பு as something that kills and that returns daily; Parimelazhagar glosses both with a man who fills his stomach each day only with great pain.

1049 says one can even sleep in the midst of fire, but in want there is no closing the eyes (நெருப்பினுள் துஞ்சலும் ஆகும்). 896 says one burned by fire may yet survive, but those who go on offending the great will not (எரியால் சுடப்படினும் உய்வுண்டாம்). Both measure a non-physical danger by granting that fire can be endured and denying the same of the thing compared.

1049 says that in poverty the eyes cannot close by any means (யாதொன்றும் கண்பாடு அரிது). In 1136 the man says his eyes will not close because of the girl, even at midnight (படல் ஒல்லா ... என் கண்). The same sign, eyes that cannot close, marks want in the Book of Wealth and longing in the Book of Love; 1136 is a lover's speech, so this is a shared figure and not a shared teaching.

Both verses speak of துப்புரவில்லார், those without means of enjoyment, and of renouncing. 378 says they would renounce if what they are due to suffer passed without afflicting them (உறற்பால ஊட்டா கழியுமெனின்). 1050 states the cost when they do not renounce fully (துவரத் துறவாமை): they are death to salt and gruel. 378 explains why the step 1050 asks for is not taken. Parimelazhagar reads the renouncing in 1050 as giving up the body, Manakkudavar as giving up attachment to goods.

344 says having nothing is natural to the vow of austerity (இயல்பாகும் நோன்பிற்கு ஒன்று இன்மை). 1050 looks at people who already have nothing and says that if they do not complete it by renouncing, they only use up others' salt and gruel. On Manakkudavar's reading, the poor have the outward condition of the renouncer without the inner letting go.

1051 says ask when you find those fit to be asked (இரத்தக்கார்க் காணின்), and if they withhold, the blame is theirs. 1067, in the chapter on the dread of begging, says: if you must beg, do not beg from those who conceal (கரப்பார் இரவன்மின்). The two chapters take opposite attitudes to begging but give the same rule about whom to ask.

1051 uses the imperative இரக்க, ask, and clears the asker of blame (தம்பழி அன்று). 222 says taking is bad even if it is called a good path (நல்லாறு எனினும் கொளல் தீது). They conflict if கொளல் in 222 covers all receiving of gifts, as Parimelazhagar's gloss ஏற்றல் allows; the conflict narrows if 1051 is confined, as he confines it, to extreme need and to rare givers.

224 speaks from the giver's side: being asked is painful (இன்னாது இரக்கப்படுதல்) until one sees the asker's glad face. 1052 speaks from the asker's side: asking is a pleasure if what is asked comes without suffering (துன்பம் உறாஅ வரின்). Each verse makes the pain or pleasure of one party depend on how the exchange goes for the other.

1052 says even asking is pleasure to a person (இன்பம் ஒருவற்கு இரத்தல்) when the thing comes without pain. 1066 says nothing is more degrading to the tongue than asking, even asking water for a cow (நாவிற்கு இரவின் இளிவந்தது இல்). They conflict if 1052 is read as commending asking under good conditions; 1052 speaks of pleasure and 1066 of disgrace, so the conflict depends on taking a disgraceful act as unable to be a pleasant one.

1053 says there is a beauty even in asking while standing before those of unconcealing heart who know what is due (கடனறிவார் முன்நின்று இரப்பும்). 708 says that if one has people who look within and understand, it is enough to stand looking at their face (முகம்நோக்கி நிற்க அமையும்). Parimelazhagar reads 1053 the same way: standing before such people is enough and nothing need be said, which is why the asking keeps some grace.

218 says those whose sight knows what is due (கடனறி காட்சியவர்) do not falter in ஒப்புரவு even when they lack means. 1053 uses the same description, கடனறிவார், for the people before whom asking has a beauty; Manakkudavar glosses them as those who know ஒப்புரவு. The pairing identifies the fit giver of the begging chapter with the person 218 describes.

1054 says asking from those who do not know concealing even in a dream is like giving (இரத்தலும் ஈதலே போலும்). 1061 takes the same givers, who give gladly without concealing and are dear as one's eyes (கரவாது உவந்தீயும் கண்ணன்னார்), and says not asking even of them is worth ten million times more (இரவாமை கோடி உறும்). 1061 limits the praise in 1054: the best case of asking still ranks below not asking.

1055 says askers take up standing before others because people who do not conceal exist in the world (கரப்பிலார் வையகத்து உண்மையால்). 1059 says givers would have no renown if there were none who wished to ask and receive (இரந்துகோள் மேவார் இலாஅக் கடை). The two verses state the dependence in both directions: asking exists because of givers, and givers' standing exists because of askers.

571 says the world exists because the beauty called kindly regard exists (கண்ணோட்டம் ... உண்மையான் உண்டிவ் வுலகு). 1055 uses the same word and construction: asking goes on because the unconcealing exist (உண்மையால்). In both, a practice or the world itself is said to rest on the existence of a disposition in some people.

1056 says that on seeing those free of the affliction of concealing, all the affliction of poverty perishes at once (நிரப்பிடும்பை எல்லாம் ஒருங்கு கெடும்). 1063 says nothing is harder than the hardness of thinking 'we will end the affliction of want by begging' (இன்மை இடும்பை இரந்து தீர்வாம்). They conflict on whether asking can end poverty's distress, if 1056 is read as a general claim; Parimelazhagar removes the conflict by reading 1063 as blaming the choice of begging over effort.

1056 gives the good outcome of asking: meeting those without concealment ends the afflictions of want. 1068 gives the other outcome: the unsafe boat called asking splits when it strikes the rock called concealment (கரவென்னும் பார்தாக்க). Both make the result of asking turn on கரவு in the person asked, so 1068 states the risk that 1056 leaves out.

1057 says the asker's heart rejoices deep within on seeing those who give without scorn or contempt (இகழ்ந்தெள்ளாது ஈவார்). 953 lists a smile, giving, sweet words and not scorning (நகை ஈகை இன்சொல் இகழாமை) as the four marks of a true lineage, and Parimelazhagar applies all four to how the poor are received. 953 gives the giver's qualities and 1057 their effect on the person asking.

228 speaks of the giver's joy, the pleasure of giving and being glad (ஈத்துவக்கும் இன்பம்), which hoarders do not know. 1057 speaks of the asker's joy, the heart glad within (உள்ளுள் உவப்பது), when the giving is free of scorn. The same verb உவ marks gladness on both sides of one act of giving.

Both verses use the wooden puppet (மரப்பாவை) for movement without life. In 1020 it is the movement of those with no shame within; in 1058 it is the coming and going of the whole world if there were no askers (மரப்பாவை சென்றுவந்தற்று). Shame in one verse and the giving that askers make possible in the other are each treated as what makes human activity alive; Parimelazhagar reads 1058 as saying people without anyone to give to are as good as lifeless.

1058 says that without askers the world would be puppets coming and going, which makes askers part of a living world; Manakkudavar draws the conclusion that asking is therefore not to be held low. 1062 says that if one must live even by begging, let the maker of the world wander and perish (பரந்து கெடுக உலகியற்றியான்). They conflict on whether a world that contains begging is as it should be; the conflict depends on reading 1058 as approval and not only as a remark about what givers need.

232 says all that speakers say in praise rests on those who give something to those who ask (இரப்பார்க்கொன்று ஈவார்மேல் நிற்கும் புகழ்). 1059 asks what standing givers would have if there were none who wished to ask and take (ஈவார்கண் என்னுண்டாம் தோற்றம்). 1059 draws the consequence of 232: if renown belongs to giving to askers, then the asker is a condition of the giver's renown.

1060 tells the asker not to be angry at a refusal, since the affliction of his own want is witness enough (நிரப்பிடும்பை தானேயும் சாலும் கரி); Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar take it as witness that means are hard to come by for anyone. 250 says that when going against someone weaker, think of yourself before those stronger (வலியார்முன் தன்னை நினைக்க). Both restrain a person by turning him to his own experience as evidence of the other's position.

1054 says that asking (இரத்தலும்) of those who do not know concealment even in a dream is 'like giving' (ஈதலே போலும்). 1061 takes exactly those givers, who give gladly without hiding (கரவாது உவந்தீயும்), and says that even with them (கண்ணும்) not asking is worth a crore more (இரவாமை கோடி உறும்). The best case that chapter 106 allows is the case 1061 ranks below not asking at all.

1035 says those who eat by the work of their hands (கைசெய்தூண் மாலையவர்) do not beg (இரவார்) and give to askers without concealing (கரவாது ஈவர்). 1061 praises not asking (இரவாமை) even from givers who do not conceal (கரவாது ஈயும்). Read together, the unconcealing giver and the one who does not ask are the same person in 1035, which shows how the higher course of 1061 is actually lived.

1058 says that without askers (இரப்பாரை இல்லாயின்) the wide world would move like a wooden puppet (மரப்பாவை சென்றுவந் தற்று); Parimelazhagar takes this as showing the world needs askers. 1062 says that if living by begging is required (இரந்தும் உயிர்வாழ்தல் வேண்டின்), the maker of the world should himself wander and perish (பரந்து கெடுக உலகியற்றியான்). The conflict holds if 1058 is read as approving a world that contains beggars; 1062 treats such an arrangement as grounds for a curse.

377 says even those who heap up crores can enjoy them only in the way the apportioner has apportioned (வகுத்தான் வகுத்த வகை). 1062 addresses the same figure as the maker of the world (உலகியற்றியான்) and curses him if what he has laid down includes living by begging; Parimelazhagar explains that he assigns each life its livelihood. 377 states the allotment as a fact, and 1062 judges the one who allots.

1056 says that on seeing those free of the affliction of concealment, all the afflictions of want perish together (நிரப்பிடும்பை எல்லாம் ஒருங்கு கெடும்). 1063 says nothing is harder than the hardness of saying 'we will end the affliction of poverty by begging' (இன்மை இடும்பை இரந்து தீர்வாம்). They conflict if 1063 is read, as Manakkudavar reads it, to mean begging does not end poverty; Parimelazhagar instead faults the choice of begging over effort.

616 says effort makes fortune and lack of effort brings want in (முயற்றின்மை இன்மை புகுத்தி விடும்); Parimelazhagar applies it to kings. 1063 calls it hardness (வன்மை) to think poverty's affliction can be ended by begging, and Parimelazhagar explains that the proper path, effort, is being set aside. 1063 applies 616's rule to the poor man and names begging as the wrong substitute for effort.

1063 calls hard the thought that poverty can be ended by begging (இரந்து தீர்வாம்). 1068 gives a picture of why: begging is a boat without safety (ஏமாப்பில் தோணி) that splits when it strikes the rock of concealment (கரவென்னும் பார்). Manakkudavar says 1068 states the cause of poverty not ending, which makes it the reason behind 1063's claim.

988 says poverty is no disgrace to a person if he has the firmness called worth (சால்பென்னும் திண்மை). 1064 says the worth (சால்பு) that will not consent to asking even when there are no means (இடமில்லாக் காலும் இரவொல்லா) is too great for all space to hold. 1064 shows one thing the firmness of 988 consists in: poverty does not disgrace the worthy because they do not turn it into begging.

218 says those who see their duty do not slacken in ஒப்புரவு even in a season without means (இடனில் பருவத்தும்). 1064 says worth does not consent to asking even at a time without means (இடமில்லாக் காலும்). The same test, what a person does when resources are gone, is applied to giving in 218 and to asking in 1064: the good neither stop giving nor start begging.

64 says the gruel (கூழ்) stirred by one's children's small hands is far sweeter than amrita (அமிழ்தினும் ஆற்ற இனிதே). 1065 says nothing is sweeter (இனியது இல்) than eating what one's own effort brought (தாள் தந்தது), though it is gruel thin as clear water (தெண்ணீர் அடுபுற்கை); Parimelazhagar adds that it equals amrita. In both, plain gruel is made sweet by whose hands are behind it, the children's in 64 and one's own labour in 1065.

1033 says only those who plough and eat (உழுதுண்டு) truly live, and all others bow and eat and walk behind (தொழுதுண்டு பின்செல்பவர்). 1065 says nothing is sweeter than eating what one's own effort gave (தாள் தந்தது உண்ணல்), however thin. Both rank food by how it was got: 1033 in terms of standing and dependence, 1065 in terms of taste.

In 1107 the man says the woman's embrace is like living in one's own home and eating one's own food after sharing it (தம்மில் இருந்து தமது பாத்து உண்டற்று); Parimelazhagar glosses 'one's own' as wealth that came by one's own effort. 1065 says nothing is sweeter than eating what one's effort gave. The lover uses as his standard of pleasure the very thing 1065 states as a rule, though his is a speech in the Book of Love and not a teaching.

222 says taking is bad even if it is called a good path (நல்லாறு எனினும் கொளல் தீது). 1066 says that even if one asks for water for a cow (ஆவிற்கு நீரென்று இரப்பினும்), nothing is more degrading to the tongue than asking; Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar both take the cow as a case of asking for the sake of virtue. Both verses deny that a good purpose removes what is wrong with asking or receiving.

656 says that even if one must see one's own mother hungry (ஈன்றாள் பசி காண்பான் ஆயினும்), one should not do what the worthy condemn. 1066 says that even asking water for a cow is degrading to the tongue (நாவிற்கு இளிவந்தது). Each picks the most sympathetic motive available, a hungry mother or a thirsty cow, and holds that it does not excuse the act.

1053 says that even asking, standing before those of unconcealing heart who know their duty, has a certain beauty (இரப்பும் ஓர் ஏஎர் உடைத்து). 1066 says nothing is more degrading to the tongue than asking (இரவின் இளிவந்தது இல்), even for a cow's water. They conflict if 1066 is read as covering every act of asking; on a narrower reading 1053 speaks only of asking from the right giver, which 1066 does not mention.

1051 says to ask if you find those fit to be asked, and if they conceal the blame is theirs and not yours (அவர்பழி தம்பழி அன்று). 1067 has the poet himself beg of all who beg (இரப்பன் இரப்பாரை எல்லாம்) not to ask of those who conceal (கரப்பார் இரவன்மின்). 1051 clears the refused asker of blame; 1067 adds that being blameless is not enough reason to ask a concealer, and Parimelazhagar says it forbids the asking that costs one's honour.

1067 asks beggars not to beg of those who conceal (கரப்பார்). 1077 describes such people from the other side: the base will not even shake a wet hand (ஈர்ங்கை விதிரார்) for anyone but those whose fist would break their jaw. 1077 shows what asking a concealer comes to, and why 1067 pleads against it.

1068 calls asking a boat without safety (ஏமாப்பில் தோணி) that splits on the rock of concealment; the commentators supply poverty as the sea it was meant to cross. In 1164 the woman says the sea of love exists but the safe raft to swim it (ஏமப் புணை) does not. Both use the figure of a sea that must be crossed and a vessel that fails, 1068 as a teaching about begging and 1164 as a lover's complaint.

306 says anger burns even the safe raft called one's own people (இனமென்னும் ஏமப் புணை). 1068 calls asking a boat without safety (ஏமாப்பில் தோணி) that breaks on concealment. The same word for safety (ஏமம், ஏமாப்பு) marks the vessel in both: one's people are the safe one in 306, and asking is named the unsafe one in 1068.

1057 says that on seeing those who give without scorn, the heart rejoices deep within (உள்ளம் உள்ளுள் உவப்பது உடைத்து). 1069 says that at the thought of asking the heart melts (உள்ளம் உருகும்), and at the thought of concealment even what remains is gone (உள்ளதூஉம் இன்றிக் கெடும்). Both follow the heart (உள்ளம்) through the act of asking; 1057 gives its state before a good giver and 1069 its state before a refusal. Parimelazhagar takes the heart in 1069 as the speaker's, while he reports others take it as the asker's.

224 says being asked is unpleasant (இன்னாது இரக்கப் படுதல்) until one sees the asker's glad face. 1069 says the heart melts at the thought of asking. Taken together they say asking is painful on both sides, for the one asked in 224 and for the one who asks or contemplates it in 1069, and that only the gift ends the pain.

230 says nothing is more bitter than dying, yet even dying is sweet when giving is not possible (ஈதல் இயையாக் கடை). 1070 says the asker's life goes at the word of refusal (சொல்லாடப் போஒம் உயிர்) and asks where the concealer's life hides (யாங்கொளிக்கும் கொல்லோ). 230 gives the giver's view that life without giving is not worth keeping; 1070 puts that standard to the one who can give and refuses, and wonders that his life stays.

223 says not uttering the misery of 'I have nothing' (இலனென்னும் எவ்வம் உரையாமை), and giving, are found in one of good family; Pope takes the words as the giver's excuse, while Parimelazhagar first takes them as the asker's plea. 1070 says the asker's life leaves when the word is spoken (சொல்லாட); Parimelazhagar takes this as the concealer saying 'no'. On Pope's reading of 223 both verses are about the word of refusal, which the well-born never say and which 1070 says kills the hearer.

993 says likeness of limbs is not likeness among people (உறுப்பொத்தல் மக்களொப்பு அன்று), and that fitting likeness is likeness of character (பண்பொத்தல்). 1071 says the base are just like people (மக்களே போல்வர்) and that no such resemblance has been seen elsewhere. 993 gives the rule and 1071 the case: Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar both explain that the base match people in form and not in qualities.

600 says those without inner drive are trees, and their being human in form is the only difference (மரம் மக்களாதலே வேறு). 1071 says the base resemble people exactly (மக்களே போல்வர்). Both treat the human shape as something that can be present without what makes a person, lacking drive in 600 and lacking character in 1071.

201 says those given to evil deeds do not fear, and the excellent do fear, the intoxication called evil deed (தீவினையார் அஞ்சார் விழுமியார் அஞ்சுவர்). 1072 says the base are more fortunate than those who know what is good, because they have no distress in the heart (நெஞ்சத்து அவலம் இலர்). 1072 puts 201's fact in mock praise: Parimelazhagar says the verse scorns by implication, and that the point is their not fearing blame.

839 says the friendship of fools is very sweet (பெரிதினிது), because parting from it gives no pain. 1072 says the base are fortunate (திருவுடையர்), because their hearts have no distress. Both verses praise a bad thing for the absence of a pain that only something of value would cause.

1073 says the base are like the gods because they too act as they please (மேவன செய்தொழுகலான்). 1075 says that where the base show proper conduct (ஆசாரம்) it is fear, and beyond that a little if there is something they desire. 1075 marks the limit on 1073's freedom: their doing as they please stops only at fear or gain; Parimelazhagar says doing what they like is their nature and conduct is not.

1072 calls the base fortunate (திருவுடையர்) for having no distress of heart, and 1073 calls them like the gods (தேவர் அனையர்) for doing as they please. Both give praise that is meant as blame; Parimelazhagar says so of each. The two together describe one condition, no inner check in 1072 and no outer one in 1073.

978 says greatness always bows and smallness adorns itself in admiration of itself (சிறுமை அணியுமாம் தன்னை வியந்து). 1074 says the base man, on seeing those worse than himself, outdoes them and swaggers (மிகப்பட்டுச் செம்மாக்கும்); this follows Parimelazhagar's reading of அகப்பட்டி as those of looser conduct, while Manakkudavar reads the word quite differently. On Parimelazhagar's reading 1074 shows where the self-admiration of 978 finds its material: in comparison with someone lower.

1016 says the high do not care for the wide world unless they have shame as their fence (நாண்வேலி). 1075 says the conduct of the base is fear (அச்சமே கீழ்களது ஆசாரம்), which Parimelazhagar takes as fear of harm from the king. Each verse names what keeps a kind of person within bounds: shame from inside for the high, fear from outside for the base.

201 says those given to evil deeds do not fear (தீவினையார் அஞ்சார்) the intoxication of evil deed. 1075 says fear is the whole of the base man's good conduct (அச்சமே). The two are consistent once the object of fear is separated: 201 means fear of the evil deed itself, and 1075, on Parimelazhagar's reading, fear of punishment.

1075 says the base behave properly out of fear. 1078 says the base, like sugar-cane, are of use only when crushed (கொல்லப் பயன்படும் கீழ்). 1078 applies the rule of 1075 to giving: what fear does for their conduct, force does for their generosity.

1076 says the base are like a beaten drum (அறைபறை அன்னர்) because they carry a secret they heard (கேட்ட மறை) to others. In 1180 the woman says the town easily gets the secret (மறை) in the heart of those like her whose eyes are beaten drums (அறைபறை கண்ணார்). The same pair of words, drum and secret, is used for a fault of character in 1076 and for a lover's eyes that give her away against her will in 1180.

221 says giving to those who have nothing is what giving is (வறியார்க்கொன்று ஈவதே ஈகை), and all other giving has the nature of a loan to be returned. 1077 says the base will not even shake a wet hand (ஈர்ங்கை விதிரார்) except for those whose bent fist would break their jaw; Parimelazhagar sums up that they give nothing to the weak and everything to those who hurt them. The base man's giving in 1077 is the reverse of 221's definition: it goes only to the strong.

1077 says the base give only to those who would break their jaw. 1078 states the same with a contrast and a figure: the worthy are of use at a word (சொல்லப் பயன்படுவர்), and the base, like sugar-cane, when crushed (கொல்லப் பயன்படும்). Parimelazhagar treats the two verses as a pair on how the base give.

1078 says the worthy are of use as soon as they are told (சொல்லப் பயன்படுவர் சான்றோர்). 223 says not uttering the misery of 'I have nothing', and giving, belong to one of good family; Parimelazhagar records a second reading on which the giver gives before the asker has to say it. On that reading 223 goes one step beyond 1078: the worthy of 1078 give at a word, and the well-born of 223 give before the word.

216 says wealth with a person of நயன் is like a fruit-bearing tree ripening in the middle of the town (பயன்மரம் உள்ளூர்ப் பழுத்தற்று). 1078 says the base are like sugar-cane (கரும்புபோல்), of use only when crushed. Both use a plant's yield (பயன்) as the figure for how a person's wealth reaches others: the tree offers its fruit in the open, and the cane gives nothing until it is pressed.

166 says the kin of one who envies a gift will perish with nothing to wear or eat (உடுப்பதூஉம் உண்பதூஉம் இன்றிக் கெடும்). 1079 says the base man, on seeing others clothed and fed (உடுப்பதூஉம் உண்பதூஉம் காணின்), is able to find a fault in them. The same phrase for clothing and food names what the envious man cannot bear to see in 1079 and what envy costs his own house in 166.

980 says greatness hides another's weak point and smallness only tells faults (சிறுமைதான் குற்றமே கூறிவிடும்). 1079 says the base man is able to see a blemish in others (பிறர்மேல் வடுக்காண வற்றாகும்) when he sees them clothed and fed. 1079 adds the motive that 980 leaves out: Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar both take it as envy of others' prosperity, and Parimelazhagar adds that the fault may be invented.

220 says that if ruin comes through ஒப்புரவு, that ruin is worth buying even by selling oneself (விற்றுக்கோள் தக்கது). 1080 says the base are fit only to sell themselves quickly (விற்றற்கு உரியர் விரைந்து) when something befalls them. Selling oneself appears in both: as the price a good person would pay to keep helping others in 220, and as the base man's first move to get out of trouble in 1080.

969 says those like the yak that will not live once its hair is lost give up life when honour is at stake (உயிர்நீப்பர் மானம் வரின்). 1080 says the base, when something befalls them (ஒன்று உற்றக்கால்), hurry to sell themselves. The two verses give opposite answers to the same moment of pressure: the honourable give up life to keep themselves, and the base give up themselves to keep life.

In 1081 the man cannot decide whether she is an அணங்கு, a choice peahen or a woman, and his heart reels (மாலும் என் நெஞ்சு). 918 says the embrace of deceiving women (மாய மகளிர் முயக்கு) is called an அணங்கு for those without discerning sense. The same word names a spirit that overpowers a man in both books: here it is a lover's wonder, there a warning, and Parimelazhagar glosses it in 918 as a divine woman who takes life through desire.

1081 only asks whether she is an அணங்கு. In 1082, once she returns his look (நோக்கெதிர் நோக்குதல்), he says it is like an attacking அணங்கு (தாக்கணங்கு) who has also brought an army. The doubt of the first verse becomes a felt assault in the second, and Parimelazhagar reads 1082 as spoken after he has settled that she is human.

In 1081 his heart reels (மாலும் நெஞ்சு) because it cannot place her among goddess, peahen and woman. In 1112 he scolds the same heart for being confused at flowers (மலர்காணின் மையாத்தி நெஞ்சே), as if her eyes were like what many can see. The confusion moves from what she is to what could be compared with her, and by 1112 he treats it as the heart's error.

1082 says her returning look is like an attacking spirit come with an army (தாக்கணங்கு தானைக்கொண் டன்னது): the look only wounds. 1091 finds two looks in her eyes (இருநோக்கு), one that gives the sickness and one that is its medicine (நோய்நோக்கு ... அந்நோய் மருந்து). The next chapter adds the healing side that 1082 leaves out.

In 775 a warrior whose glaring eye (விழித்த கண்) blinks when a spear is thrown counts that as running away. In 1082 the man looks, and her look answering his (நோக்கெதிர் நோக்குதல்) is like an army brought against him. Both treat meeting another's gaze as combat, one on the battlefield and one at first sight in love.

1082 makes her answering glance an armed host (தானை). 1113, listing her beauties, calls her kohl-lined eyes spears (வேலுண்கண்). The eye as weapon is a fixed figure of the man's praise, used first as his alarm and later as a plain item of description.

765 defines an army as the force that can stand together even if Death comes raging at it (கூற்றுடன்று மேல்வரினும்). In 1083 the man says he now knows what is called Death (கூற்று): it has womanly grace and large warring eyes (பேரமர்க் கட்டு). Both set கூற்று in a battle; the Book of Wealth imagines standing against it, and the lover says he has met it in her eyes.

1083: 'I did not know before (பண்டறியேன்) what Death is; now I know'. 1226: the woman did not know (அறிந்ததிலேன்), while her husband had not left, that evening brings sickness. In both a lover says love has taught what was only a word before, the man at first sight and the woman in separation.

326 says Death that eats life (உயிருண்ணுங் கூற்று) does not advance on the days of one who lives by not killing. 1084 says the eyes of this womanly, artless girl have a look that eats the life of those who see them (கண்டார் உயிருண்ணும் தோற்றம்). The lover gives her eyes the standing epithet of Death, which the previous verse (1083) has just named.

279: the arrow is straight but cruel, the lute bent but sweet, so judge by what a thing does (வினைபடு பாலால் கொளல்). 1084 sets a girl of womanly gentleness (பெண்டகைப் பேதை) against eyes that look as if they eat lives; Parimelazhagar takes அமர்த்தன as 'were at odds' with her nature. Both verses turn on a form that does not match its effect, one as a rule for judging ascetics and one as a lover's surprise.

1084: her eyes have a look that eats the life of those who see them (உயிருண்ணும்). 1221: the woman tells evening it is not evening but a time that eats the life of those once wed (மணந்தார் உயிருண்ணும் வேலை). The same phrase marks what kills each lover: for the man her eyes at first sight, for the woman the evening hour in his absence.

1085 asks whether her look is Death, an eye or a doe, and says it has all three (இம்மூன்றும் உடைத்து); Parimelazhagar comments that it gives pleasure and pain together. 1091 states that plainly as two looks, one the sickness and one its cure. The puzzled question of 1085 is resolved into a doubleness he can name.

In 1085 the doe (பிணை) is one of three things her look might be, beside Death. In 1089 her doe-like artless look (பிணையேர் மடநோக்கு) and her modesty are ornament enough, so added jewels are pointless. The same doe glance is first one part of a threat and then her natural adornment.

1086 wishes her brows would screen her eyes (மறைப்பின்), for then the eyes would not cause him trembling pain. 1087 says the cloth over her breasts is like the face-cloth over a rutting elephant's eyes (கட்படாம்). Both are about a covering over something that harms him: one he wishes for and one he sees, and Parimelazhagar says of the second that the cloth keeps them from killing.

In 1086 the man says her eyes cause him trembling pain (நடுங்கஞர்) and wishes them screened. In 1171 the woman asks why her own eyes weep, since they showed him to her and so gave her this unending sickness (தண்டாநோய் தாம்காட்ட). Each lover names eyes as the cause of the pain; for him it is hers, for her it is her own.

1087: the cloth over her firm breasts is the face-cloth on a rutting bull elephant (கடாஅக் களிற்றின்மேற் கட்படாம்). 24: the renouncer guards the five senses with the goad of firmness (உரனென்னும் தோட்டியான்), a goad being the elephant-driver's tool. Both draw on the dangerous elephant held in check; the ascetic chapter makes the senses the elephant, and the lover makes her covered breasts the elephant.

1088: his might (பீடு), feared even by enemies in battle, has broken (உடைந்ததே) before her bright forehead alone. 1258: the woman says the soft words of that deceiving thief are the weapon that breaks her womanly firmness (பெண்மை உடைக்கும் படை). Each lover uses the language of war and breaking for the loss of the quality they prized in themselves, his strength and her restraint.

1088 reports the first loss: his battlefield strength breaks at the sight of her forehead. 1134 says the fierce flood of love carries off the raft of shame and good manliness (நாணொடு நல்லாண்மை என்னும் புணை). The later verse generalises what 1088 exclaims, with manliness now lost along with shame.

906, in the chapter on being ruled by one's wife, says men who fear her bamboo-like shoulders (அமையார்தோள் அஞ்சுபவர்) have no worth even if they live like gods. In 1088 a lover says his might, feared in battle, has broken before her bright forehead. The same pattern, a man's standing undone by a woman's bodily feature, is a censure in the Book of Wealth and a lover's amazed complaint in the Book of Love, where it is his speech and not a ruling.

95: humility and sweet speech are a person's ornament and nothing else is (அணியல்ல மற்றுப் பிற). 1089: what use are foreign ornaments (ஏதில தந்து அணி) to one who has a doe's artless look and modesty? Both deny that added adornment counts beside an inborn quality, 95 as a rule of conduct and 1089 as a lover's praise.

1014: is not having shame an ornament to the worthy (அணியன்றோ நாணுடைமை)? 1089 counts her modesty (நாண்) with her doe-like look as adornment enough. Both call நாண் an ornament; the nearby 1011 separates the shame of bright-browed women from shame at wrong actions, so the two verses praise different kinds of நாண் with the same figure.

1085 asks whether her look is Death, an eye or a doe (பிணை). 1089 names the doe-like artless look (பிணையேர் மடநோக்கு) as her natural ornament. The chapter's doe glance appears once beside Death and once as beauty that needs nothing added.

1090: brewed liquor (அடுநறா) delights only those who drink it, not, like love, those who merely see (கண்டார் மகிழ்செய்தல் இன்று). 1281: to be elated at a thought and glad at a sight (காண மகிழ்தல்) belongs to love and not to liquor. The same contrast is made twice, at the first meeting and again by the woman late in the book, where thinking is added to seeing.

1090 puts love above liquor because it delights by sight alone. 1201 says love is sweeter than liquor (கள்ளினும் காமம் இனிது) because even thinking of it (உள்ளினும்) gives great joy that does not end. The comparison is extended from the lover who sees to the lover who is apart and only remembers.

1090 uses liquor as the lesser pleasure that love outdoes. 1288 uses it as an exact likeness: 'your chest is to us as liquor is to those who are drunk on it (களித்தார்க்குக் கள்ளற்றே), though it does shaming harm (இளித்தக்க இன்னா)'. The later verse grants what 1090 leaves unsaid, that the pull likened to drink goes on despite disgrace.

27 lists the five, taste, light, touch, sound and smell (சுவை ஒளி ஊறு ஓசை நாற்றம்), and says the world lies with the one who discerns their kinds. 1101 lists seeing, hearing, tasting, smelling and touching (கண்டு கேட்டு உண்டு உயிர்த்து உற்று) and says all five are found in this bright-bangled woman alone (ஒண்தொடி கண்ணே உள). The same inventory of the senses is used in the renouncers' chapter for mastery of them and by the lover for their complete enjoyment in one person.

65: touching one's children is joy to the body and hearing their words is joy to the ear. 1101: the objects of all five senses are in her. Both describe a loved person sense by sense; the householder's verse names two senses and children, the lover's names all five and one woman.

1091: her eyes hold two looks, one the sickness and the other its medicine (நோய்நோக்கு ... அந்நோய் மருந்து). 1102: for other diseases the medicine is something else (பிணிக்கு மருந்து பிற), but she is herself the medicine for the sickness she causes (தன்நோய்க்குத் தானே மருந்து). The idea moves from her glance to her person, and from signs before union to union itself.

15: it is rain that ruins, and rain again that stands by the ruined and lifts them up (கெடுப்பதூஉம் ... எடுப்பதூஉம் எல்லாம் மழை). 1102: she is the cure for the sickness she herself gives. Both locate harm and remedy in one source, rain for the world and the beloved for the lover.

948 tells the healer to examine the disease, then its root (நோய்முதல்), then the means that subdue it (அது தணிக்கும் வாய்), as three separate things. 1102 first grants the ordinary rule, that the medicine is other than the disease, and then says love is the exception, where cause and remedy are the same person. The lover's verse marks love's sickness as a case the method of 948 does not cover.

1103: is the world of the lotus-eyed one (தாமரைக் கண்ணான் உலகு) sweeter than sleep on the soft shoulders of the one you love? 1323: is there a land of the gods (புத்தேள் நாடு) to compare with sulking with one joined to you like water with earth? Both use the same rhetorical question to set a lover's pleasure above heaven, the first for sleep in her arms and the second for the quarrel.

213 says that in the world of the gods or here (புத்தேளுலகத்தும் ஈண்டும்) it is hard to find another good like ஒப்புரவு, doing one's part for others. 1103 asks whether the lotus-eyed one's world is as sweet as sleeping on the beloved's shoulders. Both measure an earthly thing against heaven and prefer it; in the Book of Virtue it is a duty, and here it is a lover's own claim about his pleasure.

1104: the man asks where she got this fire that burns when he moves away and is cool when he comes near (நீங்கின் தெறூஉம் குறுகுங்கால் தண்ணென்னும் தீ). 1159: fire burns only if touched; can it burn when one lets go, as love's sickness does (விடிற்சுடல் ஆற்றுமோ தீ)? The same reversed fire is described from both sides, by the man after union and in the chapter on being unable to bear parting.

691: those who serve quarrelsome kings should be like people warming at a fire, neither moving off nor coming close (அகலாது அணுகாது தீக்காய்வார் போல்க). 1104: her fire burns at a distance and cools up close. Both reason about fire and distance; the king's fire follows the ordinary rule and calls for a middle distance, while the lover says hers reverses it, so only nearness is safe.

265: austerity is practised here because whatever is wanted is obtained as it is wanted (வேண்டிய வேண்டியாங்கு எய்தலால்). 1105: her shoulders are like each desired thing at the moment of desiring it (வேட்ட பொழுதின் அவையவை போலுமே). Both describe desire met exactly as it arises, promised to the ascetic through தவம் and claimed by the lover in her embrace.

1101 says the objects of all five senses are found in her alone. 1105 says her shoulders are like whatever one craves, at the time one craves it. The first claim is about range, that she holds every kind of pleasure; the second adds timing, that she answers each wish as it comes.

78: a life with no love inside is like a dried-up tree putting out shoots on hard ground (வற்றல் மரந்தளிர்த் தற்று), which cannot happen. 1106: each time he reaches her, her touch makes his life put out shoots (உயிர்தளிர்ப்பத் தீண்டலால்), so her shoulders must be made of ambrosia. Both speak of a life sprouting like a plant; without love it cannot, and in the lover's verse it does at every embrace.

1106: his life sprouts afresh whenever he touches her. 1124: she is to his life what living is when they are together, and what dying is when she leaves (வாழ்தல் உயிர்க்கன்னள் ... சாதல் அதற்கன்னள்). Both tie his உயிர் to her presence; 1124 states the other half, which 1106's 'each time' (உறுதோறு) implies.

64: gruel stirred by the small hands of one's own children is far sweeter than ambrosia (அமிழ்தினும் ஆற்ற இனிதே). 1106: her shoulders are made of ambrosia (அமிழ்தின் இயன்றன) because their touch revives his life. Parent and lover both reach for அமிழ்து to measure the nearness of someone of their own; the parent ranks the child's gruel above it and the lover equates her with it.

1065: though it is gruel thin as clear water, nothing is sweeter than eating what one's own effort gave (தாள்தந்தது உண்ணலின் ஊங்கினியது இல்). 1107 takes that pleasure as its standard: her embrace is like living in one's own house and eating one's own after sharing (தம்மில் இருந்து தமது பாத்து உண்டற்று). The lover's simile assumes what 1065 states, that one's own food is the sweetest.

44: if a household fears blame and shares its food (பாத்தூண்), its line never fails. 1107 uses the same shared meal (பாத்து உண்டு) as the likeness for the joy of embracing her. What the Book of Virtue commends as duty with a reward, the lover treats as a known pleasure; Parimelazhagar reads the verse as his answer to her friend, who urges marriage and the householder's life.

229: eating alone to fill one's own store (தாமே தமியர் உணல்) is more bitter than begging. 1107: eating one's own after sharing it, in one's own house, is the model of sweetness, and the embrace is like it. Read together they give both halves of one judgement on eating: bitter when hoarded, sweet when shared.

1108: sweet to two who desire each other is an embrace that air cannot cut through (வளியிடை போழப் படாஅ முயக்கு). 1239: when a cool breeze did cut into their embrace (முயக்கிடைத் தண்வளி போழ), her large eyes turned pale. The same words describe the ideal and its smallest breach, and the later verse shows the cost of what 1108 rules out.

1108 praises the embrace with no gap. In 1187 the woman says she lay embracing, shifted a little (புடைபெயர்ந்தேன்), and at once pallor was on her thick enough to scoop up. The woman's verse gives a reason from her side why the unbroken embrace is the sweet one: the least separation brings the pallor of parting.

1108 specifies 'two who desire' (வீழும் இருவர்க்கு இனிதே): the close embrace is sweet to both. 1196: love on one side only is painful, and like a carrying pole it is sweet on both ends (இருதலையானும் இனிது). Both make sweetness depend on the love being mutual, 1108 in fulfilment and 1196 from the woman who lacks it.

1109: sulking, understanding and union (ஊடல் உணர்தல் புணர்தல்) are the gains of those who have come together in love. 1330, the last verse of the book: sulking is love's pleasure, and its pleasure is to join and embrace (கூடி முயங்கப் பெறின்). The early verse lists the cycle and the closing verse restates it as the nature of love's joy, so the book's final chapters develop what 1109 names in one line.

1109 names quarrel, making up and union together as rewards without ranking them. 1326 ranks them: as digesting is sweeter than eating, sulking is sweeter than union (புணர்தலின் ஊடல் இனிது). The later verse takes one item from 1109's list and gives it first place.

1109 counts sulking (ஊடல்) among the fruits of love. 1302 says sulking is like salt in the right amount, and letting it run a little long is like a little too much salt (சிறிது மிக்கற்றால் நீள விடல்). The later verse sets a limit on the first item of 1109's list: it is a gain only in measure.

783: the more one studies a book the more its worth shows (நவில்தொறும் நூல்நயம்), and so it is with the bond of people of character the more one keeps their company (பயில்தொறும்). 1110: as each act of knowing shows one's ignorance (அறிதோறு அறியாமை கண்டற்று), so is love with each closeness to her (செறிதோறும்). Both use learning, with the same -தொறும் construction, to say that a bond deepens with practice, one for friendship and one for desire.

1145: as drinking is wanted more each time one gets drunk (களித்தொறும் கள்ளுண்டல் வேட்டற்று), love is sweeter each time it is exposed. 1110: love is like finding one's ignorance each time one learns, each time he is close to her. Both say love grows by repetition and does not wear out; 1110 takes its likeness from knowledge and 1145 from drink, and they differ in what is repeated, union or exposure by gossip.

940: as a gambler loves the game more with each loss (இழத்தொறூஉம்), life loves itself more with each suffering (உழத்தொறூஉம்). 1110: each closeness shows love to be more than he knew, as each learning shows ignorance. Both describe an attachment that grows through its own repetition; the gambling chapter gives it as a warning and the lover as a delight.

In 90 the anicham is the measure of fragility: it wilts when merely smelled (மோப்பக் குழையும்), and a guest wilts at a changed face. In 1111 the man grants the flower that same good nature (நன்னீரை) and then says the woman he loves is softer still (நின்னினும் மென்னீரள்). The book's standard of delicacy in the ethics of hospitality becomes the thing a lover's praise has to exceed.

1111 says she is more delicate than the anicham (நின்னினும் மென்னீரள்); 1289 says love itself is more delicate than a flower (மலரினும் மெல்லிது காமம்) and few catch its right moment. The same comparative, softer than a flower, is applied first to the beloved's body and later to the experience of love.

In 1112 the man scolds his heart for being confused by flowers, as if her eyes were like blossoms that many can see (பலர்காணும் பூ); Parimelazhagar takes the point to be that her eyes are seen by him alone. 1119 turns the same phrase on the moon: to match her face it must not appear for many to see (பலர்காணத் தோன்றல்). Both rest on one criterion: what is open to everyone's gaze cannot equal what is his alone.

1113 lists her features as metaphors: body a tender shoot (முறி), teeth pearls, and kohl-lined eyes that are spears (வேலுண்கண்). 1084 had already noticed the mismatch this list contains: her eyes, with a look that eats the life of those who see them, are at war (அமர்த்தன) with her gentle womanly nature. Read together, the spear in the inventory of soft things is the same contradiction 1084 names outright.

1113 praises her as bamboo-shouldered (வேய்த்தோளவட்கு). 906, in the chapter on men ruled by their wives, says those who fear the wife's bamboo-like shoulders (அமையார்தோள் அஞ்சுபவர்) have no standing even if they live like the gods. The same stock epithet of beauty is admired in the Book of Love and named in the Book of Wealth as the thing an unmanned husband fears.

In 1094 the woman, when he looks at her, looks at the ground (நிலன்நோக்கும்). In 1114 the blue lilies, if they could see her, would bow and look at the ground (கவிழ்ந்து நிலன்நோக்கும்), admitting they cannot match her eyes. The flowers are given her own gesture of shyness, here as shame at being outdone.

1114 imagines lilies hanging their heads because they cannot equal her eyes (கண்ணொவ்வேம்). In 1231, during separation, the friend tells her that her eyes are now ashamed before fragrant flowers (நறுமலர் நாணின கண்); Parimelazhagar explains that weeping has dimmed them. The shame has changed sides: the superiority claimed in praise lasts only while the lovers are together.

475 warns that even a cart loaded with peacock feathers breaks its axle if the load is piled too high (அச்சிறும்). 1115 says she has worn anicham flowers without removing the stalks (கால்களையாள்), so no good drums will sound for her waist; Parimelazhagar explains that the waist will break under the weight and get the funeral drum. Both make the lightest possible load the breaking one, as counsel on overreach in 475 and as playful hyperbole about her slenderness in 1115.

1111 says she is more delicate than the anicham. 1115 pushes the claim to a comic limit: the unremoved stalks of that same flower (அனிச்சப்பூக் கால்களையாள்) are too heavy for her waist. The flower that was the standard of softness becomes a burden.

In 1081 the man, at first sight, cannot tell whether she is a goddess, a peahen or a woman, and his heart reels (மாலும் என் நெஞ்சு). In 1116 the confusion is moved to the sky: the stars cannot tell the moon from her face (அறியா) and wander from their places (பதியின் கலங்கிய). The lover's own bewilderment about what she is becomes, in the praise chapter, a bewilderment he attributes to the stars.

1116 says the stars cannot distinguish the moon from her face. 1117 immediately denies that the two are alike: the moon fills out from loss and has a spot, and her face has none (மறுவுண்டோ). Parimelazhagar reads 1117 as mocking the stars for missing an obvious difference, so the second verse withdraws the equality the first seemed to grant.

957 says a fault in the well-born shows up high and clear like the spot on the moon in the sky (மதிக்கண் மறுப்போல்). 1117 asks whether her face has any spot as the bright moon has (மறுவுண்டோ மாதர் முகத்து). The moon's mark is the book's figure for the one visible flaw in something eminent, and the lover uses it to claim she has no such flaw.

782 uses the moon's phases for friendship: with the wise it fills like the crescent, with fools it shrinks like the moon after full. 1117 mentions the same cycle, a moon that shines only after filling its lost parts (அறுவாய் நிறைந்த), as a defect that her face does not share. The waxing that is a hopeful figure in 782 counts in 1117 as evidence of the moon's inconstancy.

Both verses address the moon with வாழி மதி. In 1118 the man tells it that it could have his love if it could shine like her face; Parimelazhagar hears the blessing as mockery. In 1210 the woman, left behind, asks it not to set so that her eyes may find the man who has gone without leaving her heart. The moon is a rival to be dismissed in the time of union and a helper to be begged in separation.

In 1119 the man tells the moon that to resemble her face it must not appear for many to see (பலர்காணத் தோன்றல்). In 1311 the woman refuses the man's chest because all women feast on him in common with their eyes (கண்ணின் பொதுஉண்பர்). Each lover applies the same standard from the other side: what is shared with every onlooker is no longer one's own.

1111 opens the chapter by ranking her above the anicham in softness. 1120 closes it by making the anicham and swan's down hurt her feet like the nerunji fruit, a thorn (மாதர் அடிக்கு நெருஞ்சிப் பழம்). The flower moves from being less soft than she is to being painful to her. Parimelazhagar sets the verse in a refusal to take her on a desert elopement.

64 says the gruel one's children have stirred with their small hands is far sweeter than amrita (அமிழ்தினும் ஆற்ற இனிது). 1121 says the moisture at her white teeth is like milk mixed with honey (பாலொடு தேன்கலந் தற்று). In both, affection makes something bodily and ordinary taste better than the finest food, for a parent in one verse and a lover in the other.

1121 calls her பணிமொழி, the woman of soft, low speech, in a verse about the sweetness of her kiss. In 1258 the woman uses the same word for his speech: the soft words (பணிமொழி) of that thief of many deceits are the weapon that breaks her womanly reserve. The quality he savours in her is the one she names in him as a weapon.

Both verses use the phrase உடம்பொடு உயிரிடை நட்பு, the friendship between body and life. In 1122 the man offers it as the model of closeness for his bond with her. In 338, in the chapter on impermanence, that same friendship is like a bird flying off and leaving its shell (குடம்பை) behind. Read with 338, the lover's comparison describes a bond that is intimate and also certain to end, which fits Parimelazhagar's heading for 1122 as spoken in fear of parting.

73 says the tie of the precious life to the body (என்போடு இயைந்த தொடர்பு) is itself said to be the way of being joined with love. 1122 says the tie between the man and the woman is what the tie of body and life is. One verse explains embodiment by love and the other explains a love by embodiment, so the two comparisons run in opposite directions and support each other.

In 1122 the man claims they are as body and life. In 1209 the woman says her life is ending as she thinks about the lack of kindness in the one who used to say 'we are not separate' (வேறல்லம் என்பார்). Her line remembers a claim of exactly this kind and sets it against his absence; these are speeches in a drama, so this is her complaint in the moment, not a refutation.

In 1123 the man orders the image in the pupil of his eye (கருமணியிற் பாவாய்) to leave, since otherwise there is no room for the woman he loves. In 1126 the woman says her lover never leaves her eyes (கண்ணுள்ளின் போகார்) and is too subtle to be hurt when she blinks. Both lovers place the other inside the eye; he has to make room for her, and she has him there already.

1122 says their bond is like that of body and life. 1124 draws the consequence: together she is to his life what living is (வாழ்தல்), and when she leaves she is what dying is (சாதல்). The comparison in 1122 becomes a statement of what separation will mean.

In 1124 the man says her leaving is death to his life (சாதல் அதற்கன்னள் நீங்கும் இடத்து). In 1151 the reply to his announced journey is that news of his quick return should be told to those who will be alive then (வாழ்வார்க் குரை); Parimelazhagar gives the line to her friend, Manakkudavar to the woman. Each side says that separation is not survivable, he at a brief parting after a meeting and her side when he leaves on a long journey.

In 1125 the man says he would recall her qualities if he forgot them, but he does not know forgetting (மறப்பறியேன்). In 1207 the woman uses the same word, மறப்பறியேன், and asks what would become of her if she did forget, since even remembering burns her heart. Both deny that forgetting is possible; his version is a neat reply to her friend, and hers records what unbroken memory costs.

In 1125 the man avoids saying 'I remembered her', because remembering implies having forgotten (உள்ளுவன் மன்யான் மறப்பின்). In 1316 he says exactly that, 'I thought of you' (உள்ளினேன் என்றேன்), and she asks 'why did you forget?' (என்மறந்தீர்) and sulks. The later scene plays out the trap that the reply in 1125 was built to avoid.

In 1126 she says her lover does not leave her eyes and is not hurt even if she blinks (இமைப்பின் பருவரார்), because he is so subtle. In 1129 she will not blink, knowing he would be hidden (இமைப்பின் கரப்பாக்கு அறிவல்). The same conceit is used both ways within one chapter: blinking is harmless in the first verse and a risk in the second, which shows these are playful defences of him and not one consistent picture.

1126 says he never leaves her eyes though the town thinks him gone. 1218 says that when she sleeps he is on her shoulder and when she wakes he hurries into her heart (நெஞ்சத்தர் ஆவர் விரைந்து). Parimelazhagar frames both as her defence of him against the charge of absence: she answers by locating him somewhere inside herself at every moment.

Both verses turn on the moment of lining the eye with kohl. In 1127 she does not line her eyes at all (கண்ணும் எழுதேம்), because for that moment the lover who lives in them would be hidden. In 1285 the eye cannot see the stick while it is being lined (எழுதுங்கால் கோல்காணாக் கண்), and likewise she cannot see her husband's fault when she sees him. The same small blindness is something to avoid in one verse and the figure for love's blindness in the other.

1128 says that since her lover is in her heart (நெஞ்சத்தார் காதலவராக) she fears eating anything hot, knowing it would burn him. 1249 uses almost the same opening, உள்ளத்தார் காதலவராக, to ask her heart whom it goes out looking for when he is within it. The playful premise of 1128, said to defend him, is used in 1249 to rebuke her own restless heart.

In 1128 his presence in her heart is something she protects, to the point of avoiding hot food. In 1205 the same presence is a complaint: he keeps her out of his own heart and yet is not ashamed to come into hers without pause (எம்நெஞ்சத்து ஓவா வரல்). The later verse adds what 1128 leaves out, the question whether the dwelling is mutual.

In 1129 she does not blink for fear of losing sight of him, and for this the town calls him a stranger without love (ஏதிலர் என்னும் இவ் வூர்). In 1220 the people of the town say he has left her in waking life, and she asks whether they do not see him in dreams (கனவினால் காணார்கொல்). In both she sets the town's outward evidence against her inner experience of his presence, first in the eye and then in the dream.

1129 and 1130 end with the same line, ஏதிலர் என்னும் இவ் வூர். 1129 gives the town's ground for blame, her sleeplessness, which she explains as refusing to blink. 1130 states her answer directly: he lives gladly in her heart always (உவந்துறைவர் உள்ளத்துள் என்றும்), while the town says he lives apart.

In 1130 she is sure that he lives in her heart, and gladly (உவந்துறைவர்), against the town's talk. In 1204 she affirms the same thing, that he is always in her heart (எந்நெஞ்சத்து ஓஒ உளரே அவர்), and then asks whether she too has a place in his (யாமும் உளேங்கொல் அவர்நெஞ்சத்து). The confidence she shows the town in 1130 does not answer the doubt she admits in 1204: his presence in her heart says nothing about her place in his.

1131 has the man say that for those worn down by love there is no strength that is a safeguard (ஏமம்) except the palmyra horse (மடலல்லது இல்லை வலி). In 1164 the woman says the sea of love exists but the safe raft to swim it does not (ஏமப் புணைமன்னும் இல்). The one ஏமம் he names is a man's recourse; her verse shows a sufferer for whom even that is missing.

1131 calls the palmyra horse the only safeguard for those who suffer in love. 1137 praises womanhood that suffers a sea of desire (கடலன்ன காமம் உழந்தும்) and still does not mount it (மடலேறா). The same verb உழந்து marks the same suffering, so 1137 limits 1131: the remedy is one a woman forgoes, and forgoing it is counted as worth.

In 1132 the body and life that cannot bear it (நோனா உடம்பும் உயிரும்) will mount the palmyra horse, setting shame aside (நாணினை நீக்கி நிறுத்து). In 1163 love and shame hang balanced, with life as the carrying pole, inside 'my body that cannot bear' (நோனா உடம்பின் அகத்து). The same three terms, unbearing body, life and shame, appear in both: he ends the strain by dropping shame, she goes on carrying both loads.

In 1247 the woman tells her heart to give up either desire or shame, since she cannot bear the two together (காமம் விடு ஒன்றோ நாண்விடு). 1132 is that choice made: the man keeps desire and puts shame aside (நாணினை நீக்கி) to ride the palmyra horse. Read together, 1247 states the dilemma and 1132 shows one way out of it.

1017 says those ruled by shame give up life for shame and do not give up shame for life's sake (உயிர்ப்பொருட்டால் நாண்துறவார்). In 1132 the man's body and life, unable to endure, put shame aside (நாணினை நீக்கி) and mount the palmyra horse. They conflict only if the lover's speech is read as a claim about what one should do; taken as a dramatised speech it is an instance of exactly what 1017 says the நாணாள்பவர் never do.

In 1133 the man says he once had shame and good manliness (நாணொடு நல்லாண்மை பண்டுடையேன்) and today has the palmyra horse. In 1254 the woman says she used to say she had restraint (நிறையுடையேன் என்பேன்மன்), yet her desire passes concealment and comes out in public. Each speaker sets a former self-possession against its loss to love; his loss is நாண் and ஆண்மை, hers is நிறை.

In 1088 the man, on first seeing her, says his might (பீடு), which enemies dreaded in battle, has broken before her bright forehead. In 1133 he says the shame and good manliness he once had are replaced by the palmyra horse. The later verse carries the first collapse through to its end: what broke at first sight is now given up publicly.

1026 defines நல்லாண்மை as making oneself fit to manage the house one was born into (இல்லாண்மை ஆக்கிக் கொளல்). 1133 uses the same word for what the lover had before (நல்லாண்மை பண்டுடையேன்) and has now exchanged for the palmyra horse. Set beside 1026's definition, the lover's loss is of the capacity that makes a man of use to his family, not only of pride.

1134 says the fierce flood of love (காமக் கடும்புனல்) carries off the raft of shame and good manliness. In 1167 the woman swims the same காமக் கடும்புனல் and sees no shore. The phrase is identical: the man loses his raft to the flood, and the woman is in it with no raft and no bank in sight.

1134 has the flood of love carry away the raft called shame and good manliness (நாணொடு நல்லாண்மை என்னும் புணை). 1251 has the axe of desire break the door called restraint, bolted with the bar of shame (நிறையென்னும் நாணுத்தாழ் வீழ்த்த கதவு). Both make shame a built defence that love's force destroys, one in the man's voice and one in the woman's.

306 says anger burns the safe raft that is one's own people (இனமென்னும் ஏமப் புணையைச் சுடும்). 1134 says the flood of love sweeps off the raft that is shame and good manliness (என்னும் புணை). In both a passion destroys the thing figured as the raft that keeps a person afloat: anger in the chapter on not being angry, desire here.

In 1135 the man says the girl with small bangles gave him (தந்தாள்) the palmyra horse and the grief that evening brings. In 1183 the woman says he took her grace and shame and gave in return (கைம்மாறா ... தந்து) sickness and pallor. Each lover describes the affliction as a gift from the other, and in both verses shame is part of what is lost.

1135 speaks of the grief endured at evening (மாலை உழக்கும் துயர்). 1227 says this sickness buds in the morning, is in bud all day and blossoms in the evening (மாலை மலரும் இந்நோய்). Parimelazhagar explains 1135's 'evening' by the same idea, that love opens at evening, so 1227 supplies the reason behind the man's phrase.

In 1136 the man's eyes will not close (படல் ஒல்லா) for the girl, so even at midnight (யாமத்தும்) he thinks of riding the palmyra horse. In 1252 the woman says desire, having no pity, rules her heart at its work even at midnight (யாமத்தும் ஆளும் தொழில்). Both use midnight, when all else rests, as the proof that love allows no rest.

1049 says one may sleep even in fire, but in poverty closing the eyes at all is hard (யாதொன்றும் கண்பாடு அரிது). 1136 says the lover's eyes will not close (படல் ஒல்லா ... கண்) even at midnight. The Kural gives sleeplessness the same role in two domains: it is the measure of want in the Book of Wealth and of love here.

54 asks what is of greater worth than a woman, if she has the firmness called கற்பு (பெண்ணின் பெருந்தக்க யாவுள). 1137 says nothing is of greater worth than womanhood that suffers a sea of desire and does not mount the palmyra horse (பெண்ணின் பெருந்தக்கது இல்). The wording is reused almost exactly: the Book of Virtue rests her worth on firmness as a wife, the Book of Love on restraint under desire.

907 says a woman who has shame holds more greatness than the manhood of one who does a woman's bidding (நாணுடைப் பெண்ணே பெருமை உடைத்து). 1137 gives the highest worth to womanhood that does not ride the palmyra horse, in a chapter where the man gives up shame and manliness (1133). Both rank a woman who keeps her shame above a man who has let his go.

1138 says love, without thinking 'they are hard to overcome in restraint' or 'they deserve pity', passes concealment and comes out in the open (மறையிறந்து மன்று படும்). 1254 ends with the same words, after the woman says she used to claim she had restraint (நிறையுடையேன் என்பேன்). The shared line is stated generally in 1138 and as a personal confession in 1254; both set நிறை against it and lose.

71 asks whether there is a bolt that can shut love in (அன்பிற்கும் உண்டோ அடைக்குந்தாழ்), since the small tears of the loving make it known. 1138 says காமம் breaks through secrecy and appears in public. The Book of Virtue says of அன்பு what the Book of Love says of காமம்: neither can be kept hidden, and each publishes itself.

In 1139 the woman's love, thinking 'not everyone knows' (அறிகிலார் எல்லாரும் என்றே), goes reeling through the street (மறுகின் மறுகும்). In 1180 she says the town easily learns the secret of those whose eyes are beaten drums (அறைபறை கண்ணார்). In both the secret is given away by the lover herself and not by the town: by her love going about in 1139, by her eyes in 1180.

In 1140 the woman says the unknowing laugh where she can see, because they have not undergone what she has (யாம்பட்ட தாம்படா ஆறு). In 1219 she says those who blame him for not being gracious in waking life are those who have not seen a lover in dreams (காதலர்க் காணாதவர்). Both explain the town's judgement by its lack of the lover's experience.

877 advises not telling one's pain to those who do not know it (நோவற்க நொந்தது அறியார்க்கு). 1140 shows the reason from inside: those who have not suffered what the speaker suffered (யாம்பட்ட தாம்படா) laugh at her in plain sight. The statecraft maxim and the lover's complaint agree that pain gets no hearing from those who have not felt it.

1141 says that because gossip has risen the precious life holds on (அலரெழ ஆருயிர் நிற்கும்). 1213 says the woman's life exists because she sees in dreams the one who gives nothing in waking life (காண்டலின் உண்டென் உயிர்). In each a lover's life is kept going by something that only stands in for the beloved: the town's talk in one, a dream in the other.

1141 says life stays because the gossip has risen. 1263 says the woman still exists by longing for his return (வரல்நசைஇ இன்னும் உளேன்). Both verses name the one thing that keeps life from leaving; in 1141 it comes from outside, from the town, and in 1263 from her own hope.

In 1142 the man says the town, not knowing how hard the flower-eyed woman is to reach (அருமை அறியாது), has given him gossip (அலரெமக்கு ஈந்தது). In 1150 the speaker says the town is raising the very talk 'we want' (யாம்வேண்டும் கெளவை எடுக்கும் இவ்வூர்). Both treat the town's gossip as an unintended service; Parimelazhagar reads ஈந்தது as help given, and reads 1150 as the friend counting on it.

In 1143 the man says the gossip the town knows is like having obtained what he has not obtained (பெறாஅது பெற்றன்ன நீர்த்து). In 1213 the woman sees in dreams the man who gives nothing in waking life, and lives by it. Both take a substitute for union as if it were union: public talk for him, a dream for her.

In 1144 the man says his love thrives through gossip (கவ்வையால் கவ்விது காமம்) and without it would lose its nature and go slack. In 1147 the woman says the town's gossip is manure and her mother's words water to 'this sickness' (நீளும் இந்நோய்). Both say gossip feeds love; he calls what grows காமம் and welcomes it, she calls it நோய்.

1145 says love is sweeter each time it is exposed, as drinking is desired each time one is drunk (களித்தொறும் கள்ளுண்டல் வேட்டற்றால்). 940 says life is loved more each time it suffers, as gambling is loved more with each loss (இழத்தொறூஉம் காதலிக்கும் சூதேபோல்). The two verses have the same shape, a 'each time ... the more' simile from a vice, applied to love in one and to attachment to life in the other.

1145 takes drinking as the model for love: each exposure makes love sweeter as each bout makes drink wanted. 1281 says being intoxicated at a thought and glad at a sight belong to love and not to liquor (கள்ளுக்கில் காமத்திற்கு உண்டு). So the likeness in 1145 has a limit the book itself states: liquor works only when drunk, love without contact.

1110 says that as each new knowing shows one's earlier ignorance (அறிதோறு அறியாமை கண்டற்றால்), so is love each time one draws close to her (செறிதோறும்). 1145 says love is sweeter each time it comes out (வெளிப்படுந் தோறும் இனிது). Both use the தோறும் construction to say love increases with each repetition, in union in 1110 and in exposure in 1145.

In 1146 the woman saw him one day only, and the gossip has spread like the serpent seizing the moon (திங்களைப் பாம்புகொண்டற்று), which Parimelazhagar glosses as spreading everywhere. 957 says a fault in the well-born shows high, like the spot on the moon in the sky (மதிக்கண் மறுப்போல்). Both use the moon as the thing whose blemish everyone sees: a brief event or a small fault becomes public because of where it sits.

In 1147 the woman says the town's gossip is manure (எருவாக) and her mother's word water (நீராக) by which this sickness grows. In 1144 the man says his love thrives by gossip and would go slack without it. The claim is the same from both lovers, but she counts her mother's rebuke with the gossip and calls the growth a sickness.

1147 makes the sickness of love a crop, manured by gossip and watered by a mother's words, that grows long (நீளும் இந்நோய்). 1227 makes the same இந்நோய் a flower that buds in the morning and opens in the evening. In both the woman describes her lovesickness as a plant with its own growth, fed in 1147 and timed in 1227.

1038, on farming, says manuring is better than ploughing and guarding better than watering (எருவிடுதல் ... நீரினும்). 1147 uses the same pair, எரு and நீர், for the gossip and the mother's words that raise the sickness of love. The farmer's two inputs are turned into a figure: what is meant to check the love is what cultivates it.

1148 says that to think of putting out love with gossip is like thinking to put out fire with ghee (நெய்யால் எரி நுதுப்பேம்). 1260 asks whether those whose hearts are like fat put in fire (நிணம் தீயில் இட்டன்ன) can say they will hold out in a sulk. Both use fat meeting fire for love: in 1148 the fat feeds the fire, in 1260 the heart is the fat that melts.

1144 says love thrives by gossip and would droop without it. 1148 puts the same point as a rebuttal of those who expect gossip to end the affair: it is ghee on fire. 1148 gives the image and the opposing view that 1144's plain statement lacks.

In 1154 the woman asks whether, if he who was gracious and said 'do not fear' should leave (அளித்தஞ்சல் என்றவர் நீப்பின்), any fault lies with her for trusting his assurance. In 1149 the one who said 'do not fear' has left (அஞ்சலோம்பு என்றார் ... நீத்தக் கடை), and she asks how she can now be ashamed of gossip. The same promise is quoted before and after it is broken: the fear of 1154 has come true in 1149.

In 1149 the woman asks whether she can be ashamed at gossip (அலர்நாண ஒல்வதோ) now that he has left her. In 1297 she says she has forgotten even shame (நாணும் மறந்தேன்), caught in a heart that cannot forget him. In both her shame gives way, in 1149 because his leaving has made it pointless and in 1297 because her own heart overrides it.

1150 says the town is raising the gossip 'we want' (யாம்வேண்டும் கெளவை), and the lover will grant what is asked if he wishes. In 1143 the man asks whether the gossip the town knows is not his to have, since it is like gaining what he has not gained. Both sides welcome the talk: for him it stands in for union, and in 1150, on Parimelazhagar's reading, it is the ground for asking him to take her away.

1161: she would hide the sickness, but it rises like spring water for those who bale it out (இறைப்பவர்க்கு ஊற்றுநீர் போல மிகும்). 396: a well in sand wells up as far as it is dug, and understanding as far as one learns (தொட்டனைத்து ஊறும்). The same figure of water that increases the more it is drawn serves learning in one verse and an unconcealable pain in the other.

Both open with the same words, மறைப்பேன்மன் ('I would hide it'), and both say the attempt fails: in 1161 the pain rises like spring water under baling, in 1253 desire shows itself without her intending it, like a sneeze (குறிப்பின்றித் தும்மல்போல்). Read together, one figure says concealment makes it grow and the other that it escapes her will altogether.

1162: she cannot hide the sickness, and telling it to the one who caused it brings shame (உரைத்தலும் நாணுத் தரும்). 1200: she tells her heart that it means to tell its pain to one who is not close (உறாஅர்க்கு உறுநோய் உரைப்பாய்) and might as well fill up the sea. Parimelazhagar reads both as about sending him word; 1200 adds futility to the shame that 1162 gives as the obstacle.

Both use the carrying pole (கா). In 1196 love is painful on one end only and sweet when it is on both ends, the two lovers. In 1163 the pole is her own life (உயிர் காவா) and the two loads are love and shame hanging inside a body that cannot bear them, so the figure of balance turns from two people to two forces within one.

1163 states the deadlock: love and shame hang balanced from her life within a body that cannot bear them (நோனா உடம்பின்). 1247 is her attempt to end it: she tells her heart to let go either desire or shame, since she cannot bear the two (யானோ பொறேன் இவ்விரண்டு).

1017: those ruled by shame give up life for shame and do not give up shame for life (நாணால் உயிரைத் துறப்பர்). 1163 shows that ranking from inside: she drops neither love nor shame, and it is her life, the pole (உயிர் காவா), that takes the strain; Parimelazhagar adds that the life will snap.

1134 (the man): the fierce flood of love carries off the raft called shame and manliness (காமக் கடும்புனல் ... புணை). 1164 (the woman): the sea of love is there, and the safe raft to swim it is not (ஏமப் புணை மன்னும் இல்). The same figure of love as water and restraint or help as a raft is used by each lover, he losing his raft and she never having one.

Both use the compound ஏமப்புணை, 'raft of safety'. In 306 the raft is one's own people (இனமென்னும் ஏமப்புணை), which anger burns; in 1164 there is no such raft for the sea of love, and Parimelazhagar takes her to mean that the friend has not become one. In both the raft stands for people one relies on.

10: the great sea of birth is swum by those who reach the Lord's feet and not by others (பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல் நீந்துவர்); Parimelazhagar supplies the feet as the raft. 1164: the sea of love exists and the raft to swim it does not (அது நீந்தும் ஏமப்புணை). The same structure of a sea crossed only with a support appears in the first chapter and in a separated woman's complaint.

Both argue from the nearer case to the farther with a question. 188: those who spread even the faults of their intimates, what would they do to strangers (என்னைகொல் ஏதிலார் மாட்டு)? 1165: those who can bring grief within friendship (நட்பினுள்), what would they be in enmity (துப்பின் எவனாவர்)?

1165: she asks what those who bring grief in friendship would do as enemies; Parimelazhagar says this is aimed, in a sulk, at the friend who has not sent a message. 805 advises that when friends do something hurtful (நோதக்க நட்டார் செயின்) it should be understood as folly or as great intimacy. 805 offers the charitable reading that her question refuses.

1137 speaks of suffering a love like the sea (கடலன்ன காமம் உழந்தும்) and praises womanhood that still does not mount the palmyra horse. 1166 uses the sea twice over: love's pleasure is a sea, and when it afflicts (அடுங்கால்) the pain is greater than that. The sea is the book's measure for love, and 1166 says the measure is exceeded.

629: one who does not crave the pleasure within pleasure does not come to pain within pain (இன்பத்துள் இன்பம் விழையாதான்). 1166: the pleasure of love is a sea and its pain when it afflicts is larger still (துன்பம் அதனிற் பெரிது). The woman's experience fits the link between relishing pleasure and suffering pain that 629 states as a rule in the Book of Wealth.

1164 says the sea of love exists and there is no raft to swim it. 1167 continues the figure: she has swum the fierce flood (காமக் கடும்புனல் நீந்தி) and sees no shore (கரை காணேன்), and at midnight there is only herself. The second verse turns the missing raft into an actual, endless swim.

Both lovers are awake at midnight, with the same word யாமத்தும்.
