The man in 1136 says his eyes will not close and even at midnight he thinks of mounting the palmyra horse; the woman in 1167 says that even at midnight she alone is there (யானே உளேன்), swimming without sight of shore. Sleeplessness in the dead of night is given to both sides.

1168: the night has put all living beings to sleep and, she says with pity (அளித்து), has no companion but her. 1222: she tells the evening it looks sad-eyed (புன்கண்ணை) and asks whether its partner is as hard as hers. In both she treats a time of day as a fellow sufferer and puts her own state onto it; Parimelazhagar says as much of 1222.

1169: the nights that pass so long these days (நெடிய கழியும் இரா) are crueller than the cruel one's cruelty. 1269: for those who pine with a set day of return in mind, one day passes like seven (ஒருநாள் எழுநாள்போல்). Both say that time stretches for the one who waits.

1169: in separation the long nights are crueller than the man himself. 1329: the man, pleading with her as she sulks, wishes the night would lengthen (நீடுக மன்னோ இரா). The length of the night is a torment or a wish depending on whether the lover is present; Parimelazhagar notes at 1169 that the nights were short in the days of union.

Both use the phrase கொடியார் கொடுமை, 'the cruelty of the cruel one', for the absent man. In 1235 her shoulders, their old beauty faded, declare it; in 1169 she uses it as the measure the long nights exceed (கொடுமையின் தாம் கொடிய). 1169 moves the charge of cruelty from the man to the time itself.

1170: if her eyes could go where he is as her heart does (உள்ளம்போன்று உள்வழிச் செல்கிற்பின்), they would not be swimming in a flood of tears. 1244 turns the wish into a request: heart, take the eyes along when you go (கண்ணும் கொளச்சேறி), for they consume her in wanting to see him. Both rest on the idea that the heart can travel to him and the eyes cannot.

In 1167 she herself swims the fierce flood of love and sees no shore; in 1170 it is her eyes that swim in flood water (வெள்ளநீர் நீந்தல), which is her tears. The chapter's water figure for love ends as literal water in the eyes.

1091 (the man): her kohl-lined eyes hold two looks, one that gives the sickness and one that is its cure (நோய்நோக்கு ... மருந்து). 1171 (the woman): her own eyes showed him to her and so she came to know an unabating sickness (தண்டாநோய்), and she asks why they weep. Eyes are the source of love's sickness in both, the other's eyes for the man and her own for the woman, and only his verse has a cure.

1171: she asks why her eyes weep, since they showed him to her (தாம் காட்ட யாம் கண்டது). 1244: the eyes consume her in their wish to see him (அவர்க்காணல் உற்று). In both she speaks of her eyes as agents apart from herself, with wants of their own that she pays for.

792: the friendship of one who does not take it after examining again and again ends in grief that kills him (ஆய்ந்தாய்ந்து கொள்ளாதான் கேண்மை). 1172, on Parimelazhagar's reading: the eyes looked that day without examining and understanding what would follow (தெரிந்துணரா நோக்கிய) and now suffer. The rule about forming ties without scrutiny is applied to a look. Manakkudavar reads the first phrase differently, as having looked with knowledge.

535: one who slipped by not guarding beforehand will grieve afterwards over his own error (முன்னுறக் காவாது ... பின்னூறு இரங்கிவிடும்). 1172: the eyes that looked without foresight now toil in misery (பைதல் உழப்பது). Parimelazhagar's comment on 1172 uses the same terms, that those who do not guard against what is coming can only bear it when it arrives.

1173: the eyes looked hastily of themselves (கதுமெனத் தாம் நோக்கி) and now weep of themselves, which is laughable. 435: the life of one who does not guard before a fault comes is destroyed like straw before fire (வருமுன்னர்க் காவாதான்). Parimelazhagar explains the laughter in 1173 with that same phrase: it is laughable to those who guard before it comes.

1140: the ignorant laugh where she can see it (நகுப அறிவில்லார்), because they have not suffered what she has. 1173: she finds her own eyes' plight fit to be laughed at (நகத்தக்கது உடைத்து). Laughter at a lover's suffering comes from outsiders in one verse and from the sufferer herself in the other.

320: all pain falls on those who caused pain (நோயெல்லாம் நோய்செய்தார் மேலவாம்). 1174: the eyes that fixed an inescapable sickness in her (உய்வில்நோய் என்கண் நிறுத்து) have themselves dried up and cannot weep. Parimelazhagar reads 1174 in these terms: having done her harm first, harm came to them of itself.

319: if you do hurt to others in the forenoon, hurt comes to you in the afternoon of itself (தாமே வரும்). 1175: the eyes that made her a sickness the sea cannot hold now cannot sleep and toil in misery (படலாற்றா பைதல் உழக்கும்). Manakkudavar states the connection, saying the verse shows harm coming to those who did harm to another.

1166 says love's pain, when it afflicts, is greater than the sea (அதனிற் பெரிது). 1175 repeats the measure as an epithet, a love-sickness the sea cannot hold (கடலாற்றாக் காமநோய்), and goes on to assign blame for it to her eyes.

1173 finds it laughable that the eyes looked of themselves and weep of themselves. 1176 goes a step further: it is sweet (ஓஒ இனிதே) that the eyes which gave her this sickness have fallen into it too (தாஅம் இதற்பட்டது). The sequence moves from mockery of her eyes to satisfaction at their suffering.

1174 reports that the eyes have dried up and cannot weep (நீருலந்த). 1177 wishes exactly that on them: may the eyes that longed and melted to see him suffer on until their inner water is gone (உள்நீர் அறுக). What one verse states as their condition the other pronounces as a curse.

The two verses share most of their wording. 1178: there is one who desired without cherishing (பேணாது பெட்டார்), and her eyes cannot be at peace without seeing him (காணாது அமைவில கண்). 1283: though he disregards her and does what pleases him (பேணாது பெட்பவே செய்யினும்), her eyes will not rest without seeing her husband. Both set his lack of care against the eyes' need to see him; Manakkudavar reads the opening of 1178 differently, as a question about desiring what should not be desired.

1179: when he does not come the eyes do not sleep, and when he comes they do not sleep (வாராக்கால் துஞ்சா வரின் துஞ்சா). 1295: the heart fears not having him and, having him, fears parting (பெறாஅமை அஞ்சும் பெறின் பிரிவு அஞ்சும்). The same two-sided bind is said of the eyes and of the heart, and Parimelazhagar explains 1179 by the fear of parting that 1295 names.

1152: once his mere look was a pleasure, and now union itself holds the pain of fearing separation (பிரிவஞ்சும் புன்கண் உடைத்தால் புணர்வு). 1179 gives the bodily result: her eyes do not sleep even when he has come. 1152 supplies the reason for the second half of 1179.

Both use the beaten drum (அறைபறை) for giving away a secret (மறை). In 1076 the base are like the drum because they carry whatever secret they hear to others. In 1180 her own eyes are the drum, so the town easily gets the secret in her heart. The figure for a vice in the Book of Wealth becomes a figure for a lover's helplessness.

1180 (the woman): the town can easily learn the secret of those whose eyes are beaten drums. 1271 (the man): though she hides it, her kohl-lined eyes go beyond her control (கரப்பினும் கையிகந்து) and have something to tell. Both lovers say her eyes disclose what she means to conceal.

71: is there a bolt that can shut in love? The small tears of the loving will proclaim it (புன்கணீர் பூசல் தரும்). 1180: her eyes are beaten drums and the town easily learns her secret. The Book of Virtue says of அன்பு in general what the woman says of her own love: the eyes publish it.

1160 speaks, with irony, of the many who agree to the hard thing, endure the parting and live on afterwards (அரிதாற்றி ... பிரிவாற்றிப் பின்இருந்து வாழ்வார் பலர்); Parimelazhagar glosses அரிது ஆற்றி as consenting to the parting. 1181 is the woman who did consent (நல்காமை நேர்ந்தேன்) and now cannot bear the result. Read together, 1181 shows the cost of the consent that 1160 doubted anyone could really give.

In 1162 she cannot hide the sickness, and telling the one who caused it brings shame (உரைத்தலும் நாணுத் தரும்). In 1181 the question widens to யார்க்கு உரைக்கோ, to whom can I tell it at all, because she herself agreed to his going; Parimelazhagar adds that telling a self-made sorrow would itself be blame. The pair traces how the possible hearers for her complaint run out.

1182 has the pallor ride over her body with the pride of saying 'he gave me' (அவர்தந்தார் என்னும் தகையால்). 1183 uses the same verb of giving for an exchange: he took her grace and modesty and gave sickness and pallor (நோயும் பசலையும் தந்து). The pallor that boasts of being his gift in one verse is entered as his payment in the next.

211 says obligation wants no return, கைம்மாறு வேண்டா கடப்பாடு, and points to the rain, which the world cannot repay. 1183 uses the same word bitterly: as கைம்மாறு for the grace and modesty he took, he gave sickness and pallor. The word that names the return a good giver does not ask for is here the name of a bad bargain.

In 1133 the man says he once had shame and good manliness (நாணொடு நல்லாண்மை பண்டுடையேன்) and today has the palmyra horse. In 1183 the woman says her grace and modesty (சாயலும் நாணும்) are gone and she has sickness and pallor instead. Both lovers reckon love as a loss of நாண் and of a quality proper to their sex, replaced by a public sign of suffering.

In 1184 she thinks of him and speaks only of his merits (உள்ளுவன் ... உரைப்பது அவர்திறம்), and calls it deceit (கள்ளம்) that the pallor comes all the same. In 1250 she tells her heart that by keeping in it the man who left, she will lose still more beauty (இன்னும் இழத்தும் கவின்). 1250 states as cause and effect what 1184 finds baffling: the faithful thinking does not hold the pallor off.

1125 and 1184 open with the same words, உள்ளுவன் மன்யான். The man in 1125 says he would remember her qualities if he ever forgot them, and he does not know forgetting; the woman in 1184 says she thinks of him and yet turns pale. The same claim of constant thought is his proof of love and her complaint that such thought gives no protection.

1185 points there to the lover going and here to the pallor spreading (உவக்காண் ... இவக்காண்); Parimelazhagar takes it as an earlier occasion when he had gone only a short way. 1278 says he left only yesterday and her body has been pale seven days (நெருநற்றுச் சென்றார் ... எழுநாளேம் மேனி பசந்து). One verse measures the pallor's speed in space and the other in time.

In 1277 her bangles understood before she did that the lord of the shore had parted from her (நம்மினும் முன்னம் உணர்ந்த வளை). In 1185 the pallor spreads while he is still in sight. Both make the body register the parting faster than the mind or the facts do; 1277 pushes it to before the event.

1186 is the woman's account: pallor watches for a gap in her husband's embrace (முயக்கற்றம் பார்க்கும்) as darkness watches for a lamp to fail. 1238 is the man's memory of the same thing: he loosened the arms that held her and her forehead turned pale (முயங்கிய கைகளை ஊக்கப் பசந்தது). The two speakers confirm each other from either side of the embrace.

285 describes those who, with goods in view, watch for another's lapse (பொச்சாப்புப் பார்ப்பார்), and denies them a loving nature. 1186 gives pallor the same posture: it watches for the weak moment (அற்றம் பார்க்கும்), which Parimelazhagar notes is a figurative use of 'watch'. The book's picture of the thief waiting for inattention is the picture the woman uses for what takes her colour.

In 1187 she lay embracing him, shifted a little (புடைபெயர்ந்தேன்), and at once the pallor was thick enough to scoop up. In 1239 the man recalls that a cool breeze cutting between them in the embrace (முயக்கிடைத் தண்வளி போழ) was enough to pale her eyes. Both verses, from the two partners, set the threshold of separation at the smallest physical gap.

1108, spoken in union, calls sweet the embrace that not even air can cut through (வளியிடை போழப் படாஅ முயக்கு). 1187 shows what that closeness was guarding against: one slight turn away and the pallor seizes her. The joy of 1108 and the fear of 1187 concern the same unbroken contact.

1188 says people say only 'she has grown pale' and no one says 'he left her' (துறந்தார் அவர் என்பார் இல்). In 1220 the townspeople do say he has left her in waking life (நனவினால் நம்நீத்தார் என்பர்), and she answers that they must not see him in dreams. These are speeches at different moments, but together they show her objecting both when the town blames only her and when it blames him.

1188 complains that the talk fixes on her pallor and not on his leaving. 1190 says it is good to get the name of pallor, provided they do not spread talk of his unkindness (நல்காமை தூற்றார் எனின்); Parimelazhagar sets it as her reply when the friend has blamed him. The complaint of 1188 should therefore not be read as a wish to have him blamed: in 1190 she accepts the very imbalance she resents.

1181 puts the consent on herself: நல்காமை நேர்ந்தேன், I agreed to his absence. 1189 names him as the one who brought her to agree (நயப்பித்தார்) and says let her body pale as it will if he stands well; Parimelazhagar reads நன்னிலையர் as free of fault, while Manakkudavar reads the condition as his suffering too. On Parimelazhagar's reading the two verses share out the responsibility and she keeps the cost.

In 1189, on Parimelazhagar's reading, she accepts the pallor so long as the man who persuaded her is held blameless. In 1236 her arms thin and her bangles slip, and what pains her is hearing him called cruel (அவரைக் கொடியர் எனக்கூறல் நொந்து). In both she ranks his good name above her own wasting.

1190 says being named for her pallor is good if people do not broadcast his unkindness (நல்காமை தூற்றார் எனின்). 1236 says the hurt is in hearing him called cruel (கொடியர் எனக்கூறல் நொந்து), more than in the slipping bangles. Both verses make the talk against him, and not her own disfigurement, the thing she cannot bear.

1190 hopes that her pallor can be talked of without his நல்காமை being talked of. In 1232 the friend says her pale, weeping eyes themselves seem to tell of the unkindness of the one she desired (நயந்தவர் நல்காமை சொல்லுவ போலும்). The same word நல்காமை shows the limit of her wish: the pallor is itself the report against him.

1191 calls requited love the stoneless fruit of love (காமத்துக் காழில் கனி), fruit with nothing in it to stop the eating; Parimelazhagar explains it as enjoyment without obstruction. 1306 says love without quarrels large and small is like over-ripe and unripe fruit (கனியும் கருக்காயும் அற்று). Both judge love as fruit, and they differ on resistance: the pining woman wants none, while the later verse says a love with no friction is not at its right ripeness.

1108, spoken in union, says the close embrace is sweet to two who desire each other (வீழும் இருவர்க்கு இனிதே). 1191, spoken in separation, says those loved by the ones they love (தாம்வீழ்வார் தம்வீழப் பெற்றவர்) have the stoneless fruit. Both place love's sweetness in the desire being mutual, using the same verb வீழ்; one says it from inside and the other from outside.

1192 says the grace a beloved shows the one who loves (வீழ்வார் அளிக்கும் அளி) is like the sky yielding to those who live by it. 557 says a king's lack of அளி is to living beings what lack of rain is to the earth (துளியின்மை ... அளியின்மை). The same word and the same rain comparison describe the dependence of subjects on a king and of a lover on the beloved.

542 says the world lives looking to the sky and the people live looking to the king's sceptre (வானோக்கி வாழும் ... கோல் நோக்கி வாழும்). 1192 compares the beloved's grace to rain for those who live by it; Parimelazhagar glosses them as those who live looking to it alone. Love is described with the book's standard figure for total dependence on one source.

598 says those without drive never reach the pride of saying 'we are generous' (வள்ளியம் என்னும் செருக்கு). 1193 says the pride of saying 'we shall live' (வாழுநம் என்னும் செருக்கு) suits only those loved by the ones they love. The same construction makes a justified pride depend on a prior condition: inner drive in the one case, being loved in return in the other.

1191 says those loved by the ones they love have 'obtained' (பெற்றவர் பெற்றாரே) love's stoneless fruit; Parimelazhagar ties the word to earlier good deeds. 1194 gives the negative: even those who are esteemed are கெழீஇயிலர் if the one they love does not love them, which Parimelazhagar glosses as lacking good deeds and Manakkudavar as being without what they desire. The pair states the same condition from both sides, and shows the commentators reading it as fortune and not merit.

1195 asks what the one she loves can do for her when he has no love for her (தாம்காதல் கொள்ளாக் கடை). 1245 asks her heart whether a man who does not respond when she draws near (உற்றால் உறாஅதவர்) can be dropped as one who hates her (செற்றார் எனக் கைவிடல் உண்டோ). The second speech limits the first: finding no benefit in an unreturned love does not make her able to give it up.

1196 says love on one end only is painful and, like a carrying pole (காப் போல), sweet when on both ends. In 1163 love and shame hang from the two ends of a pole that is her life (உயிர்காவாத் தூங்கும்), in a body that cannot bear them. The same pole carries a balanced, bearable load between two lovers in one verse and two opposed weights inside one person in the other.

118 praises being level like the scale-beam and not leaning to one side (ஒருபால் கோடாமை) as the ornament of the worthy. 1196 applies the same test to love: borne on one end (ஒருதலையான்) it hurts, and on both it is sweet. Evenness between two sides is a mark of justice in the Book of Virtue and a condition of happiness here.

1252 says the thing called desire has no eye, that is no pity (கண்ணின்று), since it works her heart even at midnight. 1197 asks whether Kaman, who stays and acts on one person only, does not see her pain and misery (காணான்கொல்). The complaint moves from the feeling to the god, and both use sight as the test of his mercy.

In 1308 the man asks what use suffering is when there is no lover who knows 'this one is suffering' (அஃதறியும் காதலர் இல்லா வழி). In 1197 the woman asks whether Kaman fails to see her suffering. Both speakers treat pain as needing a witness, and each finds the one who ought to notice absent.

276 ends வஞ்சித்து வாழ்வாரின் வன்கணார் இல்: none are harder than those who live by deceiving as false renouncers. 1198 ends with the same formula, உலகத்து வாழ்வாரின் வன்கணார் இல், for those who live on without a kind word from the beloved. The phrase that condemns the hypocrite's hardness is turned by the woman on herself, for the hardness of surviving.

1160 says, with irony, that many endure the parting and afterwards stay and live (பின்இருந்து வாழ்வார் பலர்). 1198 says no one is harder than those who live on without even a kind word from the one they love. Both speeches treat staying alive in separation as something that needs explaining, and neither treats it as a virtue.

1198 calls hard those who live without receiving a sweet word from the beloved (இன்சொல் பெறாஅது). 1199 defines how little would count: though he gives no grace, any report of him is sweet to her ears (அவர்மாட்டு இசையும் இனிய செவிக்கு). Parimelazhagar reads இசை as any word at all, even that he is not coming, and links the two verses on that basis; Kalaignar takes இசை as his praise.

In 1213 her life continues because in dreams she sees the man who gives no grace in waking life (நனவினால் நல்காதவரை). In 1199 the man who gives no grace (நல்கார் எனினும்) still sweetens her ears by any word of him. In both she is sustained by a substitute for his presence, a dream or a report, while saying outright that he withholds himself.

877, in the chapters on enmity, advises: do not lament to those who do not know your pain (நோவற்க நொந்தது அறியார்க்கு). In 1200 the woman tells her heart that it is setting out to tell its great pain to one who is not close to it (உறாஅர்க்கு உறுநோய் உரைப்பாய்) and that filling the sea would be easier. The statecraft maxim and the lover's self-reproach agree that pain told to the unsympathetic is wasted.

In 1237 she asks her heart whether it will win any glory by telling the cruel one, as Pope renders it, of the uproar over her wasting shoulders (பாடு பெறுதியோ நெஞ்சே ... உரைத்து). In 1200 she tells the heart that reporting its pain to one who is not close is harder than filling the sea. Both are addresses to the heart that reject sending him word of her suffering.

1164 says the sea of love exists and the raft to cross it does not (காமக் கடல் ... ஏமப் புணை இல்). 1200 tells the heart to fill up the sea (கடலைச் செறாஅஅய்) instead of telling its pain to the unloving; Pope takes this sea as her own sorrow, while Parimelazhagar takes it as the sea that torments her. On Pope's reading the two verses share the sea as the measure of her grief, with crossing it and filling it both out of reach.

1201 (the man, for Parimelazhagar) says love is sweeter than toddy because it gives great joy that does not end even when only thought of (உள்ளினும் தீராப் பெருமகிழ்). 1281, spoken by the woman, makes the same comparison: elation at a thought and delight at a sight belong to love and not to toddy (கள்ளுக்கு இல் காமத்திற்கு உண்டு). The pairing shows the same judgment given from both sides of the couple, built on the same verb உள்ளுதல்.

1090 says brewed liquor gladdens only those who drink it (உண்டார்கண் அல்லது) and does not, like love, gladden those who merely see (கண்டார் மகிழ்செய்தல் இன்று). 1201 moves the same contrast one step further from the senses: love gladdens even at a thought (உள்ளினும்), with nothing present to see. Read together they form a series from drinking to seeing to remembering.

Both verses turn on the word உள்ளினும். In 1201 the man says remembering gives unending joy (தீராப் பெருமகிழ்); in 1207 the woman says that even while she remembers, her heart burns (உள்ளினும் உள்ளம் சுடும்), which Parimelazhagar explains as the separation burning her despite the memory. These are two speakers in two moods, so it is a limit on the first claim and not a contradiction in the book's teaching.

1202 says love is sweet in every way since no pain comes from thinking of the one you love (நினைப்ப வருவதொன்று இல், as the commentators read this edition's garbled line). In 1209 the woman's dear life is wasting because she thinks hard on his lack of tenderness (அளியின்மை ஆற்ற நினைந்து). The pairing shows that the sweetness of 1202 depends on what is remembered: the shared days, not the present neglect. Manakkudavar in fact reads 1202 as conditional, 'if no pain comes'.

1202 claims that thinking of the beloved brings no pain. In 1296 the woman says that when she sat alone and thought (தனியே இருந்து நினைத்தக்கால்), her heart stayed only to eat her (என்னைத் தினிய); Parimelazhagar specifies that what she thought of was his cruelties. The two speeches mark out the cases in which remembering comforts and in which it wounds.

In 1203 a sneeze seems to start and dies away (தும்மல் சினைப்பது போன்று கெடும்), and the woman concludes he seemed about to think of her and did not. In 1317 the man sneezes and she weeps, asking whom he was thought of by (யாருள்ளித் தும்மினீர்). Both rest on the belief, noted by Parimelazhagar at 1203, that a sneeze means someone far away is thinking of you; the same sign feeds longing in separation and jealousy in union.

1203 uses the half-formed sneeze as a sign of the lover's half-formed thought of her. 1253 uses the sneeze differently: desire, though she would hide it, appears without her intending it, like a sneeze (குறிப்பின்றித் தும்மல்போல் தோன்றி விடும்). In both the sneeze stands for what the will cannot command: in 1253 she cannot hold it back, in 1203 she cannot make it come.

1204 asks whether she too is in his heart, since he is always in hers (யாமும் உளேங்கொல் அவர்நெஞ்சத்து). 1205 gives the answer as an accusation: he has put a guard on his heart against her (தம்நெஞ்சத்து எம்மைக் கடிகொண்டார்) and yet comes unceasingly into hers. Manakkudavar reads 1205 as the woman, having doubted, now deciding that he does not think of her.

In 1130 the woman answers the town's charge of lovelessness with the fact that he lives gladly in her heart always (உவந்துறைவர் உள்ளத்துள் என்றும்). In 1204 the same fact (எந்நெஞ்சத்து ஓஒ உளரே அவர்) no longer settles anything, because she now asks about his heart and not hers. The pairing shows that his presence in her heart is evidence only of her love.

1205 complains that he keeps her out of his heart while entering hers without pause (எம்நெஞ்சத்து ஓவா வரல்). 1291 states the same imbalance to her own heart: his heart stays his (அவர்நெஞ்சு அவர்க்காதல்), so why is hers not hers? In 1205 she blames him for the unequal exchange, and in 1291 she blames her own heart.

Both verses treat the lover as physically lodged in her heart. In 1128 she fears to eat anything hot because he, being in her heart (நெஞ்சத்தார் காதலவர்), would be scalded; in 1205 the same lodger is an intruder who should be ashamed (நாணார்கொல்) to keep coming where he gives no entry in return. The image passes from tender care in the days of union to reproach in separation.

1206: she exists only by remembering the days she had with him (உற்றநாள் உள்ள உளேன்), and asks what else she could live by. 1213: her life exists because she sees in dreams the man who gives nothing in waking (கனவினால் காண்டலின் உண்டென் உயிர்). Both make survival in separation depend on a mental substitute for his presence, memory by day and dream by night.

1206 says she lives by looking back at the days of union (உள்ள உளேன்). 1263 says she still lives by longing for his return (வரல் நசைஇ இன்னும் உளேன்). The same verb உளேன் is supported in one verse by the past and in the other by the expected future; Parimelazhagar on 1206 notes that the other supports, such as a messenger from him, are missing.

The two verses share the phrases மறப்பின் and மறப்பறியேன். In 1125 the man says he would remember her qualities only if he forgot them, and he does not know forgetting; in 1207 the woman, who also does not know forgetting, asks what would become of her if she did forget, when even remembering burns. The man's unforgetting is offered as proof of love, and the woman's as a pain she still prefers to the alternative.

In both verses the woman rejects the idea of forgetting him, which Parimelazhagar says the friend had advised in each case. 1207 asks what she would become if she forgot (மறப்பின் எவனாவன்); 1262 answers concretely that if she forgot today (இன்று மறப்பின்) her beauty would go and the bangles slip from her arms. Remembering hurts, but both verses hold that forgetting would be worse.

1207 says that even as she remembers, her heart is burned (உள்ளம் சுடும்). 1159 describes the same burning as a property of love's sickness: fire burns only when touched, and cannot burn when one moves away as love does (விடிற்சுடல் ஆற்றுமோ தீ). 1159 gives the general paradox of a fire that burns at a distance, and 1207 shows it at work inside memory.

The verses share the words நினை and காய். In 1208 the woman says that however much she thinks of him he is not angry (எனைத்து நினைப்பினும் காயார்), and that this is all the honour he does her. In 1320 the man reports that when he merely sits thinking and looks at her she is angry (நினைத்திருந்து நோக்கினும் காயும்) and asks whom he is thinking of. The absent lover tolerates everything because he is not there to care, while the present one is questioned about every thought.

1199 says that though the one she longs for gives nothing (நல்கார் எனினும்), even a word about him is sweet to her ear. 1208 measures what an ungiving lover leaves her more sharply: his whole gift (சிறப்பு) is that he does not object to being thought of. Parimelazhagar takes 1208 as scorn of the friend's promise that he will come and be kind, whereas Manakkudavar takes the not-being-angry as real grace.

In 1122 the man says the bond between him and her is like that between body and life (உடம்பொடு உயிரிடை). In 1209 the woman recalls him as the one who used to say 'we are not separate' (வேறல்லம் என்பார்) and says her sweet life is perishing (விளியுமென் இன்னுயிர்) as she thinks on his lack of tenderness. His figure of body and life is taken literally in her speech: with him gone, the life is leaving.

Both verses hold the lover to his earlier words. 1154 asks whether any fault lies with those who trusted the assurance of the one who was tender and said 'do not fear' (அளித்தஞ்சல் என்றவர்), if he then leaves. 1209 sets his saying 'we are not separate' against his present அளியின்மை, the absence of that same அளி. Parimelazhagar notes at 1209 that she says her life is going not because of the parting but because of his lovelessness.

Both verses address the moon and close with the same words, வாழி மதி. In 1118 the man tells the moon it could be loved if it shone like her face; in 1210 the woman asks the moon not to set (படாஅதி), so that she may see with her eyes the man who went without leaving her heart. The man treats the moon as a rival to her face and the woman treats it as a way to reach him.

1170 says that if her eyes could go where he is, as her mind does (உள்ளம்போன்று உள்வழிச் செல்கிற்பின்), they would not be swimming in tears. 1210 looks for a way round that limit: on Parimelazhagar's reading, since both of them look at the moon, her eyes meet his there (கண்ணினால் காண). Manakkudavar reads it differently, as a complaint that the moon will not set and let her sleep and see him in a dream.

Both verses end on the word விருந்து, a feast. In 1211 the woman (for Parimelazhagar) asks what feast she can make for the dream that came bringing her lover's messenger (யாதுசெய் வேன்கொல் விருந்து). In 1268 the man, away on the king's work, looks forward to the evening feast at home once the king has won (மாலை அயர்கம் விருந்து). The real feast waits on his return, and meanwhile she can offer hospitality only to a dream.

In 1211 the dream arrives as the carrier of his message (காதலர் தூதொடு வந்த கனவு). In 1212 she wants to use the dream in the other direction: if her eyes would sleep, she would herself declare to him that she survives (உயலுண்மை சாற்றுவேன்). Parimelazhagar says this is spoken when she was thinking of sending a messenger, and that she would tell him in full what she would hold back from one.

1212 makes everything depend on a condition: if her eyes would sleep when she begs them (யானிரப்பத் துஞ்சின்). 1179 says why the condition fails: her eyes do not sleep when he does not come and do not sleep when he does (வாராக்கால் துஞ்சா வரின்துஞ்சா). Set beside chapter 122, this shows that the dream which consoles her in the following verses is not available to her at will.

1162 says she cannot hide this sickness, and telling it to the one who caused it brings shame (உரைத்தலும் நாணுத் தரும்); Parimelazhagar takes the telling there to mean sending a messenger. In 1212 she is ready to proclaim her state to him herself (சாற்றுவேன்), but only in a dream. The shame that blocks the message in waking life does not apply to speech in a dream.

1198 says no one in the world is harder than those who go on living without getting even a kind word from the one they love (வாழ்வாரின் வன்கணார் இல்). 1213 has the woman living on though he gives her nothing in waking life (நனவினால் நல்காதவரை), and explains it: her life exists because she sees him in dreams (கனவினால் காண்டலின்). The second verse answers the first's charge of hardness by naming what keeps her alive.

1170 regrets that her eyes cannot travel to where he is as her mind can. In 1214 the dream does the travelling: it seeks out the man who gives nothing in waking life and brings him (நல்காரை நாடித் தரற்கு), and so there is pleasure in the dream. Parimelazhagar spells it out: the dream goes to the country he went to, finds him and delivers him.

1201 says love gives a joy that does not end even in recollection (உள்ளினும் தீரா). 1215 says that what she saw in waking was sweet then, and the dream too is sweet just while it is seen (கண்ட பொழுதே இனிது). Manakkudavar glosses both pleasures as lasting for that moment; Parimelazhagar takes her point to be that dream and waking are therefore equal for her. On either reading the woman's sweetness is tied to the moment of seeing, where the man's persists in thought.

In 1216 the woman says that if there were no such thing as waking, her lover would not leave her in the dream (கனவினால் காதலர் நீங்கலர் மன்). In 1329 the man, in the middle of a lovers' quarrel, wishes the night would lengthen so that he can go on pleading (நீடுக மன்னோ இரா). Both wish away the end of the night and both close on the wistful particle மன்; hers is said of a dream meeting and his of a real one.

1169 calls the long nights of separation crueller than the cruel man himself (கொடியார் கொடுமையின் தாம்கொடிய). 1216 wants the night's state never to end, with waking itself abolished (நனவென ஒன்றில்லை ஆயின்). The difference is sleep: the night is an enemy when she lies awake and a refuge when it brings the dream, and Parimelazhagar accordingly has her call waking a villain (பாவி).

The two verses open with nearly the same words, நனவினால் நல்காதவரை and நனவினால் நல்காக் கொடியார், and reach opposite verdicts on the dream. In 1213 seeing him in dreams keeps her alive; in 1217 she asks why the cruel one torments her in dreams (எம்மைப் பீழிப்பது). Parimelazhagar places 1217 after she has woken and found him gone, so the dream comforts while it lasts and wounds once it has ended.

819, on bad friendship, says the tie with those whose deeds are one thing and words another is bitter even in a dream (கனவினும் இன்னாது). In 1217 the lover who gives nothing in waking life hurts her in her dreams as well (கனவினால் ... பீழிப்பது). Both take the dream as the last place a person's unreliability should reach, and both find that it reaches there: one verse in the book of polity, the other in a lover's complaint.

Both verses describe the same event: he is with her in sleep and gone on waking. In 1217 this is his cruelty; Parimelazhagar explains the torment as his being on her shoulder in the dream and vanishing when she wakes. In 1218 she tells it in his favour: asleep he is on her shoulder (தோள்மேலர்), and awake he hurries into her heart (நெஞ்சத்தர் ஆவர் விரைந்து), so he never leaves her at all. Parimelazhagar says 1218 is her defence of him after the friend had spoken against him.

1218 says that on waking he quickly becomes one who is in her heart (நெஞ்சத்தர் ஆவர்). 1249 tells her own heart that the lover is inside it (உள்ளத்தார் காதலவர்), so there is no one to go out looking for. Both use his dwelling in her heart to deny that he is absent; 1218 adds the dream so that both night and day are covered.

The two verses have the same construction: an opinion is held only by those who lack an experience. In 66, 'the flute is sweet, the lute is sweet' is said by those who have not heard their own children's prattle (மழலைச்சொல் கேளாதவர்). In 1219 those who blame the man for giving nothing in waking life are those who have not seen a lover in dreams (கனவினால் காதலர்க் காணாதவர்). Parental love in the first book and a lover's dream in the third both discredit a judgment by pointing to what its holders have not known.

In 1140 the woman says the ignorant laugh in her sight because they have not suffered what she has (யாம்பட்ட தாம்படா ஆறு). In 1219 others blame her lover because they have never seen a lover in dreams. In both she rejects outsiders' judgment of her love on the ground that they lack her experience; in 1140 what they lack is her suffering, in 1219 her consolation.

1236: with bangles and arms slackening, what pains her is hearing him called cruel (அவரைக் கொடியர் எனக்கூறல் நொந்து). 1219 goes from that pain to a rebuttal: those who blame him (நோவர்) are people who have not seen a lover in their dreams. Parimelazhagar gives both verses the same occasion, the friend speaking ill of the man, and says she puts her reply in 1219 on strangers out of displeasure with the friend.

Both verses set the town (இவ்வூர்) against the woman's private evidence. In 1130 the town says he is loveless and lives apart, while he lives gladly in her heart always; in 1220 the townspeople say he has left her in waking life (நனவினால் நம்நீத்தார்), and she asks whether they do not see him in dreams. The town's report is confined to what can be observed, and she appeals each time to something only she can witness.

In 1188 the woman complains that people only say 'she has gone pale' and no one says 'he has abandoned her' (துறந்தார் அவர் என்பார் இல்). In 1220 the townspeople do say he has left her (நம்நீத்தார் என்பர்) and she objects to it. The conflict holds only if 1188 is read as her wanting the blame to fall on him, and both are speeches of a moment, not doctrine: she resents his being excused and resents his being accused.

334 says what shows itself as a 'day' (நாளென ஒன்றுபோற் காட்டி) is a blade that saws through life (உயிர் ஈரும் வாள்), for those who perceive it. 1221 has the parted woman tell the hour it is not evening (மாலையோ அல்லை) but a thing that eats the life of those once wed (உயிருண்ணும் வேலை; Parimelazhagar takes வேலை as a final hour, Manakkudavar and Kalaignar as a spear). Both unmask a unit of time as something that consumes life, one as a general truth of impermanence, the other as one lover's experience of separation.

326 calls Death 'the life-eating' (உயிருண்ணுங் கூற்று) and says it does not advance on the days of one who does not kill. 1221 gives the same epithet, உயிருண்ணும், to the evening that comes on women parted from their husbands. The pairing shows the woman addressing evening in the book's own language for Death; Parimelazhagar's note on 1229 says she thinks of evening as கூற்றம்.

In 1168 the woman pities the night, which puts all living beings to sleep and has no companion but her (என்னல்லது இல்லை துணை). In 1222 she tells the dim evening it looks sad-eyed (புன்கண்ணை) and asks whether its partner too is hard-eyed like hers (எம்கேள்போல் வன்கண்ணதோ நின் துணை). In both she treats a time of day as a fellow sufferer and asks about its துணை, the one thing she herself lacks.

1223 says the evening that used to come budding with chill and looking wan (பனி அரும்பிப் பைதல்கொள் மாலை) now comes with revulsion budding and sorrow growing (துனி அரும்பித் துன்பம் வளர). 1227 says her sickness buds in the morning (காலை அரும்பி), swells through the day and opens in the evening. Both use அரும்பு, budding, for her pain, and together they give evening as both what brings the bud and when it opens.

1169 says the long nights now passing are crueller than the cruelty of the cruel one (கொடியார் கொடுமையின் தாம்கொடிய). 1224 says that where her lover is absent (காதலர் இல்வழி) evening comes like ஏதிலர், pitiless strangers or foes, on a killing ground (கொலைக்களத்து). Both make a stretch of time into a cruel agent set beside human cruelty, and 1224 names the condition: it is so only in his absence.

319 states a rule: hurt done to others in the forenoon (முற்பகல்) comes back to oneself in the afternoon (பிற்பகல்), of itself. In 1225 the woman asks what good she did to morning (காலைக்குச் செய்த நன்று) and what enmity she did to evening (மாலைக்குச் செய்த பகை). Her question assumes the same logic of return, that suffering answers something one did, and finds no deed of hers to explain evening's hostility.

In 1083 the man says he did not know before what Death was and now knows (பண்டறியேன் ... இனியறிந்தேன்): it has a woman's nature and warring eyes. In 1226 the woman says that while her husband had not left (மணந்தார் அகலாத காலை) she did not know that evening causes pain (அறிந்ததிலேன்). Both speakers mark love as a before and after in what they know, he at first sight and she at separation.

1147 says this sickness grows long (நீளும் இந் நோய்) with the town's gossip as manure and her mother's words as water. 1227 says this sickness (இந் நோய்) buds in the morning, is a swelling bud all day and blossoms in the evening (காலை அரும்பி ... மாலை மலரும்). Both speak of love's sickness as a plant; 1147 names what feeds it and 1227 gives its daily cycle.

In 1135 the man says the girl has given him the palmyra horse and the anguish suffered at evening (மாலை உழக்கும் துயர்). In 1227 the woman says her sickness blossoms at evening (மாலை மலரும்). The man in courtship and the woman in separation both place the height of love's pain at evening; Parimelazhagar's note on 1135 explains it by saying love blooms at evening, the image of 1227.

66 says only those who have not heard their own children's prattle call the flute sweet (குழல் இனிது). In 1228 the herdsman's flute (ஆயன் குழல்) has become the messenger of the fire-like evening and a weapon that kills (கொல்லும் படை). In both the flute's sweetness depends on the hearer: surpassed for the parent, and turned to pain for the parted woman; Parimelazhagar notes the flute had been sweet to her before.

In 1258 the woman says the soft speech (பணிமொழி) of her deceiving lover is the weapon that breaks her womanly reserve (பெண்மை உடைக்கும் படை). In 1228 the herdsman's flute is a weapon that kills (கொல்லும் படை). Both call a gentle sound a படை, one because it draws her to him and the other because it announces the evening without him.

In 1168 the night has put all living beings to sleep (மன்னுயிர் எல்லாம் துயிற்றி) and she alone is its companion, so her suffering is solitary. In 1229 she says that when evening spreads, bewildering the mind (மதிமருண்டு; Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar take this as her own mind), the whole town is bewildered and suffers (பதிமருண்டு பைதல் உழக்கும்). The two speeches picture the world around her in opposite ways, asleep and untouched in one and sharing her distress in the other.

In 1209 the woman says her dear life is perishing (விளியும் என் இன்னுயிர்) as she thinks much on the lack of kindness of one who said they were not separate. In 1230 her life, which had not died till now (மாயா உயிர்), is dying in the dim evening as she thinks of the man whose nature is wealth (பொருள்மாலையாளரை உள்ளி). Both say that thinking of him is what wears her life away, and each names him by a reproach: his broken word in one, his preference for wealth in the other.

In 1263 she says he left desiring victory with his own resolve as companion (உரன் நசைஇ உள்ளம் துணையாகச் சென்றார்), and that she still lives by desiring his return (வரல் நசைஇ இன்னும் உளேன்). In 1230 thinking of the man given to wealth makes her life die. Both name him by the aim he left for, but in one speech the thought of him keeps her alive and in the other it kills; these are two moments of the same speaker, not a doctrine.

In 1114 the man says that blue lilies, if they could see, would bow and look at the ground, saying they cannot match her eyes (கண்ணொவ்வேம் என்று). In 1231 the friend says that as she thinks of the man gone far, her eyes have grown ashamed before fragrant flowers (நறுமலர் நாணின கண்). Separation reverses the earlier praise: the flowers once shamed by her eyes now shame them, which is how Parimelazhagar glosses 1231.

71 says love cannot be bolted in, because the small tears of the loving make it public (புன்கணீர் பூசல் தரும்). 1232 says her eyes, pale and running with tears (பசந்து பனிவாரும் கண்), seem to tell of the unkindness of the one she desired (நல்காமை சொல்லுவ போலும்). The same mechanism, tears that disclose, works in both; in 71 they reveal the weeper's love, in 1232 they also accuse the absent lover.

In 1180 the woman says the town easily learns the secret of those like her whose eyes are beaten drums (அறைபறை கண்ணார்). In 1232 the friend says her pale, weeping eyes seem to be telling of his unkindness. Both treat the eyes as announcing what she would keep hidden; the woman says it of herself and the friend says it to urge her to bear up, as Parimelazhagar frames it.

In 1157 the woman asks whether the bangles slipping past her wrist do not proclaim (தூற்றாகொல்) that the lord of the shore has left her. In 1233 the shoulders that swelled on the day of union (மணந்தநாள் வீங்கிய தோள்) seem to announce fully that he has parted (தணந்தமை சால அறிவிப்ப போலும்). In both her body makes the separation public without her speaking; 1233 adds the contrast with how the same shoulders looked at union.

In 1277 her bangles understood before she did that the lord of the cool shore had parted (தணந்தமை ... முன்னம் உணர்ந்த வளை). In 1233 her shoulders announce that he has parted, with the same word தணந்தமை. In 1277 the body is first to know of the parting, and in 1233 it is the one that tells others.

1234 and 1235 share the line தொல்கவின் வாடிய தோள், shoulders whose old beauty has faded. 1234 describes the loss: with her partner gone (துணை நீங்கி) they have lost their fullness and the bangles slip. 1235 turns the same shoulders into testimony that declares the cruelty of the cruel one (கொடியார் கொடுமை உரைக்கும்), so the repeated line moves from description to accusation.

In 1262 the woman tells her friend that if she forgets him today (இன்று மறப்பின்), her beauty will leave her shoulders and her ornaments will slip off (கலங்கழியும் காரிகை நீத்து). In 1234 the beauty has faded and the bangles are slipping because her partner is gone (துணை நீங்கி). Read together, the bodily loss follows his absence whether she remembers or forgets, though in 1262 she holds that remembering is what prevents it.

In 1235 the friend, in Parimelazhagar's reading, says the shoulders with bangles lost and old beauty faded declare the cruelty of the cruel one (கொடியார் கொடுமை உரைக்கும்). In 1236 the woman answers that with bangles and shoulders slackening, what pains her is the saying that he is cruel (அவரைக் கொடியர் எனக்கூறல் நொந்து). The second verse limits the first: the body's evidence stands, but she refuses the charge drawn from it.

In 1188 the woman complains that people say only 'she has grown pale' and no one says 'he has left her' (துறந்தார் அவர் என்பார் இல்). In 1235 the wasted shoulders themselves declare his cruelty. One speech says the visible change brings talk about her alone, and the other says the same kind of change speaks against him; the difference is in who is reading the body, the town or the friend.

In 1190 the woman says it is good to be called pale, if only they will not proclaim the unkindness of the man who won her (நல்காமை தூற்றார் எனின்). In 1236 she says that as bangles and shoulders slacken, she is hurt by his being called cruel (கொடியர் எனக்கூறல் நொந்து). In both she accepts the damage to her body and resists blame of him; Parimelazhagar gives both as replies to the friend's faulting of the man.

In 1169 the woman herself speaks of the cruelty of the cruel one (கொடியார் கொடுமை) when she says the long nights are crueller still. In 1236 she is pained when he is called cruel (கொடியர்). The pair shows that she uses the word in her own lament and does not accept it from another's mouth; these are different moments of a dramatised speaker, not a contradiction in teaching.

In 1200 the woman tells her heart that it wants to tell its great pain to one who is not close (உறாஅர்க்கு உறுநோய் உரைப்பாய்), and that it might as well fill up the sea. In 1237 she asks her heart whether it will win honour (பாடு பெறுதியோ) by telling the 'cruel' one of the outcry over her wasting shoulders (வாடுதோட் பூசல் உரைத்து). Both address the heart as a possible messenger to him; 1200 dismisses the errand as futile, while 1237, as Parimelazhagar reads it, urges the heart to go, with கொடியார் used as other people's word for him.

In 1162 she says she cannot hide this sickness, and that telling it to the one who caused it brings shame (உரைத்தலும் நாணுத் தரும்). In 1237 she asks her heart whether it can gain honour by telling him of her wasting shoulders. The two give opposite values to the same act of telling him, shame in one and possible honour (பாடு) in the other; in 1237 it is the heart and not she herself who would carry the word.

In 1187 the woman says she lay embracing him and shifted a little (புல்லிக் கிடந்தேன் புடைபெயர்ந்தேன்), and at that the pallor could be scooped up. In 1238 the man recalls that when he loosened the arms that held her (முயங்கிய கைகளை ஊக்க), her forehead turned pale (பசந்தது ... நுதல்). The same event, pallor at the slightest slackening of an embrace, is told once by her and once by him.

1186 says pallor watches for a weak point in her husband's embrace (முயக்கற்றம் பார்க்கும் பசப்பு) as darkness watches for a lamp to fail. 1238 gives an instance from the man's memory: he loosened his embracing arms and her forehead paled. The simile of 1186 states the rule, and 1238 shows it happening; Parimelazhagar has the man go on to ask what a real separation will do.

In 1108 the man says that for two who desire each other, an embrace that no breeze can split is sweet (வளியிடை போழப் படாஅ முயக்கு). In 1239 he recalls that when a cool breeze did split their embrace (முயக்கிடைத் தண்வளி போழ), her large cool eyes turned pale. The same words, வளி, போழ் and முயக்கு, return: what was the measure of closeness in union becomes the smallest possible separation and already brings pallor.

1238 says that when he loosened the embracing arms her forehead turned pale. 1240 says the pallor of her eyes itself came to distress (கண்ணின் பசப்போ பருவரல் எய்தின்றே) on seeing what the bright forehead had done (ஒண்ணுதல் செய்தது கண்டு). 1240 depends on 1238 for what the forehead did; Parimelazhagar explains that the eyes' pallor was abashed that the forehead had paled sooner than they did, at a smaller cause.

In 1182 the woman says pallor spreads and rides over her body with the pride (தகையால்) that he was the one who gave it. In 1240 the man says the pallor of her eyes felt distress (பருவரல்) on seeing what her forehead had done. Both give the pallor feelings of its own, pride in one and distress in the other, so that பசப்பு is spoken of as a party to the love and not only its symptom.

In 1102 the man says that medicines for other ailments are things other than the ailment (பிணிக்கு மருந்து பிற), but she is herself the medicine for the sickness she causes (தன்நோய்க்குத் தானே மருந்து). In 1241 the woman, apart from him, asks her heart to think of any medicine at all (எனைத்தொன்றும் ... மருந்து) for her sickness. Read together, 1102 explains why her heart has nothing to offer: the only cure is the absent person who caused the illness.

1195 asks what those we love can do for us if they do not love in return (தாம் காதல் கொள்ளாக் கடை). 1242 draws the conclusion and turns it on her own heart: since he has no love (காதல் அவரிலர் ஆக), its suffering is folly (நோவது பேதைமை). The first states the uselessness of one-sided love, the second names persisting in it as foolishness.

1308, which Parimelazhagar gives to the man during a sulk, asks what use suffering is where there is no lover who recognises that one suffers (நோதல் எவன் ... அஃதறியும் காதலர் இல்லா வழி). 1242 has the woman tell her heart that suffering is folly when he has no love (நோவது பேதைமை). Both speakers, from either side of the relationship, make pain depend for its point on the other's loving awareness of it.

1243 asks the heart why it sits and suffers in thought (இருந்துள்ளி என் பரிதல்) when he has no pitying thought. 1296 says that when she sits alone and thinks (தனியே இருந்து நினைத்தக்கால்) her heart is there only to eat her (என்னைத் தினிய). Both describe sitting and remembering as self-inflicted harm, and each blames the heart for it.

1204 asks whether she too is in his heart, since he is always in hers (யாமும் உளேங்கொல் அவர் நெஞ்சத்து). 1243 gives her own bleak answer: a compassionate thought of her does not exist in the one who caused the sickness (பரிந்துள்ளல் பைதல்நோய் செய்தார்கண் இல்). The question of 1204 has by chapter 125 become a settled premise for scolding her heart.

1170 says that if her eyes could travel to where he is as her heart does (உள்ளம் போன்று உள்வழிச் செல்கிற்பின்), they would not be swimming in tears. 1244 turns the same contrast into a request: heart, take the eyes with you when you go (கண்ணும் கொளச் சேறி), because left behind they consume her with wanting to see him. Both rest on the idea that the heart can reach him by thought and the eyes cannot.

In 1244 the eyes eat her (இவை என்னைத் தின்னும்) in their longing to see him; in 1296 it is the heart that stays in order to eat her (என்னைத் தினிய இருந்தது என் நெஞ்சு). The same verb of being devoured is applied to two of her own faculties, so that between the two verses neither eyes nor heart is on her side.

1283 says that though he disregards her and does only as he pleases, her eyes will not rest without seeing him (கொண்கனைக் காணாது அமையல கண்). 1244 says the eyes, wanting to see him (அவர்க் காணல் உற்று), eat her. Both make the eyes an appetite of their own that her judgment of him does not govern.

1245 asks the heart whether one can abandon as an enemy (செற்றார் எனக் கைவிடல் உண்டோ) the man who does not respond when she draws close (யாம் உற்றால் உறாஅதவர்). 1292 complains that the heart, even having seen that he is not close (உறாஅதவர்க் கண்ட கண்ணும்), goes to him on the thought that he will not be hostile (செறாஅர் என). The two share the pair உறாதவர் / செறு, and show the same refusal to treat coldness as enmity, once owned by her and once blamed on the heart.

807, on old friendship, says that those whose bond came by the way of love do not cut off love even when ruinous things are done to them (அழிவந்த செய்யினும் அன்பறார்). 1245 asks whether she can let him go as an enemy merely because he does not return her closeness. The logic of long friendship in the Book of Wealth, that injury does not license abandonment, reappears as a lover's rhetorical question.

1246 tells the heart that when it sees the lover it cannot even sulk and then be reconciled (புலந்துணராய்), so its present anger is a false heat (பொய்க்காய்வு காய்தி). 1294 makes the same charge: the heart will not first raise a quarrel and then enjoy (துனிசெய்து துவ்வாய்), so no one will plan with it. In both the heart is accused of being incapable of the sulk it pretends to.

1286 says that when she sees him she sees no faults, and when she does not see him she sees nothing but faults (காணுங்கால் காணேன் தவறாய காணாக்கால் காணேன் தவறல்லவை). 1246 calls the heart's anger in his absence false because it never survives the sight of him (காதலர்க் கண்டால் புலந்துணராய்). 1286 states the pattern plainly; 1246 uses it to discredit the anger felt while apart.

1163 pictures desire and shame hanging from the two ends of a carrying pole that is her life, in a body that cannot bear them (காமமும் நாணும் உயிர் காவாத் தூங்கும் என் நோனா உடம்பின்). 1247 states the same double load without the image and asks her heart to drop one of them, since she cannot bear both (யானோ பொறேன் இவ்விரண்டு). The earlier verse describes the balance; this one asks for it to end.

1247 leaves open which of desire and shame is to go (காமம் விடு ஒன்றோ நாண் விடு). 1251, opening the next chapter, reports the outcome: the axe of desire breaks the door of restraint that shame had bolted (காமக் கணிச்சி உடைக்கும் ... நாணுத்தாழ் வீழ்த்த கதவு). The choice she offers her heart in 1247 is settled in 1251 by force, not by decision.

1248 calls the heart a fool for going after the man who left (பிரிந்தவர் பின்செல்வாய்) while grieving that he gives no grace. 1293 asks the heart whether it follows him as it likes (பெட்டாங்கு அவர் பின் செலல்) because the ruined have no friends. Both speak of the heart 'going behind him' as a desertion of her that she can see but not stop.

967, on honour, says that being called ruined is better than living by going behind those who do not accept one (ஒட்டார் பின் சென்று ஒருவன் வாழ்தலின்); Parimelazhagar takes this of following scorners for gain. 1248 calls her heart a fool for going behind the one who left without grace (பிரிந்தவர் பின்செல்வாய் பேதை). The standard of honour from the Book of Wealth is the one she applies to her own heart, though in love she cannot enforce it.

1128 says that because her lover is in her heart (நெஞ்சத்தார் காதலவராக) she fears to eat anything hot lest he be scalded. 1249 uses almost the same clause (உள்ளத்தார் காதலவராக) to ask the heart whom it goes out to look for. The conceit that was playful tenderness during union becomes, in separation, an argument against the heart's wandering.

1130 says he lives gladly in her heart always (உவந்துறைவர் உள்ளத்துள் என்றும்) while the town says he lives apart and is a stranger. 1249 asks her heart to whom it is going when he is inside it. In 1130 the town fails to know where he really dwells; in 1249 her own heart is the one that acts as if it did not know.

In 1250 she says that if she keeps in her heart the man who left without coming close (துறந்தாரை நெஞ்சத்து உடையேமா), she will lose still more beauty (இன்னும் இழத்தும் கவின்); Parimelazhagar frames this as a case for forgetting him. In 1262 she tells her friend that if she forgets him today, beauty will leave her and the bangles slip from her arms (இன்று மறப்பின் ... கலங்கழியும் காரிகை நீத்து). The two speeches give opposite accounts of whether remembering or forgetting costs her beauty; both are a speaker's words in the moment, and the conflict holds on Parimelazhagar's reading of the settings.

1207 says she does not know how to forget, and that even remembering burns her heart (உள்ளினும் உள்ளம் சுடும்). 1250 says that holding him in her heart will cost her yet more beauty. Both count remembering him as a harm to herself, while 1207 adds that forgetting is not available to her.

71 asks whether there is any bolt that can shut love in (அன்பிற்கும் உண்டோ அடைக்குந்தாழ்), since the tears of the loving proclaim it. 1251 uses the same word தாழ்: shame is the bolt on the door of restraint, and the axe of desire breaks the door (நாணுத்தாழ் வீழ்த்த கதவு). In the Book of Virtue affection cannot be bolted in and that is to its credit; in the Book of Love the bolt exists and its breaking is told as her defeat.

In 1134 the man says the fierce flood of desire carries off the raft of shame and manliness (காமக் கடும்புனல் உய்க்கும் நாணொடு நல்லாண்மை என்னும் புணை). In 1251 the woman says the axe of desire breaks the door of restraint bolted by shame. The two verses are built alike, with desire as a force and shame as the device that fails against it, once for the man and once for the woman.

57 says that guarding women by confinement achieves nothing and the guard their own நிறை keeps is the best (மகளிர் நிறைகாக்கும் காப்பே தலை). 1251 has a woman say that this very நிறை, pictured as a door bolted by shame, is broken by desire for her husband. The dramatised speech shows the inner guard of 57 at its limit, though here what breaks it is love for her own partner and not a lapse of fidelity.

1167 says she swims the flood of desire and sees no shore, and even at midnight only she is awake (யாமத்தும் யானே உளேன்). 1252 says desire has no pity (கண் இன்று), for it sets her heart to work even at midnight (யாமத்தும் ஆளும் தொழில்). Both mark midnight, when Parimelazhagar notes all others rest, as the hour that shows desire does not release her.

In 1136 the man says his eyes cannot close because of her, so even at midnight he thinks of mounting the palmyra horse (மடலூர்தல் யாமத்தும் உள்ளுவேன்). In 1252 the woman says desire rules and works her heart even at midnight. The sleepless midnight belongs to both sexes: for him it produces a plan for public display, for her an inward servitude.

1161 and 1253 open with the same words, 'I would hide it' (மறைப்பேன்மன் யான்). In 1161 the sickness rises like spring water the more one bales it (இறைப்பவர்க்கு ஊற்றுநீர் போல மிகும்); in 1253 desire shows itself like a sneeze without her intending it (குறிப்பின்றித் தும்மல் போல் தோன்றிவிடும்). One image gives the pressure that grows under concealment, the other the sudden involuntary release.

1253 likens desire to a sneeze that appears without one's intending it; Parimelazhagar glosses that it cannot be held in. In 1318 the man does stifle a sneeze (தும்முச் செறுப்ப), and she weeps that he is hiding from her that his people are thinking of him. The sneeze is in both an involuntary sign of what is within, and 1318 shows that even suppressing it is read as a disclosure.

1138 says desire does not consider that they are firm in restraint or deserve pity, but passes beyond secrecy and comes out in public (காமம் மறையிறந்து மன்று படும்). 1254 ends with the same words (என் காமம் மறையிறந்து மன்று படும்) after her admission that she used to call herself one who had restraint (நிறையுடையேன் என்பேன்). The general statement in 1138 becomes in 1254 her own experience of being proved wrong about herself.

1180 says it is not hard for the town to get the secret of those like her, whose eyes are beaten drums (அறைபறை கண்ணார்). 1254 says her desire goes past concealment into the public place (மன்று படும்). 1180 supplies a means by which the exposure described in 1254 happens: her own eyes announce it.

966, on honour, asks what is gained by going and standing behind those who scorn one (இகழ்வார் பின் சென்று நிலை), since it brings neither fame nor heaven. 1255 says the dignity of not going after those who have turned hostile (செற்றார் பின் செல்லாப் பெருந்தகைமை) is something the lovesick do not know. 1255 names the standard of the honour chapter as a real greatness and then places the lover outside its reach; Parimelazhagar takes 'going after' here as unbroken thinking of him.

1245 asks whether she can abandon as hostile (செற்றார் எனக் கைவிடல் உண்டோ) the man who does not answer her love. 1255 turns that private question into a general statement: not following the hostile (செற்றார் பின் செல்லா) is a dignity unknown to those with love's sickness (காமநோய் உற்றார் அறிவதொன்று அன்று). The word செற்றார் links them, and the second explains why the first could only be a rhetorical question.

1255 states in general terms that the lovesick do not know the dignity of not going after one who is hostile. 1256 applies it to herself with irony: how gracious (அளித்தரோ) is this grief, which wants her to go after the one who is hostile (செற்றவர் பின் சேறல் வேண்டி). The pair moves from a maxim about lovers to her own case, and Parimelazhagar reads அளித்து as mockery.

In 1168 she calls the night அளித்து, pitiable or kindly, because having put every living thing to sleep it has no companion but her. In 1256 she uses the same word of her grief (அளித்தரோ ... துயர்), which Parimelazhagar takes as scorn. In both she speaks to her tormentor in the language of grace and pity, which is how these monologues voice bitterness.

1297 says that, caught up with a foolish heart that cannot forget him, she has forgotten even shame (நாணும் மறந்தேன்). 1257 says she knows nothing of a thing called shame (நாண் என ஒன்றோ அறியலம்) when the one she cherishes does out of desire what she longs for. The two verses give the same loss of shame from two moments, separation in 1297 and reunion in 1257.

In 1247 she cannot bear desire and shame together and asks her heart to give up one (காமம் விடு ஒன்றோ நாண் விடு). In 1257 the matter is settled in his presence: when he does what she longs for, shame is simply not known to her. The conflict that is unbearable in his absence does not arise once he is there.

1258 asks whether the humble speech of that thief of many deceptions is not the weapon that breaks their womanhood (பெண்மை உடைக்கும் படை), which Parimelazhagar glosses as her restraint. 1324 says that within the sulk itself arises the weapon that breaks 'my' heart (உள்ளம் உடைக்கும் படை); Parimelazhagar gives it to the woman. The shared phrase உடைக்கும் படை frames her resolve as a fortification, attacked from outside by his words in 1258 and from inside the quarrel in 1324.

985 says that bowing is the strength of those who accomplish things and the weapon by which the worthy turn their opponents (பணிதல் ... மாற்றாரை மாற்றும் படை). 1258 calls her lover's lowly speech (பணிமொழி) the weapon that breaks her firmness. Humility as a படை is praised in the ethics of the worthy, and in the love poems the woman sees the same device used on her and calls its user a thief.

555 asks whether the tears of those who suffer under a ruler are not the weapon that wears away his wealth (கண்ணீர் அன்றே செல்வத்தைத் தேய்க்கும் படை). 1258 has the same form of question: are his humble words not the weapon that breaks our womanhood (பணிமொழி அன்றோ ... உடைக்கும் படை). In both a soft thing, tears or gentle speech, is named as the real weapon against something that looks strong.

1284 tells her friend that she went intending to sulk, but her heart forgot that and went to unite (ஊடற்கண் சென்றேன் ... கூடற்கண் சென்றது என் நெஞ்சு). 1259 tells the same event with one more step: she went away meaning to sulk (புலப்பல் எனச் சென்றேன்) and embraced him on seeing her heart begin to join him (நெஞ்சம் கலத்தல் உறுவது கண்டு). In 1284 the heart acts alone; in 1259 she watches it and gives in.

1290 gives the man's account: she sulked with her eyes only and then, more eager than he for the embrace, lost her composure (புல்லுதல் என்னினும் தான் விதுப்புற்று). 1259 gives hers: she set out to sulk and embraced him (புலப்பல் எனச் சென்றேன் புல்லினேன்). The two verses report the collapse of a sulk from each side and agree on what happened.

1267, spoken while he is still away, asks whether on his return she will sulk, embrace, or do both (புலப்பேன்கொல் புல்லுவேன் கொல்லோ கலப்பேன்கொல்). 1259 is the answer after the fact: she intended the first and did the second (புலப்பல் எனச் சென்றேன் புல்லினேன்). The same two verbs carry the plan in one verse and its failure in the other.

1287 asks what use it is to sulk when one knows the sulk will prove false (பொய்த்தல் அறிந்து என் புலந்து), like those who jump into a stream knowing it will carry them off. 1260 asks whether those with hearts like fat put in fire (நிணம் தீயில் இட்டன்ன நெஞ்சினார்) can ever say they will hold out in a sulk. One image is of being swept away and the other of melting, and both conclude that the sulk cannot be sustained.

1259 narrates one occasion: she went away to sulk and embraced him when she saw her heart joining him. 1260 turns it into a general question about people whose hearts melt like fat in fire, and whether 'we will stand in a sulk' (ஊடி நிற்பேம் எனல்) is even open to them. The second verse gives the reason for the first.

1261 shows the woman's finger worn (தேய்ந்த விரல்) from marking the days since he left (அவர்சென்ற நாளொற்றி); 1269 says that for those pining with the return day in mind (வருநாள்வைத்து ஏங்குபவர்க்கு) one day passes like seven. 1269 gives the felt arithmetic behind 1261's tally: the days she counts are each lived as many.

In 776 the warrior takes up his days (தன் நாளை எடுத்து) and files every day without a wound as wasted; in 1261 the wife marks off the days of his absence (நாளொற்றி) until her finger wears down. Both keep a ledger of days, the soldier's reckoned by wounds received and the waiting wife's by absence endured.

In 1262 she tells her friend that if she forgets him today (இன்று மறப்பின்) her beauty will go and her bangles slip; in 1207 she asks what would become of her if she forgot (மறப்பின் எவனாவன்), since even remembering burns. Parimelazhagar frames both as replies to a friend's advice to forget a little, and both refuse it: remembering hurts, but forgetting would be worse.

1262 says forgetting him would cost her her beauty (காரிகை நீத்து); 1250 says that keeping in her heart the man who left (நெஞ்சத்து உடையேமா) will make her lose still more of her loveliness (இன்னும் இழத்தும் கவின்), which Parimelazhagar takes as implying she ought to forget him. On that reading the two speeches assign the loss of beauty to opposite causes; both are the heroine's words in different moods, not the book's settled claim.

615 praises the man who wants the work and not pleasure (இன்பம் விழையான் வினைவிழைவான்) as a pillar to his kin; in 1263 the wife describes her husband as gone desiring victory with his own resolve for company (உரன்நசைஇ உள்ளம் துணையாக), which Parimelazhagar glosses as not desiring enjoyment. 1263 shows the same man from inside the house: she stays alive only by desiring his return (வரல்நசைஇ இன்னும் உளேன்), the same verb நசைஇ set against his.

In 1206 she lives only by thinking of the days she had with him (உற்றநாள் உள்ள உளேன்); in 1263 she is still alive by longing for his coming (வரல்நசைஇ இன்னும் உளேன்). The two give the same account of what keeps her alive in his absence, one looking back to memory and the other forward to return.

In 1263 she waits for the man who left wanting victory; in 1268, which Parimelazhagar assigns to the man away on the king's service, he wishes the king would engage and win (வினைகலந்து வென்றீக வேந்தன்) so that he can join his wife for the evening. On that reading the pair gives both ends of one separation: her longing for his return and his impatience for the work to finish.

476 warns that one who has climbed to the tip of a branch (நுனிக்கொம்பர் ஏறினார்) and pushes further loses his life; in 1264 her heart, thinking of his return, கோடுகொடு ஏறும், which Manakkudavar and Kalaignar read as climbing a tree's branches to look for him (Parimelazhagar reads it as swelling up like a tree putting out branches). On the climbing reading the same image marks reckless overreach in the book on statecraft and eager hope here.

In 1170 her heart goes to where he is, and she wishes her eyes could follow (உள்ளம்போன்று உள்வழிச் செல்கிற்பின்); in 1264 her heart rises thinking of his return (வரவுள்ளி). Both make the heart the part of her that moves toward him while she stays put; on Manakkudavar's reading of 1264 it even climbs to do the seeing her eyes cannot.

In 1187 pallor seizes her the moment she shifts a little in his embrace (புடைபெயர்ந்தேன் அவ்வளவில்); in 1265 she says the pallor on her shoulders will leave once she has seen him to her eyes' fill (கண்ணாரக் கண்டபின் நீங்கும்). Together they give pallor's rule in the Book of Love: it comes with the slightest distance and goes only with his presence, which Parimelazhagar underlines by noting that merely hearing of his return will not do.

1283 says her eyes will not rest without seeing her husband (கொண்கனைக் காணாது அமையல கண்) even though he does as he pleases; 1265 prays to see the same கொண்கன் until her eyes are full. Both make the eyes' need to see him the thing that must be satisfied before anything else can mend.

In 1102 the man says that medicine for a disease is normally something else, but she is herself the medicine for the sickness she causes (தன்நோய்க்குத் தானே மருந்து); in 1266 the woman says that if he comes for one day she will drink him in so that all her sickness is destroyed (பைதல்நோய் எல்லாம் கெட). Each lover names the other as both the cause and the only cure.

1101 says all five senses find their objects in her; in 1266 she will 'drink' him (பருகுவன்), which Parimelazhagar explains as drinking that nectar through all five gateways of sense. On his reading 1266 is the woman's version of 1101, with the five-sense enjoyment compressed into a single verb.

811 speaks of people without character who seem to drink you up (பருகுவார் போலினும்), which Parimelazhagar explains as an appearance of excess love; in 1266 she says she will drink him (பருகுவன்) when he comes. The same verb for devouring affection is a suspect show in bad friendship and a sincere vow in the wife's mouth.

1267 asks in advance whether she will sulk, embrace or mix the two when he comes (புலப்பேன்கொல் புல்லுவேன் கொல்லோ கலப்பேன்கொல்); 1259 reports what happened: she went meaning to sulk (புலப்பல் எனச்சென்றேன்) and embraced him (புல்லினேன்) on seeing her heart begin to join him. The same verbs recur, and 1259 reads as the answer to 1267's question.

1109 lists sulking, reconciling and uniting (ஊடல் உணர்தல் புணர்தல்) as the rewards of those joined in love; 1267 shows the woman, before he has even returned, unable to choose between sulking and embracing and wondering whether to combine them. What 1109 states as a sequence of pleasures, 1267 shows as one impatient wish for all of them at once, which is how Parimelazhagar explains its place in this chapter.

In 1224 evening, when the lover is absent (காதலர் இல்வழி), comes like enemies onto a killing ground; in 1268 the speaker looks forward to an evening feast once the king has won and the couple are together at home (மனைகலந்து மாலை அயர்கம் விருந்து). The pair shows that evening's cruelty in chapter 123 belongs to separation and not to the hour: the same மாலை is the time set for celebration when they are reunited.

1269 says one day passes like seven (ஒருநாள் எழுநாள்போல்) for those awaiting the return day; in 1278 she says he left only yesterday (நெருநற்று) and she has been pale for seven days (எழுநாளேம்). Both use seven days to measure how separation distorts time, stretching a day of waiting in 1269 and running ahead of the departure itself in 1278.

1169 complains that the nights now pass long (நெடிய கழியும் இரா), crueller than the man himself; 1269 says a single day goes like seven for those who pine. Both say that separation lengthens time, by night in one and by day in the other.

In 1151 he is told to announce his quick return to those who will still be alive then (வல்வரவு வாழ்வார்க் குரை); 1270 asks what use getting or embracing is once the heart has broken and spilled (உள்ளம் உடைந்துக்கக் கால்). Both say a reunion that arrives too late is worth nothing; on Parimelazhagar's reading of 1270 the man himself now voices the warning that was put to him in 1151, while Manakkudavar gives 1270 to the woman.

709 says the eye itself tells enmity and friendship (கண்ணுரைக்கும்) to those who know its kinds; in 1271 the man tells her that though she hides it, her eyes have slipped her control and have something to say (உண்கண் உரைக்கல் உறுவது). The minister's skill of reading the eye in the book on statecraft is the lover's skill here, with the same verb உரை for what the eye does.

In 1180 the woman says the town easily learns the secret of those whose eyes are beaten drums (அறைபறை கண்ணார்); in 1271 the man says her eyes go beyond her hold (கையிகந்து) and speak though she conceals (கரப்பினும்). Both hold that the eyes publish what the person tries to keep hidden, said once by the woman of herself and once by the man reading her.

71 asks if there is any bolt to shut love in, since the small tears of the loving announce it (புன்கணீர் பூசல் தரும்); 1271 says her eyes tell something despite her concealment. The claim that affection cannot be locked away and that the eyes give it out appears in the book on virtue as a general truth about அன்பு and in the Book of Love as a scene.

1272 says this girl has a great measure of womanly nature (பெண்நிறைந்த நீர்மை பெரிது), which Parimelazhagar takes as artlessness beyond the usual; 1280 says that telling love's sickness with the eyes and pleading is womanhood added to womanhood (பெண்ணினால் பெண்மை உடைத்து). The chapter's first observation about her is given its content at the end: her womanliness is her saying it with the eyes and not in words.

706 says the face shows what fills the heart as crystal shows what is next to it (அடுத்தது காட்டும் பளிங்கு); 1273 says something shows through her beauty like the thread in strung gems (மணியில் திகழ்தரு நூல்), and Parimelazhagar specifies crystal beads. Both use a transparent stone for an inner state visible from outside, as a rule for courtiers in 706 and as a lover's observation in 1273.

1273 compares her unspoken meaning to a thread that shows through the gems (திகழ்தரு); 1274 compares it to the scent inside a closed bud (முகைமொக்குள் உள்ளது நாற்றம்). Parimelazhagar distinguishes them: the first lies within yet is visible outside, the second is not visible outside at all, so the pair moves from a sign that can be seen to one that can only be inferred.

650 likens those who cannot unfold what they have learned to flowers that bloom in clusters without scent (நாறா மலர்); 1274 likens what is in her budding smile to the scent inside an unopened bud (முகைமொக்குள் நாற்றம்). Scent stands in both for the inner content of a thing: 650 has the outward bloom without it, 1274 has it present before any outward opening.

1227 describes love's sickness as budding in the morning (காலை அரும்பி), swelling through the day and flowering at evening; 1274 places an unspoken meaning inside the bud of her smile (நகைமொக்குள்). Both use the bud for a feeling that is already there and has not yet opened, pain in the one and a hidden intention in the other.

1275 says the stealth with which she acted and withdrew (செய்திறந்த கள்ளம்) holds a medicine for great sorrow; 1279 states what she did (அஃதாண்டவள் செய்தது): she looked at her bangles, her shoulders and her feet. Parimelazhagar ties the two explicitly, taking 1279's அஃது to point back to 1275, so that the silent gesture is the 'stealth' and its meaning, going with him, is the cure.

1091 finds two looks in her eyes, one that gives the sickness and one that is its medicine (அந்நோய் மருந்து); 1275 finds in her covert behaviour a medicine that ends great sorrow (உறுதுயர் தீர்க்கும் மருந்து). In both the remedy is not anything she says but something to be read in a sign she gives.

1092 values the small look her eyes steal (கண்களவு கொள்ளும் சிறுநோக்கம்) at more than half of love; 1275 says her கள்ளம், her stealth, contains a medicine. Theft is the figure for her indirect signalling in both, at first meeting in 1092 and after reunion in 1275.

1152 says his look alone was once sweet, and now union itself carries the pain of fearing separation (பிரிவஞ்சும் புன்கண் உடைத்தால் புணர்வு); 1276 says his greatly comforting, eager union contains her having to endure again and to think on his lack of love (அன்பின்மை சூழ்வது உடைத்து). Both are the woman telling her friend that she reads coming departure in his lovemaking, and both use உடைத்து for what the embrace holds within it.

827 warns not to take an enemy's bowing words at face value, because a bow's bending signals harm (வில்வணக்கம் தீங்கு குறித்தமையான்); in 1276 the woman reads his unusually great tenderness (பெரிதாற்றிப் பெட்பக் கலத்தல்) as a sign of coming absence. The same inference, that excess of kindness points to its opposite, is advice about false friends in one book and a wife's reading of her husband in the other, though she alleges no enmity.

1157 asks if the bangles slipping past her wrist do not proclaim that the lord of the shore has left her (துறைவன் துறந்தமை தூற்றாகொல்); 1277 says the bangles perceived before she did that the lord of the cool shore had parted (தணந்தமை நம்மினும் முன்னம் உணர்ந்த வளை). Same man, same bangles, in both; 1157 has them announce a departure, while 1277 has them detect one that Parimelazhagar says is so far only in his mind.

707 asks if anything is as knowing as the face, which gets there first (தான்முந்துறும்) whether one is pleased or angry; 1277 says her bangles knew before she did (நம்மினும் முன்னம் உணர்ந்த). In both the body registers a state ahead of the person, the face ahead of speech in the book on statecraft and her thinning arms ahead of her own understanding here.

In 1185 she points: there goes her lover, and here the pallor is spreading over her body (உவக்காண்… இவக்காண்), the two at the same moment; in 1278 he left yesterday and she has already been pale for seven days (மேனி பசந்து எழுநாளேம்). 1278 pushes 1185's simultaneity further: the pallor now comes before the departure, which Parimelazhagar explains as her having suspected his intention for a week.
