1277 says her bangles knew of his parting before she did; 1278 says her body has been pale for seven days though he left only yesterday. The two adjacent speeches make the same point with different signs: her body responds to his intention to leave before the leaving is an acknowledged fact.

1093 reports a wordless act and reads it: she looked, and having looked bowed her head (நோக்கினாள் நோக்கி இறைஞ்சினாள்), and that (அஃது) was water poured on their bond; 1279 reports that she looked at her bangles, her shoulders and her feet, and that (அஃது) is what she did there. Both verses consist of a sequence of looks followed by அஃது, leaving the meaning to be drawn from the gesture, at courtship in 1093 and at the threat of parting in 1279.

1234 describes separation's effect: the shoulders lose their fullness and old beauty and the bangles slip (பைந்தொடி சோரும்… தோள்); in 1279 she looks at bangles and soft shoulders (தொடிநோக்கி மென்தோளும் நோக்கி) and then at her feet. Read with 1234, her first two glances name what will happen if she is left, and the third, as Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar take it, names her alternative of walking with him.

1137 says nothing has greater worth than womanhood that suffers a sea of desire and still does not mount the palmyra horse (மடலேறாப் பெண்ணின் பெருந்தக்கது இல்); 1280 says that telling love's sickness with the eyes and pleading (கண்ணினால் காமநோய் சொல்லி இரவு) is womanhood upon womanhood. Both praise as specifically womanly the refusal to declare desire openly, 1137 by what she will not do and 1280 by the silent means she uses instead.

1100 says that when eyes agree with eyes, spoken words are of no use (வாய்ச்சொற்கள் என்ன பயனும் இல); 1280 praises her for telling her sickness with the eyes (கண்ணினால் சொல்லி). 1280 applies the general statement about lovers' eyes to a hard case, a plea not to be left, and adds a value judgment the earlier verse lacks.

1053 says that even asking has a beauty of its own (இரப்புமோர் ஏஎர் உடைத்து) when done before those who know their duty and do not withhold; 1280 says her asking (இரவு), done with the eyes, has a womanliness of its own (பெண்மை உடைத்து). The word for begging is the same, and both grant it a grace under conditions, though the chapter on begging means alms and 1280 means a lover's plea.

1281 says that rejoicing at a thought (உள்ளக் களித்தல்) and delight at a sight (காண மகிழ்தல்) belong to love and not to liquor (கள்ளுக்கில்). 1090 makes the sight half of this claim at the very start of the Book of Love: brewed liquor gladdens only those who drink it (உண்டார்கண் அல்லது), not, as love does, those who merely see (கண்டார் மகிழ்செய்தல் இன்று). The comparison that opens the courtship returns here after the separation, now with thought added to sight.

1201 says love is sweeter than liquor because even thinking of it gives great joy (உள்ளினும் தீராப் பெருமகிழ்... கள்ளினும் காமம் இனிது); 1281 says joy at a thought and at a sight is found in love and not in liquor. Together with 1090 (sight) the three verses form one argument, and 1281 joins the two halves; Parimelazhagar gives 1201 to the man and 1281 to the woman, so both lovers make the claim.

In 1281 love is set above liquor: it delights at a thought and a look, which liquor cannot do. In 1288, in the same chapter, his chest is itself like liquor to those who have got drunk on it (களித்தார்க்குக் கள்ளற்றே), wanted though it does shameful harm (இளித்தக்க இன்னா செயினும்). The chapter uses the one image both ways, first to say love exceeds drink and then to say it compels like drink.

104 says that those who understand its fruit take a help the size of a millet (தினைத்துணை) as the size of a palmyra (பனைத்துணை); 1282 says that when love comes filling to a palmyra's measure there should be no sulking even of a millet's measure. The same millet-and-palmyra pair of measures serves gratitude in one verse and love in the other, in each case to say that a large thing should not be weighed against a small one.

433 says those ashamed of blame treat a fault as small as a millet as if it were a palmyra (தினைத்துணையாங் குற்றம்... பனைத்துணையாக் கொள்வர்). 1282 uses the same two measures in the other direction: with love as large as a palmyra, even a millet of sulking over his fault is to be avoided. In 433 the small fault is magnified; in 1282 the small grievance is to be dropped.

1302 says sulking is like salt in the right amount and is spoiled only by being prolonged a little (உப்பமைந் தற்றால் புலவி). 1282 says that when love is full to a palmyra's measure, not even a millet of sulking is wanted (தினைத்துணையும் ஊடாமை வேண்டும்). Read together, 1282 states a condition, காமம் நிறைய வரின், under which the measured sulk that 1302 recommends falls to nothing; Parimelazhagar takes 1282 as the woman voicing her own haste in the form of general advice.

1178 ends காணாது அமைவில கண் and 1283 ends காணா தமையல கண்: in both her eyes cannot rest without seeing a man who desires without cherishing (பேணாது பெட்டார் in 1178, பேணாது பெட்பவே செய்யினும் in 1283). 1178 is spoken in his absence and 1283 on his return, so the pair shows the same complaint about her eyes holding on both sides of the separation.

1257 says she knows nothing of shame when the one she cherishes does, in desire, what she wants (பேணியார் பெட்ப செயின்). 1283 reuses the two words with the sense turned round: even if he does only what he himself wants, without cherishing her (பேணாது பெட்பவே செய்யினும்), her eyes will not rest without seeing him. The second verse removes the condition of the first: her yielding does not depend on his doing what pleases her.

1259: she went away saying she would sulk (புலப்பல் எனச் சென்றேன்) and embraced him on seeing her heart begin to join with him. 1284: she went to sulk (ஊடற்கண் சென்றேன்) and her heart, forgetting that, went to unite (கூடற்கண் சென்றது). The two verses report the same event in the same sentence shape, in 1259 as a failure of her restraint (the chapter is நிறையழிதல்) and in 1284 as eagerness for union.

1246 tells the heart that when it sees the lover it cannot stay in a sulk, so its present anger is false (பொய்க்காய்வு). 1284 is that prediction coming true: she set out to sulk and the heart forgot it and went to unite (அதுமறந்து கூடற்கண் சென்றது).

1284 reports to her friend that her heart forgot the sulk and went to unite. 1294 gives the consequence: since the heart will not first sulk and then enjoy (துனிசெய்து துவ்வாய்), who will consult with it about such things again (நின்னொடு சூழ்வார் யார்). The report of the heart's desertion in one chapter becomes the quarrel with the heart in the next.

1127: because her lover lives in her eyes she will not even line them with kohl (கண்ணும் எழுதேம்), knowing he would be hidden. 1285: as the eye cannot see the kohl-stick at the moment of lining (எழுதுங்கால் கோல்காணாக் கண்), she cannot see his fault when she sees him. Both build on the lining of the eye, once for his constant presence in her sight and once for her blindness to his fault when he is near.

1285 gives the image: the eye does not see the stick that is lining it, and she does not see his blame when she sees him (பழிகாணேன் கண்ட இடத்து). 1286 states the other half that the image implies: when she does not see him she sees nothing but his faults (காணாக்கால் காணேன் தவறல்லவை). Parimelazhagar's gloss on 1285 already supplies this, saying the eye has seen the stick at every other time.

190 asks what harm could come if people saw their own faults as they see strangers' faults (ஏதிலார் குற்றம்போல் தங்குற்றங் காண்கிற்பின்). 1285 says she cannot see her husband's fault when he is before her, as the eye cannot see the kohl-stick touching it. In both, what is nearest is what goes unseen; 190 treats this as a failing to correct, and 1285 as a fact about love.

1286: seeing him, she sees no faults; not seeing him, she sees nothing else. In 1297 she calls her heart மடநெஞ்சு, and Parimelazhagar defines that மடமை as exactly this reversal: remembering when he is absent, and forgetting when he is present, faults that ought to be remembered at sight and forgotten in absence. On his reading 1297 names and blames what 1286 only describes.

1134: the fierce flood of love carries off the raft of shame and manliness (காமக் கடும்புனல் உய்க்கும்). 1287: why sulk knowing it will prove false, like those who leap into a stream knowing it will carry them off (உய்த்தல் அறிந்து புனல்பாய்பவர்). The same water and the same verb, உய்த்தல், are used by the man of his restraint in 1134 and by the woman of her sulk here.

1260 asks whether those whose hearts are like fat put in fire (நிணந்தீயில் இட்டன்ன) can say they will hold out in a sulk. 1287 asks what use it is to sulk when one knows it will fail (பொய்த்தல் அறிந்தென் புலந்து). Both are rhetorical questions that deny she can keep up a sulk, one by the image of fat melting and one by the image of a current.

1145: as drinking is wanted more each time one gets drunk (களித்தொறும் கள்ளுண்டல் வேட்டற்றால்), love is sweeter each time it is exposed. 1288: his chest is as liquor is to those who have got drunk on it (களித்தார்க்குக் கள்ளற்றே), though it does shameful harm. Both take the drinker's returning appetite as the likeness for love; 1288 adds the harm and the shame that 1145 leaves out.

924 says the good woman called Shame turns her back on those with the great fault of liquor (நாண்என்னும் நல்லாள் புறங்கொடுக்கும்). 1288 likens his chest to liquor that does disgraceful harm (இளித்தக்க இன்னா) and is still wanted; Parimelazhagar names the harms as loss of shame and of self-restraint. What Book Two condemns in the drinker the love verse accepts as its own comparison.

940: as the gambler loves the game more with each loss (இழத்தொறூஉம் காதலிக்கும் சூதேபோல்), the living being loves life more with each suffering. 1288: liquor is wanted by the drunk even as it does them shameful harm, and so is his chest. Both explain an attachment that grows through injury by a vice from the same group of chapters (dice in 940, liquor in 1288).

90: the anicham withers when merely smelled, and a guest withers when looked at with a changed face. 1289: love is more delicate than a flower (மலரினும் மெல்லிது) and few reach its right moment (செவ்வி). A flower's fragility measures the guest's sensitivity in the household chapters and love's in the Book of Love, and in both the point is how little it takes to spoil the thing. (The edition's text of 90 has a typo in குழையும்.)

1289 says few attain love's செவ்வி, its right moment or condition. 1306 gives a figure for missing it on either side: without துனி and புலவி love is like fruit over-ripe or unripe (கனியும் கருக்காயும் அற்று). Parimelazhagar places 1289 in a sulk that will not yield to appeasement, so the fineness it speaks of is the same fineness of timing that 1306 puts in terms of ripeness.

In 1290 the man recalls that she sulked with her eyes alone (கண்ணின் துனித்தே) and then, more eager for the embrace than he (என்னினும் தான்விதுப் புற்று), gave way. In 1259 she tells it herself: she went off meaning to sulk and embraced him when she saw her heart begin to join with him. The same collapse of a sulk is given once from his side and once from hers.

1290 remembers her sulk ending because her eagerness to embrace was greater than his. 1327 states the rule the man later draws: in a lovers' quarrel the one who loses has won, as is seen in the union (ஊடலில் தோற்றவர் வென்றார்). Her giving way in 1290 is a case of the defeat that 1327 counts as victory.

72: the loveless belong wholly to themselves, and the loving belong to others even in their bones (அன்பிலார் எல்லாம் தமக்குரியர்). 1291: his heart is for him (அவர்நெஞ்சு அவர்க்காதல்), so why, heart, are you not for me (நீ எமக்கு ஆகாதது). The woman's complaint is 72's distinction seen from the inside: the one who loves no longer owns her own heart, and the one who does not love keeps his.

1205 asks whether he, who has shut her out of his heart (தம்நெஞ்சத்து எம்மைக் கடிகொண்டார்), is not ashamed to keep entering hers. 1291 asks her own heart why it is not hers when his heart is his. Both rest on the same imbalance of two hearts; 1205 blames him for it and 1291 blames her heart.

1245 asks the heart whether one can give him up as hostile (செற்றார் எனக் கைவிடல் உண்டோ) merely because he does not respond when she draws close (உற்றால் உறாஅதவர்). 1292 uses the same word for him, உறாஅதவர், and reverses the charge: even after seeing that he is not close, the heart goes to him saying he will not be hostile (செறாஅரென). In 1245 she argues the heart out of abandoning him; in 1292 she reproaches it for not being able to.

1255 says the dignity of not going after one who has turned away (செற்றார்பின் செல்லாப் பெருந்தகைமை) is something the lovesick cannot know. 1292 shows it: her heart goes to him (சேறி) though it has seen that he is not attached to her. 1255 gives the general statement and 1292 the instance, addressed to the heart that does the going.

752 says everyone scorns those who have nothing and everyone honours the rich (இல்லாரை எல்லாரும் எள்ளுவர்). 1293 has the woman quote the same worldly observation as a saying, கெட்டார்க்கு நட்டார் இல், and ask her heart whether that is why it leaves her and follows him. The pairing shows a hard fact from the chapter on wealth being used in the Book of Love as a taunt, with the woman as the ruined one and her heart as the fair-weather friend.

787 defines friendship as turning a friend from ruin and, when ruin comes, sharing the suffering (அழிவின்கண் அல்லல் உழப்பதாம் நட்பு). The saying in 1293, that the ruined have no friends, describes how the world behaves and not what friendship is; by the standard of 787 her heart, which goes after him as it pleases (பெட்டாங்கு அவர்பின் செலல்), has failed as a friend. The woman's question, என்பதோ, shows she is quoting the saying to reproach, not endorsing it.

798 warns against taking the friendship of those who cut away in distress (அல்லற்கண் ஆற்றறுப்பார் நட்பு). In 1293 the one who deserts in distress is her own heart, which cannot be declined as a friend. The verse turns the advice of the friendship chapters into a predicament with no remedy.

1330 says sulking is the pleasure of love, and the pleasure of sulking is to come together and embrace (ஊடுதல் காமத்திற்கு இன்பம்). 1294 has the woman want exactly that order, first make a quarrel and then enjoy (துனிசெய்து துவ்வாய்), and complain that her heart will not do it. The book's closing statement of how a sulk should work is, in 1294, a plan she cannot carry out.

1260 asks whether those with hearts like fat in fire can say they will hold out in a sulk (புணர்ந்தூடி நிற்பேம் எனல்). 1294 tells the heart that it will not sulk first and enjoy afterwards, so no one will plan such things with it. Both say the intention to sulk cannot survive her own heart; 1294 adds that she will stop consulting it.

1152 says that once his mere look was pleasure, and now union itself holds the misery of fearing separation (பிரிவஞ்சும் புன்கண் உடைத்தால் புணர்வு). 1295 says her heart fears not having him and, having him, fears parting (பெறின் பிரிவு அஞ்சும்), so its grief never ends. The fear inside union that 1152 notes before he leaves is one of the two fears in 1295 after he has come back.

1179: when he does not come her eyes do not sleep, and when he comes they do not sleep (வாராக்கால் துஞ்சா வரின்துஞ்சா), so either way they suffer. 1295: the heart fears when it lacks him and fears when it has him (பெறாஅமை அஞ்சும் பெறின்பிரிவு அஞ்சும்). The same two-sided trap is stated of the eyes in one chapter and of the heart in another; Parimelazhagar explains the eyes' sleeplessness on his coming by the same fear of parting.

1244 tells the heart to take the eyes along, since they are eating her (இவையென்னைத் தின்னும்) in their wish to see him. 1296 says that when she sat alone and thought, her heart was there as if to eat her (என்னைத் தினிய இருந்தது). The image of being eaten by a part of oneself moves from the eyes to the heart, the very one she had been addressing as an ally in 1244.

293: do not lie about what your heart knows, for after the lie your own heart will burn you (தன்நெஞ்சே தன்னைச் சுடும்). 1296: thinking alone, she finds her own heart is there to eat her. In both the tormentor is one's own heart and the setting is solitude with what one knows; 293 makes this the working of conscience, and 1296 gives it as the experience of the abandoned lover, with no fault of hers involved.

1207 says she does not know forgetting, and even remembering burns her heart (உள்ளினும் உள்ளம் சுடும்). 1296 says that when she sits alone and thinks (நினைத்தக்கால்), her heart consumes her. Both make thinking of him in his absence the source of the pain; in 1207 the heart is what is burned, in 1296 it is what does the harm.

1247 tells the heart to give up either desire or shame, since she cannot bear both (காமம் விடுஒன்றோ நாண்விடு). 1297 reports how that ended: caught up with a foolish heart that cannot forget him (அவர்மறக் கல்லா), she has forgotten even shame (நாணும் மறந்தேன்). The choice she put to the heart in 1247 is settled in 1297 by the heart's incapacity, not by her decision.

1017 says those ruled by shame give up life for shame's sake and do not give up shame for life's sake (நாண்துறவார்). In 1297 the woman has forgotten shame because her heart cannot forget him, and Parimelazhagar glosses the shame as dearer to her than life, the valuation of 1017. The pairing sets the rule from the chapter on shame beside a speaker in the Book of Love who holds that rule and reports failing it; it is her confession, not a contrary teaching.

In 1132 the man says his body and life, unable to bear it, will mount the palmyra horse, with shame set aside (நாணினை நீக்கி நிறுத்து). In 1297 the woman says she has forgotten shame through her heart's inability to forget him. Each sex is shown losing நாண் to love; the man sets it aside to act in public, and the woman finds it gone.

1255 says the dignity of not going after one who has turned away is unknown to the lovesick (செற்றார்பின் செல்லாப் பெருந்தகைமை). In 1298 her heart reasons the opposite way about where disgrace lies: it thinks that to scorn him would be a disgrace (எள்ளின் இளிவாம் என்று எண்ணி) and so keeps thinking of his side. 1298 shows the lovesick heart not merely ignorant of that dignity, as 1255 has it, but supplied with its own argument from honour for doing without it.

967 says it is better to be called ruined where one stands than to live by following those who do not accept one (ஒட்டார்பின் சென்றொருவன் வாழ்தலின்). In 1298 the heart, described as loving life (உயிர்க்காதல் நெஞ்சு), counts scorning him as the disgrace and goes on dwelling on him. The chapter on honour ranks honour above life; the heart in 1298 keeps the vocabulary of disgrace (இளிவு) but, out of attachment to life, applies it so as to stay with the one who slighted her. This is the heart's reasoning as she reports it, not a rival doctrine.

1184: she thinks of him and what she speaks of is his merit (உரைப்பது அவர்திறம்), and still the pallor comes. 1298: her heart thinks of what pertains to him (அவர்திறம் உள்ளும்), judging that to scorn him would be a disgrace. The phrase அவர் திறம் with உள்ளுதல் appears in both; in 1184 it is her own loyal practice that goes unrewarded, and in 1298 it is something her heart does that she stands apart from.

1299 asks who will be a companion in grief when one's own heart is not (தாமுடைய நெஞ்சந் துணையல் வழி). 1300 repeats the frame, தாமுடைய நெஞ்சம் தமரல் வழி, and draws the further step: then it is a small matter that strangers are not one's own. The pair moves from the loss of the nearest help to an inference about everyone else, and Parimelazhagar gives both to the man, where the first eight verses of the chapter are the woman's.

1263 describes the man as having left with his own heart or resolve for companion (உள்ளம் துணையாகச் சென்றார்). 1299 asks who can be a companion in grief when one's own heart is no companion (நெஞ்சந் துணையல் வழி). The heart as துணை is what he had on setting out and, on Parimelazhagar's assignment of 1299 to the man, what he lacks when she will not be reconciled; Manakkudavar gives 1299 to the woman.

36 says virtue, done without delay, is the companion that does not die when one dies (பொன்றுங்கால் பொன்றாத் துணை). 1299 says that in grief there is no companion if one's own heart is not one. Both verses ask what stays with a person when other support is gone; Book One answers virtue, and the lover's verse names the heart and finds it missing.

1291 opens the chapter with the woman asking her heart why it is not hers when his heart is his own (நீ எமக்கு ஆகாதது). 1300 closes it with the general form: when one's own heart is not one's kin (நெஞ்சம் தமரல் வழி), it is nothing that strangers are not. Parimelazhagar gives the first to the woman and the last to the man, so the chapter begins and ends with the same complaint from each side.

188 asks what those who spread even the faults of their closest (துன்னியார்) will do to strangers (ஏதிலார் மாட்டு). 1300 argues that when one's own heart is not one's own, strangers (ஏதிலார்) not being one's own is a slight thing. Both reason from the nearest relation to ஏதிலார்: if the bond fails at the closest point, nothing can be expected further out.

882 says do not fear enemies who are like swords, but fear the tie with enemies who are like kin (கேள்போல் பகைவர்). 1300 finds the same reversal inside one person: the heart that should be தமர், one's own people, is not, and beside that the distance of outsiders hardly counts. The lesson of the chapter on enmity within, that the danger is in what is closest, is applied in 1300 to the heart.

1301 has the friend urge the woman to hold back her embrace and sulk (புல்லாது இராப் புலத்தை) so they can watch his pain 'a little' (சிறிது). 1302 states the limit that word implies: sulking is like salt in right measure, and letting it run on (நீள விடல்) is like salt in excess. Parimelazhagar reads the சிறிது of 1301 as already pointing to this rule.

1301 proposes not embracing (புல்லாது) in order to see his அல்லல்நோய். 1303 uses the same two words from the other side: leaving the one who sulks unembraced (புல்லா விடல்) is like giving அல்லல்நோய் to those already in distress (அலந்தாரை). Read together, the pain that 1301 treats as a brief test is the pain 1303 says must not be left standing.

In 1301 the friend wants the sulk kept up so that his suffering can be seen for a while. In 1329 the man himself wishes she would go on sulking (ஊடுக மன்னோ) and the night grow long so that he may keep pleading (யாம் இரப்ப). Both sides treat the sulk as something to prolong on purpose, hers to watch and his to beg.

1302 says sulking is like salt in fitting measure (உப்பு அமைந்தற்று) and too much of it is like salt in excess. 802 says a friend's liberties are a limb of friendship and that being salt to them (உப்பாதல்) is the duty of the worthy; Parimelazhagar glosses this as being sweet toward those liberties. In both, salt is what makes a close bond palatable, but only the love verse adds that the salt can be overdone.

1302 gives the measure: a little sulking seasons, a little too long spoils. 1306 gives the two failures by name: without துனி and புலவி, love is like கனி and கருக்காய், which Manakkudavar reads as overripe fruit and unripe fruit. Together they make sulking a matter of degree, judged by taste, in both verses through a food image.

1302 allows sulking in measure, like salt. In 1282 the woman says that when love comes filling to the size of a palmyra, one should not sulk even a millet's worth (தினைத்துணையும் ஊடாமை வேண்டும்). 1282 is a speech by a woman eager for union, so it limits 1302 for that moment and does not cancel it.

1303 says that leaving unembraced those who have sulked (புலந்தாரைப் புல்லா விடல்) is like giving sharp pain to those already suffering (அலந்தாரை அல்லல்நோய் செய்தற்று). 1304 says that not appeasing those who sulk (ஊடியவரை உணராமை) is like cutting a withered creeper at the root (வாடிய வள்ளி முதல் அரிந்தற்று). The pair states one claim twice, once as added hurt and once as a finishing cut. Parimelazhagar takes both as the wife's taunt sending the man back to his other women.

1304 compares leaving a sulking lover unappeased to cutting an already withered creeper at its root (வாடிய வள்ளி முதல் அரிந்தற்று). 1030 says a family with no good man to prop it falls when trouble cuts it at the foot (இடுக்கண் கால் கொன்றிட வீழும்); Parimelazhagar takes this as an axe at the tree's base. Both picture a weakened plant that needed support and got the cut instead, once in love and once in the household.

1305 says that for men good in their qualities (நலத்தகை நல்லவர்க்கு) the beauty (ஏர்) is the sulking in flower-eyed women; Parimelazhagar reads this as 'even for the faultless, sulking is sweet'. 1325 says the same in plainer terms: though without fault (தவறிலர் ஆயினும்), being kept from the soft shoulders of the one they love has something in it (ஆங்கொன்று உடைத்து). Manakkudavar reads 1305 differently, taking நல்லவர் as the other women.

1305, on Parimelazhagar's reading, has the man find beauty in her sulk even though he is good and blameless. 1321 gives her side: he has no fault (இல்லை தவறு அவர்க்கு), yet the way he shows tenderness (அவர் அளிக்குமாறு) is what makes sulking possible. Both verses detach the sulk from any real offence.

1306 says love without துனி and புலவி is like கனி and கருக்காய்; Manakkudavar takes these as fruit gone past ripeness and fruit not yet ripe. 100 says speaking unpleasant words when pleasant ones exist is like taking the unripe fruit while the ripe is there (கனி இருப்பக் காய் கவர்ந்தற்று). In 100 ripe is simply good and unripe bad; in 1306, on that reading, both ends are faulty and the right point lies between.

1306 puts it negatively: without quarrels, serious and light, love is fruit at the wrong stage. 1330 puts it positively: sulking is the pleasure of love (ஊடுதல் காமத்திற்கு இன்பம்), and the pleasure of sulking is the embrace that follows. The chapter 133 verse states as a conclusion what 1306 argues by image.

1307 finds a pain inside sulking (ஊடலின் உண்டு ஆங்கு ஓர் துன்பம்): the thought of whether union will be delayed or not. In 1152 the woman says union itself holds the misery of fearing separation (பிரிவு அஞ்சும் புன்கண் உடைத்தால் புணர்வு). In both, a state counted as pleasant carries worry about what comes next.

1330 calls sulking the pleasure of love, provided the embrace follows (கூடி முயங்கப் பெறின்). 1307 fastens on that proviso: because one cannot be sure the union will not be long delayed (புணர்வது நீடுவது அன்றுகொல்), the sulk has its own pain. 1307 is the reservation built into 1330's praise.

1308 asks what use it is to suffer where there is no lover who knows 'this one is hurt' (நொந்தார் என்று அஃது அறியும் காதலர் இல்லா வழி). 877, in the chapter on enemies, advises: do not voice your hurt to those who do not know you are hurt (நோவற்க நொந்தது அறியார்க்கு). The same roots நோ and அறி carry one rule in love and in statecraft: displayed pain is wasted on someone who does not perceive it.

1308 says the man's hurt is useless without a lover who recognises it. 1309 gives the general form: as water is sweet in shade, sulking is sweet only with those who love (வீழுநர் கண்ணே இனிது). Parimelazhagar assigns both to the man, in a sulk that she is not answering.

In 1308 suffering is pointless when the other does not know or care that one suffers. In 1200 the woman tells her heart that reporting its great pain to one who is not close (உறாஅர்க்கு உறுநோய் உரைப்பாய்) is like trying to fill in the sea. Man and woman reach the same judgment from opposite sides of the couple.

1309 says water is sweet when it is in shade (நீரும் நிழலது இனிதே), and sulking is sweet only with those who love. 881 says even shade and water are bad if they do harm (நிழல்நீரும் இன்னாத இன்னா), and so are one's own people. Both use shade and water as the stock example of what is pleasant, and both make the pleasantness depend on a condition: love in the one, harmlessness in the other.

1309 limits the sweetness of sulking to those who love (வீழுநர் கண்ணே). 1323 asks whether any heaven matches sulking with those joined like water with earth (நிலத்தொடு நீர் இயைந்தன்னார் அகத்து). Both say the value of the sulk depends on the closeness of the two, and both use water to say it.

In 1310 the man, on Parimelazhagar's reading, says that his heart's intent to join with one who leaves him to wither in the sulk (ஊடல் உணங்க விடுவாரோடு) is just craving (அவா). In 1292 the woman scolds her heart for going to him even after seeing that he is not close to her (உறாஅதவர்க் கண்ட கண்ணும்). Each blames the heart for running to someone who has shown no care.

1304 compares the unappeased sulker to a withered creeper (வாடிய வள்ளி) cut at the root. 1310 speaks of being left to dry up in the sulk (ஊடல் உணங்க விடுவார்). The wife's warning and the man's complaint use the same picture of a plant left without water; Parimelazhagar places 1310 in a sulk she does not answer.

1310 calls the heart's wish to join with one who neglects it mere craving. In 1255 the woman says the dignity of not going after those who have turned away (செற்றார் பின் செல்லாப் பெருந்தகைமை) is something the love-sick do not know. Both admit that desire overrides self-respect toward an indifferent partner.

In 1311 the woman refuses his chest (நண்ணேன் பரத்த நின் மார்பு) because all women feed on him with their eyes in common (பொது உண்பர்). 915 says the wise will not touch the mean charms of women whose charms are common to all (பொதுநலத்தார் புன்னலம் தோயார்). She applies to a man the book's own reasoning about public women: what is பொது is not to be touched. Parimelazhagar makes this explicit by calling his chest their leavings.

In 1312 the woman says he sneezed while she was sulking, knowing (அறிந்து) she would have to say 'live long' and so speak to him. In 1253 the sneeze is the example of what happens without intention: desire comes out குறிப்பின்றித் தும்மல்போல். Parimelazhagar notes that 1312 treats a natural sneeze as a deliberate one, which is the subtlety the chapter title names.

In 1313 the man reports that even wearing a wreath makes her angry (காயும்): 'you wore it to show some woman'. In 1321 the woman says he has no fault (இல்லை தவறு அவர்க்கு), yet his way of showing tenderness can bring on a sulk. 1321 supplies from her mouth what the man's complaints in chapter 132 imply: the grounds are invented.

1311 gives her stated ground: every woman takes him in with her eyes (கண்ணின் பொது உண்பர்). 1313 shows the same worry applied to a trifle: a wreath must have been put on to be shown to another woman (ஒருத்தியைக் காட்டிய சூடினீர்). Her jealousy in both is about who sees him.

In 1314 he says 'we love more than anyone' (யாரினும் காதலம்) and she turns it on him: 'than whom, than whom?' (யாரினும் யாரினும்). 645 advises speaking a word only after knowing there is no other word that can defeat it (வெல்லுஞ்சொல் இன்மை அறிந்து). The love scene shows that rule failing in a comic way: his own word, repeated back, is the one that beats him.

In 1314 'more than anyone' is heard as implying other loves; in 1315 'we will not part in this birth' (இம்மைப் பிறப்பில் பிரியலம்) fills her eyes with tears, because she hears a parting in the next. Parimelazhagar describes the move in 1315: she takes a plain statement as a hinting one. Both verses turn a strong assurance into an offence by what it leaves unsaid.

In 1315 a promise limited to this birth (இம்மை) makes her weep. 107 says the good remember through all seven births (எழுமை எழுபிறப்பும் உள்ளுவர்) the friendship of those who removed their distress. Her complaint measures his promise against the span the book itself uses for lasting bonds.

In 1316 he says 'I thought of you' (உள்ளினேன்) and she answers 'why did you forget?' (என் மறந்தீர்). In 1125 the man himself uses that logic: he would remember her qualities if he forgot them, but he does not know forgetting (உள்ளுவன் மன் யான் மறப்பின்; மறப்பறியேன்). Her inference in 1316 is the one he made in 1125, now used against him.

1316 has her treat remembering as proof of forgetting. In 1207 the woman, alone, says she does not know forgetting (மறப்பறியேன்) and that even remembering burns. The standard she holds him to in 1316, never having forgotten at all, is the one she claims for herself in separation.

In 1203 the woman, apart from him, takes a sneeze that starts and dies away as a sign that he was about to think of her and did not (நினைப்பவர் போன்று நினையார்கொல்). In 1317 the same belief, that one sneezes when someone thinks of one, makes her weep: 'who thought of you, that you sneezed?' (யார் உள்ளித் தும்மினீர்). The sign she waited for in absence becomes evidence against him in his presence. Parimelazhagar cites this belief in his note on 1317.

In 1312 she suspects his sneeze was a trick to get the customary 'live long' out of her. In 1317 she gives that blessing (வழுத்தினாள்) and at once takes it back (அழித்து அழுதாள்) with a new suspicion. One sneeze is read two ways in the chapter, as a stratagem and as proof of another woman.

In 1317 sneezing brings the charge that some woman is thinking of him. In 1318 he holds the sneeze back (தும்முச் செறுப்ப) and she weeps anyway: 'are you hiding from me that your people think of you?' (நுமர் உள்ளல் எம்மை மறைத்திரோ). The two verses close both exits: sneezing and not sneezing are both faults.

In 1253 the woman says she would hide her desire (மறைப்பேன்) but it comes out like a sneeze. In 1318 he does manage to hold a sneeze in, and the holding in is what she reads as hiding (மறைத்திரோ). Both verses pair the sneeze with concealment; in 1253 it stands for what cannot be hidden, and in 1318 hiding it is itself the offence.

In 1319 even his effort to appease her makes her angry (உணர்த்தினும் காயும்): 'you must be like this with others too'. 693 warns those who serve kings that once suspicion has arisen, clearing it is hard for anyone (கடுத்தபின் தேற்றுதல் யார்க்கும் அரிது). The court maxim and the bedroom scene describe the same trap: reassurance offered to a suspicious mind is taken as more evidence.

1304 says not appeasing one who sulks (ஊடியவரை உணராமை) is like cutting a withered creeper at the root. In 1319 he does appease her (தன்னை உணர்த்தினும்) and that too is a fault. Taken together, the man is blamed in chapter 131 for not doing what chapter 132 shows cannot be done to her satisfaction.

1313, 1319 and 1320 share the frame '…even if I do X, she is angry (…இனும் காயும்), saying …'. In 1313 the act is wearing a wreath; in 1320 it is only sitting and looking at her (நினைத்திருந்து நோக்கினும்), which she takes as comparing her with someone (யார் உள்ளி நோக்கினீர்). The series runs from adornment down to a silent look, so that no act of his is left free of suspicion.

In 1311 her objection is to other women's eyes on him (கண்ணின் பொது உண்பர்). In 1320 it is to his eyes on her, which she thinks are really on another woman; Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar both explain that she supposes he is matching her limbs against someone else's. The chapter opens and closes on the look as the place where she locates unfaithfulness.

In 1321 the woman says he has no fault (இல்லை தவறவர்க்கு), yet the way he shows tenderness (அவர் அளிக்குமாறு) is able to produce a sulk. In 1325 the man says that even when men are faultless (தவறிலர் ஆயினும்), being kept from the soft arms of the one they love 'has a certain something' (ஆங்கொன்று உடைத்து). The chapter opens each speaker's side with the same concession: the sulk it praises needs no offence.

In 1311 the woman refuses his chest because all women 'feast on it in common with their eyes' (கண்ணின் பொதுஉண்பர்), a sulk with a stated ground. In 1321 she grants there is no fault at all and says his tenderness itself brings the sulk on; Parimelazhagar explains this as her thought that others too might receive that same tenderness. On his reading the jealousy of 1311 survives in 1321 with its ground removed.

Both verses use the rare word சிறுதுனி for a brief bad spell in something good. In 1010 the short want of the renowned rich is like the rain-cloud going dry (மாரி வறங்கூர்ந்தனையது); in 1322 the small pain that sulking brings may make his good tenderness droop (நல்லளி வாடினும்), yet it gains worth (பாடு பெறும்). In each the dryness is temporary and belongs to a giver whose giving is not in doubt.

1306 says love without துனி and புலவி is like fruit over-ripe or unripe (கனியும் கருக்காயும் அற்று), so some quarrel is needed. 1322 names the amount: only the 'small துனி' that arises in a sulk (ஊடலின் தோன்றும் சிறுதுனி), which leaves his tenderness greater even if it droops for a while. Parimelazhagar on 1306 takes துனி as the full-grown quarrel and புலவி as the young one, so 1322's சிறு marks the tolerable dose.

1322 says tenderness may wilt (வாடினும்) under the small pain of a sulk and still come to greatness. 1304 uses the same verb for the limit: not reconciling one who has sulked is like cutting an already wilted creeper at the root (வாடிய வள்ளி முதலரிந்தற்று). The wilting is harmless only if the sulk is ended; Parimelazhagar reads 1304 as the woman speaking of his other women.

1103 asks whether the world of the lotus-eyed one (தாமரைக் கண்ணான் உலகு) is as sweet as sleeping on the soft arms of the one you love. 1323 asks whether there is a land of the gods (புத்தேள்நாடு உண்டோ) like sulking with one joined to you as water to earth. The man's question at the first union and the woman's at the end of the book have the same form, and the thing set above heaven has moved from the embrace to the quarrel.

452 says water changes by the nature of the land it meets (நிலத்தியல்பால் நீர் திரிந்தற்று), and so a person's understanding takes the nature of their company. 1323 describes lovers as joined like water with land (நிலத்தொடு நீர் இயைந்தன்னார்). Parimelazhagar explains 1323 with the logic of 452, that water becomes of the nature of the ground it stands on, so the image that warns against bad company in 452 here describes a complete union.

1309 says water is sweet only in the shade, and sulking is sweet only with those who love (புலவியும் வீழுநர் கண்ணே இனிது). 1323 says the sulk that surpasses heaven is the one with those joined like water and earth (நிலத்தொடு நீர் இயைந்தன்னார் அகத்து). Both verses, each with a water image, put the sweetness of sulking under the same condition: it holds only where the bond is already secure.

In 1258 the woman calls her lover's humble words (பணிமொழி) 'the weapon that breaks our womanhood' (பெண்மை உடைக்கும் படை). 1324 says that within the sulk arises 'the weapon that breaks my heart' (என் உள்ளம் உடைக்கும் படை) and does not name it; Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar both gloss it as humble words, Parimelazhagar adding bowing. 1258 supplies the identity of the weapon that 1324 leaves unstated, though the commentators differ on whether the woman or the man speaks 1324.

828 warns that a weapon lies hidden inside an enemy's hands folded in worship (தொழுதகையுள்ளும் படையொடுங்கும்), and his tears are the same. 1324 finds a weapon (படை) inside the lovers' sulk, which Parimelazhagar explains as the other's bowing and humble words. Submission as a concealed weapon is a danger to be detected in false friendship and, in love, the means by which the sulk is ended.

1251 says the axe of desire breaks the door of restraint bolted with shame (காமக் கணிச்சி உடைக்கும் நிறையென்னும் ... கதவு). 1324 uses the same verb for the resolve to keep sulking: a weapon arises that breaks the heart (உள்ளம் உடைக்கும் படை). What was a breach forced during separation in 1251 becomes, inside the sulk, a breaking that leads to the embrace that does not let go (புல்லி விடா).

Both verses turn on the same phrase, 'the soft arms of the one they love' (தாம்வீழ்வார் மென்றோள்). In 1103 sleeping on them is set against the world of the lotus-eyed one; in 1325 being kept away from them (அகறலின்), though one is faultless, 'has a certain something' (ஆங்கொன்று உடைத்து). The repeated phrase shows the book's last chapter finding a pleasure in the very absence of what the first union praised.

1325 says that being kept from her arms by a sulk has a pleasure of its own (ஆங்கொன்று உடைத்து). 1307 says sulking also holds one pain: the thought of whether union will be delayed or not (புணர்வது நீடுவது அன்றுகொல் என்று). Parimelazhagar gives both to the man, 1325 after the making up and 1307 during the sulk, so the pleasure of 1325 is one judged in hindsight.

In 1319 the man reports that even when he tries to appease her she is angry (உணர்த்தினும் காயும்), saying he is like this with others too: a complaint that he is blamed without cause. In 1325 he grants the same situation, a man without fault (தவறிலர் ஆயினும்) kept from her arms, and finds something to enjoy in it. The groundless sulks listed in chapter 132 are re-read as a pleasure in chapter 133.

944 instructs: know that the earlier meal is digested (அற்றது அறிந்து) and eat only when thoroughly hungry (துவரப் பசித்து). 1326 says the digesting of what was eaten is sweeter than eating (உணலினும் உண்டது அறல் இனிது), and so sulking is sweeter than union. The chapter on medicine states as a rule of health what the man uses as his simile; Parimelazhagar on 1326 draws the same line, that one who eats when hungry eats more and with more relish.

1326 ranks sulking above union: ஊடல் is sweeter than புணர்தல் for love. 1330 calls sulking love's pleasure but adds that the pleasure of the sulk itself lies in being able to come together and embrace (கூடி முயங்கப் பெறின்). The closing verse makes the sulk's sweetness depend on the union that 1326 placed below it, as digestion has value for the next meal.

986 says the touchstone of worth is to accept defeat even from those who are not one's equals (தோல்வி துலையல்லார் கண்ணும் கொளல்). 1327 says that in a sulk those who lost have won (ஊடலில் தோற்றவர் வென்றார்), which is seen in the union that follows. Accepting defeat is a test of character in 986 and the winning move in 1327; Parimelazhagar glosses the loser of 1327 as the one who gave way, unable to keep opposing.

931 says not to want gambling even if you win, since what is won (வென்றதூஉம்) is like the hook a fish has swallowed. 1327 says that in a sulk the loser is the winner (தோற்றவர் வென்றார்). The two verses reverse the apparent result of a contest in opposite directions: the gambler's win is a loss that shows later, and the lover's loss is a win that shows later in union (கூடலிற் காணப்படும்).

1302 says sulking is like salt in the right amount (உப்பு அமைந்தற்றால் புலவி), and prolonging it is like a little too much. 1328 calls the pleasure of the union that follows a sulk its உப்பு, the savour that appeared in union with her forehead sweating, and asks whether sulking will win it again. Salt is the sulk as seasoning in 1302 and the resulting savour in 1328; Parimelazhagar glosses 1328's உப்பு as sweetness.

802 says intimate liberty is a limb of friendship and that 'being உப்பு to it' (அதற்கு உப்பாதல்) is the duty of the worthy; Parimelazhagar reads this as being pleasant toward that liberty. 1328 uses உப்பு for the savour of union after a sulk, which Parimelazhagar again glosses as sweetness. In both, salt stands for the relish that makes something a close companion does, a liberty or a sulk, enjoyable and not an offence.

In 1238 the man recalls that when he loosened the arms that embraced her, her forehead turned pale (பசந்தது ... பேதை நுதல்). In 1328 he recalls union so intense that her forehead sweated (நுதல் வெயர்ப்ப). Her forehead is the place where he reads both the first sign of separation and the fullness of union.

In 1169 the separated woman says the nights that now pass so long (நெடிய கழியும் இரா) are crueller than the cruelty of the man who left. In 1329 the man wishes the night to lengthen (நீடுக மன்னோ இரா) so that he may go on pleading while she sulks. The long night is the worst of separation in her mouth and a wish in his, once the lovers are together and the only distance is a sulk.

1307 names the one pain within sulking: the thought of whether union will be delayed or not (புணர்வது நீடுவது அன்றுகொல்). 1329 wishes for that delay, asking that she keep sulking and the night grow long (ஊடுக ... நீடுக). Parimelazhagar gives both to the man, 1307 during a sulk and 1329 after one has ended well, so the delay feared in the moment is desired in retrospect.

1052 says even begging is a pleasure to a person if what is begged for comes without pain (இன்பம் ஒருவற்கு இரத்தல்). In 1329 the man wants the sulk and the night prolonged so that he may beg (யாம் இரப்ப), treating the pleading itself as something to enjoy. Begging, which chapter 107 calls degrading, is here a pleasure because the giver is not in doubt, which is the condition 1052 sets.

1109 lists sulking, reconciling and uniting (ஊடல் உணர்தல் புணர்தல்) as the gains of those joined in love. 1330, the last verse of the book, orders the same elements: sulking is the pleasure of love, and the pleasure of sulking is to come together and embrace (கூடி முயங்கப் பெறின்). What 1109 gives as a list early in the Book of Love, 1330 states as a dependence of each step on the next.

1330 says the sulk's own pleasure comes if the lovers get to unite and embrace (பெறின்). 1304 states the other case: not reconciling one who has sulked (ஊடியவரை உணராமை) is like cutting a wilted creeper at the root. The conditional in 1330 is a real one, and 1304 shows what a sulk is when the condition fails.

1302 says a sulk is like salt in the right amount, and letting it run long (நீள விடல்) is like a little too much. 1330 makes the sulk love's pleasure only if embrace follows (கூடி முயங்கப் பெறின்). Parimelazhagar reads 1330's condition through this measure: the sulk must be ended at the right point, between a quarrel too ripe and one too young, and that is hard to judge.
